ASSUS

Pages 8-8
or Assos, in Ancient Geography, a town of Troas (though by others supposed to be of Mytilene), and the same with Apollonia (Pliny); but different from the Apollonia on the river Rhynchus. Ptolemy places it on the sea-coast, but Strabo more inland; if he does not mean the head of an inland bay, as appears from Diodorus Siculus. It was the country of Clearchus, the Stoic philosopher, who succeeded Zeno. St Luke and others of St Paul's companions, in his voyage (Acts xx. 13, 14.), went by sea from Troas to Alos; but St Paul went by land thither, and meeting them at Alos, they all went together to Mytilene. It is still called Alos. E. Long. 27. 3. N. 38. 30.

ASSYRIA

Pages 8-9

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, commencement, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of which, historians differ greatly in their accounts. Several ancient writers, in particular Ctesias and Diodorus Siculus, have affirmed, that the Assyrian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, under <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINUS">Ninus</a> and Semiramis, comprehended the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the known world. Had this been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it is not likely that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> would have omitted a fact so remarkable. The sacred records intimate, that none of the ancient states <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> kingdoms were of considerable extent; for neither Chedrauomer, nor any of the neighbouring princes, were tributary or subject to Assyria; and we find nothing of the greatness or power of this kingdom in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the judges and succeeding kings of Israel, though the latter kingdom was oppressed and enslaved by many different powers in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. It is highly probable, therefore, that Assyria was originally of small extent. According to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, it was bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>; on the west by the Tigris; on the south by Susiana; and on the east by Media. It is probable, that the origin and revolutions of the Assyrian monarchy were as follows.—The founder of it was Ashur, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of Shem, who went out of Shinar, either by the appointment of Nimrod, or to elude the fury of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>; conducted a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> body of adventurers into Assyria, and laid the foundation of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINEVEH">Nineveh</a> (Gen. x. 11.) These events happened not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after Nimrod had established the Chaldaean monarchy, and fixed his residence at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>. The Persian historians suppose that the kings of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> of the first dynasty were the same with the kings of Assyria, of whom Zohah, or Nimrod, was the founder of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BABEL">Babel</a>. (Herbelot Orient. Bibl. v. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>.) It does not, however, appear that Nimrod reigned in Assyria. The kingdoms of Babylon and Assyria were originally distinct and separate (<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MICAH">Micah</a>, v. 6.); and in this state they remained until Ninus conquered Babylon and made it tributary to the Assyrian empire. Ninus the successor of Ashur (Gen. x. 11., Diod. Sic. lib. i.), seized on Chaldea, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Nimrod, and united the kingdoms of Assyria and Babylon. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> is said to have subdued Asia, Persia, Media, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he did so, the effects of his conquests were of no duration; for in the days of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, we do not find that any of the neighbouring kingdoms were subject to Assyria. He was succeeded by Semiramis; a princess of an heroic mind; bold, enterprising, fortunate; but of whom many fabulous things have been recorded. It appears, however, that there were two princesses of the same name, who flourished at very different periods. One of them was the consort of Ninus; and the other lived five generations before Nitocris <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a> (Euseb. Chron. p. 58, Herod. lib. i. c. 184.). This fact has not been attended to by many writers. Whether there was an uninterrupted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of kings from Ninus to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDANAPALUS">Sardanapalus</a>, or not, is still a question. Some suspicion has arisen, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> which Ctesias has given of the Assyrian kings is not genuine; for many names in it are of Persian, Egyptian, and Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>. Nothing memorable has been recorded concerning the successors of Ninus and Semiramis. Of that effeminate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of princes it is barely said, that they ascended the throne, lived in indolence, and died in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Nineveh. Diodorus (lib. ii.) relates, that, in the reign of Teutames, the Assyrians, solicited by Priam their vassal, sent to the Trojans a supply of 20,000 foot and 200 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>, under the command of Memnon, son of Tithonus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of Persia: But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of his relation is rendered doubtful by the accounts of other writers. Sardanapalus was the last of the ancient Assyrian kings. Contemning his indolent and voluptuous course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, Arbaces, governor of Media, withdrew his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, and rose up in rebellion against him. He was encouraged in this revolt by the advice and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> of Belisis, a Chaldean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, who engaged the Babylonians to follow the example of the Medes. These powerful provinces, aided by the Persians and other allies, who despised the effeminacy, or dreaded the tyranny of their Assyrian lords, attacked the empire on all sides. Their most vigorous efforts were, in the beginning, unsuccessful. Firm and determined, however, in their opposition, they at length prevailed, defeated the Assyrian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, besieged Sardanapalus in his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, which they demolished, and became masters of the empire, B.C. 821. After the death of Sardanapalus, the Assyrian empire was divided into three kingdoms, viz. the Median, Assyrian, and Babylonian. Arbaces retained the supreme power and authority, and fixed his residence at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECBATANA">Ecbatana</a> in Media. He nominated governors in Assyria and Babylon, who were honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of kings, while they remained subject and tributary to the Median monarchs. Belisis received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Babylon as the reward of his services; and Phul was intrusted with that of Assyria. The Assyrian governor gradually enlarged the boundaries of his kingdom, and was succeeded by Tiglath-pileser, Salmanasar, and Sennacherib, who asserted and maintained their independency. After the death of Asar-haddon, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> and successor of Sennacherib, the kingdom of Assyria was split, and annexed to the kingdoms of Media and Babylon. Several tributary princes afterwards reigned in Nineveh; but no particular account of them is found in the annals of ancient nations. We hear AST Assyriam hear no more of the kings of Assyria, but of those of Babylon. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYAXARES">Cyaxares</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Media assisted Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, in the siege of Nineveh, which they took and destroyed, B.C. 606. The Chaldean or Babylonian kingdom was transferred to the Medes, after the reign of Nabonadius, son of Evil-merodach, and grandson of Nebuchadnezzar. He is styled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELSHAZZAR">Belshazzar</a> in the sacred records, and was conquered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>, B.C. 538. ASSYRIAM. See Assyriam.

ASTABAT

Pages 9-9

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, situated near the river Aras, 12 miles south of Nakhivan. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> about it is excellent, and produces very good wine. There is a root peculiar to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, called romas; which runs in the ground like liquorice, and serves for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>. It is very much used all over the Indies, and in it they have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 46° 30', N. Lat. 39° 0'.

ASTANDA

Pages 9-9

in Antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> courier <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> messenger, the same with Angarus.—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> is said by Plutarch, in his book on the fortune of Alexander, to have formerly been an astanda.

ASTAROTH

Pages 9-9
or Ashtaroth, in Antiquity, a goddess of the Sidonians.—The word is Syriac, and signifies sheep, especially when their udders are turgid with milk. From the fecundity of these animals, which in Syria continue to breed a long time, they formed the notion of a deity, whom they called Astarte, or Ashlarite. See Astarte. Astarte, in Ancient Geography, the royal residence of Og king of Bashan; whether the same with Altaroth Carnaim, is matter of doubt: if one and the same, it follows from Eusebius's account, that it lay in Bashan, and to the east of Jordan, because in the confines of Arabia. Astarte, in Pagan Mythology, (the singular of Ashlaroth), a Phoenician goddess, called in Scripture the queen of heaven, and the goddess of the Sidonians.—Solomon, in compliment to one of his queens, erected an altar to her. In the reign of Ahab, Jezebel caused her worship to be performed with much pomp and ceremony: she had 400 priests; the women were employed in weaving hangings or tabernacles for her; and Jeremiah observes, that "the children gathered the wood, the fathers kindled the fire, and the women kneaded the dough, to make cakes for the queen of heaven." Astarte, in Ancient Geography, a city on the other side Jordan; one of the names of Rabbath Ammon, in Arabia Petraea, (Stephanus).

ASTEISM

Pages 9-9

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a genteel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRONY">irony</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> handsome way of deriding another. Such, e.g.: is that of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>: Qui Bavium non odi, amet tua carmina, Mavi, &c. Diomed places the characteristic of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of irony, in that it is not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> and rustic, but ingenious and polite.

ASTELL

Pages 9-10
Mary, an English lady who was an eminent writer, was born at Newcastle upon Tyne in the year 1668. Her father, who was a merchant, committed the education of his daughter to her uncle, who was a clergyman. Convicted of the general injury done to young ladies at that period by the deficiency of their education, he taught her the Latin and French languages, and instructed her in the principles of logic, mathematics, and ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural philosophy. Having spent 20 years of her life in Newcastle, she retired to London, where she continued the pursuit of her studies; and, deeply affected with the general ignorance of her sex, she employed the first fruits of her pen to route them to a proper emulation, in a work, "A Serious Propal to the Ladies, wherein a Method is offered for the Improvement of their Minds," printed in 12mo. at London 1697. The chief object of that book was to erect a seminary for female education. A certain lady, supposed to be the queen, formed the design of devoting 10,000l. to this honourable purpose; but Bishop Burnet having suggested, that it would have too much the appearance of a nunnery, the design did not take effect. Disappointed in the article of marriage with an eminent clergyman, she next wrote a book entitled "Reflections on Marriage," which was published in 1700. This lady was a zealous advocate for the religious system commonly called orthodox; and in politics, defended the doctrine of nonresistance. About this time she published some controversial pieces, among which are the following: "Moderation truly stated;" "A Fair Way with the Dissenters;" "An Impartial Enquiry into the causes of the Rebellion;" and "A Vindication of the Royal Martyrs;" all printed in 4to in 1704. Her most finished performance was, "The Christian Religion as professed by a Daughter of the Church of England," published in 1705, in a large octavo volume. Dr Waterland speaks of this book in very favourable terms; and such was the intrepidity of this lady, that she has attacked both Locke and Tillotson in the controversial part. In the evening of her life Mrs. Astell was attacked with the severe disease of a cancer in her breast; the amputation of which she bore with singular fortitude. At the advanced age of 63 she died in the year 1731. Mrs. Astell appears to have been a woman of uncommon talents as a writer and scholar; rigid in her principles, and austere in her manners. Since a new era of female education has commenced, such an author as Mrs. Astell would have attracted little notice; but at a period of society when few women could read, and scarcely any could write, it was highly honourable for a female to suggest hints, however imperfect, for the improvement of female education. It may farther be remarked, that it deserves to be mentioned, that about a century ago a lady informed the public by her pen, that "women, who ought to be retired, are for this reason designed for speculation," and that "great improvements might be made in the sciences, were not women enviously excluded from their proper business." Deeming her time more valuable than to be walled by trifling visitors, and abhorring the practice of of teaching servants to lie, she would humorously accost such visitors by saying, "Mrs Attell is not at home." (Gen. Biog.)

ASTERABAD

Pages 10-10

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, having Tabristan on the east, part of the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and part of Jorjan on the north, Korasan on the west, and Koumas on the south. It is a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, except near the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> that almost surround it, where it is pleasant and fruitful, producing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a> of a prodigious size. In other parts the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> and barren. Afterabad is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town, which gives name to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> in the Persian sea, at the bottom of which it stands. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 54° 35'. N. Lat. 36° 50'.

ASTERIA

Pages 10-10

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a name by which some authors have called the Falco palumbarius, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> gyrfalcon. See Falco, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. ASTERIA is also the name of a gem, usually called the cat's eye, or oculus cati. It is a very singular and very beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and somewhat approaches to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the opal, in having a bright included <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which seems to be lodged deep in the body of the stone, and shifts about, as it is moved, in various directions; but it differs from the opal in all other particulars, especially in its want of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of colours seen in that gem, and in its superior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>. It is usually found between the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a> and the breadth of a sixpence; is almost always of a semicircular form, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and flat at the bottom, and rounded and convex at the top; and is naturally smooth and polished. It has only two colours, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; the brown seeming the ground, and the white playing about in it, as the fire colour in the opal. It is considerably hard, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> take a fine polish, but is usually worn with its native shape and smoothness. It is found in the East and West Indies, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORNEO">Borneo</a> affords some very fine ones, but they are usually small; they are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the sands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a> they are not unfrequently found immersed in the same matrix of jasper with the opal. ASTERIA is also the name of an extraneous fossil, called in English the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>-fish. The fossils are small, short, angular, or suctated columns, between one and two inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and seldom above a third of an inch in diameter; composed of several regular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>; when separated, each resembles a radiated star. They are, not without reason, supposed to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-fish petrified, probably the asterias or sea-star. The asteria is also called astreites, astrotites, and astereus. They may be reduced to two kinds: those whose whole bodies make the form of a star; and those which in the whole are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, but are adorned as it were with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a> in the parts. Dr Lister, for distinction's sake, only, gives the name asteria to the former sort, distinguishing the latter by the appellation of astrotites; other naturalists generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the two indiscriminately. The asteria spoken of by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, appears to be of this latter kind. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of moving in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> animated, is scarcely perceivable in the astrotites, but is signal in the asteria. The former must be broken in small pieces before it will move; but the latter will move, not only in a whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>, but in two or three knit together. The curious frequently meet with these <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> in many parts of England: at Cleydon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a> they are found rather larger than common, but of a softer substance; for, on being left a small space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in a strong acid, they may easily be separated at the joints in small plates.

ASTERIAS

Pages 10-10

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of the bittern. See Ardea, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ASTERISK

Pages 10-10

a mark in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> (*), placed over a word <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, to refer the reader to the margin, or elsewhere, for a quotation, explanation, or the like.

ASTERIUS

Pages 10-10
or Asturius, a Roman consul, in 449. We have under his name, "A Conference on the Old and New Testament," in Latin verse: in which each strophe contains, in the first verse, an historical fact in the Old Testament; and in the second, an application of that fact to some point in the New.

ASTERN

Pages 10-10

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-phrase, used to signify any thing at some distance behind the ship; being the opposite of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AHEAD">AHEAD</a>, which signifies the space before her. See AHEAD.

ASTEROPODIUM

Pages 10-10

a kind of extraneous fossil of the same substance with the asteria <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, to which they serve as a base. See ASTERIA and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">STONE</a>. ASTHMA. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ASTI

Pages 10-10

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Montferrat in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, seated on the Tanaro, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name. It is a bishop's see, and well fortified with strong walls and deep ditches; and is divided into the city, borough, citadel, and castle. There are a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many churches and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, as well as other handsome buildings; and its territory is well watered, abounding with groves, pleasant hills, and spacious fields. It was taken by the French in 1745, and retaken by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a> in 1746. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 15'. N. Lat. 54° 50'.

ASTIGI

Pages 10-10

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a colony, and conventus juridicus, of Baetica, fumigated Augusta Firma, situated on the Singulus, which falls into the Baetis; called also Colonia Adigitana (Pliny): Now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ECIJA">Ecija</a>, midway between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> and Cordova. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° N. Lat. 37° 20'.

ASTOMI

Pages 10-10

in Anthropology, a people feigned without mouths. Pliny speaks of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of Astomi in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> who lived only by the smell <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> effluvia of bodies taken in by the nose.

ASTORGA

Pages 10-10

a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Leon, with a bishop's see, is seated on the river Tuerta, and well fortified both by art and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. It stands in a most agreeable plain, about 150 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. There are excellent trouts in the river. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 20'. N. Lat. 42° 20'.

ASTRACAN

Pages 10-12

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Russia, and the most easterly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Bulgaria and Bashkiria; on the south by the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; on the west, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>, which divides it from the Nogayan Tartars and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Cossacks; and on the east, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ridge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which part it from Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. The province extends from the 46th to the 52d <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and intensely hot: the winter continues about three months. Astracan, months so severe, that the Volga is frozen hard enough to bear loaded sledges. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is rich and fertile; but the Tartars who inhabit it are strangers to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. On the western and southern sides of the Volga are heaths of a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, and uncultivated; these, however, produce vast quantities of fine transparent <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> in pits, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> bakes and incrustates it to the thickness of an inch on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. There are pits in the neighbourhood of Astracan which yield this excellent salt in such abundance, that any person may carry it off, paying at the rate of one farthing a poof, which is equal to forty pounds. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, Astracan, is situated within the boundaries of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, on an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> called Dolgoi, about 60 English miles above the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the Volga discharges itself into the Caspian sea. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> derives its name from Hadjee Tarken, a Tartar, by whom it was founded. It was conquered by Ivan Basilowitsch, recovered by the Tartars in the year 1668, and retaken by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CZAR">czar</a>, who employed for this purpose a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of flat-bottomed vessels, in which he transported his forces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the Volga from Cazan. The city of Astracan is about two miles and a half in circumference, surrounded by a brick wall, which is now in a ruinous condition; but, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we comprehend the suburbs, the circuit <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be near five miles. The number of inhabitants amounts to 70,000, including Armenians and Tartars, as well as a few Persians and Indians. The garrison consists of six regiments of the best Russian troops, who, when this place was alarmed from the side of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, had in the adjacent plain erected a great number of small batteries, to secure the fields, and obstruct the approach of the enemy. The houses of Astracan are built of wood, and generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> and inconvenient. The higher parts of the city command a prospect of the Volga, which is here about three miles in breadth, and exhibits a noble appearance. The marshy lands on the banks of it render the place very tickly in the summer; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, being impregnated with salt, is extremely fertile, and produces abundance of fruit, the immoderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of which is attended with epidemic distempers. Sickness is likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of those annual changes in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> produced by the floods in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and autumn. All round the city of Astracan, at the distance of two miles, are seen a great number of gardens, orchards, and vineyards, producing all sorts of herbs and roots. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a> are counted so delicious, that they are preserved in sand, and transported to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>-carriage at a prodigious expense; yet the wine of Astracan is very indifferent. The summer being generally dry, the inhabitants water their gardens by means of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> worked by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> horses, which raise the water to the highest part of the garden, from whence it runs in trenches to refresh the roots of every single tree and plant. The neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> produces hares and partridges, plenty of quails in summer, with wild and water-fowl of all sorts in abundance. About ten miles below Astracan is a small island called Bojmaise, on which are built large storehouses for the salt, which is made about twelve miles to the eastward, and, being brought thither in boats, is conveyed up the Volga, in order to supply the country as far as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a> and Tver. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of salt annually dug for these purposes amounts to some millions of pounds, the exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of which is claimed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and yields a considerable revenue; for the holders and bulk of the people live almost entirely on <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and salt. The neighbourhood of these salt-works is of great advantage to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, which extend from hence to the Caspian sea, and reach to the south-east as far as Yack, and even 100 miles above Zaritzen. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> fish here caught are sturgeon and beluga. These, being salted, are put on board of vessels, and sent away in the spring, for the use of the whole empire, even as far as Petersburg; but as fish may be kept fresh as long as it is frozen, the winter is no sooner set in, than they transport great quantities of it by land through all the provinces of Russia. Of the roes of the fish called beluga, which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, transparent, and of an agreeable flavour, the fishers here prepare the caviare, which is in so much esteem all over Europe. These fisheries were first established by one Tikon Demedoff, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRIER">carrier</a>, who settled in this place about 60 years ago, his whole wealth consisting of two horses. By dint of skill and industry, he soon grew the richest merchant in this country; but his success became so alluring to the crown, that of late years it hath engrossed some of the fisheries as well as the salt-works. From the latter end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> to the beginning of October, the country about Astracan is frequently infested with myriads of locusts, which darken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> in their progression from the north to the southward; and, wherever they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, consume the whole verdure of the earth. These insects can even live for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> under water; for when the wind blows across the Volga, vast numbers of them fall in clutters, and are rolled ashore; and their wings are no sooner dry, than they rise and take flight again. Heretofore the inhabitants of Astracan traded to Khuva and Bokhara; but at present these branches are lost, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is limited to Persia and the dominions of Russia. Even the trade to Persia is much diminished by the troubles of that country; nevertheless, the commerce of Astracan is still considerable. Some years ago, the city maintained about 40 vessels, from 100 to 200 tons burden, for the Caspian traffic. Some of these belong to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and are commanded by a commodore, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>. This office is generally well stocked with naval stores, which are sold occasionally to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. The trading ships convey <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> to the frontier <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Terkic and Kilic, situated on the Caspian sea; and transport merchandise to several parts of Persia. The merchants of Astracan export to Persia, chiefly on account of the Armenians, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, linens, woollen cloths, and other European <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. In return, they import the commodities of Persia, particularly those manufactured at Cazan; such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> satins intermixed with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, for the use of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a>; wrought silks and stuffs mixed with cotton; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, cotton, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RHUBARB">rhubarb</a>, and a small quantity of other drugs; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> commodity is raw silk. The government has engrossed the article of rhubarb, the greater part of which is brought into Russia by the Tartars of Yakutsk, bordering on the eastern Tartars belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. They travel through <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARA">Samara</a>, thence to Cazan, and lastly to Moscow. The revenue revenue of Astracan is computed at 150,000 rubles, or 33,000l. arising chiefly from salt and fish. The city is ruled by a governor, under the check of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>. He is nevertheless arbitrary enough, and exercises oppression with impunity. The officers of the admiralty and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> having very small sal- aries, are open to corruption, and extremely rapaci- ous. At christening feasts, which are attended with great intemperance, the guests drink a kind of cherry- brandy out of large goblets; and every person invited throws a present of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the mother, who sits up with great formality to be saluted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. The Indians have a Pagan temple at Astracan, in which they pay their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a>, and make offerings of fruit to a very ugly deformed idol. The priests of this pagod use incense, beads, cups, and prostrations. The Tartars, on the contrary, hold idol-worship in the ut- most abomination.

ASTRAEA

Pages 12-12

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a name which some give to the sign Virgo, by others called Erigone, and some- times Isis. The poets feign that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> quitted hea- ven to reside on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; but, grow- ing weary of the iniquities of mankind, she left the earth, and returned to heaven, where she commenced a constellation of stars, and from her orb still looks <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the ways of men.

ASTRAGAL

Pages 12-12

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNNERY">Gunnery</a>, a round moulding encom- passing a cannon, about half a foot from its mouth.

ASTRAGALOMANCY

Pages 12-12

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a> per- formed by throwing small pieces, with marks corre- sponding to the letters of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>; the acciden- tal disposition of which formed the answer required. This kind of divination was practised in a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, in Achaia. The word is derived from ἀστραγάλος, and μαντεία, divination.

ASTRAGALUS

Pages 12-12
MILK-VETCH, or LIQUORICE- VETCH. See Botany Index. ASTRAGALUS. See Anatomy Index.

ASTRINGENTS

Pages 12-12

in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, sub- stances distinguished by a rough astringent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and changing solutions of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, especially those made in the vitriolic acid, into a dark purple <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; such are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a>, tormentil root, bitrot root, balantines, ter- ra japonica, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACACIA">acacia</a>, &c. See Materia Medica In- dex.

ASTROGNOSIA

Pages 12-12

the science of the fixed stars, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the knowledge of their names, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a>, mag- nitudes, &c.

ASTROITES

Pages 12-12
or STAR-STONE, in Natural His- tory. See ASTERIA and STAR STONE.

ASTROLABE

Pages 12-12

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">Ancients</a>, was the same as our armillary sphere.

ASTROLOGY

Pages 12-12

a conjectural science, which teach- es to judge of the effects and influences of the stars, and to foretell future events by the situation and diffe- rent aspects of the heavenly bodies. This science has been divided into two branches, na- tural and judiciary. To the former belongs the pre- dicting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> effects; as, the changes of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, winds, storms, hurricanes, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, floods, earthquakes, &c. This art properly belongs to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; and is only to be deduced à posteriori, from phenomena and observations. Judiciary <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> judicial astrology, is that which pretends to foretell moral events; i.e. such as have a dependency on the free <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> and agency of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were directed by the stars. This art, which owed its origin to the practices of knavery on credulity, is now universally exploded by the intelli- gent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of mankind. The professors of this kind of astrology maintain, "That the heavens are one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> volume or book, wherein God has written the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the world; and in which every man may read his own fortune, and the transactions of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The art, say they, had its rise from the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> itself: while the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Assyrians, whose serene unclouded sky favoured their celestial observations, were intent on tracing the paths and periods of the heavenly bodies, they disco- vered a constant settled relation or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> between them and things below; and hence were led to con- clude these to be the Parcae, the Destinies, so much talked of, which preside at our births, and dispose of our future fate. "The laws therefore of this relation being ascer- tained by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of observations, and the share each planet has therein; by knowing the precise time of any person's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>, they were enabled, from their know- ledge in astronomy, to erect a scheme or horoscope of the situation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> at this point of time; and, hence, by considering their degrees of power and in- fluence, and how each was either strengthened or tem- pered by some other, to compute what must be the re- sult thereof." Thus the astrologers.—But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> now remaining to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> professors, is the making of calendars or almanacks. Judicial astrology is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> said to have been invented in Chaldea, and thence transmitted to the Egyptians, Greeks, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; though some will have it of Egyptian origin, and ascribe the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> to Cham. But it is to the Arabs that we owe it. At Rome

ASTRONOMY

Pages 158-172

astronomy; avoiding, at the same time, the introduction of minute details upon those subjects which are not essential, that the reader's attention might not be distracted and diverted from objects of primary importance. But for the sake of those persons who may wish to indulge their taste for practical astronomy, we have thought proper to subjoin an appendix; in which we shall give, in the first place, the rules for calculating eclipses, and in the second, a description of the most important astronomical instruments. I. Method of calculating Eclipses. The method of constructing tables for the calculation of eclipses will be understood from the following observations. The motions of the sun and moon are observed to be continually accelerated from the apogee to the perigee, and as gradually retarded from the perigee to the apogee; being swiftest of all when the mean anomaly is nothing, and slowest of all when it is six signs. When the luminary is in its apogee or perigee, its place is the same as it would be if its motion were equable in all parts of its orbit. The supposed equable motions are called mean; the unequal are justly called the true. The mean place of the sun or moon is always forwarder than the true place, whilst the luminary is moving from its apogee to its perigee; and the true place is always forwarder than the mean, whilst the luminary is moving from its perigee to its apogee. In the former case, the anomaly is always less than six signs; and in the latter case, more. It has been found, by a long series of observations, that the sun goes through the ecliptic, from the vernal equinox to the same equinox again, in 365 days 5 hours 48 minutes 55 seconds; from the first star of Aries to the same star again, in 365 days 6 hours 9 minutes 24 seconds; and from his apogee to the same again, in 365 days 6 hours 14 minutes 0 seconds. The first of these is called the solar year; the second the sidereal year; and the third the anomalistic year. So that the solar year is 20 minutes 29 seconds shorter than the sidereal; and the sidereal year is four minutes 36 seconds shorter than the anomalistic. Hence it appears, that the equinoctial point, or intersection of the ecliptic and equator at the beginning of Aries, goes backward with respect to the fixed stars, and that the sun's apogee goes forward. It is also observed, that the moon goes through her orbit, from any given fixed star to the same star again, in 27 days 7 hours 43 minutes 4 seconds at a mean rate; from her apogee to her apogee again, in 27 days 13 hours 18 minutes 43 seconds; and from the sun to the moon again, in 29 days 12 hours 44 minutes 37 seconds. This shows that the moon's apogee moves forward in the ecliptic, and that at a much quicker rate than the sun's apogee does: since the moon is 5 hours 55 minutes 39 seconds longer in revolving from her apogee to her apogee again, than from any star to the same star again. The moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic in two opposite points, which are called her nodes: and it is observed, that she revolves sooner from any node to the node again, than from any star to the star again, by 2 hours 38 minutes 27 seconds; which shows that her nodes move backward, or contrary to the order of signs in the ecliptic. The time in which the moon revolves from the sun to the sun again (or from change to change) is called a lunation; which, according to Dr. Pound's mean measures, would always consist of 29 days 12 hours 44 minutes 3 seconds 2 thirds 58 fourths, if the motions of the sun and moon were always equable. Hence 12 mean lunations contain 354 days 8 hours 48 minutes 36 seconds 35 thirds 40 fourths, which is 10 days 21 hours 11 minutes 23 seconds 24 thirds 20 fourths less than the length of a common Julian year, consisting of 365 days 6 hours; and 13 mean lunations contain 383 days 21 hours 32 minutes 59 seconds 38 thirds 38 fourths, which exceeds the length of a common Julian year, by 18 days 15 hours 32 minutes 39 seconds 38 thirds 38 fourths. The mean time of new moon being found for any given year and month, as suppose for March 1700 old style, if this mean new moon falls later than the 11th day of March, then 12 mean lunations added to the time of this mean new moon will give the time of the mean new moon in March 1701, after having thrown off 365 days. But when the mean new moon happens to be before the 11th of March, we must add 13 mean lunations, in order to have the time of mean new moon in March the year following; always taking care to subtract 365 days in common years, and 366 days in leap years, from the sum of this addition. Thus, A.D. 1700, old style, the time of mean new moon in March was the 8th day, at 16 hours 11 minutes 25 seconds after the noon of that day (viz. at 11 minutes 25 seconds past four in the morning of the 9th day), according to common reckoning. To this we must add 13 mean lunations, or 383 days 21 hours 32 minutes 39 seconds 38 thirds 38 fourths, and the sum will be 392 days 13 hours 44 minutes 4 seconds 38 thirds 38 fourths: from which subtract 365 days, because the year 1701 is a common year, and there will remain 27 days 13 hours 44 minutes 4 seconds 38 thirds 38 fourths for the time of mean new moon in March, A.D. 1701. Carrying on this addition and subtraction till A.D. 1703, we find the time of mean new moon in March that year to be on the 6th day, at 7 hours 21 minutes 17 seconds 49 thirds 46 fourths past noon; to which add 13 mean lunations, and the sum will be 390 days 4 hours 53 minutes 57 seconds 28 thirds 20 fourths; from which subtract 366 days, because the year 1704 is a leap-year, and there will remain 24 days 4 hours 53 minutes 57 seconds 28 thirds 20 fourths, for the time of mean new moon in March A.D. 1704. In this manner was the first of the following tables constructed to seconds, thirds, and fourths; and then wrote out to the nearest seconds. The reason why we chose to begin the year with March, was to avoid the inconvenience of adding a day to the tabular time in leap-years after February, or subtracting a day therefrom. Of Calculating Eclipses, &c. The mean anomalies of the sun and moon, and the sun's mean motion from the ascending node of the moon's orbit, are set down in Table III., from 1 to 13 mean lunations. These numbers, for 13 lunations, being added to the radical anomalies of the sun and moon, and to the sun's mean distance from the ascending node, at the time of mean new moon in March 1700 (Table I.), will give their mean anomalies, and the sun's mean distance from the node, at the time of mean new moon in March 1701, and being added for 12 lunations to those for 1701, give them for the time of mean new moon in March 1702. And so on as far as you please to continue the table (which is here carried on to the year 1800), always throwing off 12 signs when their sum exceeds 12, and setting down the remainder as the proper quantity. If the number belonging to A.D. 1700 (in Table I.) be subtracted from those belonging to 1800, we shall have their whole differences in 100 complete Julian years; which accordingly we find to be 4 days 8 hours 10 minutes 52 seconds 15 thirds 40 fourths, with respect to the time of mean new moon. These being added together 60 times (always taking care to throw off a whole lunation when the days exceed 29½) make up 60 centuries, or 6000 years, as in Table VI., which was carried on to seconds, thirds, and fourths; and then wrote out to the nearest seconds. In the same manner were the respective anomalies and the sun's distance from the node found, for these centurial years; and then (for want of room) wrote out only to the nearest minutes, which is sufficient in whole centuries. By means of these two tables, we may find the time of any mean new moon in March, together with the anomalies of the sun and moon, and the sun's distance from the node at these times, within the limits of 6000 years either before or after any given year in the 18th century; and the mean time of any new or full moon in any given month after March, by means of the third and fourth tables, within the same limits, as shown in the precepts for calculation. Thus it would be a very easy matter to calculate the time of any new or full moon, if the sun and moon moved equably in all parts of their orbits. But we have already shown, that their places are never the same as they would be by equable motions, except when they are in apogee or perigee; which is, when their mean anomalies are either nothing or six signs; and that their mean places are always fartherward than their true places, whilst the anomaly is less than six signs; and their two places are fartherward than the mean, whilst the anomaly is more. Hence it is evident, that whilst the sun's anomaly is less than six signs, the moon will overtake him, or be opposite to him, sooner than she could if his motion were equable; and later whilst his anomaly is more than six signs. The greatest difference that can possibly happen between the mean and true time of new or full moon, on account of the inequality of the sun's motion, is 3 hours 48 minutes 28 seconds: and that is, when the sun's anomaly is either 3 signs 1 degree, or 8 signs 29 degrees; sooner in the first case, and later in the last.—In all other signs and degrees of anomaly, the difference is gradually less, and vanishes when the anomaly is either nothing or six signs. The fun is in his apogee on the 30th of June, and in his perigee on the 30th of December, in the present age: so that he is nearer the earth in winter than in our summer.—The proportional difference of distance, deduced from the difference of the sun's apparent diameter at these times, is as 683 to 1017. The moon's orbit is dilated in winter, and contracted in summer; therefore the lunations are longer in winter than in summer. The greatest difference is found to be 22 minutes 29 seconds; the lunations increasing gradually in length whilst the sun is moving from his apogee to his perigee, and decreasing in length whilst he is moving from his perigee to his apogee.—On this account, the moon will be later every time in coming to her conjunction with the sun, or being in opposition to him, from December till June, and sooner from June till December, than if her orbit had continued of the same size all the year round. As both these differences depend on the sun's anomaly, they may be fitly put together into one table, and called The annual or first equation of the mean to the true syzygy, (See Table VII.) This equational difference is to be subtracted from the time of the mean syzygy when the sun's anomaly is less than six signs, and added when the anomaly is more.—At the greatest it is 4 hours 10 minutes 57 seconds, viz., 3 hours 48 minutes 28 seconds, on account of the sun's unequal motion, and 22 minutes 29 seconds, on account of the dilatation of the moon's orbit. This compound equation would be sufficient for reducing the mean time of new or full moon to the true time thereof, if the moon's orbit were of a circular form, and her motion quite equable in it. But the moon's orbit is more elliptical than the sun's, and her motion in it is so much the more unequal. The difference is so great, that she is sometimes in conjunction with the sun, or in opposition to him, sooner by 9 hours 47 minutes 54 seconds, than she would be if her motion were equable; and at other times as much later. The former happens when her mean anomaly is 9 signs 4 degrees, and the latter when it is 2 signs 26 degrees. See Table IX. At different distances of the sun from the moon's apogee, the figure of the moon's orbit becomes different. It is longest of all, or most eccentric, when the sun is in the same sign and degree either with the moon's apogee or perigee; shortest of all, or least eccentric, when the sun's distance from the moon's apogee is either three signs or nine signs; and at a mean state when the distance is either 1 sign 15 degrees, 4 signs 15 degrees, 7 signs 15 degrees, or 10 signs 15 degrees. When the moon's orbit is at its greatest eccentricity, her apogee distance from the earth's centre is to her perigeeal distance therefrom, as 1067 is to 933; when least eccentric, as 1043 is to 957; and when at the mean state, as 1055 is to 945. But the sun's distance from the moon's apogee is equal to the quantity of the moon's mean anomaly at the time of new moon, and by the addition of 6 signs it becomes equal in quantity to the moon's mean anomaly at the time of full moon. Therefore, a table may be constructed so as to answer to all the various inequalities depending on the different eccentricities of the moon's orbit, in the syzygies, and called The se- Appendix. Of Calculating the Equation of the Mean to the True Syzygy. (See Table IX.) And the moon's anomaly, when equated by Table VIII., may be made the proper argument for taking out this second equation of time; which must be added to the former equated time, when the moon's anomaly is less than five signs, and subtracted when the anomaly is more. There are several other inequalities in the moon's motion, which sometimes bring on the true syzygy a little sooner, and at other times keep it back a little later, than it would otherwise be; but they are so small, that they may be all omitted except two; the former of which (see Table X.) depends on the difference between the anomalies of the sun and moon in the syzygies, and the latter (see Table XI.) depends on the sun's distance from the moon's nodes at these times. The greatest difference arising from the former is 4 minutes 58 seconds; and from the latter, 1 minute 34 seconds. The tables here inserted being calculated by Mr. Ferguson according to the methods already given, he gives the following directions for their use. To calculate the true Time of New or Full Moon. Precept I. If the required time be within the limits of the 18th century, write out the mean time of new moon in March, for the proposed year, from Table I. in the old style, or from Table II. in the new; together with the mean anomalies of the sun and moon, and the sun's mean distance from the moon's ascending node. If you want the time of full moon in March, and the half lunation at the foot of Table III. with its anomalies, &c. to the former numbers, if the new moon falls before the 15th of March; but if it falls after, subtract the half lunation, with the anomalies, &c. belonging to it, from the former numbers, and write down the respective sums or remainders. II. In these additions or subtractions, observe, that 60 seconds make a minute, 60 minutes make a degree, 30 degrees make a sign, and 12 signs make a circle. When you exceed 12 signs in addition, reject 12, and set down the remainder. When the number of signs to be subtracted is greater than the number you subtract from, add 12 signs to the lesser number, and then you will have a remainder to set down. In the tables signs are marked thus *, degrees thus °, minutes thus ′, and seconds thus ″. III. When the required new or full moon is in any given month after March, write out as many lunations with their anomalies, and the sun's distance from the node from Table III. as the given month is after March, setting them in order below the number taken out for March. IV. Add all these together, and they will give the mean time of the required new or full moon, with the mean anomalies and sun's mean distance from the ascending node, which are the arguments for finding the proper equations. V. With the number of days added together, enter Table IV. under the given month; and against that number you have the day of mean new or full moon in the left-hand column, which set before the hours, minutes, and seconds, already found. But (as it will sometimes happen) if the said number of days fall short of any in the column under the given month, add one lunation and its anomalies, &c. (from Table III.) to the foresaid sums, and then you will have a new sum of days wherewith to enter Table IV. under the given month, where you are sure to find it the second time, if the first falls short. VI. With the signs and degrees of the sun's anomaly, enter Table VII. and therewith take out the annual or first equation for reducing the mean syzygy to the true; taking care to make proportions in the table for the odd minutes and seconds of anomaly, as the table gives the equation only to whole degrees. Observe, in this and every other case of finding equations, that if the signs are at the head of the table, their degrees are at the left hand, and are reckoned downwards; but if the signs are at the foot of the table, their degrees are at the right hand, and are counted upward; the equation being in the body of the table, under or over the signs, in a collateral line with the degrees. The titles Add or Subtract at the head or foot of the tables where the signs are found, show whether the equation is to be added to the mean time of new or full moon, or to be subtracted from it. In this table, the equation is to be subtracted, if the signs of the sun's anomaly are found at the head of the table; but it is to be added, if the signs are at the foot. VII. With the signs and degrees of the sun's mean anomaly, enter Table VIII. and take out the equation of the moon's mean anomaly; subtract this equation from her mean anomaly, if the signs of the sun's anomaly be at the head of the table, but add it if they are at the foot; the result will be the moon's equated anomaly, with which enter Table IX. and take out the second equation for reducing the mean to the true time of new or full moon; adding this equation, if the signs of the moon's anomaly are at the head of the table, but subtracting it if they are at the foot; and the result will give you the mean time of the required new or full moon twice equated, which will be sufficiently near for common almanacs.—But when you want to calculate an eclipse, the following equations must be used; thus, VIII. Subtract the moon's equated anomaly from the sun's mean anomaly, and with the remainder in signs and degrees enter Table X. and take out the third equation, applying it to the former equated time, as the titles Add or Subtract do direct. IX. With the sun's mean distance from the ascending node enter Table XI. and take out the equation answering to that argument, adding it to, or subtracting it from, the former equated time, as the titles direct, and the result will give the time of new or full moon, agreeing with well regulated clocks or watches very near the truth. But to make it agree with the solar, or apparent time, you must apply the equation of natural days, taken from an equation-table, as it is leap-year, or the first, second, or third after. This, however, unless in very nice calculations, needs not be regarded, as the difference between true and apparent time is never very considerable. The method of calculating the time of any new or full moon without the limits of the 18th century will be shown further on. And a few examples compared with the precepts will make the whole work plain. N.B. The tables begin the day at noon, and reckon forward from thence to the noon following.—Thus, March the 31st, at 22 h. 30 m. 25 sec. of tabular time is April 1st (in common reckoning) at 30 m. 25 sec. after 10 o'clock in the morning. May 8th at 3h. 50min. 50sec. in the morning. --- To calculate the time of New and Full Moon in a given year and month of any particular century between the Christian era and the 18th century. **Precept I.** Find a year of the same number in the 18th century with that of the year in the century proposed, and take out the mean time of new moon in March, old style, for that year, with the mean anomalies and sun's mean distance from the node at that time, as already taught. **II.** Take as many complete centuries of years from Table VI. as, when subtracted from the above said year in the 18th century, will answer to the given year; and take out the first mean new moon and its anomalies, &c. belonging to the said centuries, and set them below those taken out for March in the 18th century. **III.** Subtract the numbers belonging to these centuries from those of the 18th century, and the remainders will be the mean time and anomalies, &c. of new moon in March, in the given year of the century proposed.—Then, work in all respects for the true time of new or full moon, as shown in the above precepts and examples. **IV.** If the days annexed to these centuries exceed the number of days from the beginning of March taken out in the 18th century, add a lunation and its anomalies, &c. from Table III. to the time and anomalies of new moon in March, and then proceed in all respects as above. Appendix. ASTRONOMY. Of Calculating the true time of New or Full Moon in any given year and month after the 18th century. Precept I. Find a year of the same number in the 18th century with that of the year proposed, and take out the mean time and anomalies, &c., of new moon in March, old style, for that year, in Table I. II. Take so many years from Table VI., as when added to the above-mentioned year in the 18th century will answer to the given year in which the new or full moon is required; and take out the first new moon with its anomalies for these complete centuries. III. Add all these together, and then work in all respects as above shown, only remember to subtract a lunation and its anomalies, when the aboveaid addition carries the new moon beyond the 31st of March, as in the following example. EXAMPLE VII. Required the true time of New Moon in July, Old Style, A.D. 2180?
