Arg. 2d equation. | | Second Equation, | + 9 24 8 | | | | | Time twice equated, | 8 6' 17 51 | | | | | Third Equation, | + 3 56 | | | | | Time thrice equated, | 8 6 21 47 | | | | | Fourth Equation, | + 1 8 | | | | | True time, July, | 8 6 22 55 | | | | In keeping by the old style, we are always sure to be right, by adding or subtracting whole hundreds of years to or from any given year in the 18th century. But in the new style we may be very apt to make mistakes, on account of the leap year's not coming in regularly every fourth year; and therefore, when we go without the limits of the 18th century, we had best keep to the old style, and at the end of the calculation reduce the time to the new. Thus, in the 22nd century there will be fourteen days difference between the styles; and therefore the true time of new moon in this last example being reduced to the new style will be the 22nd of July, at 22 minutes 55 seconds past six in the evening. To calculate the true place of the Sun for any given moment of time. Precept I. In Table XII., find the next lesser year in number to that in which the sun's place is sought, and write out his mean longitude and anomaly answering thereto: to which add his mean motion and anomaly for the complete residue of years, months, days, hours, minutes, and seconds, down to the given time, and this will be the sun's mean place and anomaly at that time, in the old style, provided the said time be in any year after the Christian era. See the first following example. II. Enter Table XIII., with the sun's mean anomaly, and making proportions for the odd minutes and seconds thereof, take out the equation of the sun's centre: which, being applied to his mean place as the title Add or Subtract directs, will give his true place or longitude from the vernal equinox, at the time for which it was required. III. To calculate the sun's place for any time in a given year before the Christian era, take out his mean longitude and anomaly for the first year thereof, and from these numbers subtract the mean motions and anomalies for the complete hundreds or thousands next above the given year; and to the remainders, add those for the residue of years, months, &c., and then work in all respects as above. See the second example following. EXAMPLE **ASTRONOMY** **EXAMPLE I.** Required the Sun's true place, March 20th, Old Style, 1764, at 22 hours 30 minutes 25 seconds past Noon? In common reckoning, March 21st; at 10 hours 30 minutes in the Forenoon. | Sun's Longitude | Sun's Anomaly | |-----------------|---------------| | s°'"" | s°'"" | | 9 20 43 50 | 6 13 1 0 | | 0 0 27 12 | 11 29 26 0 | | 11 29 17 | 11 29 14 0 | | 1 28 9 11 | 1 28 9 0 | | 20 41 55 | 20 41 55 | | 54 13 | 54 13 | | 1 14 | 1 14 | | 1 | 1 | Sun's mean place at the given time Equation of the Sun's centre, add Sun's true place at the same time --- **EXAMPLE II.** Required the Sun's true place, October 23d, Old Style, at 16 hours 57 minutes past Noon, in the 4008th year before the year of Christ 1; which was the 4007th before the year of his birth, and the year of the Julian period 706. | By the Precepts. | Sun's Longitude | Sun's Anomaly | |------------------|-----------------|---------------| | s°'"" | s°'"" | | 9 7 53 10 | 6 28 48 0 | | 1 7 46 40 | 10 13 25 0 | | 8 0 6 30 | 8 15 23 0 | | 0 6 48 0 | 11 21 37 0 | | 0 0 36 16 | 11 29 15 0 | | 0 0 5 26 | 11 29 53 0 | | 8 29 4 54 | 8 29 4 0 | | 22 40 12 | 22 40 12 | | 39 26 | 39 26 | | 2 20 | 2 20 | Sun's mean place at the given time Equation of the Sun's centre subtract Sun's true place at the same time --- So that in the meridian of London, the sun was then just entering the sign of Libra, and consequently was upon the point of the autumnal equinox. If to the above time of the autumnal equinox at London, we add 2 h. 25 m. 41 sec. for the longitude of Babylon, we shall have for the time of the same equinox, at that place, October 23d, at 19 h. 22 m. 41 sec.; which, in the common way of reckoning, is October 24th, at 22 m. 41 sec. past seven in the morning. And it appears by Example VI. that in the same year the true time of full moon at Babylon was October 23d, at 42 m. 46 sec. after six in the morning; so that the autumnal equinox was on the day next after the day of full moon.—The dominical letter for that year was G, and consequently the 24th of October was on a Wednesday. To find the Sun's distance from the Moon's ascending node, at the time of any given new or full moon; and consequently, to know whether there is an eclipse at that time or not. The Sun's distance from the moon's ascending node is the argument for finding the moon's fourth equation in the zyzygies; and therefore it is taken into all the foregoing examples in finding the times thereof. Thus, at the time of mean new moon in April 1764, the Sun's mean... mean distance from the ascending node is $5^\circ 35' 2''$. See Example I. The descending node is opposite to the ascending one, and they are just six signs distant from each other. When the sun is within 17 degrees of either of the nodes at the time of new moon, he will be eclipsed at that time; and when he is within 12 degrees of either of the nodes at the time of full moon, the moon will be then eclipsed. Thus we find, that there will be an eclipse of the sun at the time of new moon in April 1764. But the true time of that new moon comes out by the equations to be 50 minutes 46 seconds later than the mean time thereof, by comparing these times in the above example: and therefore we must add the sun's motion from the node during that interval to the above mean distance $5^\circ 35' 2''$, which motion is found in Table XII. for 50 minutes 46 seconds, to be $2' 12''$. And to this we must apply the equation of the sun's mean distance from the node in Table XV. found by the sun's anomaly, which, at the mean time of new moon in Example I. is $5^\circ 1^\circ 26' 10''$; and then we shall have the sun's true distance from the node, at the true time of new moon, as follows: | Sun from Node. | | |----------------|---| | At the mean time of new moon in April 1764 | $5^\circ 35' 2''$ | | Sun's motion from the node for 50 minutes 46 seconds | $2' 12''$ | | Sun's mean distance from node at true new moon | $5^\circ 37' 14''$ | | Equation of mean distance from node, add | $2' 50''$ | | Sun's true distance from the ascending node | $5^\circ 42' 14''$ | Which being far within the above limit of 17 degrees, shows that the sun must then be eclipsed. And now we shall show how to project this, or any other eclipse, either of the sun or moon. To project an Eclipse of the Sun. In order to this, we must find the following elements by means of the tables. 1. The true time of conjunction of the sun and moon; and at that time. 2. The semidiameter of the earth's disk, as seen from the moon, which is equal to the moon's horizontal parallax. 3. The sun's distance from the solstitial colure to which he is then nearest. 4. The sun's declination. 5. The angle of the moon's visible path with the ecliptic. 6. The moon's latitude. 7. The moon's true horary motion from the sun. 8. The sun's semidiameter. 9. The moon's semidiameter of the penumbra. We shall now proceed to find these elements for the sun's eclipse in April 1764. To find the true time of new moon. This, by Example I. is found to be on the first day of the said month, at 30 minutes 25 seconds after ten in the morning. 2. To find the moon's horizontal parallax, or semidiameter of the earth's disk, as seen from the moon. Enter Table XVII. with the signs and degrees of the moon's anomaly (making proportions, because the anomaly is of calculating in the table only to every 6th degree), and thereby take out the moon's horizontal parallax; which for the above time, answering to the anomaly $11^\circ 9' 24' 21''$, is $54' 43''$. 3. To find the sun's distance from the nearest solstice, viz. the beginning of Cancer, which is $3^\circ$ or $90^\circ$ from the beginning of Aries. It appears by Example I. (where the sun's place is calculated to the above time of new moon), that the sun's longitude from the beginning of Aries is then $5^\circ 12' 10' 12''$: that is, the sun's place at that time is $9^\circ$ Aries, $12' 10' 12''$. Therefore from Subtract the sun's longitude or place Remains the sun's distance from the solstice Or $79^\circ 49' 48''$; each sign containing 30 degrees. 4. To find the sun's declination. Enter Table XIV. with the signs and degrees of the sun's true place, viz. $5^\circ 12' 10' 12''$, and making proportions for the $10' 12''$, take out the sun's declination answering to his true place, and it will be found to be $4^\circ 49'$ north. 5. To find the moon's latitude. This depends on her distance from her ascending node, which is the same as the sun's distance from it at the time of new moon; and is thereby found in Table XVI. But we have already found that the sun's equated distance from the ascending node, at the time of new moon in April 1764, is $5^\circ 7' 23' 14''$. See above. Therefore, enter Table XVI. with 0 signs at the top, and 7 and 8 degrees at the left hand, and take out $36' 49''$, the latitude for $7^\circ$; and $41' 51''$, the latitude for $8^\circ$; and by making proportions between these latitudes for the $4' 14''$, by which the moon's distance from the node exceeds 7 degrees, her true latitude will be found to be $40' 18''$ north ascending. 6. To find the moon's true horary motion from the sun. With the moon's anomaly, viz. $11^\circ 9' 24' 21''$, Table XVII. and take out the moon's horary motion; which, by making proportions in that Table, will be found to be $30' 22''$. Then, with the sun's anomaly, $9^\circ 10' 26' 10''$, take out his horary motion $2' 28''$ from the same table; and subtracting the latter from the former, there will remain $27' 54''$ for the moon's true horary motion from the sun. 7. To find the angle of the moon's visible path with the ecliptic. This, in the projection of eclipses, may be always rated at $5^\circ 35'$, without any sensible error. 8. To find the semidiameters of the sun and moon. These are found in the same table, and by the same arguments, as their horary motions. In the present case, the sun's anomaly gives his semidiameter $16' 6''$, and the moon's anomaly gives her semidiameter $14' 57''$. 9. To find the semidiameter of the penumbra. Add the moon's semidiameter to the sun's, and their sum will be the semidiameter of the penumbra, viz. $31' 9''$. Now collect these elements, that they may be found more readily when they are wanted in the construction of this eclipse. 1. True time of new moon in April, 1764 | Event | Time | |-------|------| | 1 | 10 | | 2 | 30 | | 3 | 25 | 2. Semidiameter of the earth's disk: 54° 53' 3. Sun's distance from the nearest focus: 77° 49' 48" 4. Sun's declination, north: 4° 49' 5. Moon's latitude, north ascending: 0° 40' 18" 6. Moon's horary motion from the sun: 0° 27' 54" 7. Angle of the moon's visible path with the ecliptic: 5° 35' 8. Sun's semidiameter: 16° 6' 9. Moon's semidiameter: 14° 57' 10. Semidiameter of the penumbra: 31° 3' To project an Eclipse of the Sun geometrically. Make a scale of any convenient length, as AC, and divide it into as many equal parts as the earth's semidisk contains minutes of a degree; which, at the time of the eclipse in April 1764, is 54° 53'. Then, with the whole length of the scale as a radius, describe the semicircle AMB upon the centre C; which semicircle shall represent the northern half of the earth's enlightened disk, as seen from the sun. Upon the centre C raise the straight line CH, perpendicular to the diameter ACB; so ACB shall be a part of the ecliptic, and CH its axis. Being provided with a good sector, open it to the radius CA in the line of chords; and taking from thence the chord of 23½ degrees in your compasses, set it off both ways from H, to g and to A, in the periphery of the semidisk; and draw the straight line gVb, in which the north pole of the disk will be always found. When the sun is in Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, and Virgo, the north pole of the earth is enlightened by the sun; but whilst the sun is in the other six signs, the south pole is enlightened, and the north pole is in the dark. And when the sun is in Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces, Aries, Taurus, and Gemini, the northern half of the earth's axis C XII P lies to the right hand of the axis of the ecliptic, as seen from the sun; and to the left hand, whilst the sun is in the other six signs. Open the sector till the radius (or distance of the two go's) of the fines be equal to the length of Vb, and take the fine of the sun's distance from the focus (77° 49' 48") as nearly as you can guess, in your compasses, from the line of the fines, and set off that distance from V to P in the line gVb, because the earth's axis lies to the right hand of the axis of the ecliptic in this case, the sun being in Aries; and draw the straight line C XII P for the earth's axis, of which P is the north pole. If the earth's axis had lain to the left hand from the axis of the ecliptic, the distance VP would have been set off from V towards g. To draw the parallel of latitude of any given place, as suppose London, or the path of that place on the earth's enlightened disk as seen from the sun, from sunrise till sunset, take the following method. Subtract the latitude of London, 51° 9' from 90°, and the remainder 38° 1' will be the colatitude, which take in your compasses from the line of chords, making CA or CB the radius, and set it from b (where the earth's axis meets the periphery of the disk) to VI and VI, and draw the occult or dotted line VI K VI. Then, from the points where this line meets the earth's disk, set off the chord of the sun's declination 4° 49' to D and F, and to E and G, and connect these points by the two occult lines F XII G and DLE. Bisect LK XII, and through the point K draw the black line VI K VI. Then making CB the radius of a line of fines on the sector, take the colatitude of London 38° 1' from the fines in your compasses, and set it both ways from K to VI and VI. These hours will be just in the edge of the disk at the equinoxes, but at no other time in the whole year. With the extent K VI taken into your compasses, set one foot in K (in the black line below the occult one) as a centre, and with the other foot describe the semicircle VI 7 8 9 10, &c., and divide it into 12 equal parts. Then from these points of division draw the occult lines 7a, 8a, 9a, &c., parallel to the earth's axis C XII P. With the small extent K XII as a radius, describe the quadrant arc XII f, and divide it into five equal parts, as XII, a, ab, bc, cd, de, and ef; and through the division points a, b, c, d, e, draw the occult lines VII e V, VIII d IV, IX c III, X b II, and XI, a I, all parallel to VI K VI, and meeting the former occult lines 7a, 8a, &c., in the points VII VIII IX X XI, V IV III II and I; which points shall mark the several situations of London on the earth's disk, at these hours respectively, as seen from the sun; and the elliptic curve VI VII VIII, &c., being drawn through these points, shall represent the parallel of latitude, or path of London on the disk, as seen from the sun, from its rising to its setting. N. B. If the sun's declination had been south, the diurnal path of London would have been on the upper side of the line VI K VI, and would have touched the line DLE in L. It is requisite to divide the horary spaces into quarters (as some are in the figure), and, if possible, into minutes also. Make CB the radius of a line of chords on the sector, and take therefrom the chord of 5° 35', the angle of the moon's visible path with the ecliptic, set it off from H to M on the left hand of CH, the axis of the ecliptic, because the moon's latitude is north ascending. Then draw CM for the axis of the moon's orbit, and bisect the angle MCH by the right line Cx. If the moon's latitude had been north descending, the axis of her orbit would have been on the right hand from the axis of the ecliptic.—N. B. The axis of the moon's orbit lies the same way when her latitude is south ascending as when it is north ascending; and the same way when south descending as when north descending. Take the moon's latitude 40° 18' from the scale CA in your compasses, and set it from i to x in the bisecting line Cx, making it parallel to Cy; and through x, at right angles to the axis of the moon's orbit CM, drawn the straight line N wxy S for the path of the penumbra's centre over the earth's disk.—The point w, in the axis of the moon's orbit, is that where the penumbra's centre approaches nearest to the centre of the earth's disk, and consequently in the middle of the general eclipses: the point x is that where the conjunction... Appendix. ASTRONOMY. Of calculating the sun and moon falls, according to equal time by using the tables; and the point \( y \) is the ecliptical conjunction of the sun and moon. Take the moon's true horary motion from the sun, 27° 54', in your compasses, from the scale CA (every division of which is a minute of a degree), and with that extent make marks along the path of the penumbra's centre; and divide each space from mark to mark into 60 equal parts or horary minutes, by dots; and set the hours to every 60th minute in such a manner, that the dot signifying the instant of new moon by the tables may fall into the point \( x \), half way between the axis of the moon's orbit and the axis of the ecliptic; and then the rest of the dots will show the points of the earth's disk, where the penumbra's centre is at the instants denoted by them, in its transit over the earth. Apply one side of a square to the line of the penumbra's path, and move the square backwards and forwards until the other side of it cuts the same hour and minute (as at \( m \) and \( m' \)) both in the path of London and in the path of the penumbra's centre; and the particular minute or instant which the square cuts at the same time on both paths shall be the instant of the visible conjunction of the sun and moon, or greatest obscuration of the sun, at the place for which the construction is made, namely London, in the present example; and this instant is at 37° 1/2 minutes past ten o'clock in the morning; which is 17 minutes five seconds later than the tabular time of true conjunction. Take the sun's semidiameter, 16° 6', in your compasses, from the scale CA, and setting one foot on the path of London, at \( m \), namely at 47° 1/2 minutes past ten, with the other foot describe the circle \( UY \), which shall represent the sun's disk as seen from London at the greatest obscuration. Then take the moon's semidiameter, 14° 57', in your compasses from the same scale, and setting one foot in the path of the penumbra's centre at \( m \), in the 47° 1/2 minutes after ten, with the other foot describe the circle \( TY \) for the moon's disk, as seen from London, at the time when the eclipse is at the greatest, and the portion of the sun's disk which is hid or cut off by the moon's will show the quantity of the eclipse at that time; which quantity may be measured on a line equal to the sun's diameter, and divided into 12 equal parts for digits. Lastly, take the semidiameter of the penumbra, 31° 3', from the scale CA in your compasses; and setting one foot in the line of the penumbra's centre path, on the left hand from the axis of the ecliptic, direct the other foot toward the path of London; and carry that extent backwards and forwards till both the points of the compasses fall into the same instants in both the paths: and these instants will denote the time when the eclipse begins at London. —Then do the like on the right hand of the axis of the ecliptic; and where the points of the compasses fall into the same instants in both the paths, they will show at what time the eclipse ends at London. These trials give 20 minutes after nine in the morning for the beginning of the eclipse at London, at the points N and O; 47° 1/2 minutes after ten, at the points \( m \) and \( n \), for the time of greatest obscuration; and 18 minutes after twelve, at R and S, for the time when the eclipse ends; according to mean or equal time. From these times we must subtract the equation of natural days, viz. 3 minutes 48 seconds, in leap year April 1, and we shall have the apparent times; namely, 9 hours 16 minutes 12 seconds for the beginning of the eclipse, 10 hours 43 minutes 42 seconds for the time of greatest obscuration, and 12 hours 14 minutes 12 seconds for the time when the eclipse ends. But the best way is to apply this equation to the true equal time of new moon, before the projection be begun; as is done in Example I. For the motion or position of places on the earth's disk answer to apparent or solar time. In this construction it is supposed, that the angle under which the moon's disk is seen, during the whole time of the eclipse, continues invariably the same; and that the moon's motion is uniform and rectilineal during that time. But these suppositions do not exactly agree with the truth; and therefore, supposing the elements given by the tables to be accurate, yet the times and phases of the eclipse, deduced from its construction will not answer exactly to what passeth in the heavens; but may be at least two or three minutes wrong, though done with the greatest care. Moreover, the paths of all places of considerable latitudes are nearer the centre of the earth's disk as seen from the sun than those constructions make them; because the disk is projected as if the earth were a perfect sphere, although it is known to be a spheroid. Consequently, the moon's shadow will go farther northward in all places of northern latitude, and farther southward in all places of southern latitude, than it is shown to do in these projections. —According to Meyer's Tables, this eclipse was about a quarter of an hour sooner than either these tables, or Mr Flamsteed's, or Dr Halley's, make it; and was not annular at London. But M. de la Caille's make it almost central. The projection of lunar eclipses. When the moon is within 12 degrees of either of her nodes at the time when she is full, she will be eclipsed, otherwise not. We find by Example II. that at the time of mean full moon in May 1762, the sun's distance from the ascending node was only 4° 49' 35"; and the moon being then opposite to the sun, must have been just as near her descending node, and was therefore eclipsed. The elements for constructing an eclipse of the moon are eight in number, as follows: 1. The true time of full moon; and at that time; 2. The moon's horizontal parallax. 3. The sun's semidiameter. 4. The moon's. 5. The semidiameter of the earth's shadow at the moon. 6. The moon's latitude. 7. The angle of the moon's visible path with the ecliptic. 8. The moon's true horary motion from the sun. —Therefore, 1. To find the true time of new or full moon. Work as already taught in the precepts. —Thus we have the true time of full moon in May 1762 (see Example II. page 562) on the 8th day, at 50 minutes 50 seconds past three o'clock in the morning. 2. To find the moon's horizontal parallax. Enter Table XVII. with the moon's mean anomaly (at the above full) 6° 20' 42" 42", and thereby take out her horizontal parallax; which, by making the requisite proportions, will be found to be 57' 23". 3. To find the semidiameters of the sun and moon. Enter Table XVII. with their respective anomalies, the sun's being 1° 5° 27' 4" (by the above example) and the moon's 2° 42' 42"; and thereby take out their respective semidiameters; the sun's 15° 56", and the moon's 15° 38". 5. To find the semidiameter of the earth's shadow at the moon. Add the sun's horizontal parallax, which is always 1° 23', to the moon's which in the present case is 57° 33', from which subtract the sun's semidiameter 1° 56', and there will remain 41° 37" for the semidiameter of that part of the earth's shadow which the moon then passes through. 6. To find the moon's latitude. Find the sun's true distance from the ascending node (as already taught at the true time of full moon; and this distance increased by five signs will be the moon's true distance from the same node; and consequently the argument for finding her true latitude. Thus, in Example II., the sun's mean distance from the ascending node was of 40° 49' 35", at the time of mean full moon; but it appears by the example, that the true time thereof was six hours 33 minutes 38 seconds sooner than the mean time; and therefore we must subtract the sun's motion from the node (found in Table XII.) during this interval from the above mean distance of 4° 49' 35", in order to have his mean distance from it at the true time of full moon. Then to this apply the equation of his mean distance from the node, found in Table XV., by his mean anomaly 1° 7' 27" 45"; and lastly add five signs: so shall the moon's true distance from the ascending node be found as follows: | Sun from node at mean full moon | 0° 4° 49' 35" | |-------------------------------|---------------| | His motion from it in | | | 6 hours | 1° 56' | | 33 minutes | 1° 23' | | 38 seconds | | | Sum, subtract from the uppermost line | 2° 1° 37" | | Remains his mean distance at true full moon | 0° 4° 33' 32" | | Equation of his mean distance, add | 1° 30' 0" | | Sun's true distance from the node | 0° 10' 32" | | To which add | | | And the sum will be | 0° 6° 10' 32" | Which is the moon's true distance from her ascending node at the true time of her being full; and consequently the argument for finding her true latitude at that time. Therefore, with this argument enter Table XVI., making proportions between the latitudes belonging to the 6th and 7th degree of the argument at the left hand (the signs being at top) for the 1° 32", and it will give 32° 21" for the moon's true latitude, which appears by the table to be south descending. 7. To find the angle of the moon's visible path with the ecliptic. This may be stated at 5° 35'; without any error of consequence in the projection of the eclipse. 8. To find the moon's true horary motion from the sun. With their respective anomalies take out their horary motions from Table XVII., and the sun's horary motion subtracted from the moon's, leaves remaining the moon's true horary motion from the sun: in the present case 30° 32". Now collect these elements together for use. 1. True time of full moon in May, 1762 | D.H.M.S. | |----------| | 8° 5° 50' 50" | 2. Moon's horizontal parallax | 0° 57' 23" | 3. Sun's semidiameter | 0° 15' 36" | 4. Moon's semidiameter | 0° 15' 38" | 5. Semidiameter of the earth's shadow at the moon | 0° 41' 37" | 6. Moon's true latitude, south descending | 32° 21" | 7. Angle of her visible path with the ecliptic | 5° 35' | 8. Her true horary motion from the sun | 30° 32" | These elements being found for the construction of the moon's eclipse in May 1762, proceed as follows: Make a scale of any convenient length, as WX (fig. 159, a.), and divide it into 60 equal parts, each part standing for a minute of a degree. Draw the right line ACB (fig. 160, a.) for part of the ecliptic, and CD perpendicular thereto for the southern part of its axis; the moon having south latitude. Add the semidiameters of the moon and earth's shadow together, which in this eclipse will make 5° 15"; and take this from the scale in your compasses, and setting one foot in the point C as a centre, with the other foot describe the semicircle ADB; in one point of which the moon's centre will be at the beginning of the eclipse, and in another at the end thereof. Take the semidiameter of the earth's shadow, 4° 37", in your compasses from the scale, and setting one foot in the centre C, with the other foot describe the semicircle KLM for the southern half of the earth's shadow, because the moon's latitude is south in this eclipse. Make CD equal to the radius of a line of chords on the sector, and set off the angle of the moon's visible path with the ecliptic, 5° 35', from D to E, and draw the right line CFE for the southern half of the axis of the moon's orbit lying to the right hand from the axis of the ecliptic CD, because the moon's latitude is south descending.—It would have been the same way (on the other side of the ecliptic) if her latitude had been north descending, but contrary in both cases if her latitude had been either north ascending or south ascending. Bisect the angle DCE by the right line CG, in which line the true equal time of opposition of the sun and moon falls as given by the table. Take the moon's latitude, 32° 21", from the scale with your compasses, and set it from C to G in the line CG g; and through the point G, at right angles to CFE, draw the right line PHGFN for the path of the moon's centre. Then F shall be the point in the earth's shadow, where the moon's centre is at the middle of the eclipse; G, the point where her centre is at the tabular time of her being full; and H, the point where her centre is at the instant of her ecliptical opposition. Take the moon's horary motion from the sun, 30° 52', in your compasses from the scale; and with that extent make marks along the line of the moon's path PCN: then divide each space from mark to mark into 60 equal parts, or horary minutes, and set the hours to the proper dots in such a manner, that the dot signifying the instant of full moon (viz. 50 minutes 50 seconds after III in the morning) may be in the point G, where the line of the moon's path cuts the line that bisects the angle DCE. Take the moon's semidiameter, 1° 38", in your compasses from the scale, and with that extent, as a radius, upon the points N, F, and P, as centres, describe the circle Q for the moon at the beginning of the eclipse, when she touches the earth's shadow at V; the circle R for the moon at the middle of the eclipse; and the circle S for the moon at the end of the eclipse, just leaving the earth's shadow at W. The point N denotes the instant when the eclipse began, namely, at 15 minutes 10 seconds after II in the morning; the point F the middle of the eclipse at 47 minutes 44 seconds past III; and the point P the end of the eclipse, at 18 minutes after V.—At the greatest obscuration the moon was 10 digits eclipsed. ASTROPE WELLS

Pages 240-241

near <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANBURY">Banbury</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>, are recommended as excellent in many disorders. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is a brisk, nutritious, pleasant-tasted chalybeate, and is also gently purgative. It should be drank from three to five quarts in the forenoon.

ASTROSCOPE

Pages 241-241

a kind of astronomical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, composed of two cones, on whose surface the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a>, with their stars, are delineated, by means whereof the stars may be easily known. The astroscope is the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of William Schuckhard, formerly professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> at Tubingen, who published a treatise expressly on it in 1668.

ASTRUC

Pages 241-242

John, a celebrated physician, was born in the year 1684, at the little town of Savoy, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>. His father, who was a Protestant clergyman, bestowed particular pains upon the earliest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. After which he went to the university of Montpelier, where he was created <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts in the year 1700. He then began the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of medicine; and, in two years, obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bachelor, having upon that occasion written a dissertation on the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, which he defended in a very spirited manner. On the 25th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1703 he was created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic; after which, before arriving at extensive practice he applied to the study of medical authors, both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, with uncommon assiduity. The good effects of this study soon appeared; for, in the year 1710, he published a treatise concerning muscular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, from which he acquired very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation. In the year 1717, he was appointed to teach medicine at Montpelier; which he did with such perspicuity and eloquence. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTURIAS">Asturias</a>, quence, that it was universally said he had been born to be a professor. His fame soon rose to such a height, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> assigned him an annual salary; and he was, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, appointed to superintend the mineral waters in the province of Languedoc. But as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTPELLIER">Montpellier</a> did not afford sufficient scope for his aspiring genius, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> flock of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, which he intended to publish, after subjecting them to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the learned. Soon after, however, he left it, having in the year 1729 accepted the office of first physician to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. In this capacity he remained only for a short time, and he again returned to Paris. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the celebrated Geoffroy, in the year 1731, he was appointed regius professor of medicine at Paris. The duties of this office he discharged in such a manner as to answer even the most fangnike expectations. He taught the practice of physic with so great applause, as to draw from other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> to that of Paris a great concourse of medical students, foreigners as well as natives of France. At the same time he was not more celebrated as a professor than a practitioner. And, even at an advanced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he persevered with unwearyed assiduity in that intense study which first raised his reputation. Hence it is that he has been enabled to transmit to posterity so many valuable monuments of his medical erudition. He died, universally regretted, on the 15th of May 1766, in the 82nd year of his age.

ASTURIA

Pages 242-242

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, subdued by Augustus <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Rome.—The inhabitants of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, along with those of Cantabria, asserted their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after the rest of Spain had received the Roman yoke. So <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> was their desire of liberty, that, after being closely shut up by the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, they endured the most terrible calamities of famine, even to the devouring of one another, rather than submit to the enemy. At length, however, the Asturians were for surrendering; but the Cantabrians opposed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, maintaining that they ought all to die <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> like brave men. Upon this the two nations quarrelled, notwithstanding their desperate situation; and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> ensuing, 10,000 of the Asturians were driven to the intrenchments of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, whom they begged in the most moving manner to receive them on any terms they pleased. But Tiberius the emperor's son-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> refusing to admit them into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, some of these unhappy people put an end to their lives by falling upon their own swords; others lighting great fires threw themselves into them, while some poisoned themselves by drinking the juice of a venomous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> being put an end to by winter, the next year the Asturians summoned all their strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> against the Romans; but notwithstanding their utmost efforts of valour and despair, they were entirely defeated in a most bloody battle, which lasted two days, and for that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> entirely subdued. A few years afterwards they rebelled, in conjunction with the Cantabrians; but were soon reduced by the Romans, who massacred most of the young men that were capable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> arms. This did not prevent them from revolting anew in a short time afterwards; but without succours, being obliged to submit to the Roman power, till the subversion of that empire by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>.

ASTURIAS

Pages 242-242

anciently the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Asturias, is now a principality of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a> on the east, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a> on the west, Old Castile and Leon on the south, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. Its greatest length is about 110 miles, and its breadth 54. On the south it is separated from Old Castile and Leon by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> covered with woods. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> is tolerably fertile, but thinly inhabited. The inhabitants value themselves much on being descended from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>. Even the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> peasants, who are fain to go to seek <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in other provinces, call themselves illigrious Goths and Mountaineers, thinking it ignominious to marry even with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and rich families of another <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> is flattered by the respect paid them by the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and the privileges bestowed upon them by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Spain is styled prince of the Asturias. The most remarkable places in this principality are Oviedo, Gyon, Santillana, and St. Andero.

ASTYAGES

Pages 242-242

son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYAXARES">Cyaxares</a>, the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Medes. He dreamed that from the womb of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Mandane, married to Cambyses king of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, there sprung a vine that spread itself over all <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. She being with child, he resolved to kill the infant as soon as born. Its name was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>; and Harpagus, being sent to destroy it, preferred it; which Astyages after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> hearing of, he cauled Harpagus to eat his own son. Harpagus called in Cyrus, who de-throned his grandfather, and thereby ended the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> of the Medes. See MEDIA and PERSIA.

ASTYANAX

Pages 242-242

the only son of Hector and Andromache. After the taking of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, he was thrown from the top of a tower by Ulysses's orders.

ASTYNOUMI

Pages 242-242

in Grecian Antiquity, magistrates in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, corresponding to the aediles of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; they were ten in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. See AEDILE.

ASYLUM

Pages 242-243

a sanctuary, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of refuge, where criminals shelter themselves from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. The word is compounded of the primitive particle α, and ευλογειν, I bless; because no person could be taken out of an asylum without sacrilege. The aylas of altars and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> were very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>; and likewise those of tombs, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and other monuments of considerable personages. Thus, the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> at Ephesus was a refuge for debtors, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a> for slaves. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a celebrated asylum was opened by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> between the mounts Palatine and Capitoline, in order to people Rome, for all sorts of persons indiscriminately, fugitive slaves, debtors, and criminals of every kind. The Jews had their aylas; the most remarkable of which were, the five cities of refuge, the temple, and the altar of burnt-offerings. It was customary among the Heathens to allow refuge and impunity even to the vilest and most flagrant offenders; some out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, and others for the sake of peopling their cities: and it was by this means, and with such inhabitants, that Thebes, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, and Rome, were first stocked. We even read of asylums at Lyons and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VIENNE">Vienne</a> among the ancient Gauls; and there are some cities in Germany which still preserve the Asymmetry the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of asylum. Hence on the medals of several ancient cities, particularly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, we meet with the inscription ΑΣΥΜΜΕΤΡΙΑ, to which is added ΕΠΑΓΩ. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of asylum was given them, according to M. Spanheim, in regard to their temples, and to the gods revered by them. The emperors Honorius and Theodosius granting the like immunities to churches, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> and monks laid hold of a certain tract or territory, without which they fixed the bounds of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> jurisdiction; and so well did they manage their privileges, that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> in a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> became next akin to fortresses; where the most notorious villains were in safety, and braved the power of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. These privileges at length were extended not only to the churches and churchyards, but also to the bishops' houses; whence the criminal could not be removed without a legal assurance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and an entire <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMISSION">remission</a> of the crime. The reason of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> was, that they might not be obliged to live altogether in the churches, &c., where several of the occasions of life could not be decently performed. But at length these asylums or sanctuaries were also stripped of most of their immunities, because they served to make guilt and libertinage more bold and daring. In England, particularly, they were entirely abolished: See Sanctuary.

ASYMMETRY

Pages 243-243

the want of proportion between the parts of any thing; being the contrary of symmetry. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">Or</a>, it is the relation of two quantities which have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, as between 1 and √2, or the side and diagonal of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>.

ASYMPTOTE

Pages 243-243

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a line which continually approaches nearer to another; but, though <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> infinitely, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> never meet with it: Of these there are many kinds. In strictness, however, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> asymptotes is appropriated to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, which approach nearer and nearer to some curves of which they are said to be asymptotes; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they and their curves are indefinitely continued, they will never meet. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONIC_SECTIONS">Conic Sections</a>.

ASYNDETON

Pages 243-243

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> which omits the conjunctions in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>. As in veni, vidi, vici, where ET is left out; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in that of Cicero concerning Catiline, abit, excelfit, evasit, erupit: or in that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Ferte citò flammas, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> vela, impellite remos. Asyndeton stands opposed to polyndeton, where the copulatives are multiplied.

ATABULUS

Pages 243-243

in Physiology, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> in Apulia, of a dry pinching <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and very noxious in its effects. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> naturalists speak of the Atabulus in terms of horror, on account of the ravage it made among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which it scorched <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> withered up.

ATABYRIS

Pages 243-243

a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, on which, according to Strabo and Diodorus Siculus, there stood a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Atabyrus, whose worship a colony of Rhodians carried into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, where a temple was built to the same deity at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRIGENTUM">Agrigentum</a>.

ATALANTA

Pages 243-243

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Euripus of Euboea, near the Locri Opuntii, said to have been originally a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Locri, but torn from the continent in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the earthquake, and during an eruption of Mount <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ATALANTIS">Atalantis</a>. This happened in the fourth year of the 93rd Olympiad, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> Mnemon.

ATARAXY

Pages 243-243

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by the stoics and sceptics, to denote that calmness of mind which secures us from all emotions arising from vanity and self-conceit.

ATARGATIS TANUM

Pages 243-243

the temple of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> worshipped by the Syrians and Parthians, having the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of a woman and tail of a fish, and called Derceo by the Greeks. Her temple stood in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> Bambyce, called afterwards Hieropolis. It was extremely rich, inasmuch that Craesus, in his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> against the Parthians, spent several days in weighing the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>. Vossius makes the name of this goddess Phoenician from Addir daga, "the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fish."

ATARNEA

Pages 243-243

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of Mygia, situated between Adrymytium and Pitane, remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of Ariadne with the sister <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> concubine of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> Hermias; also for the dotage of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>.

ATAXY

Pages 243-243

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the want of order: With physicians, it signifies irregularity of crises and paroxysms of fevers.

ATCHE

Pages 243-243

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a small silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, and worth only one-third of the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>.

ATCHIEVEMENT

Pages 243-243

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, denotes the arms of a person <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> family, together with all the exterior ornaments of the shield; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>, mantle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a>, scrolls, and motto, together with such quarterings as may have been acquired by alliances, all marshalled in order. ATCHIEVE. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is derived from the French achever, i.e., to finish or make an end of; but signifies, in its ordinary acceptation, to perform <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> actions or exploits.

ATE

Pages 243-243

the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of mischief, in the Pagan <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. She was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from heaven at the birth of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>. For Juno having deceived Jupiter, in causing Euritheus to be born before Hercules, Jupiter expressed his resentment on Ate, as the author of that mischief; and threw her headlong from heaven to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, swearing she should never return thither again (Homeri II. xix. 125.) The name of this goddess comes from ατεω, νοσεω, "to hurt." Her being the daughter of Jupiter, means, according to mythologists, that no evil happens to us but by the permission of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>; and her banishment to earth denotes the terrible effects of divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> among men.

ATEGUA

Pages 243-243
or ATTEUGA, an ancient town of Spain, placed by some in the road from Antiquara, now Antequera, to Hispalis, or Seville; by others near Alcala Real; which last is the more probable situation, because the Flumen Sallum, now the Salado, was in its neighbourhood. Now Tebala Vieja, or Teruela.

ATELLA

Pages 243-244

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of Campania in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, between <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPUA">Capua</a> and Neapolis. From this town the Aetellana fabula, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Aetellani ludi, took their name. These were also called Okti, from their inventor, in whose territory Atella lay. They were generally a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a>, interlarded with much ribaldry and buffoonery; and sometimes were exordia or interludes presented between between the acts of other plays. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> in these farces were not reckoned among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> players, nor deemed infamous; but retained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of their tribe, and might be fitted for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, the privilege only of free men. The ruins of this town are still to be seen about 11 miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AVERSA">Aversa</a>, which was built out of its materials.

ATEMPO GIUSTO

Pages 244-244

in *Myth*, signifies to sing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> play in an equal, true, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

ATERGATIS

Pages 244-244

in *<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>*, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of the Syrians, supposed to be the mother of Semiramis. She was represented with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> and breasts of a woman, but the rest of her body resembled a fish. Voctius says the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> signifies *without fish*, and conjectures that the votaries of this deity obtained from fish.

ATERNUM

Pages 244-244

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCANIA">Lucania</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, now *Aterni* (Claverus): also a town in the territory of the Piceni, now *Pescara*, a port-town of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, situated on the Adriatic. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15. 25. N. Lat. 42° 30'.

ATHAMADULET

Pages 244-244

the prime minister of the Persian empire, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> vizier is of the Turkish empire. He is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, superintendent of the finances, and is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with all foreign affairs.

ATHANASIA

Pages 244-244

*goldilocks*. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **ATHANASIAN CREED**: a formulary, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> confession of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> supposed to have been drawn up by Athanasius bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, in the fourth century, to justify himself against the calumnies of his Arian enemies. But it is now generally allowed among the learned not to have been his. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERLAND">Waterland</a> attributes it to Hilary bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARLES">Arles</a>, for the following among other reasons: 1. Because Honoratus of Marcellae, the writer of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, tells us, that he composed an *Exposition of the Creed*; a proper <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> for the *Athanasian* than that of *Creed* simply which it now bears. 2. Hilary was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> admirer and follower of St Austin; and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of this creed is in a manner upon St Austin's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, both with respect to the Trinity and incarnation. 3. It is agreeable to the style of Hilary, as far as we can judge from the little that is left of his works. Upon the whole, he concludes, that Hilary bishop of Arles, about the year 430, composed the *Exposition of Faith*, which now bears the name of the *Athanasian Creed*, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the Gallican clergy, and particularly those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Arles: That, about the year 570, it became famous enough to be commended upon; but that all this while, and for several years lower, it had not yet acquired the name of *Athanasian*, but was simply styled *The Catholic Faith*: That, before 670, Athanasius's admired name came in to recommend and adorn it, being in itself an excellent system of the Athanasian principles of the Trinity and incarnation, in opposition chiefly to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, Macedonians, and Apollinarians. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> of the learned author of the *Critical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Athanasian Creed*. As to the reception of this creed in the Christian Athenasian churches, we find, that it obtained in France in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Hincmar, or about 852; that it was received in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> about 100 years later than in France, and in Germany much about the same time. As to our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, we have clear and positive proofs of this creed being sung alternately in our churches in the tenth century. It was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> use in some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, particularly in the diocese of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, about the year 960, and was received at Rome about the year 1014. As to the Greek and oriental churches, it has been questioned whether any of them ever received this creed at all; though some very considerable writers are of a contrary persuasion. It appears then, that the reception of this creed has been both general and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>; and may vie with any, in that respect, except the Nicene, or Constantinopolitan, the only general creed common to all the churches. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of this creed, it is given as a summary of the true orthodox faith, and a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> of all heresies ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>. Unhappily, however, it has proved a fruitful source of unprofitable controversy and unchristian animosity even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the present time.

ATHANASIUS

Pages 244-244

St., bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and one of the greatest defenders of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. He followed St Alexander to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice, in 325, where he disputed against <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIUS">Arius</a>, and the following years was made bishop of Alexandria; but, in 335, was deposed by the council of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>: when, having recourse to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantine, the Arian deputies accused him of having hindered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of corn from Alexandria to Constantinople; on which the emperor, without suffering him to make his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, banished him to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREVES">Treves</a>. The emperor, two years after, gave orders that he should be restored to his bishopric: but, on his return to Alexandria, his enemies brought fresh accusations against him, and chose Gregory of Cappadocia to his see; which obliged Athanasius to go to Rome to reclaim it of Pope Julius. He was there declared innocent, in a council held in 342, and in that of Sardica in 347; and two years after was restored to his see by order of the emperor Constans: but after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, he was again banished by the emperor Constantius, which obliged him to retire into the deserts. The Arians then elected one George in his room; who being killed in a popular sedition under Julian in 360, St Athanasius returned to Alexandria, but was again banished under Julian, and restored to his see under Jovian. He addressed to that emperor a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, in which he proposed that the Nicene creed should be the standard of the orthodox faith, and condemned those who denied the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of the Holy Ghost. He was also banished by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENS">Valens</a> in 367, and afterwards recalled. St Athanasius died on the 2nd of May 373. His works principally contain a defence of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the Trinity, and of the incarnation and divinity of the Word and Holy Spirit. There are three editions of his works which are extant; that of Comelin, printed in 1600; that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Nannius, in 1627; and that of Father Montfaucon. As to the creed which bears his name, see the preceding article.

ATHANATI

Pages 244-245

ATHANATI, in Persian antiquity, a body of cavalry, consisting of 10,000 men, always complete. They were called athanati (a word originally Greek, and signifying immortal), because, when one of them happened to die, another was immediately appointed to succeed him. ATHANOR. Chemists have distinguished by this name a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> so constructed that it can always maintain an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and which shall last a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> without addition of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>. The body of the athanor has nothing in it particular, and is constructed like ordinary furnaces. But at one of its sides, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> its middle, there is an upright hollow tower, which communicates with the fireplace by one or more sloping openings, and which has a lid to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> its upper opening. This furnace is now rarely used.

ATHAROTH

Pages 245-245
or ATROTH, in Ancient Geography, the name of several towns. Two appear to have been in Samaria, in the tribe of Ephraim; and one four miles to the north of Sebaste, or the city of Samaria; the other in the confines of Benjamin and Ephraim, yet so as to be in the district of Ephraim rather than Benjamin (Joshua). This the Arubad-Adder mentioned by Joshua xvi. 5, from which to Upper Bethoron extends the greatest breadth of the tribe of Ephraim.

ATHEISM

Pages 245-245

the disbelief of a deity. See Atheist. Atheist, a person who does not believe the existence of a Deity. Many people, both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, have pretended to atheism, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> have been reckoned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHEISTS">atheists</a> by the world; but it is justly questioned whether any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> seriously adopted such a principle. These pretensions, therefore, must be founded on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> or affectation. Atheism, as absurd and unreasonable as it is, has had its martyrs. Lucilio Vanini, an Italian, native of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, publicly taught atheism in France, about the beginning of the 17th century; and, being convicted of it at Thoulouse, was condemned to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Being pressed to make public acknowledgment of his crime, and to ask <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> of God, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, he answered, he did not believe there was a God; that he never offended the king; and, as for justice, he wished it to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>. He confessed that he was one of twelve, who parted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> from Naples to spread their doctrine in all parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. His tongue was first cut out, and then his body burnt, April 9, 1619. Cicero represents it as a probable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that they who apply themselves to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> believe there are no gods. This must, doubtless, be meant of the academic philosophy, to which Cicero himself was attached, and which doubted of every thing. On the contrary, the Newtonian philosophers are continually recurring to a Deity, whom they always find at the end of their chain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> causes. Some foreigners have even <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> them with making too much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the notion of a God in philosophy, contrary to the rule of Horace: Nec Deus interfit, nisi dignus vindice nodus. Among us, the philosophers have been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for the existence of a Deity. Witness the writings of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, Boyle, Ray, Cheyne, Nieuwentyt, &c. To which may be added many others, who, though of the clergy (as was also Ray), yet have distinguished themselves by their philosophical pieces in behalf of the existence of a God; e.g., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a>, Bentley, Whiston, Samuel and John Clarke, Fenelon, &c. So true is that saying of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, that though a smattering of philosophy may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a man into atheism, a deep draught <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> certainly bring him back again to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of a God and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>.

ATHELING

Pages 245-245

ADELING, EDLING, ETHLING, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ETHELING, among the Anglo-Saxons, was a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, properly belonging to the heir-apparent, or presumptive, to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> appellation was first conferred by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward the Confessor on Edgar, to whom he was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> uncle, when, being without any issue of his own, he intended to make him his heir.

ATHELSTAN

Pages 245-245

a Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of England, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son of Edward the elder, and grandson of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Alfred. He succeeded to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> in 925, and reigned 16 years. There was a remarkable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> passed by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, which shows his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> sentiments of the advantages of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, as well as the early <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to it in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>: it declared, that any merchant who made three voyages on his own account beyond the British channel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> narrow seas, should be entitled to the privilege of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THANE">thane</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>. ATHENÆA, in Antiquity, a feast celebrated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, who was called Athene. ATHENÆUM, in Antiquity, a public <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where-in the professors of the liberal arts held their assemblies, the rhetoricians declaimed, and the poets rehearsed their performances. These places, of which there were a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, were built in the manner of amphitheatres, encompassed with seats, called cunei. The three most celebrated Athenæa were those at Athens, at Rome, and at Lyons, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of which was built by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Adrian. ATHENÆUS, a physician, born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Pliny, and founder of the pneumatic feet. He taught that the fire, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, are not the true elements, but that their qualities are, viz., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, moisture, and dryness; and to these he added a fifth element, which he called spirit, whence his feet had its name.

ATHENAGORAS

Pages 245-245

an Athenian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, flourished about the middle of the 2nd century, and was remarkable for his zeal for Christianity, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning, as appears from the apology which he addressed to the emperors Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Lucius Commodus.

ATHENODORUS

Pages 245-246

a famous Stoic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born at Tarus, went to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Augustus, and was made by him <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to Tiberius. Augustus had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem for him, and found him by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of virtue and probity. He used to speak very freely to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. He, before he left the court to return home, warned the emperor not to give himself up to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>, but, whenever he should be in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, to rehearse the 24 letters of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> before he resolved to say <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> do anything. He did not live to see his bad success in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of Tiberius.

ATHENOPOLIS

Pages 246-246

a town of the Massilienenses, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>. It is conjectured by Harduin to be the same with Telo Martias, now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOULON">Toulon</a>; by others to be the same with Antipolis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIBES">Antibes</a>.

ATHENRELE

Pages 246-246

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALWAY">Galway</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Connaught. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 5. N. Lat. 53. 14. It is governed by a portreeve, and hath a barrack for three companies of foot. It hath been a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of considerable strength; but, like the numerous churches and castles which surround it, has felt the ruthless force of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Some of the walls and towers, however, are still remaining, as monuments of its former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>.

ATHENS

Pages 246-251

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 24. N. Lat. 38. 5. See ATTICA. In early times, that which was afterwards called the citadel was the whole city; and went under the name of Cecropia, from its founder Cecrops, whom the Athenians in after times affirmed to have been the first builder of cities, and called this therefore by way of eminence Polis, i.e. the city. In the reign of Erichthonius it lost the name of Cecropia, and acquired that of Athens, on what account is not certain; the most probable is, that it was so named in respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, whom the Greeks call Athene, who was also esteemed its protectress. This old city was seated on the top of a rock in the midst of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and pleasant plain, which, as the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants increased, became full of buildings, which induced the distinction of Acro and Catapolis, i.e. of the upper and lower city. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the citadel was 60 stadia; it was surrounded by olive trees, and fortified, as some say, with a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALLADIUM">palladium</a>; in succeeding times it was encompassed with a strong wall, in which there were <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> gates, one very large one, and the rest small. The inside of the citadel was adorned with innumerable edifices. The most remarkable of which were, 1. The magnificent temple of Minerva, styled partenion, because that goddess was a virgin. The Persians destroyed it; but it was rebuilt with still greater splendour by the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a>, all of the finest marble, with such skill and strength, that, in spite of the rage of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and barbarous nations, it remains perhaps the first antiquity in the world, and stands a witness to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of what ancient writers have recorded of the prodigious magnificence of Athens in her flourishing state. 2.
