The temple of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> and of Minerva; for it was divided into two parts: one sacred to the god, in which was the falt fountain said to have sprung upon the stroke of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIDENT">trident</a>; the other to the goddess protectress of Athens, wherein was the sacred olive which she produced, and her image which fell <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from heaven in the reign of Erichthonius. At the back of Minerva's temple was the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, which was burnt to the ground through the knavery of the treasurers, who, having misapplied the revenues of the state, took this short method of making up accounts. The lower city comprehended all the buildings surrounding the citadel, the fort Munychia, and the haven Phalerum and Piraeus, the latter of which was joined to the city by walls five miles in length; that on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> was built by Pericles, but that on the south by Themistocles; but by degrees the turrets which were at first erected on those walls were turned into dwelling-houses for the accommodation of the Athenians, whose large city was now become too small for them. The city, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather the lower city, had 13 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> gates, with the names of which it is not necessary to trouble the reader. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> edifices which adorned it, we may reckon, 1. The temple of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>, erected by Conon, near its centre. Adjacent thereto, the young people performed their exercises. It was also a sanctuary for distressed persons, slaves or free. 2. The Olympian temple erected in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, the honour of Athens, and of all Greece. The foundation of it was laid by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISISTRATUS">Pisistratus</a>; it was carried on but slowly in succeeding times, 700 years elapsing before it was finished, which happened under the reign of Adrian, who was particularly kind to Athens: this was the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> in which the Athenians beheld pillars. 3. The pantheon, dedicated to all the gods; a most noble structure, supported by 120 marble pillars, and having over its great gate two horses carved by Praxiteles: it is yet remaining, as we shall have occasion to show hereafter when we come to speak of the present state of this famous city. In several parts of it were flaoi or porticoes, wherein people walked in rainy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and from whence a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of philosophers were denominated flaci, because their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> Zeno taught in those porticoes. There were at Athens two places called Ceramicus, from Ceramus the son of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> and Ariadne; one within the city, containing a multitude of buildings of all sorts; the other in the suburbs, in which was the academy and other edifices. The gymnasia of Athens were many; but the most remarkable were the Lyceum, Academy, and Cynoargus. The Lyceum stood on the banks of the Ilissus; some say it was built by Pittiratus, others by Pericles, others by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a>. Here <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> taught <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, instructing such as came to hear him as they walked, whence his disciples are generally thought to derive the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIPATETICS">peripatetics</a>. The ceramicus without the city was the distance of six stadia from its walls. The academy made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> thereof; as to the name of which there is some dispute. Some affirm that it was so called from Academus, an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, who, when Helen was stolen by Theseus, discovered the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where she lay hid to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>; for which reason the Lacedemonians, when they invaded Attica, always spared this place. Dioclearchus writes, that Castor and Pollux had two Arcadians in their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, the one named Echedemonus, the other Marobius; from the former of these he says this place took its name, and that the borough of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARATHON">Marathon</a> was so called from the other. It was a marily unhealthy place, till Cimon was at great pains to have it drained; and then it became extremely pleas- Athens, faint and delightful, being adorned with shady walks, where <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> read his lectures, and from thence his scholars were styled academici. The Cynoarge was a place in the suburbs not far from the Lyceum; it was famous on many accounts; but particularly for a noble gymnasion erected there, appointed for the special <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of such as were Athenians only by one side. In after times Themistocles derived to himself ill <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, by carrying many of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> with him here, because, being but of the half blood, he could exercise nowhere else but in this gymnasion. Antithenes instituted a sect of philosophers, who from the name of this district, as many think, were styled Cynics. The havens of Athens were three. First the Piraeus, which was distant about 35 or 40 stadia from the city, till joined thereto by the long walls beforementioned, after which it became the principal harbour of the city. It had three docks; Cantharos, Aphrodium, and Zea; the first was so called from an ancient hero, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> from the goddess Venus who had there two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and the third from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-corn. There were in this port five porticoes, which joining together formed one great one called from thence Macra Stoa, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> portico. There were likewise two great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> or fora: one near the long portico, the other near the city. The second port was Munichia, a promontory not far distant from Piraeus; a place very strong by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and afterwards rendered far stronger by art. It was of this that Epimenides said, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the Athenians foresaw what mischief it would one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> produce to them, they would eat it away with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>. The third was Phalerum, distant from the city, according to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> 35 stadia, but according to Pausanias only 20. This was the most ancient harbour of Athens, as Pyreus was the most capacious. Of this city, as it stands at present, we have the following account by Dr Chandler. "It is now called Athina; and is not inconsiderable, either in extent or the number of inhabitants. It enjoys a fine temperature, and a serene sky. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is clear and wholesome, though not so delicately soft as in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>. The town stands beneath the acropolis or citadel; not encompassing the rock as formerly, but spreading into the plain, chiefly on the west and north-west. Corsairs infesting it, the avenues were secured, and in 1676 the gates were regularly shut after sunset. It is now open again; but several of the gateways remain, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of Turks patrols at midnight. Some masses of brick-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, standing separate, without the town, belonged perhaps to the ancient wall, of which other traces also appear. The houses are mostly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> and straggling; many with large courts or areas before them. In the lanes, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> walls on each side, which are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>-washed, reflect strongly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. The streets are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>; and anciently were neither uniform nor handsome. They have <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> conveyed in channels from Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYMETTUS">Hymettus</a>, and in the bazar or market-place is a large fountain. The Turks have several mosques and public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. The Greeks have <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> for men and women; with many churches, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> is regularly performed; and besides these, they have numerous oratories or chapels, some in ruins or consisting of bare walls, frequented only on the anniversaries of the saints to whom they are dedicated. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of the owner on a board is placed in them on that occasion, and removed when the solemnity of the day is over. "The city of Cecrops is now a fortress with a thick irregular wall, standing on the brink of precipices, and Citadel, or enclosing a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> about twice as long as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. City of Cecrops. Some portions of the ancient wall may be discovered on the outside, particularly at the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>; and in many places it is patched with pieces of columns, and with marbles taken from the ruins. A considerable sum had been recently expended on the side next Hymettus, which was finished before we arrived. The scaffolding had been removed to the end toward Pentele; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> was wanting, and the workmen were withdrawn. The garrison consists of a few Turks who reside there with their families, and are called by the Greeks Castriani, or the holders of the castle. The rock is lofty, abrupt, and inaccessible, except the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, which is toward the Piraeus; and on that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> is a mountainous ridge, within cannon-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>. It is destitute of water fit for drinking; and supplies are daily carried up in earthen jars, on horses and asses, from one of the conduits of the town. "The acropolis furnished a very ample field to the ancient virtuosi. It was filled with monuments of Athenian <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, and exhibited an amazing display of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, of opulence, and of art; each contending as it were for the superiority. It appeared as one entire offering to the Deity, surpassing in excellence and affluence in richness. Heliodorus, named Periegetes, the guide, had employed on it 15 books. The curiosities of various kinds, with the pictures, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and pieces of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, were so many and so remarkable, as to supply <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLEMO">Polemo</a> Periegetes with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> for four volumes; and Strabo affirms, that as many would be required in treating of other portions of Athens and of Attica. In particular, the number of statues was prodigious. Tiberius Nero, who was fond of images, plundered the acropolis as well as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OLYMPIA">Olympia</a>; yet Athens, and each of these places, had not fewer than 3000 remaining in the time of Pliny. Even Pausanias seems here to be disturbed by the multiplicity of his subject. But this banquet, as it were, of the senses has long been withdrawn; and is now become like the tale of a vision. The spectator views with concern the marble ruins intermixed with mean flat-roofed cottages, and extant amid rubbish; the sad memorials of a nobler people; which, however, as visible from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, should have introduced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Athens to more early notice. They who reported it was only a small village, must, it has been surmised, have beheld the acropolis through the wrong end of their telescopes. "The acropolis has now, as formerly, only one entrance, which fronts the Piraeus. The ascent is by traverses and rude fortifications furnished with cannon, but without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, and neglected. By the second gate is the station of the guard, who sits <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-legged under cover, much at his ease, smoking his pipe, or drinking coffee, with his companions about him in like attitudes. Over this gateway is an inscription in large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> on a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> turned upside down, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> from the fires made below. It records a prefect of a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of gates. "Going farther up, you come to the ruins of the Propylaea, an edifice which graced the entrance into the citadel." citadel. This was one of the structures of Pericles, who began it when Euthymenes was archon, 435 years before Christ. It was completed in five years, at the expense of 2012 talents. It was of marble, of the Doric order, and had five doors to afford an easy passage to the multitudes which resorted on bunsels or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> to the acropolis. While this fabric was building, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> Mnesicles, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> equalled his skill, was hurt by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, and the physicians delirious of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>: but Minerva, who was propitious to the undertaking, appeared, it was said, to Pericles, and prescribed a remedy, by which he was speedily and easily cured. It was a plant or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> growing round about the acropolis, and called afterwards parthenium. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> wing of the propylaea was a temple of Victory. They related that Ægæus had stood there, viewing the sea, and anxious for the return of his son Theseus, who was gone to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> with the tributary children to be delivered to the Minotaur. The vessel which carried them had black sails failing the occasion of its voyage; and it was agreed, that, if Theseus overcame the enemy, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> should be changed to white. The neglect of this signal was fatal to Ægæus, who, on seeing the sails unaltered, threw himself down headlong from the rock, and perished. The idol was named Victory without wings; it was said, because the news of the success of Theseus did not arrive but with the conqueror. It had a pomegranate in the right <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a> in the left. As the statue was without pinions, it was hoped the goddess would remain for ever on the spot. "On the left wing of the propylaea, and fronting the temple of Victory, was a building decorated with paintings by Polygnotus, of which an account is given by Paulanias. This edifice, as well as the temple, was of the Doric order, the columns fluted, and without bases. Both contributed alike to the uniformity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; and the whole fabric, when finished, was deemed equally magnificent and ornamental. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between Pericles and Paulanias consists of several centuries. The propylaea remained entire in the time of this topographer; and, as will be shown, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> nearly so to a much later <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. It had then a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of white marble, which was unsurpassed either in the size of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> or in the beauty of their arrangement; and before each wing was an equestrian statue. "The propylaea have ceased to be the entrance of the acropolis. The passage which was between the columns in the centre, is walled up almost to their capitals, and above is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> of cannon. The way now winds before the front of the ancient structure; and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> to the left hand among rubbish and mean walls, you come to the back part, and to the five door-ways. The foil without is risen higher than the top of the two smaller. There, under the vault and cannon, lies a heap of large stones, the ruin of the roof. "The temple of Victory, standing on an abrupt rock, has its back and one side encumbered with the modern ramparts. The columns in the front being walled up, you enter it by a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> in the side, within the propylaea. It was used by the Turks as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> for powder, until about the year 1656, when a sudden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a>, occasioned by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, carried away the roof, with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> erected on it, belonging to the officer who commanded in the acropolis, whole family, except a girl, perished. The women of the aga continued to inhabit this quarter, but it is now abandoned and in ruins. "The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a> of the temple of Victory, which is of white marble, very thick, and strongly cemented, sufficiently witnesses the great violence it has undergone; the stones in many places being disjointed, as it were, and forced from their original position. Two of these making an acute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>, the exterior edges touching, without the crevice; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> abroad being much stronger than in the room, which has a modern roof and is dark; the portion in contact becoming pellucid, had illumined the vacant space with a dim colour resembling that of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>. We were desired to examine this extraordinary appearance, which the Greeks regarded as a standing miracle, and which the Turks, who could not confute them, beheld with equal astonishment. We found in the gape some coals, which had been brought on a bit of earthen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a> for the purpose of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> incense, as we supposed, and also a piece of wax-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a>, which probably had been lighted in honour of the saint and author of the wonder; but our Swil unfortunately carrying his own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> too far in, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> blackened the marble, and destroyed the phenomenon. "The building opposite to the temple has served as a foundation for a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> lofty tower of ordinary masonry. The columns of the front are walled up, and the entrance is by a low <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> gate in the side. It is now used as a place of confinement for delinquents: but in 1676 was a powder-magazine. In the wall of a rampart near it are some fragments of exquisite sculpture, representing the Athenians fighting with the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMAZONS">Amazons</a>. These belong to the frieze, which was then standing. In the second century, when Paulanias lived, much of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> was impaired by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, but some remained, and the subjects were chiefly taken from the Trojan story. The traces are since vanished. "The pediment of the temple of Victory, with that of the opposite wing, is described as remaining in 1676; but on each building a square tower had been erected. One of the steps in the front of the propylaea was entire, with the four columns, their entablature, and the pediment. The portico, to which the five door-ways belonged, consisted of a large square room, roofed with slabs of marble, which were laid on two great marble beams, and sustained by four beautiful columns. These were Ionic, the proportions of this order best fitting that purpose, as taller than the Doric; the reason it was likewise preferred in the pronaos of the temple of Victory. The roof of the propylaea, after standing above 2000 years, was probably destroyed, with all the pediments, by the Venetians in 1687, when they battered the castle in front, firing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot bullets, and took it, but were compelled to resign it again to the Turks in the following year. The exterior walls, and, in particular, a side of the temple of Victory, retain many marks of their hostilities. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ornament of the acropolis was the parthenon or great temple of Minerva, a most superb and magnificent fabric. The Persians had burned the edifice which before occupied the site, and was called hecatompedon, beatompedou, from its being 100 feet square. The zeal of Pericles and of all the Athenians was exerted in providing a far more ample and glorious residence for their favourite goddesses. The architects were Callicrates and Ictinus; and a treatise on the building was written by the latter and Carpon. It was of white marble, of the Doric order, the columns fluted and without bases, the number in front eight; and adorned with admirable sculpture. The story of the birth of Minerva was carved in the front pediment; and in the back, her contest with Neptune for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The beasts of burden, which had conveyed up the materials, were regarded as sacred, and repented with pastures; and one, which had voluntarily headed the train, was maintained during life, without labour, at the public expense. Her statue. "The statue of Minerva, made for this temple by Phidias, was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, 26 cubits or 39 feet high. It was decked with pure <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> to the amount of 44 talents, so disposed by the advice of Pericles as to be taken off and weighed if required. The goddess was represented standing, with her vestment reaching to her feet. Her helmet had a sphinx for the crest, and on the sides were griffins. The head of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEDUSA">Medusa</a> was on her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREASTPLATE">breastplate</a>. In one hand she held her spear, and in the other supported an image of Victory about four cubits high. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of the Centaurs and Lapithae was carved on her sandals; and on her shield, which lay at her feet, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of the gods and giants, and the battle of the Athenians and Amazons. By her spear was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>, in allusion to the story of Erichthonius; and on the pedestal, the birth of Pandora. The Sphinx, the Victory, and Serpent, were accounted eminently wonderful. This image was placed in the temple in the first year of the 87th Olympiad, in which the Peloponnesian war began. The gold was stripped off by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> Lycophron, when Demetrius Poliorcetes compelled him to fly. The same plunderer plucked down the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> shields in the acropolis, and carried away the golden Victories, with the precious vessels and ornaments provided for the Panathenaean festival. "The parthenon remained entire for many ages after it was deprived of the goddess. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> converted it into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and the Mahometans into a mosque. It is mentioned in the letters of Crusius, and miscalled the pantheon and the temple of the unknown God. The Venetians under Konigsmark, when they besieged the acropolis in 1687, threw a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a>, which demolished the roof, and, setting fire to some powder, did much damage to the fabric. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, which is indented, still witnesses the place of its fall. This was the sad forerunner of farther destruction; the Turks breaking the stones, and applying them to the building of a new mosque, which stands within the ruin, or to the repairing their houses and the walls of the fortresses. The vast pile of ponderous materials, which lay ready, is greatly diminished; and the whole structure will gradually be consumed and disappear. "The temple of Minerva in 1676 was, as Wheeler and Spon assert, the finest mosque in the world, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>. The Greeks had adapted the fabric to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a>, by contriving at one end a semicircular recess for the holy tables, with a window; for before it was enlightened only by the door, obscurity being preferred under the heathen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a>, except on festivals, when it yielded to splendid illuminations: the reason, it has been surmised, why temples are commonly found simple and unadorned on the inside. In the wall beneath the window were inserted two pieces of the stone called phengiter, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of marble discovered in Cappadocia in the time of Nero; and so transparent that he erected with it a temple to Fortune, which was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> within when the door was shut. These pieces were perforated, and the light which entered was tinged with a reddish or yellowish hue. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the Panagia or Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, in mosaic, on the ceiling of the recess, remained; with two jasper columns belonging to the screen, which had separated that part from the nave; and within, a canopy supported by four pillars of porphyry, with Corinthian capitals of white marble, under which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> had been placed; and behind it, beneath the window, a marble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> for the archbishop; and also a pulpit standing on four small pillars in the middle aisle. The Turks had white-washed the walls, to obliterate the portraits of saints, and the other paintings, with which the Greeks decorate their places of worship; and had erected a pulpit on the right hand for their imam or reader. The roof was disposed in square compartments; the stones <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a>; and some had fallen in. It had been sustained in the pronaos by six columns; but the place of one was then supplied by a large pile of rude masonry, the Turks not having been able to fill up the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAP">gap</a> more worthily. The roof of the naos was supported by colonnades ranging with the door, on each side; and consisting of 22 pillars below, and of 23 above. The odd one was over the entrance, which by that disposition was left wide and unembarrassed. In the portico were suspended a few lamps, to be used in the mosque at the seasons when the muezzins assemble before day-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>, or to be lighted up round the minaret, as is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> during their Ramazan or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>. "It is not easy to conceive a more striking object than the parthenon, though now a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> ruin. The co-cent ruin, lamms within the naos have all been removed: but on the floor may be seen the circles which directed the workmen in placing them; and, at the farther end is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> across it, as for one of the partitions of the cell. The recess erected by the Christians is demolished; and from the rubbish of the ceiling the Turkish boys collect bits of the mosaic, of different colours, which compose the picture. We were told at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, that this substance had taken a polish, and been set in buckles. This cell is about half demolished; and in the columns which surrounded it is a large gap near the middle. On the walls are some traces of the paintings. Before the portico is a reservoir sunk in the rock, to supply the Turks with water for the purifications customary on entering their mosques. In it, on the left hand, is the rubbish of the pile erected to supply the place of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>; and on the right, a staircase, which leads out on the architrave, and has a marble or two with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, but worn so as not to be legible. It belonged to the minaret, which has been destroyed. "The travellers, to whom we are indebted for an account of the mosque, have likewise given a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> The temple of Minerva Polias was dedicated by all Attica, and possessed the most ancient statue of the goddesses. The demi or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> had other deities, but their zeal for her suffered no diminution. The image, which they placed in the acropolis, then the city, was in after ages not only reputed consummately holy, but believed to have fallen down from heaven in the reign of Erichthonius. It was guarded by a large serpent, which was regularly served with offerings of honeyed cakes for his food. This divine reptile was of great sagacity, and attained to an extraordinary age. He wisely withdrew from the temple when in danger from the Medes; and, it is said, was living in the second century. Before this statue was an owl; and a golden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>. This continued burning day and night. It was contrived by a curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, named Callimachus, and did not require to be replenished with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> oftener than once a year. A brazen palm-tree, reaching to the roof, received its lime. Ariftion had let the holy <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> expire while Sylla besieged him, and was abhorred for his impiety. The original olive-tree, said to have been produced by Minerva, was kept in this temple. When the Medes set fire to the acropolis, it was consumed; but, they asserted, on the following day, was found to have shot up again as much as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUBIT">cubit</a>. It grew low and crooked, but was esteemed very holy. The priestess of Minerva was not allowed to eat of the new cheese of Attica; and, among her perquisites, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of wheat, and one of barley, for every birth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>. This temple was again burned when Callias was archon, 24 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Pericles. Near it was the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Cecrops, and within it Erechtheus was buried. "The ruin of the Erechtheum is of white marble; the architectural ornaments of very exquisite workmanship, and uncommonly curious. The columns of the front of the temple of Neptune are flanking with the architrave; and also the screen and portico of Minerva Polias, and with a portion of the cell retaining traces of the partition-wall. The order is Ionic. An edifice revered by ancient Attica, as holy in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, was in 1676 the dwelling of a Turkish family, and is now deserted and neglected; but many ponderous stones and much rubbish must be removed before the well and trident would appear. The former, at least, might probably be discovered. The portico is used as a powder-magazine; but we obtained permission to dig and examine the outside. The door-way of the vestibule is walled up, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> risen nearly to the top of the door-way of the pandorofeum. By the portico is a battery commanding the town, from which ascends an amusing hum. The Turks fire from it, to give notice of the commencement of Ramazan or of their Lent, and of Bairam or the holy-days, and on other public occasions. "The pandorofeum is a small, but very particular building, of which no satisfactory idea can be communicated by description. The entablature is supported by women called Caryatides. Their story is thus related. The Greeks, victorious in the Persian war, jointly destroyed Carya, a city of the Peloponnese, which had favoured the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> enemy. They cut off Athens off the males, and carried into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> the women, whom they compelled to retain their former dress and ornaments, though in a state of servitude. The architects of those times, to perpetuate the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, represented them, as in this instance, each with a burden on her head, one hand uplifted to it and the other hanging down by her side. The images were in number six, all looking toward the parthenon. The four in front, with that next to the propylea, remain, but mutilated, and their faces bejeweled with paint. The foil is raised almost to the top of the basement on which they are placed. This temple was open or latticed between the statues; and in it also was a fluted olive-tree, with an altar of Jupiter Herceus standing under it. The propylea are nearly in a line with the space dividing it from the parthenon; which disposition, besides its other effects, occasioned the front and flank of the latter edifice to be seen at once by those who approached it from the entrance of the acropolis. "The ruin of the temple of Jupiter Olympus contains gifts of prodigious columns, tall and beautiful, of the Corinthian order, fluted; some single, some supporting the architraves; with a few massive marbles beneath: the remnant of a vast heap, which only many ages could have consumed and reduced into so scanty a compass. The columns are of very extraordinary dimensions, being about five feet in diameter, and near sixty in height. The number without the cell was 116 or 120. Seventeen were standing in 1676: but a few years before we arrived, one was overturned with much difficulty, and applied to the building a new mosque in the bazaar or market-place. This violence was avenged by the bailiwick of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGROPONT">Negropont</a>, who made it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> for extorting from the vassal or governor fifteen purses; the pillar being, he alleged, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of their master the Grand Signior. It was an angular column, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in determining the dimensions of the fabric. We regretted that the fall of this mighty mast had not been postponed until we came, as it would have afforded an opportunity of inspecting and measuring some members which we found far too lofty to be attempted. On a piece of the architrave, supported by a couple of columns, are two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> walls, of modern masonry, arched about the middle, and again near the top. You are told it has been the habitation of a hermit, doublets of a flyte; but for whatever building it has been part, and for whatever purpose designed, it must have been erected thus high in air, while the immense ruin of this huge structure was yet scarcely diminished, and the heap inclined so as to render it accessible. It was remarked that two stones of a step in the front had coalesced at the extremity, so that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a> could be perceived; and the like was discovered also in a step of the parthenon. In both instances it may be attributed to a concretory fluid, which pervades the marble in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a>. Some portion remaining in the pieces, when taken green as it were, and placed in mutual contact, it exuded and united them by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> similar to that in a bone of an animal when broken and properly set. Besides the more stable antiquities, many detached pieces of sculpture are found in the town, by the fountains, in the streets, the walls, the houses, and churches. Among these are fragments of sculpture; a marble chair or two, which probably belonged to the gymnasia or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>; a sun-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAL">dial</a> at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> with the name of the maker; and, at the archiepiscopal house <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by, a very curious vessel of marble, used as a cistern to receive water, but once serving, it is likely, as public standard or measure. Many columns occur; with some ruined statues; and pedestals, several with inscriptions, and almost buried in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. A custom has prevailed, as at Chios, of fixing in the wall, over the gateways and doors of the houses, carved stones, most of which exhibit the funeral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>. In the courts of the houses <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> many round stylobates, or pillars, once placed on the graves of the Athenians; and a great number are still to be seen applied to the same use in the Turkish burying grounds before the acropolis. These generally have concise inscriptions containing the name of the person, and of the town and tribe to which the deceased belonged. Demetrius the Phalerian, who endeavoured to restrain sepulchral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, enacted, that no person should have more than one, and that the height should not exceed three cubits. Another species, which resembles our modern head stones, is sometimes adorned with sculpture, and has an epitaph in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. We <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a few mutilated Hermies. These were busts on long quadrangular bases, the heads frequently of bronzes, invented by the Athenians. At first they were made to represent only Hermes or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, and designed as guardians of the sepulchres in which they were lodged; but afterwards the houses, streets, and porticoes of Athens were adorned with them, and rendered venerable by a multitude of portraits of illustrious men and women, of heroes, and of gods: and, it is related, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIPPARCHUS">Hipparchus</a>, son of Pothinus, erected them in the demi or borough towns, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> side, inscribed with moral apophthegms in elegiac verse; thus making them vehicles of instruction." ATHERINA. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ATHEROMA

Pages 251-251

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a tumor without pain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> discoloration of the skin, containing, in a membranous bag, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> resembling pap, intermixed with hard and stony particles. These tumors are usually cured by incision.

ATHERTON

Pages 251-251
or Atherston, a town of Warwickshire in England, situated on the river Stour, in W. Long. 1° 32'. N. Lat. 52° 40'. It is a considerable town, and had formerly a monastery; but now is best known by its fair, which is the greatest in England for cheese.

ATHESIS

Pages 251-251

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a river of the Cisalpine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, which, rising in the Rhetian <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, in Mount Brenna, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Tirol, runs southwards and washes Tridentum and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, which left it divides; and after passing this, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> its course eastwards, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> with the Po, and falls into the Adriatic between Fosca Claudia and Philistina: it separated the Euganei, an ancient people from the Veneti. The people dwelling on it are called Athestini (Pliny). Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name is the Adige.

ATHLETAE

Pages 251-252

in Antiquity, persons of strength and agility, disciplined to perform in the public games. The word is originally Greek, ἀθληταῖοι: formed from ἀθλητής, certamen, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>;" whence also ἀθλητής, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> reward adjudged the victor.—Under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHLETE">athlete</a> were comprehended wrestlers, boxers, runners, leapers, throwers. Athletic throwers of the disk, and those practised in other exercises exhibited in the Olympic, Pythian, and other solemn sports; for the conquerors wherein there were established prizes.

ATHLETIC HABIT

Pages 252-252

C <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">HABIT</a> denotes a strong hale <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of body. Anciently it signified a full fleathy corpulent state, such as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHLETE">athlete</a> endeavoured to arrive at. The athletic habit is esteemed the highest pitch of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>: yet it is dangerous, and the next door to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>; since, when the body is no longer capable of being improved, the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> must be for the worse. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> object of the athletic diet, was to obtain a firm, bulky, weighty body; by force of which, more than art and agility, they frequently overpowered their antagonist: hence they fed altogether on dry, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, and viscous meats. In the earlier days, their chief food was dry figs and cheese, which was called arida saginatio, ἑπαρ τεῦθος, and ἀναγινώσκων καθάπαυσις. Oribasius, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as others lay, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, first brought this into disuse, and substituted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> in lieu thereof. They had a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> called κολατία: They exercised, ate, and drank, without ceasing: they were not allowed to leave off eating when satiated; but were obliged to cram on till they could hold no more; by which means they at length acquired a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of voracity which to us seems incredible, and a strength <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a>. Witness what Paulanias relates of the four celebrated athletes, Polydamus the Thessalian, Milo the Crotonian, Theagenes the Thasian, and Euthymus the Locrian: The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is said to have carried a bull on his back a considerable way, then to have knocked him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with a blow of his fist, and lastly, as some add, devoured him at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>.

ATHLONE

Pages 252-252

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WESTMEATH">Westmeath</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, lying in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° N. Lat. 53° 20'. It is situated on both sides of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHANNON">Shannon</a>, and both parts are united by a strong, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-raided, and well-built <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, in the middle of which stands a monument, with some figures cut in marble, together with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>'s arms, and some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> declaring the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and the founders of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. The castle was founded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> John on some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> belonging to St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, for which he granted a compensation. It is built on a high-raided round hill, resembling one of the Danish raths <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> forts. Here were formerly two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> or monasteries. Athlone was formerly strongly fortified, and considered as of very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance. In the year 1691, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the English <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> under General Ginkel, in the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the Irish who were strongly intrenched on the opposite shore, fording the river, formed, and took possession of the town, not losing more than 50 men in the attack; which is esteemed as bold and successful an enterprise as any recorded in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. There are generally two troops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and four companies of foot quartered at Athlone. This town gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the family of Ginkel, as a reward for the noble services performed by the general.

ATHOL

Pages 252-252

the most northern district of <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-PERTHSHIRE">Perthshire</a> in Scotland, extending in length 43 miles, and in breadth 30. It is bordered on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Badenoch, on the west by Lochaber, on the east and south-east by Mar and Gowrie, on the south by Strathern and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a> Proper, and on the south-west by Braidalbane. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is very rough and mountainous, and contains <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Caledonian forest; but these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are interspersed with fruitful valleys. Here are several villages, but no <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of any consideration. The most noted <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is Blair-Castle, seated on the river Tilt, near its influx into the Garry, a pleasant limpid stream that falls in the Tay. This castle belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Athol, who derives his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> from this district, and lives here with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> magnificence. In the same neighbourhood we see the palls of Gillicranky, rendered memorable by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought here in the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William's reign, between that monarch's general McKay, and the Highlanders adhering to King James. See Gillicranky.

ATHOS

Pages 252-253

a celebrated mountain of Chalcidice in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26° 20'. N. Lat. 40° 10'. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> entertained extravagant notions concerning its height. Mela affirmed it to be so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as to reach above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>; and Martianus Capellinus, that it was six miles high. It was a received <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the summit of Mount Athos was above the middle region of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and that it never rained there; because the ashes left on the altars erected near its summit were always found as they were left, dry and unscattered. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> on many accounts it was famous among the ancients, it is no less so among the moderns. The Greeks, struck with its singular situation and the venerable appearance of its towering ascent, erected to many churches, monasteries, hermitages, &c., upon it, that it became in a manner inhabited by devotees, and from thence received the name of the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>; which name it still retains, though many of those consecrated works are now decayed. According to the accounts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> travellers, this mountain advances into the Archipelago, being joined to the continent by an isthmus about half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> in breadth. It is about 30 miles in circumference, and two in perpendicular height. It may be travelled over in about three days, and may be seen 90 miles off. There is a fine prospect from the top; but, like all other high mountains, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> on its summit is excessive. It abounds with many different kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and trees, particularly the pine and fir. In the valleys grows a plant called elegia, whose branches serve to make pens for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. In short, this mountain is said to be adorned with variety of herbage and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">evergreens</a>, a multitude of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and streams, and woods growing near the shore, so as to be one of the most agreeable places in the world. It is now inhabited by Caloyers, a sort of Greek monks, of the order of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, who never marry, though others of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> do. They abstain from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and fare very hardly, their ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> being olives pickled when they are ripe. They are about 6000 in all, and inhabit several parts of the mountain, on which are 24 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> old monasteries, surrounded with high walls for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> against banditti. They are so respected, that the Turks themselves <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> often send them alms. These monks are not idle like others; but labour with the axe, spade, and sickle, dressing themselves like hermits. Formerly they had fine Greek <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>; but are now become so illiterate, that they can scarce read <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> write. Through this mountain, or rather through the isthmus behind it, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> is said to have cut Athwart cut a passage for his fleet when about to invade <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> he spent three whole years, and employed in it all the forces on board the fleet. He is also said, before the work was begun, to have written the following insolent and ridiculous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the mountain: "Athos, thou proud and aspiring mountain, that liftest up thy head to the very skies, I advise thee not to be so audacious as to put rocks and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> that cannot be cut in the way of my workmen. If thou makest that opposition, I will cut thee entirely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and throw thee headlong into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>." The directors of this enterprise are said to have been Bubaris the son of Megabyzus, and Artaceus, the son of Arbeus, both Persians; but as no traces of such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> work remain, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the whole relation has justly been called in question.

ATHWART

Pages 253-253

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with across the line of the course. ATHWART the Fore-foot, is a phrase that denotes the flight of a cannon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> from one ship across the course of another, to intercept the latter, and oblige her to shorten sail, that the former may come near enough to examine her. ATHWART-Haute, expresses the situation of a ship, when she is driven by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tide, or any other accident, across the fore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of another. ATHWART-Ships, reaching across ships from one side to the other.

ATHY

Pages 253-253

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILDARE">Kildare</a>, not far from the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN_S_COUNTY"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s county. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° O. N. Lat. 53° O. It is situated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a>; is governed by a sovereign, two bailiffs, and a recorder; and is, alternately with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAAS">Naas</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town.

ATIBAR

Pages 253-253

the name by which the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Gago in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> call <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> dust; from which word, Europeans, and especially the French, have composed the word tibiri, which also signifies gold dust among those who trade in that commodity.

ATIGNY

Pages 253-253

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of Champagne in France, where several of the kings of France had their residence. It is seated on the river Arne, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 47'. N. Lat. 49° 30'.

ATILLA

Pages 306-307
king of the Huns, surnamed the scourge of God, lived in the 5th century. He may be ranked amongst the greatest conquerors, since there was scarcely any province in Europe which did not feel the weight of his victorious arms. Attila deduced his noble, perhaps his regal, descent from the ancient Huns, who had formerly con- Gibbon's tented with the monarchs of China. His features, ac- Rome, vol. iii. cording to the observation of a Gothic historian, bore p. 357. the stamp of his national origin: and the portrait of Attila exhibits the genuine deformity of a modern Calmuck; a large head, a fleshy complexion, small deep-set eyes, a flat nose, a few hairs in the place of a beard, broad shoulders, and a short square body, of nervous strength, though of a disproportioned form. The haughty step and demeanour of the king of the Huns expressed the consciousness of his superiority above the rest of mankind; and he had a custom of fiercely rolling his eyes, as if he wished to enjoy the terror which he inspired. Yet this savage hero was not inaccessible to pity; his suppliant enemies might confide in the assurance of peace or pardon; and Attila was considered by his subjects as a just and indulgent master. He delighted in war; but, after he had ascended the throne in a mature age, his head, rather than his hand, achieved the conquest of the north; and the fame of an adventurous soldier was usefully exchanged for that of a prudent and successful general. The effects of personal valour are so inconsiderable, except in poetry or romance, that victory, even among barbarians, must depend on the degree of skill, with which the passions of the multitude are combined and guided for the service of a single man. The arts of Attila were skilfully adapted to the character of his age and country. It was natural enough, that the Scythians should adore, with peculiar devotion, the god of war; but as they were incapable of forming either an abstract idea, or a corporeal representation, they worshipped their tutelar deity under the symbol of an iron scimitar. One of the shepherds of the Huns perceived, that a heifer, who was grazing, had wounded herself in the foot; and curiously followed the track of the blood, till he discovered, among the long grass, Attila, the point of an ancient sword; which he dug out of the ground, and presented to Attila. That magnanimous, or rather that artful, prince, accepted with pious gratitude this celestial favour; and, as the rightful possessor of the sword of Mars, asserted his divine and indefeasible claim to the dominion of the earth. If the rites of Scythia were practised on this solemn occasion, a lofty altar, or rather pile of faggots, 300 yards in length and in breadth, was raised in a spacious plain; and the sword of Mars was placed erect on the summit of this rustic altar, which was annually consecrated by the blood of sheep, horses, and of the hundredth captive. Whether human sacrifices formed any part of the worship of Attila, or whether he propitiated the god of war with the victims which he continually offered in the field of battle, the favourite of Mars soon acquired a sacred character, which rendered his conquests more easy and more permanent; and the barbarian princes confessed, in the language of devotion or flattery, that they could not presume to gaze with a steady eye on the divine majesty of the king of the Huns. His brother Bleda, who reigned over a considerable part of the nation, was compelled to resign his sceptre and his life. Yet even this cruel act was attributed to a supernatural impulse; and the vigour with which Attila wielded the sword of Mars, convinced the world that it had been reserved alone for his invincible arm. But the extent of his empire affords the only remaining evidence of the number and importance of his victories; and the Scythian monarch, however ignorant of the value of science and philosophy, might perhaps lament that his illiterate subjects were destitute of the art which could perpetuate the memory of his exploits. If a line of separation were drawn between the civilized and the savage climates of the globe; between the inhabitants of cities who cultivated the earth and the hunters and shepherds who dwelt in tents; Attila might aspire to the title of supreme and sole monarch of the Barbarians. He alone, among the conquerors of ancient and modern times, united the two mighty kingdoms of Germany and Scythia; and those vague appellations, when they are applied to his reign, may be understood with an extensive latitude. Thuringia, which stretched beyond its actual limits as far as the Danube, was in the number of his provinces; he interposed, with the weight of a powerful neighbour, in the domestic affairs of the Franks; and one of his lieutenants chastified, and almost exterminated, the Burgundians of the Rhine. He subdued the islands of the ocean, the kingdoms of Scandinavia, encompassed and divided by the waters of the Baltic; and the Huns might derive a tribute of furs from that northern region, which has been protected from all other conquerors by the severity of the climate, and the courage of the natives. Towards the east, it is difficult to circumscribe the dominion of Attila over the Scythian deserts; yet we may be assured, that he reigned on the banks of the Volga; that the king of the Huns was dreaded, not only as a warrior, but as a magician; that he insulted and vanquished the khan of the formidable Geogouen; and that he sent ambassadors to negotiate an equal alliance with the empire of China. In the proud review of the nations who acknowledged the sovereignty of Attila, and who never entertained during his lifetime the thought of a revolt, the Gepidae and the Ostrogoths were distinguished by their numbers, their bravery, and the personal merit of their chiefs. The renowned Ardaric king of the Gepidae, was the faithful and sagacious counsellor of the monarch; who esteemed his intrepid genius, whilst he loved the mild and discreet virtues of the noble Walamir king of the Ostrogoths. The crowd of the vulgar kings, the leaders of so many martial tribes, who served under the standard of Attila, were ranged in the submissive order of guards and domestics round the person of their master. They watched his nod; they trembled at his frown; and at the first signal of his will, they executed without murmur or hesitation his stern and absolute commands. In time of peace, the dependent princes, with their national troops, attended the royal camp in regular succession; but when Attila collected his military force, he was able to bring into the field an army of five, or, according to another account, of seven hundred thousand Barbarians. The death of Attila was attended with singular circumstances. He had married a new wife, a beautiful virgin named Ildico. His nuptials were celebrated with great festivity, at his palace beyond the Danube, and he retired late to bed opprest with wine. In the night, a blood-veinl burst in his lungs, which suffocated him. The bride was found in the morning lying by the bedside, lamenting his death and her own danger. The body of Attila was exposed in the plain, while the Huns, singing funeral songs to his praise, marched round it in martial order. The body, enclosed in three coffins, of gold, silver, and iron, was privately interred during the night; and to prevent the violation of his remains by the discovery of the place where he was buried, all the captive slaves who were employed in the solemnity were barbarously massacred. This happened about the year 453. With Attila ended the empire of the Huns. His sons, by dissension and civil war, mutually destroyed each other, or were dispossessed by more powerful and independent chieftains. For a farther account of his exploits, see the article Huns.

ATKINS

Pages 253-253

Sir Robert, son of the preceding, was born in 1646, and was eminent for all the virtues that could adorn an English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>. He wrote The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> and Present State of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, in one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> volume in folio; and died October 29, 1711.

ATKYNS

Pages 253-253

Richard, was descended from a good family, and was born at Tuffleigh in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a> in the year 1615. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, from whence he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s Inn, and afterwards distinguished himself by his loyalty to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., for whom he raised a troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> at his own expense. At the Restoration he was made one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> lieutenants of Gloucestershire, and distinguished himself by his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. But at length being committed prisoner to the Marshalsea in Southwark for debt, he died there on the 14th of September 1677. He wrote several pieces, particularly A Treatise on the Original and Growth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">Printing</a>.

that bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> on the east, and by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> on the west. ATLANTICA. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIS">Atlantis</a>.

ATLANTIDES

Pages 253-253

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a denomination given to the Pleiades, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> stars, sometimes also called Vergilii. They are thus called, as being supposed by the poets to have been the daughters either of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a> or his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Helperus, who were translated into heaven.

ATLANTIS

Pages 253-264
ATALANTIS, or ATLANTICA, an island mentioned by Plato and some others of the ancients, concerning the real existence of which many disputes have been raised. Homer, Horace, and the other poets, make two Atlanticas, calling them Hesperides and Elysian Fields, making them the habitations of the blest. The most distinct account of this island we have in Plato's Timaeus, of which Mr Chambers gives the following abridgement. "The Atlantis was a large island in the western ocean, situated before or opposite to the straits of Gades. Out of this island there was an easy passage into some others, which lay near a large continent exceeding in bigness all Europe and Asia. Neptune settled in this island (from whose son Atlas its name was derived), and divided it among his ten sons. To the youngest fell the extremity of the island, called Gadir, which in the language of the country signifies fertile, or abundant in sheep. The descendants of Neptune reigned here from father to son for a great number of generations in the order of primogeniture, during the space of 9000 years. They also possessed several other islands; and, passing into Europe and Africa, subdued all Libya as far as Egypt, and all Europe to Asia ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor. At length the island sunk under water; and for a long time afterwards the sea thereabouts was full of rocks and shelves." Many of the moderns also are of opinion, that the existence of the Atlantis is not to be looked upon as entirely fabulous. Some take it to have been America; and from thence, as well as from a passage in Seneca's Medea, and some other obscure hints, they imagine that the new world was not unknown to the ancients. But allowing this to be the case, the above-mentioned mentioned continent, which was said to lie beyond Atlantis, would seem rather to have been the continent of America than Atlantis itself. The learned Rudbeck, professor in the university of Upsal, in a work entitled Atlantica five Manheim, endeavours to prove that Sweden and Norway are the Atlantis of the ancients; but this its situation will by no means allow us to believe. By Kircher it is supposed to have been an island extending from the Canaries quite to the Azores; that it was really swallowed up by the ocean, as Plato affirms; and that these small islands are the shattered remains of it which were left standing. Atlantis, New, is the name of a fictitious philosophical commonwealth, of which a description has been given by Lord Bacon.—The New Atlantis is supposed to be an island in the South Sea, to which the author was driven in a voyage from Peru to Japan. The composition is an ingenious fable, formed after the manner of the Utopia of Sir Thomas More, or Campanella's City of the Sun. Its chief design is to exhibit a model or description of a college, instituted for the interpretation of nature and the production of great and marvellous works, for the benefit of men, under the name of Solomon's House, or "the college of the six days' work." This much, at least, is finished; and with great beauty and magnificence. The author proposed also a frame of laws, or of the best state or mould of a commonwealth. But this part is not executed. Atlas, king of Mauritania, a great astronomer, contemporary with Moses. From his taking observations of the stars from a mountain, the poets feigned him to have been turned into a mountain, and to sustain the heavens on his shoulders. Being an excellent astronomer, and the first who taught the doctrine of the sphere, they tell us that his daughters were turned into stars: seven of them forming the Pleiades, and other seven the Hyades. Atlas, a chain of mountains in Africa, lying between the 20th and 25th degree of north latitude, and supposed almost to divide the continent from east to west. They are said to have derived their name from Atlas, king of Mauritania, who was a great astronomer. They are greatly celebrated by the ancients on account of their height, insomuch that the above-mentioned king, who is said to have been transformed into a mountain, was feigned to bear up the heavens on his shoulders. We are assured, however, by Dr Shaw, that the part of this chain of mountains which fell under his observation could not stand in competition either with the Alps or Apennines. He tells us, that if we conceive a number of hills, usually of the perpendicular height of 400, 500, or 600 yards, with an easy ascent, and several groves of fruit or forest trees, rising up in a succession of ranges above one another; and that if to this prospect we add now and then a rocky precipice, and on the summit of each imagine a miserable mud-walled village; we shall then have a just idea of the mountains of Atlas. According to M. Chenier*, this mountain is formed by an endless chain of lofty eminences, divided into different countries, inhabited by a multitude of tribes, whose ferocity permits no stranger to approach. "I have not been able (continues he) to obtain a sufficient knowledge of these mountains to describe them accurately: What Leo Africanus has said of them is very vague; and his account is the less to be regarded at present, as it is now about three centuries since he wrote, and the face of the country has been in that time totally changed. Nothing perhaps would be more interesting to the curiosity of the philosopher, or conducive more to the improvement of our knowledge in href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural history, than a journey over Mount Atlas. The climate, though extremely cold in winter, is very healthy and pleasant; the valleys are well cultivated, abound in fruits, and are diversified by forests and plentiful springs, the streams of which uniting at a little distance, form great rivers, and lose themselves in the ocean. According to the reports of the Moors, there are many quarries of marble, granite, and other valuable stone, in these mountains: It is probable there are also mines, but the inhabitants have no idea of these riches; they consider their liberty, which their situation enables them to defend, as the most invaluable of all treasures." Atlas, in Matters of Literature, denotes a book of universal geography, containing maps of all the known parts of the world. Atlas, in Commerce, a silk-fatin, manufactured in the East Indies. There are some plain, some striped, and some flowered, the flowers of which are either gold or only silk. There are atlas of all colours, but most of them false, especially the red and the crimson. The manufacture of them is admirable; the gold and silk being worked together after such a manner as no workman in Europe can imitate; yet they are very far from having that fine gloss and lustre which the French know how to give to their silk stuffs. In the Chinese manufactures of this sort, they gild paper on one side with leaf-gold; then cut it in long slips, and weave it into their silks; which makes them, with very little cost, look very rich and fine. The same long slips are twisted or turned about silk threads, so artificially, as to look finer than gold thread, though it be of no greater value. Atmosphere, a word generally used to signify the whole mass of fluid consisting of air, aqueous and other vapours, electric fluid, &c., surrounding the earth to a considerable height. The composition of that part of our atmosphere properly called air, was till lately very much unknown. In former times it was supposed to be a simple, homogeneous, and elementary fluid. The experiments of Dr Priestley discovered, that the purest kind of air, which he called deplogisticated, was in reality a compound, and might be artificially produced in various ways. His first conjectures concerning its component parts were, that it consisted of earth, nitrous acid, and phlogiston. Subsequent experiments rendered these conjectures dubious; and at last it was supposed that deplogisticated air is a pure elementary substance, the vivifying principle to animals, and the acidifying principle throughout all nature. This deplogisticated air, however, is but a small part of the composition of our atmosphere. According to the most accurate computations, the air we usually breathe is composed of only one-fourth of this deplogisticated air, or perhaps less; the other three or four parts consisting of what Dr Priestley calls phlogisticated, and M. Lavoisier respirable air. This by itself is absolutely noxious, and exceedingly poisonous to animals: though it seems only to be negatively so; for when mixed in a certain proportion with depoliticated air, it may be breathed with safety, which could not be if it contained any ingredient absolutely unfriendly to the human constitution. The other part, viz. the pure depoliticated air, seems to stand much in the same relation to plants that phlogisticated air does to animals; that is, it would prove poisonous and destroy them if they were to depend upon it entirely for their subsistence; but as they derive their nourishment partly from the air and partly from the soil, it thence happens, that the plants which are set to grow in depoliticated air do not die instantly, as animals do in the phlogisticated kind, but remain for some time weak and sickly. The other component parts of our atmosphere are so various, and of such heterogeneous natures, that they do not admit of any kind of definition or analysis, one only excepted, namely, the electric fluid. This we know pervades the whole, but appears to be much more copious in the upper than in the lower atmospherical regions. See Electricity. To measure the absolute quantity of this fluid, either in the atmosphere or any other substance, is impossible.
