in Antiquity, a kind of servants <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> officers in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> families at Rome, who had the care and inspection of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATRIUM">atrium</a> and the things lodged therein. There are otherwise called atrarii, though some make a distinction between atrienenses and atrarii; suggesting that the latter were an inferior order of servants, perhaps assistants of the atrienenses, and employed in the more servile offices of the atrium, as to attend at the door, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>, &c. The atrienenses are represented as servants of authority and command over the rest: they acted as procurators, or agents, of their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, in selling his goods, &c. To their care were committed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and images of the master's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, &c. which were placed round the atrium; and which they carried in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> at funerals, &c. In the villas, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-houses, the atrienenses had the care of the other furniture and utensils, particularly those of metal, which they were to keep bright from rust. Other things they were to hang from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, to keep them dry, &c. They were clothed in a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, to distinguish them, and prevent their loitering from home.

ATRIP

Pages 266-266

in Nautical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">Language</a>, is applied either to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sails. The anchor is atrip, when it is drawn out of the ground in a perpendicular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, either by the cable or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUOY">buoy</a>-rope. The topsails are atrip, when they are hoisted up to the mast-head, or to their utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>.

ATRIPLEX

Pages 266-266

ORACH, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">OR</a> ARACH. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATRIUM">atrium</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> Antiquity, denotes an open <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> before a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of what was called the narthex or antecella. The atrium in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> churches was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> plot of ground, surrounded with a portico or cloister, situated between the porch or vestibule of the church and the body of the church. Some have mistakenly confounded the atrium with the porch or vestibule, from which it was distinct; others with the narthex, of which it was only a part. The atrium was the mansion of those who were not suffered to enter farther into the church. More particularly, it was the place where the first class of penitents stood to beg the prayers of the faithful as they went into the church. Atrium is also used in the canon-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, for the cemetery or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we find a law prohibiting buildings to be raised in atrio ecclesiae, except for the clergy: which the glossary explains thus, id est in cimiterio, which includes the space of forty paces around a large church, or thirty round a little church or chapel.

ATROPA

Pages 266-267

DEADLY NIGHTSHADE. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Buchanan gives an account of the destruction of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of Sweno the Dane, when he invaded Scotland, by mixing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the belladonna berries with the drink which the Scots were, according to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of truce, to supply them with. This so intoxicated the Danes, that the Scots fell upon them in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, and killed the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of them, so that there were scarcely men enough left to carry off their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. There have also been many instances in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> of children being killed by eating berries of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and about the size of a small cherry, which are no other than those of belladonna. When an accident of this kind is discovered in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, a glass of warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> prevent the bad effects. Naturalists tell strange stories of this plant: but setting aside its soporific virtue, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> botanists will scarce warrant any of them, nor even that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> ordinarily ascribed to its roots, especially since the discovery of the artifice of charlatans in fashioning it, to surprize the credulity of the people. Moses informs us (Gen. xxx. 14.) that Reuben the son of Leah, being in the field, happened to find mandrakes, which he brought home to his mother. Rachel had a mind to them, and obtained them from Leah, upon condition that she should consent that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> should be Leah's bedfellow the night following. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> דָּדָיִם, dudaim, here made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by Moses, is one of those words of which the Jews at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> do not understand the true signification. Some translate it violets, others lilies, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> jeffamine. Junius calls it agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>; Codurquus makes it truffle, or mybroom; and Calmet will have it to be the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a>. Those that would support the translation of mandrakes plead, that Rachel being barren, and having a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> desire to conceive, coveted Leah's mandrakes, it may be presumed, with a view to its prolific virtues. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> have given to mandrakes the name of the apples. Atrophy apples of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, and to Venus the name of Mandragoritis; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Julian, in his epistle to Caecilius, says, that he drinks the juice of mandrakes to excite amorous inclinations.

ATROPHY

Pages 267-267

in Medicine, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, wherein the body <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some of its parts, does not receive the necessary nutriment, but wastes and decays incessantly. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ATROPUS

Pages 267-267

in Fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the name of the third of the Parce, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Fates, whose business it was to cut the thread of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>.

ATTACHMENT

Pages 267-267

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a> of England, implies the taking <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> apprehending a person by virtue of a writ or precept. It is distinguished from an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a>, by proceeding out of a higher <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> by precept or writ; whereas the latter proceeds out of an inferior court by precept only. An arrest lies only on the body of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; whereas an attachment lies often on the goods only, and sometimes on the body and goods. An attachment by writ differs from distress, in not extending to lands, as the latter does; nor does a distress touch the body, as an attachment does. Attachment out of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">Chancery</a>, is obtained upon an affidavit made, that the defendant was served with a subpoena, and made no appearance; or it issues upon not performing some order or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>. Upon the return of this attachment by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, quod non est inventus in bailiva, i.e., another attachment, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a>, issues; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he still refuses to appear, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of rebellion. Attachment of the Forest, is one of the three courts held in the forest. The lowest court is called the court of attachment, or wood-mote court; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, swanmote; and the highest, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in eyre's seat. The court of attachments has its name from the verdurers of the forest having no other authority in it, but to receive the attachments of offenders against vert and venison taken by the foresters, and to enroll them, that they may be presented or punished at the next justice in eyre's seat. This attachment is by three means: by goods and chattels; by body, pledges, or main-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>; or by the body only. This court is held every 42 days throughout the year; and is thence called forty days court. Foreign Attachment, is an attachment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> or goods found within a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, to satisfy some creditor within such liberty or city. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and several other places, a man can attach money or goods in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a stranger, to satisfy himself.

ATTACK

Pages 267-267

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> Art, is an effort made to force a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> a body of troops, &c. Attack of a Siege, is a furious assault made by the besiegers with trenches, covers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, &c., in order to make themselves masters of a fortress, by storming one of its sides. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> there are two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three attacks made at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, there should be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> betwixt them. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>.

ATTACOTTI

Pages 267-267

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMIANUS_MARCELLINUS">Ammianus Marcellinus</a> and St Jerome, as well as in the Notitia Imperii. They are represented as allies and confederates of the Scots and Picts, and therefore probably their neighbours: though their Attainder precise situation has not been determined by antiquaries.

ATTAIN

Pages 268-268

is a writ that lies after judgment against a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> of twelve men that have given false verdict in any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of record, in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> real <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> personal, where the debt or damages amounted to above 40s. Stat. 5 and 34 Edw. III. c. 7. It is called attaint, because the party that obtains it endeavours thereby to stain or taint the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of the jury with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>, by whose verdict he is grieved. The jury who are to try this false verdict must be twenty-four, and are called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-jury; for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> wills not that the oath of one jury of twelve men should be attainted or set aside by an equal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, nor by less indeed than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the former. And he that brings the attaint can give no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> to the grand jury, than what was originally given to the petit. For as their verdict is now trying, and the question is whether or no they did <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> upon the evidence that appeared to them, the law adjudged it the highest absurdity to produce any subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> upon such <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, and to condemn the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> jurisdiction for not believing evidence which they never knew. But those against whom it is brought are allowed, in the affirmance of the first verdict, to produce new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>: because the petit jury may have formed their verdict upon evidence of their own knowledge, which never appeared in court; and because very terrible was the judgment which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law inflicted upon them, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the grand jury found their verdict a false one. The judgment was, 1. That they should lose their liberam legem, and become for ever infamous. 2. That they should forfeit all their goods and chattels. 3. That their lands and tenements should be seized into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. 4. That their wives and children should be thrown out of doors. 5. That their houses should be rafed and thrown <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. 6. That their trees should be rooted up. 7. That their meadows should be ploughed. 8. That their bodies should be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into jail. 9. That the party should be restored to all that he lost by reason of the unjust verdict. But as the severity of this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> had its usual effect, in preventing the law from being executed, therefore by the statute 11 Hen. VII. c. 24, revived by 23 Hen. VIII. c. 3, and made perpetual by 13 Eliz. c. 25, it is allowed to be brought after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the party, and a more moderate punishment was inflicted upon attainted jurors: viz. perpetual infamy, and if the cause of action were above 40l. value, a forfeiture of 20l. a-piece by the jurors; or, if under 40l. then 5l. a-piece; to be divided between the king and the party injured. So that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may now bring an attaint either upon the statute or at common law, at his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>; and in both of them may reverse the former judgment. But the practice of setting aside verdicts upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and granting new trials, has so superceded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of both sorts of attaints, that there is hardly any instance of an attaint later than the 16th century.

ATTAINED

Pages 268-268

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is applied to a person's being under attainer. See ATTAINER. ATTALICÆ VESTES, in Antiquity, garments made of a kind of cloth of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. They took the denomination from Attalus, surnamed Philometer, a wealthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERGAMUS">Pergamus</a>, who was the first, according to Pliny, who procured gold to be wove into cloth.

ATTAINER

Pages 267-268

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the most terrible and highest judgment in our laws, is pronounced, the immediate inseparable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law is attainder. For when it is now clear beyond all dispute, that the criminal is no longer fit to live upon the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, but is to be exterminated as a monster and a bane to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, the law sets a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of infamy upon him, puts him out of its protection, and takes no farther care of him than barely to see him executed. He is then called attainted, attinctus, stained <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> blackened. He is no longer of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> or reputation; he cannot be a witness in any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; neither is he capable of performing the functions of another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>: for, by an anticipation of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, he is already dead in law. This is after judgment; for there is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between a man convicted and attainted; though they are frequently through inaccuracy confounded together. After conviction only, a man is liable to none of these disabilities: for there is still in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of law a possibility of his innocence. Something may be offered in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> of judgment: the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> may be erroneous, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> render his guilt uncertain, and thereupon the present conviction may be quashed: he may obtain a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, or be allowed the benefit of clergy; both which suppose some latent sparks of merit, which plead in extermination of his fault. But when judgment is once pronounced, both law and fact conspire to prove him completely guilty; and there is not the remotest possibility left of anything to be said in his favour. Upon judgment, therefore, of death, and not before, the attainder of a criminal commences: or upon such circumstances as are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to judgment of death; as judgment of outlawry on a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> crime, pronounced for absconding or fleeing from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, which tacitly confesses the guilt: and therefore, upon judgment either of outlawry, or of death, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> or felony, a man shall be said to be attainted. A person attainted of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> treason forfeits all his lands, tenements, and hereditaments; his blood is corrupted, and he and his posterity rendered base; and this corruption of blood cannot be taken off but by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. Acts of attainder of criminals have been passed in several reigns, on the discovery of plots and rebellions, from the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. when an act was made for the attainder of several persons guilty of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of King Charles I. Among acts of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, that for attaining Sir John Fenwick, for conspiring against King William, is the most remarkable; it being made to attain and convict him of high treason on the oath of one witness, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> after a law had been enacted, "That no person should be tried or attainted of high treason where corruption of blood is incurred, but by the oath of two lawful witnesses, unless the party confess, stand <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">mute</a>, &c." Stat. 7 and 8 W. III. ATTAIN. W. III. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 3. But in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of Sir John Fenwick there was something extraordinary; for he was indicted of treason on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of two witnesses, though but only one could be produced against him on his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>.

ATTALUS

Pages 268-268

the name of several kings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERGAMUS">Pergamus</a>. See PERGAMUS. ATTELABUS. See ENTOMOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ATTENTION

Pages 268-269

a due application of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the mind, to any thing said or done, in order to acquire a knowledge thereof. The word is compounded of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a>., "to," and tendo, "I stretch." Attention of mind is not properly an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the understanding; but rather of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, by which it calls the understanding from the consideration of other objects, and directs it to the thing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Nevertheless, our attention is not always voluntary: an interesting object seizes and fixes it beyond the power of control. Attention, in respect of hearing, is the stretching or straining of the membrana tympani, so as to make it more susceptible of sounds, and better prepared to catch even a feeble agitation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Or it is the adjusting the tension of that membrane to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of loudness or lowness of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> to which we are attentive. According to the degree of attention, objects make a stronger or weaker <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> (A). Attention is requisite even to the simple act of seeing; the eye can take in a considerable field at one look; but no object in the field is seen distinctly but that singly which fixes the attention: in a profound <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVERIE">reverie</a> that totally occupies the attention, we scarce see what is directly before us. In a train of perceptions, no particular object makes such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> as it would do singly and apart; for when the attention is divided among many objects, no particular object is entitled to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> share. Hence the stillness of night contributes to terror, there being nothing to divert the attention: Horror ubique animos, simul ipsa silentia terrent. Æn. ii. Zara. Silence and solitude are ev'rywhere! Through all the gloomy ways and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> doors That hither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, nor <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> (A) <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, in his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, makes the following observations. "Sounds are meliorated by the intention of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sense is collected most to the particular sense of hearing, and the sight suspended. Therefore sounds are sweeter, as well as greater, in the night than in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and I suppose they are sweeter to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> men than to others; and it is manifest, that between sleeping and waking, when all the senses are bound and suspended, music is far sweeter than when one is fully waking." Is seen or heard. A dreadful din was wont To grate the sense, when enter'd here, from groans And howls of slaves condemn'd, from clink of chains, And crash of rusty bars and creaking hinges; And ever and anon the fight was dash'd With frightful faces, and the meagre looks Of grim and ghastly executioners. Yet more this filthiness terrifies my <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, Than did that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of complicated horrors. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">Mourning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDE">Bride</a>, Act v. sc. 3. In matters of slight importance, attention is mostly directed by will; and for that reason, it is our own fault <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> trifling objects make any deep impression. Had we power equally to withhold our attention from matters of importance, we might be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> against any deep impression. But our power fails us here: an interesting object seizes and fixes the attention beyond the possibility of control; and while our attention is thus forcibly attached to one object, others may solicit for admittance; but in vain, for they will not be regarded. Thus a small misfortune is scarcely felt in presence of a greater: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAR">Lear</a>. Thou think'st 'tis much, that this contentious storm Invades us to the skin: so 'tis to thee: But where the greater malady is fix'd, The lesser is scarce felt. Thould'st thou a bear; But if thy flight lay tow'rd the roaring <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, Thould'lt meet the bear i' th' mouth. When the mind's free, The body's delicate: the tempest in my mind Doth from my senses take all feeling else, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">Save</a> what beats there. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Lear, Act iii. sc. 5.

ATTENUANTS

Pages 269-269
or ATTENUATING Medicines, are such as were supposed to subtilize and break the humours into finer parts; and thus dispose them for motion, circulation, excretion, &c.

ATTENUATION

Pages 269-269

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of attenuating; that is, of making any fluid thinner, and less consistent, than it was before. The word is compounded of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> 'to,' and tenuis 'thin.' Attenuation is defined more generally by Chavin, the dividing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> separating of the minute parts of any body, which before, by their mutual nexus or implication, formed a more continuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. Accordingly, among alchemists, we sometimes find the word used for pulverization, or the act of reducing a body into an impalpable powder, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a>, pounding, or the like.

ATTERBURY

Pages 269-274

Dr Francis, son of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Atterbury, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> in Buckinghamshire, 1662; educated at Westminster; and from thence elected to Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he soon distinguished himself by his fine genius and turn for polite literature. The year he was made M.A. 1687, he exerted himself in the controversy with the Papists, vindicated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> in the strongest manner, and showed an uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of learning, enlivened with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> vivacity. In 1690 he married Miss Osborn, a distant relation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEEDS">Leeds</a>; a lady of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, but with little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> no fortune, who lived at or in the neighbourhood of Oxford. In Feb. 1690-1, we find him resolved to "bestir himself in his office in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>;" that of censor pro- Vol. III. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. of affairs in that house. May 11, 1711, he was appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a> one of the committee for comparing Mr Whitton's doctrines with those of the church of England; and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> following, he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up "A Representation of the Present State of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>." In 1712, Dr Atterbury was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of Christ-church, notwithstanding the strong <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and warm applications of several great men in behalf of his competitor Dr Smalridge. The next year <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him at the top of his preferment, as well as of his reputation: for, in the beginning of June 1713, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, at the recommendation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARCOURT">Harcourt</a>, advanced him to the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, with the deanery of Westminster in commendam; he was confirmed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 4, and consecrated at Lambeth next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. At the beginning of the succeeding reign, his tide of prosperity began to turn; and he received a sensible mortification presently after the coronation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> George I., when, upon his offering to present his Majesty (with a view, no doubt, of standing better in his favour) with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of state or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> canopy, his own perquisites as dean of Westminster, the offer was rejected, not without some evident marks of dislike to his person. During the rebellion in Scotland, when the Pretender's <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> was dispersed, the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> in or near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, had published a Declaration of their abhorrence of the present Rebellion, and an Exhortation to the Clergy and People to be zealous in the discharge of their duties to his Majesty King George: but the bishop of Rochester refused to sign it; and engaged Bishop Smalridge in the same refusal, on account of some reflections it contained against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> church party. He appeared generally among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">protestants</a> against the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of the ministry under the king, and drew up the reasons of the protest with his own hand. In 1716, we find him advising Dean Swift in the management of a refractory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>. April 26, 1722, he sustained a severe <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> in the loss of his lady; by whom he had four children; Francis, who died an infant; Osborn, student of Christ church; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, who died September 29, 1716, aged 17; and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, who had been then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years married to Mr Maurice. In this memorable year, on a suspicion of his being concerned in a plot in favour of the Pretender, he was apprehended August 24, and committed prisoner to the Tower. Two officers, the under secretary, and a messenger, went about two o'clock in the afternoon to the bishop's house at Westminster, where he then was, with orders to bring him and his papers before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. He happened to be in his nightgown when they came in; and being made acquainted with their business, he desired <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to dress himself. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time his secretary came in; and the officers went to search for his papers; in the sealing of which the messenger brought a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, which he pretended to have found in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>-stool, and desired it might be sealed up with the rest. His Lordship observing it, and believing it to be a forged one of his own, desired the officers not to do it, and to bear witness that the paper was not found with him. Nevertheless they did it; and though they behaved themselves with some respect to Atterbury, him, they suffered the messengers to treat him in a very rough manner, threatening him, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he did not make haste to dress himself, they would carry him away undressed as he was. Upon which he ordered his secretary to see his papers all sealed up, and went himself directly to the Cock-pit, where the council waited for him. The behaviour of the messengers, upon this occasion, seems to have been very unwarrantable, if what the author of "A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> to the Clergy of the Church of England," &c., tells us be true, that the persons, directed by order of the king and council to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> his lordship and his papers, received a strict command to treat him with great respect and reverence. However this was, when he came before the council, he behaved with a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of calmness, and they with much civility towards him. He had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to speak for himself as much as he pleased, and they listened to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> with a great deal of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; and, what is more unusual, after he was withdrawn, he had twice liberty to re-enter the council chamber, to make for himself such representations and requests as he thought proper. It is said, that, while he was under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, he made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of our Saviour's answer to the Jewish council, while he stood before them; "If I tell you, ye <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not believe me; and if I also ask you, ye will not answer me, nor let me go." After three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>'s stay at the Cock-pit, he was sent to the Tower, privately, in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COACH">coach</a>, without any manner of noise or observation. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMITMENT">commitment</a> of a bishop upon a suspicion of high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, as it was a thing rarely practised since the Reformation, so it occasioned various speculations among the people. Those who were the bishop's friends, and pretended to the greatest intimacy with him, laid the whole odium of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> upon the ministry. They knew the bishop so well, they said, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the Protestant succession, his professed abhorrence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>, and settled contempt of the Pretender, and his caution, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, and circumspection, to be such, as would never allow him to engage in an attempt of subverting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, so hazardous in itself, and so repugnant to his principles; and therefore they imputed all to the malice and management of a great minister of state or two, who were resolved to remove him, on account of some personal prejudices, as well as the constant molestation he gave them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and the particular influence and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> he had shown in the late <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>. The friends to the ministry, on the other hand, were strongly of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the bishop was secretly a favourite of the Pretender's cause, and had formerly been tampering with things of that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, even in the queen's time, and while his party was excluded from power; but upon their re-admission, had relinquished that pursuit, and his confederates therein, and became a good subject again. They urged, that the influence which the late duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a> had over him, assisted by his own private ambition and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, might prompt him to many things contrary to his declared sentiments, and inconsistent with that cunning and caution which in other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> he was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of. And to obviate the difficulty, arising from the bishop's aversion to Popery, and the Pretender's bigotry to that religion, they talked of a new <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 23, 1722-3, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> was brought into the house of commons, for "inflicting certain pains and penalties on Francis Lord Bishop of Rochester;" a copy of which was sent to him, with notice that he had liberty of counsel and solicitors for making his defence. Under these circumstances the bishop applied, by petition, to the house of lords for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> and advice as to his conduct in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a>; and April 4, he acquainted the speaker of the house of commons, by a letter, that he was determined to give that house no trouble in relation to the bill depending therein; but should be ready to make his defence against it when it should be argued in another house, of which he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to be a member. On the 9th the bill passed the house of commons, and was the same day sent up to the house of lords for their concurrence. May 6th being the day appointed by the lords for the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of the bill, Bishop Atterbury was brought to Westminster to make his defence. The counsel for the bishop were, Sir Constantine Phipps and William Wynne, Esq.; for the king, Mr Reeve and Mr Weare. The proceedings <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> above a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>; and on Saturday May 11th, the bishop was permitted to plead for himself. This he did in a very eloquent speech; which he feelingly opens by complaining of the uncommon severity he had experienced in the Tower; which was carried to so great a length, that not even his son-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> Mr Morice was permitted to speak to him in any nearer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> than standing in an open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>, whilst the bishop looked out of a two-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a>-of-doors window. In the course of his defence he observes, "Here is a plot of a year or two standing, to subvert the government with an armed force; an invasion from abroad, an insurrection at home: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> when ripe for execution, it is discovered; and twelve months after the contrivance of this scheme, no consultation appears, no men corresponding together, no provision made, no arms, no officers provided, not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in arms; and yet the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> bishop has done all this. What could tempt me to step thus out of my way? Was it ambition, and a desire of climbing into a higher station in the church? There is not a man in my office farther removed from this than I am. Was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> my aim? I always despised it too much, considering what occasion I am now like to have for it: for out of a poor bishopric of 500l. per annum, I have laid out no less than 1000l. towards the repairs of the church and episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; nor did I take one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> for dilapidations. The rest of my little income has been spent, as is necessary, as I am a bishop. Was I influenced by any dislike of the established religion, and secretly inclined towards a church of greater pomp and power? I have, my lords, ever since I knew what Popery was, opposed it; and the better I knew it, the more I opposed it. I began my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, when the Popish controversy grew hot, with that immortal book of Tillotson's, when he undertook the Protestant cause in general; and as such, I esteemed him above all. You will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> me, my lords, if I mention one thing: Thirty years ago, I wrote in defense of Martin Luther; and have preached, expressed, and wrote to that purpose from my infancy; and whatever happens to me, I will fulfill anything, and, by God's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, burn at the stake, rather than depart from any material point of the Protestant religion as professed in the church of England. Once more: Can I be supposed to favour arbitrary power? The whole tenor of my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> has been otherwise: I was always a friend to the liberty of the subject; and, to the best of my power, constantly maintained it. I may have been thought mistaken in the measures I took to support it; but it matters not by what party I was called, so my actions are uniform." Afterwards, speaking of the method of proceeding against him as unconstitutional, he says: "My ruin is not of that moment to any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men, to make it worth their while to violate, or even to seem to violate, the constitution in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, which they ought to preserve against any attempts whatsoever. Though I am worthy of no regard, though whatsoever is done to me may for that reason be looked upon to be just; yet your lordships will have some regard to your own lasting interest and that of posterity. This is a proceeding with which the constitution is unacquainted; which, under the pretence of supporting it, will at last effectually destroy it. For God's sake, lay aside these extraordinary proceedings; let not up these new and dangerous precedents. I, for my part, will voluntarily and cheerfully go into perpetual banishment, and please myself that I am in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the occasion of putting a stop to such precedents, and doing some good to my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>: I will live, wherever I am, praying for its prosperity; and do, in the words of Father Paul to the state of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, say, *Eflo perpetua.* It is not my departing from it I am concerned for. Let me depart, and let my country be fixed upon the immovable foundation of law and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and stand for ever." After a solemn profession of his innocence, and an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the Searcher of Hearts for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of what he had said, he concludes thus: "If, on any account, there shall fill be thought by your lordships to be any seeming strength in the proofs against me; if, by your lordships judgments, springing from unknown motives, I shall be thought to be guilty; if, for any reasons or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of state, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and justice of which I am no competent judge, your lordships shall proceed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> this bill against me; I shall dispose myself quietly and tacitly to submit to what you do; God's will be done: Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return; and, whether he gives or takes away, blest be the name of the Lord!" On Monday the 13th he was carried for the last time from the Tower to hear the reply of the king's counsel to his defence. These were both men of great knowledge and sagacity in law, but of different talents in point of eloquence. Their speeches on this occasion were made public; and they seem to have formed their "Replies," designedly, in a different way. The former sticks close to the matter in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, and enforces the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> against the bishop with great strength. Atterbury, and perspicuity: The latter answers all his objections, and refutes the arguments brought in his defence, in an easy, soft manner, and with great simplicity of reasoning. Mr Reeve is wholly employed in facts, in comparing and uniting together circumstances, in order to corroborate the proofs of the bishop's guilt; Mr Wearg is chiefly taken up in silencing the complaints of the bishop and his counsel, and replying to everything they advance, in order to invalidate the allegations of his innocence. The one, in short, possesses the minds of the lords with strong convictions against the bishop; the other disposes them of any favourable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> that might possibly be made upon them by the artifice of his defence. And accordingly Mr Reeve is strong, nervous, and enforcing; but Mr Wearg, smooth, easy, and insinuating, both in the manner of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> and the turn of his periods. Wearg pays the highest compliments to the bishop's eloquence; but, at the same time, represents it as employed to impose upon the reason, and misguide the judgment of his hearers in proportion as it affected their passions; and he endeavours to strip the bishop's defence of all its ornaments and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>. On the 15th the bill was read the third time; and, after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and warm debate, passed on the 16th, by a majority of 83 to 43. On the 27th, the king came to the house, and confirmed it by his royal assent. June 18, 1723, this eminent prelate, having the day before taken leave of his friends, who, from the time of passing the bill against him to the day of his departure, had free access to him in the Tower (b), embarked on board the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDBOROUGH">Aldborough</a> man of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and landed (b) The following anecdote was first communicated to the public by the late Dr Maty, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of Lord Chesterfield: "I went (said Lord Chesterfield) to Mr Pope, one morning, at Twickenham, and found a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> folio <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a>, with gilt clasps, lying before him upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>; and, as I knew his way of thinking upon that book, I asked him, jocosely, if he was going to write an answer to it? It is a present, said he, or rather a legacy, from my old friend the Bishop of Rochester. I went to take my leave of him yesterday in the Tower, where I saw this bible upon his table. After the first compliments, the Bishop said to me, 'My friend Pope, considering your infirmities, and my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> and exile, it is not likely that we should ever meet again; and therefore I give you this legacy to remember me by. Take it home with you; and let me advise you to abide by it.'—Does your Lordship abide by it yourself?"—I do. 'If you do, my Lord, it is but lately. May I begin to know what new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> or arguments have prevailed with you now, to entertain an opinion so contrary to that which you entertained of that book all the former part of your life?'—The Bishop replied, 'We have not time to talk of these things; but take home the book; I will abide by it, and I recommend you to do so too; and so God bless you.' These anecdotes Mr Nichols has inserted in the "Epistolary Correspondence," vol. ii. p. 79, with the professed view of vindicating Atterbury, in the following words of an ingenious correspondent: "Dr Warton has revived this story, which he justly calls an 'uncommon' one, in his last '<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on the Genius and Writings of Pope.' It was indeed very uncommon; and I have my reasons for thinking it equally groundless and invidious. Dr Warton, though he retails the story from 'Maty's <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>,' yet candidly acknowledges, that it ought not to be implicitly relied on. That this caution was not unnecessary, will, I apprehend, be sufficiently obvious, from the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the story itself and Mr Pope's letters to the bishop. "According to Lord Chesterfield's account, this remarkable piece of conversation took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> but a few days before the Bishop went into exile: and it is intimated that Mr Pope, till that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, had not even entertained the slightest suspicion of his friend's reverence for the bible: Nay, it is asserted, that the very recommendation of it from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> so unexpected, staggered Mr Pope to such a degree, that in a mingled vein of rillery and ferioufnels, he was very eager to know the grounds and reasons of the Bishop's change of sentiment. "Unfortunately for the credit of Lord Chesterfield and his story, there is a letter on record, that was written <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months before this pretended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> took place, in which Mr Pope seriously acknowledged the Bishop's piety and generosity, in interesting himself to zealously and affectionately in matters which immediately related to his improvement in the knowledge of the holy scriptures. The passage I refer to is a very remarkable one: and you will find it in a letter, dated July 27, 1722. It appears undeniably from this letter, that the Bishop had earnestly recommended to Mr Pope the study of the bible; and had softened his zeal with an unfeigned urbanity and courtesy, in order to avoid the imputation of ill-breeding, and remove all occasion of disgust from a mind so 'tremblingly alive' as Mr Pope's. I will transcribe the passage at large. 'I ought first to prepare my mind for a better knowledge even of good profane writers, especially the moralists, &c. before I can be worthy of tafting the Supreme of books, and Sublime of all writings, in which, as in all the intermediate ones, you may (if your friendship and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> towards me continue so far) be the best guide to, Yours, A. Pope.' "The last letter of Mr Pope to the Bishop, previous to his going into exile, was written very early in June 1723. It must have been about this time that Pope paid his farewell visit to the Bishop in the Tower. But whether such a conversation as that which hath been pretended actually took place, may be left to the determination of every man of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, after comparing Lord Chesterfield's anecdote with Mr Pope's letter. "There must have been a mistake, or a wilful misrepresentation somewhere. To determine its origin, or to mark minutely the various degrees of its progress, till it issued forth into calumny and falsehood, is impossible." Atterbury landed the Friday following at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>. When he went on shore, having been informed that Lord Bolingbroke, who had, after the rising of the parliament, received the king's pardon, was arrived at the same place on his return to England, he said, with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of pleasantry, "Then I am exchanged!" and it was, in the opinion of Mr Pope on the same occasion, "a sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>'s being curiously afraid of being overrun with too much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, when it could not regain one great man but at the expense of another." But the severity of his treatment did not cease even with his banishment. The same vindictive spirit pursued him in foreign climes. No British subject was even permitted to visit him without the king's sign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a>, which Mr Morice was always obliged to solicit, not only for himself, but for every one of his family whom he carried abroad with him, for which the fees of office were very high. When Bishop Atterbury first entered upon his banishment, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> was the place destined for his residence; but, by the arts and intrigues of the British ministers, he was compelled to leave that place, and retire to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. There being solicited by the friends of the Pretender to enter into their negotiations, he changed his abode for Montpelier in 1728; and, after residing there about two years, returned to Paris, where he died Feb. 15, 1731-2. The affliction which he sustained by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> in 1729, was thought to have hastened his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>. The former event he hath himself related in a very affecting manner, in a letter to Mr Pope: "The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> desire of meeting one I dearly loved, called me abruptly to Montpelier; where, after continuing two months under the cruel torture of a sad and fruitless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>, I was forced at last to take a long journey to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a>; and even there I had missed the person I sought, had she not, with great spirit and courage, ventured all night up the Garonne to see me, which she above all things desired to do before she died. By that means she was brought where I was, between seven and eight in the morning, and lived 20 hours afterwards; which time was not lost on either side, but passed in such a manner as gave great satisfaction to both, and such as, on her part, every way became her circumstances and character: For she had her senses to the very last gasp, and exerted them to give me, in those few hours, greater marks of duty and love than she had done in all her lifetime, though she had never been wanting in either. The last words she said to me were the kindest of all; a reflection on the goodness of God, which had allowed us in this manner to meet once more, before we parted for ever. Not many minutes after that, she laid herself on her pillow, in a sleeping posture, Placidaque ibi demum morte quietit. Judge you, Sir, what I felt, and still feel, on this occasion, and spare me the trouble of describing it. At Atterbury, my age, under my infirmities, among utter strangers, how shall I find out proper reliefs and supports? I can have none, but those with which reason and religion furnish me; and those I laid hold on, and grasp as fast as I can. I hope that He who laid the burden upon me (for wife and good purpose no doubt) will enable me to bear it in like manner as I have borne others, with some degree of fortitude and firmness." How far the Bishop might have been attached in his inclinations to the Stuart family, to which he might be led by early prejudices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and the divided opinions of the times, it is not necessary here to inquire: But that he should have been weak enough to engage in a plot inconsistent with his station, and so clumsily devised (to lay the least of it, and without entering into his solemn avowal of innocence,) is utterly inconsistent with that cunning which his enemies allowed him. The duke of Wharton, it is well known, was violent against him, till convinced by his unanswerable reasoning. It has been said that Atterbury's wishes reached to the bishopric of London, or even to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> or Canterbury. But those who were better acquainted with his views, knew that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a> would have been much more desirable to him than either of the others. And there are those now living, who have been told from respectable authority, that that bishopric was offered to him whenever it should become vacant (and till that event should happen, a pension of £500l. a-year, besides an ample provision for Mr Morice), if he would cease to give the opposition he did to Sir Robert Walpole's administration, by his speeches and protests in the house of lords. When that offer was rejected by the bishop, then the contrivance for his ruin was determined on. In his speech in the house of lords, the bishop mentions his being "engaged in a correspondence with two learned men (Bishop Potter and Dr Wall) on settling the times of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the four gospels." Part of this correspondence is still in being, and will soon be published. The same subject the bishop pursued during his exile, having consulted the learned of all nations, and had nearly brought the whole to a conclusion when he died. These laudable labours are an ample <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFUTATION">confutation</a> of Bishop Newton's assertion, that Atterbury "wrote little whilst in exile but a few criticisms on French authors." His body was brought over to England, and interred on the 12th of May following in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, in a vault which in the year 1722 had been prepared by his directions. There is no memorial over his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>; nor could there well be any, unless his friends would have consented (which it is most probable they refused to do) that the words implying him to have died bishop of Rochester should have been omitted on his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>. Some I have simply stated matters of fact as they are recorded; and leave it to your readers to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> not quite so obvious and indisputable, as they may think fit. My motives in this very plain relation arose from an honest wish to remove unmerited obloquy from the dead. I should sincerely rejoice if the cloud which in other respects still shades the character of this ingenious prelate could be removed with equal facility and success. I am, dear Sir, your faithful humble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, Samuel Babcock. Some time before his death, he published a vindication of himself, Bishop Smalridge, and Dr Aldrich, from a charge brought against them by Mr Oldmixon, of having altered and interpolated the copy of Lord Clarendon's "<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Rebellion." Bishop Atterbury's "Sermons" are extant in four volumes in octavo: those contained in the two first were published by himself; and dedicated to his great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a> Trelawney bishop of Winchester; those in the two last were published after his death by Dr Thomas Moore his Lordship's chaplain. Four admirable "Visititation Charges" accompany his "Epistolary Correspondence." As to Bishop Atterbury's character, however the moral and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> part of it may have been differently represented by the opposite parties, it is universally agreed, that he was a man of great learning and uncommon abilities, a fine writer, and a most excellent preacher. His learned friend Smalridge, in the speech he made when he presented him to the upper house of convocation, as prolocutor, styles him Vir in nulla literarum genere holpes, in plurisque artibus et studiis diu et felicius exercitatus, in maxime perfectis literarum disciplinis perfectissimus. In his controversial writings, he was sometimes too severe upon his adversary, and dealt rather too much in satire and invective; but this his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> imparts more to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> fervour of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> than to any bitterness of temper or personal malice. In his sermons, however, he is not only every way unexceptionable, but highly to be commended. The truth is, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> as a preacher was so excellent and remarkable, that it may not improperly be said, that he owed his preferment to the pulpit; nor any hard matter to trace him, through his writings, to his several promotions in the church. We shall conclude Bishop Atterbury's character as a preacher, with the encomium bestowed on him by the author of "the Tatler;" who, having observed that the English clergy too much neglected the art of speaking, makes a particular exception with regard to our prelate; who, says he, "has so particular a regard to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>, that he commits to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> what he has to say to them; and has so soft and graceful a behaviour, that it must attract your attention. His person (continues this author), is to be confessed, is no small recommendation; but he is to be highly commended for not losing that advantage, and adding to propriety of speech (which might pass the criticism of Longinus) an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> which would have been approved by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>. He has a peculiar force in his way, and has affected many of his audience, who could not be intelligent hearers of his discourse were there no explanation as well as grace in his action. This art of his is used with the most exact and honest skill. He never attempts your passions, till he has convinced your reason. All the objections which you can form are laid open and dispersed before he uses the least vehemence in his sermon; but when he thinks he has your head, he very soon wins your heart, and never pretends to throw the beauty of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a>, till he has convinced you of the truth of it."—In his letters to Pope, &c. Bishop Atterbury appears in a pleasing light, both as a writer and as a man. In ease and elegance they are superior to those of Pope, which are more studied. There are in them several beautiful references to the classics. The bishop excelled in his Attestation allusions to sacred as well as profane authors.

a town in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, now called *Effo*. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 6. N. Lat. 45° 25'.

ATTIC

Pages 274-274

anything relating to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>: thus Attic <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PHILOLOGY">philology</a>, is a delicate poignant sort of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and humour peculiar to the Athenian writers; Attic witness, a witness incapable of corruption, &c. ATTIC Order. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>. ATTIC Base, a peculiar kind of base used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> architects in the Ionic order; and by Palladio, and some others, in the Doric. ATTIC Story, in Architecture; a story in the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where the windows are usually <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>.

ATTICA

Pages 274-306

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, situated along the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Saron; bounded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, &c., on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, Mount Cithaeron, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>; on the north by the gulf of Euripus, now Stratto di negro ponte, and the rest of Boeotia; and on the east by the Euripus. It extends in length from north-west to south-east about 60 miles; its breadth from north to south was 56, decreasing as it approached the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was naturally barren and craggy, though by the industry of its inhabitants it produced all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. On this account Attica was less exposed to invasion than other more fertile countries; and hence it preferred its ancient inhabitants beyond all the other kingdoms in its neighbourhood; so that they were reputed to be the spontaneous productions of the soil; and as a badge of this, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> tells us, they wore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> grasshoppers in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cities in the kingdom of Attica were A-Cities, then the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>; next to it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELEUSIS">Eleusis</a>, situated on the same gulf, near the coast of Megara; and next to that Rhamnus famed for the temple of Amphiarus and the statue of the goddes Nemesis. The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of this country, of whom we have any distinct account, was Cecrops. Others indeed are said the first to have reigned before him, particularly one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADONIS">Adonis</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Cecrops married, and in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> laid the foundation of his new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>. Cecrops is said to have been the first who deified <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, set up altars and idols, and instituted <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> among the Greeks. He is likewise affirmed to have taught his subjects <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; and for the better administration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and promoting intercourse among them, to have divided them into the first four tribes, called Cecropis, Antabiblon, Adeia, and Paralia; and he is also by some said to be the founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREOPAGUS">Areopagus</a>. From this monarch the Athenians affected to call themselves Cecropide till the reign of Erechtheus their fifth king, after whom they took the name of Erechtheidae. Cecrops dying after a reign of 50 years, left three daughters; by marrying one of whom, probably, Cranus a wealthy citizen ascended the throne. He enjoyed his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> peaceably for ten years; till, having married one of his daughters named Attis, to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AMPHICTYON">Amphictyon</a> the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>, he was by him dethroned, and forced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a private life to the last. From this Whence daughter, the country, which before had been called the country Adeia, took the name of Attica. After a reign of 10 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 12 years, Amphitryon was himself deposed by Erechthonius, said to be the son of Vulcan and Tethys. Being lame of both his feet, he is said to have invented coaches, or, as others <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it, instituted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and chariot races, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>. He is also reported to have been the first who stamped silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>. He reigned 50 years, and was succeeded by his son Pandion the father of Progne and Philomela; whose hard fate, so famous among the poets, is supposed to have broke his heart, after a reign of about 40 years. In his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> Triptolemus taught the Athenians <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, which he had learned from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>. Pandion was succeeded by his son Eretheus, who being reckoned the most powerful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of his time, Boreas king of Thrace demanded his daughter Orithya in marriage; and on being refused carried her off by force. After a reign of 50 years, Eretheus being killed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> with the Eleusians, was succeeded by his son Cecrops II., who is generally allowed to have been the first who gathered the people into <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; they having till then lived in houses and cottages scattered here and there, without order or regular distance. After a reign of 40 years he was driven out by his brethren Metion and Pandorus, who forced him to fly into Ægialea, where he died. Cecrops II. was succeeded by his son Pandion II., and he was likewise driven out by Metion, who assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Pandion in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time fled into Megara, where he married <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PELIA">Pelia</a> the daughter of Pylas king of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and was appointed successor to the kingdom. Here he had four sons, who returning to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, whether with or without their father is uncertain, expelled the sons of Metion, and after the decease of Pandion their father, divided the government among themselves; notwithstanding which, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> did in effect remain with Ægeus the eldest. Ægeus, when he ascended the throne, finding himself despised by his subjects because he had no sons, and sometimes insulted by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Pallas, who had no less than fifty, consulted the oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>. Receiving here, as was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, an answer which could not be understood without a commentator, he applied to Pittheus king of Troezen, famous for his skill in expounding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a>. This prince easily prevailed with him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> with his daughter Æthra, who proved with child; and as none but these three were privy to the secret, Ægeus, before his return to Athens, hid a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> and a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of shoes under a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, leaving orders with the princess, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the child proved a boy, she should send him to Athens with these tokens as soon as he was able to lift up that stone. He <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> her moreover to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> all imaginable secrecy, lest the sons of his brother Pallas should waylay and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> him. Æthra being delivered of a son, Pittheus gave out that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> was the father of it. This child was named <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>, and proved one of the most famous heroes of antiquity. Being arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 16, his mother brought him to the stone above mentioned; and he having lifted it with ease, was desired to take up the sword and shoes and prepare himself to go to his father.
