So he " considers centripetal powers as attractions, though, physically speaking, it were perhaps more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> to call them impulses." ib. p. 147. He adds, "that what he calls attraction may possibly be effected by impulse, though not a common or corporeal impulse, or after some other manner unknown to us," Optic. p. 322. Attraction, if considered as a quality arising from the specific forms of bodies, ought, together with sympathy, antipathy, and the whole tribe of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OCCULT">occult</a> qualities, to be exploded. But when we have set these aside, there <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> remain innumerable phenomena of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and particularly the gravity or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of bodies, or their tendency to a centre, which argue a principle of action seemingly distinct from impulse, where at least there is no sensible impulsion concerned. Nay, what is more, this action in some respects differs from all impulsion we know of; impulse being always found to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> in proportion to the surfaces of bodies, whereas gravity acts according to their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> content, and consequently must arise from some cause that penetrates or pervades the whole substance thereof. This unknown principle, unknown we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> in respect of its cause, for its phenomena and effects are most obvious, with all the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> and modifications thereof, we call attraction; which is a general name, under which all mutual tendencies, where no physical impulse appears, and which cannot therefore be accounted for from any known laws of nature, may be ranged. And hence arise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> particular kinds of attraction; as, Gravity, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNETISM">Magnetism</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>, &c. which are so many different principles acting by different laws, and only agreeing in this, that we do not see any physical causes thereof; but that, as to our senses, they may really arise from some power or efficacy in such bodies, whereby they are enabled to act even upon distant bodies, though our reason absolutely disallows of any such action. Attraction may be divided, with respect to the law it observes, into two kinds. 1. That which extends to a sensible distance. Such are the attraction of gravity, found in all bodies; and the attraction of magnetism and electricity, found in particular bodies. The several laws and phenomena of each, see under their respective <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. The attraction of gravity, called also among mathematicians the centripetal force, is one of the greatest and most universal principles in all nature. We see and feel it operate on bodies near the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and find by observation that the same power (i.e. a power which acts in the same manner, and by the same rules, viz. always proportionably to the quantities of matter, and as the squares of the distances reciprocally) does also obtain in the moon, and the other planets primary and secondary, as well as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a>; and even that this is the very power whereby they are all retained in their orbits, &c. And hence, as gravity is found in all the bodies which come under our observation, it is easily inferred, by one of the settled rules of philosophy, that it obtains in all others: and as it is found to be as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of matter in each body, it must Vol. III. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. Attraction rent bodies; stronger, e.g., between the particles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a> and those of nitric acid than those of silver, between nitric acid and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a> than <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, between iron and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> than silver or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>. So sulphuric acid acts on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, but more on iron or copper, &c. The other experiments which countenance the existence of such principle of attraction in the particles of matter are innumerable. These actions, in virtue whereof the particles of the bodies above mentioned tend towards each other, the author calls by a general indefinite name attraction; which is equally applicable to all actions whereby distant bodies tend towards one another, whether by impulse or by any other more latent power: and from hence he accounts for an infinity of phenomena, otherwise inexplicable, to which the principle of gravity is inadequate. Thus (adds our author) will nature be found very conformable to herself and very simple; performing all the great motions of the heavenly bodies by the attraction of gravity, which intercedes those bodies, and almost all the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> ones of their parts, by some other attractive power diffused through the particles thereof. Without such principles, there never would have been any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> in the world; and without the continuance thereof, motion would soon perish, there being otherwise a great decrease or diminution thereof, which is only supplied by these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> principles. We need not say how unjust it is in the generality of foreign philosophers to declare against a principle which furnishes so beautiful a view, for no other reason but because they cannot conceive how one body should act on another at a distance. It is certain, philosophy allows of no action but what is by immediate contact and impulsion (for how can a body exert any active power there where it does not exist? to suppose this of anything, even the Supreme Being himself, would perhaps imply a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>): yet we see effects without seeing any such impulse; and where there are effects, we can easily infer there are causes whether we see them or not. But a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may consider such effects without entering into the consideration of the causes, as indeed it seems the business of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> to do: for to exclude a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of phenomena which we do see, will be to leave a great chasm in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of nature; and to argue about actions which we do not see, will be to build castles in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>.—It follows, therefore, that the phenomena of attraction are matter of physical consideration, and as such entitled to a share in the system of physics; but that the causes thereof will only become so when they become sensible, i.e., when they appear to be the effect of some other higher cause (for a cause is no otherwise seen than as itself is an effect, so that the first cause must from the nature of things be invisible): we are therefore at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to suppose the causes of attractions what we please, without any injury to the effects.—The illustrious author himself seems a little irresolute as to the causes; inclining sometimes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> gravity to the action of an immaterial cause (<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, p. 343, &c.) and sometimes to that of a material one (ib. p. 325.) In his philosophy, the research into causes is the last thing, and never comes under consideration till the laws and phenomena of the effect be settled; it being to these phenomena that the cause is to be accommodated. The cause even of any, the grossest and most sensible action, is not adequately known. How impulse or percussion itself produces its effects, i.e., how motion is communicated by body to body, confounds the deepest philosophers; yet is impulse received not only into philosophy, but into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>: and accordingly the laws and phenomena of its effects make the greatest part of common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>. The other species of attraction, therefore, in which no impulse is remarkable, when their phenomena are sufficiently ascertained, have the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to be promoted from physical to mathematical consideration; and this without any previous inquiry into their causes, which our conceptions may not be proportionate to: let their causes be occult, as all causes strictly speaking are, so that their effects, which alone immediately concern us, be but apparent. Our great philosopher, then, far from adulterating science with any thing foreign or metaphysical, as many have reproached him with doing, has the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of having thrown every thing of this kind out of his system, and of having opened a new source of sublimer mechanics, which duly cultivated might be of infinitely greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> than all the mechanics yet known. It is hence alone we must expect to learn the manner of the changes, productions, generations, corruptions, &c. of natural things; with all that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of wonders opened to us by the operations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>. Some of our own countrymen have prosecuted the discovery with laudable zeal: Dr Keill particularly has endeavoured to deduce some of the laws of this new action, and applied them to solve divers of the more general phenomena of bodies, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a>, fluidity, elasticity, softness, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, coagulation, &c.; and Dr Freund, seconding him, has made a further application of the same principles, to account at once for almost all the phenomena that chemistry presents: so that some philosophers are inclined to think that the new mechanics should seem already raised to a complete science, and that nothing now can occur but what we have an immediate solution of from the attractive force. But this seems a little too precipitate: A principle so fertile should have been further explored; its particular laws, limits, &c. more industriously detected and laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, before we had proceeded to the application. Attraction in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> is so complex a thing, that it may solve a thousand different phenomena alike. The notion is but one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> more simple and precise than action itself; and, till more of its properties are ascertained, it were better to apply it less and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> it more. It may be added, that some of Sir Isaac Newton's followers have been <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with falling into that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> which he industriously avoided, viz. of considering attraction as a cause or active <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in bodies, not merely as a phenomenon or effect. Attraction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>. See Mountains. Electric Attraction. See Chemistry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Attrebatii. See Attrebatii. Attribute, in a general sense, that which agrees with some person or thing; or a quality determining something to be after a certain manner. Thus understanding is an attribute of mind, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> an attribute of body. That attribute which the mind conceives. Attributes conceives as the foundation of all the rest, is called its essential attribute; thus extension is by some, and solidity by others, esteemed the essential attribute of body or matter.

ATTRIBUTES

Pages 311-311

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">Sculpture</a>, are symbols added to several figures, to intimate their particular office and character. Thus the eagle is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>; a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>, of Juno; a caduceus, of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>; a club, of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>; and a palm, of Victory.

ATTRIBUTIVES

Pages 311-311

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, are words which are significant of attributes; and thus include <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADJECTIVES">adjectives</a>; verbs, and particles, which are attributes of substances; and adverbs, which denote the attributes only of attributes. Mr Harris, who has introduced this distribution of words, denominates the former attributives of the first order, and the latter attributives of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> order.

ATTRITION

Pages 311-311

the rubbing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> striking of bodies one against another, so as to throw off some of their superficial particles. ATURÆ, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town in the district of Novempopulana in Aquitania, on the river Aturus; now <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRE">Aire</a> in Gascogne, on the Adour. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 3. N. Lat. 43. 40.

AUBAGNE

Pages 311-311

a town of Provence in France, situated on the river Veau, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from Marceilles to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOULON">Toulon</a>. The states formerly held their sessions at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 52. N. Lat. 43. 17.

AUBAIN

Pages 311-311

in the old customs of France, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> vested in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of being heir to a foreigner that dies within his dominions. By this right the French King claimed the inheritance of all foreigners that died within his dominions, notwithstanding of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a> the deceased could make. An <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> was not subject to the right of aubaine; and the Swedes, Savoyards, Scots, and Portuguese were also exempted, being deemed natives and regnicoles.

AUBENAS

Pages 311-311

a town of France, in the department of Ardeche, situated on the river Ardeche, at the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> called the Cevennes. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 32. N. Lat. 44. 40.

AUBENTON

Pages 311-311

a town of France, in the department of Ainé, situated on the river Aube. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 25. N. Lat. 49. 51. AUBETERRÉ, a town of France in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGOUMOIS">Angoumois</a>, on the river Dronne. E. Long. 0. 10. N. Lat. 45. 15.

AUBREY

Pages 311-312

John, a famous English antiquary, descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in Wiltshire, was born in 1626. He made the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and antiquities of England his peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and delight; and contributed considerable assistance to the famous Monasticon Anglicanum. He succeeded to several good estates; but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>-suits and other misfortunes consumed them all, so that he was reduced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> want. In this extremity he found a valuable benefactor in the Lady <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a> of Draycot in Wilts, who gave him an apartment in her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and supported him to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened about the year 1700. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of considerable ability, learning, and application, a good Latin poet, an excellent naturalist, but somewhat credulous, and tinctured with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. He left many works behind him. He wrote, 1. Miscellanies. 2. A Perambulation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, in five volumes, octavo. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Mr Hobbes of Malmesbury. 4. Monumenta Britannica, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a discourse concerning <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONEHENGE">Stonehenge</a>, and Roll-Rich <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>. 5. Archiepistola Sacra; and several other works still in manuscript.

AUBURN

Pages 312-312

a market-town in Wiltshire, in England. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 20. N. Lat. 53. 20.

AUBUSSON

Pages 312-312

a small town of France, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of La Marche, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the Lyonnais, now the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREUSE">Creuse</a>. Its situation is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, on the river Creuse, in a bottom surrounded with rocks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. A manufacture of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a> is carried on here, by which the town is rendered very populous. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 15. N. Lat. 45. 58.

AUCAUGREL

Pages 312-312

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Adel in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, seated on a mountain. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 44. 25. N. Lat. 9. 10.

AUCH

Pages 312-312

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Armagnac, now the department of Gers, and the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of all Gacony. The archbishop formerly assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> of Aquitain. It lies on the summit and declivity of a very steep hill, which is surrounded by other hills that rise at a small distance; and through the vale below runs a rivulet, called the Gers. The inhabitants are about 6000; the buildings are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> and elegant; the streets, though in general narrow, yet are clean and well paved. In the centre of the city stands the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, which is one of the most magnificent in France, both as to its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and the internal decorations. The painted windows are only inferior to those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOUDA">Gouda</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. The chapels are of equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and ornamented at a prodigious expense. The revenues of the see of Auch amount annually to three hundred thousand livres. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is a very handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; and its apartments are furnished with a voluptuous splendor, rather becoming a temporal than a spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 40. N. Lat. 43. 40.

AUCTION

Pages 312-312

a kind of public <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, very much in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> goods, books, plate, &c. By this method of sale the highest bidder is always the buyer. This was originally a kind of sale among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, performed by the public crier judicat, i.e., under a spear stuck up on that occasion, and by some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, who made good the sale by delivery of the goods.

AUDEUS

Pages 312-313

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the Audeans, obtained the name of a heretic, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of banishment, for celebrating Easter in the manner of the Jews, and attributing a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> form to the Deity. He died in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, about the year 370. AUDIENCE given to ambassadors, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> observed in courts at the admission of ambassadors <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> public ministers to a hearing. In England, audience is given to ambassadors in the presence chamber; to envoys and residents, in a gallery, cloister, or in any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> happens to be. Upon being admitted, as is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of all courts, they make three bows; after which they cover and fit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; but not before the king is covered and fat down, and has given them the sign to put on their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>. When the king does not care to have them covered, and fit, he himself stands uncovered; which is taken as a slight. At Constantinople, ministers usually have audience of the prime vizier. Audience is also the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> established in the West-Indies by the Spaniards, answering in effect to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in France. These courts take in several provinces, called allo audiencier, from the name of the tribunal to which they belong. Audience is also the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> court held by the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, wherein differences upon elections, consecrations, institutions, marriages, &c. are heard. AUDIENDO & TERMINANDO, a writ, or rather a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to certain persons, when any insurrection or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> riot is committed in any place, for the appealing and punishment thereof.

AUDIENTES

Pages 313-313
or AUDITORES, in Church History, an order of catechumens; consisting of those newly instructed in the mysteries of the Christian religion, and not yet admitted to baptism.

AUDIT

Pages 313-313

a regular hearing and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of an account by some proper officers, appointed for that purpose.

AUDITOR

Pages 313-313

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, a hearer, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> one who listens or attends to anything. Auditor, according to our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is an officer of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, or some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> person, who, by examining yearly the accounts of the under officers, makes up a general book, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between their receipts and charges, and their allowances to allocations. Auditor of the Receipts, is an officer of the exchequer who files the tellers bills, makes an entry of them, and gives the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> a certificate of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> before. He also makes debentures to every teller, before they receive any money, and takes their accounts. He keeps the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> book of receipts, and the treasurer's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, and fees every teller's money locked up in the new treasury. Auditors of the Revenue, or of the exchequer, officers who take the accounts of those who collect the revenues and taxes raised by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and take the accounts of the sheriffs, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a> officers, collectors, tenants, and customers, and set them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in a book, and perfect them. Auditors of the Press and Impress, officers of the exchequer, who take and make up the accounts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, Berwick, the mint, and of any money impressed to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> for the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. They received poundage on all accounts paid by them, which amounted to a prodigious sum, especially in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. But the office is now abolished, and £1000 a-year given to the incumbents. Auditors Collegiate, Conventual, &c., officers formerly appointed in colleges, &c. to examine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> their accounts.

AUDITORES

Pages 313-313

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>. See AUDIENTES. The auditores formed one branch of the Manichean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, which was divided into elect and auditors; corresponding, according to some writers, to clergy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a>; and, according to others, to the faithful and catechumens among the Catholics. By the Manichean rule, a different course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was prescribed to the elect from that of the auditors. The latter might eat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, drink wine, bathe, marry, traffic, possess estates, bear magistracy, and the like; all which things were forbidden to the elect. The auditors were obliged to maintain the elect, and knelt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to ask their blessing. Beaufobre observes, that the elect were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, and in general such as made profession of observing certain councils, called evangelic; such as the clergy and monks; and they were called the perfect by Theodoret. The auditors were the laity, and so demominated, because they heard in the church, whilst others taught and instructed.

AUDITORIUM

Pages 313-313

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> churches, was that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> where the audientes stood to hear and be instructed. The auditorium was that part now called navis ecclesiae*. In the primitive times, the church was so strict in keeping the people together in that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, that the person who went from thence in sermon-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was ordered by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a> to be excommunicated.

AUDITORY

Pages 313-313

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Churches. See AUDITORIUM. AUDITORY Passage, (meatus auditorius), in Anatomy; the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. See ANATOMY, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. AUDITORY Nerves. See ANATOMY Index.

AUDRAN

Pages 313-315
Claude, a French engraver, the first of the celebrated artists of that name, was the son of Lewis Audran, an officer belonging to the wolf-hunters, in the reign of Henry IV. of France; and was born at Paris in 1592. He never made any great progress in that art; so that his prints are held in little or no estimation. Yet though he acquired no great reputation by his own works, it was no small honour to him to be the father of three great artists, German, Claude, and Girard; the last of whom has immortalized the name of the family. Claude Audran retired from Paris to Lyons, where he resided, and died in 1677. Audran, Carl, a very eminent engraver, was brother to the preceding, though some assert he was only his cousin-german; and was born at Paris in 1594. In his infancy he discovered much taste, and a great disposition for the arts; and to perfect himself in engraving, which he appears to have been chiefly fond of, he went to Rome, where he produced several prints that did him great honour. At his return, he adopted that species of engraving which is performed with the graver only. He settled at Paris, where he died in 1674, without having ever been married. The Abbé Marolles, who always speaks of this artist with great praise, attributes 130 prints to him: amongst which, the annunciation, a middle-sized plate, upright, from Hannibal Carracci; and the assumption, in a circle, from Domenichino, are the most esteemed. In the early part of his life he marked his prints with C, or the name of Carl, till his brother Claude published some plates with the initial only of his baptismal. Audran, Germain, the eldest son of Claude, mentioned in the preceding article but one, was born in 1631 at Lyons, where his parents then resided. Not content with the instructions of his father, he went to Paris, and perfected himself under his uncle Carl; so that, upon his return to Lyons, he published several prints which did great honour to his graver. His merit was in such estimation, that he was made a member of the academy established in that town, and chosen a professor. He died at Lyons in 1710, and left behind him four sons, all artists; namely, Claude, Benoît, John, and Louis. Audran, Claude, the second of this name, and second son to Claude above-mentioned, was born at Lyons in 1639, and went to Rome to study painting; where he succeeded so well, that at his return he was employed by Le Brun to assist him in the battles of Alexander, which he was then painting for the king of France. He was received into the Royal Academy in the year 1675, and died unmarried at Paris in 1684. His virtues (says Abbé Fontenai) were as praiseworthy as his talents were great. M. Heineken mentions this artist as an engraver, without specifying any of his works in that line. Audran, Girard, or Gerard, the most celebrated artist of the whole family of the Audrans, was the third son of Claude Audran mentioned in a preceding article, and born at Lyons in 1640. He learned from his father the first principles of design and engraving; and following the example of his brother, he left Lyons and went to Paris, where his genius soon began to manifest itself. His reputation there brought him to the knowledge of Le Brun, who employed him to engrave the battles of Conquering, and the triumph of that emperor; and for these works he obtained apartments at the Gobelins. At Rome, whither he went for improvement, he is said to have studied under Carlo Maratti, in order to perfect himself in drawing; and in that city, where he resided three years, he engraved several fine plates. M. Colbert, that great encourager of the arts, was so struck with the beauty of Audran's works whilst he resided at Rome, that he persuaded Louis XIV. to recall him. On his return, he applied himself assiduously to engraving; and was appointed engraver to the king, from whom he received great encouragement. In the year 1681 he was named councillor of the Royal Academy; and died at Paris in 1703. He had been married; but left no male issue behind him. The great excellency of this artist above that of any other engraver was, that though he drew admirably himself, yet he contrived no manner of his own; but transcribed on copper simply, with great truth and spirit, the style of the master whose pictures he copied. On viewing his prints you lose sight of the engraver, and naturally say, it is Le Brun, it is Poullin, it is Mignard, or it is Le Sueur, &c. as you turn to the prints which he engraved from those masters. Let any one examine the battles above-mentioned from Le Brun, the preservation of the young Pyrrhus from Nicholas Poullin, the peafowl from Mignard, and the martyrdom of St Lawrence from Le Sueur, and then judge candidly of the truth of this observation. The following judicious observations by the Abbé Fontenai, taken chiefly from M. Bafan, with some small variation and additions, will fully illustrate the merits of Gerard Audran. "This sublime artificer, far from conceiving that a servile arrangement of strokes, and the too frequently cold and affected clearness of the graver, were the great essentials of historical engraving, gave worth to his works by a bold mixture of free hatchings and dots, placed together apparently without order, but with an inimitable degree of taste; and has left to posterity most admirable examples of the style in which grand compositions ought to be treated. His greatest works, which have not a very flattering appearance to the ignorant eye, are the admiration of true connoisseurs and persons of fine taste. He acquired the most profound knowledge of the art by the constant attention and study which he bestowed upon the science of design, and the frequent use he made of painting from nature. This great man always knew how to penetrate into the genius of the painter he copied from; often improved upon, and sometimes even surpassed him. Without exception, he was the most celebrated engraver that ever existed in the historical line. We have several subjects which he engraved from his own designs, that manifested as much taste as character and facility. But, in the battles of Alexander, he surpassed even the expectations of Le Brun himself." These consist of three very large prints, lengthwise, each consisting of four plates, which join together, from Le Brun; namely, the passage of the Granicus; the battle of Arbela; Porus brought to Alexander, after his defeat. To this set are added two more large prints lengthwise, on two plates each, also from Le Brun, as follow: Alexander entering the tent of Darius; and The triumphal entry of Alexander into Babylon. The former was engraved by Gerard Edelink, and the latter by Gerard Audran. It is to be remarked of all these plates, that those impressions are generally most esteemed which have the name of Guyon the printer marked upon them. The Peafowl from Peter Mignard, a large plate, lengthwise, also deserves particular notice. In the first impressions, the figure in the clouds is Juno with her peacock behind her; in the latter, the peacock is obliterated, and the wings of an angel are added to the figure. Audran, Benoît, the second son of Germain Audran, was born at Lyons in 1661, where he learned the first principles of design and engraving under the instruction of his father. But soon after going to Paris, his uncle Gerard Audran took him under his tuition; and Benoît so greatly profited by his instructions, that though he never equalled the sublime style of his tutor, yet he deservedly acquired great reputation. Nay, the Abbé Fontenai adds this eulogy: "We admire in his works a share of those beauties which we find in the engravings of the illustrious Gerard." He was honoured with the appellation of the king's engraver, and received the royal pension. He was made an academician, and admitted into the council in 1715. He died unmarried at Louzouer, where he had an estate, in 1721. His manner was founded upon the bold clear style of his uncle. His outlines were firm and determined; his drawing correct; the heads of his figures are in general very expressive; and the Audran, the other extremities well marked. His works, when compared with those of his uncle, appear to want that mellowness and harmony which are so conspicuous in the latter; they are more dry; and the round dots with which he finished his flesh upon the lights are often too predominant. In his most finished plates, we find the mechanical part of the engraving extremely neat, and managed with great taste and judgment. Among his neatest prints may be reckoned that which represents Alexander sick, drinking from the cup which his physician presents to him: a circular plate, from Le Sueur. Audran, John, the third son of Germain Audran, was born at Lyons in 1667; and, after having received instructions from his father, went to Paris to perfect himself in the art of engraving under his uncle Gerard Audran. At the age of 20 years, the genius of this great artist began to display itself in a surprising manner; and his future success was such, that in 1707, he obtained the title of engraver to the king, and had a pension allowed him by his majesty, with apartments in the Gobelins; and the following year he was made a member of the Royal Academy. He was 80 years of age before he quitted the graver; and near 90 when he died at his apartments assigned him by the king. He left three sons behind him; one of whom was also an engraver, as we shall see below. "The most masterly and best prints of this artist (in Mr Strutt's opinion) are those which are not so pleasing to the eye at first sight. In these the etching constitutes a great part; and he has finished them in a bold rough style. The scientific hand of the master appears in them on examination. The drawing of the human figure, where it is shown, is correct. The heads are expressive and finely finished; the other extremities well marked. He has not, however, equaled his uncle. He wants that harmony in the effect; his lights are too much and too equally covered; and there is not sufficient difference between the style in which he has engraved his backgrounds and his draperies. This observation refers to a fine print by him of Athaliah, and such as he engraved in that style. At other times he seems almost to have quitted the point, and substituted the graver. But here I think he has not so well succeeded. The effect is cold and silvery: see, for example, the Andromache from Sylvestre. One of his best finished prints, in this neat style, seems to me to be Cupid and Psyche from Ant. Corneil." Audran, Louis, the last son of Germain Audran, was born at Lyons in 1670; from whence he went to Paris, after the example of his brothers, to complete his studies in the school of his uncle Gerard. He died suddenly at Paris in 1712, before he had produced any great number of prints by his own hand. He assisted, it is presumed, his brothers in their more extensive works. Among the most esteemed prints by this artist are the seven acts of mercy, on seven middling sized plates, lengthwise, from Sebastian Bourdon. Audran, Benoît, the second engraver of that name, was the son of John Audran, and nephew to the former Benoît; and was also established at Paris. He engraved but a few plates. It is necessary, however, to be careful not to confound him with his uncle. But a little attention will easily prevent this mistake; for the second Benoît is vastly inferior to the first in point of merit. We have some few portraits by this artist; and among other plates, the different from the crofs, from a picture of Poussin.

AUKLAND

Pages 327-327

Bishop's, a town in the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a> in England, situated on the river Wear. It is a sanctuary for debtors; and here the bishop has a princely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> and a noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 55'. N. Lat. 54° 44'.

AULCESTER

Pages 327-327

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a> in England. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 47'. N. Lat. 52° 15'.

AULETES

Pages 327-327

in antiquity, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>-player. One of the Ptolemies, kings of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, father of Cleopatra, bore the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> denomination of Auletes.

AULIC

Pages 328-328

in the Sorbonne and foreign <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> which a young divine maintains upon being admitted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. It begins by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARANGUE">harangue</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, addressed to the young doctor, after which he receives the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, and prefides at the aulic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disputation.

AULIS

Pages 328-328

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, over against Chalcis of Euboea, on the Euripus, where that strait is narrowest; and which was sometimes joined with Chalcis together by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> causeway, (Diodorus Siculus): a craggy situation, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NONNUS">Nonnus</a>); and a village of the Tanagraei, (Strabo), distant from Chalcis three miles: A harbour famous for the rendezvous of the Grecian fleet under Agamemnon, previous to the Trojan expedition, (Livy, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Pliny.) Now entirely destroyed. AULNEGER. See Alnager.

AULON

Pages 328-328
or Aulona, anciently a town of Elis, in Peloponnesus on the confines of Messenia. Here stood a temple of Æsculapius; hence the epithet Aulonius given that divinity, (Pausanias).

AULPS

Pages 328-328

a town of Provence in France, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Frejus, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a vigurie. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 25' N. Lat. 43° 40'. AULUS GELLIUS. See Gellius.

AUNCLEWEIGHT

Pages 328-328

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kind of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> now out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, being prohibited by several statutes, on account of the many deceits practised by it. It consisted of scales hanging on hooks, fastened at each end of a beam, which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> lifted up on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. In many parts of England, auncle-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> signifies meat sold by the hand, without scales.

AUNGERVYLL

Pages 328-328

RICHARD, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known by the name of Richard de <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">Bury</a>, was born in 1281 at St Edmund's Bury in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, and educated at the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>: After which he entered into the order of Benedictine monks, and became <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward III. Upon the accession of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> pupil to the throne he was first appointed cofferer, then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the wardrobe, archdeacon of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTON">Northampton</a>, prebendary of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, Sarum, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a>, keeper of the privy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>, and last of all was promoted to the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>. He likewise enjoyed the offices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, and treasurer of England; and discharged two important embassies at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of France. Learned himself, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of the learned, he maintained a correspondence with some of the greatest geniuses of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, particularly with the celebrated Italian poet Petrarch. He was also of a most humane and benevolent temper, and performed many signal acts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> he made eight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of wheat into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, and gave it to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. Whenever he travelled between Durham and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, he distributed eight pounds <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> in alms: between Durham and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKTON">Stockton</a> five pounds, between Durham and Auckland five marks, and between Durham and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLEHAM">Middleham</a> five pounds. He founded a public library at Oxford, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the students, which he furnished with the best collection of books then in England; and appointed five keepers, to whom he granted yearly salaries. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses in the reign of Henry VIII. Durham <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, where he fixed the library, being dissolved among the rest, some of the books were removed to the public library, some to Balliol college, and some came into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Dr George Owen, a physician of Godstow, who bought that college of King Edward VI. Bishop Aungervyle died at his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of Auckland, April 24, 1345, and was buried in the south <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the choir aisle of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Durham, to which he had been a benefactor. He wrote, 1. Philobiblon, containing directions for the management of his library at Oxford, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in praise of learning, in bad Latin. 2. Epistolae familiarium; some of which are written to the famous Petrarch. 3. Orationes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> principes; mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">Bale</a> and Pits.

AUNIS

Pages 328-328

the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in France, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Poitou, on the west by the ocean, on the east and south by Saintonge, of which it was formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>. It is watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Seure and Sarente, the former of which has its source at Seure in Poitou. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of this small district has the advantage of several ports, the most remarkable of which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHEFORT">Rochefort</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a>, Brouge, St Martin de Re, Tremblade, Tonrai, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is dry, yet produces good corn and plenty of wine. The marshes feed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cattle, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> marshes yield the best salt in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

AURACH

Pages 329-329

a town of Germany with a good castle, in the south <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Swabia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Würtemberg. It is the usual residence of the youngest sons of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Würtemberg, and is seated at the foot of a mountain on the rivulet Ernst. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 20'. N. Lat. 48° 25'. AURÆ, in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to the nymphs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. They are mostly to be found in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> paintings of ceilings; where they are represented as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a>, generally with long robes and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> veils of some lively <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other, and fluttering about in the rare and pleasing element assigned to them. They are characterized as sportive and happy in themselves, and wellwisher to mankind.

AURANCHES

Pages 329-329

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a territory called Auranchin, about 30 miles in length, in Lower Normandy in France, now the department of the Channel. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>; but its situation very fine, being on an eminence, near which the river Se runs, about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half from the ocean. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> stands on a hill, which terminates abruptly; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> extending to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> verge of it, and overhanging the precipice. It bears the marks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> antiquity; but the towers are decayed in many places, though its original <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> has been wonderfully strong. Here, you are told, the English Henry II. received <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTION">absolution</a> from the Papal nuncio for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of St. Thomas-a-Becket in 1172, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> on which he knelt during the performance of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> is shown to strangers. Its length is about 30 inches, and the breadth 12. It stands before the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> portal, and on it is engraved a chalice in commemoration of the event. The ruins of the castle of Auranches are very extensive; and beneath lies a rich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, abounding in grain and covered with orchards, from the fruit of which is made the best cider in Normandy. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 20'. N. Lat. 48° 5'.

AURAY

Pages 329-329

a small seaport town of Lower Brittany in France, situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORBIHAN">Morbihan</a>, and in the department of the same name. It consists of only one handsome street, and is chiefly known for its trade. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 25'. N. Lat. 47° 48'.

AURELIA

Pages 329-329

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the same with what is more usually called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRYSALIS">chrysalis</a>, and sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a>. See Chrysalis, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

AURELIANUS

Pages 329-329

Lucius Domitius, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Rome, was one of the greatest generals of antiquity, and commanded the armies of the emperor Claudius with such <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, that after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that emperor all the legions agreed to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> him on the throne: this happened in the year 270. He carried the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> from the east to the west, with as much facility, says a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writer, as a body of troops marches from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALSACE">Alsace</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>. He defeated the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, Sarmatians, Aurelius Marcomanni, the Persians, Egyptians, and Vandals; conquered Zenobia <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of the Palmyreans, and Tetricus general of the Gauls; both of whom were made to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> his triumph, in the year 274. He was killed by one of his generals in Thrace in the year 275, when he was preparing to enter <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. See Rome. AURELIUS VICTOR. See Victor.

AURENGABAD

Pages 329-329

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the East Indies, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Balagate, in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul. It is furnished with handsome mosques and caravanseras. The buildings are chiefly of freestone, and pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and the streets planted on each side with trees. They have <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> gardens well stocked with fruit trees and vines. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> about it is also very fertile, and the sheep fed in its neighbourhood are remarkably large and strong. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 75° 30'. N. Lat. 19° 10'.

AUREOLA

Pages 329-329

in its original signification, signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEWEL">jewel</a>, which is proposed as a reward of victory in some public dispute. Hence the Roman schoolmen applied it to denote the reward bestowed on martyrs, virgins, and doctors, on account of their works of supererogation; and painters <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it to signify the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> with which they adorn the heads of saints, confessors, &c.

AUREUS

Pages 329-329

a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, equal in value to 25 denarii. According to Ainsworth, the aureus of the higher empire weighed near five pennyweights; and in the lower empire, little more than half that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. We learn from Suetonius, that it was customary to give aurei to the victors in the chariot races.

AUREUS MONS

Pages 329-329

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a mountain in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> west of Corsica, whose ridge runs out to the north-east and south-east, forming an elbow.—Another mountain of Moesia Superior, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a> (Peutinger), to the south of the Danube, with a cognominal town at its foot on the same river. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Probus planted this mountain with vines (Europius).

AURICK

Pages 329-329

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany; in East Frieland, in the circle of Westphalia; to which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> claims a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. It is situated in a plain surrounded with forests full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 50'. N. Lat. 53° 28'.

AURICLE

Pages 329-329

in Anatomy, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> which is prominent from the head, called by many authors auris externa. Auricles are likewise two mucular bags situated at the basis of the heart, and intended as diverticula for the blood during the diaetole.

AURIFLAMMA

Pages 329-329

in the French <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, properly denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> standard belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St. Denis, suspended over the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of that saint, which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> on occasion of any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of their lands or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, and gave it to their protector or advocate, to be borne at the head of their forces. Auriflamma is also sometimes used to denote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> flag or standard in any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>.

AURIGA

Pages 329-330

the Waggoner, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AURILLAC">Aurillac</a>, a town of France in the Lower Auvergne, now the department of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANTAL">Cantal</a>, seated on a small river called Jourdan. It is one of the most considerable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, has six gates, is very populous, and yet has but one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>. The castle is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and commands the town. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Aurillac, and had episcopal jurisdiction; and was also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the town. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is remarkable for having produced several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 33. N. Lat. 44. 55.

AURISCALPIUM

Pages 330-330

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> to clean the ears, and serving also for other operations in disorders of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>.

AURORA

Pages 330-335

the morning twilight, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that faint <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> which appears in the morning when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is within 18 degrees of the horizon. Aurora, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of the morning, according to the Pagan <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>. She was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Hyperion and Theia, according to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>; but of Titan and Terra, according to others. It was under this name that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> denoted the light which foretells the rising of the sun above our hemisphere. The poets represent her as rising out of the ocean, in a chariot, with rosy fingers dropping gentle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> describes her ascending in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>-coloured chariot with four horses. Aurora, one of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in which Mr Forster supposes the Peak d'Etoile mentioned by Mr Bougainville to be situated. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is inhabited; but none of its inhabitants came off to visit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is woody, and the vegetation seems to be excessively luxuriant. It is about 12 leagues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, but not above five miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>; lying nearly <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and south. The middle lies in S. Lat. 15. 6. E. Long. 168. 24. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AURORA_BOREALIS">Aurora Borealis</a>, Northern Twilight, or Streamers; a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a> appearing in the northern part of the heavens, mostly in the winter-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and in frosty <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. It is now so generally known, that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> is requisite of the appearance which it usually makes in this country. But it is in the arctic regions that it appears in perfection, particularly during the solstice. In the Shetland islands, the merry dancers, as they are there called, are the constant attendants of clear evenings, and prove <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reliefs amidst the gloom of the long winter nights. They <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> appear at twilight near the horizon, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUN">dun</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, approaching to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; sometimes continuing in that state for several hours without any sensible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; after which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out into streams of stronger light, spreading into columns, and altering slowly into ten thousand different shapes, varying their colours from all the tints of yellow to the obscurest ruddiness. They often cover the whole hemisphere, and then make the most brilliant appearance. Their motions at these times are most amazingly quick; and they astonish the spectator with the rapid change of their form. They break out in places where none were seen before (skimming briskly along the heavens) are suddenly extinguished, and leave behind an uniform dusky tract. This again is brilliantly illuminated in the same manner, and as suddenly left a dull blank. In certain nights they assume the appearance of vast columns, on one side of the deepest yellow, on the other declining away till it becomes undistinguishable from the sky. They have generally a strong tremulous motion from end to end, which continues till the whole vanishes. In a word, we, who only see the extremities of these northern phenomena, have but a faint idea of their splendour and their motions. According to the state of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, they differ in colours. They often put on the colour of blood, and make a most dreadful appearance. The ruddy tinges become prophetic, and terrify the gazing spectators with the dread of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, pestilence, and famine. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> was not peculiar to the northern islands; nor are these appearances of recent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a>. The ancients called them Chasmata, and Trabes, and Bolides, according to their forms or colours. In old times they were extremely rare, and on that account were the more taken notice of. From the days of Plutarch to those of our sage historian Sir Richard Baker, they were supposed to have been portentous of great events, and timid imagination flamed them into aerial conflicts: Fierce fiery warriors fight upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> In ranks and squadrons and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> form of war. Dr Halley tells us, that when he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a great aurora borealis in 1716, he had begun to despair of ever seeing one at all; none having appeared, at least in any considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, from the time he was born till then. Notwithstanding this long <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>, however, it seems that in some periods the aurora borealis had been seen much more frequently; and perhaps this, as well as other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> phenomena, may have some stated times of returning. The only thing that resembles a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this phenomenon, is what we have from the learned Dr Halley, Phil. Trans. No. 347. The first account he gives, is of the appearance of what is called by the author <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> spears, and was seen at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 30th, 1560. This account is taken from a book entitled, A Description of Meteors, by W. F. D. D., and reprinted at London in 1654. The next appearance, on the testimony of Stow, was on October 7th, 1564. In 1574 also, according to Camden, and Stow above-mentioned, an aurora borealis was observed two nights successively, viz. on the 14th and 15th of November, with much the same appearances as described by Dr Halley in 1716, and which we now so frequently observe. Again, the same was twice seen in Brabant, in the year 1575; viz. on the 13th of February and 28th of September. Its appearances at both these times were described by Cornelius Gemma, professor of medicine in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>, who compares them to spears, fortified cities, and armies fighting in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. After this, Michael Maestlin, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to the great Kepler, assures us, that at Bakenang in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Wurttemberg in Germany, these phenomena, which he styles chasmata, were seen by himself no less than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> times in 1580. In 1581, they again appeared in an extraordinary manner in April and September, and in a less degree at some other times of the same year. In 1621, September 2d, this phenomenon was observed all over France, France, and described by Gassendus, who gave it the name of aurora borealis: yet neither this, nor any similar appearances <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> to 1574, are described by English writers till the year 1707; which, as Dr Halley observes, shows the prodigious neglect of curious matters which at that time prevailed. From 1621 to 1707, indeed, there is no mention made of an aurora borealis being seen by any body; and considering the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of astronomers who during that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> were in a manner continually poring on the heavens, we may very reasonably conclude that no such thing did make its appearance till after an interval of 86 years. In 1707, a small one was seen in November; and during that year and the next, the same appearances were repeated five times. The next on record is that mentioned by Dr Halley in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1715—16, the brilliancy of which attracted universal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and by the vulgar was considered as marking the introduction of a foreign <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of princes. Since that time those meteors have been so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, that no accounts have been kept of them. It was for a long time a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of doubt whether this meteor made its appearance only in the northern hemisphere, or whether it was also to be observed near the south pole. This is now ascertained by Mr Foster; who in his late voyage round the world along with Captain Cook, affirms us, that he observed them in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> southern latitudes, though with phenomena somewhat different from those which are seen here. On Feb. 17, 1773, as they were in Lat. 58° south, "A beautiful phenomenon (says he) was observed during the preceding night, which appeared again this and several following nights. It consisted of long columns of a clear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> light, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> up from the horizon to the eastward, almost to the zenith, and gradually spreading on the whole southern part of the sky. These columns were sometimes bent sidewise at their upper extremities; and though in most respects similar to the northern lights (aurora borealis) of our hemisphere, yet differed from them in being always of a whitish colour, whereas ours affume various tints, especially those of a fiery and purple hue. The sky was generally clear when they appeared, and the air sharp and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, the thermometer standing at the freezing point." Dr Halley observed that the aurora borealis described by him arose to a prodigious height, it being seen from the west of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> to the confines of Russia and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> on the east; nor did he know how much further it might have been visible; so that it extended at least 30 degrees in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and from Lat. 50° north it was seen over all the northern part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and what was very surprising, in all those places where it was visible, the same appearances were exhibited which Dr Halley observed at London. He observes, with seeming regret, that he could by no means determine its height, for want of observations made at different places; otherwise he might as easily have calculated the height of this aurora borealis, as he did of the fiery globe in 1719*. To other philosophers, however, he gives the following exhortation. "When therefore for the future any such thing shall happen, all those that are curious in astronomical matters are hereby admonished and entreated to let their clocks to the apparent time at London, for example, by allowing for many minutes as is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of meridians; and then to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, at the end of every half <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> precisely, the exact situation of what at that time appears remarkable in the sky; and particularly the azimuths of those very tall pyramids so eminent above the rest, and therefore likely to be seen furthest: to the intent that, by comparing these observations taken at the same moment in distant places, the difference of their azimuths may serve to determine how far these pyramids are distant from us." This advice of Dr Halley seems to have been totally neglected by all the philosophical people in his country. In other countries, however, they have been more industrious. Father Boscovich has determined the height of an aurora borealis, observed on the 16th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1737 by the marquis of Poletti, to have been 825 miles high; the celebrated Mr Bergman, from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> of 30 computations, makes the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> height of the aurora borealis to be 70 Swedish, or upwards of 450 English miles. Euler supposes it to be several thousands of miles high; and Mairet also affirms them a very elevated region. In the 7th volume of the Philosophical Transactions, Dr Blagden, when speaking of the height of some fiery meteors, tells us, that the "aurora borealis appears to occupy as high, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not a higher region above the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, as may be judged from the very distant countries to which it has been visible at the same time." The height of these meteors, however, none of which appear to have exceeded or even arrived at the height of a hundred miles, must appear trifling in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of the vast elevations above mentioned. But these enormous heights, varying so exceedingly, show that the calculators have not had proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATA">data</a> to proceed upon; and indeed the immense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of space occupied by the aurora borealis itself, with its constant motion, must make it infinitely more difficult to determine the height of it than of a fiery globe, which occupies but a small portion of the visible heavens. The most certain method of making a comparison between the aurora borealis and the meteors already mentioned, would be, if a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of fire should happen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the same part of the heavens where an aurora borealis was; when the comparative height of both could easily be ascertained.
