One instance of this only has come under our observation, where one of the small meteors, called falling stars, was evidently obscured by an aurora borealis; and therefore must have been higher than the lower part of the latter at least. A singularity in this meteor was, that it did not proceed in a straight line through the heavens, as is usual with falling stars, but described a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of a circle, rising in the north-west, and proceeding southward a considerable way in the arch of a circle, and disappearing in the north. Its edges were ill defined, and five or six coruscations seemed to issue from it like the rays painted as issuing from stars. The aurora borealis was not in motion, but had degenerated into a crepuscule in the northern part of the hemisphere. Indeed, in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> this kind of crepuscule appears so plainly to be connected with the clouds, that we can scarcely avoid supposing it to proceed from them. We cannot, however, argue from this to the height of the aurora borealis when it moves with great velocity, because it then may, and very probably does, ascend much higher. Dr Blagden, in Aurora Borealis <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, informs us, that instances are recorded, where the northern lights have been seen to join, and form <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> balls, darting about with great velocity, and even leaving a train like the common <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIRE_BALLS">fire-balls</a>. It would seem, therefore, that the highest regions of the aurora borealis are the same with those in which fire balls move. With regard to the cause of the aurora borealis naturally occurring was, that it was occasioned by the ascent of inflammable sulphureous vapours from the earth. To this supposition Dr Halley objects the immense extent of such phenomena, and that they are constantly observed to proceed from north to south, but never from south to north. This made him very reasonably conclude, that there was some connexion between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> of the earth and the aurora borealis; but being unacquainted with the electric power, he supposed, that this earth was hollow, having within it a magnetic sphere, which corresponded in virtue with all the natural and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> magnets on the surface; and the magnetic effluvia passing through the earth, from one pole of the central magnet to another, might sometimes become visible, in their course, which he thought was from north to south, and thus exhibit the beautiful coruscations of the aurora borealis. Had Dr Halley, however, known that a stroke of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a> would give polarity to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> that had it not, or reverse the poles of one that had it before, he would undoubtedly have concluded the electric and magnetic effluvia to be the same, and that the aurora borealis was this fluid performing its circulation from one pole of the earth to the other. In fact, this very <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> is adapted by S. Beccaria; and by the supposed circulation of the electric fluid he accounts for the phenomena of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNETISM">magnetism</a> and the aurora borealis in a manner perfectly similar to that of Dr Halley, only changing the phrase magnetic effluvia for electric fluid. The following is the account given us by Dr Priestley of Beccaria's sentiments on this matter. "Since a sudden stroke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> gives polarity to magnets, he conjectures, that a regular and constant circulation of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of the fluid from north to south may be the original cause of magnetism in general. "That this ethereal current is insensible to us, is no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of its non-existence, since we ourselves are involved in it. He had seen birds fly near a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>-cloud, as he was sure they would not have done had they been affected by its atmosphere. "This current he would suppose to arise from one source, but from several, in the northern hemisphere, of the earth; and he thinks that the aurora borealis may be this electric matter performing its circulation in such a state of the atmosphere as renders it visible, or approaching the earth nearer than usual. Accordingly, very vivid appearances of this kind have been observed to occasion a fluctuation in the magnetic needle." A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> disproof of this circulation, however, is furnished by the observation of Mr Forster already mentioned: with which, though neither Dr Halley nor S. Beccaria could be acquainted, they might have thought of it as a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> proof either of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> or falsehood of their hypothesis.—If the aurora borealis is no other than the electric fluid performing the above-mentioned circulation, it ought to dart from the horizon towards the zenith in the northern hemisphere, and from the zenith to the horizon in the southern one: but Mr Forster plainly tells us, that the columns <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> up from the horizon towards the zenith as well in the southern hemisphere as in the northern; so that if the aurora borealis is to be reckoned the flittings of electric matter, its course is plainly directed from both poles toward the equator, and not from one pole to the other. Concerning the cause of this phenomenon, Mr <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">Canton</a> has the following query: "Is not the aurora borealis the flashing of electrical fire from positive towards <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> clouds at a great distance, through the upper part of the atmosphere where the refraction is least?" But to this we must reply in the negative; for in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it would flash in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> according to the position of the clouds, as well as from north to south. Besides this query, he conjectures, that when the needle is disturbed by the aurora borealis, that phenomenon proceeds from the electricity of the heated air; and supposes the air to have the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of becoming electric by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, like the tourmalin. But neither does this hypothesis appear at all probable; because, in such a case, the aurora borealis ought to be most frequent in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> when the air is most heated, whereas it is found to be the reverse. Lastly, with these electrical hypotheses we shall <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> that of Mr Mairan, who imagined this phenomenon to proceed from the atmosphere of the sun, particles of which were thrown off by its centrifugal force acquired by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> on his axis; and that these particles falling upon the atmosphere of the earth near its equatorial parts, were from thence propelled by the diurnal motion of the earth towards the polar regions, where they formed the aurora borealis. This hypothesis, besides its being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> supposition unsupported by one single appearance in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, is liable to the objection already mentioned; for in this case the light should dart from the equator to the poles, and not from the poles to the equator: or if we should suppose this matter to be gradually accumulated at each of the poles, we must then make other suppositions equally vague and ill founded, concerning its getting back with such surprising rapidity in direct opposition to the power which once brought it thither. The first person who seems to have endeavoured to find any positive proof of the electrical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the aurora borealis, was Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. He observes, that though this phenomenon is commonly supposed to be electrical, yet he had not seen any attempt to prove that it is so; but the only proof he himself brings is an experiment of Mr Hawkesbee, by which the electric fluid is shown to put on appearances somewhat like the aurora borealis, when it passes through a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>. He observed, that when the air was most perfectly exhausted, the streams of electric matter were then quite white; but when a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of air was let in, the light assumed more of a purple colour. The flashing of this light therefore from the dense regions of the atmosphere into such as are more rare, and the transitions through mediums of different density, he reckons the cause of the aurora borealis, and of the different colours it assumes. Dr Hamilton's proof, then, of the electricity of the the aurora borealis consists entirely in the resemblance the two lights bear to one another; and if to this we add, that, during the time of an aurora borealis, the magnetic needle hath been disturbed, electric fire ob- tained from the atmosphere in plenty, and at some times different kinds of rumbling and hissing sounds heard, we have the sum of all the positive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> in favour of the electric hypothesis. Was the aurora borealis the first natural pheno- menon the solution of which had been attempted by elec- tricity, no doubt the proofs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> now adduced would be very insufficient; but when it is considered, that we have indisputable evidence of the identity of the phe- nomena of thunder and of electricity; when we also consider, that the higher parts of our atmosphere are continually in a strongly electrified state; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> becomes so strong that we can scarce doubt of the au- ora borealis arising from the same cause. The only difficulty is, to give a good reason why the electricity of the atmosphere should be constantly found to direct its course from the poles towards the equator, and not from the equator to the poles; and this we think may be done in the following manner. 1. It is found that all electric bodies, when consi- derably heated, become conductors of electricity; thus hot air, hot glass, melted rosin, sealing-wax, &c., are all conductors, till their heat is dissipated, and then they again become electrics. 2. As the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> of every true proposition ought also to be true, it follows from the above one, that if electricity when heated become conductors, then non- electricity when subjected to violent degrees of cold ought to become electric. In one instance this has been verified by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which is a conduc- tor when warm or not violently cooled, is found to be- come electric when cooled to 20° below 0 of Fahrenheit's thermometer. With regard to metallic substan- ces, indeed, no experiments have as yet been made to determine whether their conducting power is affected by cold or not. Very probably we might not be able to produce such a degree of cold as sensibly to lessen their conducting power; but still the analogy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> hold; and, as we are by no means able to produce the greatest degree of cold possible, reason will always sug- gest to us, that if a certain degree of cold changes one conductor into an electric, a sufficient degree of it will also change all others into electrics. 3. If cold is sufficient to change conducting sub- stances into electrics, it must also increase the electric power of such substances as are already electric; that is to say, very cold air, glass, rosin, &c., provided they are dry, will be more electric than when they are warmer. With regard to air, which is most to our present purpose, this is rendered extremely probable, by considering that clear frosty weather is of all others the most favourable for electric experiments. They may be made indeed to equal advantage almost in any state of the atmosphere, provided sufficient pains are used, but in dry hard frosts they will succeed much more easily than at any other time. These three axioms being allowed, the cause of the aurora borealis is easily deduced from them. The air, all round the globe, at a certain height above its sur- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, is found to be exceedingly cold, and, as far as experiments have yet determined, exceedingly electro- cal also. The inferior parts of the atmosphere between the tropics, are violently heated during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>-time by the reflection of the sun's rays from the earth. Such air will therefore be a kind of conductor, and much more readily part with its electricity to the clouds and vapours floating in it, than the colder air towards the north and south poles. Hence the prodig- ious appearances of electricity in these regions, show- ing itself in thunder and other tempests of the most terrible kind. Immense quantities of the electric fluid are thus communicated to the earth; and the inferior warm atmosphere having once exhausted itself, must ne- cessarily be recruited from the upper and colder re- gion. This becomes very probable from what the French mathematicians observed when on the top of one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDES">Andes</a>. They were often involved in clouds, which, sinking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into the warmer air, ap- peared there to be highly electrified, and discharged themselves in violent tempests of thunder and light- ning; while in the mean time, on the top of the mountain, they enjoyed a calm and serene sky. In the temperate and frigid zones, the inferior parts of the atmosphere never being so strongly heated, do not part with their electricity so easily as in the torrid zone, and consequently do not require such recruits from the upper regions; but notwithstanding the difference of heat observed in different parts of the earth near the surface, it is very probable that at considerable heights the degrees of cold are nearly equal all round it. Were there a like equality in the heat of the under part, there could never be any considerable loss of equili- brium in the electricity of the atmosphere; but as the hot air of the torrid zone is perpetually bringing down vast quantities of electric matter from the cold air that lies directly above it; and as the inferior parts of the atmosphere lying towards the north and south poles do not conduct in any great degree; it thence follows, that the upper parts of the atmosphere lying over the torrid zone will continually require a supply from the northern and southern regions. This easily shows the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of an electric current in the upper parts of the atmosphere from each pole towards the equator; and thus we are also furnished with a reason why the au- ora borealis appears more frequently in winter than in summer; namely, because at that time the electric power of the inferior atmosphere is greater on account of the cold than in summer; and consequently the abundant electricity of the upper regions must go al- most wholly off to the equatorial parts, it being impos- sible for it to get down to the earth; hence also the aurora borealis appears very frequent and bright in the frigid zones, the degree of cold in the upper and un- der regions of the atmosphere being much more nearly equal in these parts than in any other. In some parts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a> particularly, this meteor appears constantly from October to Christmas, and its coruscations are said to be very terrifying. Travellers agree, that here the aurora borealis appears in greatest perfection; and it is to be remarked, that Siberia is the coldest coun- try on earth. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of this, it may also be observed, that, from the experiments hitherto made with the electrical <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KITE">kite</a>, the air appears considerably more electrical in winter than in summer, though the clouds are known to be often most violently electrified in the summer time; a proof, that the electricity natu- rally Aurora Borealis. turally belonging to the air is in summer much more powerfully drawn off by the clouds than in the winter, owing to the excess of heat in summer, as already observed. A considerable difficulty, however, still remains from the upright position which the streams of the aurora borealis are generally supposed to have; whereas, according to the hypothesis above mentioned, they ought rather to run directly from north to south. This difficulty occurred to Dr Halley; but he answers it by supposing his magnetic effluvia to pass from one pole to another in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of great circles, arising to a vast height above the earth, and consequently darting from the places whence they arose almost like the radii of a circle; in which case, being sent off in a direction nearly perpendicular to the surface of the earth, they must necessarily appear erect to those who see them from any part of the surface, as is demonstrated by mathematicians. It is also reasonable to think that they will take this direction rather than any other, on account of their meeting with less resistance in the very high regions of the air than in such as are lower. But the greatest difficulty still remains: for we have supposed the equilibrium of the atmosphere to be broken in the daytime, and restored only in the night; whereas, considering the immense velocity with which the electric fluid moves, the equilibrium ought to be restored in all parts almost instantaneously; yet the aurora borealis never appears except in the night, although its brightness is such as must sometimes make it visible to us did it really exist in the daytime. In answer to this it must be observed, that though the passage of electricity through a good conductor is instantaneous, yet through a bad conductor it is observed to take some time in passing. As our atmosphere therefore, though very violently heated, is but a bad conductor of electricity; though the equilibrium in it is broken, it can by no means be instantaneously restored. Add to this, that as it is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the sun which breaks the equilibrium, so the same action, extending over half the globe, prevents almost any attempt to restore it till night, when flashes arise from various parts of the atmosphere, gradually extending themselves with a variety of undulations towards the equator. It now remains to explain only one particularity of the aurora borealis, namely, that its streams do not always move with rapidity; sometimes appearing quite <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a> for a considerable time, and sometimes being carried in different directions with a slow motion. To this indeed we can give no other reply, than that weak electric lights have been sometimes observed to put on the same appearance at the surface of the earth; and much more may we suppose them capable of doing so at great heights above it, where the conductors are both fewer in number and much more imperfect. When M. de Romas was making experiments with an electric kite in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> of blue light about four or five inches diameter was observed surrounding the string. This was in the daytime; but had it been night, he imagined it must have been four or five feet in diameter; and as the string was 780 feet long, it would probably have seemed pyramidal, pointing upwards like one of the streams of the aurora borealis. A still more remarkable appearance, Dr Priestley tells us, was observed by Mr Hartman. He had been making electrical experiments for four or five hours together in a very small room; and upon going out of it, and returning with a light in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, walking pretty quick, he perceived a small flame following him at about three feet distance. Being alarmed at this appearance, he stopped to examine it, upon which it vanished. This last instance is very remarkable, and singular in its kind: from both, however, we are sufficiently warranted to conclude, that final portions of our atmosphere may by various causes be so much electrified as to shine, and likewise be moved from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another without parting with the electricity they have received, for a considerable time. The corona, or circle, which is often formed near the zenith by the aurora borealis, is easily accounted for in the same manner. As this corona is commonly stationary for some time, we imagine it would be a very proper mark whereby to determine the distance of the meteor itself. If an aurora borealis, for instance, was observed by two persons, one at London, and the other at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>; by noting the stars among which the corona was observed at each place, its true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> from the surface of the earth could easily be determined by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">trigonometry</a>. Under the article Atmosphere it was suggested, that no good proof had been as yet brought for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> rarity of the air usually supposed to take place at no very great heights above the earth. The brightness of the meteor there mentioned at 70 miles perpendicular from the surface, as also its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, seemed to prove the air considerably denser at that distance from the earth. Though the height of the aurora borealis has never been determined, we can scarce imagine it to be greater than that of this meteor, or indeed so great; but although its streams resemble the passage of electric light through a vacuum, it cannot be from thence inferred, that the air is at all in a state similar to the vacuum of an air-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> in those places where the aurora borealis is produced; seeing we have instances of similar appearances being produced in very dense air. The plate of an electrophorus is often so highly electrified, as to throw out flashes from different parts as soon as it is lifted up, and by proper management it may be always made to emit long and broad flashes which shall scarcely be felt by the finger, instead of small, dense, and pungent sparks; so that, though long flashes may be produced in rarefied air, it by no means follows, that the same may not also be produced in denser air. As little can we infer anything from the colours; for we observe the electric spark sometimes white, sometimes blue, and sometimes purple, in the very same state of the atmosphere, and from the same substance. The aurora borealis is said to be attended with a peculiar hissing noise in some very cold climates; Gmelin speaks of it in the most pointed terms, as frequent and very loud in the north-eastern parts of Siberia; and other travellers have related similar facts. Gmelin's account is very remarkable. "These northern lights (says he) begin with single bright pillars, rising in the north, and almost at the same time in the north-east, which gradually increasing, comprehend a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> space of the heavens, rush about from place to place with incredible velocity, and finally almost cover the whole sky." sky up to the zenith. The streams are then seen meeting together in the zenith, and produce an appearance as if a vast extent was expanded in the heavens, glittering with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, rubies, and sapphire. A more beautiful spectacle cannot be painted; but whoever should see such a northern light for the first time, could not behold it without terror. For however fine the illumination may be, it is attended, as I have learned from the relation of many persons, with such a hissing, cracking, and rushing noise throughout the air, as if the largest fireworks were playing off. To describe what they then hear, they make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, Spolachi ebodjat, that is, 'the raging <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLT">holt</a> is puffing.' The hunters who pursue the white and blue foxes on the confines of the icy sea, are often overtaken in their course by these northern lights. Their dogs are then so much frightened, that they will not move, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> obstinately on the ground till the noise has passed. Commonly clear and calm weather follows this kind of northern lights. I have heard this account, not from one person only, but confirmed by the uniform testimony of many, who have spent part of several years in these very northern regions, and inhabited different countries from the Yenesei to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENA">Lena</a>; so that no doubt of its truth can remain. This seems indeed to be the real birthplace of the aurora borealis." The hissing or rushing noise above described, Dr Blagden is inclined to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to small streams of electric matter running off to the earth from the mists or accumulations of electricity by which the northern lights are supposed to be produced. We shall conclude this article with an account of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> presented to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> by Mr Winn, in 1772, wherein he says that the appearance of an aurora borealis is a certain sign of a hard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALE">gale</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> from the south-west. This he never found to fail in 23 instances; and even thinks, that from the splendour of the meteor, some judgment may be formed concerning the ensuing tempest. If the aurora is very bright, the gale will come on within twenty-four hours, but will be of no long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>; if the light is faint and dull, the gale will be less violent, and longer in coming on, but it will also last longer. His observations were made in the English channel, where such winds are very dangerous; and by attending to the aurora, he says he often got easily out of it, when others narrowly escaped being wrecked. This is an exceedingly useful observation for sailors: but it cannot be expected that the winds succeeding these meteors should in all places blow from the south-west; though no doubt a careful observation of what winds succeed the aurora borealis, and other meteors, in different parts of the world, might contribute in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to lessen the dangers of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. That the aurora borealis ought to be succeeded by winds, may be easily deduced from the hypothesis last mentioned. If this phenomenon is occasioned by the vast quantity of electric matter conveyed to the equatorial parts of the earth, it is certain that the earth cannot receive any great quantity of this matter at one place without emitting it at another. The electricity, therefore, which is constantly received at the equator, must be emitted nearer the poles, in order to perform its course, otherwise there could not be a constant supply of it for the common operations of nature. It is observed, that electrified bodies are always surrounded by a blast of air, which is sent forth from them in all directions; hence, if the electric matter find a more ready passage through one part of the earth than another, a wind will be found to blow from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. If therefore one of these places happens to be in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a> near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of France, or in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>, the electric matter which has been received at the equator during an aurora borealis will be discharged there some time after, and consequently a wind will blow from that quarter, which will be from the south-west to those ships which are in the English channel. It cannot be imagined, however, that all the matter can be discharged from one place; and therefore according to the different situations of these electrical vents, winds may blow in different directions; and thus the same aurora borealis may produce a south-west wind in the English channel, and a north-west one in Scotland. AURUM. See GOLD, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">CHEMISTRY</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. This metal was introduced into medicine by the Arabians, who esteemed it one of the greatest cordials and comforters of the nerves. From them Europe received it without any diminution of its character; in foreign pharmacopoeias it is still retained, and even mixed with the ingredients from which simple waters are to be distilled. But no one, it is presumed, at this time expects any singular virtues from it, since it certainly is not alterable in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body. Mr Geoffroy, though unwilling to reject it from the cordial preparations, honestly acknowledges that he has no other reason for retaining it than complaisance to the Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. The chemists have endeavoured, by many elaborate processes, to extract what they call a sulphur or anima of gold: but no method is as yet known of separating the component parts of this metal; all the tinctures of it, and aurum petteabile, which have hitherto appeared, are real solutions of it in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> regia, diluted with spirit of wine or other liquors, and prove injurious to the body rather than beneficial. A place, however, is now given in some of the foreign pharmacopoeias to the aurum fulminans; and it has of late been recommended as a remedy in some convulsive diseases, particularly in the chorea famili viti. AURUM Fulminans. See CHEMISTRY Index. AURUM Mofacium. See CHEMISTRY Index.

AURUNCI

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a people of Latium, towards Campania; the name with the Aufones, at least so intermixed as not to be easily distinguishable, though Pliny separates them.

AUSI

Pages 335-338

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and very <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> tells us that they were unacquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, and had all their women in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. The children were brought up by their mothers till they were able to walk: after which they were introduced to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the men, who met every three months; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to whom any child first spoke, acknowledged himself its father. They celebrated annually a feast in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, in which the girls divided into two companies, fought with sticks... and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and those who died of their wounds were concluded not to have been virgins. **Ausimum**, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> **Aximum**, an ancient Roman colony in the Picenum; now Qfino or Qfino, in the marquisate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15° N. Lat. 43° 20'. **Ausitae**, or **Aesitae**, a tribe of ancient Arabs, supposed by Bochart to have inhabited the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Uz mentioned in Scripture. **Ausona**, in *Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, a town of the Ausones, a people who anciently occupied all the Lower Italy, from the Promontorium Circeum <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> (Livy), but were afterwards reduced to a much narrower compass; namely, between the Montes Circei and Massici: nor did they occupy the whole of this, but other people were intermixed. Concerning Ausona or its remains there is nothing particular recorded. **Ausonia**, the ancient name of Italy, from its most ancient inhabitants the Ausones (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Servius). **Ausoneum Mare**, in *Ancient Geography*, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Ionian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, extending southwards from the promontory Japygium to Sicily, which it washes on the east, as it does the Bruttii and Magna Graecia on the south and east. It is separated from the Tuscan sea by the strait of Messina. **Ausonius** (in Latin, Decius, or rather Decimus, Magnus Ausonius), one of the best poets of the fourth century, was the son of an eminent physician, and born at Bordeaux. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> care was taken of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, the whole family interesting themselves in it, either because his genius was very promising, or that the scheme of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>, which had been <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> by his grandfather on the mother's side, made them imagine that he would rise to great honour. He made an uncommon progress in classical learning, and at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 30 was chosen to teach <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> at Bordeaux. He was promoted some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after to be professor of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>; in which office he acquired great reputation, that he was sent for to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to be preceptor to Gratian the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">Valentinian</a>'s son. The rewards and honours conferred on him for the faithful discharge of his office prove the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of Juvenal's maxim, that when Fortune pleases, she can raise a man from a rhetorician to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>. He was actually appointed consul by the emperor Gratian, in the year 379, after having filled other considerable posts; for besides the dignity of quaestor, to which he had been nominated by Valentinian, he was made prefect of the praetorium in Italy and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> after that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. His speech returning thanks to Gratian on his promotion to the consulship is highly commended. The time of his death is uncertain; he was still living in 392, and lived to a great age. The emperor Theodosius had a great esteem for Ausonius, and praised him to publish his poems. There is a great inequality in his works; and in his manner and his style there is a harshness which was perhaps rather the defect of the times he lived in than of his genius. Had he lived in Augustus's reign, his verses, according to good judges, would have equalled the most finished of that age. He is generally supposed to have been a Christian; some ingenious authors indeed think otherwise, but, according to Mr Bayle, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> reason. The best edition of his poems is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1671. **Auspeix**, a name originally given to those who were afterwards denominated augurs. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the word is supposed to be formed from avus, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>," and inspiciere, "to inspect"; auspices, q. d. avispices. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> therefore have auspices properly to denote those who foretell future events from the flight of birds. **Auspiciun**, **Auspicy**, the same with augury. **Auster**, one of the four <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> winds, as Servius calls them, blowing from the south, (Pliny, Ovid, Manilius.) **Austere**, rough, stringent. Thus an austere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is such as one as constringes the mouth and tongue; as that of unripe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, harsh wines, &c. **Austerity**, among moral writers, implies severity and rigour. Thus we say, austerity of manners, austerities of the monastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, &c. **Austin, Sr.** See St. Augustine. **Austral**, **Australis**, the same with southern. The word is derived from auster, "south <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>." Thus austral signs are the six last signs of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>; so called because they are on the south side of the equinoctial. **Australis Piscis**, the Southern Fish, is a constellation of the southern hemisphere, not visible in our latitude; whose stars in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue are 18, and in the Britannic catalogue 24. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>**, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> provinces of the empire of Germany towards the east; from which situation it takes its name Oost-rych, in the German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signifying the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">Country</a>. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAVIA">Moravia</a>; on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>; on the south by Stiria; and on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>. It is divided into Upper and Lower. Upper Austria is situated on the south, and Lower Austria on the north side of the Danube. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is in Upper Austria, which contains several other very considerable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. The country is very fertile, has a great many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, and produces vast quantities of sulphur. In the ninth and tenth centuries, Austria was the frontier of the empire against the barbarians. In 928, the emperor Henry the Fowler, perceiving that it was of great importance to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> some person in Austria who might oppose these incursions, invested Leopold, named the illustrious, with that country. Otho I. erected Austria into a marquisate in favour of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> Leopold, whose descendant Henry II. was created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Austria by the emperor Frederic Barbarossa. His posterity becoming extinct in 1240, the states of the country, in order to defend themselves from the incursions of the Bavarians and Hungarians, resolved to put themselves under the protection of Henry marquis of Münster, but Othochar II., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, being likewise invited by a party in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>, took possession of it, alleging not only the invitation of the states, but also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of his wife, heiress of Frederic the last duke. The emperor Rodolphus I., pretending a right to this duchy, refused to give Othochar the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a> of it; and afterwards killing him in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, procured the right of it to his own family. From this Rodolphus the present <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Austria is descended, which for several centuries past has rendered itself so famous and so powerful, having given 14 emperors to Germany, and five kings to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. In 1477, Austria was erected into an archduchy by the emperor Frederic the Pacific for his son Maximilian, with these privileges: That these shall be judged to have obtained the investiture of the states, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they do not receive it after having demanded it three times; that if they receive it from the emperor, or the imperial ambassadors, they are to be on horseback, clad in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> mantle, having in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> of command, and upon their head a ducal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, and surrounded with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> like that of the imperial crown. The archduke is born privy-counsellor to the emperor, and his states cannot be put to the ban of the empire. All attempts against his person are punished as crimes of lese-majesty, in the same manner as those against the king of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, or electors. No one dared to challenge him to single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>. It is in his choice to assist at the assemblies, or to be absent; and he has the privilege of being exempt from contributions and public taxes, excepting 12 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> which he is obliged to maintain against the Turks for one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. He has <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> immediately after the electors; and exercises <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in his states without <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>, by virtue of a privilege granted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. His subjects cannot even be summoned out of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> upon account of law-suits, to give witness, or to receive the investiture of fiefs. Any of the lands of the empire may be alienated in his favour, even those that are feudal; and he has a right to create counts, barons, gentlemen, poets, and notaries. In the succession to his states, the right of birth takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and, failing males, the females succeed according to the lineal right, and, if no heir be found, they may dispose of their lands as they please. Upper Austria, properly so called, has throughout the appearance of a happy country. Here are no signs of the striking <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> betwixt poverty and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> which offends so much in Hungary. All the inhabitants, those of the capital only excepted, enjoy that happy mediocrity which is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a gentle and wise administration. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> has <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, who enjoy a kind of lower judicial power, are well defined. The south and south-west parts of the country are bounded by a ridge of hills, the inhabitants of which enjoy a share of prosperity unknown to those of the interior parts of France. There are many villages and market towns, the inhabitants of which have bought themselves off from vassalage, are now their own governors, and belong some of them to the estates of the country. The cloisters, the prelates of which belong to the estates of the country, are the richest in Germany, after the immediate prelacies and abbeys of the empire. One of the greatest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a> is worth upwards of 4000 millions of French livres, half of which goes to the exchequer of the country. Lower Austria yearly exports more than two millions guilders worth of wine to Moravia, Bohemia, Upper Austria, Bavaria, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALZBURG">Salzburg</a>, and part of Styria and Carinthia. This wine is fine, but has a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of strength, and may be carried all over the world without danger; when it is ten or twenty years old it is very good. This country is very well peopled. Mr Schloesser, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">Political</a> Journal, which contains an account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Austria, estimates that of this country at 2,100,000 men. The revenue amounts to about 14,000,000 florins, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Vienna contributes above five, as one man in the capital earns as much as three in the country. The southern parts of Austria are covered with hills, which rise gradually from the banks of the Danube to the borders of Styria, and are covered with woods. They lose themselves in the mists of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which run to the south of Germany, and stretch through all Styria, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARNIOLA">Carniola</a>, Carinthia, and Tyrol, to the Swiss <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>; and probably, after Savoy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, the highest part of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The inhabitants of this extensive ridge of mountains are all very much alike; they are a strong, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and, the Goitres excepted, a very handsome people. The characteristic of the inhabitants of all this country is striking bigotry, united with striking sensuality. You need only see what is going forwards here to be convinced that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> taught by the monks is as ruinous to the morals as it is repugnant to Christianity. The Cicibos accompany the married women from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them to the very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFESSIONAL">confessional</a>. The bigotry of the public in the interior parts of Austria, which from the mixture of gallantry with it, is still to be found even amongst people of rank, degenerates amongst the common people into the grossest and most abominable buffoonery. The Windes, who are mixed with the Germans in these countries, distinguish themselves by a superstitious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> that does little honour to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> understanding, and would be incredible if we had not the most unequivocal proofs of the fact before our eyes. Many years ago, they set out in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with some Hungarian enthusiasts to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, which is about 120 German miles distant, to cut off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRUCIFIX">crucifix</a> there. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years this operation is repeated, as in this space of time the beard grows again to its former length. The rich persons of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> send the poorer ones as their deputies, and the magistrates of Cologne receive them as ambassadors from a foreign prince. They are entertained at the expense of the state, and a counsellor shows them the most remarkable things in the town. This <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a> brings in large sums of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> at stated times, and may therefore deserve political encouragement; but still, however, it is the most miserable and meanest way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> that can be imagined. These Windes have alone the right to shave our Saviour, and the beard grows only for them. They firmly believe, that if they did not do this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the crucifix the earth would be shut to them for the next seven years, and there would be no harvests. For this reason they are obliged to carry the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> home with them, as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of having fulfilled their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, the returns of which are distributed among the different communities, and preserved as holy relics. The imperial court has for a long time endeavoured in vain to prevent this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMIGRATION">emigration</a>, which deprives <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> of so many useful <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. When the Windes could not go openly, they would go clandestinely. At length the court thought of the expedient of forbidding the regency of Cologne to let them enter the town. This happened six years ago, and the numerous embassy was obliged to beg its way back again without the wonderful beard; which without doubt the Capuchins, to whom the crucifix belonged, used to put together from their own. The trade which the monks carry on with holy salves, oils, &c. is still very considerable; a prohibition of the court, lately published, has rather lessened it, but it cannot be entirely suppressed till next <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. It is now carried on secretly, but perhaps to nearly as great an amount as formerly.

AUSTROMANCY

Pages 338-338

AUSTROMANTIA, properly denotes foothsaying, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a vain method of predicting futurity, from observations of the winds. AUTERFOITS ACQUIT. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">PLEA</a> to AUTERFOITS Attain. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">Indictment</a>.

AUTHENTIC

Pages 338-338

something of acknowledged and received authority. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, it signifies something clothed in all its formalities, and attested by persons to whom <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> has been regularly given. Thus we say, authentic papers, authentic instruments.

AUTHOR

Pages 338-338

in matters of literature, a person who has composed some book <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>.

AUTHORITY

Pages 338-338

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to command, and make one's self obeyed. In which sense we say, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> authority, the episcopal authority, the authority of a father, &c. It denotes also the testimony of an author, some apophthegm <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of an eminent person quoted in a discourse by way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. Authority is represented, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> matron sitting in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of state, richly clothed in a garment embroidered with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, holding in her right <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and in her left a sceptre. By her side is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> trophy of books and arms.

AUTOCHTHONES

Pages 338-338

an appellation assumed by some nations, importing that they sprung, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> were produced, from the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> which they still inhabited. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, Autochthonous amounts to the same with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABORIGINES">Aborigines</a>. The Athenians valued themselves on their being Autochthonous, self-born, or γεννημένοι, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>-born; it being the prevailing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, that, in the beginning, the earth, by some prolific power, produced men, as it still does <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The proper Autochthonous were those primitive men who had no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> beside the earth. But the name was also assumed by the descendants of these men, provided they never changed their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> state, nor suffered other nations to mix with them. In this sense it was that the Greeks, and especially the Athenians, pretended to be Autochthonous; and as a badge thereof, wore a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> grasshopper woven in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, an insect supposed to have the same origin.

AUTOCRATOR

Pages 338-338

a person vested with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> independent power, by which he is rendered unaccountable to any other for his actions. The power of the Athenian generals, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> commanders, was usually limited; so that, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of their office, they were liable to render an account of their administration. But, on some extraordinary occasions, they were exempted from this restraint, and went with a full and uncontrollable authority: in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> they were styled Aslangolotes. The same people also applied the name to some of their ambassadors, who were vested with a full power of determining matters according to their own <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. These were denominated Ἱεροβυτλοί, Aslangolotes, and resembled our plenipotentiaries.

AUTODIDACTUS

Pages 338-338

a person self-taught, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> who has had no <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> or assistant of his studies besides himself.

AUTOGRAPH

Pages 338-338

denotes a person's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the original manuscript of any book, &c.

AUTOLITHOTOMUS

Pages 338-338

he who cuts himself for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. Of this we have a very extraordinary instance given by Reifelius, in the Ephemerides of the Academia Naturae Curiosorum, dec. i. ann. 3. obs. 192.

AUTOMATE

Pages 338-338

called also Hiero, one of the Cyclades, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> (Pliny), said to have emerged out of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> Thera and Thera, in the fifth year of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> 30 stadia, (Orofius).

AUTOMATION

Pages 338-339

(from autos itself, and μακεῖν εἰς) a self-moving machine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> one so constructed, by means of weights, levers, pulleys, &c. as to move for a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, as though endowed with animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. According to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, clocks, watches, and all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> of that kind, are automata. Under the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDROIDES">ANDROIDES</a> we observed that the highest perfection to which automata could be carried was to imitate exactly the motions and actions of living creatures, especially of mankind, which are more difficultly imitated than those of other animals. Very surprising imitations, however, have been made of other creatures. So <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago as 400 years before Christ, Archytas of Tarentum is said to have made a wooden pigeon that could fly; nor <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> this appear at all incredible, when we consider the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>-player made by M. Vaucanson, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESS">chess</a>-player by M. Kempell. Dr Hook is also said to have made the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> chariot, capable of supporting itself in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. But M. Vaucanson above-mentioned hath distinguished himself still more eminently. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, encouraged by the favourable reception of his flute-player, made a duck, which was capable of eating, drinking, and imitating exactly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> one. Nay, what is still more surprising, the food it swallowed was evacuated in a digested state; not that it was really in a state of natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCREMENT">excrement</a>, but only considerably altered from what it was when swallowed; and this digestion was performed on the principles of solution, not of trituration. The wings, viscera, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, of this <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> duck, were also formed so as very strongly to resemble those of a living animal. Even in the actions of eating and drinking, this resemblance was preserved; the artificial duck swallowed with avidity and vastly quick motions of the head and throat; and likewise muddled the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> with its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, exactly like a natural one. M. le Droz of La Chaux de Fonds in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Neufchatel, hath also executed some very curious pieces of mechanism, which well deserve to be ranked with those already mentioned. One was a clock, which was presented to his Spanish majesty; and had among other curiosities, a sheep, which imitated the bleating of a natural one; and a dog watching a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of fruit. When any one attempted to purloin the fruit, the dog gnashed Autonomia gnashed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> and barked; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was actually taken away he never ceased <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARKING">barking</a> till it was refored. Besides this, he made a variety of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> figures, which exhibited motions truly surprising; but all inferior to Mr Kempell's chefs-player, which may justly be looked upon as the greatest masterpiece in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> that ever appeared. See ANDROIDES.

AUTONOMIA

Pages 339-339

a power of living <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> being governed by our own laws and magistrates. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the cities which lived under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and protection of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, confided in their autonomia, i.e., they were allowed to make their own laws, and elect their own magistrates; by whom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> was to be administered, and not by Roman presidents or judges, as was done in other places which were not indulged the autonomia.

AUTOPYROS

Pages 339-339

from ἀυτός, and ὑπό, under; in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> diet, an epithet given to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, wherein the whole substance of the wheat was retained without retrenching any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the bran. Galen describes it otherwise, viz., as bread where only the coarser bran was taken out.—And thus it was a medium between the finest bread, called similisimum, and the coarsest called furfuraceus. This was also called autopyrites and syncomiflus. AUTRE-ÉGLISE, a village of Brabant, in the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>; to which the left wing of the French <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> extended, when the confederates obtained the victory at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAMILLIES">Ramillies</a>, in 1706. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 50'. N. Lat. 50° 40'.

AUTRICUM

Pages 339-339

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Carnutes, a people of Gallia Celtica; afterwards called Carnotena, Carnotenae, and Civitas Carnotenum; now Chartres, in the Orléanais on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EURE">Eure</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 32'. N. Lat. 48° 47'.

AUTUMN

Pages 339-339

the third season of the year, when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> are gathered in. Autumn is represented in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> at perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, clothed like the vernal, and likewise girded with a starry girdle; holding in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of scales equally poised, with a globe in each; in the other hand a bunch of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> fruits and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>. His age denotes the perfection of this season; and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>, that sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a> which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> enters when our autumn begins. Autumn begins on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> when the sun's meridian distance from the zenith, being on the decrease, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> between the greatest and the least; which in these countries is supposed to happen when the sun enters Libra. Its end coincides with the beginning of winter. Several nations have computed the years by autumns; the English Saxons, by winters. Tacitus tells us, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Germans were acquainted with all the other seasons of the year, but had no notion of autumn. Lidya observes of the beginning of the several seasons of the year, that Dat Clemens hyemen, dat Petrus ver catbedratus, Afluat Urbanus, autumnat Bartholomeus. Autumn has always been reputed an unhealthy season, Tertullian calls it tentator valeudinum; and the satyrift speaks of it in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. Autumnus Libitineque flos acerbe.

AUTUMNAL POINT

Pages 339-339

is that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the equinox from which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> begins to descend towards the south pole.

AUTUMNAL SIGNS

Pages 339-339

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, are the signs Li, Autumnal bra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, through which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> passes during the autumn.

AUTUN

Pages 339-339

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, in the department of Saone and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Autunais, with a bishop's see. The length of this city is about three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a>, and its breadth nearly equal. The river Arroux washes its ancient walls, whose ruins are so firm, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> so closely united, that they seem almost to be cut out of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rock. In this city are the ruins of three ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, one of which was dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a>, and another to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>. Here are likewise a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>, which last is probably a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>; it stands in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called the field of urns, because several urns had been found there. Here are also two antiques gates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. The city lies at the foot of three great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 15'. N. Lat. 45° 50'.

AUTURA

Pages 339-339
or Audura, a river of Gallia Celtica, only mentioned in the Lives of the Saints. Now the Eure, which falls into the Seine, on the left-hand or south side.

AUVERGNE

Pages 339-339

a late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, about 100 miles in length and 75 in breadth. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Bourbonnois; on the east by Torez and Velay; on the west, by Limosin, Quercy, and La Marche; and on the south, by Auvergne and the Cevennes. It is divided into upper and lower; the latter, otherwise called Limagne, is one of the finest countries in the world. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Higher Auvergne render it less fruitful; but they afford good pasture, which feeds <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of cattle, which are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Auvergne supplies Lyons and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> with fat cattle, makes a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of cheese, and has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of several kinds. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the whole province is Clermont. It is now divided into the departments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANTAL">Cantal</a> and Puy de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">Dome</a>.

AUVERNAS

Pages 339-339

a very deep-coloured heavy wine, made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> raisins so called, which comes from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>. It is not fit to drink before it is above a year old; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> kept two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three years, it becomes excellent.

AUXERRE

Pages 339-339

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of France in the department of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YONNE">Yonne</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Auxerrois, and lately a bishop's see. The episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> was one of the finest in France, and the churches were also very beautiful. This town is advantageously situated for trade with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, on the river Yonne. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 35'. N. Lat. 47° 54'.

AUXESIS

Pages 339-339

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> worshipped by the inhabitants of Egina, and mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> and Pausanias. Auxesis, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> whereby anything is magnified too much.

AUXILIARY VERBS

Pages 339-339

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, are such as help to form <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conjugate others; that is, are prefixed to them, to form or denote the modes or tenses thereof; as, to have and to be, in the English; être and avoir, in the French; ho and sono in the Italian, &c. In the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>,

AVA

Pages 311-311

formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the same name, is situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 96. 30. N. Lat. 21. 0. It is pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>; the houses built with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bamboo canes, with thatched roofs, and floors made of teak plank or split bamboo. The streets are very straight, with rows of trees planted on each side. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is an exact quadrangle, each side of which is 800 paces, and is surrounded with a brick wall; but the palace itself is of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. It has four gates: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> gate, through which all ambassadors enter; the gate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, through which the people bring petitions, accusations, or complaints; the gate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, through which those who have received any favours, or have been acquitted of crimes laid to their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>; and the gate of state, through which his majesty himself passes when he shows himself to the people.

AVA AVA

Pages 311-311

a plant so called by the inhabitants of Otaheite, in the South-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, from the leaves of which they express an intoxicating juice. It is drunk very freely by the chiefs and other considerable persons, who vie with each other in drinking the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of draughts, each draught being about a pint; but it is carefully kept from their women.

AVADOUTAS

Pages 311-311

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> Brahmans, who Avadoutas in austerity surpass all the rest. The other sects retain earthen vessels for holding their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and a stick to lean on; but none of these are used by the Avadoutas; they only cover their nakedness with a piece of cloth; and some of them lay even that aside, and go stark naked, befouling their bodies with cow-dung. When hungry, some go into houses, and, without speaking, hold out their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; eating on the spot whatever is given them. Others retire to the sides of holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and there expect the peasants to bring them provisions, which they generally do very liberally.

AVAIL OF MARRIAGE

Pages 311-311

in Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, that causality in wardholding, by which the superior was entitled to a certain sum from his vassal, upon his attaining the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of puberty, as the value <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> avail of his tocher. avalanches, a name given to prodigious snow-balls that frequently roll <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in Savoy, particularly Mount Blanc, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> danger of such adventurous travellers as attempt to ascend those stupendous heights. Some of the avalanches are about 200 feet diameter; being fragments of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>-rocks which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> by their own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> from the tops of the precipices. See Mount Blanc.

AVALON

Pages 311-311

a small but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a> in France, about 500 paces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 300 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. E. Long. 3. 5. N. Lat. 47. 38.

AVANIA

Pages 311-311

in the Turkish legislature, a fine for crimes and on deaths, paid to the governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. In the places wherein several nations live together under a Turkish governor, he takes this profitable method of punishing all crimes among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Jews, unless it be the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of a Turk.

AVARICUM

Pages 311-311

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of the Bituriges in Gallia Celtica, situated on the rivulet Avara, in a very fertile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> (Castrum). Now <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURGES">Bourges</a>, in Berry. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 30. N. Lat. 47. 15.

AVAST

Pages 311-311
