in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> requiring to flop <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to stay.

AVE-MARIA

Pages 316-316

the angel Gabriel's salutation of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, when he brought her the tidings of the incarnation.—It is become a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The chaplets and rosaries are divided into so many ave-marias, and so many pater-nosters, to which the Papists ascribe a wonderful efficacy.

AVEIRO

Pages 315-315

a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, seated near the head of a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> formed by the tide at the mouth of the river Vouga. This river forms a small haven with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, over which vessels may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> that do not draw above eight <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> feet <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The city stands in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> plain well watered, and very fertile. This plain is nine miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, from Porto to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIMBRA">Coimbra</a>; and is bounded on the east by a chain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERRA">Serra</a> d'Alcoba, which reach from the one town to the other. Near this city there is <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> made in sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> to serve two or three provinces. Here is a remarkable nunnery, where none are received but the daughters of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. The inhabitants of Aveiro have the singular privilege, that no stranger whatever can pass a night there without leave of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. W. Long. 9. 8. N. L. 40. 30.

AVELLANE

Pages 315-315

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a crofs, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of which somewhat resemble a filbert-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>. Sylvanus Morgan says, that it is the crofs which ensigns the mound of authority, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the sovereign's globe.

AVELLINO

Pages 315-316

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, with a bishop's see. It was almost ruined by an earthquake in 1694. It is, however, at present a pretty considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, extending a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in length <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the declivity of a hill, with ugly streets, but tolerable houses. The churches have nothing to recommend them, being crowded with monstrous ornaments, in a barbarous style, which the Neapolitans seem to have borrowed from the Spaniards. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, in a wretched situation, with little to attract the eye. The good people here need not run to Naples to see the blood of St Januarius: for they have a statue of St Lawrence, with a phial of his blood, which for eight days in August entertains them with a similar miraculous liquefaction. Their only edifice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> is a public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANARY">granary</a>, of the Composite order, adorned with antique <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and a very elegant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a> one of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, while a boy, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> by Cavalier Cosimo. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants amounts to 8000, some say 10,000. The bishop's revenue is about 6000 ducats (112,1.) a-year. The magistracy consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNDIC">Syndic</a> and four Eletti, all annual; which offices are engrossed by a certain number of families of some distinction, that neither intermarry nor associate with the rest of the burghers. There is a considerable manufacture of cloth here of various qualities and colours, but chiefly blue. Many wealthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> have a concern in this business, some with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of eighty thousand ducats (15,000l.). The poor women who spin the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> must <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> very hard to earn above four grana a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> article of trade is maccaroni and paste of many kinds, which being of an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, are in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> repute all over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Wooden chairs are also made and sold here in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities. Avellino abounds with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> of every sort; each street is supplied with wholesome <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; the wine is but indifferent. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of this district, which consists chiefly of volcanic substances, produces little corn, but fruit in abundance, of which the apple is deservedly held in great esteem. The most profitable, however, of all its fruit-trees is the hazel. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">Nut</a> bushes cover the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the valley, and in good AVE-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">MARIA</a> good years bring in a profit of sixty thousand ducats (11,250l.). The nuts are mostly of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> round <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of filbert, which we call Spanish. These bushes were originally imported into Italy from Pontus, and known among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by the appellation of Nux Pontica, which in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was changed into that of Nux Aveliana, from the place where they had been propagated with the greatest success. The proprietors plant them in rows, and by dressing, form them into large bushes of many items. Every year they refresh the roots with new <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and prune off the straggling shoots with great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>.

AVENACEOUS

Pages 316-316

something belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> partaking of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of oats.

AVENAGE

Pages 316-316

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of oats paid by a tenant to a landlord, instead of rent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some other duties.

AVENCHE

Pages 316-316

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of Bern, formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of all Switzerland, but now shows its former greatness only by its ruins. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 7. N. Lat. 46. 50.

AVENES

Pages 316-316

a small but strong town in French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Hainault, seated on the river Thespis. It contains about 2,000 inhabitants; but the houses are wretchedly built, and the streets <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>. It was fortified by M. Vauban in a strong regular manner. About this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> proper for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and used by sculptors for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>; they are known by the name of Stones of Avenes. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 40. N. Lat. 50. 10.

AVENIO

Pages 316-316

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of the Cavares, and one of the most opulent in Gallia Narbonensis; now <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a>, in Provence. See AVIGNON.

AVENOR

Pages 316-316

an officer belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s stables, who provides oats for the horses. He acts by warrant from the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>.

AVENTINE

Pages 316-316

JOHN, author of the Annals of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, was born of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> parentage, in the year 1466, at Abenberg in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> named. He studied first at Ingolstadt, and afterwards in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. In 1503, he privately taught eloquence and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>; and in 1507 he publicly taught Greek at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. In 1509, he read lectures on some Cicero's works at Ingolstadt: and in 1512, was appointed to be preceptor to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> and Prince Ernest, sons of Albert the Wise, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Bavaria, and travelled with the latter of these two princes. After this he undertook to write the annals of Bavaria; being encouraged by the dukes of that name, who settled a pension upon him, and gave him hopes that they would defray the charges of the book. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which gained its author <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation, was first published in 1554, by Jerome Zieglerus, professor of poetry in the university of Ingolstadt; and afterwards at Basle in 1580, by Nicholas Cipner. An affront which Aventine received in the year 1529, struck by him all the rest of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>: he was forcibly taken out of his Aventine father's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Abenberg, and hurried to jail; the true cause of which violence was never known: but it would probably have been carried to a much greater length, had not the duke of Bavaria interfered, and taken this learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> into his protection. Mr Bayle remarks, that the incurable melancholy which from this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> possessed Aventine, was so far from determining him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a life of celibacy, as he had done till he was 64, that it induced him perhaps to think of marrying. The violence of his new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> was not, however, so great, but that it suffered him to advise with two of his friends, and consult certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> relative to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. The result was, that it was best for him to marry; and having already lost too much time, considering his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he took the first woman he met with, who happened to be his own maid, ill-tempered, ugly, and extremely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. He died in 1534, aged 68; leaving one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, who was then but two months old. He had a son, who died before.

AVENTINUS MONS

Pages 316-316

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hills on which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Rome stood. The origin of the name Aventinus is uncertain: but this hill was also called <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURCIA">Murcia</a>, from Murcia the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of sloth, who had a little chapel there; and Collis Diane, from the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>; likewise Remonius, from Remus, who wanted to build the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and who was buried there. It was taken within the compass of the city by Ancus Martius. To the east it had the city walls; to the south, the Campus Figulinus; to the west, the Tiber; and to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, Mons Palatinus, in circuit two miles and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>.

AVENUE

Pages 316-317

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a walk planted on each side with trees, and leading to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, garden-gate, wood, &c. and generally terminated by some distant object. All avenues that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to a house ought to be at least as wide as the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the house, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> wider they are better still; and avenues to woods and prospects ought not to be less than 60 feet wide. The trees should not be planted nearer to one another than 35 feet, especially if they are trees of a spreading kind; and the same ought to be the distance, if they are for a regular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>. The trees most proper for avenues with us, are the English elm, the lime, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-chestnut, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> chestnut, the beech, and the ash. The English elm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> do in all grounds, except such as are very wet and shallow; and this is preferred to all other trees, because it will bear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>, heading, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lopping in any manner, better than most others. The rough or smooth Dutch elm is approved by some, because of its quick growth. This is a tree which will bear removing very well; it is also green almost as soon as any plant whatever in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and continues so as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as any, and it makes an incomparable hedge, and is preferable to all other trees for lofty espaliers. The lime is valued for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> growth and fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. The horse-chestnut is proper for all places that are not too much exposed to rough winds. The common chestnut will do very well in a good <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>; and rises to a considerable height, when planted somewhat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>; though, when it stands single, it is rather inclined to spread than to grow tall. Avenzoar. The beech is a beautiful tree, and naturally grows well with us in its wild state; but it is less to be chosen for avenues than the before-mentioned, because it does not bear transplanting well, but is very subject to miscarriage. Lastly, the ash is fit for any soil, and is the quickest grower of any forest-tree. It seldom fails in transplanting; and succeeds very well in wet soils, in which the others are apt to fail. The oak is but little used for avenues, because of its slow growth. The old method of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> avenues was with regular rows of trees, and this has been always kept to till of late: but we have now a much more magnificent way of planting avenues; this is by setting the trees in clumps, or plantings, making the opening much wider than before, and placing the clumps of trees at about 300 feet distant from one another. In each of these clumps there should be planted either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> trees; but it is to be observed, that this is only to be practised where the avenue is to be of some considerable length, for in short walks this will not appear so tightly as single rows of trees. The avenues made by clumps are fittest of all for parks. The trees in each clump should be planted about 30 feet asunder; and a trench should be thrown up round the whole clump, to prevent the deer from coming to the trees to bark them.

AVENZOAR

Pages 317-317

ABU MERWAN ABDALMALEC EBN ZOHR, an eminent Arabian physician, flourished about the end of the eleventh <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the beginning of the twelfth century. He was of noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, where he exercised his profession with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation. His grandfather and father were both physicians. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> estate he inherited from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, set him above practicing altogether for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>: he therefore took no fees from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, or from artificers, though he refused not the presents of princes and great men. His liberality was extended even to his enemies; for which reason he used to say, that they hated him not for any fault of his, but rather out of envy. Dr Freind writes, that he lived to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 135; that he began to practise at 49, or (as others say) at 20; and had the advantage of a longer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> than almost any one ever had, for he enjoyed perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> to his last <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. He left a son, known also by the name of Ebn Zohr, who followed his father's profession, was in great favour with Al Manzur <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>, and wrote several treatises of physic. Avenzoar was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AVICENNA">Avicenna</a>, who, according to Leo Africanus, heard the lectures of the former, and learned physic of him; this seems the more probable, because Avicenna more than once gives Avenzoar a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and deserved eulogium, calling him admirable, glorious, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of all knowledge, and the most supreme in physic from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Galen to his own. Avenzoar, notwithstanding, is by the generality of writers reckoned an empiric: But Dr Freind observes, that this character suits him less than any of the rest of the Arabians. "He was bred," continues that author, "in a physical family, his father and grandfather being both practitioners, whom he always remembers with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. We have his own testimony that he had a regular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; and that he not only learned what properly belongs to a physician, but, out of a great desire of knowledge, everything besides which relates to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>." Dr Freind afterwards observes, "that he was adverse to quackery, and rejects the idle superstitions of astrologers; and throughout all his works professes himself so much of the dogmatical or rational <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, which was directly opposite to the empirical, that he has a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of reasoning about the causes and symptoms of distempers; and as in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> he chiefly, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not only, follows Galen, so he quotes him upon all occasions, oftener than the rest of the Arabians do. Notwithstanding he is so Galenic, there are several particulars in him which seldom or never occur in other authors; and there are some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> which he relates from his own experience, which are worth perusing." He wrote a book entitled, Tayaffur fi'malawat walradibir, i.e., "The method of preparing medicines and diet;" which is much esteemed. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was translated into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, in the year of Christ 1280, and thence into Latin by Paracelsus, whose version has had several editions. The author added a supplement to it, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Jami', or a Collection. He also wrote a treatise Fi'ladwiyat wa'taughbdiyat, i.e., "Of Medicines and Food;" wherein he treats of their qualities.

AVERAGE

Pages 317-317

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, signifies the accidents and misfortunes which happen to ships and their cargoes, from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their loading and sailing to their return and unloading; and is divided into three kinds. 1. The simple <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> particular average, which consists in the extraordinary expenses incurred for the ship alone, or for the merchandise alone. Such is the loss of anchors, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, and rigging, occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> accidents at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; the damages which happen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> by storm, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>, shipwreck, wet, or rotting; all which must be borne and paid by the thing which suffered the damage. 2. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and common average, being those expenses incurred, and damages sustained, for the common good and security both of the merchandises and vessels, consequently to be borne by the ship and cargo, and to be regulated upon the whole. Of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> are the goods or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> given for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> of the ship and cargo, things thrown overboard for the safety of the ship, the expenses for unloading for entering into a river or harbour, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and hire of the sailors when the ship is put under an embargo. 3. The small averages, which are the expenses for towing and piloting the ship out of or into harbours, creeks, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, one third of which must be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> to the ship, and two thirds to the cargo. Average is more particularly used for a certain contribution that merchants make proportionally to their losses, who have had their goods <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into the sea in the time of a tempest. It also signifies a small duty which those merchants, who send goods in another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s ship, pay to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> for his care of them over and above the freight. Hence it is expressed in the bills of lading, paying so much freight for the said goods, with primeage and average accustomed. AVERDUPOIS. See AVORDUPOIS.

AVERNUS

Pages 317-318

a lake of Campania in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, near Baiae, famous among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> for its poisonous qualities. It is described by Strabo as lying within the Lucrine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, deep and darksome, surrounded with steep banks that hang threatening over it, and only accessible Ave accessible by the narrow passage through which you <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> aged groves stretched their boughs over the watery <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a>, and with impenetrable foliage excluded almost every ray of wholesome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; mephitic vapours ascending from the hot bowels of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, being denied free pallage to the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, floated along the surface in poisonous mists. These circumstances produced horrors fit for such gloomy deities; a colony of Cimmerians, as well suited to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> as the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> itself, cut dwellings in the bosom of the surrounding hills, and officiated as priests of Tartarus. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">Superstition</a> always delighting in dark <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, early and eagerly feasted upon this spot, and hither she led her trembling votaries to celebrate her dismal orgies; here she evoked the manes of departed heroes—here she offered sacrifices to the gods of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, and attempted to dive into the secrets of futurity. Poets enlarged upon the popular theme, and painted its awful scenery with the strongest colours of their art. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> brings Ulysses to Avernus, as to the mouth of the infernal abodes; and in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Grecian bard, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> conducts his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> to the same ground. Whoever failed thither, first did sacrifice; and endeavoured to propitiate the infernal powers, with the assistance of some priests who attended upon the place, and directed the mystic performance. Within, a fountain of pure <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> broke out <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which was fancied to be a vein of the river Styx; near this fountain was the oracle; and the hot waters frequent in those parts were supposed to be branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> Phlegthon. The poisonous effluvia from this lake were said to be so strong, that they proved fatal to birds endeavouring to fly over it. Virgil ascribes the exhalation not to the lake itself, but to the cavern near it, which was called Avernus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cave of the Sibyl, and through which the poets feigned a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> to hell. Hence the proper name of the lake is Lacus Averni, the "lake near the cavern," as it is called by some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> of these shades remained unimpaired for many ages: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> marched his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> to offer incense at this altar; but it may be suspected he was led to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> rather by the hopes of surprising the garrison of Puteoli, than by his piety. After a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> reign of undisturbed gloom and celebrity, a sudden glare of light was let in upon Avernus; the horrors were dispelled, and with them vanished the sanctity of the lake: the axe of Agrippa brought its forest to the ground, disturbed its sleepy waters with ships, and gave room for all its malignant effluvia to escape. The virulence of these exhalations, as described by ancient authors, has appeared so very extraordinary, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writers, who know the place in a cleared state only, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> these accounts with exaggeration; but Mr Swinburn thinks them entitled to more respect; for even now, he observes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is feverish and dangerous, as the jaundiced faces of the vine-dreflers, who have succeeded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIBYLS">Sibyls</a> and the Cimmerians in the possession of the temple, most ruefully testify. Boccaccio relates, that, during his residence at the Neapolitan <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, the surface of this lake was suddenly covered with dead fish, black and fanged, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> killed by some subaqueous eruption of fire. At present the lake abounds with tench; the Lucrine is abundant with eels. The change of fortune in these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> is singular. In the splendid days of imperial Rome the Lucrine was the chosen spot for the brilliant parties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of a voluptuous court; now, a flimsy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of rushes covers the scattered pools of this once beautiful sheet of water; while the once dusky Avernus is clear and serene, offering a most alluring surface and charming <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> for similar amusements. Opposite to the temple is a cave usually styled the Sibyl's grotto; but apparently more likely to have been the mouth of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between Cuma and Avernus, than the abode of a prophetess; especially as the Sibyl is positively said by historians to have dwelt in a cavern under the Cumae citadel. AVERROES. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

AVERROES

Pages 318-318

one of the most sublime philosophers that ever appeared among the Arabs, flourished at the end of the 11th and beginning of the 12th century. He was the son of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> judge of Cordova in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; he was educated in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>; and studied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, medicine, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, he enjoyed his posts; but notwithstanding his being exceeding rich, his liberality to men of letters in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, whether they were his friends <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> his enemies, made him always in debt. He was afterwards stripped of all his posts, and thrown into prison, for hereby; but the oppressions of the judge who succeeded him, caused him to be restored to his former employments. He died at Morocco in the year 1206. He was excessively fat, though he ate but once a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. He spent all his nights in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of philosophy; and when he was fatigued, amused himself with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. He was never seen to play at any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, or to partake in any diversion. He was extremely fond of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s works, and wrote commentaries on them; whence he was styled, the commentator, by way of eminence. He likewise wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on the whole art of physic, and many amorous verses; but when he grew old, he threw these last into the fire. His other poems are lost, except a small piece, in which he says, "That when he was young, he acted against his reason; but that when he was in years, he followed its dictates;" upon which he utters this wish; "Would to God I had been born old, and that in my youth I had been in a state of perfection!" As to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, his opinions were, that Christianity is absurd; Judaism, the religion of children; Mahometanism, the religion of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRVINE">Irvine</a>.

AVERROISTS

Pages 318-319

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of peripatetic philosophers, who appeared in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before the restoration of learning, and attacked the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. They took their denomination from Averroes, the celebrated interpreter of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> (see the preceding article), from whom they borrowed their distinguishing doctrine. The Averroists, who held the soul was mortal, according to reason <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, yet pretended to submit to the Christian <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, which declares it immortal. But this distinction was held suspicious; and this divorce of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> from reason was rejected by the doctors of that time, and condemned by the last <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of the Lateran under Leo X. AVERRUNCI (DEI); certain gods, whose business it was, according to the Pagan theology, to avert misfortunes. fortunes. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> were of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of these gods among the Greeks; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AVERSA">Aversa</a>**, a town of Italy in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, with a bishop's see. It is situated in a very fine plain, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 20', N. Lat. 41°. **Aversion**, according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kames, is opposed to affection, and not to desire, as it <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> is. We have an affection to one person; we have an aversion to another; the former disposes us to do good to its object, the latter to do ill. **Averti**, in Horsemanhip, is applied to a regular step or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> enjoined in the lemons. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> they say pas averte, sometimes pas ecoue, and pas d'ecole, which all denote the same. The word is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> French, and signifies adverted.

AVES

Pages 319-319

one of the Carribbee <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, 451 miles south of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORTO_RICO">Porto Rico</a>, with a good harbour for careening of ships. It is so called from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of birds that frequent it. There is another of the same name lying to the northward of this, in N. Lat. 15° 0'; and a third near the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Newfoundland, in N. Lat. 50° 5'. **Arres, Birds**, the name of Linneus's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> class of animals. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>.

AVESBURY

Pages 319-319

Robert**, an English historian, of whom little more is known than that he was keeper of the regitery of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> in the reign of Edward III. and consequently that he lived in the 14th century. He wrote, *Memoriale seu magnifici regis Angliae domini Eduardi tertii poët conquecum, procerumque; taehis primitius quibusdam gestis de tempore patriæ sui domini Eduardi secundi, qua in regnis Anglie, Scotiae, et Franciae, ac in Aquitania et Britannia, non humana sed Dei <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POTENTIA">potentia</a>, contiguerunt, per Robertum de Aveshury*. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> ends with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Poictiers, about the year 1356. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in manuscript till the year 1720, when it was printed by the industrious Thomas Hearne at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, from a manuscript belonging to Sir Thomas Seabright. It is now become very scarce.

AVEZZANO

Pages 319-326

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> in the Farther Abruzzo. It is built on an almost imperceptible declivity, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the lake of Celano, to which an avenue of poplars leads from the baronial castle. This edifice stands at a little distance from the town, is <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and flanked with towers; it was erected by Virgilio Orsini, to which family this and many other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lordships belonged, before they were wrested from them in times of civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and transferred to the Colonnes. Avezzano was founded in 860, and contains 2700 inhabitants, and two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> communities within its walls, which are indeed in a ruinous condition. The houses are in general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>; but there are some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> buildings and opulent families of the class of gentlemen, not possessed of fees held in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPITE">capite</a>. **Auge**, a territory of Normandy in France, which gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to a vicount. It extends from Falaise and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGENTON">Argenton</a> as far as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Dives, Vie, and Tongues. The arable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is stiff, and produces but little good corn; but they sow <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>; which succeeds so well that they have five good crops successively; they likewise sow flax and hemp; and have a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of apples, with which they make cider. Horses are bred here in great numbers; and Auges, the inhabitants fatten the oxen which come from Poictou and Brittany. **Augias**, in Fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>, and particularly famed for his stable, which contained 3000 oxen, and had not been cleaned for 30 years. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> was desired to clear away the filth from this stable in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and Augias promised, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he performed it, to give him a tenth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the cattle. This task Hercules is said to have executed by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the course of the river Alpheus through the stable; when Augias refusing to stand by his engagement, Hercules flew him with his arrows, and gave his kingdom to Phyleus his son, who had shown an abhorrence of his father's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a>. **Augment**, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, an accident of certain tenses of Greek verbs, being either the prefixing of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an increase of the quantity of the initial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a>. **Augmentation**, in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of adding or joining something to another with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to render it large. **Augmentation** is also used for the addition of anything added. **Augmentation** was also the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> created 27 Hen. VIII. so called from the augmentation of the revenues of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, by the suppression of religious houses; and the office still remains, wherein there are many curious records, though the court has been dissolved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> since. **Augmentation**, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, are additional charges to a coat-armour, frequently given as particular marks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and generally borne either in the escutcheon or a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a>; as have all the baronets of England, who have borne the arms of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. **Augre**, or Awre, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used by carpenters and joiners to bore large round holes; and consisting of a wooden handle, and an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> blade terminated at bottom with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> bit. **Augsburg**, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the circle of Sunbia, seated near the confluence of the Ardesh and Lech, in one of the most beautiful plains that can be imagined. It is one of the largest and handsomest cities of the empire; but the fortifications are after the old manner, and very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>; the streets are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and straight; the houses mostly of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, plastered and whitened without, or adorned with paintings; the rest are of freestone; the churches and fountains are generally ornamented with fine figures of brats. Many of the churches are stately, and adorned within with curious workmanship and paintings. That part of the city erected by the noble family of the Fuggers, who are lords of the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, consists of several streets crosswise, containing 106 houses; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people that inhabit them are maintained by an annual pension. Its magnificent town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is little inferior to that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, it being a vast square <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, with a marble portico; at the top of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, within the pediment, is a large spread eagle, holding a sceptre and globe in its talons, of brats gilt, said to weigh 2200 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; the great portal is of a very beautiful reddish marble, over which is a balcony of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, supported by two pillars of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble; over the gate there are two large griffins of Augsburg: most of the rooms are wainscotted and ceiled with very fine timber; the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> is very magnificent, and paved with marble; it is 110 feet long, 58 broad, and 52 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is supported by eight columns of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> marble; the ceiling of the upper wall is of very curious workmanship of polished ash, consisting of compartments, the squares and panels of which are enriched with gilded sculptures, and filled with pictures and other ornaments; this is likewise supported by eight pillars with bases and chapiters of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>; the other rooms are handsomely adorned with very fine paintings. In the square, near the town-house, is the fountain of Augustus, which is a marble basin, surrounded with iron balustrades finely wrought; at the four corners are four brass <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> as big as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, two of which are women and two men; in the middle of the basin is a pedestal, at the foot of which are four large sphinxes squirting <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> out of their breasts; a little above these are four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> holding four dolphins in their arms, which pour water out of their mouths; and over these infants are festoons and pine-apples all of brass; upon the pedestal is the statue of Augustus as large as the life. The fountain most remarkable next to this is that of Hercules, which is a hexagon basin with several brass figures, particularly Hercules engaging the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRA">hydra</a>. Another curiosity is the secret gate, which was contrived to let in persons safely in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of war; it has so many engines and divisions with gates and keys, and apartments for guards at some distance from each other, where passengers are examined, that it is impossible for the town to be surprized this way; the gates are bolted and unbolted, opened and shut, by unseen operators, inasmuch that it looks like enchantment. The water-towers are also very curious, of which there are three seated on a branch of the river Lech, which runs through the city in such a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a> as to drive many <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of pumps that raise the water in large leaden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> to the tops of the towers; one of these fends water to the public fountains, and the rest to near 1000 houses in the city. The Lutherans have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> here, which is a vast square building, with a fine clock on the top of the front. In this there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> different classes, a hall for public disputations, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> for dramatic representations. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is a large, gloomy, Gothic building, with two spire steeples; it is adorned with paintings upon whimsical subjects, and has a great gate all of brass, over which are several scripture <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> well represented in baso-relief. The Jesuits had a splendid college here, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> full of gilding, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, and carving; and a fine library. Though half the inhabitants are Lutherans, there are a great many Popish processions. There are no Jews in the town, nor are they suffered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> there; but they inhabit a village at about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> distance, and pay so much an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of trading in the daytime. The Benedictine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> is a vast Gothic building, the ceiling of which is said to be the highest in Germany, and overlooks all the rest of the churches; it is adorned with several statues, and has one very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> altar. The church of St Croix is one of the handsomest in Augsburg for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, painting, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, gilding, and a fine spire. The inhabitants look upon Augustus Caesar as the founder of the town: it is true, that that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> sent a colony there; but the town was already founded, though he gave it the name of Augusta Vindelicorum. Augsburg, indeed, is one of the oldest <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in Germany, and one of the most remarkable of them, as it is there and at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> that you meet with the oldest marks of German art and industry. In the 14th and 15th centuries, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of this town was the most extensive of any part of south Germany, and contributed much to the civilization of the country by the works of art and variety of necessaries to the comfort and convenience of life which it was the means of introducing. Many things originated in this town which have had a great influence on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of mankind. Not to mention the many important diets of the empire held here; here, in 952, did a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> confirm the order for the celibacy of priests; here, in 1530, was the confession of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> laid before the emperor and other estates of Germany; and here, in 1555, was signed the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of peace, by which religious liberty was secured to Germany. Though the Protestants were very powerful at Augsburg, they could not keep their ground: for the Bavarians drove them from thence: but Gustavus Adolphus restored them again in 1632; since which time they have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> there, and share the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> with the Catholics. In 1703, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a> took the city after a siege of seven days, and demolished the fortifications: however the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Hochstedt restored their liberty, which they yet enjoy under the government of their own magistrates, the bishop having no temporal dominion in the city. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> is composed of persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, who are to bring proofs of their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. The canons have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of electing their own bishop, who is a sovereign, in the same manner as several of the German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is very good: and though the town has no territory, it has no debts. Augsburg is, however, no longer what it was. It no longer has a Fugger and a Welser in it to lend the emperor millions. In this large and handsome town, formerly one of the greatest trading towns in Germany, there are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> at present to be found who have capitals of more than 20,000l. The others, most of whom must have their coaches, go creeping on with capitals of 300l. or 400l. and do the business of brokers and commissioners. Some houses, however, carry on a little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANKING">banking</a> trade; and the way through Tyrol and Graubunden occasions some little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> between this place and Germany. After these brokers and doers of business by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, the engravers, statuaries, and painters, are the most reputable of the labouring part of the city. Their productions, like the toys of Nuremberg, go everywhere. There are always some people of genius amongst them; but the small demand for their art affords them so little encouragement, that to prevent starving they are mostly confined to the small religious works which are done elsewhere by Capuchin monks. They furnish all Germany with little pictures for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> books, and to hang in the citizens' houses. There is an academy of arts instituted here under the protection of the magistrates: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> aim of which is to produce good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, and preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of the city. This town, which is 9½ miles in circumference, contains, according to Mr. Riebeck, hardly 30,000 inhabitants; but Mr Nicolai makes them about 35,000. This city has its drinking water from the river Lech, which runs at some distance from it; and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a> which convey the water are much to be admired. As the court of Bavaria has it in its power to cut off this indispensable <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, by threatening the town with doing so, it often lays it under contribution. But as it has, besides this, other means of keeping the high council in a state of dependence, to secure itself from this oppression, the city seeks the emperor's protection, upon whom it makes itself as dependent on the other side, so as to be indeed only a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> which both courts play with. The emperor's minister to the circle of Swabia generally resides here, and by so doing secures to his court a perpetual influence. There are always Austrian and Prussian recruiting parties quartered here, and the partiality of the government to the former is very remarkable. In the war of 1756, the citizens were divided into equal parties for the two courts. The Catholics considered the emperor as their god, and the Protestants did the same by the king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> had almost kindled a bloody civil war amongst them.—The bishop takes his name from this town, but resides at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILLINGEN">Dillingen</a>. He has an income of about 20,000l. per annum. As a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the catholicism of this place, the Pope throughout his whole progress met nowhere with such honours as he did here. This he owed to his friends the Jesuits, who have still great influence. E. Long. 10. 58. N. Lat. 48° 24'. Augsburg Confession, denotes a celebrated confession of faith drawn up by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> and Melanchthon, on behalf of themselves and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> reformers, and presented in 1530 to the emperor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. at the diet of Augsburg or Augsburg, in the name of the evangelic body. This confession contains 28 chapters; of which the greatest part is employed in representing, with perspicuity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, the religious opinions of the Protestants, and the rest in pointing out the errors and abuses that occasioned their separation from the church of Rome. Augur, an officer among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> appointed to foretell future events, by the chattering, flight, and feeding of birds. There was a college or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of them, consisting originally of three members with respect to the three tribes, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCERES">Luceres</a>, Ramnenses, and Titites; afterwards the number was increased to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, four of whom were patricians and five plebeians. They bore an augural <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> or wand, as the ensign of their authority; and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> was so much respected, that they were never deposed, or any substituted in their place, though they should be convicted of the most enormous crimes. See Augury. Augural, something relating to the augurs.—The augural instruments are represented on several ancient medals. Augural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a>, that given by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> on his first admission into the order, called also by Varro Adjectalis. Augural Books, those wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> and rules of augury were laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. Augurale, the place in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> where the general took auspicia. This answered to the Augurato, Augurale rium in the city. Augurale is also used in Seneca for the ensign or badge of an augur, as the latus. Auguratorium, a building on the Palatine mount, where public auguries were taken. Augury, in its proper sense, the art of foretelling future events by observations taken from the chattering, singing, feeding, and flight, of birds; though it is used by some writers in a more general signification, as comprising all the different kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>. Augury was a very ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. We know from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>, that husbandry was in part regulated by the coming or going of birds: and most probably it had been in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> long before his time, as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> was then in its infancy. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, these animals seem to have gained a greater and very wonderful authority, till at last no affair of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, either of private or public concern, was undertaken without consulting them. They were looked upon as the interpreters of the gods; and those who were qualified to understand their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> were held among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> men in the Greek and Roman states, and became the advisers of kings, and even of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> himself. However absurd such an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> as a college of augurs may appear in our eyes, yet, like all other extravagant institutions, it had in part its origin from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. When men considered the wonderful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a> of birds, how they disappeared at once, and appeared again at stated times, and could give no guess where they went, it was almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to suppose, that they retired somewhither out of the sphere of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and perhaps approached the ethereal regions, where they might <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with the gods, and thence be enabled to predict events. It was almost natural for a superstitious people to imagine this; at least to believe it, as soon as some impostor was impudent enough to affect it. Add to this, that the disposition in some birds to imitate the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, must contribute much to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of such a doctrine. This institution of augury seems to have been much more ancient than that of auspicy; for we find many instances of the former in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, but not a single one of the latter, though frequent mention is made of sacrifices in that author. From the whole of what has been observed, it seems probable that natural augury gave rise to religious augury, and this to auspicy, as the mind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> makes a very easy transition from a little truth to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>. A passage in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a> gave the hint for these observations. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> of the Birds, he makes one of them say this: 'The greatest blessings which can happen to you, mortals, are derived from us; first we show you the seasons, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, winter, autumn. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRANE">crane</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out the time for sowing, when she flies with her warning notes into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; she bids the sailor hang up his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a> and take his raft, and every prudent man provide himself with winter garments. Next the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KITE">kite</a> appearing, proclaims another season, viz. when it is time to shear his sheep. After that the swallow informs you when it is time to put on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> clothes. We are to you, (adds the chorus), <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DODONA">Dodona</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>: for, after consulting us, you undertake every thing; merchandise, purchases, marriages, August marriages, &c. Now, it seems not improbable, that the same transition was made in the speculations of men which appears in the poet's words; and that they were easily induced to think, that the surprising foresight of birds, as to the time of migration, indicated something of a divine nature in them; which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, as an Epicurean, thinks fit to enter his protest against, when he says, Haud equidem credo, quia sit divinitas illis ingenium. But to return to Aristophanes. The first part of the chorus, from whence the fore-cited passage is taken, seems, with all its wildness, to contain the fabulous cant, which the augurs made use of in order to account for their impudent impositions on mankind. It sets out with a cosmogony; and says, That in the beginning were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">Chaos</a> and Night, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EREBUS">Erebus</a> and Tartarus: That there was neither water, nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, nor sky: That Night laid an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, from whence, after a time, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> arose: That Love, in conjunction with Erebus, produced a third kind; and that they were the first of the immortal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, &c. Augustus, (augustus), in a general sense, something majestic, venerable, or sacred. The appellation was first conferred by the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> upon Octavius, after his being confirmed by them in the sovereign power. It was conceived as expressing something divine, or elevated above the pitch of mankind, being derived from the verb augo, "I increase," tanquam supra humanam formam auctus. See Augustus. August, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of our year, containing 31 days. August was dedicated to the honour of Augustus Caesar, because, in the same month, he was created <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, thrice triumphed in Rome, subdued Egypt to the Roman empire, and made an end of civil wars, being before called Sextilis, or the sixth month from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. Augusta, or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AOSTA">Aosta</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Adriatic sea on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAGUSA">Ragusa</a>, subject to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. E. Long. 17° 50'. N. Lat. 42° 35'. Augusta, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. See Georgia. Augusta Aeglorum, a town of Aquitania, so named out of compliment to Augustus, being originally called Climentum, which name it afterwards retained. In the middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, it took the name of the people, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSI">Ausi</a>; and is now called Auch, the capital of Gascony. Augusta Emerita, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUSITANIA">Lusitania</a> on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANAS">Anas</a>, the capital of the province; a colony of the Emeriti, or such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> as had served out their legal time, were men of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, or had received marks of favour. The colony was founded by Augustus; and is now called Merida, a city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in Extremadura, on the river Guadiana. See Merida. Augusta Praetoria, a town and colony of Gallia Cisalpina, and capital of the Salassi; seated at the foot of the Alpes Graiae, on the Duria. Now Aoste in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>. See Aoste. Augusta Rauracorum, a town of Gallia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>; now a small village called Augusta, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> northwards, but from the ruins, which are still to be seen, appears to have been a considerable colony, at the distance of six miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> to the Augusta castrum. Augusta Suevorum, a town of Gallia Belgica, on the Axona; so called from Augustus, and with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> supposed to be the Noviodunum Suevorum of Caesar. Now <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOISSONS">Soissons</a>, on the river Aisne, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France. See Soissons. Augusta Taurinorum, a town of the Taurini at the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, where the Duria <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a> falls into the Po; now <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>, the capital of Piedmont. Augusta Trebonia, a town of the Æqui, near the spring of the river Anio in Italy; now Trevi, in Umbria, or in the east of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> di Roma. Augusta Treviorum, a town of the Treviri, a people inhabiting between the Rhine and the Meuse, but especially about the Moselle; now Trèves, or Trèves, in the circle of the Lower Rhine, on the Moselle. Augusta Vindelicorum, a town of the Licates on the Licus; called by Tacitus a noble colony of Rhaetia; now Augsburg, capital of Swabia. Augusta Historia, is the history of the Roman emperors from the time of Adrian to Carinus, that is, from the year of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> 157 to 285, composed by five Latin writers, AEI. Spartianus, Julius Capitolinus, AEI. Lampridius, Vulcatius Gallicanus, Trebellius Pollio, and Flavius Vopiscus. Augustales, in Roman Antiquity, an epithet given to the flamens or priests appointed to sacrifice to Augustus after his deification; and also to the ludi or games celebrated in honour of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> on the fourth of the ides of October. Augustalia, a festival instituted by the Romans in honour of Augustus Caesar, on his return to Rome, after having settled peace in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a>; on which occasion they likewise built an altar to him, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> Fortune reduci. Augustalis praefectus, a title peculiar to a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> who governed Egypt, with a power much like that of a proconsul in other provinces. Augustan Confession. See Augsburg Confession. Augustin, or Austin, St., the first archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, was originally a monk in the convent of St Andrew at Rome, and educated under St Gregory, afterwards Pope Gregory I. by whom he was despatched into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> with forty other monks of the same order, about the year 596, to convert the English Saxons to Christianity. They landed in the isle of Thanet; and having sent some French interpreters to King <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ETHELBERT">Ethelbert</a> with an account of their errand, the king gave them leave to convert as many of his subjects as they could, and assigned their place of residence, at Dorovernum, since called Canterbury; to which they were confined till the king himself was converted, whose example had a powerful influence in promoting the conversion of his subjects; but though he was extremely pleased at their becoming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, he never attempted to compel them. He despatched a priest and a monk to Rome, to acquaint the pope with the success of his mission, and to desire his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of certain questions. These men brought back with them a pall, and several books, vestments, utensils, and ornaments for the churches. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a>, by the fame messengers, Augustine messengers, gave Augustine directions concerning the settling of episcopal sees in Britain; and ordered him not to pull down the idol-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, but to convert them into Christian churches; only destroying the idols, and sprinkling the place with holy water, that the natives, by frequenting the temples they had been always accustomed to, might be the less flocked at their entrance into Christianity. Augustine resided principally at Canterbury, which thus became the metropolitan church of England; and having established bishops in several of the cities, he died on the 26th May, 607. The Popish writers ascribe several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> to him. The observation of the festival of St Augustine was first enjoined in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> held under Cuthbert archbishop of Canterbury, and afterwards by the pope's bull in the reign of King Edward III. Augustine, Sr., an illustrious father of the church, was born at Thagaste, a city of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a>, on the 13th of November 354. His father, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGESS">burgess</a> of that city, was called Patricius; and his mother, Monica, who being a woman of great virtue, instructed him in the principles of the Christian religion. In his early youth he was in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of the catechumens; and falling dangerously ill, earnestly desired to be baptized; but the violence of the distemper ceasing, his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> was delayed. His father, who was not yet baptized, made him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> at Thagaste, Madaura, and afterwards at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>.
