Augustine having read Cicero's books of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, began to entertain a love for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and applied himself to the study of the Holy Scriptures; nevertheless, he suffered himself to be seduced by the Manicheans. At the age of 19, he returned to Thagaste, and taught grammar, and also frequented the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>; he afterwards taught <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> at Carthage with applause. The insolence of the scholars at Carthage made him take a resolution to go to Rome, though against his mother's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>. Here also he had many scholars; but disliking them, he quitted Rome, and settled at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, and was chosen public professor of rhetoric in that city. Here he had opportunities of hearing the sermons of St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a>, which, together with the study of St Paul's epistles, and the conversion of two of his friends, determined him to retract his errors, and quit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Manicheans; this was in the 32nd year of his age. In the vacation of the year 386, he retired to the house of a friend of his, named Persecundus, where he seriously applied himself to the study of the Christian religion, in order to prepare himself for baptism, which he received at Easter in the year 387. Soon after this, his mother came to see him at Milan, and invite him back to Carthage; but at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSTIA">Ostia</a>, whither he went to embark in order to his return, she died. He arrived in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> about the end of the year 388; and having obtained a garden-plot without the walls of the city of Hippo, he associated himself with 11 other persons of eminent sanctity, who distinguished themselves by wearing leathern girdles, and lived there in a monastic way for the space of three years, exercising themselves in fasting, prayer, study, and meditation, day and night: from hence sprung up the Augustinian friars, or eremitae of St Augustine, being the first order of mendicants; those of St Jerome, the Carmelites, and others, being but branches of this of St Augustine. About this time, or before, Valerius bishop of Hippo, against his will, ordained him priest; nevertheless, he continued to reside in his little Augustinian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, with his brethren, who, renouncing all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, possessed their goods in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. Valerius, who had appointed St Augustine to preach in his place, allowed him to do it in his presence, contrary to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the churches in Africa. He explained the creed, in a general council of Africa, held in 393. Two years after, Valerius, fearing he might be preferred to be bishop of another church, appointed him his coadjutor or colleague, and caused him to be ordained bishop of Hippo, by Megalus bishop of Calame, then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> of Numidia. St Augustine died the 28th day of August, 430, aged 76 years, having had the misfortune to see his country invaded by the Vandals, and the city where he was bishop besieged for seven months. The works of St Augustine make ten volumes: the best edition of them is that of Maurin, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, in 1700. They are but little read at this time, except by the clergy of the Greek church and in the Spanish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>. The bookellers of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> receive frequent commissions for them, and indeed for the most of the fathers, from Russia, and also from Spain. Augustine, Sr., a fort of North America, on the east coast of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>, situated in W. Long. 81° 10'. N. Lat. 30° 0'. This fort was built by the Spaniards; who were scarce well established there when they were attacked by Sir Francis Drake in 1586, who reduced and pillaged the fort and town adjacent. In 1665, it underwent a similar fate, being attacked by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Davis at the head of a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of buccaneers. In 1702 an attempt was made by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> More to annex St Augustine to the British dominions. He invested it with only 500 English and 700 Indians; which small force, however, would have been sufficient to reduce the place, had not succours arrived when it was on the point of surrendering. Even then, it is thought that he might have defeated the reinforcement which arrived; but he chose to raise the siege, and retire with precipitation. In 1740, another unsuccessful attempt was made on this fort by General Oglethorpe: it was, however, together with the whole country of Florida, ceded to Great Britain by the treaty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1763; but has since been restored to Spain by the treaty of peace 1783. Augustine, a cape of South America. W. Long. 35° 4'. S. Lat. 8° 30'. Augustins, or Augustinians, an order of religious; thus called from St Augustine, whose rule they observe. The Augustins, popularly also called Auffin friars, were originally hermits, whom Pope Alexander IV. first congregated into one body, under their general Lanfranc, in 1256. Soon after their institution, this order was brought into England, where they had about thirty-two houses at the time of their suppression. The Augustins are clothed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and make one of the four orders of mendicants. From these arose a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a>, under the denomination of bare-foot Augustins, or Minorites, or Friars minor. There are also canons regular of St Augustine, who are clothed in white, excepting their cope, which is black. At Paris they were known under the denomination of religious of Genevieve; that abbey was the chief of of the order. There are also nuns and canons, who observe the rules of St Augustin. Augustinians are also those divines who maintain, on the authority of St Augustin, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> is effectual from its nature, absolutely and morally, and not relatively and gradually. They are divided into rigid and relaxed. Augustobona, a city of the Tricassiers in ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, from whom it was afterwards called Tricasses, and Treccasse; and still farther corrupted to Throare, or Treci; whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-TROYES">Troyes</a>, in Champagne, on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>. See Troyes. Augustodunum, the capital of the Aedui, where there was a famous academy or school for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of youth; now <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUTUN">Autun</a>, or Autun, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, on the Arroux. See Autun. Augustomagus, an ancient town of Gallia Belgica; now Sentin, in the Isle of France. E. Long. 2° 30'. N. Lat. 49° 10'. Augustoritum, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, according to some authors the capital of the Pictones, afterwards called Picavi; now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POITIERS">Poitiers</a>. But by Antonine's Itinerary from Burdigala to Argantomagus (or Argenton, as it is interpreted by many), it can be no other but the capital of the Lemovices, now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMOGES">Limoges</a>, situated between Velluna of the Petrocorii, or Perigeux, and Argantomagus. E. Long. 1° 22'. Lat. 45° 52'. Augustow, a small but strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in the duchy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of Polakia, seated on the river Narie. E. Long. 24° 2'. N. Lat. 53° 25'. Augustus, Fort, a small fortress seated on a plain at the head of Lochness in Scotland, between the rivers Taarf and Oich; the last is a considerable stream, and has over it a stone <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. The fort consists of four battions: within is the governor's house, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a> for 400 men; it was taken by the rebels in 1746, who immediately deserted it after demolishing what they could. The name of this fort in Erse is Kill Chumain, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> place of the Cummins. It lies on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to the isle of Sky, which is about 52 miles off; but on the whole way there is not a place fit for the reception of man or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. Augustus, the appellation conferred upon Caesar Octavianus, the first Roman emperor. See Octavianus and Rome. The obscure name of Octavianus, Mr Gibbon observes, he derived from a mean family, in the little town of Aricia. It was stained with the blood of the proscription; and he was desirous, had it been possible, to erase all <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his former life. The illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Cæsar he had assumed, as the adopted son of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>; but he had too much good sense either to hope to be confounded, or to wish to be compared, with that extraordinary man. It was proposed in the senate, to dignify their minister with a new appellation; and after a very serious discussion, that of Augustus was chosen among several others, as being the most expressive of the character of peace and sanctity, which he uniformly affected. Augustus was therefore a personal, Cæsara family, distinction. The former should naturally have expired with the prince on whom it was bestowed; and however the latter was diffused by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>, Nero was the last prince who could allege any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> claims to the honour of the Julian line. But at the time of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the practice of a century had inseparably connected those appellations with the imperial dignity, and they have been preserved by a long succession of emperors, Romans, Greeks, Franks, and Germans, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the republic to the present time. A distinction was, however, soon introduced. The sacred title of Augustus was always reserved for the monarch; the name of Cæsar was more freely communicated to his relations; and from the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a> at least, was appropriated to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> person in the state, who was considered as the presumptive heir of the empire. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AVIARY">Aviary</a>, a place set apart for feeding and propagating birds. It should be so large as to give the birds some freedom of flight; and turfed, to avoid the appearance of foulness on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AVICENNA">Avicenna</a>, or Avicen, the prince of Arabian philosophers and physicians, was born at Afifna, a village in the neighbourhood of Bokhara. His father was from Balkh in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and had married at Bokhara. The first years of Avicenna were devoted to the study of the Koran and the belles lettres. He soon showed what he was likely to become afterwards; and the progress he made was so rapid, that when he was but ten years old, he was perfectly intelligent in the most hidden tenets of the Koran. Abou-Abdallah, a native of Napoous in Syria, at that time professed philosophy at Bokhara with the greatest reputation. Avicenna studied under him the principles of logic; but soon, disgusted with the slow manner of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, he set about studying alone, and read all the authors that had written on philosophy, without any other help than that of their commentators. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a> had no fewer charms for him; and after <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> the first five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> of Euclid, he got alone to the last, having made himself perfect <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of them, and treasured up all of them equally in his memory. Possessed with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> avidity to be acquainted with all sorts of sciences, he likewise devoted himself to the study of medicine. Persuaded that this divine art consisted as much in practice as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>, he sought all opportunities of seeing the sick; and afterwards confessed, that he had learned more from experience than from all the old books he had read. He was now in his 16th year, and already was celebrated for being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of his age. He resolved at this age to resume his studies of philosophy, which medicine had made him neglect; and he spent a year and a half in this painful labour, without ever sleeping all this time a whole night together. If he felt himself oppressed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, or exhausted by study, a glass of wine refreshed his wasted spirits, and gave him new vigour for study; if in spite of him his eyes, for a few minutes shut out the light, it then happened to him to recollect and meditate upon all the things that had occupied his thoughts before sleep. At the age of 21, he conceived the bold design of incorporating, in one work, all the objects of human knowledge; and carried it into execution in an Encyclopaedia of 20 volumes, to which he gave the title of the Utility of Utilities. Several great princes had been taken dangerously ill, and Avicenna was the only one that could know their ailments. Avicenna, ailments and cure them. His reputation increased daily, and all the kings of Asia desired to retain him in their families. Mahmud, the son of Sabektekin, the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of the dynasty of the Samanides, was then the most powerful prince of the east. Imagining that an implicit obedience should be paid by all manner of persons to the injunctions of his will, he wrote a haughty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Mamun sultan of Kharazm, ordering him to send Avicenna to him, who was at his court, with several other learned men. Philosophy, the friend of liberty and independence, looks down with scorn on the shackles of compulsion and restraint. Avicenna, accustomed to the most flattering distinctions among the great, could not endure the imperious manner of Mahmud's inviting him to his court, and refused to go there. But the sultan of Kharazm, who dreaded his resentment, obliged the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> to depart with others whom that prince had demanded to be sent to him. Avicenna pretended to obey; but instead of repairing to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAZNA">Gazna</a>, he took the route of Giorgian. Mahmud, who had gloried in the thoughts of keeping him at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, was greatly irritated at his flight. He dispatched portraits done in crayons of this philosopher to all the princes of Asia, with orders to have him conducted to Gazna, if he appeared in their courts. But Avicenna had fortunately escaped the most diligent search after him. He arrived in the capital of Giorgian, where under a disguised name he performed many admirable cures. Cabous then reigned in that country. A nephew, whom he was extremely fond of, being fallen sick, the most able physicians were called in, and none of them were able to know his ailment, or give him any ease. Avicenna was at last consulted. So soon as he had felt the young prince's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, he was confident with himself, that his illness proceeded from a violent love, which he dared not to declare. Avicenna commanded the person who had the care of the different apartments in the palace, to name them all in their respective order. A more lively <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> in the prince's pulse, at hearing mentioned one of these apartments, betrayed a part of his secret. The keeper then had orders to name all the slaves that inhabited that apartment. At the name of one of those beauties, the young Cabous could not contain himself; an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> of his pulse completed the discovery of what he in vain desired to keep concealed. Avicenna, now fully assured that this slave was the cause of the prince's illness, declared, that she alone had the power to cure him. The sultan's consent was necessary, and he of course was curious to see his nephew's physician. He had scarce looked at him, when he knew in his features those of the crayoned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> sent him by Mahmud; but Cabous, far from forcing Avicenna to repair to Gazna, retained him for some time with him, and heaped honours and presents on him. This philosopher passed afterwards into the court of Nedjmeddevle, sultan of the race of the Bouides. Being appointed first physician to that prince, he found means to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> his confidence to so great a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that he raised him to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of grand vizir. But he did not long enjoy that illustrious dignity. Too great an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to pleasures, especially those of love and Avicenna, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, made him lose at the same time his post and his master's favour. From that time Avicenna felt all the rigours of adversity, which he had brought upon himself by his ill conduct. He wandered about as a fugitive, and was often obliged to shift the place of his habitation to secure his life from danger. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMADAN">Hamadan</a>, aged 58 years, in the 428th year of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a>, and of Christ 1036. The perfect knowledge he had of physic did not secure him from the ailments that afflict human nature. He was attacked by several maladies in the course of his life, and particularly was very subject to the colic. His excesses in pleasures, and his infirmities, made a poet say who wrote his epitaph, that the profound study of philosophy had not taught him good morals, nor that of medicine the art of preserving his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. No one composed with greater facility than Avicenna, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, when he sat down to it, 50 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> generally in a day, without fatiguing himself. The doctors of Schiras, having made a collection of objections against one of his metaphysical works, sent it to him at Ifpanah by Cafem. This learned man, not arriving till towards evening, came to Avicenna's house, with whom he sat discoursing till midnight. When Cafem had retired, he wrote an answer to the objections of the Schirazians, and finished it before sunrise. He immediately delivered it to Cafem, telling him, that he had made all possible despatch in order not to detain him any longer at Ifpanah. Avicenna, after his death, enjoyed so great a reputation, that till the 12th century he was preferred for the study of philosophy and medicine to all his predecessors. His works were the only writings in vogue in schools, even in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The following are the titles: 1. Of the Utility and Advantage of Science, twenty books. 2. Of Innocence and Criminality, two books. 3. Of Health and Remedies, eighteen books. 4. Canons of Physic, fourteen books. 5. On Astronomical Observations, one book. 6. On Mathematical Sciences. 7. Of Theorems, or Mathematical and Theological Demonstrations, one Book. 8. On the Arabic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">Language</a>, and its Properties, ten books. 9. On the Last Judgment. 10. On the Origin of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">Soul</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">Resurrection</a> of Bodies. 11. Of the end we should propose to ourselves in Harangues and Philosophical Argumentations. 12. Demoustration of the collateral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">Lines</a> in the Sphere. 13. Abridgement of Euclid. 14. On Infinity and Infinity. 15. On Physics and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>. 16. On Animals and Vegetables, &c. 17. Encyclopedie, 20 volumes—Some, however, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> him with having stolen what he published from a celebrated physician who had been his master. This man had acquired so much honour and wealth, that he was solicited by many to take their sons to be his scholars, or even his servants; but being resolved not to discover the secrets of his art, he would receive none of them. Avicenna's mother formed the following stratagem: she offered him her son as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, pretending he was naturally <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEAF_AND_DUMB">deaf and dumb</a>; and the youth by his mother's instructions, counterfeited those defects so well, that the physician, after making several trials to discover the reality of them, took the boy into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and by degrees trusted him. Avicen him so far as to leave his writings open in his room when he went abroad: Avicenes took that opportunity to transcribe them, and carried the copies to his mother; and after death of his master he published them under his own name. Indeed if we reflect that he lived but 58 years, that he was a wanderer and a fugitive, and that he was much addicted to his pleasures, we shall have some difficulty to conceive how he could find time to compose so many works. Physic, however, is indebted to him for the discovery of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CASSIS">cassis</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RHUBARB">rhubarb</a>, mirabolans, tamarinds; and from him also, it is said, came to us the art of making <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>.

AVICENIA

Pages 326-326

Eastern Anacardium. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. AVIGATO <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">PEAR</a>. See Laurus, Botany Index.

AVIGLIANO

Pages 326-326

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 5. N. Lat. 44. 40.

AVIGNON

Pages 326-327

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, in the department of Vaucluse, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Venafin, and seated on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>. It was formerly an archbishop's see; and the residence of several popes at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for 70 years has rendered it considerable. Near the Rhone there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> rock, within the circumference of the walls, upon which is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a>, from whence may be had a prospect of the whole city and the places about it. This city is about three miles and two furlongs in circumference, and is in general ill built, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, and devoid of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. But it is surrounded by handsome battlemented walls and turrets, not unlike those of Rome; and its public edifices are large, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the fourteenth century could make them. Several popes and anti-popes, who, during their lives, shook the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> with violence and mutual altercation, repose quietly near each other in the various monasteries of the place. The church of the Cordeliers contains, in an obscure corner, the almost defaced <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Petrarch's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAURA">Laura</a> and her husband Hugh de Sade; and nearly opposite is the tomb of the brave Gullon, so well known for his invincible courage as well as for his inviolable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to his sovereign Henry IV. Many productions of Rene of Anjou are to be seen in the city; whose inhabitants amount to about 30,000, of whom 1000 are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> and some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> Jews. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the vice-legate is composed of several large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> towers, and he gives audience in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> which is full of fine paintings, as is also the chapel and the apartments. The arsenal is near the palace. The church of Notre Dame is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, but not large, and is one of the best adorned in the city. After having ascended about 50 steps, you come to a very ancient portico, which sustains a great tower; as you enter the church on the left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, you see paintings which equal the finest in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. The great altar is very magnificent, and is adorned with a shrine that contains the relics of whom we know not how many saints. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of the sacristy is worthy of the curiosity of the traveller. The little palace where the archbishop resides is formed of three bodies of lodgings, accompanied with courts and small pavilions. It overlooks the Rhone, the city, and the fields. These buildings and the mint adorn a large square, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> walk of the inhabitants. In Avignon they reckon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> gates, seven palaces, seven colleges, seven <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, seven monasteries, seven nunneries, and seven popes who have lived there in 70 years. The steeples are numerous, and the bells are never at rest; one of silver is rung only on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of a pope. The church of the Celestines is very magnificent, and full of fine monuments, and the rest are not without their curiosities. The university has four colleges; and the place where the Jews live is a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, from whence the Jews who pay tribute dare not stir out without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, and the women must have something yellow about their heads, to distinguish them from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. Their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> is very considerable in a very confined place, where the only way of enlarging their abodes is by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> their houses higher. Their synagogue is so dark, that they are obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> lamps. However, they are forced to hear a monk preach a sermon every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. Across the Rhone, here, extend the ruined and decayed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> against which Madame de Grignan was so near being loit, and of which Madame de Sevigne makes terrified mention. It was demolished in 1699 by one of the inundations common to the Rhone. When entire, it was not less than a quarter of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in length; but being so narrow as not to permit two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, it had previously become almost useless; and motives of policy prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of a new bridge, while Avignon belongs to the papal see. The curious that travel this way go to see the fountain of Vaucluse, where the river Sorgues, which passes through this city, has its source; and whither Petrarch so often retired to indulge his grief and hopeless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. It is situated in a valley five miles distant from the city. The sides of the river are skirted by meadows of the most lively green; above which rise abrupt and lofty rocks, that seem designed to exclude it from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> view. The valley becomes gradually narrower toward the extremity, and winding continually describes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-hoe. The view is at length terminated by an enormous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of rock, forming a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> across it, of a prodigious height, and absolutely perpendicular. Through its vast recesses run the streams which supply the fountain of Vaucluse, and at its feet appears a basin of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, several hundred feet in circumference, stretched like an expanse, silent and quiet. The sides are very steep, and it is said that in the middle no bottom can be discovered, though attempts have been often made for that purpose; a circumstance probably resulting from the violence with which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> bubble up, which prevents any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> from descending beyond a certain depth. Though the fountain is clearer in itself than crystal, yet the incumbent rock casts a continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, approaching to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, over its surface. The water escaping from this state of inaction by a narrow passage, is immediately precipitated in a cascade <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a rocky channel, where it foams over a number of vast detached <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which intercept and impede its progress. They are covered with a deep green moss of many ages, and have probably tumbled from the mountain that overhangs the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>. The rocks themselves, which surround and invest this romantic Avignon, a mantic spot, are worn by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and the inclemency of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> into a thousand extraordinary and fantastic forms, to which imagination gives shape and figure. On one of the pointed extremities, and in a situation which appears almost inaccessible, are seen the remains of an ancient castle, projecting over the water. The peasants call it "Il Castello di Petrarcha"; and add, with great simplicity, that Laura lived upon the opposite side of the river, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of which was a subterranean passage by which the two lovers visited each other. Nothing is however more certain, than that these are the ruins of the chateau belonging to the lords <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> seigneurs of Avignon; and the bishop of Cavaillon resided in it during the frequent visits which he used to make to Petrarch.—The poet's dwelling was much lower down, and nearer to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Sorgue, as evidently appears from his minute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it, and the relation he gives of his quarrel with the Naiads of the stream, who encroached during the winter on his little adjoining territory. No remains of it are now to be discerned. Below the bridge there is an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> where the Sorgues joins the Rhone, in which are several houses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 59'. N. Lat. 43° 57'. Avignon-Berry, the fruit of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of lycium; growing plentifully near Avignon and in other parts of France. The berry is somewhat less than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>; its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is green, approaching towards a yellow; and it is of an agreeable and bitter taste.—It is much used by the dyers, who stain a yellow colour with it; and by the painters, who also make a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> yellow of it.

AVILA

Pages 327-327

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Old Castile, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, seated on an eminence on the banks of the river Adaja, and in sight of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Pico. It is fortified both by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art, having a wall 9075 feet in circumference, adorned with 26 lofty towers, and 10 handsome gates. There are 17 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> streets, the houses in which are generally good, and some of them stately. It hath <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> squares, 2000 houses, nine parishes, as many monasteries, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> nunneries, two colleges, nine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, 18 chapels, and an allowance of 10,000 ducats yearly for the maintenance of orphans and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people. It has an university, and a considerable bishopric; besides a noble <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, which has eight dignitaries, 20 canons, and the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> canons. It stands in the middle of a fine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> plain surrounded with mountains, and covered with fruit-trees and vineyards. There is likewise a manufacture of cloth. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 13'. N. Lat. 40° 35'.

AVIS

Pages 327-327

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALENTEJO">Alentejo</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, seated on an eminence with a castle near the river Avis. Hence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> order of the knights of Avis have their name. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 0'. N. Lat. 38° 40'. Avis (Knights d'Avis), an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> in Portugal established about the year 1162. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EVORA">Evora</a> was taken from the Moors, in the reign of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Portugal, it was garrisoned by several persons who assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of knights of St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> of Evora, which was soon after changed for that of knights d'Avis, which the king gave them, and whither they removed from Evora. The badge of the order is a green <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> flory, and they observe the rule of St Benedict.

AVISO

Pages 327-327

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> chiefly used in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> to denote an advertisement, an advice, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> piece of intelligence.

AVISON

Pages 327-327
Charles, organist of Newcastle, and a disciple of Geminiani, was the author of an essay on musical expression, published in the year 1752, in which are some judicious reflections on music in general, but his division of the modern authors into classes is rather fanciful than just. Throughout his book he celebrates Marcello and Geminiani; the latter frequently in prejudice to Mr Handel. In the year 1753 came out remarks on Mr Avion's essay on musical expression, the author whereof first points out sundry errors against the rules of composition in the works of Avion. In the same year Avion republished his essay, with a reply to the author of the remarks; and a letter containing a number of loose particulars relating to music, collected in a course of various reading, unquestionably written by Dr Jortin. Avion promoted and assisted in the publication of Marcello's music to the psalms adapted to English words. Of his own composition there are extant five collections of concertos for violins, 44 in number; and two sets of sonatas for the harpsichord and two violins, a species of composition little known in England till his time. The music of Avion is light and elegant, but it wants originality; a necessary consequence of his too close attachment to the style of Geminiani, which in a few particulars only he was able to imitate.

AVOCATORIA

Pages 328-328

a mandate of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Germany, addressed to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, in order to stop his unlawful proceedings in any cause appealed to him.

AVOIDANCE

Pages 328-328

in the Canon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is when a benefice becomes void of an incumbent; which happens either in fact, as by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the person; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in law, as by cession, deprivation, resignation, &c. In the first of these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> must take notice of the avoidance at his peril; but in avoidance by law, the ordinary is obliged to give notice to the patron, in order to prevent a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a>. AVOIRDUPOIS. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> for the larger and coarser commodities, such as groceries, cheese, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAKERS">Bakers</a>, who live not in corporation <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, are to make their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> by avoirdupois weight, those in corporations by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">troy</a> weight. Apothecaries buy by avoirdupois weight, but sell by troy. The proportion of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> avoirdupois to a pound troy is as 17 to 14. AVOSETTA. See Recurvirostra, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

AVOWEE

Pages 328-329

one who has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to present to a benefice. He is thus called in contradistinction to those AUR Avowry those who only have the lands to which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOWSON">advowson</a> belongs for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of years, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by virtue of intrusion or disfavour.

AVOWRY

Pages 329-329

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is where a person distrained sues out a replevin; for then the distrainer must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a>, and justify his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a>, which is called his avowry.

AVVENTURE

Pages 316-316

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a> Books, means a mischance causing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of a person without felony.

AWARD

Pages 340-340

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the judgment of an arbitrator, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of one who is not appointed by the law a judge, but chosen by the parties themselves for terminating their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>. See ARBITER and ARBITRATION.

AWLAN

Pages 340-340

a small imperial town of Germany, in the circle of Suabia, seated on the river Kochen. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 15'. N. Lat. 48° 52'.

AWNING

Pages 340-340

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">Language</a>, is the hanging a sail, tarpawling, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, over any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ship, to keep off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>.

AX

Pages 340-340

a carpenter's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, serving to hew wood. The ax differs from the joiner's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCHET">hatchet</a>, in that it is made larger and heavier, as serving to hew <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> stuff; and its edge tapering into the middle of its blade. It is furnished with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> handle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> helve, as being to be used with both <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">Battle</a>-Ax. See Celt.

AXAMENTA

Pages 340-340
or Affimenta, in Ancient Music, hymns or songs performed wholly with human voices.

AXATI

Pages 340-340

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Baetica, on the Baetis; now Lora, a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, seated on the Gaudalquivier. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 26'. N. Lat. 37° 20'.

AXAYACATL

Pages 340-340

the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fly, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, about the lake; the eggs of which being deposited in immense quantities, upon the rushes and corn-flats, form <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> matts, which are taken up by fishermen and carried to market for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. This caviare, called abuautli, which has much the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> with the caviare of fish, used to be eaten by the Mexicans, and is now a common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a> among the Spaniards. The Mexicans eat not only the eggs, but the flies themselves, made up together into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, and prepared with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>.

AXBRIDGE

Pages 340-340

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a> in England, consisting of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> narrow street. W. Long. 2° 20'. N. Lat. 51° 30'.

AXHOLM

Pages 340-340

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a> in England. It is formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, Idle, and Dan; and is about ten miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The lower part is marshy, but produces an odoriferous shrub called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALL">gall</a>; the middle is rich and fruitful, yielding <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance, as also alabaster which is used for making lime. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is called Axey, and is now very thinly inhabited.

AXIAE

Pages 340-340

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of Sarmatia Europae; now Oczakow, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Budziac <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 32° 30'. N. Lat. 46° 0'.

AXILLA

Pages 340-340

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, is the space comprehended between the stems of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and their leaves. Hence we say those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> grow in the axilla of the leaves; i.e. at the base of the leaves, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of their pedicles.

AXILLARY

Pages 340-340

something belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lying near the axilla. Thus, axillary artery is that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the subclavian branches of the ascending <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of the aorta which passes under the arm-pits; axillary glands are situated under the arm-pits, enveloped in fat, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by the axillary vessels; and axillary vein is one of the subclavians which passes under the arm-pit, dividing itself into several branches, which are spread over the arm.

AXIM

Pages 340-340

a small territory on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> here is so excessively moist, that it is proverbially said to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> 11 months and 29 days of the year. This excessive moisture renders it very unhealthy; but it produces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, watermelons, lemons, oranges, &c. Here are also produced vast numbers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, goats, sheep, tame pigeons, &c. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is filled with beautiful and populous villages, and the intermediate lands well cultivated; besides which, the natives are very wealthy, from the constant traffic carried on with them by the Europeans for their gold. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, which is also called Axim, by some Achombone, stands under the cannon of the Dutch fort St Antonio. Behind, it is secured by a thick wood that covers over the whole declivity of a neighbouring hill. Between the town and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> runs an even and spacious shore of beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> sand. All the houses are separated by groves of cocoa and other fruit trees, planted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, each of an equal width, and forming an elegant vista. The little river Axim crosses the town; and the coast is defended by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small pointed rocks, which project from the shore, and render all access to it dangerous. The capital is situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 24° 0'. N. Lat. 5° 0'. This <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> is a kind of republic, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> being

AXINOMANCY

Pages 340-341

AXINOMANTIA, from ἀξίων, σερυσις, and μαντεία, divinatio; an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a method of foretelling future events by means of an ax or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCHET">hatchet</a>. This art was in considerable repute among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; and was performed, according to some, by laying an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> on a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot hatchet; and also by fixing a hatchet on a round flake so as to be exactly poised; then the names of those that were suspected were repeated, and he at whose name the hatchet moved was pronounced guilty.

AXIPOLIS

Pages 341-341

a town of the Triballi in Mæsia Inferior; now Axiopolis, in Bulgaria. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 34° 0'. N. Lat. 45° 40'.

AXIS

Pages 341-341

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>. Spiral axis, is the axis of a twisted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> drawn spirally in order to trace the circumvolutions without. Axis of the Ionic <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, is a line passing perpendicularly through the middle of the eye of the volute. Axis of a Veil, is an imaginary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line passing through the middle of it perpendicularly to its base, and equally distant from its sides. Axis, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> column placed in the centre of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> catkins, about which the other parts are disposed. Axis, in Anatomy, the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> vertebra of the neck; it hath a tooth which goes into the first vertebra, and this tooth is by some called the axis.

AXMINSTER

Pages 341-341

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, situated on the river Ax, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 15'. N. Lat. 50° 40'. It was a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Saxons, but now contains only about 200 houses. Here is a small manufactory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and narrow cloths, and some carpets are also manufactured after the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> manner. AXOLOTLE. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACERTA">LACERTA</a>.

AXONNE

Pages 340-340

a small fortified town in France, in the department of Cote d'<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">Or</a>; seated on the river Saone, over which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of 23 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, to facilitate the running off of the waters after the overflowing of the river. At the end of the bridge is a causeway 2250 paces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. E. Long. 5° 22'. N. Lat. 47° 11'. AXY; the French give the name of auxy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> to that which is spun in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBEVILLE">Abbeville</a>, by those workmen who are called boupiers. It is a very fine and beautiful wool, which is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used to make the finest stockings.

AXUMA

Pages 341-341

formerly a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, but now reduced to a miserable village scarcely containing 100 inhabitants. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 36° 4'. N. Lat. 14° 13'.

AXUNGIA

Pages 341-341

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes old <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the driest and hardest of any fat in the bodies of animals; but more properly it signifies only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOG">hog</a>'s lard. AXUNGLA Viri, Sandiver, or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">Salt</a> of Glafs, a kind of salt which separates from the glafs while it is in fusion. It is of an acrimonious and biting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. The farriers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it for cleansing the eyes of horses. It is also made use of for cleansing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; and it is sometimes applied to running ulcers, the herpes, or the itch, by way of deificative. AXYRIS. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

AY

Pages 341-341

a town of France in Champagne, near the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, remarkable for its excellent wines. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 15'. N. Lat. 49° 4'. AYAMONTÉ, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, with a strong castle built on a rock; seated on the mouth of the river Gaudiana. It has a commodious harbour, fruitful vineyards, and excellent wine. W. Long. 8° 5'. N. Lat. 37° 9'. AYENIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AYLESBURY">AYLESBURY</a>. See AILESBOURNE. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> gave <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the noble family of Bruce, now to a branch of Brudenals by succession.

AYLMER

Pages 341-342

JOHN, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, was born in the year 1521, at Aylmer-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Tilney, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>. Whilst a boy, he was distinguished for his quick parts by the marquis of Dorset afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>; who sent him to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, made him his chaplain and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to his children. One of these children was the unfortunate Lady Jane Gray, who soon became perfectly acquainted with the Latin and Greek languages. His first preferment was to the archdeaconry of Stow, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, which gave him a seat in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a> held in the first year of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, where he resolutely opposed the return to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>, to which the generality of the clergy were inclined. He was soon after obliged to fly his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and take shelter among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. On the accession of Queen Elizabeth, he returned to England. In 1562, he obtained the archdeaconry. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYR">AYR</a> deaconry of Lincoln; and was a member of the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> of that year, which reformed and settled the doctrine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England. In the year 1576, he was consecrated bishop of London. He died in the year 1594, aged 73; and was buried in St Paul's. He was a learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, a zealous father of the church, and a bitter enemy to the Puritans. He published a piece entitled, An barbrowe for faithful and trewe subiects against the late bloune blaste concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of women, &c. This was written whilst he was abroad in answer to Knox, who published a book in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a> under this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, The first blast against the monstrous regiment and empire of women. He is by Strype supposed to have published Lady Jane Gray's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Hardinge. He also assisted Fox in translating his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Martyrs into Latin.

AYR

Pages 342-342

a river in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Muirkirk, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYRSHIRE">Ayrshire</a>; which after a course of about eighteen miles nearly due west falls into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at Ayr, where its estuary forms a fine harbour. It is for a considerable course only a small rivulet; but joined by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENOCK">Greenock</a> and Garpel, tributary streams, it becomes a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> body of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It frequently floods its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and does considerable damage by its encroachments. Its banks are steep and very romantic; and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of seats which ornament them present a fine picturesque scenery. Sorn-castle, Auchincriuie, and Auchinleck, may be mentioned as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> beauties of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>. The village of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CATRINE">Catrine</a> is situated on its banks. It forms the boundary between the districts of Ayrshire, denominated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KYLE">Kyle</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRICK">Carrick</a>.

AYRSHIRE

Pages 342-343

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Scotland, which is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the county of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RENFREW">Renfrew</a>; on the east by the shires of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LANARK">Lanark</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUMFRIES">Dumfries</a>; on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>; and on the west by the Irish channel, and the frith of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> in length is about 65 miles, and about 36 in breadth. It is divided into three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> districts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stewartries, which bear the names of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KYLE">Kyle</a>, Cunningham, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRICK">Carrick</a>. These divisions are not altogether <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>; the river <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYR">Ayr</a>, on which is the town of Ayr, forming the separation between Carrick and Kyle (or Ayrshire Proper), and the river <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRVINE">Irvine</a> (at the mouth of which is a borough of the same name) is the limit between Kyle and Cunningham. AYR These districts are very different from each other in appearance. Carrick, and the interior parts of Kyle, are mountainous, and more fitted for pasture; while the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Kyle, and the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Cunningham, exhibit a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, interperled with numerous villages and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> coast is mostly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, with flint rocks, possessing several good harbours. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AILSA">Ailsa</a> is in this county. From the ridge, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Carrick are a part, rise almost all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of the south of Scotland. The Tweed, the Els, the Nith, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNAN">Annan</a>, the Urr, &c., flow to the east and south, while the Stinchar, the Girvan, the Doon, the Ayr, and the Lugar, pouring into the Irish channel, intersect the county of Ayr with their copious streams. Besides these, the Irvine and other smaller rivulets, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> the more northerly parts of the county. Ayrshire has two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> boroughs, viz. Ayr and Irvine; and several populous towns and villages, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILMARNOCK">Kilmarnock</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEITH">Beith</a>, Saltcoats, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KILWINNING">Kilwinning</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGS">Largs</a>, Girvan, and Ballantrae, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. Fitted as Ayrshire is in every respect for the carrying on of trade, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of agricultural improvements, it is only of late years that much has been done in that way. Possessing valuable seams of excellent coal, and enriched with the returns from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>, little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was paid to the culture of the ground. The establishment of the Douglas and Heron <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">Bank</a>, though ruinous to the proprietors, contributed greatly to promote the improvement of Ayrshire. The abundance of wealth which it fallaciously seemed to pour into the country, and the ready command of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> it gave, set all the proprietors towards improving and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> their estates, furnished means for raising and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> lime for manure, and above all, with the money from the bank, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> were opened through every part of the county. Upon the failure of that extravagant and ill-conducted speculation, the proprietors of many estates <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> brought to the hammer, and the greater part of their lands purchased by new proprietors. After the general distress, consequent on so disastrous a scheme, was somewhat relieved, the improvement which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> had received during the profusion of money, enabled the proprietors to continue the improvement, and the new settlers being mostly men of great fortune, allowed no expense to be wanting to produce the same end; and hence the improvement of the country was rather promoted than retarded, by an event which threatened to overwhelm not only Ayrshire, but the greater part of Scotland, into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of bankruptcy. Ayrshire, besides the inexhaustible seams of coal with which it abounds, possesses several other valuable minerals; as freestone, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>, ironstone, several rich ores of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. A few curious specimens are also to be found in the hills of Carrick, of agates, porphyries, and of calcareous petrifactions. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Stair, galena and plumbago have been found; and in several parts of the county is found that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of whetstone, known by the name of Ayr-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. There is plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a> in most of the lochs; the chief of which is Loch Doon, from which the river of that name takes its rise. There is annually a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sea weed thrown ashore, from which many tons of kelp are made. All the rivers of Ayrshire abound with salmon, and the coasts are admirably adapted for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>. The following is a statement of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Ayrshire, this county at two different periods. | Parish | Population in 1755 | Population in 1790-1798 | |--------|------------------|-----------------------| | Ardrossan | 1207 | 1518 | | Auchinleck | 887 | 775 | | Ayr | 2064 | 4647 | | Ballantrae | 1049 | 770 | | Barr | 858 | 730 | | Beith | 2064 | 2872 | | Cumbranes | 259 | 509 | | Colmonell | 1814 | 1102 | | Coylton | 527 | 667 | | Craigie | 551 | 700 | | Cumnock, New | 1497 | 1200 | | Cumnock, Old | 1336 | 1632 | | Dalry | 839 | 1007 | | Dalmellington | 739 | 681 | | Dalry | 1498 | 2000 | | Dalrymple | 439 | 380 | | Dreghorn | 887 | 830 | | Dundonald | 983 | 1317 | | Dunlop | 796 | 779 | | Fenwick | 1113 | 1281 | | Galston | 1013 | 1577 | | Girvan | 1193 | 1725 | | Irvine | 4025 | 4500 | | Kilbirney | 651 | 700 | | Kilbride, West | 885 | 698 | | Kilmarnock | 4433 | 6776 | | Kilmuir | 1004 | 1147 | | Kilwinning | 2511 | 2560 | | Kirkmichael | 710 | 956 | | Kirkoswald | 1168 | 1335 | | Largs | 1104 | 1025 | | Loudoun | 1494 | 2308 | | Mauchline | 1169 | 1800 | | Maybole | 2018 | 3750 | | Monkton | 582 | 717 | | Muirkirk | 745 | 1100 | | Newtown on Ayr | 581 | 1089 | | Ochiltree | 1210 | 1150 | | Riccarton | 745 | 1320 | | St Quivox | 499 | 1450 | | Sorn | 1494 | 2779 | | Stair | 369 | 518 | | Stevenston | 1412 | 2425 | | Stewarton | 2819 | 3000 | | Straiton | 1123 | 934 | | Symington | 359 | 610 | | Tarbolton | 1365 | 1100 | Total, 59,268 | 75,544 | Increase, 16,276

AYSCUE

Pages 343-344

Sir George, a gallant English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, descended from a good family in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>. He obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., which, however, did not withhold him from adhering adhering to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>: he was by them constituted admiral of the Irish seas, where he is said to have done <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, and to have contributed much to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. In 1651 he reduced Barbadoes and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, then held for the king, to the obedience of the parliament; and soon after the restoration behaved with great honour in the war with the Dutch. In the famous engagement in the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1666, when Sir George was admiral of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> squadron, his ship the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> ran upon the Gallop-sand; where, being surrounded with enemies, his men obliged him to strike. He went no more to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> after this, but spent the rest of his days in retirement. AYMOUTH. See EYMOUTH. AYTONIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

AZAMOR

Pages 344-344

a small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. It is situated on the river Morbeya, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Daguella, at some considerable distance from its mouth. This town, though formerly very considerable, is not proper for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, because the entrance of the river is dangerous. It was unsuccessfully besieged by the Portuguese in 1528; it was taken, however, in 1513, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRAGANZA">Braganza</a>, but abandoned about the end of the 16th century. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7°. O. N. Lat. 32°. 50'.

AZARAKITES

Pages 344-344

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Mahometan Arabs. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">ARABIA</a>, No. 143, et seq.

AZARIAH

Pages 344-344
or UZZIAH, king of Judah, succeeded his father Amaziah, 815 years before Christ. He assembled an army of above 300,000 men, with which he conquered the Philistines, and demolished the walls of Gath, Jabniel, and Ashdod; built up the walls of Jerusalem; furnished the city with conduits; and planted gardens and vineyards: but at last, being elated with his prosperity, and resolving to usurp the office of high-priest, he was struck with a leprosy, which obliged him to remain shut up in his palace for the rest of his days. He died about 759 years before the Christian era, and was succeeded by Jonathan his son.—There are several other persons of this name mentioned in the sacred Scriptures. AZAZEL. The word relates to the history of the scape-goat, under the Jewish religion. Some call the goat itself by this name, as St Jerome and Theodoret. Dr Spenser says, the scape-goat was to be sent to Azazel; by which is meant the devil. Mr Le Clerc translates it precipitum, making it to be that steep and inaccessible place to which the goat was sent, and where it was supposed to perish.

AZEKA

Pages 344-344

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Amorites, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of Judah; situated between Eleutheropolis and Aelia (Jerome); where the five kings of the Amorites and their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> were destroyed by hailstones from heaven, (Joshua).

AZEM

Pages 344-344

ASSEM, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSAM">ASSAM</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ACHAM, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVA">Ava</a>, but which is very little known to Europeans. It is said to be very fertile, and to contain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, all Azimuth which belong to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, who, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of enjoying the produce, requires no taxes from his people. They have also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> lac, and coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. It is also thought that the inhabitants of Azem were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago the inventors of cannon and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-powder; and that from them the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> passed to the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEGU">Pegu</a> and from thence to the Chinese.

AZIMUTH

Pages 344-344
