in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of the horizon intercepted between the meridian of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and the azimuth, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vertical circle passing through the centre of the object, which is equal to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the zenith, formed by the meridian and vertical circle: or it is found by this proportion, As the radius to the tangent of the latitude of the place, so is the tangent of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a>, for instance, to the cosine of the azimuth from the south, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the equinox. Magnetical Azimuth, an arch of the horizon intercepted between the azimuth, or vertical circle, passing through the centre of any heavenly body and the magnetic meridian. This is found by observing the object with an azimuth compass. Azimuth-Compass, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for finding either the magnetical azimuth or amplitude of a heavenly object. The learned Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">Knight</a> invented some time since a very accurate and useful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-compass, which is at present used in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. This instrument, with another invented by the ingenious Mr Smeaton, answers the purposes of an azimuth amplitude compass. See Compass. Azimuth Circles, called also azimaths, or vertical circles, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> circles of the sphere intersecting each other in the zenith and nadir, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the horizon at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>. These azimaths are represented by the rhumbs on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sea-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a>, and on the globe they are represented by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a> of altitude, when viewed in the zenith. On these azimaths is reckoned the height of the stars and of the sun when not in the meridian.

AZMER

Pages 344-344

a town of the East Indies in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the same name, with a very strong castle. It is pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and sometimes visited by the Mogul himself. It is about 62 leagues distant from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGRA">Agra</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> trade of this province is in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>. ASOGA ships, are those Spanish ships <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the quicksilver ships, from their carrying quicksilver to the Spanish West Indies, in order to extract the silver out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. These ships, strictly speaking, are not to carry any goods unless for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>'s account.

AZONI

Pages 344-344

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a name applied by the Greeks to such of the gods as were deities at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, not appropriated to the worship of any particular town <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but acknowledged in general by all countries, and worshipped by every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. These the Latins called dii communes. Of this sort were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNA">Luna</a>, &c.

AZORES

Pages 344-344
islands in the Atlantic ocean, lying between 25° and 33° degrees of west longitude, and between 36° and 40° degrees of north latitude. They belong to the Portuguese, and are also called the Western

AZOTH

Pages 344-345

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> of a metal; more particularly that which they call the mercury of philosophers, which they pretended to draw from all sorts of metallic bodies.

AZOTUS

Pages 345-345

AZOTH, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ASHDOD, one of the five cities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>, and a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port on the Mediterranean, situated about 14 or 15 miles south of Ekron, between that and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASCALON">Ascalon</a>. It was in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> that the idol <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAGON">Dagon</a> fell <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> before the ark: and so strong a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> it was, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may believe <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, that it sustained a siege of 29 years by Phaemmeticus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. It was, however, taken by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACCABEES">Maccabees</a> in a much shorter <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; who burnt both city and temple, and with them about 1000 men. The town is now called by the Arabs Ashdun. It is but thinly inhabited, though the situation is very pleasant: with regard to the houses, those that were built in the time of Christianity, and which are now inhabited by Mahometans, still preserve some claim to admiration; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> buildings, though generally of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, have nothing in them which can attract the notice of a traveller. The streets are pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, the inhabitants mostly Mahometans, with a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, who have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> under the jurisdiction of the archbishop of Gaza. The town is about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in circumference; and has in it a mosque, a public bath, a market-place, and two inns. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the inhabitants is between two and three thousand. The most remarkable things in this place is an old structure with fine marble pillars, which the inhabitants say was the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> that Samson pulled down; and to the south-east, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> out of the town, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in which the eunuch Candace was baptized by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>: besides these two, there are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> buildings, with capitals and pillars standing.

AZURE

Pages 345-345

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the blue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the sky. See Sky and Blue. Azure, among Painters. This word, which at present signifies in general a fine blue colour, was formerly applied to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> lazuli, called azure <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and to the blue prepared from it. But since a blue has been extracted from cobalt, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> has applied to it the name of azure, although it differs considerably from the former, and is incapable of being used for the same purposes, and particularly for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. The former at present is called lapis lazuli, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> only lapis; and the blue prepared from it for painting in oil, is called <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ULTRAMARINE">ultramarine</a>.—The name azure is generally applied to the blue glass made from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> of cobalt and vitrifiable matters. This glass, which is called <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMALT">smalt</a> when in masses, is called azure only when it is reduced to a fine powder. Several kinds of azure are distinguished, according to its degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, by the names of fine azure, powdered azure, and azure of four fires. In general, the more intense the colour, and the finer the powder, the more beautiful and dear it is. Azure is employed to colour <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>; hence it has also been called starch blue. It is used for painting with colours, and for a blue enamel. Azure, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, the blue colour in the arms of any person below the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a baron. In the escutcheon of a nobleman, it is called sapphire; and in that of a sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. In engraving, this colour is expressed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> or strokes drawn horizontally.—This colour may signify <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a>, Perseverance, and Vigilance; but according to G. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEIGH">Leigh</a>, when compounded with | Or | Arg. | Gul. | Ver. | Pur. | Sab. | |----|-----|------|-----|-----|-----| | | | | | | | | Cheerfulness. | Vigilance. | Readiness. | Enterprise. | Goodness. | Mournfulness. | French heralds, M. Upton, and his followers, rank this colour before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULES">gules</a>.

AZYGOS

Pages 345-345

in Anatomy, a vein rising within the thorax, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> side, having no fellow on the left; whence it is called azygos, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vena sine pari.

AZYMITES

Pages 345-345

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> who administer the eucharist with unleavened <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. The word is formed from the Greek α priv. and ζύμη, ferment.—This appellation is given to the Latin by the Greek church, because the members of the former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> fermented bread in the celebration of the eucharist. They also call the Armenians and Maronites by the same name, and for the same reason.

AZYMOUS

Pages 345-346

something unfermented, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> made without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAVEN">leaven</a>; as unleavened <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> biscuit is of this kind; and therefore, according to Galen, less wholesome than bread that has been fermented. B. B, THE <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the English and most other alphabets. It is the first consonant, and first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">mute</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> is supposed to resemble the bleating of a sheep; upon which account Pierius tells us in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>, that the Egyptians represented the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of this letter by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of that animal. B is also one of those letters which the eastern grammarians call labial, because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> organs employed in its pronunciation are the lips. It is pronounced ced by pressing the whole length of them together, and forcing them open with a strong breath. It has a near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with the other labials P and V, and is often used for P both by the Armenians and other orientals, as in Betrus for Petrus, opferos for abfens, &c.; and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> for V, as in amalit for amavit, bernia for verma, &c., whence arose that jest of Aurelian on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Bonosus, Non ut vivat natura eft, fed ut libat. Plutarch observes, that the Macedonians changed Φ into B, and pronounced Bilip, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERENICE">Berenice</a>, &c. for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, Pherecine, &c.; and those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHOS">Delphos</a> used B instead of Π, βαλιν for παλιν, βάρος for πάρος, &c.—The Latins said fuppono, oppono, for fulpono, obpono; and pronounced optimum, though they wrote obtinuit, as Quintilian has observed.—They also used B for F or Pf; thus, in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inscription mentioned by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GRUTER">Gruter</a>, Obrendario, is used for Ofrendario. As a numeral B was used by the Greeks and Hebrews to denote 2; but among the Romans for 300, and with a dash over it (thus B) for 3000. B is also used as an abbreviation. Thus B.A. stands for bachelor of arts; B.L. for bachelor of laws; and B.D. for bachelor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. B.F. in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the decrees or senatus consults of the old Romans signified bonum factum. In music, B stands for the tone above A; as B♭, or bB, does for B flat, or the semitone <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> above A. B also stands for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a>; and B.C. for bass continuo, or thorough bass.

BAAL

Pages 346-346

the same as Bel, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Belus; an idol of the Chaldeans, and Phoenicians or Canaanites. The former worshipped <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> under this name, according to Josephus*; who, speaking of Thurus the successor of Nimus, says, "To this Mars the Assyrians erected the first statue, and worshipped him as a god, calling him Baal." It is probable the Phoenicians worshipped the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> under the name of Baal; for Josiah, willing to make some amends for the wickedness of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>, in worshipping Baal, and all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOST">host</a> of heaven, put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> the idolatrous priests that burnt incense unto Baal, to the sun, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, and to all the host of heaven. He likewise took away the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun, and burnt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> of the sun with fire†. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> consecrated to this god, are called in the Scripture Chamanim, which signifies places enclosed with walls in which was kept a perpetual fire. Maundrell, in his journey from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, observed some traces of these enclosures in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. In most of them were no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>; in a few there were some, but of no uniform <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The word baal (in the Punic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>), signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; and doubtless meant the supreme Deity, the Lord and Master of the universe. It is often joined with the name of some false god, as Baal-berith, Baal-petor, Baal-zephon, and the like. This deity passed from the Phoenicians to the Carthaginians, who were a colony of the Phoenicians; as appears from the Carthaginian names, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>, Asdrubal, &c., according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the east, where kings and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men added to their own names those of their gods. This false deity is frequently mentioned in Scripture in the plural <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> (Baalim); which may signify, either that the name Baal was given to several different gods; or that there were many statues, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> different appellations, consecrated to this idol. Arnobius tells us, that Baal was of an uncertain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; and that his votaries, when they called upon him, invoked him thus: Hear us, whether thou art a god or a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>. Some learned men think, that the Baal of the Phoenicians is the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> of the Greeks; which is probable enough from the conformity there is between the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> sacrifices offered to Saturn and those which the Scripture tells us were offered to Baal. Others are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that Baal was the Phoenician or Tyrian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, a god of great antiquity in Phoenicia.

BAAL-BERITH

Pages 346-346

the god of the Shechemites. Bochart conjectures, that Berith is the same as Beroe, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Venus and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADONIS">Adonis</a>, who was given in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>; and that she gave her name to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Berith in Phoenicia, and became afterwards the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of it. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAAL">Baal</a>-berith signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> of the covenant, and may be taken for the god who presides over alliances and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a>, in like manner as the Greeks had their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZEUS">Zeus</a> oikos, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> their Deus Fidius, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Pillius. The idolatrous Israelites, we are told, made Baal-berith their god, Judg. viii. 33.

BAAL-PEOR

Pages 346-346
Baal-phegor, or Beel-phegor, an idol of the Moabites and Midianites. We are told, that Israel joined himself to Baal-peor; and that Solomon erected an altar to this idol upon the mount of Olives. Baal-peor has been supposed to be no other than a Priapus, and that the worship of him consisted in the most obscene practices. Others have thought, that as Baal is a general name signifying Lord, Peor may be the name of some great prince deified after his death. Mede imagines, that Peor being the name of a mountain in the country of Moab, on which the temple of Baal was built, Baal-peor may be only another name of that deity, taken from the situation of his temple; in like manner as Jupiter is styled Olympius, because he was worshipped in a temple built on Mount Olympus. Selden, who is of this latter opinion, conjectures likewise, that Baal-peor is the same with Pluto; which he grounds upon these words of the Psalmist*, They joined themselves unto Baal-peor, and ate the offerings of the dead; though by the sacrifices or offerings of the dead, in this passage, may be meant no more than sacrifices or offerings made to idols, or false gods, who are very properly called the dead, in contradiction to the true God, who is styled in Scripture the living God.

BAAL-ZEUBU

Pages 346-346

Beel-zebul, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Belzebul; the idol, or god, of the Ekronites. In Scripture he is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of Devils. His name is rendered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> of Flies, or the God-fly; which some think was a mock appellation bestowed on him by the Jews. He had a famous temple and oracle at Ekron. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AHAZIAH">Ahaziah</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Israel, having fallen from the terrace of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> into a lower room, and being dangerously hurt, sent to consult this deity, to know <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he should be cured of his wounds. The worship of this false god must have prevailed in our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, since the Jews accused him of driving out devils in the name of Belzebul their prince. Scaliger derives the name of this deity from Baalim-zebahim, which signifies the Lord of sacrificers.

BABBLING

Pages 346-346

among Hunters, is when the hounds are too busy after they have found a good scent.

BABEL MANDEL

Pages 347-347

the gate of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>; a famous strait in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Felix in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and that of Adel and Zeila in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, at the entrance into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. By some it is also called the Straits of Moka. It is narrow, and difficult to sail through, on account of the sand banks. At the mouth of the strait is a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> called also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BABEL">Babel</a> Mandel, which is little else than a barren rock. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 44. 30. N. Lat. 12. 40.

BABENHAUSEN

Pages 347-347

a town of Germany in Swabia. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 16. N. Lat. 48. 39.

BABINA

Pages 347-347

COMMONWEALTH OF, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> ludicrously so called, which was founded in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> in the reign of Sigismund Augustus, in the 16th century. It took its rise from a set of gentlemen, inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUBLIN">Lublin</a>, who had agreed to meet at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called Babina, merely for the purposes of mirth and jollity. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> increased, and they formed themselves into a regular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, under the presidency of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. The magistrates were elected from something which appeared ridiculous in the character <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conduct of any of the members. For instance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any person was meddling or officious, he was immediately created an archbishop; a blundering or disputations member was promoted to the speaker's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>; a boaster of his own courage, and vain-glorious Thraso, was honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERALISSIMO">generalissimo</a>, which was presented him with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> by the subordinate heroes. Those who declined the office for which they were declared qualified were persecuted with hisings, and abandoned by the society. Thus every vice and every foible was attacked with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>; and Babina became in a short time the terror, the admiration, and the reformer, of the Polish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>: genius flourished, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> was cultivated, and the abuses which had crept into government and society were corrected by the judicious application of good humoured satire. Never did any <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> become so general or so useful; but at length it degenerated into a set of buffoons, and banterers of every thing sacred or profane. For several years it was patronized by the kings of Poland, and Sigismund himself became a member; the starosta of Babina telling him jocularly, that "his majesty had certain qualities which entitled him to the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in the commonwealth." Not the least remnant of the society now remains, though it was honoured with extraordinary privileges by kings and emperors.

BABINGTON

Pages 347-348

Gervase, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, wa Baboon, was born, according to Fuller, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a>; but in what year is uncertain. He was sent to Trinity <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, of which he was made fellow; and, in 1578, was incorporated <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. He appears, however, to have made Cambridge the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his residence, where he became an eminent preacher; and, being now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> chaplain to Henry <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>. In this station he is supposed to have assisted the countess in her translation of the Psalms. In 1588 he was installed prebend of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>, and in 1591 consecrated bishop of Landaff. In 1564 he was translated to the see of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, and thence to Worcester in 1597. About this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> soon after, he was made <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s counsellor for the marches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. He was a considerable benefactor to the library belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of Worcester, where he was buried in May 1610 without a monument. The several historians who have mentioned this prelate agree in giving him the character of a learned and pious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. His writings, like those of most of his contemporaries, abound with puns and quaint expressions. His works were printed both in folio and quarto in 1615, and again in folio in 1637, under this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>: The works of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> reverend father in God Gervase Babington, late bishop of Worcester, containing comfortable notes upon the five books of Moses, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>, &c. As also an exposition upon the Creed, the Ten Commandments, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">Prayer</a>; with a conference betwixt man's frailties and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and three sermons, &c.

BABYLON

Pages 348-351

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Chaldea, and supposed to have stood in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 44° N. Lat. 32° O. Semiramis is said by some, and Belus by others, to have founded this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. But, by whomsoever it was founded, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a> was the person who put the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to it, and made it one of the wonders of the world. The most famous works in and about it were the walls of the city, the temple of Belus, Nebuchadnezzar's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, the hanging-gardens, the banks of the river, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> lake, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>. The city was surrounded with walls, in thickness 87 feet, in height 350 feet; and in compass 480 furlongs or 60 of our miles. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, who was himself at Babylon; and though some disagree with him in these dimensions, yet most writers give us the same, or nearly the same, as he does. Diodorus Siculus diminishes the circumference of these walls very considerably, and takes somewhat from the height of them, as in Herodotus; though he seems to add to their breadth by saying, that six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> might drive abreast thereon: while the former writes, that one chariot only might turn upon them; but then he places buildings on each side of the top of these walls, which, according to him, were but one story <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; which may pretty well reconcile them together in this respect. It is observed, that those who give the height of these walls but at 50 cubits, speak of them only as they were after the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> Hystaspis, who had caused them to be beaten <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>. These walls formed an exact <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, each side of which was 120 furlongs, or 15 miles, in length; and were all built of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bricks cemented together with bitumen, which in a short time grows harder than the very brick and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> which it cements. The city was encompassed, without the walls, with a vast ditch filled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and lined with bricks on both sides; and, as the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> that was dug out of it served to make the bricks, we may judge of the depth and largeness of the ditch from the height and thickness of the walls. In the whole compass of the wall there were 100 gates, that is, 25 on each of the four sides, all made of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bricks. Between every two of these gates, at proper distances, were three towers, and four more at the four corners of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> square, and three between each of these corners and the next gate on either side, and each of these towers was ten feet higher than the walls. But this is to be understood only of those parts of the walls where towers were needful for defense. For some parts of them being upon a morass, and inaccessible by an enemy, there the labour and cost was spared, which, though it must have spoiled the symmetry of the whole, must be allowed to have favoured of good economy; though that is what one would not have expected from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> who had been so determined, as Nebuchadnezzar must have been, to make the city complete both for strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, then, of these towers amounted to no more than 250; whereas a much greater number would have been necessary to have made the uniformity complete all round. From each of the 25 gates on each side of this square, there was a straight street, extending to the corresponding gate in the opposite wall; whence the whole number of the streets must have been but 50; but then they were each about 15 miles long, 25 of them crossing the other 25 exactly at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>. Besides these whole streets, we must reckon four half streets, which were but rows of houses facing the four inner faces of the walls. These four half streets were properly the four sides of the city within the walls, and were each of them 200 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, the whole streets being about 150 of the same. By this interposition of the 50 streets, the city was divided into 676 squares, each of four furlongs and a half on each side, or two miles and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> in compass. Round these squares, on every side towards the streets, stood the houses, all of three or four stories in height, and beautified with all manner of ornaments; and the space within each of these squares was all void, and taken up by yards, or gardens, and the like, either for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> or convenience. A branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> divided the city into two, running through the midst of it, from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south; over which, in the very middle of the city, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURLONG">furlong</a> in length, or rather more; and indeed much more, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we hearken to others, who say it was no less than five stades or furlongs in length, though but 30 feet broad, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> we shall never be able to decide. This bridge, however, is said to have been built with wonderful art, to supply a defect in the bottom of the river, which was all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>. At each end of this bridge were two palaces: the old palace on the east side, the new one on the west side of the river; the former of which took up four of the squares above-mentioned, and the latter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>. The temple of Belus, which stood next to the old palace, took up another of the same squares. The whole city stood in a large flat or plain, in a very fat and deep <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>: that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> or half of it on the east side of the river was the old city, and the other on the west was added by Nebuchadnezzar, both being included within the vast square bounded by the walls aforesaid. The form of the whole was seemingly borrowed from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINEVEH">Nineveh</a>, which was also 450 furlongs; but though it was equal in dimensions to this city, it was less with respect to its form, which was a parallelogram, whereas that of Babylon was an exact square. It is supposed, that Nebuchadnezzar, who had destroyed that old seat of the Assyrian empire, proposed that this new one should rather exceed it; and that it was in order to fill it with inhabitants, that he transported such numbers of the captives from other countries hither; though that is what may be disputed, seeing he therein only followed the constant practice of the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, who thought this the most certain means of ensuring their conquests either to themselves or their posterity. But it plainly appears, that it was never wholly inhabited; so that, even in the meridian of its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, it may be compared with the flower of the field, which flourishes to-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and to-morrow is no more. It never had time to grow up to what Nebuchadnezzar visibly intended to have made it; for, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> removing the seat of the empire soon after Shulman, Babylon fell by degrees to utter decay: yet it must be owned, that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was better able to support so vast and populous a city, had it been completed up to its first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. But so far was it from being finished according to its original design, that, when Alexander came to Babylon, Q. Curtius tells us, "No more than 90 furlongs of it were then built;" which can be no otherwise understood than of so much in length; and, if we allow the breadth to be as much as the length (which is the utmost that can be allowed), it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> follow, that no more than 8100 square furlongs were then built upon: but the whole space within the walls contained 14,400 square furlongs; and therefore there must have been 6300 square furlongs remaining unbuilt, which, Curtius tells us, were ploughed and sown. And, besides this, the houses were not contiguous, but all built with a void space on each side, between <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and house. The next great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Nebuchadnezzar was the temple of Belus. The wonderful tower, however, that stood in the middle of it, was not his work, but was built many ages before; that, and the famous tower of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BABEL">Babel</a>, being, as is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> supposed, one and the same structure. This tower is said to have been composed of eight pyramidal ones raised above one another, and by Herodotus said to have been a furlong in height; but as there is an ambiguity in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, it has been disputed whether each of the towers was a furlong in height, or the whole of them taken together. On the latter supposition, which is the most probable, this tower must have exceeded the height of the Egyptian pyramids by 170 feet, though it fell short of its breadth at the basis by 33. The way to go up was by stairs on the outside round it; whence it seems most likely, that the whole ascent was, by the benching in, drawn in a sloping line from the bottom to the top eight times round it; and that this made the appearance of eight towers, one above the other. Till the times of Nebuchadnezzar, it is thought this tower was all the temple of Belus; but as he did by the other ancient buildings of the city, so he did by Babylon, this, making great additions thereto, by vast edifices erected round it, in a square of two furlongs on every side, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in circumference, which exceeded the square at the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> by 1800 feet. On the outside of these buildings was a wall, which enclosed the whole; and, in consideration of the regularity wherewith this city was to all appearance marked out, it is supposed, that this wall was equal to the square of the city wherein it stood, and so is concluded to have been two miles and a half in circumference. In this wall were several gates leading into the temple, and all of solid <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>; which it is thought may have been made out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZEN_SEA">brazen <a </a>class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and brazen pillars, and other vessels and ornaments of the kind, which Nebuchadnezzar had transported from Jerusalem; for in this temple he is said to have dedicated his spoils from that of Jerusalem. In this temple were several images or idols of maffy idols of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and one of them, as we have seen, 40 feet in height; the same, as supposed, with that which Nebuchadnezzar consecrated in the plains of Dura. For though this last is said to have been 60 cubits, or 90 feet high, these dimensions appear so incredible, that it has been attempted to reconcile them into one, by supposing, that in the 90 feet the height of the pedestal is included, and that the 40 feet are for the height of the statue without the pedestal; and being said to have weighed 1000 talents of Babylon, it is thence computed, that it was worth three millions and a half of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. In a word, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and decorations, in Diodorus Siculus, amounting to 3000 and odd talents in gold, the whole is estimated at above 21,000,000. of our money; and a sum about equal to the same, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, utensils, and ornaments, not mentioned, is allowed for. Next to this temple, on the east side of the river, stood the old palace of the kings of Babylon, being four miles in circumference. Exactly opposite to it, on the other side of the river, was the new palace built by Nebuchadnezzar, eight miles in circumference, and consequently four times as big as the old one. But nothing was more wonderful at Babylon than the hanging-gardens, which Nebuchadnezzar made in gardens, compliance to his wife Amyte; who, being a Mede, and retaining a strong inclination for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and forests of her own country, was desirous of having something like them at Babylon. They are said to have contained a square of four plethra, or 400 feet, on each side; and to have consisted of terraces one above another, carried up to the height of the wall of the city, the ascent from terrace to terrace being by steps ten feet wide. The whole pile consisted of substantial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> upon arches, and was strengthened by a wall surrounding it on every side, 22 feet thick; and the floors on each of them were laid in this order; first, on the tops of the arches was laid a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> or pavement of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> 16 feet long, and four feet broad; over this was a layer of reed mixed with a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of bitumen; and over this two courses of brick, closely cemented together with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>; and over all these were thick fleeces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and on these the earth or mould of the garden. This floorage was designed to retain the moisture of the mould; which was so deep, as to give root to the greatest trees which were planted up. on every terrace, together with great variety of other vegetables pleasing to the eye. Upon the uppermost of these terraces was a reservoir, supplied by a certain engine with water from the river, from whence the gardens on the other terraces were supplied. The other works attributed to Nebuchadnezzar by Berossus and Abydenus, were the banks of the river, the artificial canals, and the great artificial lake said to have been sunk by Semiramis. The canals were cut out on the east side of the Euphrates, to convey the water of the river, when it overflowed its banks, into the Tigris, before they reached Babylon. The lake was on the west side of Babylon; and, according to the lowest computation, 40 miles square, 160 in compass, and in depth 35 feet, as we read in Herodotus, or 75, as Megasthenes will have it; the former, perhaps, measured from the surface of the sides, and the latter from the tops of the banks that were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> up upon them. This lake was dug to receive the waters of the river, while the banks were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> on each side of it. But both the lake, and the canal which led to it, were preferred after that work was completed, being found of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, not only to prevent all overflows, but to keep water all the year, as in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> reservoir, to be let out, on proper occasions, by sluices, for the improvement of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. The banks were built of brick and bitumen, on both sides of the river, to keep it within its channel; and extended on each side throughout the whole length of the city, and even farther, according to some, who reckon they extended 160 furlongs, or twenty miles; whence it is concluded they must have begun two miles and a half above the city, and have been <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> an equal distance below it, the length of the city being no more than 15 miles. Within the city they were built from the bottom of the river, and of the same thickness with the walls of the city itself. Opposite to each street, on either side of the river, was a brazen gate in the said wall, with stairs leading down from it to the river: these gates were open by day, and shut by night. Berossus, Megasthenes, and Abydenus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> all these works to Nebuchadnezzar; but Herodotus tells us, the bridge, the banks, and the lake, were the work of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> after him, called Nitocris, who may have finished what Nebuchadnezzar left imperfect, and thence have had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> this historian gives her of the whole. The tower or temple stood till the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a>. But that prince, on his return from the Grecian expedition, having first plundered it of its immense wealth, demolished the whole, and laid it in ruins. Alexander, on his return to Babylon from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> expedition, proposed to rebuild it, and accordingly set 10,000 men to work to clear away the rubbish. But his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> happening soon after, a stop was put to all further proceedings in that design. After the death of that conqueror, the city of Babylon began to decline apace; which was chiefly owing to the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>, built by Seleucus Nicator, as is said, out of state to the Babylonians, and peopled with 500,000 persons drawn from Babylon, by which that means continued declining till the very people of the country were at a loss to tell where it had stood. Such is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> we have by ancient historians of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of this city; which, if these accounts are not exaggerated, must have exceeded every piece of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> grandeur that hath yet appeared. Many of the moderns, however, are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that these magnificent descriptions are very far from being true; although it is certain that few other arguments can be brought against the reality of them, than that we do not see things of a similar kind executed in our own days. The following are the arguments used on this subject by the present Goguet. "Authors have greatly extolled the public works and edifices which once rendered Babylon one of the wonders of the world. We may reduce all these objects to five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> heads: 1. the height of its walls; 2. the temple of Belus; 3. the hanging gardens; 4. the bridge built over the river Euphrates, and the quays which lined the river; 5. the lake and canals dug by the hand of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to distribute the waters of the Euphrates. "All these works, so marvellous in the judgment of Goguet's antiquity, appear to me to have been extremely exaggerated by the authors who have spoke of them. How can we conceive, in effect, that the walls of Babylon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the could have been 318 feet high, and 81 in thickness, in relation to a compass of near ten leagues? "I shall lay the fame of that square building, known under the name of the temple of Belus. It was composed of eight towers placed one above another, diminishing always as they went up. Herodotus does not tell us what was the height of this monument. Diodorus says, that it surpassed all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>. Strabo fixes it to one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADIUM">stadium</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> which answers nearly to 600 of our feet. For in the time of this geographer the Iliad were much more considerable than in the first ages. The entire <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of this building ought to have been antipodal to its excessive height; and this is also the idea that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> designed to give us of it. We may judge by the following fact. Xerxes had entirely demolished this temple. Alexander undertook to rebuild it. He designed to begin by clearing the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and removing the ruins. Ten thousand workmen who were employed two months in this work, were not, say they, able to finish it. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> enclosed in the temple of Belus were proportioned to its immensity. Without speaking of the tables and censers, the cups and other sacred vases, of maffy gold, there was a statue 40 feet high, which alone weighed 1000 Babylonish talents. In short, according to the inventory that the ancients have given us of the riches contained in this temple, the total sum would amount to two hundred and twenty millions and a half of French livres. Exaggerations like these destroy themselves. "As to the hanging gardens, according to all appearance they never existed. The silence of Herodotus on a work so singular and so remarkable, determines one to place in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of fables all that the other writers have delivered upon this pretended wonder. Herodotus had carefully visited Babylon. He enters into such details as prove that he has omitted none of the rarities of that city. Can we presume that he would have passed over in silence such a work as the hanging gardens? All the authors who have spoken of it are of much later <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> than this great historian. None of them except Berossus speaks on his own testimony." mony. It is always on the report of others. Diodorus had extracted from Ctesias what he says of these famous gardens. There is also great appearance that Strabo had drawn from the same source. In a word, the manner in which Quintus Curtius expresses himself sufficiently shows how much the existence of these gardens appeared to him suspicious. He judged they owed the greatest part of it to the imagination of the Greeks. "Let us now speak of the bridge of Babylon, which the ancients have placed in the number of the most marvellous works of the east. It was near 100 fathoms in length, and almost four in breadth. We cannot deny but that a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of art and labour was necessary to lay the foundations, which it could not be easy to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in the bed of an extremely deep and rapid river, which also rolls along a prodigious quantity of mud, and whose bottom is entirely sandy. They had therefore taken many precautions to secure the piers of the bridge of Babylon. They were built of stones joined and fastened together with cramps of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> filled with melted lead. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the piers, turned towards the current of the Euphrates, was defended by buttresses extremely advanced, which diminished the weight and force of the water, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> it at a great distance. Such was the bridge of Babylon. "While we do <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to the skill of the Babylonians in conducting these works, we cannot help remarking the bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> which at all times reigned in the works of the eastern nations. The bridge of Babylon furnishes a striking instance of it. This edifice was absolutely without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, or any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of majesty. The breadth of it was in no sort of proportion to its length. The distance between the piers was also very ill contrived. They were distant from each other only 11 feet and a half. Finally, this bridge was not arched. We may judge of its effect on the view. "The Babylonians, however, were not the only people who were ignorant of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>. This secret, as far as I can find, was unknown to all the people of remote antiquity, who, generally speaking, do not appear to have been very skilful in stone-cutting. "As for the quays which lined the Euphrates, we may believe that they were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and magnificent; but I shall not easily believe that they surpassed those which we have daily under our eye. In this respect, I believe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> may dispute it for magnificence, and for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the work, with all the cities of the universe." Babylon, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> near the eastmost branch of the river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, now supposed to be Grand <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, or this city to stand near its ruins. E. Long. 31. 12. N. Lat. 30. 5.

BABYLONIA

Pages 351-353
or Chaldea, a kingdom of Asia, and the most ancient in the world, being founded by Nimrod the grandson of Ham, who also, according to the margin of our Bibles, founded Nineveh the capital of the kingdom of Assyria. Indeed, these two kingdoms seem to have always continued in such a state of friendship, that we can scarce help thinking they must have been the same, or perhaps Babylonia was for some time a province of Assyria. Nothing certain is known concerning either of them, except what may be gathered from Scripture. From thence we learn, that in the days of Abraham there was a king of Shinar, called Amraphel, who, under the king of Elam or Persia, made war upon the Canaanites. From this time we have nothing that can be depended upon till the days of Nabonassar, the first king of Babylon mentioned in Ptolemy's canon. It is plain, indeed, both from Scripture and profane history, that Babylonia subsisted as a distinct kingdom from Assyria even when the latter was in all its glory. The most probable account of the matter is this: The empire of Assyria was founded by Pul, on the ruins of that of Damascus or Syria, in the days of Manahem king of Judah. This king left two sons, Tiglath-Pileser, and Nabonassar. To the former he bequeathed the empire of Assyria, and to the latter that of Babylon. Tiglath-Pileser resided at Nineveh, the original seat of the Assyrian empire; while Nabonassar, who was the younger brother, held his residence at Babylon. As the two kingdoms were governed by princes of the same family, we may well suppose a perfect harmony to have reigned between them, the younger branch at Babylon acknowledging a kind of subjection to the elder at Nineveh. That the Babylonian empire was of Assyrian origin, we are assured by the prophet Isaiah, in the following words: "Behold the land of the Chaldeans: this people was not till the Assyrians founded it for them that dwelt in the wilderness: they set up the towers thereof; they built the palace thereof." As to the kingdom of Assyria, the Scripture mentions only five kings, viz. Pul, Tiglath-Pileser, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, and Esarhaddon; whose history, as related by the sacred writers, it is needless to mention particularly here. From the days of Nabonassar to Nabopolassar, that is, from the year before Christ 747 to 626, the kings of Babylon made no figure, and were therefore probably in a state of dependence on the kings of Assyria; but at that time, in the reign of Chynnadan, the Sardanapalus of the Greeks, Nineveh was taken and destroyed by the Medes and Babylonians, and the seat of the empire transferred to Babylon. This Nabopolassar was the father of the famous Nebuchadnezzar, for whose history we must refer to the sacred writers; and from his time to that of the Belshazzar of Daniel, and Nabonadius of other authors, the history of Babylon is little better than a mere blank. Of the reduction of Babylon by Cyrus, which happened at this time, we have the following account. War had been begun betwixt the Medes, Persians, and Babylonians, in the reign of Neriglissar the father of Nabonadius, which had been carried on with very bad success on the side of the Babylonians. Cyrus, who commanded the Median and Persian army, having subdued the several nations inhabiting the great continent from the Aegean sea to the Euphrates, bent his march towards Babylon. Nabonadius, hearing of his march, immediately advanced against him with an army. In the engagement which ensued, the Babylonians were defeated; and the king, retreating to his metropolis, was blockaded and closely besieged by Cyrus. The reduction of this city was no easy enterprise. The walls were of a prodigious height, the number of men to defend them very great, and the place stored with all sorts of provisions for 20 years. Cyrus, despairing of being able to take such a city by storm, caused a line of circumvallation to be drawn quite round it, with a large and deep ditch; reckoning, that if all communication with the country were cut off, the besieged would be obliged to surrender through famine. That his troops might not be too much fatigued, he divided his army into twelve bodies, appointing each body its month to guard the trenches; but the besieged, looking upon themselves to be out of all danger by reason of their high walls and magazines, insulted him from the ramparts, and looked upon all the trouble he gave himself as so much unprofitable labour. After Cyrus had spent two whole years before Babylon, without making any progress in the siege, he at last thought of the following stratagem, which put him in possession of it. He was informed, that a great annual solemnity was to be held at Babylon; and that the inhabitants on that occasion were accustomed to spend the whole night in drinking and debauchery. This he therefore thought a proper time for surprising them; and accordingly sent a strong detachment to the head of the canal leading to the great lake, with orders, at a certain time, to break down the great bank which was between the lake and the canal, and to turn the whole current into the lake. At the same time he appointed one body of troops at the place where the river entered the city, and another where it came out; ordering them to march in by the bed of the river as soon as they should find it fordable. Towards the evening he opened the head of the trenches on both sides the river above the city, that the water might discharge itself into them; by which means, and the breaking down of the great dam, the river was soon drained. Then the two above-mentioned bodies of troops, according to their orders, entered the channel; the one commanded by Gobryas and the other by Gadates: and finding the gates all left open by reason of the disorders of that riotous night, they penetrated into the very heart of the city without opposition; and meeting, according to agreement, at the palace, they surprised the guards, and cut them in pieces. Those who were in the palace opening the gates to know the cause of this confusion, the Persians rushed in, took the palace, and killed the king, who came out to meet them sword in hand. Thus an end was put to the Babylonian empire; and Cyrus took possession of Babylon for one called in Scripture Darius the Mede, most probably Cyaxares II., uncle to Cyrus. From this time Babylonia never was erected into a distinct kingdom, but hath always followed the fortune of those great conquerors who at different times have appeared in Asia. It is now frequently the object of contention between the Turks and Persians. See Assyria. Concerning the nature of the country, manners, customs, &c. of the ancient Babylonians, the following account is collected by M. Sabbathier. "As all the nations under the dominion of Cyrus, beside the ordinary tributes, were obliged to maintain him and his army, the monarch and his troops were supported by all Asia. The country of Babylon alone was obliged to maintain him four months of the year; its fertility, therefore, yielded a third of the produce of Asia. The government of this country, which the Persians termed satrapy, was richer and more extensive than any of the rest. It maintained for the king, besides the war-horses, a stud of 800 stallions, and 16,000 mares. So great a number of Indian dogs Babylonia were likewise bred in this province for the king, that four of its cities kept those animals; and in return, they were exempted from all taxes and tributes. "It rained very seldom in this country, according to Herodotus. The earth was watered by the river, which was here diffused by human industry, as the Nile is over Egypt by nature; for all the country of Babylon was divided by canals, the greatest of which was navigable, and flowed from south to north, from the Euphrates to the Tigris. In short, it was one of the finest countries for corn in the world; but for producing trees, the fig-tree, the vine, and the olive, it was not famous. It was so luxuriant in grain, that it commonly yielded a hundred times more than what was sown; and in good years it yielded three hundred times more than it received. The leaves of its wheat and barley were four inches broad. 'Though I know,' says Herodotus, 'that the millet and the fame of that country grow to the size of trees, I will not describe them particularly; lest those who have not been in Babylonia should think my account fabulous.' "They had no oil but what they made from Indian corn. The country abounded with palm-trees, which grew spontaneously; and most of them bore fruit, of which the inhabitants made bread, wine, and honey. They cultivated these trees and their fig-trees in the same manner. Some of them, as of other trees, the Greeks called male ones. They tied the fruit of the male to the trees which bore dates; that the mosquito, leaving the male, might cause the date to ripen, by penetrating it; for without that affluence it came not to maturity. Mosquitos bred in the male palms as in the wild fig-trees. "But we must not here omit to give an account of the peculiar and surprising construction of their boats of skins, in which they sailed along the river to Babylon. These boats were invented by the Armenians, whose country lay north from Babylonia. They made them with poles of willow, which they bent, and covered with skins; the bare side of the skins they put outwards; and they made them so tight, that they resembled boards. The boats had neither prow nor stern, but were of a round form like a buckler. They put straw on the bottom. Two men, each with an oar, rowed them down the river, laden with different wares, but chiefly with palm wine. Of these boats some were very large, and some very small. The largest carried the weight of 500 talents. There was room for an ass in one of their small boats; they put many into a large one. When they had unloaded, after their arrival at Babylon, they sold the poles of their boats and the straw; and loading their asses with the skins, returned to Armenia; for they could not fail up the river, its current was so rapid. For this reason they made their boats of skins, instead of wood; and on their return to Armenia with their asses, they applied the skins to their former use. "As to their dress, they wore a linen shirt, which came down to their feet. Over it they wore a woollen robe; their outer garment was a white vest. Their shoes resembled those of the Thebans. They let their hair grow. On their heads they wore a turban. They rubbed their bodies all over with fragrant liquors. Each Each man had a ring on his finger, and an elegant cane in his hand, with an apple at the top, or a rose, a lily, or an eagle, or some other figure; for they were not suffered to use canes without devices. "With regard to their policy, Herodotus thinks that their best law was one which the Heneti, an Illyrian people, likewise observed in every town and village. When the girls were marriageable, they were ordered to meet in a certain place, where the young men likewise assembled. They were then sold by the public crier; but he first sold the most beautiful one. When he had sold her at an immense price, he put up others to sale, according to their degrees of beauty. The rich Babylonians were emulous to carry off the finest women, who were sold to the highest bidders. But as the young men who were poor could not aspire to have fine women, they were content to take the ugliest with the money which was given them; for when the crier had sold the handsomest, he ordered the ugliest of all the women to be brought; and asked, if any one was willing to take her with a small sum of money. Thus she became the wife of him who was most easily satisfied; and thus the finest women were sold; and from the money which they brought, small fortunes were given to the ugliest, and to those who had any bodily infirmity. A father could not marry his daughter as he pleased; nor was he who bought her allowed to take her home, without giving security that he would marry her. But, after the sale, if the parties were not agreeable to each other, the law enjoined that the purchase-money should be restored. The inhabitants of any of their towns were permitted to marry wives at these auctions. Such were the early customs of the Babylonians. "But they afterwards made a law, which prohibited the inhabitants of different towns to intermarry, and by which husbands were punished for treating their wives ill. When they had become poor by the ruin of their metropolis, fathers used to prostitute their daughters for gain. There was a sensible custom among the Babylonians, worthy to be related. They brought their sick into the forum, to consult those who passed on their diseases; for they had no physicians. They asked those who approached the sick, if they ever had the same distemper? If they knew any one who had it? and how he was cured? Hence, in this country, every one who saw a sick person was obliged to go to him and inquire into his distemper. "They embalmed their dead with honey; and their mourning was like that of the Egyptians. "There were three Babylonian tribes, who lived only upon fish, and who prepared them in the following manner: they dried them in the sun, and then beat them in a mortar to a kind of flour, which after they had sifted through linen, they baked it in rolls. "The Babylonians at first worshipped only the sun and the moon; but they soon multiplied their deities. They deified Baal, Bel, or Belus, one of their kings, and Merodach-Baladan. They also worshipped Venus, under the name of Mylitta. She and Belus were the principal deities of the Babylonians. They counted their days from sunrise to sunrise. They solemnized five days of the year with great magnificence, and almost the same ceremonies with which the Romans celebrated their Saturnalia. "The Babylonians were very much addicted to judicial astrology. Their priests who openly professed that art, were obliged to commit to writing all the events of the lives of their illustrious men; and on a fancied connection between those events and the motions of the heavenly bodies, the principles of their art were founded. They pretended that some of their books, in which their historical transactions and revolutions were accurately compared with the courses of the stars, were thousands of years old. This assertion of their judicial astrologers we may reasonably dispute; but that their astronomers had made a long series of observation, is incontestably true. It is certain that some of those observations were extant in the days of Aristotle, and that they were older than the empire of the Babylonians." See History of Astronomy.

BABYLONIAN

Pages 353-353

BABYLONIUS, is used in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers for an astrologer, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> anything related to astrology. Hence <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a> cura, the art of casting nativities; and numeri Babylonii, the computation of astrologers.

BABYLONICA TEXTA

Pages 353-353

a rich sort of weavings, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hangings, denominated from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, where the practice of interweaving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> colours in their hangings first obtained. Hence also Babylonics garments, Babylonic skins, Babylonic carpets, hangings, &c. Babylonic solana, coverings laid over couches, &c., painted with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, purple, and other colours.

BABYLONICS

Pages 353-353

BABYLONICA, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a fragment of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> history of the world, ending at 267 years before Christ; and composed by Berossus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Berothus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Alexander. Babylonics are sometimes also cited in ancient writers by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Chaldaicae. The Babylonics were very consonant with Scripture, as Josephus and the ancient Christian chronologers affirm; whence the author is usually supposed to have consulted the Jewish writers. Berossus speaks of an universal deluge, an ark, &c. He reckons ten generations between the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and the deluge; and marks the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the several generations by saroi, or periods of 223 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> months; which reduced to years, differ not much from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> of Moses.—The Babylonics consisted of three books, including the history of the ancient Babylonians, Medes, &c. But only a few imperfect extracts are now remaining of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; preserved chiefly by Josephus and Syncellus, where all the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of citations of ancient authors out of Berossus are collected with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> exactness. Annius of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VITERBO">Viterbo</a>, to supply the loss, forged a complete Berossus out of his own head. The world has not thanked him for the imposture.

BAC

Pages 353-354

in Distillery, vessels into which the liquor to be fermented is pumped from the cooler, in order to be worked with yeast. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> Maker, is one who makes liquor-bacs, under-bacs, coolers, math-tuns, working-tuns, &c., for the brewers. The workmanship is partly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARPENTRY">carpentry</a>, in a particular manner, for it must be tight enough to hold liquor; and partly cooperage, viz., the math-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUN">tun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vat, which is hooped. There are not many of this trade; and it requires chiefly strength, with a little art. A small stock of stuff, besides tools, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> set a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> up tolerably well; but with 200l. or 300l. he will make a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in business.

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Crime <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, and, as the khan usually takes up his residence there, it may be considered as the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. in middle-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, denotes a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-farms, consisting of several manors.
