BACCARACH

Pages 354-354

a town of Germany in the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a>; formerly imperial and free, but now subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> Palatine. It is famous for excellent wine; and is situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 5'. N. Lat. 49° 57'. BACCHÆ, in Antiquity, the priestesses of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, who celebrated the orgia <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of that god. The word was also used for the ivy crowns or garlands worn by the priests of Bacchus, in offering sacrifices to him.

BACCHANALIA

Pages 354-354

feasts celebrated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. The two most remarkable were called the greater and lesser. The latter called lenae, from a word signifying a wine-pref, were held in the open fields about autumn; the greater, called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIONYSIA">Dionysia</a>, from one of the names of Bacchus, were celebrated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, about the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Both these feasts were accompanied with games, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a>, and theatrical representations; and it was at this time the poets contended for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. Those who were initiated into the celebration of these feasts, represented, some Silenus; others, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>; others, Satyrs; and in this manner appeared in public, night and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, counterfeiting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUNKENNESS">drunkenness</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> obscenely, and committing all kinds of licentiousness and debauchery. See Bacchus.

BACCHI

Pages 354-354

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, in form of goats, used by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, in his wars against the giants. Rudbeck describes two kinds of bacchi, one made like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERING">battering</a>-ram, wherewith Jupiter demolished the enemy's fortifications; the other contrived to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> fire out of, from whence the Greeks are conjectured to have framed their idea of the chimera.

BACCHIC

Pages 354-354

something relating to the ceremonies of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. The celebrated intaglio, called Michael Angelo's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>, is representation of a Bacchic feast. Bacchic song, is sometimes used for a chanon à boire, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> to inspire jollity. But in a more proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is restrained to a dithyrambic ode or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a>.

BACCHINI

Pages 354-354

Benedict, a Benedictine monk, and one of the most learned men in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORGO">Borgo</a> San Domino in 1651; and wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of books in Latin and Italian, the most considerable of which is a Literary Journal. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a> in 1721, aged 70.

BACCHUS

Pages 354-355

in Heathen <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, the god of wine, with whose fabulous adventures every school-boy is acquainted. This personage is seldom named in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times but as a sensual encourager of feasting and jollity; but he was regarded in a more respectable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, who worshipped him in different countries under the following appellations: in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, he was called Ophiris; in Mycia, Fanaces; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, Dianysus; in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>; and Pentheus, by the Lucanians. Mythologists furnish reasons for all these different names given to the same god, which may be seen in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of Banier's Mythology. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to suppose that the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, as usual, bestowed upon the one Bacchus which they worshipped, the several actions and attributes of the many divinities known by that name, and by other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> denominations in different countries. However, Bacchus, ever, antiquity chiefly distinguished two gods under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Bacchus: that of Egypt, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a>, and the same as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>; and that of Thebes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Semele. The Egyptian Bacchus was brought up at Nysa, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Arabia Felix, whence he acquired the name of Dionysius, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the god of Nysa; and this was the conqueror of India. Though this Bacchus of the Egyptians was one of the elder gods of Egypt, yet the son of Semele was the youngest of the Grecian deities. Diodorus Siculus tells us, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a> first deified the son of Semele by the name of Bacchus, and appointed his ceremonies in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, in order to render the family of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a>, the grandfather of the Grecian Bacchus, illustrious. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Bacchus, according to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, flourished but one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> before the Argonautic expedition. This Bacchus, says Hermippus, was potent at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, conquered eastward as far as India, returned in triumph, brought his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> over the Hellespont, conquered Thrace, and left music, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> there. And, according to Diodorus Siculus, it was the son of Semele who invented farces and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>, and who first established a music school, excepting from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> functions such musicians as discovered great abilities in their art; on which account, says the same author, musicians formed into companies have since frequently enjoyed great privileges. Dr Burney * observes, that the dithyrambs which gave birth to dramatic representations, are as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> as the worship of Bacchus in Greece; and there is little doubt but that the ceremonies of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> gave rise to the pomp and illusions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. Many of the most splendid exhibitions upon the stage for the entertainment of the people of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and Rome, being performed upon the festivals of Bacchus, gave occasion to the calling all those that were employed in them, whether for singing, dancing, or reciting, servants of Bacchus. Paulanias, in his Attics, speaks of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at Athens consecrated to Bacchus the finger; thus named, he says, for the same reason as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> and conductor of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>. Whence it should seem that Bacchus was regarded by the Athenians not only as the god of wine, but of song; and it must be owned, that his followers, in their cups, have been much inclined to fingering ever since. Indeed we are certain, that in none of the orgies, processions, triumphs, and festivals, instituted by the ancients to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of bons vivants, music was forgotten, as may be still gathered from ancient <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, where we find not only that musicians, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, regaled him with the lyre, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>, and with song; but that he was accompanied by fawns and satyrs playing upon timbrels, cymbals, bagpipes, and horns; these Suidas calls his ministrils; and Strabo gives them the appellations of Bacchi, Sileni, Satyri, Bacche, Leucos, Thyrs, Mamillones, Naiades, Nymphae, and Titiri. These representations have furnished subjects for the finest remains of ancient sculpture; and the most voluptuous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of ancient poetry are descriptions of the orgies and festivals of Bacchus. See ORIGIA.

BACCHYLIDES

Pages 355-355

a famous Greek poet, was the nephew of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIMONIDES">Simonides</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> and rival of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>. Both sung the victories of Hiero at the public games. Besides odes to athletic victors, he was author of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> Verses; Profodies; Dithyrambs; Hymns; Peans; Hyparchmes; Parthenia, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> songs to be sung by a chorus of virgins at festivals. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> of Eusebius places the birth of Bacchylides in the 82nd Olympiad, about 450 B.C.

BACCIO

Pages 355-355

FRA. Bartolomeo, called Bartolemei di S. Marco, a celebrated painter of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAVIGNANO">Savignano</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in 1469, and was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Cosimo Rofelli; but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> knowledge in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> was derived from Leonardo da Vinci. He understood the true principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> better than most masters of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and was also a considerable painter in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>; which induced Raphael to have recourse to him after he had quitted the school of Perugino; and under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> likewise Raphael studied the art of managing and uniting colours, as well as the rules of perspective. Some years after the departure of Raphael from Florence, Baccio visited Rome; and by the observations he made on the antiques, and the works of Raphael which were then the admiration of the whole world, he was extremely improved, and manifested his acquired abilities by a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of S. Sebastian, which he finished at his return to Florence. It was so well designed, so naturally and beautifully coloured, and had so strong an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of pain and agony, that it was removed from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it was publicly seen (in the chapel of a convent), as it had been observed to have made too strong an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the imaginations of many women who beheld it. He was very laborious, and made <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> his perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; he designed the naked correctly; his figures had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, and his colouring was admirable. He is accounted to have been the first inventor of that machine called a layman by the artists, and which to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> is in general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Upon that he placed his draperies, to observe with greater exactness their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and their more elegant folds. A <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> picture of the ascension by Baccio, is in the Florentine collection. He died in 1517.

BACCULE

Pages 366-366

in Fortification, a kind of portcullis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> gate, made like a pit-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> with a counterpoise, and supported by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> stakes. It is usually made before the corpade-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, not far from the gate of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.

BACHELOR

Pages 355-357
or Batchelor, a common term for a man not married, or who is yet in a state of celibacy.—The Roman censors frequently imposed fines on old bachelors. Dion Halicarnassus mentions an old constitution, by which all persons of full age were obliged to marry. But the most celebrated law of this kind, was that made under Augustus, called the lex Julia de maritandis ordinibus; by which bachelors were made incapable of legacies or inheritances by will, unless from their near relations. This brought many to marry, according to Plutarch's observation, not so much for the sake of raising heirs to their own estates, as to make themselves capable of inheriting those of other men.—The rabbins maintain, that, by the laws of Moses, every body, except some few particulars, is obliged in conscience to marry at 20 years of age: this makes Bachelor makes one of their 613 precepts. Hence those maxims so frequent among their casuists, that he who does not take the necessary measures to leave heirs behind him, is not a man, but ought to be reputed a homicide.—Lycurgus was not more favourable; by his laws, bachelors are branded with infamy, excluded from all offices civil and military, and even from the shows and public sports. At certain feasts they were forced to appear, to be exposed to the public derision, and led round the market place. At one of their feasts, the women led them in this condition to the altars, where they obliged them to make amende honorable to nature, accompanied with a number of blows and lashes with a rod at discretion. To complete the affront, they forced them to sing certain songs composed in their own derision.—The Christian religion is more indulgent to the bachelor state: the ancient church recommended it as in some circumstances preferable to, and more perfect than, the matrimonial. In the canon law, we find injunctions on bachelors, when arrived at puberty, either to marry or to turn monks and profess chastity in earnest.—In England, there was a tax on bachelors, after 25 years of age, 12l. 10s. for a duke, a common person 1s. by 7 Will. III. 1695. In Britain, at present, they are taxed by an extra-duty on their servants. Every man of the age of 21 years and upwards, never having been married, who shall keep one male servant or more, shall pay 1l. 5s. for each above or in addition to the ordinary duties leviable for servants. Every man of the age of 21 years and upwards, never having been married, keeping one female servant, shall pay 2s. 6d. in addition to the former 2s. 6d.; 5s. in addition for each, if he has two female servants; and 10s. in addition for each for three or more female servants. Bachelor, was anciently a denomination given to those who had attained to knighthood, but had not a number of vassals sufficient to have their banner carried before them in the field of battle; or if they were not of the order of Bannerets, were not of age to display their own banner, but obliged to march to battle under another's banner. It was also a title given to young cavaliers, who having made their first campaign, received the military girdle accordingly. And it served to denominate him who had overcome another in a tournament the first time he ever engaged.—The word bachelor, in a military sense, is derived by Cujas from buccelarius, a kind of cavalry, anciently in great esteem. Du Cange deduces it from baccalaria, a kind of fees or farms, consisting of several pieces of ground, each whereof contained 12 acres, or as much as two oxen would plough: the possessors of which baccalaria were called bachelors. Cafeauve and Altaferra derive bachelor from baculus, or bacillus, "a staff," because the young cavaliers exercised themselves in fighting with staves. Martinius derives it from baccalareus, i.e. lacca laurae donatus, in allusion to the ancient custom of crowning poets with laurel, baccis lauri; as was the case with Petrarch at Rome in 1341. Alciat and Vives are of the same opinion: nor is this etymology improbable. Knights-Bachelors, the most ancient, but the lowest order of knights in England; known by the name of knights only. They are styled knights-bachelors, either (according to some) as denoting their degree, quasi bas chevaliers; or, according to others, because this title Bachelor does not descend to their posterity. The custom of the ancient Germans was to give their young men a shield and a lance in the great council: this was equivalent to the toga virilis of the Romans. Before this, they were not permitted to bear arms, but were accounted as part of the father's household; after it, as part of the public. Hence some derive the usage of knighting, which has prevailed all over the western world, since its reduction by colonies, from those northern heroes. Knights are called in Latin equites aurati; aurati, from the gilt spurs they wore; and equites, because they always served on horseback: for it is observable, that almost all nations call their knights by some appellation derived from a horse. They are also called in our law militiae, because they formed a part, or indeed the whole, of the royal army, in virtue of their feudal tenures; one condition of which was, that every one who held a knight's fee (which in Henry II.'s time amounted to 20l. per annum) was obliged to be knighted, and attend the king in his wars; or pay a fine for his non-compliance. The exertion of this prerogative, as an expedient to raise money in the reign of Charles I. gave great offence, though warranted by law and the recent example of Queen Elizabeth. At the Reformation, it was, together with all other military branches of the feudal law, abolished: and it now only exists as an honorary title; though, on account of its indiscriminate attainment, not very generally regarded. It is conferred indiscriminately upon gownsmen, burglers, and physicians, by the king's lightly touching the person, who is then kneeling, on the right shoulder with a drawn sword, and saying, Rife Sir. See the articles Knight and Nobility. Bachelors, in a university sense, are persons that have attained to the baccalaureate, or who have taken the first degree in the liberal arts and sciences. The degree of bachelor was first introduced in the 13th century by Pope Gregory IX. but it remains still unknown in Italy. At Oxford, before a person is entitled to the degree of bachelor of arts, he must have studied there four years; three years more to become master of arts; and seven more to commence bachelor of divinity.—At Cambridge, to commence bachelor of arts, he must have been admitted near four years; and above three years more before he commence master; and seven more still to become bachelor of divinity. He may commence bachelor of law after having studied it six years.—At Paris, to pass bachelor in theology, a person must have studied two years in philosophy and three years in theology, and held two acts of examination in the Sorbonne.—Bachelors in the canon law are admitted after two years study in the same, and sustaining an act according to the forms. A bachelor of physic must have studied two years in medicine after having been four years master of arts in the university, and have stood an examination; after which he is invested with the sur, in order to be licensed.—In the university of Paris, before the foundation of divinity-professorships, those who had studied divinity five years were admitted to go through their course, whence they were called baccalarii cursores; and as there were two courses, the first employed in explaining the Bible during... Bachelors during three successive years, the second for explaining the matter of the sentences for one year, those who were in their Bible-course were called baccalarii Biblii, and those arrived at the sentences baccalarii sententiarii. And, lastly, those who had gone through both were denominated baccalarii formati, or formed bachelors. At present, formed bachelor denotes a person who has taken the degree regularly after the due course of study and exercises required by the statutes; by way of opposition to a current bachelor, who is admitted in the way of grace, or by diploma. We also find mention of bachelors of the church, baccalarii ecclesiae. The bishop with his canons and baccalarii, cum confoilio et consensu omnium canoniciorum fuiorum et baccalariorum.

BACHELORS

Pages 357-357

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a> companies of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, are those not yet admitted to the livery. These companies generally consist of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, two wardens, the livery, and the bachelors, who are yet but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and have their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> only in attendance on the master and wardens. They are also called yeomen. Bachelor is also a name given in the six companies of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> to the elders, and such as, having served the offices, have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to be called by the masters and wardens to be present with them, and assist them in some of the functions, particularly in what relates to the chef-d'œuvre <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>-pieces of such as are candidates for being admitted masters.

BACHERAC

Pages 357-357

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, situated on the western shore of that river, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7°, and N. Lat. 58°. It is remarkable for excellent wine, from thence called Bacherac.

BACHIAN

Pages 357-357

one of the Molucca <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, belonging to the Dutch; situated under the equator, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12°.

BACHU

Pages 357-357

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Shirvan in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and the best haven in the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It is defended by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> wall, as also by a ditch and redoubts, made by the Russians when they were masters of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. It had a sumptuous cattle, but it is reduced to a ruinous state by the Russians. Formerly many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> resided here, and carried on a considerable traffic in raw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>; but that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is now given up. All the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> round is much impregnated with sulphur, which renders the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> very unpleasant. The neighbourhood of this city supplies the countries adjacent with naphtha, brimstone, and rock-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; and is the only place thereabouts which produces saffron. Round Bachu are several very steep craggy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, on which are strong watch-towers. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 49°. S. N. Lat. 40°.

BACK

Pages 357-363

BACK-BONE, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> SPINE. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Back, in the Manege, and among Farriers. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s back should be straight, not hollow, which is called saddle-backed: horses of this kind are generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and carry their heads <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, but want in strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. A horse with a weak back is apt to stumble. In the French riding-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, to mount a horse à dos, is to mount him bare-backed, without a saddle. Back-Gammon, an ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> played with dice, upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, by two persons. Manner of playing the game. The table is divided into two parts, upon which there are 24 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> spaces, called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. Each adversary has 15 men, black and white, to distinguish them; and they are disposed of in the following manner: Supposing the game to be played into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> table, two are placed upon the ace-point in the adversary's table, five upon the fix point in the opposite table, three upon the cinque point in the hitherto table, and five on the fix point in the right-hand table. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> object in this game is for each player to bring his men round into his right-hand table, by throwing with a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of dice those throws that contribute towards it, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> prevent the adversary doing the like. The first best throw upon the dice is esteemed aces, because it stops the fix point in the outer table, and secures the cinque in the thrower's table; whereby the adversary's two men upon the thrower's ace point cannot get out with either quatre, cinque, or fix. This throw is an advantage often given to the antagonist by the superior player. When he carries his men home in order to lose no point, he is to carry the most distant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to his adversary's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> point, that being the first stage he is to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> it on; the next stage is fix points farther, viz. in the place where the adversary's five men are first placed out of his tables. He must go on in this method till all his men are brought home, except two, when by losing a point, he may often <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the gammon, by throwing two fours or two fives. When a <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> is only played for, he should endeavour to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> either his own or adversary's cinque point; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> that fails by his being hit by the adversary, and he finds him forwarder than himself, in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> he must throw more men into the adversary's tables; which is done in this manner: He must put a man upon his cinque or bar point; and if the adversary neglects to hit it, he may then gain a forward game instead of a back game: but if the adversary hits him, he should play for a back game; and then the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men which are taken up makes his game the better, because by these means he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> preserve his game at home: and then he should endeavour to gain both his adversary's ace and trois points, or his ace and deuce points, and take care to keep three men upon the adversary's ace point, that in case he hits him from thence, that point may remain still secure to himself. A back game should not be played for at the beginning of a set, because it would be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disadvantage, the player running the risk of a gammon to win a single hit. Rules for playing at setting out all the throws on the dice, when the player is to play for a gammon or for a single hit (A). 1. Two aces are to be played on the cinque (a) The rules marked thus + are for a gammon only; those marked thus * are for a hit only. cinqe point and bar point, for a gammon or for a hit. 2. Two fixes, to be played on the adversary's bar point and on the thrower's bar point, for a gammon or for a hit. 3. + Two trois, to be played on the cinqe point, and the other two on the trois point in his own tables, for a gammon only. 4. + Two deuces, to be played on the quatre point in his own tables, and two to be brought over from the five men placed in the adversary's tables for a gammon only. 5. + Two fours, to be brought over from the five men placed in the adversary's tables, and to be put upon the cinqe point in his own tables for a gammon only. 6. Two fives, to be brought over from the five men placed in the adversary's tables, and to be put on the trois point in his own tables, for a gammon or for a hit. 7. Size ace, he must take his bar point for a gammon or for a hit. 8. Size deuce, a man to be brought from the five men placed in the adversary's tables, and to be placed in the cinqe point in his own tables, for a gammon or for a hit. 9. Six and three, a man to be brought from the adversary's ace point, as far as he will go, for a gammon or for a hit. 10. Six and four, a man to be brought from the adversary's ace point, as far as he will go, for a gammon or for a hit. 11. Six and five, a man to be carried from the adversary's ace point, as far as he can go, for a gammon or for a hit. 12. Cinqe and quatre, a man to be carried from the adversary's ace point, as far as he can go, for a gammon or for a hit. 13. Cinqe trois, to make the trois point in his table, for a gammon or for a hit. 14. Cinqe deuce, to play two men from the five placed in the adversary's tables, for a gammon or for a hit. 15. + Cinqe ace, to bring one man from the five placed in the adversary's tables for the cinqe, and to play one man <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the cinqe point in his own tables for the ace, for a gammon only. 16. Quatre trois, two men to be brought from the five placed in the adversary's tables, for a gammon or for a hit. 17. Quatre deuce, to make the quatre point in his own tables, for a gammon or for a hit. 18. + Quatre ace, to play a man from the five placed in the adversary's tables for the quatre; and for the ace, to play a man down upon the cinqe point in his own tables, for a gammon only. 19. + Trois deuce, two men to be brought from the five placed in the adversary's tables, for a gammon only. 20. Trois ace, to make the cinqe point in his own tables, for a gammon or for a hit. 21. + Deuce ace, to play one man from the five men placed in the adversary's table for the deuce; and for the ace to play a man down upon the cinqe point in his own tables, for a gammon only. 22. * Two trois, two of them to be played on the cinqe point in his own tables, and with the other two he is to take the quatre point in the adversary's tables. 23. * Two deuces, two of them are to be played on the quatre point in his own tables, and with the other two he is to take the trois point in the adversary's tables. By playing these two <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> in this manner, the player avoids being shut up in the adversary's tables, and has the chance of throwing out the tables to win the hit. 24. * Two fours, two of them are to take the adversary's cinqe point in the adversary's tables, and for the other two, two men are to be brought from the five placed in the adversary's tables. 25. * Cinqe ace, the cinqe should be played from the five men placed in the adversary's tables, and the ace from the adversary's ace point. 26. * Quatre ace, the quatre to be played from the five men placed in the adversary's ace point. 27. * Deuce ace, the deuce to be played from the five men placed in the adversary's tables, and the ace from the adversary's ace point. The three last chances are played in this manner; because an ace being laid down in the adversary's tables, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of throwing deuce ace, trois deuce, quatre trois, or size cinqe, in two or three throws; either of which throws secures a point, and gives the player the best of the hit. Cautions, &c. The player must understand by the directions given to play for a gammon, that he is to make some blots on purpose, the odds being in his favour that they are not hit: but if it should happen that any blot is hit, as in this case there will be three men in the adversary's tables, he must then endeavour to secure the adversary's cinqe, quatre, or trois point, to prevent a gammon, and must be very cautious of his fourth man's not being taken up. He must not crowd his game at any time if he can help it; that is to say, he should not put many men either upon the trois or deuce points in his own tables, being the same as losing those men, not having them in play. Besides, by crowding the game, and attempting to save a gammon, the player is often gammoned. His game being crowded in his own tables, the adversary has room to play as he thinks proper. The following calculations will show the odds of entering a single man upon any certain number of points; and accordingly the game should be played. It is necessary to know that there are thirty-six chances upon two dice, and the points that are upon these thirty-six chances are as follow: | Viz. | Points | |------|--------| | 2 Aces | - | 4 | | 2 Deuces | - | 8 | | 2 Trois | - | 12 | | 2 Fours | - | 16 | | 2 Fives | - | 20 | | 2 Sixes | - | 24 | | 6 And 5 twice | - | 22 | | 6 And 4 twice | - | 20 | | 6 And 3 twice | - | 18 | | 6 And 2 twice | - | 16 | | 6 And 1 twice | - | 14 | | 5 And 4 twice | - | 18 | | 5 And 3 twice | - | 16 | | 5 And 2 twice | - | 14 | | 5 And 1 twice | - | 12 | | 4 And 3 twice | - | 14 | | 4 And 2 twice | - | 12 | | 4 And 1 twice | - | 10 | | 3 And 2 twice | - | 10 | | 3 And 1 twice | - | 8 | | 2 And 1 twice | - | 6 | Divide by 36)294(8 and it proves, that upon an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> the player has a right to 8 points each throw. The odds on the hits. | 2 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> is about | - | 5 to 2 | | 2 to 1 is | - | 2 1 | | 1 Love is | - | 3 2 | Directions for the player to bear his men. If a player has taken up two of the adversary's men, and happens to have two, three, or more points made in his own tables, he should spread his men, that he either may take a new point in his tables, or be ready to hit the man which the adversary may happen to enter. If he finds upon the adversary's entering, that the game is upon a par, or that the advantage is on his own side, he should take the adversary's man up whenever he can, it being 25 to 11 that he is not hit: except when he is playing for a single hit only; then, if playing the throw otherwise gives him a better chance for it, he ought to do it. It being five to one against his being hit with double dice, he should never be deterred from taking up any one man of the adversary's. If he has taken up one of the adversary's men, and should happen to have five points in his own tables, and forced to leave a blot out of his tables, he should endeavour to leave it upon doublets preferable to any other chance, because in that case the odds are 35 to one that he is not hit; whereas it is only 17 to one but he is hit upon any other chance. When the adversary is very forward, a player should never move a man from his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, trois, or deuce points, thinking to bear that man from the point where he put it, as nothing but high doublets can give him any chance for the hit. Instead of playing an ace or a deuce from any of those points, he should play them from his own size or highest points, so that throwing two fives, or two fours, his size and cinque points being eased, would be a considerable advantage. to him; whereas had they been loaded, he must have been obliged to play otherwife. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the adversary to take up the player as soon as he enters. The blot should be left upon the adversary's lowest point; that is to say, upon his deuce point rather than upon his trois point; or upon his trois point rather than his quatre point, or upon his quatre point preferable to his cinque point, for a reason before mentioned; all the men the adversary plays upon his trois or his deuce points are deemed lost, being greatly out of play; so that those men not having it in their power to make his cinque point, and his game being crowded in one place and open in another, the adversary must be greatly annoyed by the player. If the player has two of the adversary's men in his tables, he has a better chance for a hit than if he had more, provided his game is forwarder than that of his antagonist's; for if he had three or more of the adversary's men in his tables, he would stand a worse chance to be hit. When a player is running to save the gammon, if he should have two men upon his ace point, and several men abroad, although he should lose one point or two in putting his men into his tables, it is his interest to leave a man upon the adversary's ace point, because it will prevent his adversary from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> his men to the greatest advantage, and at the same time the player will have a chance of the adversary's making a blot, which he may chance to hit. However, if a player finds upon a throw, that he has a probability of saving his gammon, he should never wait for a blot, as the odds are greatly against his hitting it, but should embrace that opportunity. How to calculate the odds of saving or winning the gammon. Suppose the adversary has so many men abroad as require three throws to put them into his tables, and at the same time that the player's tables are made up, and that he has taken up one of the adversary's men; in this case, it is about an equal wager that the adversary is gammoned. For in all probability the player has bore two men before he opens his tables, and when he bears the third man, he will be obliged to open his size or cinque point. It is then probable, that the adversary is obliged to throw twice before he enters his men in the player's tables, twice more before he puts that man into his own tables, and three throws more to put the men which are abroad into his own tables, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> throws. Now the player having 12 men to bear, he may be forced to make an ace or a deuce twice before he can bear all his men, and consequently will require seven throws in bearing them; so that, upon the whole, it is about equal whether the adversary is gammoned or not. Suppose a player has three men upon his adversary's ace point and five points in his own tables, and that the adversary has all his men in his tables, three upon each of his five highest points. Has the player a probability of gammoning his adversary or not? Points. For bearing three men from his 6th point is 18 From his 5th point 15 Carried forward From his 4th point 33 From his 3d point 12 From his 2d point 6 In all 60 Bringing his three men from the adversary's ace point to his size point in his own tables, being 18 points each, and making together 54 There must remain 6 It is plain from this calculation, that the player has much the best of the probability of the gammon, exclusive of one or more blots which the adversary is liable to make in bearing his men, supposing at the same time the throws to be upon an equality. Suppose two blots are left, either of which cannot be hit but by double dice; one must be hit by throwing eight and the other by throwing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>; so that the adversary has only one die to hit either of them. What are the odds of hitting either of them? The chances of two dice being in all 36 The chances to hit 8 are 6 and 2 twice 2 5 and 3 twice 2 2 Deuces 1 2 Fours 1 The chances to hit 9 are 6 and 3 twice 2 5 and 4 twice 2 2 Trois 1 For hitting in all 11 Chances for not hitting, remain 25 So that the odds are 25 to 11 against hitting either of these blots. This method may be taken to find out the odds of hitting three, four, or five blots upon double dice; or blots made upon double and single dice at the same time. After knowing how many chances there are to hit any of those blots, they must be added all together, and then subtracted from the number 36, which are the chances of the two dice, and the question is solved. A critical case for a Back-game. Suppose the foregame to be played by A, and that all his men are placed as usual; B has fourteen of his men placed upon his adversary's ace point and one man upon his adversary's deuce point, and B is to throw. Who has the best of the hit?—Answer: A has the best of it, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> to silver: because, if B does not throw an ace to take his adversary's deuce point, which is 25 to 11 against him, A will take up B's men in his tables, either singly or to make points; and then if B secures either A's deuce or trois point, A will put as many men down as possible, in order to hit, and thereby get a back-game. It is evident that the back-game is very powerful; consequently, whoever practises it must become a greater proficient at the game than he could by any other means. Another critical case. Suppose A to have five men placed upon his size point, as many upon his quatre point, and the same number upon his deuce point, all in his own tables. At the same time, let us suppose B to have three men placed upon A's ace point, as many many upon A's trois point, and the same number upon A's cinque point, in his own tables, and three men placed as usual out of his tables. Who has the best of the hit? — Answer: The game is equal till B has gained his cinque and quatre points in his own tables; which if he can effect, and by playing two men from A's cinque point, in order to force his adversary to blot by throwing an ace, which should B hit, he will have the best of the hit. A case of curiosity and instruction: in which is shown the probability of making the hit last by one of the players for many hours, although they shall both play as fast as usual. Suppose B to have bore 13 men, and that A has his fifteen men in B's tables, viz. three men upon his five point, as many upon his cinque point, three upon his quatre point, the same number upon his trois point, two upon his deuce point, and one upon his ace point. A in this situation can prolong it, as aforesaid by bringing his 15 men home, always securing six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> points till B has entered his two men, and brought them upon any certain point; as soon as B has gained that point, A will open an ace, deuce, or trois point, or all of them; which done, B hits one of them, and A taking care to have two or three men in B's tables, is ready to hit that man; and also being certain of taking up the other man, has it in his power to prolong the hit almost to any length, provided he takes care not to open such points as two fours, two fives, or two sixes, but always to open the ace, deuce, or trois points, for B to hit him. A critical game to play. Suppose A and B place their men for a hit in the following manner: A to have three men upon the five point in his own tables, three men out of his tables upon the usual point, and nine men upon his adversary's ace, deuce, and trois points; that is, three upon each: and suppose B's men to be placed in his own and his adversary's tables in the same order. So situated, the best player should win the hit. The game being so equal, that in this case the dice should be thrown for. Now if A throws first, he should endeavour to gain his adversary's cinque point: this being done, he should lay as many blots as possible, to tempt B to hit him, as it puts him backward, and A thereby gains an advantage. A should always endeavour to have three men upon each of his adversary's ace and deuce points; because when B makes a blot, these points will remain secure, and when A has bore five, six, or more men, A yet may secure six close points out of his tables, in order to prevent B from getting his man home, at which time he should calculate who has the best of the hit. If he finds that B is foremost, he should then try to lay such blots as may be taken up by his adversary, that he may have a chance of taking up another man, in case B should happen to have a blot at home. Laws of Back-gammon. 1. If a man is taken from any point, it must be played; if two men are taken from it, they also must be played. 2. A man is not supposed to be played till it is placed upon a point and quitted. 3. If a player has only fourteen men in play, there is no penalty inflicted, because by his playing with a lesser number than he is entitled to, he plays to a disadvantage for want of the deficient man to make up his tables. 4. If he bears any number of men before he has entered a man taken up, and which of course he was obliged to enter, such men to borne must be entered again in the adversary's tables as well as the man taken up. 5. If he has mistaken his throw and played it, and his adversary has thrown, it is not in the choice of either of the players to alter it, unless they both agree so to do. Back-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, the method of painting mezzotinto <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>, pasted on glass, with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>-colours. See Mezzotinto. The art consists chiefly in laying the print upon a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>-glass, of such a size as fits the print. In order to do this, take your print, and lay it in clean <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> for two days and two nights, if the print be on very strong, clothe, and hard gummed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>; but if upon an open, soft, spongy paper, two hours will sometimes suffice, or more, according as the paper is. The paper or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> having been sufficiently soaked, take it out and lay it upon two sheets of paper, and cover it with two more; and let it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> there a little to suck out the moisture. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, take the glass the picture is to be put upon, and set it near the fire to warm; take <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a> turpentine, warm it over the fire till it is grown fluid, then with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOG">hog</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> spread the turpentine very smoothly and evenly on the glass. When this has been done, take the mezzotinto print from between the papers, and lay it upon the glass; beginning first at one end, rubbing it down gently as you go on, till it lie close, and there be no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> bladders between. Then, with your fingers, rub or roll off the paper from the backside of the print, till it looks black, i.e., till you can see nothing but the print, like a thin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILM">film</a>, left upon the glass, and let it by to dry. When it is dry, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> it over with some white transparent varnish, that the print may be seen through it; and then it is fit for painting. The utmost care will be necessary in rubbing or rolling the paper off the print, so as not to tear it, especially in the light parts. You may, instead of soaking your prints two days and two nights, roll them up and boil them for about two hours, more or less, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the paper, in water; and that will render it as fit for rubbing, rolling, or peeling, as the other way. This being done, and your oil-colours prepared, ground very fine, and tempered up very stiff, lay on the back side of the transparent prints such colours as each particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> requires; letting the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of the print still guide your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, and to each particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> will lie fair to the eye on the other side of the glass, and look almost as well as a painted piece, if it be done neatly. The shadows of the print are generally sufficient for the shadow of every colour; but if you have a mind to give a shadow by your pencil, then let the shadows be laid on first, and the other colours afterward. In laying on colours in this kind of back-painting, you need not be curious as to the laying them on smooth. This is not at all requisite here, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> aim is only to have the colours appear well on the fore side of the print; and therefore the only care to Back-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> be used in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, is to lay the colours on thick enough, that its body may strike the colour of it plainly through the glass. Back-Staff, a name formerly given to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a> invented by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Davis; because the back of the artifit is turned towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> at the time of observation. See Quadrant. Back-Slats, of a ship, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> belonging to the main-mast and fore-mast, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> belonging to them; serving to keep them from pitching forwards or overboard. Back-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TACK">Tack</a>, in Scotch <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>: When a wadsetter, instead of selling the wadset-lands, grants a tack thereof to the reverer for payment of a certain sum in name of tack-duty, that tack is called a back-tack. Back-Worm. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILANDERS">Filanders</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BACKER">Backer</a>, or Barker, Jacques, a painter of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1530; and learned the principles of painting from his father, who was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> very knowing in his profession, though his works were in no great estimation. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, he lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Jacopo Palermo, a dealer in pictures, who avociously took care to keep him incessantly employed, and sent his paintings to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> to be disposed of, where they happened to be exceedingly admired. The judicious were very eager to purchase them; and though the tranactor sold them at a great price, yet the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> artist was not proportionally rewarded, but <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the same obscure and deprested condition. His merit, indeed, was universally allowed, but his name, and the narrowness of his circumstances, were as universally unknown. He had a clean light manner of pencilling, and a tint of colour that was extremely agreeable.—He died in 1560. Backer, or Barker, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, painter of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> and history, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARLINGEN">Harlingen</a> in 1609, but spent the greatest part of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>; and by all the writers on this subject, he is mentioned as an extraordinary painter, particularly of portraits, which he executed with strength, spirit, and a graceful resemblance. He was remarkable for an uncommon readiness of hand and freedom of pencil; and his incredible expedition in his manner of painting, appeared even in one portrait of a lady from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAARLEM">Haarlem</a>, that he painted at half length, which was begun and finished in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, though he adorned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> with rich drapery and several ornamental jewels. He also painted historical subjects with good success; and in that style there is a fine picture of Cimon and Iphigenia, which is accounted by the connoisseurs an excellent performance. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> academy figures his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> was so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>, and his outline so correct, that he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> from all his competitors; and his works are still bought up at very high prices in the Low Countries. In the collection of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">Elector</a> Palatine there is an excellent head of Brouwer, painted by this master; and in the Carmelites <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at Antwerp is preserved a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> picture of the Last Judgment, which is well designed and well coloured. He died in 1651. Backereel, called Bacquerelli, William, a painter of history, was born at Antwerp, and was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Rubens, at the same time that Vandyck was educated in that school. When each of them quitted that master, and commenced painters, Backereel was very little inferior to Vandyck, if not nearly his equal. And this may be manifestly seen in the works of the former, which are in the church of the Augustin monks at Antwerp; where those two great artists painted in competition, and both were praised for their merit in their different ways; but the superiority was never determined in favour either of the one or the other. He had likewise a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; but, by exercising that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> too freely, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> satires against the Jesuits, these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> pursued him with unremitting <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, till they compelled him to fly from Antwerp; and by that means deprived his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of such paintings as would have contributed to its perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>.—Sandrart takes notice, that in his time there were seven or eight painters, who were very eminent, of the name of Backereel, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and the Low Countries. Backhuyzen, Ludolph, an eminent painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMDEN">Emden</a> in 1631, and received his earliest instruction from Albert Van Everdingen; but acquired his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> knowledge by frequenting the painting rooms of different great masters, and observing their various methods of touching and colouring. One of these masters was Henry Dubbels, whose understanding in his art was very extensive; and he was as remarkably communicative of his knowledge to others. From him Backhuyzen obtained more real benefit than from all the painters of his time, either by studying their works, or personally conversing with them. His subjects were sea-pieces, ships, and sea-ports. He had not practised very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> when he became the object of general admiration; so that even his drawings were fought after, and several of them were bought up at 100 florins a-piece. It was observed of him, that while he was painting, he would not suffer even his most intimate friends to have access to him, lest his fancy might be disturbed, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> he had formed in his mind be interrupted. He studied <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> attentively in all her forms; in gales, calms, storms, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, rocks, skies, lights, and shadows; and he expressed every subject with so sweet a pencil, and such transparency and lustre, as placed him above all the artists of his time in that style, except the younger Vandervelde, who is deservedly esteemed the first in that manner of painting. It was a frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> with Backhuyzen, whenever he could procure resolute mariners, to go to sea in a storm, in order to store his mind with grand images, directly copied from nature, of such scenes as would have filled any other head and heart with terror and dismay; and the moment he landed he always impatiently ran to his palette to secure those incidents of which the traces might by delay be obliterated.—He perfectly understood the management of the chiaroscuro, and by his skill in that part of his art, gave uncommon force and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> to his objects. He observed strictly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, in the distances of his vessels, the receding of the grounds on the shores, and the different buildings which he described in the sea-ports; whether they were the result of his own imagination, or sketched, as he usually did, after nature. His works may easily be distinguished by an observant eye, from the freedom and neatness of his touch; from the clearness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> agitation or quiescence of the water; from a peculiar tint in his clouds and skies; and also from the exact proportions of his ships, and the gracefulness of their position. For the burgomasters of Amsterdam he painted a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> picture, with a multitude of vessels, and a view of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> at a distance, for which they gave him thirteen hundred guilders, and a considerable present; which picture they afterwards presented to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France, who placed it in the Louvre. No painter was ever more honoured by the visits of kings and princes than Backhuyzen; the king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> was one of the number; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great took delight to see him paint, and often endeavoured to draw after vessels which he had designed. He was remarkably affiduous, and yet it seems astonishing to consider the number of pictures which he finished, and the exquisite manner in which they are painted. He died in 1709.

BACKING

Pages 363-363

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">Horsemanship</a>. See Horsemanship. BACKING the Sails, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>; to arrange them in a situation that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> force the ship to retreat, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> move backwards. This is, however, only done in narrow channels, when a ship is carried along sidewise by the tide or current, and wants to avoid any thing that may interrupt her progress, as shoals, vessels at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, &c. or in the line of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, when a ship wants to be immediately opposite to another with which she is engaged.

BACKS

Pages 363-363

among dealers in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, denote the thickest and best tanned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, used chiefly for soles of shoes.

BACNOLAS

Pages 380-380

a town of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, now the department of Hérault in France. It has a very handsome <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and two fountains which rise in the middle of the town; the waters of which, being received in a basin, are conveyed by a canal out of town, and from thence to the lands about it. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 43. N. Lat. 44. 10.

BACON

Pages 365-365

Sir Nathaniel, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the bath, and an excellent painter, was a younger son of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> keeper, and half <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Sir Francis. He travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and studied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> there; but his manner and colouring approaches nearer to the style of the Flemish school. Mr Walpole observes, that at Culford, where he lived, are preserved some of his works; and at Gorhambury, his father's seat, is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> by him in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, of a cook-maid with a dead fowl, admirably painted, with great <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, neatness, and lustre of colouring. In the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is a whole length of him, by himself, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> and pallet hung up, and a half length of his mother by him.

BACONTHORP

Pages 365-365

John, called the refolute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>, a learned monk, was born towards the end of the 13th century at Baconthorp, a village in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>. He spent the early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in the convent of Blackney, near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALSINGHAM">Walsingham</a> in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; whence he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and from thence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; where being distinguished for his learning, he obtained degrees in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and laws, and was esteemed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of the Avroffits*. In 1329 he returned to England, and was immediately chosen twelfth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> of the English Carmelites. In 1333 he was sent for to Rome; where, we are told, he first maintained the pope's sovereign authority in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of divorce, but that he afterward retracted his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. He died in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in the year 1346. Leland, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">Bale</a>, and Pits, unanimously gave him the character of a monk of genius and learning. He wrote, 1. Commentaria seu quaestiones super quattuor libros sententiarum; and, 2. Compendium legis Christi, et quodilibet; both which underwent several editions at Paris, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREMONA">Cremona</a>. Leland, Bale, and Pits, mention a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his works never published.

BACTRIA

Pages 365-365
or Bactriana, now Chorassan or Khoreasan, an ancient kingdom of Asia, bounded on the west by Margiana, on the north by the river Oxus, on the south by Mount Paropamisus, and on the east by the Aastic Scythia and the country of the Massagetae. It was a large, fruitful, and well-peopled country, containing according to Ammianus Marcellinus 100 cities, though of these only a few are particularly mentioned by historians, of which that formerly called Maracanda, now Samarcand, is the most considerable. Of the history of this country we know but little. Authors agree that it was subdued first by the Assyrians, afterwards by Cyrus, and then by Alexander the Great. Afterwards it remained subject to Seleucus Nicator and his successors till the time of Antiochus Theos; when Theodorus, from governor of that province, became king, and strengthened himself so effectually in his kingdom, while Antiochus was engaged in a war with Ptolemy Philadelphus king of Egypt, that he could never afterwards dispossess him of his acquisitions. His posterity continued to enjoy the kingdom.

BACTROPERATA

Pages 365-366

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> appellation given to philosophers by way of contempt, denoting a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> and a budget. We suppose it is of the same people that Pauchasius Radbertus speaks under the corrupt name of Bacoperita <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Bacchionita, whom he described as philosophers who had so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a contempt for all earthly things, that they kept nothing but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a> to drink out of; and that one of this order feeding a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a> scooping up the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, threw away his cup as a superfluity: which is nothing but the old story of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> the Cynic.

BACULARIUS

Pages 363-363

in writers of the middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> apparitor, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> verger; who carries a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, baculus, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, as an ensign of his office.

BACULOMETRY

Pages 366-366

the art of measuring accessible <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> inaccessible heights, by the help of one or more baculi, staves, or rods. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>.

BACURIUS

Pages 366-366
or Baturius, king of the Iberians, a people on the side of the Caftian sea. One day being a-hunting, he lost sight of his company, through a great storm and sudden darkness; upon which he vowed to the God of his Christian faith, that if he were delivered he would worship him alone: the day breaking up immediately, he made good his promise, and became the apostle of his country.

BADAGSHAN

Pages 366-366

a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Bukharia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Balkh, situated at the foot of those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which separate Indofian from Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. The city is exceedingly strong by its situation; and belongs to the khan of Proper Bukharia, who uses it as a kind of state-prison to secure those he is jealous of. The town is not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, but well built, and very populous. It stands on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the river Amu, about 100 miles from its source, and is a great thoroughfare for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> travelling to Little Bukharia. The inhabitants are enriched by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and rubies, which are in the neighbourhood; and those who live at the foot of the mountains gather a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of gold and silver dust brought <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> by torrents occasioned by the melting of the snow on the top.

BADAJOZ

Pages 366-366

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and strong town, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Extremadura in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It is seated on the river Guadiana, over which there is a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> built by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. On this bridge the Portuguese were defeated in 1661, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> John of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Badajoz is computed at near 9,000 inhabitants, but a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> in proportion to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. Most of the streets are extremely narrow, and the houses small and crowded. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 3'. N. Lat. 38° 35'.

BADELONA

Pages 366-366

a town of Catalonia in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, seated on the Mediterranean. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Peterborough landed here in 1704, when, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Spain, he laid siege to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a>, from which it is ten miles distant. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 20'. N. Lat. 41° 12'.

BADEN

Pages 366-368

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the above district, is an agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, moderately <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, seated on the side of the Limmat, in a plain flanked by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hills, between which the river runs. This city owes its rise to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, which were famous before the Christian era. Several monuments of antiquity have been found here from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time, particularly in 1240. When they were opening the large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the baths, they found <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of several heathen gods, made of alabaster; Roman coins, made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>, of Augustus, Vespasian, Decius, &c.; and several medals of the Roman emperors, of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and bronze. There are two churches in Baden; one of which is collegiate, and makes a good appearance; the other is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of the Capuchins, near the townhouse. This last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> serves not only for the assemblies of their own <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, but also for those of the cantons. The diet assemblies there in a handsome room made for that purpose; the deputies of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a> sit at the bottom behind a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, as the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; the ambassadors of foreign powers are seated on one side to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, and the deputies of the other cantons are ranged on each side the room. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> of Baden resides in a castle at the end of a handsome wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, which is covered in. Before this castle there is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> pillar, erected in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Trajan, who paved a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> 85 Italian miles in length. The inhabitants are rigid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman catholics</a>, and formerly behaved in a most insolent manner, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, but they are now obliged by their masters to be more more submissive. The baths which are on each side of the river are a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> from the city. Joining to the small baths there is a village, and to the large a town which may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Baden. It is seated on a hill, of which the ascent is steep. There the baths are brought into inns and private houses, by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, which are about 60 in all. There are also public baths in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, from a spring which rises in the street, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> bathe gratis, but they are exposed quite naked to all that pass by. All the baths are hot, and one to go <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> as to scald the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and they are impregnated with a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of sulphur, with some <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> and nitre.
