They are useful for drinking as well as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>; and are said to cure all diseases from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> cause, headaches, vertigoes, &c. They strengthen the senses, cure diseases of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> and bowels, asthma, and obstructions. They are peculiarly excellent for women's diseases. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 25. N. Lat. 47. 27. Baden, the Margravate of, in the circle of Swabia, in Germany, is bounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK_FOREST"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Forest, on the east; by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, on the south; and by the Rhine, which divides it from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALSACE">Alsace</a>, on the east: and is about 90 miles in length, from north to south; but not above 20 in breadth, where it is widest. It is a very populous and fruitful country, abounding in corn and wine. Venison and wild fowl are so plentiful, that they are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> diet of the peasants. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> this territory, are the Rhine, Ens, Wurmbs, and Phintis, which yield plenty of fish. They feed their hogs with chestnuts, which make the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">bacon</a> excellent. They have free-stone for building, and marble of all colours. They have some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>, and great quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> towns are Baden, Durlach, Stolhafen, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RASTADT">Rastadt</a>, Gerbach, Pforzheim, and Hochberg. Baden, the chief city of the above margravate, has a castle that stands on the top of a hill, which is the residence of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. The town is seated among hills, on rocky and uneven ground, which renders the streets inconvenient and crooked. It is famous for its baths, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of which are said to be above 300. Some of them are hot, and accounted to be very good in nervous <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. They partake of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, alum, and sulphur. E. Long. 9. 24. N. Lat. 48. 50. Baden, a town of Germany, in the archduchy of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, seated on the Little Suechat, is a neat little walled town, standing in a plain not far from a ridge of hills which run out from the mountain Cetius. It is much frequented by the people of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, and the neighbouring parts, on account of its baths. The springs supply two convenient baths within the town, five without the walls, and one beyond the river. They are good for distempers of the head, the gout, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a>, and most chronic diseases. E. Long. 17. 10. N. Lat. 48. 0. Badenoch, the most easterly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERNESS_SHIRE"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>-shire, in Scotland, extending about 33 miles in length from east to west, and 27 from north-east to south-west where broadest. It has no considerable town, and is very barren and hilly, but abounds with deer, and other kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>. Baden-Weiller, a town of Germany, belonging to the lower margravate of Baden. E. Long. 7. 50. N. Lat. 47. 55. Badens, Francis, historical and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1571; and the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the art were communicated to him by his father, who was but an ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. However, he visited Rome, and several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and then formed a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and a manner exceedingly pleasing. When he returned to his own country his merit procured for him great employment, and still greater reputation, and he was usually distinguished by the name of the Italian painter. His touch was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and spirited, and his colouring warm; and he had the honour of being the first who introduced a good taste of colouring among his countrymen. While his acknowledged merit was rewarded with every public testimony of esteem and applause, unhappily he received an account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, who had been afflicted on a journey; and the intelligence affected him so violently, that it occasioned his own death, to the inexplicable regret of every lover of the art, in 1603. Badge, in naval <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, signifies a sort of ornament placed on the outside of small ships, very near the stern, containing either a window for the convenience of the cabin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a representation of it. It is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> decorated with marine figures, martial instruments, or such like emblems. Badger, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the English name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-URSUS">ursus</a>. See Ursus. Badger, in old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>-books, one that was licensed to buy corn in one place and carry it to another to sell, without incurring the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of an engroffer. Badia, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of Bastica, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANAS">Anas</a>; now supposed to be <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BADAJOZ">Badajoz</a> on the Guadiana. Badiga, in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a> the name of a sort of spongy plant, common in the shops in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>, and some other northern kingdoms. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it is the taking away of livid marks from blows and bruises, which the powder of this plant is said to do in a night's time. Badiane, or Bandian, the seed of a tree which grows in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, and smells like aniseed. The Chinese, and the Dutch in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of them, sometimes use the badiane to give their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a> an aromatic taste. Badigeon, a mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> and free-stone, well ground together, and fitted; used by statuaries to fill up the little holes, and repair the defects in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, whereof they make their statues and other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is also used by joiners for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>-dust mixed with strong <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>, wherewith they fill up the chaps and other defects in wood after it is wrought. Badile, Antonio, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and portrait painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a> in 1480, and by great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and application acquired a more extensive knowledge of the true principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> than any of his predecessors. He was confessedly a most eminent artist; but he derived greater honour from having two such disciples as Paolo Veronese and Baptista Zelotti, than he did even from the excellence of his own compositions. He died in 1560. His colouring was admirably good; his carnations beautiful; and his portraits preferred the perfect resemblance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> and real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>: nor had he any cause to envy the acknowledged merit. merit of Titian, Giorgione, or the best of his cotemporaries.

BADIS

Pages 368-368

a fortress of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, subject to Russia. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23. 10. N. Lat. 59. 15.

BADIUS

Pages 368-368
Conrad, and Stephen Robert, his brother; French refugees; celebrated as printers at Geneva, and Conrad as an author. The latter died in 1566. BAECKEA. See Botany Index.

BAEBEL

Pages 346-347

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and tower undertaken to be built <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BABEL">Babel</a> by the whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> soon after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, and remarkable for the miraculous frustration of the attempt by the confusion of languages. As to the situation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Babel, most authors are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that it was exactly in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the celebrated city of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> afterwards stood. That it was in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, appears indisputably from Scripture; but that it was exactly in the same place is what cannot be proved, nor is it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. Authors have been much divided about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> by which the whole race of mankind were induced to join as one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in such an undertaking. Some have imagined that it was out of fear of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> deluge; others, that they knew beforehand that they were to be dispersed through all the different countries of the world, and built this tower in order to defeat the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the Deity, because having a tower of such vast height as they proposed, those who were at a distance could easily find their way back again. Had either of these been their design, however, it is probable they would have chosen an eminence rather than a plain for the situation of their tower, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> indeed that they would have chosen some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain, such as Ararat, for their mark, rather than any tower at all: for though it is said that they designed the top of their tower to reach to heaven, we can scarce suppose them to have been so absurd, as to imagine this possible in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we understand it; and must therefore rather take it in the limited sense in which it is often used by Moses and his countrymen, where they speak of cities walled up to heaven. Others there are who imagine that the top of this tower was not to reach up to heaven, but to be consecrated to the heavens, i.e., to the worship of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> and stars; of the fire, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, &c. and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> powers, as deities; and therefore that the true Deity interposed in order to prevent a total and irrecoverable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFECTION">defection</a>. Certain it is, that the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of idolatry which takes for the objects of its worship those natural agents, as it is the most ancient, so it is by far the most rational, and the most difficult to be disproved. It is much more difficult, for instance, to prove that the sun, which by his enlivening beams gives vigour to the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, is not a deity, than that a log of wood is not one: and hence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> such a system of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> became universally established among mankind, it would be impossible ever afterwards to eradicate it. Indeed that the scheme of Babel, whatever it was, could have been put into execution by man, seems evident from the interpolation of the Deity on the occasion; for we cannot suppose that he would have worked a miracle on purpose to defeat that which would have defeated itself if he had let it alone; and he expressly says, That now nothing could be restrained from them; which intimates very plainly, that, had this scheme gone on, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> which God had laid for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the world would have been totally frustrated: and agreeable to this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> Dr Tenison supposes that the tower was of a pyramidal form, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the spires of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>; and that it was erected in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the sun, as being the most probable cause of drying up the flood. As to the materials made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of this tower, the Scripture informs us that they were bricks and lime or bitumen. According to an eastern <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, three years were taken up in making the bricks, each of which was 13 cubits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, 10 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and five thick. Oriental writers say, that the city was 373 fathoms in length, and 151 in breadth; that the walls were 5533 fathoms high, and 33 in breadth; and that the tower itself was no less than 10,000 fathoms, or 12 miles high. Even St Jerome affirms from the testimony of eye-witnesses, who as he says had examined the remains of the tower, that it was four miles high; but Ado makes the height to have been no less than 5000 miles. The only account of its dimensions which can be at all depended upon (supposing it to have been the same which afterwards stood in the midst of the city of Babylon, and round which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a> built the temple of Belus), is that given under the article BABYLON.

BAETERRAE

Pages 368-368

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of the Tertofages in Gallia Narbonensis; now Belfort, on the east <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Obris, now Orbis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Orbe, in Lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>.

BAETICA

Pages 368-368

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, so called from the famed river Baetis, afterwards Tartessus, now Guadalquivir, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> river. It was bounded on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUSITANIA">Lusitania</a>; on the south, by the Mediterranean, and Sinus Gadianus; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Cantabric <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, now the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>. On the east and north-east, its limits cannot be so well ascertained as they are very reasonably thought to have been in a continual state of fluctuation, as each petty monarch had an opportunity of encroaching upon his neighbour. The province was divided in two by the river Baetis already mentioned. On the one side of which, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANAS">Anas</a>, were situated the Turdetani, from whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> was called Turdetania, though more generally known by the name of Baeturia. On the other side were situated the Baetuli, Baetetani, and Contentani, along the Mediterranean coasts. The Baetuli were supposed to be of Phoenician extract, and dwelt along the coasts of the Mediterranean, till, driven from thence by the Moors, they fled into the mountainous parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, which they then called from their own name Baetulia. The Baetetani were seated higher up, on the same coasts. The territories of both these made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of what has since become the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>; in which there is a ridge of very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, called from the above-mentioned people, the Baetetanian mountains. Mention is also made of their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> Batetiana; a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of such strength, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Ferdinand was six months besieging it before he could take it from the Moors. The whole province of Baetica, according to the most probable account, contained what is now called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, part of the kingdom of Granada, and the outward boundaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a>. BAETIS. See BAETICA.

BAETULO

Pages 368-368

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in the Terraconensis; now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BADALONA">Badalona</a> in Catalonia.

BAETYLLIA

Pages 368-368

anointed <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, worshipped by the Phoenicians, by the Greeks before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Cecrops, and by other barbarous nations. They were <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and consecrated to some god, as <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>, &c. Some are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the true original of these idols is to be derived from the pillar of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> erected at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BETHEL">Bethel</a>, and which was afterwards worshipped by the Jews. These baetylia were much the object of the veneration of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heathens. Many of their idols were no other. In reality, no sort of idol was more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the eastern countries, than that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> stones erected, and hence termed by the Greeks, xionos, pillar. In some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> they were planted on both sides of the highways. In the temple of Heliogaba- lus, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, there was one pretended to have fallen from heaven. There was also a famous black stone in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, said to have fallen from heaven. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> sent for it and the priests belonging to it with much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, Scipio Nasica being at the head of the embassy.

BAEZA

Pages 368-368

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hill three miles from the Guadalquivir; it is the see of a bishop, and has a kind of university founded by John d'<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVILA">Avila</a>. It was taken from the Moors about the end of the 15th century. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 15. N. Lat. 37. 45.

BAFFETAS

Pages 368-368
or Bastas, a cloth made of coarse white cotton thread, which comes from the East Indies. That of Surat is the best.

BAFFIN'S BAY

Pages 368-368

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, running north-east from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Farewell in West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a>, from 6° to 8° of north latitude.

BAFFO

Pages 368-368

a considerable town in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cyprus, with a fort built near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Paphos, of which some considerable ruins yet remain, particularly some broken columns, which probably belonged to the temple of Venus. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 32. 20. N. Lat. 34. 50.

BAG

Pages 368-368

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> signifying a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of some particular commodity: a bag of almonds, for instance, is about 300 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; of aniseeds, from 300 to 400, &c. Bags, are used in most countries to put several sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, either of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">Bankers</a>, and others, who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> much in current cash, label their bags of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, by tying a ticket or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> at the mouth of the bag, signifying the coin therein contained, the sum total, its weight, and of whom it was received. Tare is allowed for the bag. Bag, among Farriers, is when, in order to retrieve a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s lost appetite, they put in an ounce of saffron-tida, and as much powder of savin, into a bag, to be tied to the bit, keeping him bridled for two hours, several times a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; as soon as the bag is taken off he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to eating. The same bag will serve a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

BAG-PIPE

Pages 380-381

a musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> kind, chiefly used in Scotland and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. The peculiarity of the bag-pipe, and from which it takes its name, is, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> which blows it is collected into a leathern bag, from whence it is pressed out by the arm into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>. These pipes consist of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a>, and tenor <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather treble; and are different according to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the pipe. The bass <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRONE">drone</a>, and the tenor or treble part the chanter. In all the species, the bass never varies from its uniform <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, and therefore very deservedly gets the name of drone; and the compass of the chanter is likewise very limited. There is a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the Highland and Lowland bag-pipes of Scotland; the former being blown with the mouth, and the latter with a small bellows; though this difference is not essential, every species of bag-pipes being capable, by a proper <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the reeds, of producing music either with the mouth or bellows. The following are the species of bag-pipes most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. 1. The Irish Pipe. This is the softest, and in some respects the most melodious of any, so that music-books have been published with directions how to play on it. The chanter, like that of all the rest, has eight holes like the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>, and is played on by opening and shutting the holes as occasion requires; the bass consists of two short drones and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> one. The lowest note of the chanter is D on the German flute, being the open note on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>-string of a violin; the small drone (one of them commonly being stopped up) is tuned in unison with the note above this, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> one to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a> below; so that a bag-pipe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> length is required in order to produce such a low note, on which account the drone hath sometimes two or three turns. The instrument is tuned by lengthening or shortening the drone till it finds the note desired. 2. The Highland Bag-Pipe. This consists of a chanter and two short drones, which found in union the lowest note of the chanter except one. This is exceedingly loud, and almost deafening <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> played in a room; and is therefore mostly used in the field, for marches, &c. It requires a prodigious blast to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> it; so that those unaccustomed to it cannot imagine how Highland pipers can continue to play for hours together, as they are often known to do. For the same reason, those who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the instrument are obliged either to stand on their feet or walk when they play. This instrument hath but <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> notes; its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, however, hath not yet been reduced to a regular standard by comparing it with that of other instruments, so that we can say nothing about its compass. Those who are best acquainted with it, however, affirm that it plays only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> notes, without being capable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> by flats or sharps. 3. The Scots Lowland Pipe. This is likewise a very loud instrument, though less so than the former. It is blown with bellows, and hath a bass like the Irish pipe. This species is different from all the rest, as it cannot play the natural notes, but hath F and C sharp. The lowest note of a good bag-pipe of this kind is unison with C sharp on the tenor of a violin tuned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a>-pitch; and, as it hath but nine notes, the highest is D in alt. From this peculiar construction, the Highland and Lowland bag-pipes play two species of music essentially different from one another, as each of them also is from every other species of music in the world. Hence these two species of bag-pipes deserve notice as curiosities; for the music which they play is accompanied with such peculiar ornaments, or what are intended as such, as neither violin, or even organ, can imitate, but in a very imperfect manner. This kind of bag-pipe was formerly very much used in Scotland at weddings and other festivals; being indeed extremely well calculated for playing that peculiar species of Scots music called reels. It has been often a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of surprize how this was possible, as the instrument has only a compass of nine or ten notes at the utmost, and which cannot be varied as in other instruments. In this respect, however, it has a very great compass, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> play an inconceivable variety of tunes. As its notes are naturally so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, there is scarce any one tune but what is naturally transposed by it, so that what would be a flat note on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> proper for the violin, may be a sharp one on the bag-pipe; and though the latter cannot play any flat note, it may nevertheless in this manner play tunes which on other instruments would be flat, to as great perfection as these instruments themselves. 4. The Small Pipe. This is remarkable for its smallness, the chanter not exceeding eight inches in length; for which reason, the holes are so near each other, that it is with difficulty they can be closed. This hath only eight notes, the lower end of the chanter being commonly stopped. The reason of this is, to prevent the flurring of all the notes, which is unavoidable in the other other species; so that in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a bad player they become the most shocking and unintelligible instruments imaginable: but this, by having the lower hole closed, and also by the peculiar way in which the notes are expressed, plays all its tunes in the way called by the Italians flaccato, and cannot flur at all. It hath no species of music peculiar to itself; and can play nothing which cannot be much better done upon other instruments; though it is surprising what volatility some performers on this instrument will display, and how much they will overcome the natural disadvantages of it. Some of this species, instead of having drones like the others, have their bass parts consisting of a winding cavity in a kind of short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and are tuned by opening them to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> by means of sliding covers; from which contrivance they are called flute-pipes. Besides these there are a variety of others, called Italian, German, Organ, &c., bag-pipes, which have nothing different in their construction from those above described, nor any good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to recommend them. As to the origin of bag-pipe music, some are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that it is to be derived from the Danes; but Mr Pennant thinks differently, and gives the following reasons for deriving it from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Neither of these instruments (the Highland and Lowland bag-pipes above described) were the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the Danes, or, as is commonly supposed, of any of the northern nations; for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers prove them to have been animated by the clangor tubarum. Notwithstanding they have had their feck pipe long amongst them, as their old songs prove, yet we cannot allow them the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of inventing this melodious instrument, but must assert, that they borrowed it from the invaded Caledonians. We must still go farther, and derive even that ancient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>; and derive its origin from the mild <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of Italy, perhaps from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. There is now in Rome a most beautiful bas relievo, a Grecian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> of the highest antiquity, of a bag-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIPER">piper</a> playing on his instrument, exactly like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGHLANDER">Highlander</a>. The Greeks had their Aερανδρος, or instrument, composed of a pipe and blown-up skin: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> borrowed it from them, and introduced it among their swains, who still use it under the names of piva and cornu-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSA">musa</a>. That <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of music, Nero, used one; and had not the empire been so suddenly deprived of that great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, he would (as he graciously declared his intention) have treated the people with a concert, and among other curious instruments, would have introduced the utricularius or bag-pipe. Nero perished; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the instrument is preserved on one of his coins, but highly improved by that great master: it has the bag and two of the vulgar pipes; but was blown with a bellows like an organ, and had on one side a row of nine unequal pipes, resembling the syrinx of the god <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>. The bag-pipe, in the unimproved state, is also represented in an ancient sculpture; and appears to have had two long pipes or drones, and a single short pipe for the fingers. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">Tradition</a> says, that the kind played on by the mouth was introduced by the Danes; as theirs was wind-music, we will admit that they might have made improvement, but more we cannot allow: they were skilled in the use of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>; the Highlanders in the pibroch, or bag-pipe. Non tuba in usu illis, conjuncta at tibia in utrem Dat belli signum, et martem vocat horrida in arma.* * Melvini Topogr. Scot. The bag-pipe appears to have been an instrument of great antiquity in Ireland, though it is uncertain whence they derived it. Mr Pennant, by means of an antique found at Richborough in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, has determined that the bag-pipe was introduced at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; whence it is probable that both Irish and Danes might borrow the instrument from the Caledonians with whom they had such frequent intercourse. Arithides Quintilianus informs us, that it prevailed in the highlands in very early ages; and indeed the genius of the people seems to render the opinion highly probable. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> of that people to their music called pibrachs is almost incredible, and on some occasions is said to have produced effects little less marvellous than those ascribed to the ancient music. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Quebec in 1760, while the British troops were retreating in great disorder, the general complained to a field officer in Frazer's regiment of the bad behaviour of his corps. "Sir (said he with some warmth), you did very wrong in forbidding the pipers to play this morning: nothing encourages the Highlanders so much in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. Nay, even now they would be of use."—"Let them blow like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>, then (replies the general), if it will bring back the men." The pipers were then ordered to play a favourite martial air; and the Highlanders, the moment they heard the music, returned and formed with alacrity in the rear. In the late <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, Sir Eyre Coote, aware of the attachment of the Highlanders to their favourite instrument, gave them 50l. to buy a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of bag-pipes after the battle of Porto Nuovo. Formerly there was a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SKYE">Skye</a>, where the highland bag-pipe was taught; the teachers making use of pins stuck into the ground instead of musical notes. This college, however, has been for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> entirely dissolved, and the use of the Highland pipe became much less general than before. At last a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of gentlemen, thinking it perhaps impolitic to allow the ancient martial music of the country to decline, resolved to revive it by giving an annual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> to the best performers on the instrument. These competitions were first held at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALKIRK">Falkirk</a>, but for a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>; where the only surviving member of the ancient college of Skye is now professor of bag-pipe music. The Lowland pipe, as has been already observed, is an instrument essentially different from the Highland pipe; it was reformed, and the music improved by George Mackie, who is said to have attended the college of Skye <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years. He had before been the best performer on that instrument in that part of the country where he lived; but, while attending the college at Skye, he adapted the graces of the Highland music to the Lowland pipe. Upon his return, he was heard with astonishment and admiration; but unluckily, not being able to commit his improvements to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, and indeed the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the instrument scarcely admitting of it, the knowledge of this kind of music hath <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to decay ever since, and will probably soon wear out altogether. What contributes much to this is, that bag-pipers, not content with the natural nine notes which their instrument can play easily,

BAGAMADER

Pages 368-368
or BAGAMEDRI, a province of the kingdom of Abyssinia in Africa. It is said to receive its name from the great number of sheep bred in it; meder signifying land or earth, and bag a sheep. Its length is estimated about 60 leagues, and its breadth 20: but formerly it was much more extensive; several of its provinces having been dismembered from it, and joined to that of Tigre. A great part of it, especially towards the east, is inhabited by wandering Gallas and Caffres. BAGAUDÆ, or BACAUDE, an ancient faction of peasants, or malecontents, who ravaged Gaul. The Gauls being oppressed with taxes, rose about the year of Christ 290, under the command of Amand and Elian; and assumed the name bagaudæ, which, according, to some authors, signified in the Gallic language forced rebels; according to others, tributes; according to others, robbers; which last signification others allow the word had, but then it was only after the time of the bagaudæ, and doubters took its rise from them.

BAGDAD

Pages 368-379

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IRAK">Irak</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, seated on the eastern banks of the Tigris, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 43. 40. N. Lat. 33. 15. By many authors this city is very very improperly called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>. The latter stood on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> at a considerable distance. This city, for many years the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Saracen empire, was founded by the caliph Al Mansur, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Al Abbas, after an attempt by the Rawandians to assassinate him, as already mentioned. See Arabia, No. 184. The reasons assigned by the Arabian historians for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the city of Bagdad are, That the above-mentioned attempt to assassinate the caliph had disgusted him at his Arabian subjects in general, and that the spot where Bagdad stood was at a considerable distance from the city of Cufa particularly; the inhabitants of which were remarkable for their treachery and inconstancy, Al Mansur himself having felt several instances of it. Besides the people of Irac, who had always <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> faithful to him, represented, that by building his capital near the confluence of the Euphrates and Tigris, it would be in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> secured from the insults and attacks of those who should have an inclination to dispute the caliphate with him; and that by being situated as it were in the middle of the tract comprehending the districts of Bafrah, Cufa, Walet, Mawfel, and Swada, at no great distance from these cities, it would be plentifully supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> by means of the aforesaid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. Concerning the origin of the name Bagdad, there are various accounts, which, being equally uncertain and trifling, merit no <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. The first city that went by this name was situated on the western <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Tigris; from whence Al Mansur despatched his son Al Mohdi with a body of Mollem troops to the opposite bank. Here the young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, and fortified the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on which he had encamped with a wall, in order to cover his troops, as well as the workmen employed by his father on the other side of the river, from the incursions of the Persians, who seemed to have taken umbrage at the erection of a new <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> so near the frontiers of their dominions. Hence that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the city soon after built on the eastern banks of the Tigris, received the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">Camp</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Fortresses of Al Mohdi. The caliph had a superb and magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> both in the eastern and western part of the town. The eastern palace was surrounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> side by a semicircular wall that had six gates; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which seems to have been called the gate of prefects, whose entrance was generally kissed by the princes and ambassadors that came to the caliph's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. The western part of the city was entirely round, with the caliph's palace in the centre, and having the great mosque annexed to it. The eastern part consisted of an interior and exterior town, each of which was surrounded by a wall. For some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the building of the city went but slowly on, owing to a scarcity of materials for building; for which reason the caliph was sometimes inclined to remove the materials of Al Madayen, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> metropolis of the Persian empire. But, upon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, he found the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> to be of such immense size, that the removal of them to Bagdad would be attended with great difficulty and expense; besides, he considered that it would be a reflection upon himself to have it said that he could not finish his metropolis without destroying such a pile of building as perhaps could not be paralleled in the whole world; for which reasons he at length gave over his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and erected the city of Bagdad most probably out of the ruins of the ancient cities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a> and Ctesiphon, putting an end to his undertaking in the 149th year of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a>, or four years after the city was begun. From the building of the city of Bagdad to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Al Mansur nothing very remarkable happened, excepting some irruptions made into the territories of the Greeks, and by the Arabs into some of the caliph's other territories. In the 157th year of the Hegira also, a grievous famine was felt in Mesopotamia, which was quickly after followed by a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> that destroyed great numbers. This year likewise, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who had been all along very severely dealt with by Al Mansur, were treated with the utmost rigour by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSA">Musa</a> Ebn Moaafab the caliph's governor; every one who was unable to pay the enormous tribute exacted of them being thrown into prison without distinction. The next year, being the 158th of the Hegira, the death of Al Mansur set out from Bagdad, in order to perform the pilgrimage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>; but being taken ill on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, he expired at Bir Maimun, whence his body was carried to Mecca; where, after a hundred graves had been dug, that his sepulchre might be concealed, he was interred, having lived according to some 63, according to others 68 years, and reigned 22. He is said to have been extremely covetous, and to have left in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> 600,000,000 dirhems, and 24,000,000 dinars. He is reported to have paid his cook by afflicting him the heads and legs of the animals drest in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>, and to have obliged him to procure at his own expense all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> and vessels he had occasion for. When Al Mansur expired at Bir Maimun, he had succeeded only his domestics and Rabi his freedman with him, by Al Mohdi. The latter of these, for some time, kept his death concealed, and pretended to have a conference with him, in which, as he gave out, the caliph commanded him to exact an oath of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to Al Mohdi his son, as his immediate successor, and to Isa Ebn Musa his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>-german, as the next apparent heir to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. He then despatched a courier to Bagdad with the news of Al Mansur's death; upon which Al Mohdi was unanimously proclaimed caliph. Isa Ebn Musa, however, no sooner heard this news, than he began to entertain thoughts of setting up for himself at Cufa, where he then resided; and in order to facilitate the execution of his scheme, fortified himself in that city. But Al Mohdi being apprised of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFECTION">defection</a>, sent a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of 1000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> to bring him to Bagdad; which being done, Al Mohdi not only prevailed upon him to own his allegiance to him, but also to give up his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the succession for 10,000 according to some, or according to others for 10,000,000 dinars. From the accession of Al Mohdi to the 146th year of the Hegira, the most remarkable event was the rebellion of Al Mokanna. This impious impostor, whose true name was Hakem Ebn Heyham, came originally from Khorasan, and had been an under secretary to Abu Mollem governor of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. He afterwards turned soldier, and passed thence into Mawarannah, where he gave himself out for a prophet. The name of Al Mokanna, as also that of Al Borkai, that is, the veiled, he took from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of covering his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> with a veil or girdle mask, to conceal his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a>; he having lost an eye in the wars, and being otherwise... otherwise of a despicable appearance; though his followers pretended he did this for the same reason that Moles did, viz. left the splendour of his countenance should dazzle the eyes of his beholders. In some places he made a great many profelytes, deluding the people with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of juggling tricks which they swallowed as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, and particularly by causing the appearance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> to rise out of a well for many nights together; whence he was also called in the Persian tongue, Sazendeb mak, or the moon-maker. This wretch, not content with being reckoned a prophet, arrogated to himself divine honours; pretending that the Deity resided in his person, having proceeded to him from Abu Mollem, in whom he had taken up his residence before. At last this impostor raised an open rebellion against the caliph, and made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of several fortified places in Khurasan, so that Al Mohdi was obliged to send one of his generals with an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> against him. Upon the approach of the caliph's troops, Al Mokamma retired into one of his strong fortresses which he had well provided for a siege; and sent his emissaries abroad to persuade the people that he raised the dead to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and foretold future events. But being closely besieged by the caliph's forces, and seeing no possibility of escaping, he gave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> in wine to his whole family and all that were with him, in the castle; when they were dead, he burnt their bodies, together with all their furniture, provisions, and cattle; and lastly, he threw himself into the flames, or, as others say, into a tub of aquafortis, or some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, which consumed every part of him except the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. When the besiegers therefore entered the place, they found no living creature in it, except one of Al Mokanna's concubines, who, suspecting his design, had hid herself, and now discovered the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. This terrible contrivance, however, failed not to produce the desired effect. He had promised his followers, that his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> should transmigrate into the form of an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> riding on a greyhul coloured beast, and that after so many years he would return and give them the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> for their possession; which ridiculous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> kept the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> in being for several years. All this time <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> had been carried on with the Greeks, but without any remarkable success on either side. In the 164th year of the Hegira, however, Al Mohdi ordered his son Harun Al Rafchid to penetrate into the Greek territories with an army of 95,000 men. Harun, then, having entered the dominions of the empress Irene, defeated one of her commanders that advanced against him; after which he laid waste several of the imperial provinces with fire and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and even threatened the city of Constantinople itself. By this the empress was so terrified, that she purchased a peace with the caliph by paying him an annual tribute of 70,000 pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; which, for the present at least, delivered her from the depredations of these barbarians. After the signing of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, Harun returned home laden with spoils and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. This year, according to some of the oriental historians, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, a little after his rising, totally lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> in a moment, without being eclipsed, when neither any fog nor any cloud of dust appeared to obscure him. This frightful darkness continued till noon, to the great astonishment of the people settled in the countries where it happened. In the 166th year of the Hegira, Al Mohdi was poisoned, though undefendedly, by one of his concubines named Hafanab. She had designed to destroy him; one of her rivals whom she imagined to have too great an ascendant over the caliph by giving her a poisoned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>. This the latter, not suspecting anything, gave to the caliph; who had no sooner eaten it than he felt himself in exquisite torture, and soon after expired. On the death of Al Mohdi, he was succeeded by his eldest son Al Hadi; who having formed a design to succeed, deprived his younger <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Harun Al Rafchid of his right of succession, and even to affiancement him, was poisoned by his vizier in the 17th year of the Hegira; and on his death the celebrated caliph Harun Al Rafchid ascended the throne. This was one of the best and wisest princes that Harun Al Rafchid ever sat on the throne of Bagdad. He was also extremely fortunate in all his undertakings, though he did not much extend his dominions by conquest. In his time the Mollem empire may be said to have been in its most flourishing state, though by the independency of the Mollems in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, who had formerly set up a caliph of the house of Omniyah, his territories were not quite so extensive as those of some of his predecessors. He possessed the provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, Arabia, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a>, Media or Adurbijan, Babylon, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, Sindia, Sijiljan, Khorasan, Tabristan, Jorjan, Zablestan or Sablestan, Mawaralnahr or Great Bukharia, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>, &c.; so that his empire was by far the most powerful of any in the world, and extended farther than the Roman empire ever had done. The first influence of Harun's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, and which was taken for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> of a prosperous and happy reign, was his finding a valuable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> which he had thrown into the Tigris to avoid being deprived of it by his brother Al Hadi. He was able to give the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> than by throwing a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of Bagdad, about the same place of the river in which he had thrown the ring; notwithstanding which, they found it without any great difficulty. In the 186th year of the Hegira, beginning <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 802, the caliph divided the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> among his three sons, in the following manner: To Al Amin the eldest, he assigned the provinces of Syria, Irak, the three Arabias, Mesopotamia, Assyria, Media, Palestine, Egypt, and all that part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> extending from the confines of Egypt and Ethiopia to the straits of Gibraltar, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of caliph; to Al Mamun the second, he assigned Persia, Kerman, the Indies, Khorasan, Tabristan, Calestan, and Zablestan, together with the vast province of Mawaralnahr; and to this third son Al Kalem, he gave Armenia, Natolia, Jorjan, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, Circassia, and all the Mollem territories bordering upon the Euxine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. As to the order of succession, Al Amin was to ascend the throne immediately after his father's decease; after him, Al Mamun; and then Al Kafem, whom he had nicknamed Al Mutaman. The most considerable exploit performed by this caliph caliph were against the Greeks, who by their perfidy provoked him to make war upon them, and whom he always overcame. In the 18th year of the Hegira, the caliph received a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Nicephorus soon after he had been advanced to the imperial dignity, commanding him to return all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> he had extorted from the empress Irene, though that had been secured to him by the last treaty concluded with that princess, or expect soon to see an imperial army in the heart of his territories. This insolent letter so exasperated Harun, that he immediately assembled his forces and advanced to Heraclia, laying the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> through which he passed waste with fire and sword. For some time also he kept that city straitly besieged; which so terrified the Greek emperor, that he submitted to pay an annual tribute. Upon this Harun granted him a peace, and returned with his army. But a hard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a> soon after happening in these parts, Nicephorus took for granted that Al-Rafid would not pay him another visit, and therefore broke the treaty he had concluded. Of this the caliph receiving advice, he instantly put himself in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; and, notwithstanding the inclemency of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, forced the emperor to accept of the terms proposed. According to a Persian historian, before the hostilities at this time commenced, Nicephorus made the caliph a present of several fine swords, giving him thereby plainly to understand that he was more inclinable to come to blows than to make peace with him. All these swords Harun cut asunder with his famous sword Samiramah, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had been so many radishes, after which severe <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> there did not appear the least flaw in the blade; a clear proof of the goodness of the sword, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the others with it was of the strength of Harun's arm. This sword had fallen into Al-Rafid's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> among the spoils of Ebn Dakikan, one of the last Hamaritic princes of Yaman; but is said to have belonged originally to a valiant Arab named Amru Ebn Maadi Karb, by whose name it generally went among the Molems. This man is said to have performed very extraordinary feats with his sword, which induced a certain prince to borrow it from him; but not being able to perform any thing remarkable with it, complained to Amru that it had not the desired effect; upon which that brave man took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to tell him, that he had not sent him his arm along with his sword. In the 18th year of the Hegira, war was renewed with the Greeks, and Nicephorus with a great army attacked the caliph's forces with the utmost fury. He was, however, defeated with the loss of 40,000 men, and received three wounds in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; after which the Molems committed terrible ravages in his territories, and returned home laden with spoils. The next year Harun invaded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>; defeated an imperial army sent to oppose him; and having ravaged the country, returned without any considerable loss. In the 19th year of the Hegira, commencing November 27, 805, the caliph marched into the imperial territories with an army of 135,000 men, besides a great number of volunteers and others who were not enrolled among his troops. He first took the city of Heraclia, from whence he is said to have carried 16,000 prisoners; after which he made himself master of several other places; and in the conclusion of the expedition, he made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cyprus, which he plundered in a terrible manner. This success so intimidated Nicephorus, that he immediately sent the tribute due to Harun, the withholding of which had been the cause of the war, and concluded a peace upon the caliph's own terms; one of which was, that the city of Heraclia should never be rebuilt. This perhaps Harun would not have so readily granted, had not one Rebellion Rafe Ebn Al <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEITH">Leith</a> revolted against him at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARCAND">Samarcand</a>, in Khora, and assembled a considerable force to support him in his defection. The next year being the 19th of the Hegira, the caliph removed the governor of Khorsan from his employment, because he had not been sufficiently attentive to the motions of the rebel Rafe Ebn Al Leith. As this governor had also tyrannized over his subjects in the most cruel manner, his successor no sooner arrived than he sent him in chains to the caliph; but notwithstanding all Harun's care, the rebels made this year a great progress in the conquest of Khorasan. Next year the caliph found it necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> in person against the rebels, who were daily becoming more formidable. The general rendezvous of his troops was in the plains of Rakka, from whence he advanced at the head of them to Bagdad. Having at that place supplied the troops with everything necessary, he continued his march to the frontiers of Jorjan, where he was seized with an illness which grew more violent after he had entered that province. Finding himself therefore unable to pursue his journey, he resigned the command of the army to his son Al Mamun, retiring himself to Tus in Khorsan. We are told by Khondemir, that, before the caliph departed from Rakka, he had a dream, wherein he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> over his head full of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> earth, and at the same time heard a person pronouncing these words, "See the earth where Harun is to be buried." Upon this he demanded where he was to be buried; and was instantly answered, "At Tus." This dream greatly discomposing him, he communicated it to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> physician, who endeavoured to divert him, telling the caliph that the dream had been occasioned by the thoughts of his expedition against the rebels. He therefore advised him to pursue some favourite diversion that might draw his attention another way. The caliph accordingly, by his physician's advice, prepared a magnificent regale for his courtiers, which lasted several days. After this, he put himself at the head of his forces, and advanced to the confines of Jorjan, where he was attacked by the distemper that proved fatal to him. As his disorder increased, he found himself obliged to retire to Tus; where being arrived, he sent for his physician, and said to him, "Gabriel, do you remember my dream at Rakka? we are now arrived at Tus, the place, according to what was predicted in that dream, of my <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a>. Send one of my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a> to fetch me a handful of earth in the neighbourhood of this city." Upon this, Mafur, one of his favourite eunuchs, was despatched to bring a little of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of the place to the caliph. He soon returned and brought a handful of red earth, which he presented to the caliph with his arm half bare. At the sight of this Harun instantly cried out, "In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> this is the earth, and this the very spot, that I saw in my dream. His spirits immediately failing, and his malady being greatly increased by the perturbation of mind ensuing upon Bagdad, upon this fight, he died three days after, and was buried in the same place. According to Abul Faraj, Bahr Ebn Al Leith the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-rebel's brother was brought in chains to the caliph, who was then at the point of death. At the fight of whom Harun declared, that if he could speak only two words he would say kill him; and immediately ordered him to be cut to pieces in his presence. This being done, the caliph soon after expired, in the year of the Hegira 193, having reigned 23 years. The distemper that put an end to his days is said to have been the bloody-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a>. Upon the arrival of a courier from Tus, with the news of Al Rafhid's death, his son Al Amin was immediately proclaimed caliph; and was no sooner seated on the throne, than he formed a design of excluding his brother Al Mamun from the succession. Accordingly he deprived him of the furniture of the imperial palace of Khorasan; and in open violation of his father's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, who had bestowed on Al Mamun the perpetual government of Khorasan, and of all the troops in that province, he ordered these forces to march directly to Bagdad. Upon the arrival of this order, Al Mamun expostulated with the general Al Fadl Ebn Rabbi who commanded his troops, and endeavoured to prevent his marching to Bagdad; but without effect, for he punctually obeyed the orders sent by the caliph. Al Mamun, however, took care not to be wanting in fidelity to his brother. He obliged the people of Khorasan to take an oath of fidelity to Al Amin, and reduced some who had actually excited a considerable body of the people to revolt, while the general Al Fadl having ingratiated himself with the caliph by his ready compliance with his orders, was chosen prime vizir, and governed with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> sway: Al Amin abandoning himself entirely to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUNKENNESS">drunkenness</a>. Al Fadl was a very able minister; though fearing Al Mamun's resentment if ever he should ascend the throne, he gave Al Amin such advice as proved in the end the ruin of them both. He told him that his brother had gained the affection of the people of Khorasan by the good order and <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> he had established among them; that his unwearied application to the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> had so attracted their esteem, that the whole province was entirely at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>; that his own conduct was by no means relished by his subjects, whose minds were almost totally alienated from him; and therefore that he had but one part to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, which was to deprive Al Mamun of the right of succession that had been given him by his father, and transfer it to his own son Mufa, though then but an infant. Agreeable to this pernicious advice, the caliph sent for his brother Al Kasem from Mesopotamia, and recalled Al Mamun from Khorasan, pretending he had occasion for him as an assistant in his councils. By this treatment Al Mamun was so much provoked, that he resolved to come to an open rupture with his brother, in order if possible to frustrate his wicked designs. Instead, therefore, of going to Bagdad as he had been commanded, he cut off all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between his own province and that capital: pretending, that as his father Harun had assigned him the lieutenancy of Khorasan, he was responsible for all the disorders that might happen there during his absence. He also coined money, and would not suffer Al Amin's name to be impressed upon any of the dirhems or dinars struck in that province. Not content with this, he prevailed upon Rafe Ebn Al Leith, who had been for some time in rebellion, to join him with a body of troops; whose example was soon after followed by Harthema Ebn Aafan; which put him in possession of all the vast territory of Khorasan. Here he governed with an absolute sway, officiated in the mosque as Imam, and from the pulpit constantly harangued the people. The following year, being the 19th year of the Hegira, beginning October 4, 810, the caliph Al-Amin, finding that his brother set him at defiance, declared war against him, and sent his general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a> Ebn Ishaq with an army of 60,000 men to invade Khorasan. Al Mamun, being informed that Ali was advancing against him with such a powerful army, put on foot forces of all the troops he could raise, and gave the command to Thaher Ebn Hoefin, one of the greatest generals of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Thaher being a man of undaunted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, chose only 4000 men whom he led against Al Amin's army. Ali, seeing so small a number of troops advancing against him, was transported with joy, and promised himself an easy victory. Defying his enemies, therefore, he behaved in a secure and careless manner; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which was, that his army was entirely defeated, and himself killed, his head being afterwards sent as a present to Al Mamun, who amply rewarded Thaher and Harthema for their services. After this victory, Al Mamun assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of caliph, ordered Al Amin's name to be omitted in the public prayers, and made all necessary preparations for carrying the war into the very heart of his brother's dominions. For this purpose he divided his forces into two bodies, and commanded them to march into Irak by different routes. One of them obeyed the orders of Thaher, and the other of Harthema. The first directed his march towards Ahwas, and the other towards Holwan, both of them proposing to meet in the neighbourhood of Bagdad, and after their junction to besiege that city. In the 196th year of the Hegira, Thaher Ebn Hoefin made a most rapid progress with the troops under his command. Having advanced towards Ahwas, he there defeated a body of the caliph's forces; and though the victory was by no means decisive, it intimidated the commander of Ahwas, that he thought fit to surrender that fortress to him. This opened him a way to Wafet upon the Tigris, and facilitated the conquest of that place. After this he marched with his army to Al Madayen; the inhabitants of which immediately opened their gates to him. The rapidity of these conquests, and the infamous conduct of Al Amin, excited the people of Egypt, Syria, Hejaz, and Yaman, unanimously to declare for Al Mamun; who was accordingly proclaimed caliph in all the provinces. The next year, Al Mamun's forces under Thaher laid siege of and Harthema, laid siege to Bagdad. As the caliph was shut up in that place, and it had a numerous garrison, the besieged made a vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, and destroyed a great number of their enemies. The besiegers, however, incessantly played upon the town with their catapults and other engines, though they were in their turn not a little annoyed by the garrison with the same sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>. The latter likewise made continual continual fallies, and fought like men in despair, though they were always at last beaten back into the town with considerable loss. In short the siege continued during the whole of this year, in which the greatest part of the eastern city, called the Camp of Al Mohdi, was demolished or reduced to ashes. The citizens, as well as the garrison, were reduced to the last extremity, by the length and violence of the siege. In the beginning of the 108th year of the Hegira, Al Amin finding himself deserted by his troops, as well as by the principal men of Bagdad, who had kept a private correspondence with Thaher, was obliged to retire to the old town on the west bank of the Tigris. He did not, however, take this step, before the inhabitants of the new town had formally depopulated him, and proclaimed his brother Al Mamun caliph. Thaher, receiving advice of this, caused the old town to be immediately invested, planted his engines against it, and at last starved it to surrender. Al Amin being thus reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of putting himself into the hands of one of the generals, chose to implore the protection of Harthema, whom he judged to be of a more humane disposition than Thaher. Having obtained this, he embarked in a small vessel in order to arrive at that part of the camp where Harthema was posted; but Thaher being informed of his design, which, if put in execution, he thought would eclipse the glory he had acquired, laid an ambush for him, which he had not the good fortune to escape. Upon his arrival in the neighbourhood of Harthema's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a>, Thaher's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> rushed upon him, drowned all his attendants, and put himself in prison. Here he was soon after massacred by Thaher's servants, who carried his head in triumph to their master, by whose order it was afterwards exposed to public view in the streets of Bagdad. Thaher afterwards sent to Al Mamun in Khorasan, together with the ring or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of the caliphate, the sceptre, and the imperial robe. At the theft of these, Al Mamun fell <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, and returned thanks to God for his success; making the courier who brought them a present of a million of dirhems, in value about 100,000 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. The same day that Al Amin was assassinated, his brother Al Mamun was proclaimed caliph at Bagdad. He had not long been seated on the throne when he was alarmed by rebellions breaking out in different parts of the empire.
