These, however, were at last happily extinguished; after which, Thaher Ebn Hofein had the government of Khorasan conferred upon him and his descendants with almost absolute and unlimited power. This happened in the 25th year of the Hegira, from which time we may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> the dismemberment of that province from the empire of the caliphs. During the reign of this caliph nothing remarkable happened; only the African Molems invaded the island of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, where they made themselves masters of several places. He died of a surfeit in the 28th year of the Hegira, having reigned 20, and lived 43 or 49 years. On the death of Al Mamun, his brother Al Motafsem, by some of the oriental historians named Billah, was saluted caliph. He succeeded by virtue of Al Mamun's express nomination of him to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of his own son Al Abbas and his other brother Al Kafein, who had been appointed by Harun Al Raschid. In the beginning of his reign he was obliged to employ the whole forces of his empire against one Babec, who had been for a considerable time in rebellion in Persia and Perisan Irak. This Babec first appeared in the year of the Hegira 201, when he began to take upon new caliph him the title of a prophet. What his particular doctrine and name was, is now unknown; but his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is said to have differed from all others then known in Alfa. He gained a great number of proficients in Aderbijan and the Persian Irak, where he soon grew powerful enough to wage war with the caliph Al Mamun, whose troops he often <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a>, so that he was now become extremely formidable. The general sent by Al Motafsem to reduce him was Haider Ebn Kaus, surnamed Afshin, a Turk by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, who had been brought a slave to the caliph's court, and having been employed in disciplining the Turkish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> there, had acquired the reputation of a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>. By him Babec was defeated with prodigious slaughter, no fewer than 60,000 men Babec being killed in the first engagement. The next year, being the 220th of the Hegira, he received a still greater overthrow, losing 100,000 men either killed or taken prisoners. By this defeat he was obliged to retire into the Gordyean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; where he fortified himself in such a manner, that Afshin found it impossible to reduce him till the year of the Hegira 222. This commander having reduced with invincible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> all Babec's castles one after another, the impostor was obliged to shut himself up in a strong fortress called Ca'abad, which was now his last resource. Here he defended himself with great bravery for several months; but at last finding he should be obliged to surrender, he made his escape into a neighbouring wood, from whence he soon after came to Afshin, upon that general's promising him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>. But Afshin no sooner had him in his power, than he first caused his finger and hands and feet, and afterwards his head, to be cut off; put to death. Babec had supported himself against the power of the caliphs for upwards of 20 years, during which time he had cruelly massacred 250,000 people; it being his He destroy custom to spare neither man, woman, nor child, of the evil Mahometans or their allies. Amongst the prisoners numbers of taken at Ca'abad there was one Nad, who had been one of Babec's executioners, and who owned that in obedience to his master's commands he had destroyed 20,000 Molems with his own hands; to which he added, that vast numbers had also been executed by his companions, but that of these he could give no precise account. In the 223rd year of the Hegira, the Greek emperor Theophilus invaded the caliph's territories, where he behaved with the greatest cruelty, and by destroying Sozopetra the place of Al Motafsem's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>, notwithstanding his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> entreaties to the contrary, occasioned the terrible destruction of Amorium mentioned under that article. The rest of this caliph's reign is remarkable for nothing but the execution of Afshin, who was accused of holding correspondence with the caliph's enemies. After his death a great number of idols were found in his house, which were immediately burned, as also several books said to contain impious and detestable opinions. In the 227th year of the Hegira died the caliph Al Death of Motafsem, in the 48th or 49th year of his age. He Al Motafsem reigned eight years eight months and eight days, was born Baghdad, born in the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the year, fought eight battles, had 800 slaves, and had 8,000,000 dinars and 80,000 dirhems in his treasury at his death, whence the oriental historians give him the name of Al Motbammen, or the Generous. He is said to have been robust, that he once carried a burden of 1000 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> several paces. As the people of Baghdad disturbed him with frequent revolts and commotions, he took the resolution to abandon that city, and build another for his own residence. The new city he built was first called Samarra, and afterwards Sarra Manray, and stood in the Arabian Irak. He was attached to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the Motaizites, who maintain the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of the Koran; and both he and his predecessor cruelly persecuted those who believed it to be eternal. Al Motalem was succeeded by Al Wathek Bilah, who the following year, being the 228th of the Hegira, invaded and conquered Sicily. Nothing remarkable happened during the rest of his reign; he died in the 232nd year of the Hegira, and was succeeded by his brother Al Motawakkil. The new caliph began his reign with an act of the greatest cruelty. The late caliph's vizir having treated Al Motawakkil ill in his brother's lifetime, and opposed his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> to the caliphate, was on that account now sent to prison. Here the caliph ordered him to be kept awake for several days and nights together; after this, being suffered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> asleep, he slept a whole day and a night; and after he awoke was thrown into an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> lined with spikes or nails heated red hot, where he was miserably burnt to death. During this reign nothing remarkable happened, except wars with the Greeks, which were carried on with various success. In the year 859 too, being the 245th of the Hegira, violent earthquakes happened in many provinces of the Moslem dominions; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> at Mecca failed to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that the celebrated well Zemzem was almost dried up, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> sold for 100 dirhems a bottle. In the 247th year of the Hegira, the caliph was assassinated at the instance of his son Al Montafer; who succeeded him, and died in six months after. He was succeeded by Al Mollan, who in the year of the Hegira 252 was forced to abdicate the throne by his brother Al Motazz, who afterwards caused him to be privately murdered. He did not long enjoy the dignity of which he had so iniquitously possessed himself; being deplored by the Turkish militia (who now began to set up and depose caliphs as they pleased) in the 255th year of the Hegira. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a>, he was sent under escort from Sarra Manray to Baghdad, where he died of thirst or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, after a reign of four years and about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months. The fate of this caliph was peculiarly hard; the Turkish troops had mutinied for their pay; and Al Motazz, not having money to satisfy their demands, applied to his mother named Kabiha for 50,000 dinars. This she refused, telling him that she had no money at all, although it afterwards appeared that she was possessed of immense treasures. After his deposition, however, she was obliged to discover them, and even depose them in the hands of the new caliph Al Mokhtadi. They consisted of 1,000,000 dinars, a bushel of emeralds, and another of pearls, and three pounds and three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of rubies of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of fire. Al Mokhtadi, the new caliph, was the son of one of Baghdad. Al Wathek's concubines named Korb, or Karb, who is by some supposed to have been a Christian. The beginning of his reign is remarkable for the irruption of the Zenjians, a people of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUBIA">Nubia</a>, Ethiopia, and the jins in country of the Caffres, into Arabia, where they penetrated into the neighbourhood of Bafra and Cufa. The chief of this gang of robbers, who, according to some historians, differed but little from wild beasts, was Ali Ebn Mohammed Ebn Abdalrahman, who falsely gave himself out to be of the family of Ali Ebn Abu Taleb. This made such an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon the Shites in those parts, that they flocked to him in great numbers; which enabled him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> upon the cities of Bafra and Ramla, and even to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the Tigris at the head of a formidable army. He then took the title of Prince of the Zenjians, in order to ingratiate himself with those barbarians, of whom his army was principally composed. In the 267th year of the Hegira, Al Mokhtadi was barbarously murdered by the Turks who had raised him to the throne, and was succeeded by Al Montafer, the son of Al Motawakkil. This year the prince of the Zenjians, Ali, or as he is also called Al Habib, made incursions to the very gates of Baghdad, doing prodigious mischief wherever he passed. The caliph therefore sent against him one Jolan with a considerable army; he was overthrown, however, with very great slaughter by the Zenjians, who made himself master of 24 of the caliph's largest ships in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Bafra, put a vast number of the inhabitants of Obolla to the sword, and feasted upon the town. Not content with this, he set fire to it, and soon reduced it to ashes, the houses mostly consisting of the wood of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> tree called by the Arabians Sag. From thence he marched to Abadan, which likewise surrendered to him. Here he found immense <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, which enabled him to possess himself of the whole district of Ahwaz. In short, his forces being now increased to 80,000 strong, most of the adjacent territories, and even the caliph's court itself, were struck with terror. In the 257th year of the Hegira, Al Habib continued victorious, defeated several armies sent against him by the caliph, reduced the city of Bafra, and put 20,000 of the inhabitants to the sword. The following year, the caliph, supported by his brother Al Mowaffek, had formed a design of circumferring the power of the Turkish soldiery, who had for some time given <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> to the caliphs themselves. But this year the Zenjians made so rapid a progress in Persia, Arabia, and Irak, that he was obliged to suspend the execution of his design, and even to employ the Turkish troops to assist his brother Al Mowaffek in opposing these robbers. The first of the caliph's generals who encountered Al Habib this year, was defeated in several engagements, and had his army at last entirely destroyed. After this Al Mowaffek and another general named Moheh advanced against him. In the first engagement Moheh being killed by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>, the caliph's troops retired; but Al Mowaffek put them afterwards in such a posture of defence, that the enemy durst not renew the attack. Several other sharp encounters happened this year, in which neither party gained great advantage; but, at last, some contagious distempers breaking out out in Al Mowaffek's army, he was obliged to conclude a truce, and retire to Walet to refresh his troops. In the 259th year of the Hegira, commencing Nov. 7, 872, the war between the caliph and Al Habib still continued. Al Mowaffek, upon his arrival at Bagdad, sent Mohammed furnished Al Mowalled with a powerful army to act against the Zenjians; but he could not hinder them from ravaging the province of Ahwaz, cutting off about 50,000 of the caliph's subjects, and dismantling the city of Ahwaz; and notwithstanding the utmost efforts of all the caliph's generals, no considerable advantages could be gained either this or the following year. In the 261st year of the Hegira, beginning October 16, 874, Mohammed Ebn Wafel, who had killed the caliph's governor of Pars, and afterwards made himself master of that province, had several engagements with Al Habib, but with what success is not known. The caliph, having been apprized of the state of affairs on that side, annexed the government of Pars, Ahwaz, and Bafra, to the prefecture he had given to Musa Ebn Baga, whom he looked upon as one of the best generals he had. Musa, soon after his nomination to that post, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> Abdalrahman Ebn Molleh as his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> to Ahwaz, giving him as a colleague and assistant one Tifam, a Turk. Mohammed Ebn Wafel, however, refusing to obey the orders of Abdalrahman and Tifam, a fierce conflict ensued, in which the latter was defeated, and Abdalrahman taken prisoner. After this victory, Mohammed advanced against Musa Ebn Boga himself; but that general finding he could not take possession of his new government without a vast <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of blood, recalled the deputies from their provinces, and made the best of his way to Sarra Manray. After this, Yakub Ebn Al Leit, having taken Khorasan from the descendants of Thaher, attacked and defeated Mohammed Ebn Wafel, seizing on his palace, where he found a sum of money amounting to 40,000,000 dirhems. The next year Yakub Ebn Leit being grown formidable by the acquisition of Ahwaz and a considerable portion of Pars, or at least the Persian Irak, declared war against the caliph. Against him Al Motamed dispatched Al Mowaffek; who having defeated him with prodigious slaughter, plundered his camp, and pursued him into Khorasan; where meeting with no opposition, he entered Nifabur, and released Mahomet the Thaherian, whom Yakub had detained in prison three years. As for Yakub himself, he made his escape with great difficulty, though he and his family continued several years in possession of many of the conquests he had made. This war with Yakub proved a scataneous diversion in favour of Al Habib, who this year defeated all the forces sent against him, and ravaged the district of Walet. The following year, being the 263d of the Hegira, beginning September 24, 876, the caliph's forces, under the command of Ahmed Ebn Lehuna, gained two considerable advantages over Al Habib; but being at last drawn into an ambuscade, they were almost totally destroyed, their general himself making his escape with the utmost difficulty; nor were the caliph's forces able, during the course of the next year, to make the least impression upon these rebels. In the 265th year of the Hegira, beginning September 3, 878, Ahmed Ebn Tolun rebelled against the caliph, and set up for himself in Egypt. Having assembled a considerable force, he marched to Antioch, and besieged Sima the governor of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a> and all the rebellious provinces known among the Arabs by the name of Al Egypt Awajem, in that city. As the beleaguered found that he whom they resolved to carry the place by assault, they thought not be sup- fit, after a short defense, to submit, and to put Sima prilled into his hands. Ahmed no sooner had that officer in his power, than he caused him to be beheaded; after which he advanced to Aleppo, the gates of which were immediately opened unto him. Soon after, he reduced Damascus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMS">Hems</a>, Hamath, Kinusfrin, and Al Rakka, situated upon the eastern bank of the Euphrates. This rebellion so exasperated Al Motamed, that he caused Ahmed to be publicly curled in all the mosques belonging to Bagdad and Irak; and Ahmed on his part ordered the same malediction to be thundered out against the caliph in all the mosques within his jurisdiction. This year also a detachment of Al Habib's troops penetrated into Irak, and made themselves masters of four of the caliph's ships laden with corn; then they advanced to Al Nomanic, laid the greatest part of it in ashes, and carried off with them several of the inhabitants prisoners. After this they possessed themselves of Jarfaraya, where they found many prisoners more, and destroyed all the adjacent territory with fire and sword. This year there were four independent powers in the Four independent dominions, besides the house of Ommiyah in pendent Spain, viz. The African Moilems, or Aglabites, who bowers had for a long time acted independently; Ahmed in Syria and Egypt; Al Leit in Khorasan; and Al Ha-minions, bibr in Arabia and Irak. In the 266th year of the Hegira, beginning August 23, 879, Al Habib reduced Ramhormoz, burnt the fatly mosque there to the ground, put a vast number of the inhabitants to the sword, and carried away great numbers, as well as a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of spoil. This was his last successful <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>; for the following, Al Mowaffek, attended by his son Abul <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">Ad</a>-bad succes bas, having attacked him with a body of 10,000 horse and death, and a few infantry, notwithstanding the vast disparity of numbers (Al Habib's army amounting to 100,000 men), defeated him in several battles, recovered most of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> he had taken, together with an immense quantity of spoil, and released 5000 women that had been thrown into prison by these barbarians. After these victories, Al Mowaffek took post before the city of Al Mabiya', built by Al Habib, and the place of his residence; burnt all the ships in the harbour; thoroughly pillaged the town; and then entirely dismantled it. After the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of this place, in which he found immense treasures, Al Mowaffek pursued the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> Zenjians, put several of their chiefs to the sword, and advanced to Al Mokhtara, a city built by Al Habib. As the place was strongly fortified, and Al Habib was posted in its neighbourhood, with an army, according to Abu Jafer Al Tabari, of 300,000 men, Al Mowaffek perceived that the reduction of it would be a matter of some difficulty. He therefore built a fortress opposite to it, where he erected a mosque, and coined money. The new city, from its founder, was called by the Arabs Al Mowaffekkia, and soon rendered considerable by the settlement of several wealthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> there. The city of Al Mokhtara being reduced to great straits was at last taken by storm, and given up to Bagdad, be plundered by the caliph's troops; after which Al Mowafek defeated the numerous forces of Al Habib in such a manner, that they could no more be rallied during that campaign. The following year, being the 268th of the Hegira, Al Mowafek penetrated again into Al Mabiya', and demolished the fortifications which had been raised since its former reduction, though the rebels disputed every inch of ground. Next year he again attacked Al Habib with great bravery; and would have entirely defeated him, had he not been wounded in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> with an arrow, which obliged him to find a retreat. However, as soon as he was cured of his wound, Al Mowafek advanced a third time to Al Mabiya', made himself master of that metropolis, threw down the walls that had been raised, put many of the inhabitants to the sword, and carried a vast number of them into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>. The 27th year of the Hegira, commencing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 11th 883, proved fatal to the rebel Al Habib. Al Mowafek made himself a fourth time master of Al Mabiya', burnt Al Habib's palace, seized upon his family, and sent them to Sarra Manam. As for the usurper himself, he had the good fortune to escape at this time; but being closely pursued by Al Mowafek into the province of Ahwaz, where the shattered remains of his forces were entirely defeated, he at last fell into the hands of the victor, who ordered his head to be cut off, and carried through a great part of that region which he had so long disturbed. By this complete victory Al Mowafek obtained the title of Al Najir Lidmilhab, that is, the protector of Mohommetanifin. This year also died Ahmed Ebn Tolun, who had feigned upon Egypt and Syria, as we have already observed: and was succeeded by his son Khamarawiyah. The next year, a bloody engagement happened between the caliph's forces commanded by Al Mowafek's son, and those of Khamarawiyah, who had made an irruption into the caliph's territories. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> was fought between Al Ramla and Damascus. In the beginning, Khamarawiyah found himself so hard pressed, that his men were obliged to give way; upon which, taking for granted that all was lost, he fled with great precipitation, even to the borders of Egypt; but, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, his troops being ignorant of the flight of their general, returned to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, and gained a complete victory. After this, Khamarawiyah, by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and mild administration, gained the affections of his subjects, that the caliph found it impossible to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the least advantage over him. In the 27th year of the Hegira, he overthrew one of the caliph's generals named Abul Saj, at Al Bathia near the city of Damascus; after which he advanced to Al Rakka on the Euphrates, and made himself master of that place. Having annexed several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> provinces to his former dominions, and left some of his friends in whom he could confide to govern them, he then returned into Egypt, the principal part of his empire, which now extended from the Euphrates to the borders of Nubia and Ethiopia. The following year, being the 278th of the Hegira, was remarkable for the death of Al Mowafek. He died of the elephantiasis or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a>; and while in his last illness, could not help observing, that of 100,000 men whom he commanded, there was not one to mis-able as himself. This year is also remarkable for the first disturbances raised in the Moism empire by the Karmanians. The origin of this fact is not certainly known; but the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> opinion is, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> fellow, of some called Karmata, came from Khuzestan to the villages near Cufi, and there pretended great sanctity, and strictness of life, and that God had enjoined him to pray 50 times a day; pretending also to invite people to the obedience of a certain Imam of the family of Mahomet; and this way of life he continued till he had made a very great party, out of whom he chose twelve as his apostles to govern the rest, and to propagate his doctrines. He also assumed the title of prince, and obliged every one of his earlier followers to pay him a dinar a-year. But Al Haidam, the governor of that province, finding men neglected their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and their husbandry in particular, to say those 50 prayers a-day, seized the fellow, and having put him in prison, swore that he should die. This being overheard by a girl belonging to the governor, she, out of compassion, took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the dungeon at night from under her master's head, released the man, and restored the key to its place while her master slept. The next morning the governor found his prisoner gone; and the accident being publicly known, raised great admiration; Karmata's adherents giving out that God had taken him into heaven. After this he appeared in another province, and declared to a great number of people he got about him, that it was not in the power of any person to do him hurt; notwithstanding which, his courage failing him, he retired into Syria, and was never heard of any more. After his disappearance, the sect continued and increased; his disciples pretending that their matter had manifested itself to be a true prophet, and had left them a new law, wherein he had changed the ceremonies and form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> used by the Moismans, &c. From this year, 278, these sectaries gave almost continual disturbance to the caliphs and their subjects, committing great disorders in Chaldea, Arabia, and Mesopotamia, and at length established a considerable principality. In the 279th year of the Hegira died the caliph Al <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> of Motamed; and was succeeded by Al Motaded, son to Al Mowafek. The first year of his reign, Al Motaded demanded in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Khamarawiyah, the caliph sultan, or caliph, of Egypt; which was agreed to by Al Motaded him with the utmost joy, and their nuptials were celebrated with great pomp in the 282nd year of the Hegira. He carried on a war with the Karmatians; but very unsuccessfully, his forces being defeated with great slaughter, and his general Al Abbas taken prisoner. This caliph also granted to Harun, son to Khamarawiyah, the perpetual possession of Awasam and Kinnifin, which he annexed to that of Egypt and Syria, upon condition that he paid him an annual tribute of 45,000 dinars. He died in the year of the Hegira 289, and was succeeded by his son Al Moctaffi. This caliph proved a warlike and successful prince. He gained several advantages over the Karmatians, but was not able to reduce them. The Turks, however, having invaded the province of Mawaradnah, were defeated with great slaughter; after which, Al Moctaffi carried on a successful war against the Greeks, from whom he took Seleucia. After this he invaded Syria and Bagdad, and Egypt, which provinces he recovered from the house of Ahmed Ebn Tolun. The reduction of Egypt happened in the 292nd year of the Hegira, after which the war was renewed with success against the Greeks and Karmatians. The caliph died in the 295th year of the Hegira, after a reign of about six years and a half. He was the last of the caliphs who made any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> by their warlike exploits. His successors Al Moktader, Al Kaher, and Al Radi, were so distressed by the Karmatians and numberless usurpers who were every day starting up, that by the 325th year of the Hegira they had nothing left but the city of Bagdad. In the 324th year of the Hegira, commencing November 30, 935, the caliph Al Radi, finding himself distressed on all sides by usurpers, and having a vizir of no capacity, instituted a new office superior to that of vizir, which he entitled Emir Al Omra, or Commandant of commandants. This great officer was trusted with the management of all military affairs, and had the entire management of the finances in a much more absolute and unlimited manner than any of the caliph's vizirs ever had. Nay, he officiated for the caliph in the great mosque at Bagdad, and had his name mentioned in the public prayers throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. In short, the caliph was so much under the power of this officer, that he could not apply a single dinar to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> without the leave of the Emir Al Omra. In the year 325, the Mollem empire, once so great and powerful, was shared among the following usurpers: The cities of Wasit, Bafra, and Cufa, with the rest of the Arabian Irak, were considered as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the Emir Al Omra, though they had been in the beginning of the year seized upon by a rebel called Al Baridi, who could not be driven out of them. The country of Pars, Farfelan, or Perfa properly so called, was possessed by Amado'ddawla Ali Ebn Buyla, who resided in the city of Shiraz. Part of the tract denominated Al Jabol, together with Persian Irak, which is the mountainous part of Perfa, and the country of the ancient Parthians, obeyed Rueno'ddowla, the brother of Amado'ddawla, who resided at Hipahan. The other part of that country was possessed by Wallmakin the Deylamite. Diyar Rahia, Diyar Becr, Diyar Modar, and the city of Al Mawcel, or Morul, acknowledged for their sovereigns a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of princes called Hamdanites. Egypt and Syria no longer obeyed the caliphs, but Mahomet Ebn Taj, who had formerly been appointed governor of these provinces. Africa and Spain had long been independent. Sicily and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> were governed by princes of their own. The provinces of Khorsan and Mawaralnahr were under the dominion of Al Nafr Ebn Ahmed, of the dynasty of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SAMARITANS">Samaritans</a>. The provinces of Tabreitan, Jorjan, or Georgia, and Mazanderan, had kings of the first dynasty of the Deylamites. The province of Kerman was occupied by Abu Ali Mahomet Ebn Eyila Al Sammani, who had made himself master of it a short time before. And, Lastly, the provinces of Yamama and Bahrain, including the district of Hajar, were in the possession of Abu Thaher the Karmatian. Thus the caliphs were deprived of all their dominions, and reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of sovereign pontiffs; in which light, though they continued for some time to be regarded by the neighbouring princes, yet their power never arrived to any height. In this low state the caliphs continued till the year of the Hegira 656, commencing January 8, 1238. This year was rendered remarkable by the taking of Bagdad by Hulaku the Mogul or Tartar; who likewise abolished the caliphate, putting the reigning caliph Al Mo'tafem Bilah to a most cruel death. These diabolical conquerors, after this, they had taken the city, massacred, according to custom, a vast number of the inhabitants; and after they had plundered it, set it on fire. The spoil they took from thence was prodigiously great, Bagdad being then looked upon as the first city in the world. Bagdad remained in the hands of the Tartars or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOGULS">Moguls</a> to the year of the Hegira 795, of Christ 1392, the city when it was taken by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a> from Sultan Ahmed since that time. Ibn Weis; who being incapable of making head against Tamerlane's numerous forces, found himself obliged to send all his baggage over the Tigris, and abandoned his capital to the conqueror. He was, however, hotly pursued by his enemy's detachments to the plain of Karbella, where several skirmishes happened, and a considerable number of men were lost on both sides. Notwithstanding this disaster, he found means to escape the fury of his pursuers, took refuge in the territories of the Greek emperor, and afterwards repossessed himself of the city of Bagdad. There he remained till the year of the Hegira 803, when the city was taken a second time by Tamerlane; who nevertheless restored it to him, and he continued sovereign of the place till driven from thence by Miram Shaw. Still, however, he found means to return; but in the 81st year of the Hegira was finally expelled by Kara Yulef the Turcman. The descendants of Kara Yulef continued masters of Bagdad till the year of the Hegira 875, of Christ 1470, when they were driven out by Ulun Cassim. The family of this prince continued till the year of the Hegira 914, of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> 1508, when Shah Ithmael, furred Sufi or Safi, the first prince of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family reigning in Iran or Perfa, till the dethroning of the late Shah Hofeim, made himself master of it. From that time to this Bagdad has continued to be a bone of contention between the Turks and Persians. It was taken by Soliman furred the magnificent, and retaken by Shah Abbas the great, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Perfa; but being at length besieged by Amruth or Morad IV. with a formidable army, it was finally obliged to surrender to him in the year 1638; since which time the Persians have never been able to make themselves masters of it for any length of time. The city is large and populous; and the advantage of the Tigris is so considerable, with regard to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, that although the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is excessively hot, and in other respects far from being agreeable, yet the number of its inhabitants is computed at 300,000; but before the plague broke out there, they were supposed to be four times that number. It is governed by a baishaw, whose authority extends as far as Curdistan. The revenues would be immense if the government were mild; but instead thereof, oppression rules here with the most despotic sway. The baishaw is continually extorting money from the poor inhabitants, and none diffuse. Bagdad. suffer more than the unfortunate Jews and Christians, many of whom are put to the most cruel tortures in order to force their property from them. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of tyranny and oppression has almost entirely driven them out of the city; in consequence of which the trade must suffer very considerably, they being generally the principal merchants in the place. In the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, July, and August, the weather is so extremely hot, as to oblige the inhabitants to live for these months in subterranean apartments, which are arched over, to admit the freer circulation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The houses are generally large, built of brick and cement, and are arched over. Many of the windows are made of elegant Venetian glass; the ceilings are usually ornamented with a kind of chequered work, which has generally a noble appearance; most of the houses have a court-yard before them, in the middle of which is a little plantation of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> trees, &c., that has a very pleasing effect. The soil, which would produce not only every convenience in life, but almost every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, is through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> indolence of the Turks, and the many faults in the government of the country, in a great measure uncultivated and neglected. The revenues are computed at 125 lacks of piastres, or £562,500 sterling; but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> part of this is not collected, owing to the slothfulness of the Turks, who suffer the Arabs to plunder them of the remainder. This in some measure accounts for the cruelties and extortions that are continually practised here. As the baihaw lives in all the splendour of a sovereign prince, and maintains a very large army, he could not be able to defray his expenses, was he not to have recourse to oppression and injustice; and he, by his extensive power, acting almost independent of the Porte, only acknowledges it to bring in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> from thence yearly in his favour. The bazars or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> here are large and extensive; being covered over with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> built of masonry, and divided into different streets, filled with shops of all kinds of merchandise, to the number of 12,000. Everything a person can have occasion for may be had there. The number of houses in the city is computed at near 80,000; and each house and shop pay an annual tribute to the baihaw, which is calculated to produce the sum of 300,000 sterling. Besides these immense revenues that are collected, the baihaw pretends, that by repairs on the fortifications 30,000l. or 40,000l. are annually expended, when not so many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> are taken out of his coffers for that purpose. Likewise clearing the river and mending the bridge become a charge greater than their income, and probably not the value of an English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> is expended. To support the expense of the feraglio, their clothes, caparisons of their horses, and every outward pomp, the amount is considerable. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the town stands the citadel, which commands the river; and consists of curtains and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>, on which some very long cannon are mounted, with two mortars in each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>, placed on no other beds than the ground, and in very bad condition. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> of the guns are likewise so unwieldy, and in such a shattered condition, that from their appearance they would not support one firing, but would be shaken in pieces. Their elevations were from 30 to 40 degrees, but they had no quoins to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> them. There are, besides, a number of small towers, and loop-holes for musketry, placed at certain distances, all well encompassed by a ditch of 25 feet deep, which can be filled at any time by the waters of the Tigris. The citadel is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the houses, that it might be easily taken if possession was once gained of the town; but an attack made towards the land would not probably be successful, as sluices might with the greatest facility be cut into the ditch, and so overflow the country for miles round; but it is said an advantageous attack might be made from the water. The city, which is fortified by lofty thick walls of brick covered with earth, and strengthened by great towers much resembling cavalier battions, the whole being surrounded by a deep ditch, is in the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; but the walls in many places are broken down, occasioned by the disputes which happened on the death of Abdulla <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BASHAW">Bashaw</a> a few years ago, when two competitors arose in Bagdad for the baihawic, who fought several times in the town and citadel, and laid great part of it in ruins. In the interim, the governor of Mouful and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINEVEH">Nineveh</a> being appointed bashaw by the Porte, came hither with a considerable army, and took possession of the sovereignty, vanquishing his two opponents. Opposite to the city, on the other side of the river, are very extensive suburbs, from whence shells might be thrown into the town, which would have a dreadful effect on a place so closely built. There is a communication between the city and suburbs by a bridge of boats; the only kind of bridge which that river will admit of, as it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and deep, and in its ordinary course very rapid. At certain seasons it swells to a prodigious height, and overflowing the country occasions many miseries on that side opposite to the city. Among these are several towns and villages, whose inhabitants are said to be the ancient Chaldeans: they are of a particular religion, which they pretend is that of Seth. The inhabitants of this city are composed chiefly of Persians, Armenians, Turks, Arabs, and Jews, which last act in the capacity of schroffs, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>, to the merchants. The Jews, notwithstanding the severe treatment they meet with from the government, are induced to live here from a reverence to the prophet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a> they pretend is a day's journey from the city. Besides the Jews who reside here, there are many that come every year out of devotion to visit the prophet's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>. There are also two European gentlemen, a Venetian and a Frenchman, with five Romish priests, who are Frenchmen and Italians. Two chapels are permitted for those of the Romish and Greek persuasions; at the former the five priests officiate. In the city are several large beautiful mosques, but into which Christians are never suffered to enter if known to be such, for fear it should defile them. The Mahometan women are very richly dressed, wearing bracelets on their arms and jewels in their ears: the Arabian women have the partition between their nostrils bored, wherein they wear rings. There are also a number of antique buildings. At the distance of about ten miles stand the ruins of an ancient tower called the Tower of Nimrod. Whether this tower was at first of a square or round form is now difficult to determine; though the former is most probable, Baggage, babble, because all the remaining bricks are placed square, and not in the least circular. The bricks are all twelve inches square and four and a half thick. The cement is of mud or lime, mixed with broken reed, as we mix hair with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>; which flume might either have been had from one of the great rivers, or taken out of one of the swamps in the plain, with which the country hereabout very much abounds. The height of the ruin is 126 feet; the diameter of the largest and middle part about 100 feet. It would appear to be <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> to the centre; yet near the top there is a regular opening of an oval form. The circumference of that part of the tower which remains, and is above the rubbish, is about 300 feet; but probably could the foundation be come at, it would be found of far greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. The present Turks, Jews, and Arabians, are fond of believing this to be the identical ruin of the ancient tower of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BABEL">Babel</a>, for which they assign a variety of reasons; but all so void of the appearance of truth, that to fet about confuting them would be losing time in trifles. It appears to have been a beacon or watch-tower, to give notice of the approach of an enemy: or perhaps was used as an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> to inspect the various motions of the heavenly bodies; which science was so much cultivated among the ancient inhabitants of this country, that even the Grecians, though deafened of being esteemed the inventors of all arts and sciences, could never deny the Babylonians the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of having laid the foundations of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>.

BAGGAGE

Pages 379-379

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> Affairs, denotes the clothes, tents, utensils of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> sorts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and other necessaries belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. Before a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, the waggons with the baggage are marshalled according to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> which the several regiments bear in the army; being sometimes ordered to follow the respective columns of the army, sometimes to follow the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, and sometimes to form a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> by themselves. The general's baggage marches first; and each waggon has a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>, showing the regiment to which it belongs. Packing up the Baggage, uasa colligere, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, for preparing to go to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to be ready for an expedition. The Romans distinguished two sorts of baggage; a greater and less. The lesser was carried by the soldier on his back, and called sarcina; consisting of the things most necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and which he could not do without. Hence colligere sarcinam, packing up the baggage, is used for decamping, edtra movere. The greater and heavier was carried on horses and vehicles, and called onera. Hence onera vehiculorum, sarcinae hominum. The baggage-horses were denominated fagmentarii equi. The Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in their marches were heavy loaded; insomuch, that they were called by way of jest muli mariani, and cervus. They had four sorts of luggage, which they never went without, viz. corn or baccellatum, utensils, valli, and arms. Cicero observes, that they used to carry with them above half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>'s provisions; and we have instances in Livy, where they carried provisions for a whole month. Their utensils comprehended those proper for gathering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, dressing their meat, and even for fortification or intrenchment; and what is more, a chain for binding captives. For arms, the foot carried a spear, shield, Bagiana <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASKET">basket</a>, rurum, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCHET">hatchet</a>, lorum, falx, &c. Also stakes or pales, valli, for the sudden fortifying a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or even twelve of these pales were carried by each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, though generally, as Polybius tells us, only three or four. On Trajan's column we see soldiers represented with this fardle of corn, utensils, pales, &c., gathered into a bundle and laid on their shoulders. Thus insured to labour, they grew strong, and able to undergo any fatigue in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of which never tired them, or put them out of breath. In aftertimes, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> grew slack, this luggage was thrown on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> and porters' shoulders. The Macedonians were not less insured to hardship than the Romans: when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> first formed an army, he forbade all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of carriages; yet, with all their load, they would march, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, 20 miles in military rank.

BAGLANA

Pages 379-379
or Buglana, a province of the kingdom of Dekkan in the Mogul's empire. It is bounded on the north and east by Guzerat and Ballagat; and on the south and west by that part of Vifapour called Konbau, belonging to the Mahrattas. It ends in a point at the sea coast between Daman and Balfora, and is the least province in the kingdom. The Portuguese territories begin in this province at the port Daman, 21 leagues south of Surat; and run along the coast by Balaim, Bombay, and Chawli, to Dadul, almost 50 leagues to the north of Goa.

BAGLIVI

Pages 379-379

GEORGE, a most illustrious physician of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, was a native of Apulia, and born about the year 1668. He studied at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, where he became <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>; and then went to Rome, where he was chosen professor of anatomy. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of most uncommon force of understanding, of which he gave ample proofs in many curious and accurate productions, philosophical as well as medicinal. He died at Rome 1706, in the flower of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and when he was no more than 38. A collection of his works was printed first in 1710, quarto; and has since been reprinted, in the same size, at various places. His Praxis Medica, and De Fibra Matricis, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> pieces. He wrote a Dissertation upon the Anatomy, Bite, and Effects, of the Tarantula, which is the production of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and gave a particular account of the earthquake at Rome and the adjacent cities in 1703. His works are all in Latin.

BAGNAGAR

Pages 379-379

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Golconda in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on this side the Ganges. The inhabitants within the town are the better sort; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and meaner people inhabiting the suburbs, which is three miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. It is chiefly remarkable for a magnificent reservoir of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, surrounded with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONNADE">colonnade</a> supported by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. It is seated on the river Newa, in E. Long. 96°. N. Lat. 15°. 30'.

BAGNARA

Pages 379-379

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, in the farther <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16°. 8'. N. Lat. 38°. 15'.

BAGNAREA

Pages 379-379

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s patri- mony, and in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORVIETO">Orvieto</a>, with a bishop's see. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12°. 10'. N. Lat. 42°. 36'.

BAGNERES

Pages 379-380

a town of France in Gascony, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGNIALACK">Bagnialack</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Bigorre, now the department of the Upper Pyrenees, so called from its mineral waters, which are much resorted to. It is seated on the river Adour, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 12. N. Lat. 43. 3.

BAGNIALACK

Pages 380-380

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bosnia. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 18. 10. N. Lat. 44. 9.

BAGNIIO

Pages 380-380

an Italian word, signifying a bath. We <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> with conveniences for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>, cupping, sweating, and otherwise cleansing the body; and sometimes for worse purposes. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> it becomes a general name for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a> where the slaves are enclosed, it being usual in these prisons to have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>.

BAGNOLIANS

Pages 380-380
or BAGNOLANSES, in Church History, a sect of heretics, who in reality were Manichees, though they somewhat disguised their errors. They rejected the Old Testament and part of the New; held the world to be eternal; and affirmed that God did not create the soul when he infused it into the body.

BAGOI

Pages 380-380

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Persians, were the same with those called by the Latins phalanges, viz. a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>, in whom the canal of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENIS">penis</a> was so contorted by a tight <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINCULUM">vinculum</a>, that they could not emit the semen.

BAHAMA

Pages 381-382
or Lucaya, Islands, are the easternmost of the Antilles, lying in the Atlantic ocean. They are situated to the south of Carolina, between 22 and 27 degrees N. Lat. and 73 and 81 degrees W. Long. They extend along the coast of Florida quite down to the isle of Cuba, and are said to be 500 in number, some of them only bare rocks; but twelve of them are large, fertile, and in nothing different from the soil of Carolina: all are, however, uninhabited except Providence, which is 200 miles east of the Floridas; though some others are larger and more fertile, on which the English have plantations. Between them and the continent of Florida is the gulf of Bahama, or Florida, through which the Spanish galleons sail in their passage to Europe. These islands are the first fruits of Columbus's discoveries; but they were not known to the English till 1667, when Captain Seyle, being driven among them in his passage to Carolina, gave his name to one of them; and being a second time driven upon it, gave it the name of Providence. The English, observing the advantageous situation of these islands for being a check on the French and Spaniards, attempted to settle them in the reign of Charles II. Some unlucky accidents prevented this settlement from being of any advantage; and the isle of Providence became an harbour for the bucaniers or pirates, who for a long time infested the American navigation. This obliged the government in 1718 to send out Captain Woodes Rogers with a fleet to dislodge the pirates, and for making a settlement. This the captain effected; a fort was erected, and an independent company was stationed in the island. Ever since this last settlement these islands have been improving, though they advance but slowly. In time of war, people gain considerably by the prizes condemned there; and at all times by the wrecks, which are frequent in this labyrinth of rocks and shelves. The Spaniards and Americans captured these islands during the last war; but they were retaken by a detachment from St Augustine, April 7, 1783. Cotton has been introduced into the Bahamas, where it is now successfully cultivated. The quantity exported in 1792 was 5047 bales which amounted to 1,162,822 pounds.

BAHAR

Pages 382-382
or Barre, in Commerce, weights used in several places in the East Indies. There are two of these weights; one the great bahar, with which they weigh pepper, cloves, nutmegs, ginger, &c. and contains 530 pounds of Portugal, or about 524lb. 9oz. avoirdupois weight. With the little bahar, they weigh quicksilver, vermilion, ivory, silk, &c. It contains about 437lb. 9oz. avoirdupois weight.

BAHARIN

Pages 382-382

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 50° 0' N. Lat. 26° 0'. This island is chiefly remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>-fishery, and has often changed its masters. It fell with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMUS">Ormus</a> under the dominion of the Portuguese, was again restored to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> by Thomas Khoulai Kan; and after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> the confusion into which his empire was thrown, gave an opportunity to an enterprising and ambitious Arab of taking possession of the island, where he still maintains his authority. Baharen was famous for its pearl-fishery even at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when pearls were found at Ormus, Karek, Kaffry, and other places in the Persian gulf; but it is now become of much greater <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>; all the other banks having been exhausted, while this has suffered no sensible diminution. The time of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> begins in April, and ends in October. It is confined to a tract four <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> five leagues in breadth. The pearls taken at Baharen, though not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> as those of Ceylon or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, are much larger than those of the former <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and more regularly shaped than those of the latter. They have a yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; but have also this good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, that they preserve their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> hue, whereas the whiter kind lose much of their lustre by keeping, especially in hot countries. The annual revenue from the Baharen pearl fishery is computed at about 157,500l. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the pearls that are uneven are carried to Constantinople and other ports of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, where the larger go to compose ornaments for head-dresses, and the smaller are used in embroideries. The perfect pearls must be reserved for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a>, whence they are distributed through all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>.

BAHI

Pages 382-382

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Luzon <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANILLA">Manilla</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIPPINE_ISLANDS">Philippine <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the East Indies, belonging to the Spaniards. It is remarkable for producing excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BETEL">betel</a>, which the inhabitants, Spaniards as well as natives, perpetually chew from morning till night. It is also the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where most of the ships are built. But the natives suffer much from this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of them being constantly employed in it, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, or at the port of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol6.html#article-CAVITE">Cavite</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> allows these labourers a piece-of-eight per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, with a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>. The whole province contains about 6000 tributary natives.

BAHIA

Pages 382-382

de todos los santos, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, belonging to the Portuguese, and the richest in the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but unhappily the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> do not correspond with other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> advantages; yet so fertile is the province in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> and other commercial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, that the Portuguese flock hither not only as it is the seat of influence, but also of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, called St Salvador, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ciudad de Bahia, is populous, magnificent, and beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> the most gay and opulent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in Brazil. It stands on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> in S. Lat. 12° 11', is strong by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, well fortified, and always defended by a numerous garrison. It contains 12,000 or 14,000 Portuguese, and about three times as many <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, besides people of different nations who choose to reside in that city.

BAHIR

Pages 382-382

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> signifying famous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> illustrious; but particularly used for a book of the Jews, treating of the profound <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the cabbala, being the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> of the Rabbinical works.

BAHUS

Pages 382-382

a strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the same name, seated on a rock in a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 10' N. Lat. 57° 52'.

BAIANUS SINUS

Pages 383-384

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> so called from Baise, (Suetonius); Portus Batarum, (Pliny); which was enlarged by Augustus, by giving entrance to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> into the Lacus Lucrinus, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERNUS">Avernus</a>, ordering it to be called Portus Julius apud Batae, (Suetonius). We also read Baianus Lacus in Tacitus, which some interpret the Lucrinus. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name is Golfo di Pozzuoli. From the highest point that forms the bay, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> castle commands the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, where foreign ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> usually ride at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, the harbour of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> not being spacious enough for the reception of a fleet: here they enjoy good shelter, watering, and victualling; but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> risk the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of their crews, on account of the unwholesomeness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. BAJAZET I., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of the Turks, a renowned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> but a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, was conquered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a>, and exposed by him in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> cage; the fate he had destined (it is said) for his adversary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had been the victor. The iron cage, however, so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and so often repeated as a moral lesson, has been rejected as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> by modern writers, who smile at the vulgar credulity. They <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Sherefeddin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>, of which a French version has been given, and from which Mr Gibbon has collected the following more specious narrative of this memorable transaction. "No sooner was Timour informed that the captive Ottoman was at the door of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a>, than he graciously stepped forwards to receive him, seated him by his side, and mingled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> reproaches a soothing pity for his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and misfortune. 'Alas!' (said the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>), the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of fate is now accomplished by your own fault: it is the web which you have woven, the thorns of the tree which yourself have planted. I wished to spare, and even to affix, the champion of the Molems; you braved our threats, you despised our friend- Bajazet, ship; you forced us to enter your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> with our invincible armies. Behold the event. Had you vanquished, I am not ignorant of the fate which you reserved for myself and my troops. But I diddian to retaliate: your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> are secure; and I shall express my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to God by my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>." The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> captive showed some signs of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>, accepted the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMILIATION">humiliation</a> of a robe of honour, and embraced with tears his son Moufa, who, at his request, was sought and found among the captives of the field. The Ottoman princes were lodged in a splendid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a>; and the respect of the guards could be surpassed only by their vigilance. On the arrival of the haram from Bourfa, Timour restored the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> Despina and her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to their father and husband; but he privately requested, that the Servian princes, who had hitherto been indulged in the profession of Chritianity, should embrace without delay the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the prophet. In the feast of victory, to which Bajazet was invited, the Mogul emperor placed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on his head and a sceptre in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, with a solemn assurance of restoring him with an increase of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> to the throne of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. But the effect of this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> was disappointed by the sultan's untimely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; amidst the care of the most skilful physicians, he expired of an apoplexy at Akkhehr, the Antioch of Piidria, about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months after his defeat. The victor dropped a tear over his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>; his body, with royal pomp, was conveyed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a> which he had erected at Bourfa; and his son Moufa, after receiving a rich present of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and jewels, of horses and arms, was invested by a patent in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a> with the kingdom of Anatolia. "Such is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of a generous conqueror, which has been extracted from his own <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>, and dedicated to his son and grandson, 19 years after his decease; and, at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> was remembered by thousands, a manifest falsehood would have implied a satire on his real conduct. On the other hand, of the harsh and ignominious treatment of Bajazet there is also a variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>. The Turkish annals in particular, which have been consulted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> transcribed by Leucavius, Pocock, and Cantemir, unanimously deplore the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> of the iron cage; and some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> may be allowed to national historians, who cannot stigmatize the Tartar without uncovering the shame of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>." From these opposite premises, Mr Gibbon thinks a fair and moderate conclusion may be deduced. He is satisfied that Sherefeddin Ali has faithfully described the first oftentimes interview, in which the conqueror, whose spirits were harmonized by success, affected the character of generosity. But his mind was insensibly alienated by the unfeigned arrogance of Bajazet; the complaints of his enemies, the Anatolian princes, were just and vehement; and Timour betrayed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of leading his royal captive in triumph to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARCAND">Samarcand</a>. An attempt to facilitate his escape by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> a mine under the tent, provoked the Mogul emperor to impose a harsher restraint; and in his perpetual marches, an iron cage on a waggon might be invented, not as a wanton insult, but as a rigorous precaution. Timour had read in some fabulous history a similar treatment of one of his predecessors, a king of Peria; and Bajazet was condemned to represent the person and expiate the guilt of the Roman Caesar. But the strength of his mind and body fainted under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, and his premature death might without injustice be ascribed to the severity of Timour. He warred not, however, with the dead; a tear and a sepulchre were all that he could bestow on a captive who was delivered from his power; and if Moufa, the son of Bajazet, was permitted to reign over the ruins of Bourfa, the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Anatolia had been restored by the conqueror to their lawful sovereigns.

BAIKAL

Pages 384-384

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lake in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, lying between 52 and 55 degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. It is reckoned to be 500 werfs in length; but only 20 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 30 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and in some places not above 15. It is environed on all sides by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. In one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, which lies near the river Barguian, it throws up an inflammable sulphureous liquid called malba, which the people of the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> burn in their lamps. There are likewise several sulphureous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> near this lake. Its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> at a distance appears of a green <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>: it is fresh; and so clear, that objects may be seen in it several fathoms deep. It does not begin to freeze till near the latter end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, and thaws again about the beginning of May: from which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> till September, a ship is seldom known to be wrecked on it; but by the high winds which then blow, many shipwrecks happen. This lake is called by the neighbouring people Sviatoje More, or the Holy Lake; and they imagine, that when storms happen on it, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be preserved from all danger by complimenting it with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. When it is frozen over, people travel upon it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; but they must be very sharp shod, otherwise they cannot stand upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, which is exceedingly smooth. Notwithstanding that the ice on this lake is sometimes two ells thick, there are some open places in it to which tempestuous winds will often drive those who are crossing it; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they are irrecoverably lost. The camels that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> along have a particular kind of shoes sharp at bottom, and the oxen have sharp irons driven through their hoofs, without which it would be impossible for them to pass. Here are plenty of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sturgeon and pike; with many feasts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, but none of the spotted, kind. It contains several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; and the borders are frequented by black fables and civet-cats.

BAIL

Pages 384-385

bailium, (from the French bailier, which comes of the Greek βαλλειον, and signifies to deliver into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>), is used in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> for the freeing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> setting at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of one arrested or imprisoned upon any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, either civil or criminal, on surety taken for his appearance at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> certain. The reason why it is called bail, is because by this means the party restrained is delivered into the hands of those that bind themselves for his forthcoming, in order to a safe-keeping or protection from prison; and the end of bail is to satisfy the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> and costs, or render the defendant to prison. With respect to bail in civil <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, it is to be observed, that there is both common and special bail. Common bail is an action of small concernment, being called common, because any sureties in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> are taken; whereas in causes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, as actions upon bonds, or specialty, &c., where the debt amounts to 10l. special bail or surety must be taken, such such as subsidy men at least, and they according to the value.
