The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMITMENT">commitment</a> of a person being only for safe custody, wherever bail <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> answer the same intention, it ought to be taken, as in most of the inferior crimes; but in felonies, and other offences of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, no bail can be a security <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to the actual custody of the person. For what is there that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may not be induced to forfeit to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>? and what satisfaction or indemnity is it to the public, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> the effects of them who have bailed a murderer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the murderer himself be suffered to escape with impunity? Upon a principle similar to which, the Athenian magistrates, when they took a solemn oath never to keep a citizen in bonds that could give three sureties of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> with himself, did it with an exception to such as had embezzled the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, or been guilty of treasonable practices. Bail may be taken either in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, or, in some particular cases, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>; but mostly used by the justices of the peace. To refuse or delay to bail any person bailable, is an offence against the liberty of the subject, in any magistrate, by the common law; as well as by the statute Westm. I. c. 15, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABEAS_CORPUS">habeas corpus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, 31 Car. II. c. 2. And, lest the intention of the law should be frustrated by the justices requiring bail to a greater amount than the nature of the case demands, it is expressly declared by statute 1 W. and M. st. 2, c. 1, that excessive bail ought not to be required; though what bail shall be called excessive, must be left to the courts, on considering the circumstances of the case, to determine. And on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, if the magistrate takes insufficient bail he is liable to be fined, if the criminal doth not appear. In civil cases, every defendant is bailable. But it is otherwise in Criminal matters. Regularly, in all offences, either against the common law or act of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, that are below felony, the offender ought to be admitted to bail unless it be prohibited by some special act of parliament.—By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> common law, before and since the Conquest, all felonies were bailable, till <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> was excepted by statute: so that persons might be admitted to bail almost in every case. But the statute Westm. I. c. 15, takes away the power of bailing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> instances of felony. The statutes 23 Hen. VI. c. 9, and 1 and 2 Ph. and Mar. c. 13, gave farther regulations in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; and upon the whole we may collect, that no justices of the peace can bail, 1. Upon an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> of treason: nor, 2. Of murder: nor 3. In case of manslaughter, if the prisoner be clearly the slayer, and not barely suspected to be so; or if any <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> be found against him; nor, 4. Such as, being committed for felony, have broken prison; because it not only carries a presumption of guilt, but is also superadding one felony to another: 5. Persons outlawed: 6. Such as have abjured the realm: 7. Persons taken with the mainour, or in the fact of felony: 8. Persons <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with arson: 9. Excommunicated persons, taken by writ de excommunicato capiendo: all which are clearly not admissible to bail by the justices. Others are of a dubious nature; as, 10. Thieves openly defamed and known: 11. Persons charged with other felonies, or manifest and enormous offences, not being of good fame: and, 12. Accessories to felony, that labour under the same want of reputation. These seem to be in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the justices, whether bailable or not. The last class are such as may be bailed upon offering sufficient surety; as, 13. Persons of good fame, charged with a bare suspicion of manslaughter, or other infamous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMICIDE">homicide</a>: 14. Such persons being charged with petit larceny or any felony, not before specified: or, 15. With being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCESSORY">accessory</a> to any felony. Lastly, it is agreed, that the court of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> (or any judge thereof in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of vacation) may bail for any crime whatsoever, be it treason, murder, or any other offence, according to the circumstances of the case. And herein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of the law is very manifest. To allow bail to be taken <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> for such enormous crimes, would greatly tend to elude the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>: and yet there are cases, though they rarely happen, in which it would be hard and unjust to confine a man in prison, though accused even of the greatest offence. The law has therefore provided one court, and only one, which has a discretionary power of bailing in any case: except only, even to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> jurisdiction, and of course to all inferior ones, such persons as are committed by either <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of parliament, so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the session lasts; or such as are committed for contempts by any of the king's superior courts of justice. See Law. Clerk of the Bails, is an officer belonging to the court of the king's bench; he files the bail-pieces taken in that court, and attends for that purpose. Bail, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">Bale</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The seamen call throwing the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> by hand out of the ship's or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>'s hold, bailing. They also call those hoops that bear up the tilt of a boat, its bails.

BAILIE

Pages 385-385

in Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a judge anciently appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> over such lands not erected into a regality as happened to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> by forfeiture <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> otherwise, now abolished. It is also the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> boroughs, and of the judge appointed by a baron over lands erected into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a>. See Law.

BAILLIE

Pages 385-388

(balliœ), from the French word <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, that is, prefectus provinciae; and as the names, so the office itself was answerable to that of France; where there are eight parliaments, which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> courts from whence there lies no <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>, and within the precincts of the several parts of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> which belong to each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> there are several provinces to which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> is administered by certain officers called bailiffs: and in England there are several counties in which justice hath been administered to the inhabitants by the officer who is now called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wifecount (one of which names descends from the Saxons, the other from the Normans); and though the sheriff is not called bailiff, yet it is probable that was one of his names also, because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> is often called bailiwick. And in the statute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">Magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTA">Charta</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 28, and 14 Ed. III. c. 9, the word bailiff seems to comprise as well sheriffs as bailiffs of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>. As the realm is divided into counties, so every county is divided into hundreds; within which in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times the people had justice ministered to them by the officers of every hundred. But now the hundred courts, except certain franchises, are swallowed in the county-courts; and the bailiff's... bailiff's name and office is grown into contempt, they being generally officers to serve writs, &c., within their liberties. Though, in other respects, the name is still in good esteem; for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> magistrates in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are called bailiffs or baillies; and sometimes the persons to whom the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s cattle are committed are termed bailiffs, as the bailiff of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> Castle, &c. Of the ordinary bailiffs there are several sorts, viz. sheriff's bailiffs, bailiffs of liberties, &c. Sheriff's bailiffs, or sheriff's officers, are either bailiffs of hundreds, or special bailiffs. Bailiffs of hundreds are officers appointed over those respective districts by the sheriffs, to collect fines therein; to summon jurors; to attend the judges and justices at the assizes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-sessions; and also to execute writs and processes in the several hundreds. But as they are generally plain men, and not thoroughly skilful in this latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their office, that of serving writs, and making arrests and executions, it is now usual to join special bailiffs with them; who are generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> persons employed by the sheriffs on account only of their adroitness and dexterity in hunting and seizing of their prey. Bailiffs of liberties are those bailiffs who are appointed by every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> within his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, to execute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, and do such offices therein as the bailiff errant doth at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in the county; but bailiffs errant or itinerant, to go up and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the county to serve process, are out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. There are also bailiffs of forests, and bailiffs of manors, who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> husbandry, fell trees, gather rents, pay quit-rents, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a>-Bailiff, an officer appointed in all ports, towns, for the searching of ships, gathering the toll for anchorage, &c., and arresting persons for debt, &c., on the water. Bailii, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, painter of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> views and portraits, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Bailii, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>; and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1584. From his father he learned to draw and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; but he was afterwards placed under the care of Adrian Verburg, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> with him for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and when he quitted that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, he studied to much greater advantage with Cornelius Vandervoort, an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a>-painter, and with him he spent about five years. As Vandervoort possessed many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> paintings of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> masters, Bailii, for his own improvement, copied them with critical care and observation; and particularly copied one perspective view of the inside of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, originally painted by Steenwyck, which he finished with such accuracy, that even Steenwyck himself could scarce determine which was the original, or which the copy, when both were placed before him. He travelled through several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> to see the works of the celebrated masters of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and for a few years resided at Rome; and abroad, as well as in his own country, the correctness of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, and the delicate handling and finishing of his pictures, procured him employment, admirers, and friends. In the latter part of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he discontinued <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, and only drew portraits on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, which he heightened with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and gave them wonderful force and roundness. He died in 1638. Bailliewick, that liberty which is exempted from the sheriff of the county; over which liberty the lord thereof appoints his own bailiff, with the like power within his precinct as an under sheriff exercises under the sheriff of the county: Or it signifies the precinct of a bailiff, or the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> within which his jurisdiction is terminated. Baillet, Adrian, a very learned French writer and critic, born in 1649 at the village of Neuville near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUVAIS">Beauvais</a> in Picardy. His parents were too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> to give him a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, which however he obtained by the favour of the bishop of Beauvais, who afterwards presented him with a small vicarage. In 1683 he was appointed librarian to M. de Lamoginon, advocate-general to the parliament of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; of whose library he made a copious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> in 35 vols. folio, all written with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. He died in 1766, after <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> many works, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> from 1609, to the peace of Nimeguen in 1679, 4 vols 12mo; Lives of the Saints, 3 vols folio, which he professed to have purged from fables; Jugesmens des Savants, which he extended to 9 vols 12mo; and The life of Des Cartes, 2 vols 4to, which he abridged, and reduced to one vol. 12mo. Baillieul, a town of France, in the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>, formerly very strong, but now without any fortifications. It has been several times burnt by accident, and contains now only about 500 houses. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 55. N. Lat. 40. 35. Bailly, Jean Sylvain, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and astronomer, was born at Paris on the 15th September 1736. He was originally intended for the profession of painting, which his family had pursued for several generations, and he even had made some progress in the art. But the bias of his mind leaned too much to literary pursuits, especially to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and works of imagination, to permit him to give that application which is necessary to secure success and eminence in any profession. The friends of Bailly, who had witnessed the early dawn of his genius, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that it was equally fitted to appear with advantage in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of polite literature, or to shine in the walks of science; and recommended the latter chiefly to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. His acquaintance with La Caille the celebrated geometer commenced, and this at once decided the object of his studies, which were now almost entirely devoted to scientific investigations. The first of his labours was the calculation of the comet which appeared in the year 1759. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1763, he was admitted a member of the Academy of Sciences; and in the same year he published a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of the observations made by La Caille in 1760 and 1761 on the zodiacal stars, an elaborate compilation, and of extensive utility. His attention was afterwards directed to the consideration of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>'s satellites. La Grange, who now promised to be the first mathematician in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, was the formidable rival of Bailly in the competition for this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> question in 1764. The results of his investigations were collected into a treatise, which also contained the history of that part of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, and were published in 1766. In 1771 appeared his interesting and important memoir on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a> of the satellites, which was marked with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of precision and accuracy, till that time altogether unknown in the observations of their eclipses. The studies of Bailly were not entirely limited to the cultivation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> science, or to profound physical Bailly's fysical speculations; his genius shone with equal lustre in those departments of literature which require the rare <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> of nice discrimination of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> power of eloquence, to reach excellence. The eloges which he composed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. Corneille, Leibnitz, Moliere, Cook, La Caille, and Grézet, were universally admired as valuable specimens of fine writing, and added much to his reputation. The distinguished place of secretary of the Academy of Sciences became vacant in 1771; and, supported by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> and influence of Buffon, he offered himself a candidate. But here he was unsuccessful. Condorcet, who was then rising into reputation, and was supported by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> influence of D'Alembert, was preferred to the office. In the year 1775, he published at Paris the first volume of the "History of Ancient Astronomy." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> appeared in 1787. In 1779 he gave to the world his "History of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> Astronomy," from the foundation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">Alexandrian</a> school to the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. These works are of ineffable value, distinguished by animated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a>, and interesting detail. He also published a work entitled, "Letters on the Origin of the Sciences, and of the People of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>;" which was afterwards followed by another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of "Letters on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIS">Atlantis</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, and the Ancient History of Asia," as a continuation of the same work. These volumes were addressed to Voltaire, with whom he had commenced an ingenious correspondence and discussion on this curious subject. The coincidence of his opinions with those of Buffon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> respecting some of the favourite theories of the latter, brought him into an intimate acquaintance and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> friendship with that celebrated naturalist, which, however, declined and was entirely dissolved, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the opposition which Bailly made to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of the Abbé Maury into the French Academy. Bailly had been chosen secretary of this academy in 1784; and in the following year he was admitted into the Academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">Inscriptions</a> and Belles-Lettres. This was the only instance, since the time of Fontenelle, of the same person being at once a member of all the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>. In the year 1784 he was nominated one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to investigate the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the animal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNETISM">magnetism</a> of Mesmer, which was practised by Delon; and he drew up an elegant report, which was presented to the Academy of Sciences. This report, which was soon afterwards translated into English, not only marked the acuteness and discernment of the author, and contained the most satisfactory and decisive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> with regard to its object, but may be held up as an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> for those who are engaged in similar investigations. In developing the physical effects produced by moral causes, it is of the greatest value; and it is particularly interesting when we consider the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> influence which causes of this nature have impeded on the general opinions of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and even on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a> of nations. Hitherto we have contemplated Bailly in the shades of retirement, and in the calm undisturbed retreats of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, employing the energy of a vigorous and comprehensive mind in the profound researches of physical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>: we are now to follow him in his political <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a>, and behold him struggling with the adverse interests of party <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a>, and contending with the unbridled fury of a lawless mob, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of a people whose minds were not prepared to understand, and whose habits were not yet formed to enjoy, the blessings of rational liberty. He was one of the first and most zealous promoters of the revolution in France,—a revolution which not only astonished and convulsed all Europe, but of which the immediate consequences to themselves, and to their country, were neither foreseen nor imagined by those who embarked in it, nor can its ultimate effects even at the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> be appreciated or conjectured,—a revolution which holds out an awful lesson to the leaders of popular faction to curb and repress, rather than to excite and encourage, that spirit of tumult and disorder among a people thrown loose from the necessary restraints of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, which bursts forth with ungovernable fury, and at last involves all in one general ruin. In the part which he acted in this bloody struggle, Bailly has had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to be well spoken of by opposite parties. He has not been <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with want of integrity or selfish designs in any part of his conduct; but actuated by a misguided zeal, and dazzled with the prospect of freedom which the warmth of imagination held out, he rashly stepped forward in a cause which he espoused with enthusiasm, and supported with his utmost exertions. But in that cause he fell a sacrifice to the unrelenting spirit of violence and party faction which had been roused, and which could neither be subdued nor regulated. When the states-general of France were assembled in 1789, he was elected a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> to the Tiers État, was afterwards chosen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>; and when the national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> was constituted, he continued in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, and was president at the time that the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> was issued ordering them to disperse. During the struggle which took place between the popular part of the assemblies and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, Bailly was among the most forward in afflicting those popular rights which were then new in France; and he dictated the famous oath to the members of the Tiers État, "to resist tyrants and tyranny, and never to separate till they had obtained a free <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>." On the 14th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> following, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> on which the Batte was stormed and taken by the people, he was appointed with universal consent, mayor of Paris. In this high office, he is allowed to have discharged the arduous and difficult duties of it with great integrity, courage, and moderation. And while he held this conspicuous situation, he was a powerful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> in promoting the various <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> by which the popular party prevailed over that of the court; and for this, and various other popular actions, he obtained a high degree of favour among the people. But the tide of public <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> now swelled beyond all bounds; no restraint could oppose its violent course. The multitude, unhackled by the fetters of despotism, fond of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>, and with enthusiastic and unsettled notions of freedom, daily panting for change, could bear no opposition. Bailly, who perhaps now saw when it was too late the general disposition of the people to anarchy, still wished the laws to be respected, and hoped by their vigorous execution to restore and preserve tranquillity. He ordered some deputies from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> insurgents at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NANCY">Nancy</a> to be arrested, and he firmly opposed the rash proceedings of Marat and Hubert; he be- Bailly came a member of a less promiscuous club than that of the Jacobins; and exerted himself strongly to persuade the populace to permit the king and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family to depart to St Cloud. By these measures, which were little relished by a frantic and lawless people, he lost their confidence and favour. But what finally destroyed his popularity, was the tumultuous meeting of the populace on the 17th of July 1791, to demand the abolition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, when, being called by the national assembly to disperse the mob, who had assaulted the soldiery, he ordered the latter to fire, by which 40 persons were killed and above 100 wounded. Thus become obnoxious to the people whom he had faithfully served, it was no longer desirable for him to hold his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. He therefore resigned his office at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the constituent assembly in the end of the year 1791. After this period he lived in retirement, having resumed his philosophical researches. But the times of bloody proscription approached, and he must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> a sacrifice to the ferocious vengeance of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> who now bore unlimited sway. He was accordingly denounced as an enemy to the republic, apprehended and thrown into prison. He was arraigned before a fangirninary tribunal, summarily condemned to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> as a conspirator, and was executed the day following, near the spot where he had given the order for the military to fire on the people. On the day of execution, his sufferings, which he bore with the utmost calmness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>, were ludicrously protracted. Instead of that sympathy and compassion which even the worst and the lowest criminal often experiences when he is about to expiate his offences with his life, he was treated by an incensed and barbarous populace, with the most ignominious indignity and cruelty. He wore the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> shirt, or badge of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a>, and was placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CART">cart</a>, with his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> tied behind his back. During the whole time of his progress to the place of execution, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> poured incessantly on his head. The populace as he passed threw mud at him, and cruelly insulted him with every kind of opprobrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. It was found necessary to remove the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUILLOTINE">guillotine</a> from the place where it was first erected to firmer ground. During this time he was forced to get out of the cart, and walk round the field, to gratify more fully the implacable and unrelenting malice of the mob. When he was ascending the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a>, a spectator who was near him, in a tone of insult exclaimed, "Bailly, you tremble?" "Yes (he instantly replied), but not with fear." Thus perished Bailly in the 57th year of his age. In his person he was tall, and of a sedate but striking countenance. He possessed great firmness and decision of character, but far removed from fulness or apathy. Few philosophers have been more distinguished in so many various departments of science and literature, or have acquired such deserved reputation. In his public stations, as well as in the retirement of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> life, his integrity and disinterestedness remained pure and untainted. In the time of his magistracy he spent part of his fortune in relieving the wants of the poor. His wife, whom he married in 1787, survived him. She was the widow of Raymond Gaye, who had been his intimate friend 25 years.

BAILMENT

Pages 388-388

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a delivery of goods in trust, upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, expressed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> implied, that the trust shall be faithfully executed on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the bailee. As <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> cloth be delivered, or (in our legal dialect) bailed, to a tailor to make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of clothes, he has it upon an implied contract to render it again when made, and that in a workmanly manner. If <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> or goods be delivered to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRIER">carrier</a> to convey from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, or from Glasgow to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, &c., he is under a contract in law to pay, or carry them to the person appointed. If a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or other goods be delivered to an innkeeper or his servants, he is bound to keep them safely and restore them when his guest leaves the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. If a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> takes in a horse, or other cattle, to graze and depasture in his grounds, which the law calls agistment, he takes them upon an implied contract to return them on demand to the owner. If a pawnbroker receives plate or jewels as a pledge or security for the repayment of money <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> thereon at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> certain, he has them upon an express contract or condition to restore them if the pledger performs his part by redeeming them in due <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; for the due execution of which contract, many useful regulations are made by statute 3 Geo. II. c. 24. And so, if a landlord distrains goods for rent, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> officer for taxes, these for a time are only a pledge in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the distrainers; and they are bound by an implied contract in law to restore them on payment of the debt, duty and expenses, before the time of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>; or when sold, to render back the overplus. If a friend delivers anything to his friend to keep for him, the receiver is bound to restore it on demand: and it was formerly held, that in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time he was answerable for any damage or loss it might sustain, whether by accident or otherwise; unless he expressly undertook to keep it only with the same care as his own goods, and then he should not be answerable for theft or other accidents. But now the law seems to be settled on a much more rational footing; that such a general bailment <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> the bailee with any loss, unless it happens by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> neglect, which is construed to be an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of fraud: but if the bailee undertakes specially to keep the goods safely and securely, he is bound to answer all perils and damages that may befall them for want of the same care with which a prudent man would keep his own. BAILO; thus they style at Constantinople the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> of the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, who resides at the Porte. This minister, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> charge, acts there the part of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> of Venice.

BAINBRIDGE

Pages 388-388

Dr. John, an eminent physician and astronomer, born at Ashby de la Zouche in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, in 1582. He taught a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school for some years, and practiced physic, employing his leisure hours in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, which was his favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>: at length he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, was admitted a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of physicians, and raised his character by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the comet in 1618. The next year Sir Henry Savile appointed him his first professor of astronomy at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and the masters and fellows of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERTON">Merton</a>-college made him first junior, and then superior, reader of Linacre's lecture. He died in 1643, having written many works, some of which have never been published: but the MSS. are preserved in the library of Trinity-college, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>.

BAIOCAO

Pages 388-389

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, current at Rome, and throughout the whole state of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, ten of which make a julio, and a hundred a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>.

BAIRAM

Pages 389-389
or BIRAM, a Turkish word which signifies a solemn feast. The Mahometans have two Bairams, the Great and the Little. The Little Bairam is properly that held at the close of the fast Ramazan, beginning with the first full moon in the following month Shawal. This is called in Arabic Id al Fete, or the Feast of breaking the Fast; by European writers, the Turkish Easter, because it succeeds Ramazan, which is their Lent, more usually the Great Bairam, because observed with great ceremony and rejoicing at Constantinople, and through Turkey, for three days, and in Persia for five or six days, at least by the common people, to make themselves amends for the mortification of the preceding month. The feast commencing with the new moon, the Mahometans are very scrupulous in observing the time when the new moon commences; to which purpose, observers are sent to the tops of the highest mountains, who the moment they spy the appearance of a new moon, run to the city, and proclaim Muzaladat, “welcome news;” as it is the signal for beginning the festivity.—The Great Bairam, is properly that held by the pilgrims at Mecca, commencing on the tenth of Dhu Thaqa, when the victims are slain, and lasting three days. This is called by the Arabs, Id al adba, that is, the feast of sacrifice, as being celebrated in memory of the sacrifice of Abram, whose God redeemed with a great victim. By European writers it is called the Lesser Bairam, as being less taken notice of by the generality of the people who are not struck with it, because the ceremonies it is observed withal, are performed at Mecca, the only scene of the solemnity.—On the feast of Bairam, after throwing little stones, one after another, into the valley of Mina, they usually kill one or more sheep, some a goat, bullock, or even a camel; and after giving a part thereof to the poor, eat the rest with their friends. After this, they shave themselves. The second is a day of rest. On the third, they set out on their return home. BAIRUT. See BEERROOT.

BAITING

Pages 389-389

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of smaller <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> weaker beasts attacking and harassing greater and stronger. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we hear of the baiting of bulls or bears by mastiffs or bull-dogs with short noses, that they may take the better hold. Utility is pled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a> of bull-baiting. This animal is rarely killed without being first baited; the chafing and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> whereof makes his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> tenderer and more digestible. In reality, it disposes it for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>; so that, unless taken in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, baited flesh is soon lost. But a spirit of barbarism had the greatest share in supporting the sport: bulls are kept on purpose, and exhibited as standing <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a> for the public entertainment. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> beasts have not fair play: they are not only tied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to a stake, with a collar about their necks and a short rope, which gives them not above four or five yards play; but they are alarmed too, and the tips of their horns cut off, or covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, to prevent their hurting the dogs. In this sport, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> aim of the dog is to catch the bull by the nose, and hold him down; to which end he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> even creep on his belly: the bull’s aim, on the contrary, is, with equal industry, to defend his nose; in order to which, he thrusts it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the ground, where his horns are also in readiness to toss the dog.—Bull-baiting was first introduced into England as an amusement in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> John, about 1209.

BAJA

Pages 382-383

Bayjah, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Begia, a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Vacea of Salust, and Oppidum Veggenfe of Pliny. It was BAJA was formerly, and still continues to be, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> market of the kingdom for corn; of which the adjacent territories produce such abundance, that they can supply more than the whole kingdom with it; and the Tunisians say, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there was in the kingdom such another town as this for plenty of corn, it would become as cheap as sand. Here is also a great annual fair, to which the most distant Arabian tribes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> with their families and flocks. Notwithstanding all this, however, the inhabitants are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> about the town remains uncultivated, through the cruel exactions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and the frequent incursions of the Arabs, who are very powerful in these parts. The town stands on the declivity of a hill on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Constantina, about 10 leagues from the northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and 56 south-west from Tunis; and hath the convenience of being well watered. On the highest part is a citadel that commands the whole place, but is now of no great strength. The walls were raised out of the ruins of the ancient Vacca, and have some ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>.

BAJADOR

Pages 383-383

a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> on the west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, south of the Canary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15. 20. N. Lat. 27. 0.

BAJULUS

Pages 389-389

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the Greek emperors. There were several degrees of bajuli; as, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> bajulus, who was preceptor to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>; and the simple bajuli, who were sub-preceptors. The word is derived from the Latin verb bajulare, “to carry <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bear a thing on the arms or on the shoulders;” and the origin of the office is thus traced by antiquaries. Children, and especially those of condition, had anciently, beside their nurse, a woman called gerula, as appears from several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of Tertullian; when weaned, or ready to be weaned, they had men to carry them about and take care of them, who were called gerula and bajuli, a gerendo et bajulando. Hence it is, that governors of princes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lords were still denominated bajuli, and their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> bajulatio, even after their pupils were grown too big to be carried about. The word passed in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. Bajulus is also used by Latin writers in the several other senses wherein <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAILIFF">Bailiff</a> is used among us. Bajulus was also the name of a conventual officer in the ancient monasteries, to whom belonged the charge of gathering and distributing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and legacies left for masses and obits; whence he was also denominated bajulus obituum novorum.

BAKAN

Pages 389-389

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> in the East Indies, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVA">Ava</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 98. c. N. Lat. 19. 33.

BAKER

Pages 389-392

Sir Richard, author of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a> of the Kings of England, was born at Sefflingham, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, about the year 1568. After going through the usual course of academical learning at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HART">Hart</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, he travelled into foreign parts; and upon his return home was created <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts, and soon after, in 1603, received from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. In 1620, he was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>; but engaging to pay some of the debts of his wife’s family, he was reduced to poverty, and obliged to betake himself for shelter to the Fleet prison, where he composed several books; among which are, 1. Meditations and Dispositions on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>’s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">Prayer</a>. 2. Meditations, &c. on several of the Psalms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>. 3. Meditations and Prayers upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> Days of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">Week</a>. 4. Cato Variegatus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cato’s Moral Difficulties varied, &c.—Mr Granger observes, that his Chronicle of the Kings of England was ever more esteemed by readers of a lower class than by such as had a critical knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of it was, in this reign, called polite; and it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> maintained its reputation, especially among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> gentlemen. The author seems to have been sometimes more studious to please than to inform, and with that view to have sacrificed even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> itself to method. In 1658, Edward Phillips, nephew to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, published a third edition of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, with the addition of the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. It has been several times reprinted since, and is now carried as low as the reign of George I. Sir Richard also translated several works from the French and Italian; and died very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> in the Fleet prison, on the 18th of February 1645. Baker, Thomas, an eminent mathematician, was born at Ilton in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a> about the year 1625, and entered at Magdalen hall, Oxon, in 1640; after which he was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of Bishop's Nymmet, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, where he wrote The Geometrical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">Key</a>, or the Gate of Equations unlocked; by which he gained a considerable reputation. A little before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the members of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> sent him some mathematical queries, to which he returned so satisfactory an answer, that they presented him a medal with an inscription full of honour and respect. He died at Bishop's Nymmet on the 5th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1690. Baker, Thomas, a very ingenious and learned antiquary, descended from a family <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and well esteemed, distinguished by its loyalty and affection for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, was born at Crook in 1656. He was educated at the free school at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, and thence removed to St John's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> in 1674. He proceeded B.A. 1677; M.A. 1681; was elected fellow, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1679-80; ordained deacon by Bishop Compton of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 20. 1685; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> by Bishop Barlow of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, December 19. 1686. Dr Watson, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> of the college, who was nominated, but not yet consecrated, bishop of St David's, offered to take him for his chaplain, which he declined, probably on the prospect of a like offer from Lord Crew bishop of Durham, which he soon after accepted. His lordship collated him to the rectory of Long-Newton in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, and the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, June 1687; and, as Dr Grey was informed by some of the bishop's family, intended to have given him that of Sedgefield, worth £600l. or £700l. a-year, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> prebend, had he not incurred his displeasure and left his family for refusing to read King James II.'s <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>. The bishop, who disgraced him for this refusal, and was excepted out of King William's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> to that king, and kept his bishopric till his death. Mr Baker resigned Long-Newton August 1. 1693, refusing to take the oaths; and retired to his fellowship at St John's, in which he was protected till <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 20. 1716-17, when, with one-and-twenty others, he was disfranchised of it. After the passing the Registering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">Act</a> 1723, he was desired to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> his annuity of £40, which the last act required before it was amended and explained. Though this annuity, left him by his father for his fortune, with £20 per annum out of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COLLIERIES">collieries</a> by his elder <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of his death August 1699, for the remaining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the leafe, which determined at Whitcombide 1722, was now his whole subsistence, he could not be prevailed on to secure himself against the act. He retained a lively resentment of his deprivations; and wrote himself in all his books, as well as in those which he gave to the college library, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> ejectus, and in some ejectus rector. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to reside in the college as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a>-master till his death, which happened <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 2. 1740, of a paralytic stroke, being found on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of his chamber. In the afternoon of June 29, being alone in his chamber, he was struck with a slight apoplectic fit; which abating a little, he recovered his senses, and knew all about him, who were his nephew Burton, Drs <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a> and Heberden. He seemed perfectly satisfied and resigned; and when Dr Bedford desired him to take some medicine then ordered, he declined it, saying, he would only take his usual sustenance, which his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>-maker knew the times and quantities of giving; he was thankful for the affection and care his friends showed him; but, hoping the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> was at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, would by no means endeavour to retard it. His disorder increased, and the third day from this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZURE">seizure</a> he departed. Being appointed one of the executors of his elder brother's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, by which a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum was bequeathed to pious uses, he prevailed on the other two executors, who were his other brother Francis and the Hon. Charles Montague, to lay out £130l. of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> upon an estate to be settled upon St John's college for six exhibitioners. He likewise gave the college £100l. for the consideration of £1. a year (then only legal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>) for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and to the library several choice books, both printed and MS. medals, and coins; besides what he left to it by his will); which were "all such books, printed and MS. as he had, and were wanting there." All that Mr Baker printed was, 1. "Reflections on Learning, shewing the insufficiency thereof in its several particulars, in order to evince the usefulness and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a>," Lond. 1759-1760" (which went through eight editions: and Mr Boivin, in his "Method of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">Study</a>," ranks it among the English classics for purity of style); and, 2. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to Bishop Fisher's Funeral Sermon for Margaret Countess of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>, 1758; both without his name. Dr Grey had the original MS of both in his own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. The latter piece is a sufficient specimen of the editor's skill in antiquities to make us regret that he did not live to publish his "History of St John's College from the foundation of old St John's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> to the present time; with some occasional and incidental account of the affairs of the university, and of such private colleges as held <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> or intercourse with the old house or college; collected principally from MSS. and carried on through a succession of matters to the end of Bishop Gunning's mastership, 1670." The original, fit for the press, is among the Harleian MSS. No. 7228. His MS. collections relative to the history and antiquities of the university of Cambridge, amounting to 49 volumes in folio and three in quarto, are divided between the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a> and the public library at Cambridge; the former possesses 23 volumes, which he bequeathed to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Oxford, his friend and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>; the latter 16 in folio and three in quarto, which he bequeathed to the university. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">Knight</a> styles him "the greatest master of the antiquities of this our university;" and Hearne says, Optandum est ut sive quoque collectanea de antiquitatibus Cantabrigiensibus juris faciatur publici Cl. Bakerus, quippe qui eruditione summa jucundique acri et subaeque pollet. Mr Baker intended something like an Athena Cantabrigiensis, on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the Athena Oxoniensis. Baker, Henry, an ingenious and diligent naturalist, was born in Fleet-street London, either near the end of the last, or very early in the beginning of the present, century. His father's profession is not known; but his mother was, in her time, a midwife of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> practice. He was brought up under an eminent bookbinder, who preceded the elder Dodley, to the business of a bookbinder; in which, however, he appears Baker pears not to have engaged at all after his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a>; or, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he did, it was soon relinquished by him: for though it was in his power to have drawn away all his master's best customers, he would not set up against him. Mr Baker being of a philosophical turn of mind, and having diligently attended to the methods which might be practicable and useful in the cure of stammering, and especially in teaching <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEAF_AND_DUMB">deaf and dumb</a> persons to speak, he made this the employment of his life. In the prosecution of so valuable and difficult an undertaking, he was very successful; and several of his pupils, who are still living, bear testimony to the ability and good effect of his instructions. He married Sophia, youngest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the famous Daniel Defoe, who brought him two sons, both of whom he survived. On the 29th of January 1740 Mr Baker was elected a fellow of the Society of Antiquaries; and, on the 12th of March following, the same honour was conferred upon him by the Royal Society. In 1744, Sir Godfrey Copley's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> medal was bestowed upon him, for having, by his microscopical experiments on the crystallizations and configuration of saline particles, produced the most extraordinary discovery during that year. Having led a very useful and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> life, he died at his apartments in the Strand on the 25th of November 1774, being then above 70 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His wife had been dead some time before; and he only left one grandson, William Baker, who was born February 17, 1763, and to whom, on his living to the age of 21, he bequeathed the bulk of his fortune, which he had acquired by his profession of teaching deaf and dumb persons to speak. His furniture, printed books (but not MSS.), curiosities, and collections of every sort, he directed should be sold, which was accordingly done. His fine collection of native and foreign fossils, petrifications, shells, corals, vegetables, ores, &c., with some antiquities and other curiosities, were sold by auction March 13, 1775, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> following days. He was buried, as he desired, in an inexpensive manner, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>-le-Strand; within which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, on the south wall, he ordered a small tablet to be erected to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. "An inscription for it (he said) would probably be found among his papers; if not, he hoped some learned friend would write one agreeable to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>." This friendly office, however, remains as yet to be performed. Mr Baker was a constant and useful attendant at the meetings of the Royal and Antiquarian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">Societies</a>, and in both was frequently chosen one of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. He was peculiarly attentive to all the new improvements which were made in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> science, and very solicitous for the prosecution of them. Several of his communications are printed in the Philosophical Transactions; and, besides the papers written by himself, he was the means, by his extensive correspondence, of conveying to the society the intelligence and observations of other inquisitive and philosophical men, both at home and abroad. The Society for the encouragement of arts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, is under singular obligations to our worthy naturalist. As he was one of the earliest members of it, so he contributed in no small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to its rise and establishment. At its first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> he officiated for some time gratis as secretary. He was many years chairman of the committee of accounts; and he took an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> part in the general deliberations of the society. He drew up a short account of the original of this society, and of the concern he himself had in forming it; which was read before the society of antiquaries, and would be a pleasing present to the public. Mr Baker was a poetical writer in the early part of his life. His Invocation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">Health</a> got abroad without his knowledge; but was reprinted by himself in his Original Poems, serious and humorous, Part I. 8vo. 1725. Part II. came out in 1726. Among these poems are some tales as witty and as loose as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">Prior</a>'s. He was the author likewise of The Universe, a poem intended to restrain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; which has been several times reprinted. His account of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-pot, which was originally published in the Philosophical Transactions, was afterwards enlarged into a separate treatise, and hath gone through several editions. But this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> publications are, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICROSCOPE">Microscope</a> made Easy, and Employment for the Microscope. The first of these, which was originally published in 1742 or 1743, hath gone through six editions. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of the other, which, to say the least of it, is equally pleasing and instructive, appeared in 1764. These treatises, and especially the latter, contain the most curious and important of the observations and experiments which Mr Baker either laid before the Royal Society or published separately. It has been said of Mr Baker, that he was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> in little things. If it was intended by this language to lessen his reputation, there is no propriety in the stricture. He was an intelligent, upright, and benevolent man, much respected by those who knew him best. His friends were the friends of science and virtue: and it will always be remembered by his contemporaries, that no one was more ready than himself to afford those with whom he was conversant in their various researches, and endeavours for the advancement of knowledge and the benefit of society. Baker, David-Erskine, son to the former, was a young man of genius and learning. Having been adopted by an uncle, who was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>-throwster in Spitalfields, he succeeded him in the business; but wanted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> which are necessary to secure prosperity in trade. He married the daughter of Mr Clendon, a reverend empiric. Like his father, he was both a philosopher and a poet; and wrote several occasional poems in the periodical collections, some of which were much admired at the time; but so violent was his turn for dramatic performance, that he repeatedly engaged with the lowest strolling companies, in spite of every effort of his father to reclaim him. The public was indebted to him for "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">Companion</a> to the Play-house," in two volumes, 1764, 12mo; a work which, though imperfect, had considerable merit, and showed that he possessed a very extensive knowledge of our dramatic authors; and which has since (under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "Biographia Dramatica") been considerably improved by the attention of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> in every respect well qualified for the undertaking. Baker, a person whose occupation or business is to bake <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">Baking</a> and Bread. The learned are in great doubt about the time when baking first became a particular profession and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a> were introduced. It is however generally agreed, that they had their rise in the east, and passed from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> BAK to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> after the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with Pyrrhus, about the year of Rome 583. Till which time every housewife was her own baker; for the word pifior, which we find in Roman authors before that time, signified a person who ground or pounded the grain in a mill or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> to prepare it for baking, as Varro observes. According to Athenæus, the Cappadocians were the most applauded bakers, after them the Lydians, then the Phœnicians.—To the foreign bakers brought into Rome, were added a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of freed men, who were incorporated into a body, or, as they called it, a college; from which neither they nor their children were allowed to withdraw. They held their effects in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, and could not dispose of any part of them. Each bake-house had a patronus, who had the superintendency thereof; and these patroni elected one out of their number each year, who had superintendence over all the rest, and the care of the college. Out of the body of the bakers every now and then one was admitted among the senators.—To preserve honour and honesty in the college of bakers, they were expressly prohibited all <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with comedians and gladiators; each had his shop or bake-house, and they were distributed into fourteen regions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. They were excluded from guardianships and other offices, which might divert them from their employment.—By our own statutes bakers are declared not to be handicrafts. No man for using the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> or sciences of baking, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREWING">brewing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, shall be interpreted a handicraft. The bakers were a brotherhood in England before the year 1155, in the reign of King Henry II. though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> bakers were not incorporated till 1427, by King Edward III. and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> bakers not till 1621, in King James I.'s time. Their hall is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">Harp</a>-lane, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>-street; and their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-day on the first Monday of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>.—They make the 19th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; and consist of a warden, 4 maters, 30 assistants, and 140 men on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a>, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a>.—The French had formerly a great baker, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> panetier de France, who had the superintendency of all the bakers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. But since the beginning of this century, they have been put under the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general de <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>. In some provinces of France, the lord is the only baker in his seigneurie; keeping a public oven, to which all the tenants are obliged to bring their bread. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> is called furnagium, or furnaticum, and makes part of the bannalite.

BAKEWELL

Pages 392-392

a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a> in England, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WYE">Wye</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the Peak. It has a considerable trade in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 30. N. Lat. 55. 15.

BAKING

Pages 392-393

the art of preparing <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> reducing meals of any kind, whether simple or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, into bread. See the article Bread. The various forms of baking among us may be reduced into two, the one for unleavened, the other for leavened bread. For the first, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> is manchet-baking; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> whereof is as follows: The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, ground and bolted, is put into a trough; and to every bushel are poured in about three pints of warm ale, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARM">barm</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> to season it. This is kneaded well together with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> through the brake; or, for want thereof, with the feet, through a cloth; after which, having lain an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> to swell, it is moulded into manchets; which, scorched in the middle, and pricked up at top, to give room to rise, are baked in the oven by a gentle fire.—For the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, sometimes called cheat-bread baking, it is thus: Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAVEN">leaven</a> (saved from a former batch) filled with salt, laid up to four, and at length dissolved in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, is strained through a cloth into a hole made in the middle of the heap of meal in the trough; then it is worked with some of the flour into a moderate consistency: this is covered up with meal, where it lies all night; and in the morning the whole heap is stirred up, and mixed with a little warm water, barm, and salt, by which it is seasoned, softened, and brought to an even leaven: it is then kneaded, moulded, and baked, as before. Method of raising a bushel of flour with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>-spoonful of barm; by James <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMPTHILL">Ampthill</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>.—Suppose you want to bake a bushel of flour, and have but one tea-spoonful of barm.
