Put your flour into your kneading-trough or trendle; then take about three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a pint of warm water, and take the tea-spoonful of thick fleady barm and put it into the water, stir it until it is thoroughly mixed with the water; then make a hole in the middle of the flour <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> enough to contain two gallons of water; pour in your small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>; then take a stick about two feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, (which you may keep for that purpose,) and stir in some of the flour, until it is as thick as you would make batter for a pudding; then throw some of the dry flour over it, and go about your usual businels for about an hour: then take about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUART">quart</a> of warm water more, and pour in; for in one hour you <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find that small quantity raised so, that it will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> through the dry flour which you throw over it; and when you have poured in the quart of warm water, take your stick as before, and stir in some more flour, until it is as thick as before; then shake some more dry flour over it, and leave it for two hours more, and then you will find it rise and break through the dry flour again; then you may add three quarts or a gallon of water more, and stir in the flour and make it as thick as at first, and cover it with dry flour again; in about three or four hours more you may mix up your dough, and then cover it up warm; and in four or five hours more you may put it into the oven, and you will have as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> bread as though you had put a pint of barm. It does not take above a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an hour more <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> than the usual way of baking, for there is no time lost but that of adding water three or four times. The author of this method affirms us that he constantly bakes this way in the morning about six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> o'clock, puts the flour out, and puts this small quantity of barm into the before-mentioned quantity of water, in an hour's time some more, in two hours more a greater quantity, about noon makes up the dough, and about six in the evening it is put into the oven, and he has always good bread, never heavy nor bitter. When you find, he says, your body of flour spunged large enough, before you put in the rest of your water, you should, with both your hands, mix that which is spunged and the dry flour altogether, and then add the remainder of warm water, and your dough will rise the better and easier. The reason he affirms why people make heavy bread is, not because they have not barm enough, but because they do not know that barm is the same to flour BAK as fire is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>; that, as a spark of fire will kindle a large body by only blowing of it up, so will a thimble-full of barn, by adding of warm water, raise or spunge any body of flour; for warm water gives fresh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to that which is before at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; so that the reason of making bread heavy is, because the body spunged is not large enough, but was made up and put into the oven before it was ripe. In regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of seasons, he prescribes, that in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> you should put your water blood-warm; and in winter, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> frosty <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, as warm as you can bear your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in it without making it smart; being sure you cover up your dough very warm in the winter, and your covering of it with dry flour every time you add warm water, will keep in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; when you have added six or eight quarts of warm water, as before-mentioned, in such a gradual way, you will find all the body of flour which is mixed with the warm water, by virtue of that one tea-spoonful of barn, brought into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> agitation, waxing or fermenting; for it is to the flour what the spirit is to the body. It soon fills it with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>.

BAKOU

Pages 393-393
or BAKU, a town of Persia, in the province of Shirvan, situated at the extremity of the gulf of Ghilan on the Caspian sea. It is esteemed the most commodious haven in this sea, as vessels may there ride securely at anchor in seven fathom water; but the number of shoals, islands, and sand-banks, render the entrance in some places extremely difficult and dangerous, particularly to the Russians, who are not very expert sailors. Baku is a fortress surrounded with high brick walls; its inhabitants, like those of Derbent, are Persians, Tartars, and a few Armenian merchants. The principal articles of exportation which support the trade of this place are naphtha, and the finest rock salt, of both which there are mines on the east side of the bay. The inhabitants cultivate saffron and the cotton tree, but not to any considerable advantage. The trade of Baku, though more valuable than that of Derbent, is still inconsiderable, and chiefly carried on with Shamakiee, from whence it draws raw silk and filken stuffs. A Russian consul is resident at this place. In 1777 Baku belonged to Melik-Mehmed, who was tributary to Feth Ali khan of Kuba; the latter possessed the whole province of Shirvan, and was the most powerful prince, next to the khan of Ghilan, upon the coast of the Caspian. Before we quit the province of Shirvan, it may not be improper to mention its capital, the inland town of Shamakiee, which is only 65 miles from Baku, and supplies that port with raw silk and filken stuffs. It owed its former commercial importance to the silk which is cultivated in the neighbouring district; this rich production still preserves the town from ruin; though its traffic is greatly reduced by the exorbitant exactions of the khan of Kuba. Formerly the Russians had a factory at this place; and it was also crowded with Turkish and Greek merchants; but at present there are only a few Armenian and Indian traders. The inhabitants manufacture silk and cotton stuffs, but far inferior to those made at this place in the beginning of the present century. The silk of this province is exported into the interior part of Persia, Turkey, Georgia, and Russia. E. Long. 51° 30' N. Lat. 40° 20'.

BALAAM

Pages 393-394

a prophet and diviner of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Pethah upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, whose practices with Balak <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Moabites are recorded in the book of Numbers, chap. xxii. It is a question much debated among divines, whether Balaam was a true prophet of God, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> no more than a magician or fortune-teller. The Jews indeed are generally of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that he was a busy and pretended astrologer, who, observing when men were under a bad aspect of the stars, pronounced a curse upon them; which sometimes coming to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, gained him in some neighbouring nations a reputation in his way. Several of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> fathers suppose him to be no more than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> soothsayer, who undertook to tell future events, and discover secrets, and by no very justifiable arts. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> needs have it, that he was no prophet, but only one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>'s sorcerers, and that of him he went to inquire; but that God was pleased to prevent him, and put what answers he pleased into his mouth. It cannot be denied, however, that the scripture expressly calls him a prophet (Pet. ii. 5.) and therefore some later writers have imagined that he had once been a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and true prophet, till loving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> of iniquity, and profiting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his office to covetousness, he apostatized from God, and betaking himself to idolatrous practices, fell under the delusion of the devil, of whom he learned all his magical enchantments, though at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a>, when the preservation of his people was concerned, it might be consistent with God's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> to appear to him, and vouchsafe his revelations. As to what passed between him and his ass, when that animal was miraculously enabled to speak to its <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, commentators are divided in their opinions concerning this fact, whether it really and literally happened as Moses relates it; or whether it be an allegory only, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> imagination or vision of Balaam. This indeed is so wonderful an instance, that several of the Jewish doctors, who upon other occasions are fond enough of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, seem as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they would hardly be induced to assent to this. Philo, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Moses, passes it over in silence; and Maimonides pretends that it happened to Balaam in a prophetic vision only. But St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> (2 Pet. ii. 16.) speaks of this fact as literal and certain, and so all interpreters explain it. St Austin, who understands it exactly according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, finds nothing in the whole account more surprising than the stupidity of Balaam, who heard his ass speak to him, and answered it as if he talked with a reasonable person. He is of opinion, that this diviner was accustomed to prodigies like this, or that he was strangely blinded by his avarice not to be stopped by an event of so extraordinary a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Le Clerc thinks, that Balaam might probably have imbibed the doctrine of transmigration of souls, which was certainly very common in the east; and from thence he might be the less astonished at hearing a brute speak. And Dr Patrick thinks that Balaam was in such a rage and fury at the supposed perverseness of his beast crushing his foot, that for the present he could think of nothing else; though the conciseness of Moses's relation, who must be presumed to have omitted many circumstances, which if rightly known would dispel this and many more difficulties that may be imagined in this transaction, does certainly furnish us with a better and more satisfactory answer. St Austin is of opinion, that God had not given the ass a reasonable foul; but permitted it to pronounce nounce certain words, in order to reprove the prophet's covetousness. Gregory of Nyssa seems to think that the afs did not utter any word articulately or distinctly; but that, having brayed as usual, the diviner, whose practice it had been to draw preludes from the cries of beasts and singing of birds, comprehended easily the afs's meaning by its noise; Moses, deigning to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> this superstitious art of augurs and footstaplers, as if the afs really spoke in words articulate. We must own, says Calmet, that this is a miraculous fact related by an inspired writer, whose authority we are not allowed to call in question in the least particular: but we should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> such ways of explaining it as are most conformable to reason, and most proper to solve the difficulties of it, without attacking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Now it is very possible for God to make an afs speak articulately; it is indeed miraculous, and above the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of this animal, but not against the laws of nature.

BALADAN

Pages 394-394

the scripture name for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> (1sa. xxxix. 1. 2 Kings xx. 12.), called by profane authors Belusius <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Belefs, Nabonafar or Nangrus. Baladan at first was no more than governor of Babylon; but entering into a confederacy with Arbaces governor of Media, and rebelling against <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDANAPALUS">Sardanapalus</a> king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, these two generals marched against him with an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 400,000 men, and were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> in three different battles. But the Bactrians defeating the king, and coming over to Baladan and Arbaces, the rebels attacked the enemy in the night, and made themselves masters of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. After this misfortune, Sardanapalus retreated to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINEVEH">Nineveh</a>, and left the command of his army to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> Salamenes. The conspirators attacked Salamenes, and defeated him in two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> battles; after which they laid siege to Nineveh. Sardanapalus sustained the siege for three years; but the Tigris, in the third year, overflowing its banks, beat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> 20 furlongs of the walls; whereupon the conspirators entered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and took possession of it, after Sardanapalus had burnt himself and all his most valuable effects upon a funeral pile erected for that purpose in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. Baladan was acknowledged king of Babylon as Arbaces was of Media. Berodach-baladan, who sent ambassadors to Hezekiah (2 Kings xx.), was the son of Baladan.

BALAGATE

Pages 394-394

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Mogul empire, and the largest of the three that compose the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Dekkan. It has Kandish and Barar to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, Tellinga to the east, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGLANA">Baglana</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Guzerat to the west, and Viziapour to the south. It is a fruitful and pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, abounding with cotton and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. Here they have sheep without horns; but so strong, that when bridled and saddled they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> carry boys of ten years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Its present <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is Aurangabad, but formerly was Dowlet Abad; and from the latter the whole province is sometimes called Dowlet-Abad. BALAGATE <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, a chain of mountains which divides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Malabar from that of Coromandel, running almost the whole length of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on this side the Ganges. Some parts of them are covered with fine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which is blown by the strong west winds as far as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ceylon; and when the rays of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> are reflected from these mountains, they seem to be all on fire. They make surprising alterations in the feelings; for on the north side of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Comorin, it is winter in May, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, August, and September, in which months it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> on the south side of the cape; on one side there are continual tempests, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, while the other enjoys a constant serenity. When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> are gathered about the mountains, they are followed by sudden <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, which causes the overflowing of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and chokes them up with sand, insomuch that they are unnavigable for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> afterwards. The buildings and clothes of the inhabitants are scarce sufficient to defend them from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. They live upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, roots, and herbs, with very little meat; they have likewise a sort of small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARRACK">arrack</a>, but are never given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUNKENNESS">drunkenness</a>; nor do they import foreign vices, for they never travel abroad.

BALAGNIA

Pages 394-394

a town of Mucovy in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Little Novgorod, seated on the Wolga. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 45. 5. N. Lat. 50. 36.

BALAGUER

Pages 394-394

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Catalonia in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river Segra, at the foot of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain, on which there was formerly a fortress. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 48. N. Lat. 41. 38.

BALAMBUAN

Pages 394-394
or PADAMBUAN, a strong town of Asia, in the Indies, on the east end of the island of Java, and capital of a territory of the same name. E. Long. 115. 30. S. Lat. 7. 50.

BALANCE

Pages 394-399
or Balance, one of the six simple powers in mechanics, principally used in determining the equality or difference of weights in heavy bodies, and consequently their masses or quantities of matter. The balance is of two kinds: the ancient and the modern. The ancient or Roman, called also the patera Romana, or steel-yard, consists of a lever or beam, moveable on a centre, and suspended near one of its extremities; the bodies to be weighed are applied on one side of the centre; and their weight is shown by the division marked on the beam, where the weight, which is moveable along the lever, keeps the steel-yard in equilibrium. This balance is still frequently used in weighing heavy bodies. The modern balance now generally used consists of a lever or beam suspended exactly in the middle, having scales or basins hung to each extremity. The lever is called the jugum or beam; and the two moieties thereof on each side the axis, the brachia or arms. The line on which the beam turns, or which divides its brachia, is called the axis; and when considered with regard to the length of the brachia, is esteemed a point only, and called the centre of the balance; the handle whereby it is held, or by which the whole apparatus is suspended, is called trutina; and the slender part perpendicular to the beam, whereby either the equilibrium or preponderancy of bodies is indicated, is called the tongue of the balance. Thus in fig. 1. Pl. 84. ab is the beam, divided into two equal brachia or arms by the white spot in the centre, which is the axis or centre of the balance, and c is the tongue. The trutina, on which the axis is suspended, is not represented in this figure, in order to render the other parts more conspicuous. It follows, from what has been observed, therefore, that in the Roman balance, the weight used for a counterpoise is the same, but the point of application varies; in the common balance the counterpoise is various, and the point of application the same. The principle on which each is founded, may be very easily understood from the following observations, and the general properties of the lever. See Lever. The beam A B (fig. 2.), is a lever of the first kind; but instead of resting on a fulcrum, is suspended by something fastened to its centre of motion: consequently the mechanism of the balance depends on the same theorems as the lever. Hence as the quantity of matter in a known weight is to its distance from the centre of motion, so is the distance of the unknown weight to its quantity of matter. Hence the nature and use of the steel-yard is easily known. Let AB (fig. 2.) represent an instrument of this kind; a, the trutina, or handle on which the beam turns; k, a ring on which the balance may be suspended on a nail or hook; f, the hook on which the body to be weighed is hung; e, a collar or guard by which the hook f is fastened to the beam; g, a moveable collar; b, a swivel; i, the counterpoise. From what has been said it evidently follows, that if the body to be weighed be fastened to the hook f, and the whole suspended by the ring k, the division on which the counterpoise is placed to maintain an equilibrium in the balance, will show the weight of the body required; provided the weight of the counterpoise i be known, and the large divisions, 1, 2, 3, &c., be equal to the distance between the centre of the balance and the screw which fastens the guard e to the shorter arm of the balance. It will also be necessary that the steel-yard itself, with its whole apparatus, exclusive of the counterpoise, be in equilibrium, when suspended on the ring k. If the body to be weighed be heavier than the divisions on the longer arm will indicate, the balance is turned the lower side upwards, and suspended on the other ring b; by which means the divisions become shorter, because the distance between the trutina d, and the screw on which the guard e moves, is less; the divisions in the figure on this side extending to 17, whereas they extend only to 6 on the other. It will be unnecessary perhaps to observe, that the same precaution, with regard to the centre of gravity when the balance is suspended, is also necessary when this side of the balance is used, as we before mentioned with regard to the other. We have already observed, that in the common scales the two brachia or arms of the balance, e f, e g, fig. 3, are equal to each other, and consequently equal weights placed in the scales d, d, will be in equilibrium when the balance is suspended on its centre e, as in the figure, where the ring at the extremity of the trutina is hung on the tapering rod a b, fixed in the foot or base c. The Deceitful Balance, or that which cheats by the inequality of its brachia, is founded on the same principle as the steel-yard. Let there be, for example, a balance so constructed, that both the brachia with their scales shall equiponderate, but that the length of the one arm shall be to that of the other as 10 to 9. In this case, a weight of nine pounds put into the longest arm, will counterpoise one of ten pounds put into the shorter one; but the cheat is immediately discovered by shifting the weight from one scale to the other; in which case, the balance will no longer remain in equilibrium. Assay-Balance, a very nice balance used in documentary operations, to determine exactly the weight of minute bodies; see fig. 4. This balance should be made of the best steel, and of the hardest kind; because that metal is not so easily spoiled with rust as iron; and it is more apt than any other to take a perfect polish, which at the same time prevents the rust. The structure of the assayist's scale is little different from that of common scales, otherwise than by its nicety and smallness. The longer the beam of it is, the more exact may the weight of a body be found; however, 10 or 12 inches are sufficient length. Let the thickness of it be so little, that two drachms may hardly be hung at either of its extremities without its bending; for the largest weight put upon it seldom exceeds one dram. The whole surface of this beam must be altogether without ornaments, which only increase the weight and gather dust, &c. The beam is suspended in a fork, the two legs of which are steel springs joined at top, but kept together below with a brass plate clasp, parallel, and two lines and a half distant from each other. This clasp being taken off, and the legs of the fork being stretched out, the axis of the beam may be put into two holes made for that purpose at the ends of the legs, or be taken away from them. Let a very sharp needle be fixed in the head of the fork, standing perpendicularly downwards, if the fork is suspended, and so long, as that it may almost touch the top of the tongue of the beam put into the fork when in equilibrium. This needle is the mark of the equilibrium; and that the artists may be able to observe this, the legs of the fork must be broader in that place, and have an opening two or three lines wide; this fork may be adorned at pleasure, provided the motion of the balance is not hindered by such ornaments: then take two scales made of thin plate of silver, one inch and a half in diameter, hanging on three small silk strings, almost as long as the beam, tied together at top, with a silver hook in form of an S, and hang them to the extremities of the beam: a smaller silver dish or blued steel, somewhat less than one inch in diameter, belongs to each of these scales. You first put into these dishes, with a pair of pincers, the bodies to be weighed, or with a spoon or a small shovel, when they are pounded, and then you put them into the scales; therefore the small dishes must be perfectly equal in weight. We use them, that bodies may be more conveniently put into and taken out of the scales, and that those which are vastly thin may not be bent or spoiled, and thence rendered false by wiping. This balance is suspended on a moveable brass or copper support, which consists of a pedestal, and of a column set upon it about 20 inches high, at the top of which comes out at right angles an arm one inch long. At the extremity of this arm, put a small pulley three lines in diameter, another at the top of the column, and a third near the bottom of it; all which pulleys must turn very easily on their axes. At the distance of one inch and a half below the upper arm, let another arm one inch and a half long come out of the column at right angles, having a hole through it two lines long, a quarter of a line broad, and placed perpendicularly... pendicularly below the pulley of the upper arm, to receive a small plate, one inch and a half long; and of such breadth and thickness, as that it may freely move up and down, and yet not have too much play within the hole. This plate must also have a small hook at each extremity. And as such a balance will hardly stand still in the open air, and becomes false when spoiled with dust, it must be put, together with its support, into a small case as represented in fig. 4, having glasses, \(a\), \(a\), at top, and all round it, that you may see what is within. Manner of using the Alloy-Balance.—Pass a silk string over the three pulleys of the support, and tie it at its upper extremity to the small hook introduced into the hole of the inferior arm; then put the support in the middle of the small case, and pass the other extremity of the silk string below, through a hole bored in the middle of the lower part of the frame, containing the window in the fore-part of the case, and fasten it to a small weight of a cubic form. Suspend the fork of the balance on the inferior hook of the plate. By this means if you move backwards and forwards the weight fastened to the string, placed upon the top of the drawer jutting out beyond the fore-part of the case, the balance within is either lifted up or let down. But you must put the bodies to be weighed, and the weights themselves, into the small silver dishes; and these, when loaded, into the scales, through the side-windows, which must be opened for that purpose. When any thing is to be added to or taken out of them, you do it with the small pincers; or, if it is powder, with the small shovel or spoon; but you must let the balance down every time anything is to be added or taken away, that the scales may rest upon the bottom of the case; and thus the windows before the balance is lifted up again, especially if the air is not perfectly calm. Hydrostatic Balance, an instrument contrived to determine accurately the specific gravity of both solid and fluid bodies. It is constructed in various forms; but we shall content ourselves here with describing that which appears of all others the most accurate. VCG (fig. 5.) is the stand or pillar of this hydrostatic balance, which is to be fixed in a table. From the top A hangs, by two silk strings, the horizontal bar BB, from which it is suspended by a ring i, the fine beam of a balance b; which is prevented from descending too low on either side by the gently springing piece txyz, fixed on the support M. The harness is annulated at o, to show distinctly the perpendicular position of the examen, by the small pointed index fixed above it. The strings by which the balance is suspended, passing over two pulleys, one on each side the piece at A, go down to the bottom on the other side, and are hung over the hook at v; which hook, by means of a screw P, is moveable about one inch and a quarter, backward and forward, and therefore the balance may be raised or depressed so much. But if a greater elevation or depression be required, the sliding piece S, which carries the screw P, is readily moved to any part of the square brass rod VK, and fixed by means of a screw. The motion of the balance being thus adjusted, the rest of the apparatus is as follows. HH is a small board, fixed upon the piece D, under the scales d and e, and is moveable up and down in a low slit in the pillar above C, and fastened at any part by a screw behind. From the point in the middle of the bottom of each scale hangs, by a fine hook, a brass wire ad and ac. These pass through two holes mm in the table. To the wire ad is fastened a curious cylindrical wire r, perforated at each end for that purpose: this wire r is covered with paper, graduated by equal divisions, and is about five inches long. In the corner of the board at E, is fixed a brass tube, on which a round wire b l is adapted so as to move neither too tight nor too free, by its flat head I. Upon the lower part of this moves another tube Q, which has sufficient friction to make it remain in any position required: to this is fixed an index T, moving horizontally when the wire b l is turned about, and therefore may be easily set to the graduated wire r s. To the lower end of the wire r s hangs a weight L; and to that a wire pn, with a final brass ball g about one-fourth of an inch diameter. On the other side, to the wire ac, hangs a large glass bubble R, by a horse-hair. Let us first suppose the weight L taken away, and the wire pn suspended from S: and, on the other side, let the bubble R be taken away, and the weight F, suspended at c, in its room. This weight F we suppose to be sufficient to keep the several parts hanging to the other scale in equilibrium; at the same time that the middle point of the wire pn is at the surface of the water in the vessel N. The wire pn is to be of such a size, that the length of one inch shall weigh four grains. Now it is evident, since brass is eight times heavier than water, that for every inch the wire sinks in the water it will become half a grain lighter, and half a grain heavier for every inch it rises out of the water: consequently, by sinking two inches below the middle point, or rising two inches above it, the wire will become one grain lighter or heavier. Therefore, if, when the middle point is at the surface of the water in equilibrium, the index T be set to the middle point a of the graduated wire r s, and the distance on each side ar and ac contains 100 equal parts: then, if in weighing bodies the weight is required to the hundredth part of a grain, it may be easily had by proceeding in the following manner. Let the body to be weighed be placed in the scale d. Put the weight X in the scale e; and let this be so determined, that one grain more shall be too much, and one grain less too little. Then the balance being moved gently up or down, by the screw P, till the equilibrium be nicely shown at o; if the index T be at the middle point a of the wire r s, it shows that the weights put into the scale e are just equal to the weight of the body. By this method we find the absolute weight of the body; the relative weight is found by weighing it hydrostatically in water, as follows. Instead of putting the body into the scale e, as before, let it hang with the weight F, at the hook c, by a horse-hair, as at R, supposing the vessel O of water were away. The equilibrium being then made, the index T standing between a and r, at the 36 division, Balancerion shows the weight of the body put in to be 1095.36 grains. As it thus hangs, let it be immersed in the water of the vessel O, and it will become much lighter: the scale will descend till the beam of the balance rest on the support Z. Then suppose 100 grams put into the scale before the equilibrium precisely, so that the index T stand at the 36 division above A; it is evident that the weight of an equal bulk of water would, in this case, be exactly 100 grams. After a like manner this balance may be applied to find the specific gravity of liquids, as is easy to conceive from what has been said. Balance of Trade. That which is commonly meant by the balance of trade, is the equal importing of foreign commodities with the exporting of the native. And it is reckoned that nation has the advantage in the balance of trade, which exports more of the native commodities, and imports less of the foreign. The reason of this is, that, if the native commodities be of a greater value than are imported, the balance of that account must be made up in bullion or money; and the nation grows so much richer, as the balance of that account amounts to. Balance of a Clock, or Watch, is that part which regulates the beats. See Clock-Making. Balance-Fly. See Squalus, Ichthyology Index.

BALANCER

Pages 399-399

in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of insects, a style, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> body, ending in a protuberance or head, found under each wing of the two-winged flies; there, it is supposed, serve to poise the body of the fly.

BALANCING

Pages 399-399

among Seamen, the contracting a sail into a narrower compass, in a storm, by retrenching, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> folding up a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it at one corner: this method is used in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to reefing, which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sails; whereas balancing is peculiar to few, such as the mizen of a ship, and the main sail of those vessels wherein it is extended by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOM">boom</a>. See Boom and Reef.—The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> of the mizen is thus performed: the mizen yard is lowered a little, then a small portion of the sail is rolled up at the peak or upper corner, and fastened to the yard about one-fifth inward from the outer end or yard-arm toward the mast. See Mizen.—A boom main-sail is balanced, after all its reefs are taken in, by rolling up a similar portion of the hindmost or aftmost lower corner called the clin, and fastening it strongly to the boom, having previously wrapped a piece of old canvas round the part (which is done in both <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>) to prevent the sail from being fretted by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> which fastens it.

BALANUS

Pages 399-399

the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of lepas. See Lepas, <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BALAYAN

Pages 399-399

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANILLA">Manilla</a> in the East Indies, belonging to the Spaniards.—It lies next to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Manilla, and extends along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> on the east side of the island, a little beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Batangas. There were formerly <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> in it, but they have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> since abandoned. It is inhabited by about 2,000 tributary Indians, and abounds in cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, and palm-trees. The province is well cultivated; and the Spaniards, generally speaking, have Balayanes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-houses in it.

BALBASTRO

Pages 399-399

an episcopal town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Arragon, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a district of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 20. N. Lat. 41. 50.

BALBEC

Pages 399-401

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, anciently called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a>, and by the Arabians The wonder of Syria. It is situated at the foot of Anti-Lebanon, precisely on the last rising ground where the mountain terminates in the plain. As we arrive from the south we discover the city only at the distance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> and a half, behind a hedge of trees, over the verdant tops of which appears a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> edging of domes and minarets. After an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>'s journey we reach these trees, which are very fine walnuts; and soon after, crossing some ill cultivated gardens, by winding paths, arrive at the entrance of the city. We there perceive a ruined wall, flanked with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> towers, which ascends the declivity to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, and traces the precincts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> city. This wall, which is only ten <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> twelve feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, permits us to have a view of those void spaces and heaps of ruins which are the invariable appendage of every Turkish city; but what principally attracts our <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> edifice on the left, which, by its lofty walls and rich columns, manifestly appears to be one of those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> which antiquity has left for our admiration. These ruins, which are some of the most beautiful and best preserved of any in Asia, merit a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. To give a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> idea of them, we must suppose ourselves descending from the interior of the town. After having crossed the rubbish and huts with which it is filled, we arrive at a vacant <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which appears to have been a square; there, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, towards the west, we perceive a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> ruin, which consists of two pavilions ornamented with pilasters, joined at their bottom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> by a wall 160 feet in length. This front commands the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from a fort of terrace, on the edge of which we distinguish with difficulty the bases of twelve columns, which formerly extended from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a> to the other, and formed a portico. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> gate is obstructed by heaps of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; but, that obstacle surmounted, we enter an empty space, which is a hexagonal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of 180 feet diameter. This court is fired with broken columns, mutilated capitals, and the remains of pilasters, entablatures, and cornices; around it is a row of ruined edifices, which display all the ornaments of the richest <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. At the end of this court, opposite the west, is an outlet, which formerly was a gate, through which we perceive a still more extensive range of ruins, whose magnificence strongly excites curiosity. To have a full prospect of these, we must ascend a slope, up which were the steps to this gate; and we then arrive at the entrance of a square court, much more spacious than the former, being 350 feet wide and 336 in length. The eye is first attracted by the end of this court, where six enormous and majestic columns render the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> astonishingly grand and picturesque. Another object not less interesting is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> range of columns to the left, which appear to have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the peristyle of a temple; but before we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> thither, we cannot refuse particular attention to the edifices which enclose this court on each side. They form a sort of gallery. gallery which contains various chambers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> of which may be reckoned in each of the principal wings, viz. two in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> and five in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> square. The bottom of these apartments still retains pediments of niches and tabernacles, the supports of which are destroyed. On the side of the court they are open, and present only four and six columns totally destroyed. It is not easy to conceive the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of these apartments; but this does not diminish our admiration at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of their pilasters and the richness of the frieze of the entablature. Neither is it possible to avoid remarking the singular effect which results from the mixture of the garlands, the large foliage of the capitals, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> of wild <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> with which they are everywhere ornamented. In traversing the length of the court, we find in the middle a little square esplanade, where was a pavilion, of which nothing remains but the foundation. At length we arrive at the foot of the six columns; and then first conceive all the boldness of their elevation and the richness of their workmanship. Their shafts are 21 feet eight inches in circumference and 58 high; so that the total height, including the entablature, is from 71 to 72 feet. The sight of this superb ruin, thus solitary and unaccompanied, at first strikes us with astonishment; but, on a more attentive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, we discover a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of foundations, which mark an oblong square of 268 feet in length and 146 wide, and which, it seems probable, was the peristyle of a grand temple, the primary purpose of this whole structure. It presented to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> court, that is to the east, a front of ten columns, with 19 on each side, which, with the other six, make in all 54. The ground on which it stood was an oblong square, on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with this court, but narrower than it, so that there was only a terrace of 27 feet wide round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONNADE">colonnade</a>; the esplanade this produces fronts the open country toward the west, by a sloping wall of about 30 feet. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, as you approach the city, becomes less steep, so that the foundation of the pavilion is on a level with the termination of the hill; whence it is evident that the whole ground of the courts has been artificially raised. Such was the former state of this edifice; but the southern side of the grand temple was afterwards blocked up to build a smaller one, the peristyle and walls of which are still remaining. This temple, situated somewhat lower than the other, presents a side of 13 columns by eight in front (in all 34), which are likewise of the Corinthian order; their shafts are 15 feet eight inches in circumference, and 44 in height. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> they surround is an oblong square, the front of which, turned towards the east, is out of the line of the left wing of the great court. To reach it you must <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> trunks of columns, heaps of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and a ruinous wall by which it is now hid. After surmounting these obstacles you arrive at the gate, where you may survey the enclosure which was once the habitation of a god; but instead of the awful scene of a prostrate people and sacrifices offered by a multitude of priests, the sky is seen through the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, which lets in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to show a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a> of ruins covered with dust and weeds. The walls, formerly enriched with all the ornaments of the Corinthian order, now present nothing but pediments of niches and tabernacles, of which almost all the supports are fallen to the ground. Between these niches is a range of fluted pilasters, whose capitals support a broken entablature; but what remains of it displays a rich frize of foliage resting on the heads of satyrs, horses, bulls, &c. Over this entablature was the ancient roof, which was 57 feet wide and 110 in length. The walls which supported it are 31 feet high, and without a window. It is impossible to form any idea of the ornaments of this roof, except from the fragments lying on the ground; but it could not have been richer than the gallery of the peristyle: the principal remaining parts contain tablets in the form of lozenges, on which are represented <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> seated on his eagle; Leda carried by the swan; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> with her bow and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>; and several busts which seem to be figures of emperors and empresses. It would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us too far to enter more minutely into the description of this astonishing edifice. The lovers of the arts <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find it described with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and accuracy in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> published at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1757, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Ruins of Balbec. This work, compiled by Mr Robert Wood, the world owes to the attention and liberality of Mr Dawkins, who in 1757 visited Balbec and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALMYRA">Palmyra</a>. But several changes, however, have taken place since their journey; for example, they found <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> large columns standing, and in 1784 Mr Volney found but six. They reckoned 29 at the lesser temple, but there now remain but 20; the others have been overthrown by the earthquake of 1759. It has likewise shaken the walls of the lesser temple, that the stone of the soffit, or cross stone at the top of the gate, has slid between the two adjoining ones, and descended eight inches; by which means the body of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> sculptured on that stone is suspended, detached from its wings and the two garlands which hang from its beak, and terminated in two genii. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> alone has not effected this devastation; the Turks have had their share in the destruction of the columns. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> is to procure the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> cramps, which serve to join the several blocks of which each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> is composed. These cramps answer so well the end intended, that several of the columns are not even disjointed by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>; one, among others, as Mr Wood observes, has penetrated a stone of the temple wall without giving way; nothing can surpass the workmanship of these columns; they are joined without any cement, yet there is not room for the blade of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> between their interstices. After so many ages, they in general still retain their original whiteness. But what is still more astonishing, is the enormous stones which compose the sloping wall. To the west the second layer is formed of stones which are from 28 to 35 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, by about nine in height. Over this layer, at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west angle, there are three stones which alone occupy a space of 175½ feet; viz. the first 58 feet seven inches, the second 58 feet 11, and the third exactly 58 feet; and each of these is 12 feet thick. These stones are of a white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, with large thinning flakes like gypsum; there is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a> of this kind of stone under the whole city and in the adjacent mountain, which is open in several places, and among others on the right, as we approach the city. There is still lying there a stone, hewn on three sides, which is 69 feet two inches long, 12 feet 10 inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and 13 feet three in thickness. By what means could the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> move these enormous masses? This is doubt- Balbec, lefs a problem in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> curious to resolve. The inhabitants of Balbec have a very commodious manner of explaining it, by supposing these edifices to have been constructed by Dioneus, or genii, who obeyed the orders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>; adding, that the motive of such immense works was to conceal in subterraneous caverns vast treasures, which still remain there. To discover these, many have descended into the vaults which range under the whole edifice: but the utility of their researches, added to the oppressions and exactions of the governors, who have made their supposed discoveries a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a>, have at length disheartened them; but they imagine the Europeans would be more successful, nor would it be possible to persuade them but that we are possessed of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> art of destroying talismans. It is in vain to oppose reason to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>: and it would be no less ridiculous to attempt to prove to them that Solomon never was acquainted with the Corinthian order, which was only in use under the Roman emperors. But their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> on the subject of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> may suggest three important observations. First, That all tradition relative to high antiquity is as false among the Orientals as the Europeans. With them, as with us, facts which happened 100 years before, when not preserved in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, are altered, mutilated, or forgotten. To expect information from them with respect to events in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> or Alexander, would be as absurd as to make inquiries of the Flemish peasants concerning Clovis or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>. Secondly, That throughout Syria, the Mahometans, as well as the Jews and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> every great work to Solomon: not that the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of him still remains by tradition in those countries, but from certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; which, with the gospel, is the source of almost all their tradition, as these are the only historical books read or known; but as their expounders are very ignorant, their applications of what they are told are generally very remote from truth. By an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of this kind they pretend Balbec is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of the forest of Lebanon built by Solomon: nor do they approach nearer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, when they attribute to that king the well of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a> and the buildings of Palmyra. Thirdly, That the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> in hidden treasures has been confirmed by discoveries which have been really made from time to time. It is not many years since a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a> was found at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBRON">Hebron</a> full of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver medals, with an ancient Arabic book on medicine. In the country of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUSES">Druses</a> an individual discovered likewise, some time since, a jar with gold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> in the form of a crescent; but as the chiefs and governors claim a right to these discoveries, and ruin those who have made them, under pretext of obliging them to make reformation, those who find anything endeavour carefully to conceal it; they secretly melt the antique coins, nay frequently <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> them again in the same place where they found them, from the same fears which caused their first concealment, and which prove the same tyranny formerly existed in these countries. When we consider the extraordinary magnificence of the temple of Balbec, we cannot but be astonished at the silence of the Greek and Roman authors. Mr Wood, who has carefully examined all the ancient writers, has found no mention of it except in a fragment of John of Antioch, who attributes the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of this edifice to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">Antoninus Pius</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> which remain corroborate this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, which perfectly accounts for the constant use of the Corinthian order, since that order was not in general use before the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Rome; but we ought by no means to allege as an additional <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> the bird sculptured over the gate; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> his crooked beak, large claws, and the caduceus he bears, give him the appearance of an eagle, the tuft of feathers on his head, like that of certain pigeons, proves that he is not the Roman eagle: besides that the same bird is found in the temple of Palmyra; and is therefore evidently an Oriental eagle, consecrated to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, who was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> adored in both these temples. His worship existed at Balbec in the most remote antiquity. His statue, which resembled that of Oliris, had been transported there from the Heliopolis of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and the ceremonies with which he was worshipped there have been described by Macrobius, in his curious work entitled Saturnalia. Mr Wood supposes with reason, that the name of Balbec, which in Syriac signifies City of Bal, or of the sun, originated in this worship. The Greeks, by naming it Heliopolis, have in this instance only given a literal translation of the oriental word: a practice to which they have not always adhered. We are ignorant of the state of this city in remote antiquity; but it is to be presumed, that its situation on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from Tyre to Palmyra, gave it some part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of these opulent capitals. Under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, in the time of Augustus, it is mentioned as a garrison town; and there is still remaining, on the wall of the southern gate, on the right, as we enter, an inscription which proves the truth of this, the words KENTURIA PRIMA, in Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, being very legible. One hundred and forty years after, Antoninus built there the present temple, instead of the ancient one, which was doubtless falling into ruins: but Christianity having gained the ascendancy under Constantine, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> temple was neglected, and afterwards converted into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; a wall of which is now remaining, that hid the sanctuary of the idols. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> thus until the invasion of the Arabs, when it is probable they envied the Christians so beautiful a building. The church being less frequented fell to decay; wars succeeded; and it was converted into a place of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a> were built on the wall which surrounded it, on the pavilions and at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> which still subsist; and from that time, the temple, exposed to the fate of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, fell rapidly to ruin. The state of the city is not less deplorable. The wretched <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the emirs of the house of Harfouche had already greatly impaired it, and the earthquake of 1739 completed its destruction. The wars of the Emir Youlef and Djezzar have rendered it still more deserted and ruinous. Of 5000 inhabitants, at which <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> they were estimated in 1751, not 1200 are now remaining; and all these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, without industry or commerce, and cultivating nothing but a little cotton, some maize, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-melons.

BALBINUS

Pages 401-401

Decimus Coelius, the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, being chosen by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> in 237, was assassinated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, who had a dislike to such emperors as were elected only by the senators. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> was eloquent, and wrote pretty good verses.

BALBOA

Pages 401-402

Vasco Nunez de, a Castilian; a celebrated celebrated navigator, and one of the first discoverers of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. He was beheaded by the Spanish governor of St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, through jealousy of his growing reputation, in 1517, aged 42.

BALBUS

Pages 402-402

Lucius Cornelius Theophanes, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>, and distinguished himself by his valour in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> carried on by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> against Sertorius and the Lusitanians, on which account Pompey gave him the privileges of a Roman citizen. He was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> in the 714th year of Rome, and was the first foreigner on whom that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> was conferred. He was the friend of Pompey, Caesar, Crassus, and Cicero.—There were many other illustrious Romans of the name of Balbus.

BALCONY

Pages 402-402

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a projection in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, supported by pillars or consoles, and encompassed with a balustrade.

BALDACHIN

Pages 402-402
or Baldaquin, in Architecture, a building in form of a canopy, supported by pillars, and frequently used as a covering to insulated altars. Some also use the term baldachin for the shelf over a door.

BALDINUCCI

Pages 402-402
Philip, of Florence; a connoisseur in the polite arts, and the continuator of Valari's Lives of the Painters. He died in 1696, aged 72.

BALDIVIA

Pages 402-402
or Valdivia, a sea port town of Chili, in America, belonging to the Spaniards. It is situated between the rivers Callacules and Portero, where they fall into the South Sea. W. Long. 80. 5. S. Lat. 40. 5. It was built in 1551 by the Spanish general Baldivia, from whom it takes its name. We may judge of its importance from the sum granted annually by the king for maintaining the garrison and keeping the fortifications in repair, being no less than 300,000 pieces of eight. It is defended by four strong castles, mounting 100 pieces of fine brass cannon. Notwithstanding which, however, as the garrison is composed mostly of transported criminals, on whom no dependence can be placed, and generally ill supplied with ammunition, &c., it could make but a poor defence. In 1643 it was easily taken by the Dutch, who would probably have maintained their conquest against all the power of the Spanish viceroy, had they not been obliged to relinquish it through sickness and famine. The inhabitants of Baldivia amount to about 2000. The trade is less considerable than formerly, because the gold mines in the neighbourhood are shut up: yet several large ships are employed in the trade between this port and that of Lima, which consists of gold, corn, hides, and salt provisions, which are exchanged for slaves, sugar, chocolate, and European commodities and manufactures.

BALDNESS

Pages 402-402

a defect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, chiefly on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>. It differs from alopecia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>, ophiasis, and tinea, as these all arise from some vice in the nutritious humour; baldness, from the defect of it. When the eyelids shed their hair, it is called a pilosis. Among the causes of baldness, immoderate venery is reputed one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>; old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> usually brings it on of course. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have the proximate cause of baldness to be the dryness of the brain, and its shrinking from the cranium; it having been observed, that in bald persons there is always a vacancy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> empty space between the skull and the brain.—Calvus, bald-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATE">pate</a>, was a frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of reproach among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; among whom this defect was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disrepute. Hence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> arts to conceal it, as false hair, a galericula contrived on purpose. The later Romans, however, seem to have been reconciled to baldness; for we find among them a kind of officers, or servants, called glabrates or glabriarii, whose business was to take off the hair from all parts, even from the head. In an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inscription, there is mention of one <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIOPHANTUS">Diophantus</a>, TI. CAESARIS, ORNATOR GLABR., that is, Ornator Glabriarius.

BALDOC

Pages 402-402

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, in England, chiefly noted for its trading in malt. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 10. N. Lat. 51. 55.

BALDOCK

Pages 402-402

Ralph de, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in the reigns of Edward I. and II. was educated at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERTON">Merton</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; became <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of St Paul's; was afterwards promoted to the see of London; and at last was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of England. He had a very amiable character both for morals and learning; and wrote Historia Anglica, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the British Affairs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and, A Collection of the Statutes and Constitutions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Paul. Bishop Baldock died at <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol20.html#article-STEPNEY">Stepney</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 24, 1313.

BALDWIN

Pages 402-402

archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, was born of obscure parents at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, where, in the early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he taught a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school; after which he took orders, and was made archdeacon of Exeter; but he resigned that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and became a Cisterian monk in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Ford in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, of which in a few years he was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>. In the year 1180, he was consecrated bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>. In 1184, he was promoted to the see of Canterbury by Pope Lucius III. and by his successor Urban III. was appointed legate for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>. He laid the foundation of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and monastery in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Thomas Becket, at Hackington, near Canterbury, for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> priests; but, being opposed by the monks of Canterbury and the pope, was obliged to desist. In 1190 he crowned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Richard I. at Westminster; and soon after followed that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> to the holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, where he died at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMAIS">Ptolemais</a>. Giraldus Cambrensis, who accompanied him in this expedition, says, he was of a mild disposition, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a>. He wrote various tracts on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> subjects, which were collected and published by Bertrand Tiffler in 1662.

BALE

Pages 402-403

John, bishop of Offory in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, was born at Cove, near Dunwich in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, in the year 1495. At 12 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> he was entered in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Carmelites at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, and was thence sent to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. He was educated a Roman catholic, but was converted to the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> by Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Wentworth. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Lord Cromwell, favourite of Henry VIII. who protected him from the persecutions of the Roman clergy, he was obliged to retire into the Low Countries, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> eight years. Soon after the accession of Edward VI. he was recalled; and being first presented to the living of Bishop's Stocke in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>, in 1552, he was nominated to the see of Offory. During his residence in Ireland he was remarkably industrious in propagating the Protestant doctrines; but to very little purpose, and frequently at the hazard of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Once, in particular, they murdered five of his domestics, who were making hay in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> near his his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and would probably have done the same by him, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the sovereign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILKENNY">Kilkenny</a> had not come to his assistance with 100 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and 300 foot. On the accession of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, the tide of opposition became so powerful, that, to avoid affiliation, he embarked for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, but was very unfortunate in his escape. First he was taken by a Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and robbed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of all his effects. Then, being forced by tempests of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> into St Ives's in Cornwall, he was confined on suspicion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>. Being, however, released after a few days confinement, the ship anchored in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, where he was again seized on a false <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a>. After his arrival in Holland, he was kept prisoner for three weeks, and at length obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> on paying 30l. From Holland he travelled to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, where he continued till Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> ascended the throne. After his return to England, he was in 1560 made prebendary of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, probably not choosing to return to his former flock of wolves. He died in November 1563, at Canterbury, in the 68th year of his age. He was so severe a writer against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, that his books are particularly prohibited in the expurgatory <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>, in folio, in the year 1667. He is the earliest dramatic writer in the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least author of the first pieces of that kind that we find in print. Of his writings in that way no fewer than 21 have been enumerated; only three of them, however, have been seen in print, viz. 1. God's Promises, an interlude; 2. St John Baptist, an interlude; 3. Concerning the Laws of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> corrupted: the first of which has been reprinted by Doddrey in the first volume of his collection of old plays, and the only copy extant of the last is preserved in St Sepulchre's library in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. As to the rest, they are mentioned by himself as his own, in his account of the writers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> before mentioned. He also translated the tragedies of Pammachius. His other works are very numerous; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> is his catalogue of British Authors: a book of some merit, as it contains some information which is not elsewhere to be found; but he has destroyed his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> by his intemperate Billinggate abuse of all those who differed from him in religion. The authentic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is transcribed from Leland. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of it is, Illustrium Majoris Britanniae scriptorum catalogus, à Japheto sanctissimi Noa filio <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> an. Dom. 1557. Bale, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>. Any goods packed up in cloth, and corded round very tight, in order to keep them from breaking, or preserve them from the weather, is called a bale.—A bale of cotton yarn is from 300 to 400 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; of raw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, is from 100 to 400; of lockram or dowlas, either three, three and a half, or four pieces. Bale-Goods, among the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, are all such as are imported or exported in bales; but the French give that name to certain hardwares and other sorts of merchandise which come to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made by bad workmen of indifferent materials. BALEARES insulae, or the Balearic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>. The appellation is commonly derived from Balearis, because the inhabitants were excellent flingers.
