But Bochart makes the name of Punic or Phoenician original, as were the people: <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAAL">Baal</a>-jare, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, or skilful at throwing; the Phoenicians and Hebrews being dexterous at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLING">sling</a>. The Greeks called these islands Gymneche (Strabo); because in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> the inhabitants went naked (Diodorus, Livy), or rather because only armed with a sling in war (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HESYCHIUS">Hesychius</a>). They are two in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, the Greater and the Lesser, or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>; and hence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> names <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJORCA">Majorca</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINORCA">Minorca</a>. The Major is distant from the Minor 30 miles to the west, in length 40 miles, and in circuit 150 (Pliny). They were subdued by Quintus Metellus, thence surnamed Balearicus, in the year 120 B.C. The Baleares, together with the adjacent islands, were a part of the Provincia Citerior or Tarraconensis, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of the Conventus Carthaginensis or New <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>. These islands are called Choerarades by Apollonius, and Choerarades by Strabo, i.e. "rocky." See MAJORCA and MINORCA. BALEARIC ISLANDS. See the preceding article.

BALECHOU

Pages 403-403

JOHN <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">JOSEPH</a>, a very celebrated and well known French engraver, flourished about 1750. He died, according to Basan, some few years since at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a>. This extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> worked entirely with the graver; and he was perfectly <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. The clearness of his strokes, and the depth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> which he produced, are far beyond any production <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to his own. The two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> plates which he did from Vernet, one representing a storm, the other a calm, must ever be considered as very astonishing exertions of the artist. They are too well known, and too much admired, to need any further eulogium; and were never equalled until they were perhaps surpassed by our countryman Woollett.

BALEN

Pages 404-404

John Van, painter of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, landscapes, and boys, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1611; and derived his knowledge of the art, and his fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, from his father Hendrick Van Balen; but as soon as he had made a competent progress, he travelled to Rome, and lived for several years in that and other cities of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. There he acquired a good gusto of design, though he was sometimes incorrect; and his particular merit was shown in his naked figures of boys, cupids, nymphs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hunting, of which subjects he painted a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; and he procured both praise and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> by his landscapes and histories. His pictures were well handled, his trees touched with spirit, and his herbage and verdure looked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and lively. The carnations of his figures were clear and fresh; his colouring in general was transparent; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> of his heads were in the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANO">Albano</a>.

BALES

Pages 404-404
Peter, a famous master in the art of penmanship, or fair writing; and one of the first inventors of short-hand writing. He was born in 1547, and is styled by Anthony Wood "a most dexterous person in his profession, to the great wonder of scholars and others;" who adds, that "he spent several years in sciences among Oxonians, particularly as it seems in Gloucester-hall: but that study, which he used for a diversion only, proved at length an employment of profit." He is recorded for his skill in micrography, or miniature-writing, in Hollinshed's Chronicle, anno 1575; and Mr Evelyn also has celebrated his wonderful skill in this delicate operation of the hand. "Hadrian Julius speaking as a miracle of somebody, who wrote the Apostles Creed, and the beginning of St John's Gospel, within the compass of a farthing: what would he have said," says Mr Evelyn, "of our famous Peter Bales; who, in the year 1575, wrote the Lord's Prayer, the Creed, Decalogue, with two short prayers in Latin, his own name, motto, day of the month, year of the Lord, and reign of the Queen, to whom he presented it at Hampton Court, all of it written within the circle of a single penny, inclosed in a ring and borders of gold; and covered with a crystal so accurately wrought, as to be very plainly legible, to the great admiration of her Majesty, the whole Privy s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">Council, and several ambassadors then at Court?" He was farther very dexterous in imitating hand-writing, and about 1586, was employed by Secretary Walsingham in certain political manoeuvres. We find him at the head of a school, near the Old Bailey, London, in 1590; in which year he published his "Writing Schoolmaster, in three parts: the first teaching swift writing; the second, true writing; the third, fair writing." In 1595, he had a great trial of skill in the Black-friars with one Daniel Johnson, for a golden pen of 20l. value, and won it; and a contemporary author farther relates, that he had also the arms of Calligraphy given him, which are Azure, a Pen, Or, as a prize, at a trial of skill in this art among the best penmen in London. In 1597, he republished his "Writing Schoolmaster;" which was in such high reputation, that no less than eighteen copies of commendatory verses composed by learned and ingenious men of that time, were printed before it. Wood says, that he was engaged in Essex's treasons in 1603; but Wood was mistaken: he was only engaged, and very innocently so, in serving the treacherous purposes of one of that earl's mercenary dependants. We know little more of this curious person, but that he seems to have died about the year 1610.

BALESTRA

Pages 404-404

Antonio, an excellent historical painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a> in 1666. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 21 he went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, where he entered himself in the school of Antonio Bellucci, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for three years under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; but from thence he visited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a> and Rome, and at the latter became the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Carlo Maratti. Under the tuition of so eminent a genius, he made a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> proficiency, and exerted himself for some hours of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> after the antiques, after Raphael, Correggio, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> Carracci, and other admired painters; by which conduct he so effectually confirmed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and freedom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, that he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of merit in the Academy of St Luke, in the year 1694, when he was only 25 years of age. From that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> his reputation was established, and he received sufficient encouragement; being engaged to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> for most of the churches, and in the palaces of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and his paintings were admired in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. His style is sweet and agreeable, not unlike that of Maratti; and the judicious observe in the works of Balestra, a certain mixture of the several manners of Raphael, Correggio, and Carracci. He died in 1740. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Santa <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> Mater Domini at Venice, there is one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> performances of Balestra, representing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a> of our Saviour. It is designed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> style, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is excellent, and has a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>. The heads are peculiarly fine; and the whole has a noble effect, with remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>. In a chapel belonging to the church of S. Geminiano, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, there is a dead Christ in the arms of the Virgin, painted by this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in a grand taste; and although the composition consists but of a few figures, they are finely designed; and in every part of it there is sufficient merit to claim and justify applause.

BALEY

Pages 404-404

Walter, the son of Henry Baley of Warnwell in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, was born at Pottham in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a> school. From thence he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and, after two years probation, was admitted perpetual fellow of New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> in the year 1550. Having taken his degrees in arts, he practised physic, and in 1558 was proctor of the university. About this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he obtained a prebend of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>, which he resigned in 1579. In the year 1561 he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s professor of physic, in 1563 proceeded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, and afterwards became one of her majesty's physicians in ordinary. He was thought skilful in his profession, and had considerable practice. He died in 1592, aged 63; and was buried in the inner chapel of New College. His works are, 1. A discourse of three kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, 1588, 8vo. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">Brief</a> treatise of the preservation of the eye-sight; first printed in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, in 12mo; afterwards at Oxford in 1616 and 1624, 8vo. 3. Directions for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>;

BALI

Pages 404-405

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the East Indies, forming the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, through which the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> ships sometimes return from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; but the passage is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> difficult on account of contrary winds. The island is extremely populous, and abounds in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> and other productions peculiar to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. The inhabitants are Pagans, and very warlike. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 115° 30'. S. Lat. 9° 0'.

BALIOL

Pages 405-405

BALLIOL, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> BOILLIOL, John, the competitor with Robert Bruce for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Scotland, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> grandson of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Huntington, third son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> David I. See SCOTLAND.

BALISORE

Pages 405-405

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the East Indies, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>. It is about four miles from the sea by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, but 20 by the river; feared in a very fruitful <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, producing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, wheat, aromatic seeds, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, &c. The inhabitants make several sorts of stuffs of cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>. The English, French, and Dutch, have factories here; but they are now of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> account. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 85° 20'. N. Lat. 21° 30'. BALISTES. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BALIVO AMOVENDO

Pages 405-405

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, was a writ for removing a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> from his office, for want of having sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> in this bailiwick to answer the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> and his people, according to the statute of Westminster, 2 reg. Orig. 78.

BALK

Pages 405-405

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the above-mentioned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, situated on the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 65° 20'. N. Lat. 37° 0. It is probably the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Bactra, capital of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACTRIA">Bactria</a>; and is said by the Persians to have been founded by Kay-umaraz the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Persia, because he met his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> upon the spot where it stood, after he had been lost for a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; balkhiden, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> balghiden, in the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, signifying to receive and embrace a friend. The first kings of Persia who resided in the province of Media or Ardabilian, considered this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> as one of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> frontiers on the side of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a>. In the 27th year of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a>, of Christ 647, Balk was reduced by the Arabs, under the command of Abdallah Ebn Amer. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> subject to Arab princes till the year of the Hegira 432, of Christ 1041; when it was reduced by Togrol Beg, the Tangrolipix of the Greeks, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the Seljukian dynasty. It was taken by Jenghiz Khan, A.D. 1221, who with his usual and unparalleled cruelty caused all the inhabitants to be brought without the walls and massacred without mercy. In 1369, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> Hofsin, the last of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of Jenghiz Khan, was driven from Balk by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a>, whose successors were driven out by the Uzbeks in the 15th century. It was afterwards redeemed by Shah Ismael Safi; but finally wrested out of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> by the Uzbek Tartars, between whom and the Persians it is the occasion of almost continual wars. It was not long since the residence of a khan of Tartars. It is the most considerable city possessed in these parts by the Mahometan Tartars, is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, well built, and populous, the houses consisting for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or brick. The fortifications consist of bulwarks of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, fenced without with a strong wall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> enough to cover the foldiers employed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of those fortifications. As this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of all the business transacted between the Indies and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Bukharia, trade flourishes extremely at Balk; especially as it has a fine river passing through its suburbs, which is of vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the town. This river falls into the Amu, in N. Lat. 38° 30', upon the confines of Great Bukharia and Kowarazim. The khan's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, or castle, is a large edifice built after the oriental manner; and consists almost entirely of marble, of which there are fine quarries in the neighbourhood. The khan of Balk, however, was obliged in 1739 to submit to the Persians under Khouli Kan; but since that time has most probably regained his independency.

BALKERS

Pages 405-405

in the fishery, persons placed on rocks and eminences at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to spy the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> droves, and give notice to the fishermen, by waving boughs, whatever way they go, and where they may be found.

BALL

Pages 405-407

in Pyrotechnics, is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of various BAL rious combustible ingredients, serving to burn, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, &c. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we read of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIRE_BALLS">fire-balls</a>, light-balls, smoke-balls, flint-balls, sky-balls, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-balls, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>-balls. Ball, among the Cornish miners, signifies a tinmine. Ball, among Printers, a kind of wooden tunnel stuffed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, contained in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> cover, which is nailed to the wood, with which the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a> is applied on the forms to be wrought off. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">Printing</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">Horse</a>-Balls, among Farriers. Horses have a very nice <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; it is therefore proper to give the more disagreeable drugs in the form of balls, and to make drenches of the more palatable. Balls should be of an oval shape, not exceeding the size of a pullet's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>; and should be dipped in sweet <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> to make them slip <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the easier. Some horses have a strict gullet, which makes them very averse to a ball being thrust down their throats; such horses had better have drenches given them, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> their medicines may be mixed with bran, or in their mashes. See Farriery, psalm. Ball-Vein, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>, a name given by the miners of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a> to a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> ore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> there, and wrought to considerable advantage. It yields not any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of metal, but what it has runs freely in the fire; it is usually found in loose masses, not in the form of a stratum, and is often covered with one or more crusts. It generally contains some sparkling particles; and is usually of a circular form in the perfect masses, thickest in the middle, and gradually thinner as it approaches the sides. The ores of Sussex in general are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, but they require very little trouble in the working; so that a considerable profit is made annually from them. Ball and Socket, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> made of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, with a perpetual screw, so as to move horizontally, vertically, and obliquely; and is generally used for the managing of surveying or astronomical instruments. Puff-Ball, the English name of the lycoperdon. See Lycoperdon, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Martial Balls, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, are a mixture of filings of iron and cream of tartar, formed into a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> confluence and form of a ball, which is used to impregnate water or other liquids with iron dissolved by the tartaric acid. To make these balls, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of filings of iron and two parts powdered cream of tartar are mixed well together, and put into an earthen or iron vessel with some water. This mixture is to be stirred from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time, till it becomes almost dry; and then it is to receive more water, and to be stirred as before. This treatment is to be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till it acquires, when nearly dry, somewhat of the confluence and tenacity of softened rosin. Then it is rolled up in the form of a ball, which is generally kept tied up in rag; and when intended to be used, it is to be infused in water, till it gives some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to that liquid. The infusion of martial balls is tonic, vulnerary, diuretic, and aperitive; and is employed both internally and externally. Iron being soluble in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, is attacked in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> by the tartaric acid, which reduces it to a kind of neutral <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> not crystallizable. This salt would remain liquid, and would form a soluble martial tartar, called tartarized tincture of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> proper proportions of filings of iron and cream of tartar be used, and treated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough for an entire and complete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a>, nothing would be obtained but a liquor or magma, which could not be preserved in a solid form, but would be continually moist. Therefore, in the martial ball there is a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of the cream of tartar and filings of iron not combined together, by which its solidity is preserved. Mercurial Balls, in Pharmacy, are an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMALGAM">amalgam</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> and tin, sufficiently solid to be moulded, and to preserve a given form. The method of making them is by adding mercury to melted tin, and pouring the fluid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> into a round hollow mould. These balls are employed to purify water, in which they are boiled; for which purpose travellers often carry some along with them. Nothing, however, can be more pernicious than such a practice, should the water contain any nitrous acid, which it very often does. Balls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">Silk</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> and Spiders, are little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> or cones of silk, wherein those insects deposit their eggs. Spiders are extremely tender of their balls, which they carry about with them, adhering to the papillae about their anus. Grew mentions balls or bags of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of silk-worms in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> as big as hens' eggs, and containing each four aurelias. Zoologists speak of a sort of balls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> covered over with a smooth shining coat or shell, found in the stomachs of oxen, cows, calves, horses, sheep, and goats. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEZOAR">Bezoar</a>. Balls of Fire, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">Meteorology</a>. See Fire, Balls of. Balls, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>, are two pieces of cork, or pith of elder, nicely turned in a lathe to the size of a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>, and suspended by fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> threads; intended as electrometers, and of excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to discover small degrees of electricity, to observe the changes of it from positive to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, and vice versa; and to estimate the force of a shock before the discharge, so that the operator should always be able to tell very nearly before the discharge, by knowing how <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> he has <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> his jars, what the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be. Fire-Balls, are bags of canvas filled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, sulphur, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, pitch, &c. to be thrown by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, or out of mortars, in order to fire the houses incommoding trenches, advanced posts, or the like.—The Greeks had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> kinds of fire-balls, or Πυροβόλα κεφαλή; one kind called, more particularly, οξύλαιμα, or οξύλαιματα, made of wood, sometimes a foot or even a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUBIT">cubit</a> long; their heads being armed with spikes of iron, beneath which were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, pitch, and other combustibles, which being set on fire, they were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> among the enemy. The preparations of fire-balls, among the moderns, consist of several operations, viz. making the bag, preparing the composition, tying, and, lastly, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> the ball. 1. The bags for this purpose are either oval or round. 2. The composition wherewith fire-balls are filled is various: To ten pounds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>-gunpowder add two of saltpetre, one of sulphur, and one of colophony; or to five pounds of gunpowder, add four of saltpetre, four of sulphur, one of powdered glass, half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, as much camphor, an ounce of sal-ammoniac, and four of common salt, all pulverised. Sometimes they even fill fire-balls with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> grenades. 3. For tying the fire-balls, they prepare two iron rings, one fitted round the aperture, Light-Balls aperture, where the ball is to be lighted, the other near its base. A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> is tied to these rings in such a manner, as that the several turns represent semicircles of the sphere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the globe through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>; over the cords, extended according to the length of the ball, others are tied, cutting the former at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to each other, making a knot at each intersection: lastly, after putting in a leaden bullet, the reft of the space is filled with tow or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. 4. Thus completed, the fire-ball remains to be dipped in a composition of melted pitch four pounds, colophony two, and linseed oil or oil of turpentine two; after dipping, they cover it round with tow, and dip again, till it be brought to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> diameter required. Light-Balls, are such as diffuse an intense light around; or they are balls which, being cast out of the hand or a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, burn for some time, and illuminate the adjacent parts. 1. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUMINOUS">Luminous</a> or light-balls for the hand are made of ground powder, saltpetre, brimstone, camphor, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, all sprinkled with oil, and moulded into a mass with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>; and this is wrapped up in tow, with a sheet of strong paper over it. To fire it, they make a hole into it with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BODKIN">bodkin</a>, into which they put some priming that will burn slow. Its use is to be cast into any works they would discover in the night-time. 2. For the larger light-balls, or those to be thrown to a greater distance, they melt equal quantities of sulphur, turpentine, and pitch; and therein dip an earthen or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> ball, of a diameter much less than that of the mortar out of which the fire-ball is to be cast; then rolling it in gunpowder, and covering it round with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>, they dip it again, and repeat the rest till it come to fit the cavity of the mortar: lastly, they sprinkle it around with gunpowder. This, being once kindled, will strongly illuminate all around the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it is thrown, and give opportunity to examine the state and condition thereof. Smoke or Dark-Balls, those which fill the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> with smoke, and thus darken a place to prevent discoveries. To prepare a darkening ball, make an oval or spherical bag; melt rosin over the coals, and add an equal part of saltpetre not purified, also of sulphur, and a fifth part of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>. The whole being well incorporated, put in tow first shred, and fill the bags with this composition, and dip it after the same manner as a fire-ball. Stink-Balls, those which yield a great stench when fired to annoy the enemy. Their preparation is thus: Melt ten pounds of pitch, six of rosin, twenty of saltpetre, eight of gunpowder, and four of colophony; to these add two of charcoal, six of horlic-roots cut small, three of asafoetida, one of stinking-fenacen, and any other offensive ingredients. The rest as in the former. Sky-Balls, those cast on high out of mortars, and which, when arrived at their height, bursting like rockets, afford a spectacle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a>. Sky-balls are made of a wooden shell, filled with various compositions, particularly that of the stars of rockets. These are sometimes intermixed with crackers and other combustibles, making rains of fire, &c. Water-Balls, those which swim and burn a considerable time in the water, and at length burst therein. These are made in a wooden shell, the cavity of which is filled with refined saltpetre, sulphur, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>-dust boiled Land-Balls in water of saltpetre, and dried; to which sometimes other ingredients are added, as iron filings, Greek pitch, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> dust, powdered glats, and camphor. The ingredients are to be ground, mixed up, and moistened with linseed oil, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> oil, olive oil, hempseed oil, or petrol. At the bottom is placed an iron <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, filled with whole gunpowder, that the ball may at last burst with a greater noise: and, lastly, the ball is by the addition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> or otherwise, made of the same specific gravity with water. Land-Balls are those which, being thrown out of a mortar, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to the ground, burn, and burst there. The ingredients are much the same as in the water-balls, only the specific gravity is not attended to.

BALLAD

Pages 407-407

a kind of song, adapted to the capacity of the lower class of people; who, being mightily taken with this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, are thereby not a little influenced in the conduct of their lives. Hence we find, that seditious and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> men never fail to spread ballads among the people, with a view to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> them over to their side.

BALLAGE

Pages 408-408
or BAILAGE, in Commerce, a small duty paid to the city of London by aliens, and even denizens, for certain commodities exported by them.

BALLAGHAN

Pages 407-407

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLIGO">Sligo</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Connaught. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 50'. N. Lat. 53° 48'.

BALLAN

Pages 407-407

a town of France, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Mons, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORNE">Orne</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 25'. N. Lat. 48° 10'.

BALLAST

Pages 407-408

any heavy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, gravel, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, &c., thrown into the hold of a ship, in order to make her sink a proper depth in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, that she may be capable of carrying a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sail without overfetting. There is often <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the proportion of ballast required to prepare ships of equal burden for a voyage; the quantity being always more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less according to the sharpness or flatness of the ship's bottom, which seamen call the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>. The knowledge of ballasting a ship with propriety, is certainly an article that deserves the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the skilful mariner: for although it is known, that ships in general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not carry a sufficient quantity of sail till they are laden so deep that the surface of the water will nearly glance on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> breadth amidships, yet there is more than this general knowledge required; since, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she has a great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of heavy ballast, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, iron, &c., in the bottom, it will <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the centre of gravity too low in the hold; and although this will enable her to carry a great sail, she will nevertheless fail very heavily, and run the risk of being dismasted by her violent rolling. To ballast a ship, therefore, is the art of disposing those materials so that she may be duly poised, and maintain a proper equilibrium on the water, so as neither to be too stiff nor too crank, qualities equally pernicious: as in the first, although the ship may be fitted to carry a great sail, yet her velocity will not be proportionally increased; whilst her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> are more endangered by her sudden jerks and excessive labouring; and in the last, she will be incapable of carrying sail, without the risk of overfetting. Stiffness, in ballasting, is occasioned by disposing a great quantity of heavy ballast, as lead, iron, &c., in the bottom, which naturally places the centre of gravity very near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>; and that being the centre about which the vibrations are made, the lower it is placed, the more violent will be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of rolling. Cranks, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, is occasioned by having too little ballast, or by disposing the ship's lading so as to raise the centre of gravity too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, which also endangers the main in carrying sail when it blows hard: for when the masts lose their perpendicular height, they strain on the shrouds in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVER">lever</a>, which increases as the sine of their obliquity; and a ship that loses her masts is in great danger of being lost. The whole art of ballasting, therefore, consists in placing the centre of the gravity to correspond with the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a> and shape of the vessel, so as neither to be too high nor too low; neither too far forward nor too far aft, and to make the ship deep, that the surface of the water may nearly rise to the extreme breadth amidships; and thus she will be enabled to carry a good sail, incline but little, and ply well to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a>. Ships are said to be in ballast when they have no other loading. Masters of vessels are obliged to declare the quantity of ballast they bear, and to unload it at certain places. They are prohibited unloading their ballast in havens, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, &c., the neglect of which has ruined many excellent ports.—Ships and vessels taking in ballast in the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> are to pay so much a ton to Trinity-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a>; who shall employ ballastmen, and regulate them; and their lighters to be marked, &c. on pain of 10l.

BALLATOONS

Pages 408-408
large heavy luggage-boats used for carrying wood by the river from Africane and the Caspian sea to Moscow. These will carry from 100 to 200 tons, and have from 100 to 120 men employed to row and tow them along.

BALLENDEN

Pages 408-408

Sir John, a Scottish poet, in the reign of James V. of Scotland, was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. His father, Mr Thomas Ballenden of Auchinoul, was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> in the year 1540, and clerk <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> in 1541. Where our poet was educated, we are not informed; but from one of his poems we learn, that in his youth he had some employment at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James V. and that he was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> favour with that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. Having taken orders, and being created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, at the Sorbonne, he was made canon of Rothes, and archdeacon of Moray. He likewise obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of clerk-register, but was afterwards deprived of that employment by the factions of the times; however, in the succeeding reign of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, he recovered that office, and was one of the lords of session. Being a zealous papist, he, in conjunction with Dr Laing, was extremely affiduous in retarding the progress of the reformation; till at last, finding the opposition too powerful, he quitted Scotland, and went to Rome, where he died in the year 1550. He is generally esteemed one of the best Scottish poets of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His works are, 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and chronicles of Scotland of Hector Boeis (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a>), translated by Mr John Ballenden, Edinb. 1536. This is not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> translation; Ballenden having corrected several mistakes of his author, and made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> additions. It is in folio, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>. 2. Cosmography to the history of Scotland, with a poetical poem. 3. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANY">Albany</a>. 4. Translation of Boethius's description of Scotland. 5. Epistles to King James V. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">Bale</a> says he had seen these letters. 6. Several poems in Carmichael's collection of Scottish poems; besides many others in manuscript, in private <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> in Scotland. Virtue and Vice, a poem addressed to King James V.

BALLET

Pages 408-408

BALET, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> BALLETTO, a kind of dramatic poem, representing some fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> or subject divided into several entries; wherein several persons appear, and recite things under the name of some deity, or other illustrious character. BALLET is more particularly used for a kind of comic dance, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> of different kinds of movements, which together represent some subject or action. They are performed chiefly by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASKS">masks</a> representing satyrs, tritons, nymphs, shepherds, and the like; and consist of three parts, the entry, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and the retreat. The word is of Greek origin, formed from βαλλειν, jaceret, to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>, throw, or toss; whence also in writers of the middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, we find ballatones for salutation, dancings; and bailare for salare, to dance.

BALLICONNEL

Pages 408-408

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cavan, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 45'. N. Lat. 54° 6'.

BALLISHANNON

Pages 408-408

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DONEGAL">Donegal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Tyrconnel, with a good haven. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 25'. N. Lat. 54° 25'.

BALLISTA

Pages 408-408

a machine used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> darts; it resembled in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> our crossbow. The word is Latin, signifying a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-bow; and is derived from the Greek, βαλλειν, to shoot, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> throw. Vegetius informs us, that the ballista discharged darts with such rapidity and violence, that nothing could resist their force: and Athenaeus adds, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGIS">Agis</a> made one of little more than two feet in length which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> darts 500 paces. In Plate LXXXIV. is represented the ballista used in sieges, according to the chevalier Folard: 2, 2, the base of the ballista; 3, 4, upright beams; 5, 6, transverse beams; 7, 7, the two capitals in the upper transverse beam, (the lower transverse beam has also two similar capitals, which cannot be seen in this transverse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>); 9, 9, two pots or supports for strengthening the transverse beams; 10, 10, two skeins of cords fastened to the capitals; 11, 11, two arms inserted between the two skeins, or parts of the skeins; 12, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> fastened to the two arms; 13, darts which are shot by the ballista; 14, 14, curves in the upright beams, and in the concavity of which cushions are fastened, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the force of the arms which strike against them with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force when the dart is discharged; 16, the arbor of the machine, in which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> or canal perfectly straight is formed, and in which the darts are placed in order to their being shot by the ballista; 17, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> of the trigger; 18, the roll or windlass, about which the cord is wound; 19, a hook, by which the cord is drawn towards the centre, and the ballista cocked; 20, a stage or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> on which the arbor is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> sustained.

BALLISTEUM

Pages 408-408
or BALLISTEA, in antiquity, a military song or dance used on occasions of victory. Vopiscus has preferred the ballistea sung in honour of Aurelian, who, in the Sarmatian war, was said to have

BALLOON

Pages 409-409

BALLOON, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> BALLOT, in the French glafls-trade, signifies a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of glafls-plates, smaller or greater according to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. The ballon of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> glafl contains 25 bundles, of fix plates per bundle; but the ballon of coloured glafl is only of 12½ bundles, and of three plates to a bundle.

BALLOTADE

Pages 409-409

in the Manege, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> between two pillars, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> upon a straight line, made with jutnells of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, with the aid of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and the calves of the legs: and in such a manner, that when his fore-feet are in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, he shows nothing but the thoes of his hinder-feet without yerking out.

BALLOTING

Pages 409-409

a method of voting at elections, &c. by means of little balls usually of different colours, by the French called ballots, which are put into a box privately.

BALLS

Pages 409-409
or BALLOTS, in Heraldry, a frequent bearing in coats of arms, usually denominated, according to their colour, bezantes, plates, hurts, &c.

BALLUSTRADE

Pages 409-409

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> row of ballusters, joined by a rail; serving as well for a rest to the elbows as for a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> or enclosure to balconies, altars, staircases, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, No. 74. BALM. See Melissa, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Balm, or Balsam. See Balsam. Balm of Gilead. See Amyris, Botany Index.

BALNAVES

Pages 409-409

HENRY, a Scottish Protestant divine, born in the shire of Fife, in the reign of James V. and educated at the university of St Andrew's. He went afterwards to France in order to finish his studies; and returning to Scotland, was admitted into the family of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARRAN">Arran</a>, who at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> governed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>: but in the year 1542 the earl disfirmed him for having embraced the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. In 1564, he joined, says Mackenzie, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Beaton; for which he was declared a traitor, and excommunicated. Whilst that party were besieged in the castle of St Andrew's, they sent Balnaves to England, who returned with a considerable supply of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; but being at last obliged to surrender to the French, he was sent with the rest of the garrison to France. He returned to Scotland, about the year 1559; and having joined the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">Congregation</a>, he was appointed one of the commissioners to treat with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. In 1563 he was made one of the lords of session, and appointed by the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, with other learned men, to revise the Book of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">Discipline</a>. Knox, his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a>, and fellow-labourer, gives him the character of a very learned and pious divine. He died...

BALNEARIUS FUR

Pages 409-410

in antiquity, a kind of thief who practised stealing the clothes of persons in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>; sometimes also called fur balnearum. The crime of these thieves was a kind of sacrilege; for the hot baths were sacred; hence they were more severely punished than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> thieves who stole out of private houses. The latter were acquitted with paying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the value of the thing stolen; whereas the former were punished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>.

BALNEUM

Pages 410-410

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by chemists to signify a vessel filled with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, in which another is placed that requires a more gentle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> than the naked fire.

BALSA

Pages 410-410

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUSITANIA">Lusitania</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGER">Ager</a> Cumeus; now Tavira, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Algarva.

BALSAM

Pages 410-410
or NATIVE BALSAM, an oily, resinous, liquid substance, flowing either spontaneously, or by means of incision, from certain plants. There are a great variety of balsams, generally denominated from the substances from which they are obtained; and which are explained under their names as they occur. BALSAMICS. Balmamica is a Latin word which signifies mitigating. The term balsamic is a very lax one; it includes medicines of very different qualities, as emollients, detergents, reformatorys, &c. but in medicines of all these kinds there seems to be this requisite in them, viz. that they be soft, yielding, and adhesive, also that by their smallness they have a ready disposition to motion. Medicines of this tribe are generally required for complaints whose seat is in the viscera; and as they cannot be conveyed there but by the common road of the circulation, it follows, that no great effects can be expected from them but by their long continuation. Hoffman calls by the name of balmamics those medicines which are hot and acid, also the natural balsams, gums, &c. by which the vital heat is increased. BALSORA. See BASSORA.

BALTAGI

Pages 410-410

among the Turks, porters, and hewers of wood, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior; who also mount on horseback when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> rides out. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> of them also, who, for that purpose, must be castrated, keep watch at the gates of the first and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> courts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERAGLIO">seraglio</a>. The first are called capigii, and their commander capigi pasha.

BALTIC SEA

Pages 410-410

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> surrounded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, Russia, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, Pomerania, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Denmark levies a tax at Elsinore on every ship that enters the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It is remarkable that this sea neither ebbs nor flows, and there is always a current sets through the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a> into the ocean. It is generally frozen over three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four months in the year. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">Yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> is found in plenty on this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>.

BALTIMORE

Pages 410-410
county and town of, Maryland in America. BALTIMORE Bird. See Oriolus, Ornithology Index.

BALTZAR

Pages 410-410

THOMAS, a native of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUBEC">Lubec</a>, was an eminent musical composer, and esteemed the finest performer on the violin of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. He came into England in the year 1658, and lived about two years in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Sir Anthony Cope of Hanwell in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>. He was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> competitor of Davis Mell, who, though a clockmaker by trade, was till Baltzar came hither, allowed to be the finest performer on the violin in England; and after his arrival he divided with him the public applause, it being agreed that Mell excelled in the fineness of his tone and the sweetness of his manner, and Baltzar in the power of execution and command of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. Moreover, it is said of the latter, that he first taught the English the practice of shifting, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the finger-board. Baltzar was given to intemperance, and is said to have shortened his days by excessive drinking: he was buried in Westminster-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> on the 27th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1663.

BALUCLAVO

Pages 410-410
or JAMBOL, a sea-port town of Crimea on the "xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black sea, where they build ships for the grand signior. E. Long. 35° 15'. N. Lat. 44° 50'.

BALUZE

Pages 410-410

STEPHEN, a French writer, born in 1651, and some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> librarian to M. Colbert. In 1693 he obtained a pension, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the lives of the popes of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a>; both which advantages he soon lost in the fluctuation of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> parties. M. Baluze is much more noted for collecting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> MSS. and illustrating them by notes, than famed for his own compositions.

BALYUR

Pages 410-411
or BALIUR, a sea-port of Africa in the kingdom of Dancali, about 14 hours journey west from Babel-Mandel. It is remarkable only for being the landing place of the Abyssinian patriarch Alphonsus Mendez, with his Jesuits and Portuguese, on April 3rd 1724. The king, who had received orders from the Abyssinian emperor to give them a proper reception, despatched his son to meet them and conduct them to him. The royal palace they found to consist of about half a dozen of tents, and a score of huts, fenced about with a thorn hedge, and shaded by some wild kinds of trees. Near the palace was a river, which was then quite dried up, and no water to be found but what was dugged for in the channel. The hall of audience was only a large tent about a musket-flot from the rest. At the upper end was a kind of throne made of stones and clay, covered with a carpet, and two velvet cushions. At the other end was his majesty's horse, with the saddle and other accoutrements hanging on one side; it being the custom of this country for the master and horse to lie together, whether king or subject. Around the hall were about 50 young men sitting cross-legged; and when the Portuguese ambassadors were admitted, they were made to sit down in the same posture. Soon after came the king preceded by some of his domestics, one having an earthen pitcher full of hydromel, hydromel, another a cup made of porcelain, a third carrying a cocon-shell full of tobacco, and a fourth bringing a silver tobacco-pipe with some fire. Next to them was the king, dressed in a light silk stuff, having on his head a turban, from the rims of which hung a parcel of rings nicely wrought, which dangled before his face. He had in his hand a short kind of javelin, and was followed by all the chief officers of his court and household. The respect paid him at his coming in was by standing on their feet, and squatting down again twice, after which they went forward to kiss his hand.

BALZAC

Pages 411-411

JOHN <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">LEWIS</a> GUEZ DE, born at Angoulême in 1595. Voltaire allows him the merit of having given numbers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> to the French prose, but censures his style as somewhat bombastic. The critics of his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> gave him no little disquiet; and he gave them no little advantage over him by his sallies of vanity, and some particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> which were a little dangerous. M. Balzac, getting rid of these disputes by his moderation, settled at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-seat; refined his style and genius; and got by his letters and other writings which he published from time to time, the reputation of being the first writer in France. He was at length drawn from his retirement by the hopes of making his fortune under <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Richelieu, who had formerly courted his friendship; but in a few years he retired again, disgusted with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> dependence of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. All he obtained from the court was a pension of 2000 livres, with the titles of counsellor of state and historiographer of France. He died in 1654; and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> of Notre Dame des Anges, to which he bequeathed 12,000 livres. He left an estate of 100 francs per annum; for a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> medal to be bestowed every two years for the best discourse on some moral subject. Besides his letters he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> called Oeuvres Diverses, i.e., on various subjects; The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a>; The Christian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, &c.; and many other pieces; all of which have been published in two vols folio.

BAMBA

Pages 411-411

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONGO">Congo</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>.—It is situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of Ambrif and Lofe; the last of which parts it from Pemba on the east, as the Ambrif does from the province of Sogno on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. Along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> it extends itself northward to the river Lelanda; and on the south to that of Dauda, which parts it from the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a>. The governors of this province bear the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of dukes, and are always some of the princes of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family. They are as despotic and arbitrary as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were really kings, notwithstanding the care and pains their monarchs have taken to keep them within due bounds. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of this province is very fertile; and would produce all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty, were the inhabitants but industrious in its cultivation. The sea-coasts produce a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, which could be purified with little trouble, and would yield an extraordinary revenue if the duties were duly paid; but these the governors find means to sink mostly into their own coffers.—Here is also the fishery of the zimbos, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> little sea-snail, whose shell is the current <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> not only in this and the neighbouring kingdoms, but also in the most distant parts of Africa. Here are also said to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, quicksilver, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, tin, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; but none except the iron mines Bamberg, Bambooccio, are allowed to be worked.

BAMBERG

Pages 411-411

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> handsome town of Franconia in Germany, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a bishopric of the same name. It was formerly imperial, but is now subject to the bishop. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about it produces plenty of corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and liquorice. It has an university, founded in 1685; and is situated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Main and Reidnitz. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 15. N. Lat. 50. 10. Bamberg, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, situated at the foot of a mountain. E. Long. 16. 50. N. Lat. 49. 53.

BAMBOCCIO

Pages 411-411

a celebrated painter of conversations, landscapes, cattle, &c., was born at Laerden, near Narden, in 1613. His name was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Van Laer; but in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> they gave him the name of Bamboccio, on account of the uncommon shape of his body, the lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> being one third part longer than the upper, and his neck so short that it was buried between his shoulders. He had, however, an ample amends for the uneasiness of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, in the superior beauties of his mind: he was endowed with an extensive genius; and, indeed, had an universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for every part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. He resided at Rome for fifteen years successively; every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> studying to improve himself by those beautiful models which were continually open to his observation, and by the lovely scenery in the environs of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He was held in the highest esteem by all ranks of men, as well as by those of his own profession; not only on account of his extraordinary abilities, but also for the amiable qualities of his mind. He studied <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> incessantly; observing with a curious exactness every effect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on different objects, at different hours of the day; and whatsoever incident afforded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to his imagination, his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> for ever perfectly retained. His style of painting is sweet and true; and his touch delicate, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> transparency of colouring. His figures are always of a small size, well proportioned, and correctly designed; and although his subjects are taken but from the lower kind of nature, such as plunderings, playing at bowls, inns, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARRIER">farrier</a> shops, cattle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conversations; yet whatever he painted was so excellently designed, so happily executed, and so highly finished, that his manner was adopted by many of the Italian painters of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. His works are still universally admired, and he is justly ranked among the first class of the eminent masters. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> was as quick as his imagination, so that he rarely made sketches or designs for any of his works; he only marked the subject with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRAYON">crayon</a> on the canvas, and finished it without more delay. His memory was amazing: for whatever objects he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he considered them with any intention to infuse them in his compositions, the idea of them was so strongly impressed on his mind, that he could represent them with as much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> as if they were placed before his eyes. Sandrart observes, that although painters who are accustomed to a small size are frequently inaccurate in the disposition of the different parts of their subject, seeming content if the whole appears <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>; yet Bamboccio was as minutely exact in having his figures, trees, grounds, and distances, determined with the utmost precision and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> truth, as the best masters usually are in pictures of the largest size; which

BAMBOE

Pages 411-412

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of arundo. See ARUNDO, BOTANY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. BAMBOS-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">Habit</a>; a Chinese contrivance by which a person who cannot swim may easily keep himself above <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The following account of it is from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the author of the Seaman's Preservative. "In the year 1730, I was passenger in a ship from Batavia to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, burden about 400 tons, called the Pradae, Francisco Xavier commander, freighted by English, Chinese, and Portuguese. Near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of China we met one of those storms called a tuftoon (tau-fong), <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, which carried away all our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, bowsprit, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a>; and in our hold we had six feet of water, expecting every moment the ship would founder.—We consequently were consulting our preservation: the English and Portuguese stood in their shirts only, ready to be thrown off; but the Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> came upon deck, not in a cork-jacket, but I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> call it a bambos-babit, which had lain ready in their chests against such dangers; and it was thus constructed; four bamboes, two before and two behind their bodies, were placed horizontally, and projected about 28 inches. These were crooked on each side by two others, and the whole properly secured, leaving a space for their body; so that they had only to put it over their heads, and tie the same securely, which was done in two minutes, and we were satisfied they could not possibly sink." The shape is here subjoined.

BAMBOROUGH

Pages 412-412

an inconsiderable village in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, 14 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALNWICK">Alnwick</a>, was once a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough, and sent two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>: it even gave name to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tract extending southward, which was called Bamboroughshire. It had also three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> foundations; a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of friars preachers founded by Henry III., a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a> of canons regular of St Austin, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. Its very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> castle stands on an almost perpendicular rock <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the sea, and accessible only on the south-east side, on a spot where, according to the monkish historians, there stood the castle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the kings of Northumberland; built, as it is said, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Ida, who began his reign about the year 559. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> of the present ruins are by some supposed to be the remains of King Ida's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The ancient name of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was, it is said, Bamborough; which name Camden, from the authority of Bede, imagines borrowed from Bebba, Ida's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>; but the author of the additions to that writer is of a contrary <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, as in the Saxon copy it is called Cynelcanberg, or the "royal manion." According to Florilegus, King Ida at first fenced it only with a wooden enclosure, but afterwards surrounded it with a wall. It is thus described by Roger Hoveden, who wrote in the year 1192: "Bebba is a very strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, but not exceeding large; containing not more than two or three acres of ground. It has but one hollow entrance into it, which is admirably raised by steps. On the top of the hill stands a fair <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; and in the western point is a well curiously adorned, and of sweet clean <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>." This castle was besieged anno 642 by Penda, the Pagan king of the Mercians, who, as the story goes, attempted to burn it: for which purpose he laid vast quantities of wood under the walls, and set fire to it as soon as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> was favourable; but no sooner was it kindled, than by the prayers of St Adian, the wind changed and carried the flames into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, so that he was obliged to raise the siege.
