In 710, King Offred, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Alfred his father, took shelter in this castle with Britthric his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a>; one Edulph having seized the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, by whom, with his partizans, they were unsuccessfully besieged. Britthric made so gallant a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, that the siege was turned into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCKADE">blockade</a>, which gave the loyal subjects <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to arm in defence of their young king. On their marching hither to his relief, Edulph fled; but was followed, taken, and put to death by Britthric, who thereby securely seated Offred on the throne, when this castle became his palace. In the reign of Egbert, Kenulph bishop of Lindisfarne was confined here 30 years from 750 to 780. In 933, it was plundered and totally ruined by the Danes; but being of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance in defending the northern parts against the continual incursions of the Scots, it was soon after repaired, and made a place of considerable strength. It is said to have been in good repair at the time of the Conquest, when it was probably put into the custody of some trusty Norman, and had in all likelihood some additions made to its works; and this is the more probable, as the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>, contained within its walls, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> upwards of 80 acres, instead of three, as when described by Hoveden. About the year 1095 it was in possession of Robert de Mowbray <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Northumberland, who engaging in some treasonable practices against William Rufus, that king laid siege to it, and obliged it to surrender. In the next reign it was intrusted by Henry I. to Luitace Fitz-John, who was dispossessed of it and his other employments by King Stephen, that king being jealous of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to Maud, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Henry I. Irritated at this, Fitz-John delivered the castle of Alnwick to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> king of Scotland, and brought to his aid all the forces he could raise; he was, however, afterward reconciled to King Stephen, and held the manors of Burg and Knaresborough in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, but never recovered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of this castle. In the 16th of Henry II. some great repairs seem to have been done here, as in Madox's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the exchequer, under the article of Amercements, it appears one William, son of Waldef, was fined five marks for refusing his assistance in the king's works at Baenburg castle.

BAMBUCK

Pages 412-413

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, of which the Bambock, following account is given by the Abbé Raynal, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> traveller whom he does not name. "In the interior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Africa, under the 12th <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 13th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, there is (says a modern traveller) a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> country, known by the name of Bambuck. It is not subject to a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>; but governed by village lords, called farims. These <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> and independent chiefs are all obliged to unite for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the state, when it is either attacked as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, or only in one of its branches. "The territory of this aristocratical state is dry and barren. It produces neither maize, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, nor <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>. The insupportable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> it is subject to, proceeds in part from its being surrounded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> from refreshing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is as unwholesome as it is disagreeable: vapours, which continually issue from the bowels of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> replete with minerals, render this country unfit to live in, especially to strangers. "It is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> that hath made this miserable country an object worthy of notice; gold, which in the eyes of the covetous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> seems to compensate for all the evils of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, though in reality it increases them all. This metal is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in this country, that it is found almost indiscriminately everywhere. To obtain it, sometimes it is sufficient to scrape the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which is clayish, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and mixed with sand. When the mine is very rich, it is dugged only to the depth of a few feet, and never deeper; though it has been observed, that the lower it was digged, the more gold the soil afforded. The miners are too indolent to pursue a toil which constantly becomes more tedious, and too ignorant to perceive the inconveniences it would be attended with. Their negligence and their folly are in this instance so extraordinary, that in washing the gold, in order to separate it from the earth, they only preserve the larger pieces: the light parts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> away with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which flows <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INCLINED_PLANE">inclined <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>. "The inhabitants of Bambuck do not <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> at all times, nor are they at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to do it when they please. They are obliged to wait till private or public wants determine the farims to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> this permission. When it is proclaimed, all who are able to avail themselves of this advantage meet at the appointed <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. When their work is finished, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> is made. Half of the gold goes to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, and the remainder is equally distributed among the labourers. Those who want gold at any other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> than that of the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a>, search for it in the beds of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, where it is very common. "The French and English have successively been desirous of appropriating to themselves these real or imaginary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>. Some thought they could reach this country by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a>, others by the Salsum. Far from having succeeded in their attempts of becoming masters of this country, they have not yet ascertained its existence. The unsuccessfulness of past efforts hath redoubled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of fainthearted minds; sensible and judicious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> have chosen to limit themselves to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> much more important, which is that of slaves."

BAMFF

Pages 414-414

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the shire of that name in Scotland, is pleasantly situated on the side of a hill, at the mouth of the river Devon. It has several streets; of which that with the town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in it, adorned with a new spire, is very handsome. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was erected into a borough by virtue of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> from Robert II., dated October 7, 1372, endowing it with the same privileges, and putting it on the same footing, with the burgh of Aberdeen; but <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> says it was founded in the reign of Malcolm Canmore. It gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of baron to a branch of the Ogilvie family. The harbour is very bad, as the entrance at the mouth of the Devon is very uncertain, being often flopped by the shifting of the sands, which are continually changing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> storms; the pier is therefore placed on the outside. Much salmon is exported from hence. About Troophead fone kelp is made; and the adventurers pay the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> 50l. per annum for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of collecting the materials. Near the town is a most magnificent seat lately built by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Fife. It lies in a beautiful plain washed by the Devon, the lofty banks of which, clothed with wood on the opposite side, afford a delightful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> to the loit vale beneath. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 5. N. Lat. 57. 40.

BAMIER

Pages 414-414

the name of a plant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. It produces a pyramidal husk, with several compartments, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of a lemon, and filled with musky seeds. This husk dressed with meat is a wholesome food, and has a very agreeable flavour. The Egyptians make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it in their ragouts.

BAMIYAN

Pages 414-415

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Zablestan, 10 days journey from Balkh, and eight from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAZNA">Gazna</a>. It is remarkable only for its dreadful catastrophe when taken by Jenghiz Khan in 1221. At that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the city belonged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> Jalalodin, the last of the famous Mahmud Gazni's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. Jenghiz Khan was at that time about to attack Gazna, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>; but was flopped by the garrison of Gazna, which he had hoped would give him no trouble. In this, however, he was disappointed. The people had for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time expected an attack; and had therefore ruined the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> for five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> six leagues round, while the peasants had carried away the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and every thing that could be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to the besiegers. Accordingly, Accordingly, Jenghiz Khan having erected wooden towers, and planted his engines upon them, was in a short time obliged to give over his attacks till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILLSTONES">millstones</a> and other materials could be brought from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance. The walls of the city were very strong, so that the engines of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOGULS">Moguls</a> made but little <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>; and the garrison making frequent and furious fallies, cut off whole squadrons of their enemies, and frequently overthrew their towers and engines. This exceedingly charmed Jenghiz Khan; who one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> returning from a fruitless attack, and hearing of the defeat of one of his generals by Jalaluddin, swore to be revenged on Bamiyan. This fury cost the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of one of his grandchildren; who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> himself too much, to please his grandfather, was slain with an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>.—At last, however, by the numberless multitude of the Moguls, who <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the attacks without intermission, the city was taken, after its walls had been ruined in many places, and the bravest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> and officers of the garrison slain in its defense. The mother of the young prince who had been killed entering with the troops, and more deserving the name of a fiend than a woman, caused the throats of all the inhabitants to be cut, without excepting one. She even gave orders to rip up the bellies of all the women with child, that not an infant might be left alive. In short, to gratify the rage of this inhuman monster, the buildings were all levelled with the ground; the cattle, and every living creature, destroyed; insomuch that the hardened Moguls themselves gave this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the name of Mauabulig, which in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signifies the unfortunate city. A strong castle has since been built out of its ruins.

BAMOTH-BAAL

Pages 415-415

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of the tribe of Reuben, which seems also to have had a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAAL">Baal</a> on an eminence; lying eastwards, and not far from the river Arnon, and the territory of Moab. Jerome calls it Bamoth, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Amorites, beyond Jordan, in the possession of the sons of Reuben. Whether the same with that mentioned Numb. xxi. is doubtful, from the disagreement of interpreters; and yet we may admit it to be the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of encampment of the Israelites, and of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALAAM">Balaam</a>’s first station, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> where he had the first view of the rear of the people.

BAMPTON

Pages 415-415

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, situated in a bottom surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hills. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 25. N. Lat. 51. 5.

BANARES

Pages 415-415
or Benares, a handsome town of Asia, in the dominions of the Great Mogul, greatly celebrated for its sanctity, and being the university of the Indian Bramins. It is seated on the north side of the river Ganges, in E. Long. 82. 30. N. Lat. 26. 20. See Observatory.

BANBURY

Pages 415-415

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a> in England, situated on the river Charwell, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 20. N. Lat. 52. 0. It sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>.

BANC

Pages 415-415
or Bence, in Law, denotes a tribunal, or judgment-seat; hence king’s banc is the same with the court of king’s bench, and common banc with that of common pleas. BANCI jus, or the privilege of having a bench, was anciently only allowed to the king’s judges, qui summam adminiftrant jufitiam. Inferior courts, as courts-baron, hundred courts, &c. were not allowed that prerogative; and even at this day the hundred-court at Freibridge in Norfolk is held under an oak at Gey-wood; and that of Woolfry in Herefordshire, under an oak near Ashton in that county, called Hundred oak.

BANCA

Pages 415-415

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> in the East Indies, between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORNEO">Borneo</a>; from the first of which it is separated only by a narrow channel. This island is famous on account of its tin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the island, who is also possessor of the territory of Palambang on the river of the same name in Sumatra, where he has his constant residence, had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> with the Dutch by whose troops his authority and independence are preserved, for the tin which he compels his subjects to deliver to him at a low price. Their profit it is said, was not less than 150,000l. annually. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the perfection which the miners had arrived at in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of the ore, the tin of this island was preferred to the tin from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">Canton</a> market. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 105. 10. N. Lat. 13. 25.

BANCALIS

Pages 415-415

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town on the east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>, where the Dutch have a settlement. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 99. 7. N. Lat. 1. 5.

BANCK

Pages 415-415
Peter Vander, an engraver of considerable repute, was born at Paris, and received his instructions in the art from the celebrated Francois de Poilly. He came over into England with Gaspar the painter, about the year 1674; and married the sister of a gentleman of estate in Hertfordshire, named Foster. He was a laborious artist; but the pay he received for his plates being by no means adequate to the time he bestowed upon them, he was reduced to want; and, retiring from business, sought an asylum in the house of his brother-in-law. He died at Bradfield, and was buried in the church there, in 1674; leaving his widow in possession of the chief part of his plates, which he disposed of to Brown, a printeller, to great advantage, and left an easy fortune.—His chief employment was engraving of portraits; and, according to Virtue’s account of this artist published by the Hon. Mr Walpole, he was the first in England who engraved them on so large a scale. But even their novelty, it seems, added to their merit, could not sufficiently recommend them to support the artist. Like many of Poilly’s disciples, his great merit, according to Mr Strutt, consists in the laboured neatness and management of the mechanical part of the art. Freedom, harmony, and chasteness of outline, are by no means the characteristic of his prints. However, though they cannot rank with the superior productions of Edelink or Nantueil, &c. they have their share of merit; and doubtless will be always esteemed in England, as preserving the best resemblance of many eminent persons who were living at that time.

BANCO

Pages 415-415

an Italian word which signifies <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>. It is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used to signify the bank of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>.

BANDAGE

Pages 415-416

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILLET">fillet</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> swath, used in dressing and binding up wounds, restraining dangerous hemorrhagies, and in joining fractured and dislocated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>.

BANDELEER

Pages 416-416
or Bandelear, in Military Affairs, a large leathern belt, thrown over the right shoulder, and hanging under the left arm; worn by the ancient musqueteers, both for the sustaining of their fire-arms, and for the carriage of their musket charges, which being put up in little wooden cases, coated with leather, were hung, to the number of twelve, to each bandaleer.

BANDELET

Pages 416-416
or Bandlet, in Architecture, any little band, or flat moulding, as that which crowns the Doric architrave.

BANDER CONGO

Pages 416-416

a small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, seated on the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 54. 10. N. Lat. 19. 0.

BANDERET

Pages 416-416

a general, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> one of the commanders in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the forces.—This appellation is given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> commanders of the troops of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of Bern in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, where there are four banderets, who command all the forces of that canton.

BANDEROLL

Pages 416-416

a little <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>, in form of a guidon, extended more in length than in breadth, used to be hung out on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> of vessels, &c.

BANDITTI

Pages 416-417

from the Italian bandito; persons proscribed, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as we call it, outlawed: sometimes denominated banniti or foris banniti. It is also a denomination given to highwaymen or robbers who infest the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> in troops, especially in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, France, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. Mr Brydone, in his Tour through Sicily, informs us, that in the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, called Val Demoni, from the devils that are supposed to inhabit Mount Aetna, it has ever been found altogether impracticable to extirpate the banditti; there being numberless caverns and subterraneous pallages round that mountain, where no troops could possibly pursue them: besides, they are known to be perfectly determined and resolute, never failing to take a dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> on all who have offended them. Hence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Villa Franca has embraced it, not only as the safest, but likewise as the wisest and most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> scheme, to become their declared <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> and protector: and such of them as think proper to leave their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and forests, though perhaps only for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, are sure to meet with good encouragement and a certain protection in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, where they enjoy the most unbounded confidence, which, in no instance, they have ever yet been found to make an improper or a dishonest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of. They are clothed in the prince's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> and green, with silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACE">lace</a>; and wear likewise a badge of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> order, which entitles them to universal fear and respect from the people. In some circumstances, these banditti are the most respectable people of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and have by much the highest and most romantic notions of what they call their point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. However criminal they may be with regard to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> in general; yet, with respect to one another, and to every person to whom they have once professed it, they have ever maintained the most unshaken fidelity. The magistrates have often been obliged to protect them, and pay them <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, as they are known to be perfectly determined and desperate, and so extremely vindictive, that they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> certainly put any person to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> that has ever given given them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> cause of provocation. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, it never was known that any person who had put himself under their protection, and showed that he had confidence in them, had cause to repent of it, or was injured by any of them in the most minute trifle; but, on the contrary, they will protect him from impositions of every kind, and scorn to go halves with the landlord, like most other conductors and travelling servants, and will defend him with their lives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there is occasion. Those of their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> who have thus enlisted themselves in the service of society, are known and respected by the other banditti all over the island; and the persons of those who accompany are ever held sacred. For these reasons, most travellers choose to hire a couple of them from town to town; and may thus travel over the whole island in safety.

BANDORA

Pages 417-417

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Salset, on the west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on this side the Ganges. It is separated from the island of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a> by a narrow channel, and subject to the Portuguese. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 72° 30'. N. Lat. 19° 0'.

BANDORE

Pages 417-417

the name of a musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> with strings, resembling a lute, and said to be invented in the fourth year of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, by John Rose, a citizen of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>.

BANDY-LEGS

Pages 417-417

from the French bander, 'to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a>,' a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTORTION">distortion</a> of the legs, when they turn either inward <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> outward on either side; arising from some defect in the birth, or imprudence in the nurse, endeavouring to make a child stand or walk before his legs were strong enough or sustain the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of his body. See Valgus.

BANE

Pages 417-417

signifies destruction <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> overthrow. Thus, "I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the bane of such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>," is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> saying. So, when a person receives a mortal injury by anything, we say, "it was his bane;" and he who is the cause of another man's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, is said to be le bane, i.e., a malefactor. BANFF. See BAMFF.

BANGHIR

Pages 417-417

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHANNON">Shannon</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 5'. N. Lat. 53° 10'.

BANGLE EARS

Pages 417-417

an imperfection in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, remedied in the following manner. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">Place</a> his ears in such a manner as you would have them stand; bind them with two little boards so fast that they cannot stir, and then clip away all the empty wrinkled skin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by the head.

BANGOR

Pages 417-417

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">Down</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster. It is seated on the south shore of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRICK">Carrick</a> Fergus, opposite to the town of that name; and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° N. Lat. 54° 42'.

BANGUE

Pages 417-417

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of opiate, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> throughout the east, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROWNING">drowning</a> cares and inspiring joy.—This by the Persians is called bang; by the Arabs, effrar, corruptly affrar, and affarth; by the Turks, bengizie, and vulgarly called maftack; by the European naturalists, bangue <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hang.—It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of a kind of wild <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, growing in the countries of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>; it differs little, either as to leaf or seed, from our hemp, except in size. Some have mistaken it for a species of althea. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> manners of preparing it, in different countries. Olearius describes the method used in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">Sale</a> tells us, that, among the Arabs, the leaf is made into pills, or conveves. But the most distinct account is that given by Alexander Maurocordato, counsellor and physician of the Ottoman Porte, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Wedelius. According to this author, hangue is made of the leaves of wild hemp, dried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, then ground to powder; put into a pot wherein <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> has been kept; let in an oven till it begin to torrify; then taken out, and pulverized again; thus to be used occasionally, as much at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on the point of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>. Such is the Turkish hangue.—The effects of this drug are, To confound the understanding; fet the imagination loose; induce a kind of folly and forgetfulness, wherein all cares are left, and joy and gaiety take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> thereof. Bangue, in reality, is a succedaneum to wine, and obtains in those countries where Mahometanism is established; which prohibiting the use of that liquor absolutely, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> mulefetans are forced to have recourse to succedanea, to rouse their spirits. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> are opium and this hangue. As to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> among Europeans, that the Turks prepare themselves for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> by a dose of hangue, which roules their courage, and drives them, with eagerness, to certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; Dr Maurocordato affirms us, that it is a popular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>; the Turks think they are then going affrightly to receive the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of martyrdom; and would not, for any consideration, lose the merit of it, which they would do, by eating the hangue, as being held unlawful by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>, among other things which intoxicate. Z z 2 BANIALUCH,

BANGUS

Pages 417-417

THOMAS, a Danish divine, and an elegant Latin writer on the origin of languages and a variety other subjects. He died in 1661.

BANIALUCH

Pages 417-418
or BAGNALUCH, a city of European Turkey, the capital of Bosnia, upon the frontiers of Dalmatia, near the river Scitna. E. Long. 18° 20'. N. Lat. 44° 20'. BANIAN-TREE. See Ficus, Botany Index.

BANIANS

Pages 418-418

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> in the empire of the Mogul, who believe a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEMPSYCHOSIS">metempsychosis</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> therefore eat no living creature, nor kill even noxious animals, but endeavour to release them when in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of others.—The name of Banian is used with some diversity, which has occasioned much confusion, and many mistakes. Sometimes it is taken in a less proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, and extended to all the idolaters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, as contradistinguished from the Mahometans: in which sense, Banians includes the Bramins and other castes. Banians, in a more proper sense, is restrained to a peculiar caste, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tribe, of Indians, whose office or profession is trade and merchandise: in which sense, Banians stand contradistinguished from Bramins, Cutters, and Wyfe, the three other castes into which the Indians are divided. The four castes are absolutely separate as to occupation, relation, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, &c., though all of the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; which is more properly denominated the religion of the Bramins, who make the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> tribe, than of the Banians, who make the mercantile. The proper Banians are called, in the fassler, or book of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, by the name of Shuddery; under which are comprehended all who live after the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, or that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> and transact for others, as brokers; exclusive of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, or artificers, who make another caste, called Wyfe. These Banians have no peculiar sect or religion, unless it be, that two of the eight general precepts given by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> Brahma to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, are, on account of the profession of the Banians, supposed more immediately to relate to them, viz. those which enjoin veracity in their word and dealings, and avoiding all practices of circumvention in buying and selling. Some of the Banians, quitting their profession, and retiring from the world, commence religious, assume a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and devote themselves more immediately to God, under the denomination of Vertea. These, though they do not hereby change their caste, are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> reckoned as bramins of a more devout kind; much as monks in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, though frequently not in orders, are reputed as a more sacred order than the regular clergy. The name Banian imports as much, in the Bramin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> (wherein their law is written), as a people innocent and harmless; void of all guile; so gentle, that they cannot endure to see either a fly or a worm injured; and who, when struck, will patiently bear it, without resisting or returning the blow.—Their mien and appearance is described by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> *, in terms a little precise, but very significant: "A people presented themselves to my eyes clothed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> garments, somewhat low defending; of a goitre and garb, as I may say, maidenly, and well nigh effeminiate; of a countenance shy and somewhat estranged." Gemelli Careri divides the Banians into 22 tribes, all distinct, and not allowed to marry with each other. Lord assures us they are divided into 82 castes or tribes, correspondent to the castes or divisions of the Bramins or priests, under whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> they are as to religious matters; though the generality of the Banians choose to be under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the two Bramin tribes, the Vifalnagranaugers and Vulnagranaugers. The Banians are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> factors, by whom most of the trade of India is managed; in this respect, comparable to the Jews and Armenians, and not behind either, in point of skill and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, in whatever relates to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. Nothing is bought but by their mediation. They seem to claim a kind of jus divinum to the administration of the traffic of the nation, grounded on their sacred books, as the Bramins do that of religion. They are dispersed, for this purpose, through all parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and abound in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, particularly at Isfahan and Gombroon, where many of them are extremely rich, yet not above acting as brokers, where a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> is to be got. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> agents of the English, Dutch, and French East India Companies, are of this nation; they are faithful, and are generally trusted with the cash of those companies in their keeping. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> also as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>, and can give bills of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for most cities in the East Indies. Their form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> in buying and selling is remarkable; being done without words, in the profoundest silence, only by touching each other's fingers: the buyer loosing his panner or girdle, spreads it on his knee, and both he and the seller having their hands underneath, by the intercourse of the fingers, mark the price of pounds, shillings, &c. demanded, offered, and at length agreed on. When the seller takes the buyer's whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, it denotes a thousand; and, as many times as he squeezes it, as many thousand pagodas, or rupees, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> in question, are demanded: when he only takes the five fingers, it denotes five hundred; and when only one, one hundred: taking only half a finger, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>, denotes fifty; the small end of the finger, to the first joint, stands for ten.

BANIE

Pages 418-418

ANTHONY, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICENTIATE">licentiate</a> in laws, member of the academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> and belles lettres, and ecclesiastic of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Clermont in Auvergne; died in November 1741, aged 69. He is principally celebrated for his translation of the Metamorphoses of Ovid, with historical remarks and explanations; which was published in 1732, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, in folio, finely ornamented with copperplates, by Picart; and reprinted at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> 1738, in two vols 4to: and for his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Fables of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">Ancients</a>, explained by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> full of the most important information, which was translated into English, and printed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1741, in 4 vols 8vo.

BANISHMENT

Pages 418-418

exile, among us is of two kinds: the one voluntary, and upon oath; the other by compulsion, for some offence <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> crime. The former properly called abjuration, is now ceased; the latter is chiefly enjoined by judgment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. Yet outlawing and transportation may also be considered as <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of exile.

BANISTER

Pages 418-419

JOHN, a physician and surgeon in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where, says Anthony Wood, he studied logicals for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but afterwards applied himself solely to physic and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>. In 1573 he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bachelor of physic; and, obtaining a license from the university to practice, settled at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, where he lived many years in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> repute, and wrote several medical treatises. BAN <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">Bank</a> treaties. His works were collected and published in 1633, 4to. BANISTERIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BANK

Pages 419-425

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> repository, where many persons agree to keep their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, to be always ready at their call <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; or, certain <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> or communities, who take the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of other people's money, either to improve it, or to keep it secure. The first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of banks was in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where the Lombard Jews kept benches in the market-places for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> of money and bills; and banco being the Italian name for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, banks took their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> from this word. Banks are of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> kinds. 1. One sort is either public, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of moneyed men, who being duly established, and incorporated by the laws of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, agree to deposit a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> stock, to be employed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, as in lending money upon good security, buying and selling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BULLION">bullion</a>, discounting bills of exchange, &c.; or private, i.e., set up by private persons, or partnerships, who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in the same way as the former upon their own single stock and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. The greatest bank of circulation in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> is the Bank of England. The company was incorporated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in the fifth and sixth years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William regulations, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, by the name of The Governors and Company of the Bank of England: in consideration of the loan of 1,200,000l. granted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; for which the subscribers received almost 8 per cent. By this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>, the company are not to borrow under their common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, unless by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament; they are not to trade, or suffer any person in trust for them to trade, in any goods or merchandise; but they may deal in bills of exchange, in buying or selling bullion, and foreign <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, &c. By an act of parliament passed in the 8th and 9th years of William III. they were empowered to enlarge their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> stock to 2,201,771l. 10s. It was then also enacted, that bank-stock should be a personal, and not a real estate; that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> either in word or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> for buying or selling bank-stock, should be good in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, unless registered in the books of the bank within 7 days, and the stock transferred in 14 days; and that it shall be felony, without benefit of clergy, to counterfeit the common seal of the bank, or any sealed bank-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, or any bank-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, or to alter or erase such bills or notes. By another act passed in the 7th of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, the company were empowered to augment their capital to 4,402,343l. and they then advanced 400,000 more to the government; and in 1714, they advanced another loan of 1,500,000l. In the third year of the reign of King George I. the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of their capital stock was reduced to 5 per cent. when the bank agreed to deliver up as many exchequer bills as amounted to 2,000,000l. and to accept an annuity of 100,000l. and it was declared lawful for the bank to call from their members, in proportion to their interests in the capital stock, such sums of money as in a general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> should be found necessary. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any member should neglect to pay his share of the moneys so called for, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> appointed by notice in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> Gazette, and fixed upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Exchange, it should be lawful for the bank, not only to stop the dividend of such member, and to apply it towards payment of the money in question, but also to stop the transfers of the share of such defaulter, and to charge him with an interest of 5 per cent. per annum, for the money so omitted to be paid; and if the principal and interest should be three months unpaid, the bank should then have power to sell so much of the stock belonging to the defaulter as would satisfy the same. After this, the bank reduced the interest of the 2,000,000l. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> to the government, from 5 to 4 per cent. and purchased several other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a>, which were afterwards redeemed by the government, and the national debt due to the bank reduced to 1,600,000l. But in 1742, the company engaged to supply the government with 1,600,000l. at 3 per cent. which is now called the 3 per cent. annuities; so that the government was now indebted to the company 3,200,000l. the one half carrying 4, and the other 3 per cent. In the year 1746, the company agreed that the sum of 986,800l. due to them in the exchequer bills unsatisfied, on the duties for licenses to sell spirituous liquors by retail, should be cancelled, and in lieu thereof to accept of an annuity of 39,442l. the interest of that sum at 4 per cent. The company also agreed to advance the further sum of 1,000,000l. into the exchequer, upon the credit of the duties arising by the malt and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> tax at 4 per cent. for exchequer bills to be issued for that purpose; in consideration of which, the company were enabled to augment their capital with 986,800l. the interest of which, as well as that of the other annuities, was reduced to 3½ per cent. till the 26th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1757, and from that time to carry only 3 per cent. And in order to enable them to circulate the said exchequer bills, they established what is now called bank circulation. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of which may be understood from what follows. The company of the bank are obliged to keep cash sufficient not only to answer the common, but also any extraordinary demand that may be made upon them; and whatever money they have by them, over and above the sum imposed necessary for these purposes, they employ in what may be called the trade of the company; that is to say, in discounting bills of exchange, in buying of gold and silver, and in government securities, &c. But when the bank entered into the above mentioned contract, as they did not keep unemployed a larger sum of money than what they deemed necessary to answer their ordinary and extraordinary demands, they could not conveniently take out of their current cash so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> a sum as a million, with which they were obliged to furnish the government, without either lessening that sum they employed in discounting, buying gold and silver, &c. (which would have been very disadvantageous to them), or inventing some method that should answer all the purposes of keeping the million in cash. The method which they chose, and which fully answers their end, was as follows: They opened a subscription, which they renew annually, for a million of money; wherein the subscribers advance 10 per cent. and enter into a contract to pay the remainder, or any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> thereof, whenever the bank shall call upon them, under penalty of forfeiting the 10 per cent. so advanced; in consideration of which, the bank pays the subscribers 4 per cent. interest for the the money paid in, and \( \frac{1}{4} \) per cent. for the whole sum they agree to furnish; and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> a call shall be made upon them for the whole, or any part thereof, the bank further agrees to pay them at the rate of \( \frac{5}{4} \) per cent. per annum for such sum till they repay it, which they are under an obligation to do at the end of the year. By this means the bank obtains all the purposes of keeping a million of money by them; and though the subscribers, if no call is made upon them (which is in general the case), receive \( \frac{6}{4} \) per cent. for the money they advance, yet the company gains the sum of \( 23,500 \) per annum by the contract; as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear by the following account: The bank receives from the government for the advance of a million \( £30,000 \) The bank pays the subscribers who advance \( 100,000l. \) and engage to pay (when called for) \( 900,000l. \) more \( 6,500 \) The clear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> to the bank thereof is \( 23,500 \) This is the state of the case, provided the company should make no call on the subscribers; which they will be very unwilling to do, because it would not only lessen their profit, but affect the public credit in general. Bank-stock may not improperly be called a trading stock, since with this they deal very largely in foreign gold and silver, in discounting bills of exchange, &c. Besides which, they are allowed by the government very considerable sums annually for the management of the annuities paid at their office. All which advantages render a share in their stock very valuable; though it is not equal in value to the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> stock. The company make dividends of the profits half yearly, of which notice is publicly given; when those who have occasion for their money may readily receive it; but private persons, if they judge convenient, are permitted to continue their funds, and to have their interest added to the principal. This company is under the direction of a governor, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>-governor, and 24 directors, who are annually elected by the general court, in the same manner as in the East India Company. Thirteen, or more, compose a court of directors for managing the affairs of the company. The officers of this company are very numerous. The stability of the bank of England is equal to that of the British government. All that it has advanced to the public must be lost before its creditors can sustain any loss. No other <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANKING">banking</a> company in England can be established by act of parliament, or can consist of more than five members. It acts, not only as an ordinary bank, but (as we have already seen) as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> engine of state; receiving and paying the greater part of the annuities which are due to the creditors of the public; circulating exchequer bills; and advancing to government the annual amount of the land and malt taxes, which are frequently not paid up till some years thereafter. It likewise has, upon several different occasions, supported the credit of the principal houses, not only in England, but of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. Upon one occasion it is said to have advanced for this purpose, in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, about \( 1,600,000l. \) a great part of it in bullion. In Scotland there are two public banks, both at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. The one, called The Bank of Scotland, was established by act of parliament in 1695; the other, called The Royal Bank, by royal charter in 1727. Within these 30 years there have also been erected private banking companies in almost every considerable town, and even in some villages. Hence the business of the country is almost entirely carried on by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> currency, i.e., by the notes of those different banking companies; with which purchases and payments of all kinds are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made. Silver very seldom appears, except in the change of a twenty-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> bank-note, and gold still seldom. But though the conduct of all those different companies has not been unexceptionable, and has accordingly required an act of parliament to regulate it; the country, notwithstanding, has evidently derived great benefit from their trade. It has been asserted, that the trade of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Glasgow doubled in about 15 years after the first erection of the banks there; and that the trade of Scotland has more than quadrupled since the first erection of the two public banks at Edinburgh. Whether the trade, either of Scotland in general, or of the city of Glasgow in particular, has really increased in so great a proportion, during so short a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, we do not pretend to know. If either of them has increased in this proportion, it seems to be an effect too great to be accounted for by the sole operation of this cause. That the trade and industry of Scotland, however, have increased very considerably during this period, and that the banks have contributed a good deal to this increase, cannot be doubted. The value of the silver money which circulated in Smith's Scotland before the Union in 1707, and which immediately after it was brought into the bank of Scotland Nations, in order to be recoined, amounted to \( 411,117l. 10s. 9d. \) <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>. No account has been got of the gold coin; but it appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> accounts of the mint of Scotland, that the value of the gold annually coined somewhat exceeded that of the silver. There were a good many people too upon this occasion, who, from a diffidence of repayment, did not bring their silver into the bank of Scotland; and there was, besides, some English coin, which was not called in. The whole value of the gold and silver, therefore, which circulated in Scotland before the Union, cannot be estimated at less than a million Sterling. It seems to have constituted almost the whole circulation of that country; for though the circulation of the bank of Scotland, which had then no rival, was considerable, it seems to have made but a very small part of the whole. In the present times, the whole circulation of Scotland cannot be estimated at less than two millions, of which that part which consists of gold and silver most probably does not amount to half a million. But though the circulating gold and silver of Scotland have suffered to great a diminution during this period, its real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> and prosperity do not appear to have suffered any. Its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and trade, on the contrary, the annual produce of its land and labour, have evidently been augmented. It is chiefly by discounting bills of exchange, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCOUNT">Discount</a> is, by advancing money upon them before they are due, that the greater part of banks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a> issue their promissory notes. They deduct always upon whatever ever sum they advance, the legal interest till the bill shall become due. The payment of the bill, when it becomes due, replaces to the bank the value of what had been advanced, together with a clear profit of the interest. The banker, who advances to the merchant whose bill he discounts not gold and silver, but his own promissory notes, has the advantage of being able to discount to a greater amount, by the whole value of his promissory notes, which he finds by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> are commonly in circulation. He is thereby enabled to make his clear gain of interest on so much larger a sum. The commerce of Scotland, which at present is not very great, was still more inconsiderable when the two first banking companies were established; and those companies would have had but little trade, had they confined their business to the discounting of bills of exchange. They invented, therefore, another method of issuing their promissory notes, by granting what they called cash accounts; that is, by giving credit to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of a certain sum (200l. or 300l. for example), to any individual who could procure two persons of undoubted credit and good landed estate to become surety for him, that whatever money should be advanced to him within the sum for which the credit had been given should be repaid upon demand, together with the legal interest. Credits of this kind are commonly granted by banks and bankers in all different parts of the world. But the easy terms on which the Scots banking companies accept of repayment are peculiar to them, and have perhaps been the principal cause, both of the great trade of those companies and of the benefit which the country has received from it. Whoever has a credit of this kind with one of those companies, and borrows 100l. upon it, for example, may repay this sum piecemeal, by 20l. and 30l. at a time, the company discounting a proportionate part of the interest of the great sum from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> on which each of those small sums is paid in, till the whole be in this manner repaid. All <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, therefore, and almost all men of business, find it convenient to keep such cash-accounts with them; and are thereby interested to promote the trade of those companies, by readily receiving their notes in all payments, and by encouraging all those with whom they have any influence to do the same. The banks, when their customers apply to them for money, generally advance it to them in their own promissory notes. These the merchants pay away to the manufacturers for goods, the manufacturers to the farmers for materials and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, the farmers to their landlords for rent, the landlords repay them to the merchants for the conveniences and luxuries with which they supply them, and the merchants again return them to the banks in order to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> their cash-accounts, or to replace what they may have borrowed of them; and thus almost the whole money-business of the country is transacted by means of them. Hence the great trade of those companies. By means of those cash-accounts, every merchant can, without imprudence, carry on a greater trade than he otherwise could do. If there are two merchants, one in London and the other in Edinburgh, who employ equal stocks in the same branch of trade, the Edinburgh merchant can, without imprudence, carry on a greater trade, and give employment to a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people, than the London merchant. The London merchant must always keep by him a considerable sum of money, either in his own coffers, or in those of his banker (who gives him no interest for it), in order to answer the demands continually coming upon him for payment of the goods which he purchases upon credit. Let the ordinary amount of this sum be supposed 500l. The value of the goods in his warehouse must always be less by 500l. than it would have been, had he not been obliged to keep such a sum unemployed. Let us suppose that he generally disposes of his whole stock upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, or of goods to the value of his whole stock upon hand, once in the year. By being obliged to keep such a great sum unemployed, he must sell in a year 500l. worth less goods than he might otherwise have done. His annual profits must be less by all that he could have made by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of 500l. worth more goods; and the number of people employed in preparing his goods for the market, must be less by all those that 500l. more stock could have employed. The merchant in Edinburgh, on the other hand, keeps no money unemployed for answering such occasional demands. When they actually come upon him, he satisfies them from his cash-account with the bank, and gradually replaces the sum borrowed with the money or paper which comes in from the occasional sales of his goods. With the same stock, therefore, he can, without imprudence, have at all times in his warehouse a larger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of goods than the London merchant; and can thereby both make a greater profit himself, and give constant employment to a greater number of industrious people who prepare those goods for the market. Hence the great benefit which the country has derived from this trade. The late multiplication of banking companies in both parts of the united <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, an event by which many people have been much alarmed, instead of diminishing, increases the security of the public. It obliges all of them to be more circumspect in their conduct, and, by not extending their currency beyond its due proportion to their cash, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> themselves against those malicious runs which the rivalryship of so many competitors is always ready to bring upon them. It restrains the circulation of each particular company within a narrower circle, and reduces their circulating notes to a smaller number. By dividing the whole circulation into a greater number of parts, the failure of any one company, an accident which, in the course of things, must sometimes happen, becomes of less <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to the public. This free competition too obliges all bankers to be more liberal in their dealings with their customers, lest their rivals should carry them away. In general, if any branch of trade, or any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of labour, be advantageous to the public, the freer and more general the competition, it will always be the more so. See further, the article <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAPER_MONEY">Paper-money</a>. 2. The other kind of banks consist of such as are instituted wholly on the public account, and are called deposit. Banks of Deposit; the nature of which not being generally understood, the following particular explanation may not be unacceptable. The currency of a great state, such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, generally generally consists almost entirely of its own coin. Should this currency, therefore, be at any time worn, clipped, or otherwise degraded below its standard value, the state by a reformation of its coin can effectually re-establish its currency. But the currency of a small state, such as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a> or Hamburg, can seldom consist altogether in its own coin, but must be made up, in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, of the coins of all the neighbouring states with which its inhabitants have a continual intercourse. Such a state, therefore, by reforming its coin, will not always be able to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> its currency. If foreign bills of exchange are paid in this currency, the uncertain value of any sum, of what is in its own nature so uncertain, must render the exchange always very much against such a state, its currency being, in all foreign states, necessarily valued even below what it is worth. In order to remedy the inconvenience to which this disadvantageous exchange must have subjected their merchants, such small states, when they began to attend to the interest of trade, have frequently enacted, that foreign bills of exchange of a certain value should be paid, not in common currency, but by an order upon, or by a transfer in, the books of a certain bank, established upon the credit and under the protection of the state; this bank being always obliged to pay, in good and true money, exactly according to the standard of the state. The banks of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, Genoa, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, Hamburg, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a>, seem to have been all originally established with this view, though some of them may have afterwards been made subservient to other purposes. The money of such banks, being better than the common currency of the country, necessarily bore an agio, which was greater or smaller, according as the currency was supposed to be more or less degraded below the standard of the state. The agio of the bank of Hamburg, for example, which is said to be commonly about 14 per cent., is the supposed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the good standard money of the state, and the clipped, worn, and diminished currency poured into it from all the neighbouring states. Before 1659, the great quantity of clipped and worn foreign coin, which the extensive trade of Amsterdam brought from all parts of Europe, reduced the value of its currency about 9 per cent. below that of good money fresh from the mint. Such money no sooner appeared, that it was melted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> or carried away, as it always is in such circumstances. The merchants, with plenty of currency, could not always find a sufficient quantity of good money to pay their bills of exchange; and the value of those bills, in spite of several regulations which were made to prevent it, became in a great measure uncertain. In order to remedy these inconveniences, a bank was established in 1659 under the guarantee of the city. The bank received both foreign coin, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and worn coin of the country, at its real and intrinsic value in the good standard money of the country, deducting only so much as was necessary for defraying the expense of coining, and other necessary expense of management. For the value which remained after this small deduction was made, it gave a credit in its books. This credit was called bank-money; which, as it represented money exactly according to the standard of the mint, was always of the same real value, and intrinsically worth more than current money. It was at the same time enacted, that all bills drawn upon or negociated at Amsterdam of the value of 600 guilders and upwards should be paid in bank-money, which at once took away all uncertainty in the value of those bills. Every merchant, in consequence of this regulation, was obliged to keep an account with the bank in order to pay his foreign bills of exchange, which necessarily occasioned a certain demand for bank-money. Bank-money, over and above both its intrinsic superiority to currency, and the additional value which this demand necessarily gives it, has likewise some other advantages. It is secure from fire, robbery, and other accidents; the city of Amsterdam is bound for it; it can be paid away by a simple transfer, without the trouble of counting, or the risk of transporting it from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another. In consequence of these different advantages, it seems from the beginning to have borne an agio; and it is generally believed that all the money originally deposited in the bank was allowed to remain there, nobody caring to demand payment of a debt which he could sell for a premium in the market. Besides, this money could not be brought from those coffer, as it will appear by and by, without previously paying for the keeping. Those deposits of coin, or which the bank was bound to restore in coin, constituted the original capital of the bank, or the whole value of what was represented by what is called bank-money. At present they are supposed to constitute but a very small part of it. In order to facilitate the trade in bullion, the bank has been for these many years in the practice of giving credit in its books upon deposits of gold and silver bullion. This credit is generally about 5 per cent. below the mint price of such bullion. The bank grants at the same time what is called a receipt or receipt, entitling the person who makes the deposit, or the bearer, to take out the bullion again at any time within six months, upon re-transferring to the bank a quantity of bank-money equal to that for which credit had been given in its books when the deposit was made, and upon paying ½ per cent. for the keeping if the deposit was in silver, and ¼ per cent. if it was in gold; but at the same time declaring, that in default of such payment, and upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, the deposit should belong to the bank at the price at which it had been received, or for which credit had been given in the transfer books. What is thus paid for the keeping of the deposit may be considered as a sort of warehouse-rent; and why this warehouse-rent should be so much dearer for gold than for silver, several different reasons have been assigned. The fineness of gold, it has been said, is more difficult to be ascertained than that of silver. Frauds are more easily practised, and occasion a greater loss in the more precious metal. Silver, besides, being the standard metal, the state, it has been said, wishes to encourage more the making of deposits of silver than those of gold. Deposits of bullion are most commonly made when the price is somewhat lower than ordinary; and they are taken out again when it happens to rise. In Holland the market price of bullion is generally above the mint price, for the same reason that it was so in England before the late reformation of the gold coin. The difference is said to be commonly from about five to fifteen... sixteen flivers upon the mark, or eight ounces of silver of eleven parts fine and one part alloy. The bank-price, or the credit which the bank gives for deposits of such silver (when made in foreign coin, of which the fineness is well known and ascertained, such as <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> dollars), is 22 gilders the mark; the mint-price is about 23 gilders; and the market-price is from 23 gilders five flivers to 23 gilders ten flivers, or from 2 to 3 per cent. above the mint-price. The proportions between the bank-price, the mint-price, and the market-price, of gold bullion, are nearly the same. A person can generally tell his receipt for the difference between the mint-price of bullion and the market-price. A receipt for bullion is almost always worth something; and it very seldom happens, therefore, that anybody suffers his receipt to expire, or allows his bullion to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to the bank at the price at which it had been received, either by not taking it out before the end of the six months, or by neglecting to pay the 1/4 or 1/2 per cent. in order to obtain a new receipt for another six months. This, however, though it seldom happens, is said to happen sometimes, and more frequently with regard to gold than with regard to silver, on account of the higher warehouse-rent which is paid for the keeping of the more precious metal. The person who by making a deposit of bullion obtains both a bank-credit and a receipt, pays his bills of exchange as they become due with his bank-credit; and either sells or keeps his receipt, according as he judges that the price of bullion is likely to rise or to fall. The receipt and the bank-credit seldom keep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> together, and there is no occasion that they should. The person who has a receipt, and who wants to take out bullion, finds always plenty of bank-credits, or bank-money, to buy at the ordinary price; and the person who has bank-money, and wants to take out bullion, finds receipts always in equal abundance.
