The owners of bank-credits and the holders of receipts constitute two different sorts of creditors against the bank. The holder of a receipt cannot draw out the bullion for which it is granted, without re-affirming to the bank a sum of bank-money equal to the price at which the bullion had been received. If he has no bank-money of his own, he must purchase it of those who have it. The owner of bank-money cannot draw out bullion without producing to the bank receipts for the quantity which he wants. If he has none of his own, he must buy them of those who have them. The holder of a receipt, when he purchases bank-money, purchases the power of taking out a quantity of bullion, of which the mint-price is 5 per cent. above the bank-price. The agio of 5 per cent., therefore, which he commonly pays for it, is paid, not for an imaginary, but for a real value. The owner of bank-money, when he purchases a receipt, purchases the power of taking out a quantity of bullion, of which the market-price is commonly from 2 to 3 per cent. above the mint-price. The price which he pays for it, therefore, is paid likewise for a real value. The price of the receipt, and the price of the bank-money, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> or make up between them the full value or price of the bullion. Upon deposits of the coin current in the country, the bank grants receipts likewise as well as bank-credits; but those receipts are frequently of no value, and will bring no price in the market. Upon ducatoons, for example, which in the currency <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for three gilders three flivers each, the bank gives a credit of three gilders only, or 5 per cent. below their current value. It grants a receipt likewise entitling the bearer to take out the number of ducatoons deposited at any time within six months, upon paying 1/4 per cent. for the keeping. This receipt will frequently bring no price in the market. Three gilders bank-money generally fell in the market for three gilders three flivers, the full value of the ducatoons if they were taken out of the bank; and before they can be taken out; 1/4 per cent. must be paid for the keeping, which would be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> loss to the holder of the receipt. If the agio of the bank, however, should at any time fall to 3 per cent., such receipts might bring some price in the market, and might sell for 1 1/2 per cent. But the agio of the bank being now generally about 5 per cent. such receipts are frequently allowed to expire, or, as they express it, to fall to the bank. The 5 per cent. which the bank gains, when deposits either of coin or bullion are allowed to fall to it, may be considered as the warehouse rent for the perpetual keeping of such deposits. The sum of bank-money for which the receipts are expired must be very considerable. It must comprehend the whole original capital of the bank, which, it is generally supposed, has been allowed to remain there from the time it was first deposited, nobody caring either to renew his receipt or to take out his deposit, as, for the reasons already assigned, neither the one nor the other could be done without loss. But whatever may be the amount of this sum, the proportion which it bears to the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of bank-money is supposed to be very small. The bank of Amsterdam has for these many years past been the great warehouse of Europe for bullion, for which the receipts are very seldom allowed to expire, or, as they express it, to fall to the bank. The far greater part of the bank-money, or of the credits upon the books of the bank, is supposed to have been created, for these many years past, by such deposits which the dealers in bullion are continually both making and withdrawing. No demand can be made upon the bank but by means of a receipt or receipt. The smaller mass of bank-money, for which the receipts are expired, is mixed and confounded with the much greater mass for which they are still in force; so that, though there may be a considerable sum of bank-money for which there are no receipts, there is no specific sum or portion of it which may not at any time be demanded by one. The bank cannot be debtor to two persons for the same thing; and the owner of bank-money who has no receipt cannot demand payment of the bank till he buys one. In ordinary and quiet times, he can find no difficulty in getting one to buy at the market-price, which generally corresponds with the price at what he can sell the coin or bullion it entitles him to take out of the bank. It might be otherwise during a public calamity: an invasion, for example, such as that of the French in 1672. The owners of bank-money being then all eager to draw it out of the bank, in order to have it in their own keeping, the demand for receipts might raise their price to an exorbitant height. The holders of them Bank might form extravagant expectations, and instead of 2 or 5 per cent. demand half the bank-money for which credit had been given upon the deposits that the receipts had respectively been granted for. The enemy, informed of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the bank, might even buy them up in order to prevent the carrying away of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>. In such emergencies, the bank, it is supposed, would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> through its ordinary rule of making payment only to the holders of receipts. The holders of receipts, who had no bank-money, must have received within 2 or 3 per cent. of the value of the deposit for which their respective receipts had been granted. The bank, therefore, it is said, would in this case make no scruple of paying, either with money or bullion, the full value of what the owners of bank-money who could get no receipts were credited for in its books; paying at the same time 2 or 3 per cent. to such holders of receipts as had no bank-money, that being the whole value which in this state of things could justly be supposed due to them. Even in ordinary and quiet times it is the interest of the holders of receipts to depress the agio, in order either to buy bank-money (and consequently the bullion which their receipts would then enable them to take out of the bank) so much cheaper, or to sell their receipts to those who have bank-money, and who want to take out bullion, so much dearer; the price of a receipt being generally equal to the difference between the market-price of bank-money and that of the coin or bullion for which the receipt had been granted. It is the interest of the owners of bank-money, on the contrary, to raise the agio, in order either to sell their bank-money so much dearer, or to buy a receipt so much cheaper. To prevent the stock-jobbing tricks which those opposite interests might sometimes occasion, the bank has of late years come to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to sell at all times bank-money for currency, at 5 per cent. agio, and to buy it again at 4 per cent. agio. In consequence of this resolution, the agio can never either rise above 5 or sink below 4 per cent., and the proportion between the market-price of the bank and that of current money is kept at all times very near to the proportion between their intrinsic values. Before this resolution was taken, the market-price of money used sometimes to rise to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as 9 per cent. agio, and sometimes to sink so low as par, according as opposite interests happened to influence the market. The bank of Amsterdam professes to lend out no part of what is deposited with it, but, for every gilder for which it gives credit in its books, to keep in its repositories the value of a gilder either in money or bullion. That it keeps in its repositories all the money or bullion for which there are receipts in force, for which it is at all times liable to be called upon, and which, in reality, is continually going from it and returning to it again, cannot well be doubted. But whether it does so likewise with regard to that part of its capital for which the receipts are long ago expired, for which in ordinary and quiet times it cannot be called upon, and which in reality is very likely to remain with it forever, or as long as the States of the United Provinces subsist, may appear perhaps more uncertain. At Amsterdam, however, no part of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> is better established, than that for every gilder circulated as bank-money there is a correspondent gilder in gold and silver to be found in the treasure of the bank. The city is guaranteed that it should be so. The bank is under the direction of the four reigning burgomasters, who are changed every year. Each new set of burgomasters visits the treasure, compares it with the books, receives it upon oath, and delivers it over, with the same awful solemnity, to the set which succeeds it; and in that sober and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> country <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> are not yet disregarded. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> of this kind seems alone a sufficient security against any practices which cannot be avowed. Amidst all the revolutions which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> has ever occasioned in the government of Amsterdam, the prevailing party has at no time accused their predecessors of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a> in the administration of the bank. No <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> could have affected more deeply the reputation and fortune of the disgraced party; and if such an accusation could have been supported, we may be assured that it would have been brought. In 1672, when the French king was at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, the bank of Amsterdam paid to readily as left no doubt of the fidelity with which it had observed its engagements. Some of the pieces which were then brought from its repositories appeared to have been scorched with the fire which happened in the town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> soon after the bank was established. Those pieces, therefore, must have lain there from that time. What may be the amount of the treasure in the bank is a question which has long employed the speculations of the curious. Nothing but conjecture can be offered concerning it. It is generally reckoned, that there are about 2000 people who keep accounts with the bank; and allowing them to have, one with another, the value of 1500l. lying upon their respective accounts (a very large allowance), the whole quantity of bank-money, and consequently of treasure in the bank, will amount to 3,000,000l. or, at 11 gilders the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> Sterling, 33,000,000 of gilders; a great sum, and sufficient to carry on a very extensive circulation, but vastly below the extravagant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> which some people have formed of this treasure. The city of Amsterdam derives a considerable revenue from the bank. Besides what may be called the warehousrent above-mentioned, each person, upon first opening an account with the bank, pays a fee of 10 gilders; and for every new account, 3 gilders 3 florins; for every transfer, 2 florins; and if the transfer is for less than 300 gilders, 6 florins; in order to discourage the multiplicity of small transactions. The person who neglects to balance his accounts twice in the year forfeits 25 gilders. The person who orders a transfer for more than is upon his account, is obliged to pay 3 per cent. for the sum overdraft, and his order is set aside into the bargain. The bank is supposed, too, to make a considerable profit by the sale of the foreign coin or bullion which sometimes falls to it by the expiring of receipts, and which is always kept till it can be sold with advantage. It makes a profit likewise by selling bank-money at 5 per cent. agio, and buying it in at 4. These different emoluments amount to a good deal more than what is necessary for paying the salaries of officers, and defraying the expense of management. What is paid for the keeping of bullion upon receipts, is alone supposed to amount to a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a> annual revenue of between 150,000 and 200,000 gilders. Public utility, however, and not revenue, was the original object of this BANK Banker's object was to relieve the merchants from the inconvenience of a disadvantageous exchange. The revenue which has arisen from it was unforeseen, and may be considered as accidental. Bank, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> affairs, denotes an elevation of the ground or bottom of the sea, so as sometimes to surmount the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or at least to leave the water so shallow as usually not to allow a vessel to remain afloat over it.—In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, bank amounts to much the same as flat, shoal, &c. There are banks of sand, and others of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, called also shelves, or rocks. In the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> sea they also speak of banks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, which are large pieces of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> floating.

BANKER

Pages 425-425

a person who traffics and negotiates in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; who receives and remits money from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> from correspondents, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by means of bills or letters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a> were called argentarii, and nummularii; by the Greeks, ἀργυραῖοι, κόλλαβοι, and ἀγγελοποιοι. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> business was to put out the money of private persons to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>; they had their boards and benches, for this purpose, in all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> and public places, where they took in the money from some to lend it to others.

BANKING

Pages 425-425

the making of banks to oppose the force of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, and secure the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> from being overflowed thereby. With respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> which is to be kept out, this is called banking; with respect to the land, which is hereby to be defended, embanking. Banking is also applied to the keeping a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, or the employment of a banker. Banking, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies the trading in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, or remitting it from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place, by means of bills of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. This answers to what the French call faire la banque. In France, every body is allowed to bank, whether merchant or not; even foreigners are indulged in this kind of traffic. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, banking does not derogate from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, especially in the republican states; whence it is, that most of the younger sons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> families engage in it. In reality, it was the nobility of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, that, for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a> in the other countries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

BANKISH

Pages 425-427

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Mogul's dominions, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, lying southwest of the province of Caffinere. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKRUPT">Bankrupt</a>, (hancus ruptus), is so called, because, when the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stock is broken or exhausted, the owner is said to be a bankrupt. And this word bankrupt is derived from the French banqueroute, which signifies a breaking or failing in the world: banque in French is as much as mensa in Latin, and route is the same as velfigium; and this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is said to have been taken originally from the Roman mensaria, which were set in public places; and when a tradesman flipped away, with an intention to deceive his creditors, he left only some velfigia or signs of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> or shop behind him. But a bankrupt with us, from the several descriptions given of him in our statute-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, may be defined "a trader, who feigns himself, or does certain acts tending to defraud his creditors." For the better understanding of this article, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be proper to consider, 1. Who may become a bankrupt. 2. What acts make a bankrupt. 3. The proceedings on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of bankruptcy: and, 4. In what manner an estate in goods and chattels may be transferred by bankruptcy. —But of these, the two last being treated under the article Commission of Bankruptcy, the two first only belong to this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. 1. A bankrupt was formerly considered merely in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of a criminal or offender; and in this spirit we are told by Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>, that we have fetched as well the name, as the wickedness, of bankrupts from foreign nations. But at present the laws of bankruptcy are considered as laws calculated for the benefit of trade, and founded on the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> as well as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; and to that end they confer some privileges not only on the creditors, but also on the bankrupt or debtor himself. On the creditors; by compelling the bankrupt to give up all his effects to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, without any fraudulent concealment: on the debtor, by exempting him from the rigour of the general law, whereby his person might be confined at the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of his creditor, though in reality he has nothing to satisfy the debt; whereas the law of bankrupts, taking into consideration the sudden and unavoidable accidents to which men in trade are liable, has given them the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of their persons, and some pecuniary emoluments, upon condition they surrender up their whole estate to be divided among their creditors. In this respect our legislature seems to have attended to the example of the Roman law. We <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> not the Blackstone law of the twelve tables, whereby the creditors Comm. II. might cut the debtor's body into pieces, and each of them take his proportionable share: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> indeed that law, de debito in partes secando, is to be understood in so very butcherly a light; which many learned men have with reason doubted. Nor do we mean those less inhuman laws (if they may be called so, as their meaning is indubitably certain), of imprisoning the debtor's person in chains; subjecting him to stripes and hard labour, at the mercy of his rigid creditor; and sometimes selling him, his wife, and children, to perpetual foreign <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> trans Tiberim (a): an oppression which produced so many popular insurrections, and secessions to the mons facer. But we mean the law of cession, introduced by the Christian emperors; whereby, if a debtor ceded or yielded up all his fortune to his creditors, he was secured from being dragged to a gaol, "omni quoque corporali cruciati fero." For, as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> justly observes, "inhumanum est stipulationem fortunis suis in folium damnari." Thus far was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and reasonable: but as the departing from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> is apt to produce its opposite, we find it afterwards enacted, that if the debtor by any unforeseen accident was reduced to low circumstances, and would swear that he had not sufficient left to pay his debts, he should not be compelled to cede or give up even that (a) In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEGU">Pegu</a>, and the adjacent countries in the East Indies, the creditor is entitled to dispose of the debtor himself, and likewise of his wife and children; insomuch, that he may even violate with impunity the chastity of the debtor's wife; but then, by so doing, the debt is understood to be discharged. Bankrupt, which he had in his possession; a law which, under a false notion of humanity, seems to be fertile of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>, injustice, and absurdity. The laws of England, more wisely, have steered in the middle between both extremes: providing at once against the inhumanity of the creditor, who is not suffered to confine an honest bankrupt after his effects are delivered up; and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> taking care that all his just debts shall be paid, so far as the effects will extend. But still they are cautious of encouraging prodigality and extravagance by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> to debtors: and therefore they allow the benefit of the laws of bankruptcy to none but actual traders; since that set of men are, generally speaking, the only persons liable to accidental losses, and to an inability of paying their debts, without any fault of their own. If persons in other situations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> run in debt without the power of payment, they must take the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their own indiscretion, even though they meet with sudden accidents that may reduce their fortunes: for the law holds it to be an unjustifiable practice, for any person but a trader to encumber himself with debts of any considerable value. If a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, or one in a liberal profession, at the time of contracting his debts, has a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> to pay them, the delay of payment is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of dishonesty, and a temporary injustice to his creditors: and if, at such time, he has not sufficient fund, the dishonesty and injustice is the greater. He cannot therefore murmur, if he suffers the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> which he has voluntarily drawn upon himself. But in mercantile transactions the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is far otherwise. Trade cannot be carried on without mutual <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> on both sides; the contracting of debts is therefore here not only justifiable but necessary. And if, by accidental calamities, as by the loss of a ship in a tempest, the failure of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-traders, or by the non-payment of persons out of trade, a merchant or trader becomes incapable of discharging his own debts, it is his misfortune and not his fault. To the misfortunes therefore of debtors, the law has given a compassionate remedy, but denied it to their faults: since, at the same time that it provides for the security of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, by enacting that every considerable trader may be declared a bankrupt, for the benefit of his creditors as well as himself, it has also, to discourage extravagance, declared that no one shall be capable of being made a bankrupt, but only a trader; nor capable of receiving the full benefit of the statutes, but only an industrious trader. In the interpretation of the several statutes made concerning English bankrupts, it hath been held, that buying only, or selling only, will not qualify a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to be a bankrupt; but it must be both buying and selling, and also getting a livelihood by it: as, by exercising the calling of a merchant, a grocer, a Mercer, or, in one general word, a Chapman, who is one that buys and sells anything. But no handicraft occupation (where nothing is bought or sold, and therefore an extensive credit, for the stock in trade, is not necessary to be had) will make a man a regular bankrupt; as that of a husbandman, a gardener, and the like, who are paid for their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> and labour. Also an innkeeper cannot, as such, be a bankrupt: for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> or livelihood does not arise from buying and selling in the way of merchandise, but greatly from the use of his rooms and furniture, his attendance, and the Bankrupt-like; and though he may buy corn and victuals, to sell again at a profit, yet that no more makes him a trader, than a schoolmaster or other person is, that keeps a boarding-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and makes considerable gains by buying and selling what he spends in the house, and such a one is clearly not within the statutes. But where persons buy goods, and make them up into saleable commodities, as shoemakers, smiths, and the like; here, though part of the gain is by bodily labour, and not by buying and selling, yet they are within the statutes of bankrupts; for the labour is only in melioration of the commodity, and rendering it more fit for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. 2. To learn what the acts of bankruptcy are which render a man a bankrupt, we must consult the several statutes, and the resolutions formed by the courts thereon. Among these may therefore be reckoned, 1. Departing from the realm, whereby a man withdraws himself from the jurisdiction and coercion of the law, with an intent to defraud his creditors. 2. Departing from his own house, with an intent to secrete himself and avoid his creditors. 3. Keeping in his own house, privately (except for just and necessary cause), so as not to be seen or spoken with by his creditors; which is likewise construed to be an intention to defraud his creditors, by avoiding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of the law. 4. Procuring or suffering himself willingly to be arrested, or outlawed, or imprisoned, without just and lawful cause; which is likewise deemed an attempt to defraud his creditors. 5. Procuring his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, goods, chattels, and effects, to be attached or sequestrated by any legal process; which is another plain and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> endeavour to disappoint his creditors of their security. 6. Making any fraudulent conveyance to a friend, or secret trustee, of his lands, tenements, goods, or chattels: which is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the same culpable <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with the last. 7. Procuring any protection, not being himself privileged by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, in order to screen his person from arrests; which also is an endeavour to elude the justice of the law. 8. Endeavouring, or desiring, by any petition to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> exhibited in any of the king's courts against any creditors, to compel them to take less than their just debts; or to procrastinate the time of payment, originally contracted for; which are an acknowledgment of either his poverty or his knavery. 9. Living in prison for two months, or more, upon <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> or other detention for debt, without finding bail, in order to obtain his liberty. For the inability to procure bail argues a strong deficiency in his credit, owing either to his suspected poverty, or ill character; and his neglect to do it, if able, can arise only from a fraudulent intention: in either of which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> time for his creditors to look to themselves, and compel a distribution of his effects. 10. Escaping from prison after an arrest for a just debt of 100l. or upwards. For no man would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> prison, that was able and desirous to procure bail; which brings it within the reason of the last case. 11. Neglecting to make satisfaction for any just debt to the amount of 100l. within two months after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of legal process, for such debt, upon any trader having privilege of parliament. These are the several acts of bankruptcy expressly defined by the statutes relating to this article; which being being so numerous, and the whole law of bankrupts being an innovation on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, our courts of justice have been tender of extending or multiplying acts of bankruptcy by any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> or implication. And therefore Sir John <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLT">Holt</a> held, that a man's removing his goods privately to prevent their being feized in execution, was no act of bankruptcy. For the statutes mention only fraudulent gifts to third persons, and procuring them to be seized by them processes, in order to defraud creditors: but this, though a palpable fraud, yet, falling within neither of those cases, cannot be adjudged an act of bankruptcy. So also it has been determined expressly, that a banker's stopping or refusing payment is no act of bankruptcy: for it is not within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of any of the statutes; and there may be good reasons for his doing so, as suspicion of forgery, and the like: and if, in consequence of such refusal, he is arrested, and puts in bail, still it is no act of bankruptcy; but if he goes to prison, and lies there two months, then, and not before, is he become a bankrupt. As to the consequences resulting from the unhappy situation of a bankrupt, see the article Commission of Bankruptcy.

BANKS

Pages 427-427

JOHN, a dramatic writer, was bred to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of Gray's Inn; but this profession not suiting his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> disposition, he quitted it for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>. Here, however, he found his rewards by no means adequate to his deserts. His emoluments at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> were precarious, and the various successes of his pieces too frequently convinced him of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in his choice. This, however, did not prevent him from pursuing with cheerfulness the path he had taken; his thirst of fame, and warmth of poetic enthusiasm, alleviating to his imagination many disagreeable circumstances into which indigence, the too frequent attendant on poetical pursuits, frequently threw him. His turn was entirely to tragedy; his merit in which is of a peculiar kind. For at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> must be confessed to be extremely unpoetical, and his numbers uncouth and unharmorous; nay, even his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> very far from being strongly marked <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> distinguished, and his episodes extremely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>: yet it is impossible to avoid being deeply affected at the representation, and even at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, of his tragic pieces. This is owing in the general to a happy choice of his subjects; which are all borrowed from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, either real or romantic; and indeed the most of them from circumstances in the annals of our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which, not only from their being familiar to our continual recollection, but even from their having some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of relation to ourselves, we are apt to receive with a kind of partial prepossession, and a pre-determination to be pleased. He has constantly chosen as the basis of his plays such tales as were in themselves and their well-known catastrophes most truly adapted to the purposes of the drama. He has indeed but little varied from the strictness of historical facts; yet he seems to have made it his constant rule to keep the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> perpetually alive, and never suffer his characters to droop. His <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> is not <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, but prose run mad. Yet <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> the false gem sometimes approach so near in glitter to the true one, at least in the eyes of all but real connoisseurs (and how small a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of an audience are to be ranked in this class! it will need no ghost to inform us,) that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOMBAST">bombast</a> will frequently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for the true sublime; and where it is rendered the vehicle of incidents in themselves affecting, and in which the heart is apt to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> itself, it will perhaps be found to have a stronger power on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> passions than even that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> to which it is in reality no more than a bare succedaneum. And from these principles it is that we must account for Mr Banks's writings having in the general drawn more tears from, and excited more terror in, even judicious audiences, than those of much more correct and more truly poetical authors. The tragedies he has left behind him are, 1. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBION">Albion</a> Queens. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. 3. Destruction of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>. 4. Innocent Usurper. 5. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a> Queens. This is only the Albion Queens altered. 6. Rival Kings. 7. Virtue Betrayed. 8. Unhappy Favourite. The Albion Queens was rejected by the managers in 1684; but was acted by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s command in 1706, with great applause, and has been several times revived. The Unhappy Favourite <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till very lately a flock tragedy at the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>; but gives way at present to the latter tragedies from the same story, by Jones and Brooke.—Neither the time of the birth, nor that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, of this author, are ascertained. His remains, however, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> interred in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St James's, Westminster.

BANKS'S ISLAND

Pages 427-427

a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, discovered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook in 1770, in S. Lat. 53° 32'. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 186° 30'. It is of a circular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and about 24 leagues in compass: it is sufficiently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> to be seen at the distance of 12 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 15 leagues; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> has a broken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> surface, with the appearance of barrenness rather than fertility. It is, however, inhabited; as some straggling savages were observed upon it. BANKSIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BANN

Pages 427-428
or BAN (from the Brit. ban, i.e. clamour), is a proclamation or public notice; any public summons or edict, whereby a thing is commanded or forbidden. It is a word ordinary among the feudists; and there is both bannus and banum, which signify two several things.—The word bannus is particularly used in England in publishing matrimonial contracts; which is done in the church before marriage, to the end that if any persons can speak against the intention of the parties, either in respect of kindred, precontract, or for other just cause, they may take their exception in time, before the marriage is consummated; and in the canon law, Banne sunt proclamationes sponsi et sponsae in ecclesiis fieri solitis. But there may be a faculty or licence for the marriage, and then this ceremony is omitted: and ministers are not to celebrate matrimony between any persons without a licence, except the bans have been first published three several times, upon pain of suspension, &c. Can. 62. The use of matrimonial bans is said to have been first introduced in the Gallican church, though something like it obtained even in the primitive times; and it is this that Tertullian is supposed to mean by minuenda promulgatio. The council of Lateran first extended, and made the usage general. By the ordinance of Blois, no person could validly contract marriage, without a preceding proclamation of three bans; nor could any person whatever be dispensed with, except... BANN cept for the two last. But the French themselves have abated much of this severity; and only minors are now under an absolute necessity of submitting to the formality of banns. For majors, or those of age, after publication of the first banns, the two latter are easily bought off. BANN is also used to denote procription or banishment for a crime proved; because anciently published by sound of trumpet; or, as Vossius thinks, because those who did not appear at the above-mentioned summons, were punished by procription. Hence, to put a prince under the bann of the empire, is to declare him divested of all his dignities. The sentence only denotes an interdict of all intercourse, and offices of humanity, with the offender; the form of which seems taken from that of the Romans, who banished persons by forbidding them the use of fire and water. Sometimes also cities are put under the imperial bann; that is, stripped of their rights and privileges.

BANN ALSO

Pages 428-428

N also denotes a pecuniary mulct, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> penalty, laid on a delinquent for offending against a bann.

BANNER

Pages 428-428

R denotes either a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> standard belonging to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. We find a multiplicity of opinions concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of the word banner; some deriving it from the Latin bandum, "a band or flag;" others from the word bann, "to summons the vassals to appear in arms;" others again from the German ban, "a field or tenement," because landed men alone were allowed a banner; and finally, there are some who think it is a corruption of panniere, from pannus, "cloth," because banners were originally made of cloth. The Banner of France, was the largest and richest of all the flags borne by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kings in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> expeditions. St Martin's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> 600 years as the banner of France; it was made of taffety, painted with the image of that saint, and laid one or two days on his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> to prepare it for use. About the year 1100 came in a more pompous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>. The banner <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> was fastened to the top of a mast, or some tall tree, planted on a scaffold, borne on a carriage drawn by oxen, covered with velvet hangings, decorated with devices or cyphers of the prince reigning. At the foot of the tree was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, who said <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> early every morning. Ten knights mounted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> on the scaffold night and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and as many trumpets at the foot of the tree never ceased flourishing, to animate the troops. This cumbersome machine, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of which was brought from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in use about 130 years. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> was in the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. And here it was that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> feats were performed, to carry off and defend the royal banner; for there was no victory without it, nor was any army reputed vanquished till they had lost this banner.

BANNERETS

Pages 428-430

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> order of knights, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> feudal lords; who, possessing several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fees, led their vassals to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> under their own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> or banner, when summoned thereto by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. The word seems formed from banner, "a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> flag;" or from band, which anciently denoted a flag.—Bannerets are also called in ancient writers milites vexilliferi, and vexillarii bannerarii, bannarii, banderifii, &c. Anciently there were two kinds of knights, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and little; the first whereof were called bannerets, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> bachelors; the first composed the upper, the second the middle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. The banneret was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> allowed to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> under his own flag, whereas the bachelarius eques followed that of another. To be qualified for a banneret, one must be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of family, and must have a power to raise to certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of armed men, with estate enough to subsist at least 28 or 30 men. This must have been very considerable in those days; because each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, besides his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, had two horsemen to wait on him armed, the one with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-bow, the other with a bow and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCHET">hatchet</a>. As he was not allowed to be a baron who had not above 13 knights fees, so he was not admitted to be a banneret <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had less than 10. Banneret, according to Spelman, was a middle order between a baron and a simple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>; called sometimes also vexillarius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>, to distinguish him from the greater, that is, from the baron, to whom alone properly belonged the jus vexilli, or privilege of the square flag. Hence the banneret was also called bannercetus, quasi baro minor; a word frequently used by English writers in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> as banneret was by the French, though neither of them occur before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Edward II. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have bannerets to have originally been persons who had some portion of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> assigned them; and enjoyed it under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of baro proximus, and that with the same prerogatives as the baron himself. Some, again, find the origin of bannerets in France, others in Brittany, others in England. These last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of bannerets to Conan, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of Maximus, who commanded the Roman legions in England under the empire of Gratian in 383. This general, lay they, revolting, divided England into 40 cantons, and in these cantons distributed 40 knights; to whom he gave a power of assembling, on occasion, under their several banners, as many of the effective men as were found in their respective districts: whence they are called bannerets. However this be, it appears from Froissart, &c. that anciently such of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> men as were rich enough to raise and subsist a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of armed men, and had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to do so, were called bannerets. Not, however, that these qualifications rendered them knights, but only bannerets; the appellation of knight being only added thereto, because they were simple knights before. Bannerets were second to none but knights of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">garter</a>. They were reputed the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> below the nobility; and were allowed to bear arms with supporters, which none else may under the degree of a baron. In France, it is said, the dignity was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>; but in England it died with the person that gained BAN Banneret gained it. The order dwindled on the institution of baronets by King James I. and at length became extinct. The last person created banneret was Sir John Smith, made so after Edghill fight, for rescuing the standard of King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. The form of the banneret's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> was this. On a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of battle, the candidate presented his flag to the king or general; who, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the train or skirt thereof, and making it a square, returned it again, the proper banner of bannerets; who are hence sometimes called knights of the square flag. There seem to have been bannerets created either in a different manner, or by others than the sovereign; since King James, in the patents of baronets, gives them precedence to all knights bannerets, except such as are created by the king himself in the field; which implies, either that there are some of this order created out of the field, or by inferior persons. Banneret is also the name of an officer or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of Rome towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 14th century. —The people of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and throughout the territory of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, during the disputes of the antipopes, had formed a kind of republican <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; where the whole power was lodged in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a magistrate called senator, and twelve heads of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> called bannerets, by reason of the banners which each raised in his district. Bannock, a kind of oat-cake, baked in the embers, or on a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> placed before the fire. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the northern parts of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Bannum, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies the utmost bounds of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> or town. Banquet, a feast or entertainment where people regale themselves with pleasant foods or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. Banquet, in the Manege, that small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the branch of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a> that is under the eye; which being rounded like a small rod, gathers and joins the extremities of the bit to the branch, in such a manner that the banquet is not seen, but covered by the cope, or that part of the bit that is next the branch. Banquet-Line, an imaginary line drawn, in making a bit, along the banquet, and prolonged up or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, to adjust the designed force or weaknesses of the branch, in order to make it stiff or easy. Banquet, or Banquette, in Fortification, a little foot-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, or elevation of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, forming a path which runs along the inside of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>, upon which the musketeers get up, in order to discover the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTERSCARP">counterscarp</a>, or to fire on the enemy, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOAT">moat</a> or in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">covert</a>-way. Banqueting Room or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALOON">Saloon</a>. The ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> supped in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATRIUM">atrium</a>, or vestibule, of their houses; but, in after-times, magnificent saloons, or banqueting-rooms, were built, for the more commodious and splendid entertainment of their guests. Lucullus had several of these, each distinguished by the name of some god; and there was a particular rate of expense appropriated to each. Plutarch relates with what magnificence he entertained Cicero and Pompey, who went with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to surprize him, by only telling a slave who waited, that the cloth should be laid in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius, among others, had a splendid banqueting-room named <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>. But everything of this kind was outdone by the lustre of that celebrated banqueting-house of Nero, called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOMUS">domus</a> au- BANSTICKLE. See Gasterosteus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANTAM">Bantam</a>, a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, in the East Indies, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 105° 16'. S. Lat. 6° 20'. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a kingdom of the same name, with a harbour and cattle; but the harbour is now so choked up that it is inaccessible to vessels of any great burden. It is divided into two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> separated by a river, and one of them inhabited by the Chinese. Bantam once enjoyed a flourishing trade. It was a great mart for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a> and other spices; but this trade, as well as the power of its sovereign, had fallen to decay. For its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, &c. see Java. Bantam-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, a kind of painted or carved work, resembling that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, only more gaudy. There are two sorts of Bantam, as well as of Japan work. As, in the latter, some are flat, lying even with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and others <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and embossed; so, in Bantam-work, some are flat and others in-cut, or carved into the wood, as we find in many large screens: with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that the Japan artists work chiefly in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>; and those of Bantam generally in colours, with a small sprinkling of gold here and there: for the flat Bantam-work is done in colours, mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, proper for the thing designed to be imitated. For the carved, or in-cut kind, the method of performing it is thus described by an ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>: 1. The wood is to be primed with whiting and size, so often till the primer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> near a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an inch thick; then it is to be water-plained, i.e. rubbed with a fine wet cloth, and, some time after, rubbed very smooth, the blacks laid on, varnished up with a good body, and polished well, though with a gentle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. This done, the design is to be traced out with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a> and gum-water, exactly in the manner wherein it is intended to be cut; the figures, trees, buildings, &c. in their due proportion: then the graver is applied, with other tools, of proper shapes, differing according to the workman's fancy: with these he cuts deep or shallow, as is found convenient, but never deeper than the whiting lies, the wood being never to feel the edge of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">Lines</a>, or parts of the black, are still to be left for the draperies, and other outlines, and for the distinction of one thing from another; the rule being to cut where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> is, and leave the black untouched. The carving being finished, then take to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, with which the colours are laid into the cut-work; after this, the gold is to be laid in those places which the design requires; for which purpose, a strong thick gum-arabic water is taken and laid with a pencil on the work; and, while this remains wet, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>-gold is cut with a sharp smooth edged <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, in little pieces, shaped to the bigness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the places where they are to be laid. These being taken up with a little cotton, they daub them with the same close to the gum-water, which affords a rich luster. The work thus finished, they clear up the black with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, taking care not to touch the colours. The European workmen ordinarily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> bras-duft, which is less bright and beautiful. Bantry, Bantry, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cork, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>. It is seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the same name, in W. Long. 9. 15. N. Lat.

BAOBAB

Pages 430-430

the name given by Prosper Alpinus to the African calabash-tree, since called Adansonia. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BAPTISM

Pages 430-435

in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of washing; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a sacrament, by which a person is initiated into the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>.—The word is formed from the Greek βαπτίζω, of βάπτω to dip or wash. Baptism is known, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> other names and titles. Sometimes it is called palingenesis, or layer of regeneration; sometimes salut, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>; sometimes σημεῖον, signaculum Domini, and Bingham's signaculum fidei, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; sometimes ablutio, Orig. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLES">Eccles</a>. Autely mylterium, and sacramentum; sometimes the sacrament of faith; sometimes viaticum, from its being administered to departing persons; sometimes sacerdotium laici, or the lay priesthood, because allowed, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, to be conferred by laymen: sometimes it is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> circumcision, because it was imagined to succeed in the room of circumcision, and to be a seal of the Christian covenant, as that was the seal of the covenant made with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>: so, in regard that baptism had Christ for its author, and not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, it was anciently known by the name of Δαγός και Χριστός, the gift of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>: sometimes it was simply called δώρον, without any other addition, by way of eminence, because it was both a gratuitous and singular gift of Christ: in reference to the making men complete members of Christ's body, the church, it had the name of τέκνον, and ἁγιασμός, the consecration, and consummation; because it gave men the perfection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to partake of the ἀρτὸς τοῦ κυρίου, which was the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a>: it had also the name of πνεύμα και πνεύματος, the initiation, because it was the admittance of men to all the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the Christian religion. Baptism has been supposed by many learned authors to have had its origin from the Jewish church, in which, as they maintain, it was the practice <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, to baptize proselytes or converts to their faith, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ceremony of their admission; a practice which, according to some, obtains among them to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; a person <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> Jew, is first circumcised, and, when healed, is bathed, or baptized in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, in presence of their rabbins; after which he is reputed a good Jew. Others, however, insist that the Jewish proselyte baptism is not far off <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and that John the Baptist was the first administrator of baptism among the Jews. Of this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> were Deylingius, J. G. Carpzovius, Boernerus, Wermdorfius, Zeltnerus, Owen, Knatchbull, Jennings, Gill, and others. Grotius is of opinion, that the rite of baptism had its original from the time of the deluge; immediately after which, he thinks, it was instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the world having been purged by water. Some learned men think it was added to circumcision, soon after the Samaritan schism, as a mark of distinction to the orthodox Jews. Spencer, who is fond of deriving the rites of the Jewish religion from the ceremonies of the Pagans, lays it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as a probable supposition, that the Jews received the baptism of proselytes from the neighbouring nations, who were wont to prepare candidates for the more sacred functions of their religion, by a solemn ablution; that by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> of sacred rites, they might draw the Gentiles to embrace their religion, and that the proselytes (in gaining of whom they were extremely diligent) might the more easily comply with the transition from Gentilism to Judaism. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of this opinion, he observes, first, that there is no divine precept for the baptism of proselytes, God having enjoined only the rite of circumcision for the admission of strangers into the Jewish religion. Secondly, that, among foreign nations, the Egyptians, Persians, Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and others, it was customary that those who were to be initiated into their mysteries, or sacred rites, should be first purified by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> their whole body in water. That learned writer adds, as a farther confirmation of his opinion, that the cup of blessing likewise, added to the paschal supper, seems plainly to have been derived from a pagan original: for the Greeks, at their feasts, had one cup, called ἀρτὸς τοῦ κυρίου, the cup of the good demon or god, which they drank at the conclusion of their entertainment, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> was removed. Since then, a rite of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENTILE">Gentile</a> origin was added to one of the Jewish sacraments, viz. the paschal, there can be no absurdity in supposing, that baptism, which was added to the other sacrament, namely circumcision, might be derived from the same source. In the last <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, he observes, that Christ, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of his sacraments, paid a peculiar regard to those rites which were borrowed from the Gentiles: for rejecting circumcision and the paschal supper, he adopted into his religion baptism and the sacred cup; thus preparing the way for the conversion and reception of the Gentiles into his church. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the Jewish baptism, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> baptism be practised by them, is supposed to be, to import a regeneration, whereby the proselyte is rendered a new man, and of a slave becomes free. The effect of it is, to cancel all former relations; so that those who were before akin to the person, after the ceremony ceased to be so. It is to this ceremony Christ is supposed to have alluded, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> to Nicodemus, that it was necessary that he should be born again, in order to become his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>.—The necessity of baptism to salvation, is grounded on those two sayings of our Saviour: He that believeth, and is baptized, shall be saved; and, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of God. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> did not generally think the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> want of baptism, where the profession was impracticable, excluded men absolutely from the hopes of eternal salvation. Some few of them, indeed, are pretty severe upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> dying without baptism; and some others seem also, in general terms, to deny eternal life to adult persons dying without it; but when they interpret themselves, and speak more distinctly, they make some allowances, and except several cases, in which the want of baptism may be supplied by other means. Such are, martyrdom, which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> goes by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> baptism in men's own blood, in the writings of the ancients; because of the power and efficacy it was thought to have to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> men by the invisible baptism of the Spirit, without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> element of water. Faith, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>, were also esteemed a supplement to the want of baptism, in such catechumens as died while they were piously preparing themselves for baptism. Constantly communicating Baptism. communicating with the church, was thought to supply the want of baptism, in persons who had been admitted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, on a presumption of their being duly baptized, though the contrary afterwards appeared. For infants dying without baptism, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> was thought more dangerous; as here, no personal faith, repentance, or the like, could be pleaded, to supply the defect, and wash away original sin: on this account, they who spoke most favourably of them, as Greg. Nazianzen, and Severus bishop of Antioch, only assigned them a middle state, neither in heaven nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. But the Latins, as St. Augustin, Fulgentius, Marius Mercator, &c., who never received the opinion of a middle state, concluded, as they could not be received into heaven, they must go to hell. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PELAGIUS">Pelagius</a>, and his followers, who denied original sin, affirmed, that they might be admitted to eternal life and salvation, though not to the kingdom of heaven; between which they distinguished. Where the fault was not on the side of the child, nor his parents, but of the minister, or where any unavoidable accident rendered baptism absolutely impossible, Hincmar, and others, make an exception, in holding the child saved without baptism. The receiving baptism is not limited to any time, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of life. Some contend for its being administered like circumcision, precisely on the eighth day, as Greg. Nazianzen; and others would have it deferred till the child is three years of age, and able to hear the mystic words, and make answer thereto, though he do not understand them. In the canon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> we find divers injunctions against deferring the baptism of infants beyond the 37th day, 30th day, and the 9th day; some of them under pecuniary forfeitures. Salmans, and Suicerus from him, deliver it as authentic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that for the two first ages, no one received baptism, who was not first instructed in the faith and doctrine of Christ, so as to be able to answer for himself, that he believed; because of those words, He that believeth, and is baptized; which, in effect, is to say, that no infant, for the first two ages, was ever admitted to Christian baptism. But, afterwards, they own, that pedo-baptism came in, upon the opinion that baptism was necessary to salvation. But Vossius, Dr Forbes, Dr Hammond, Mr Walker, and especially Mr Wall, who has exactly considered the testimony and authority of almost every ancient writer that has said anything upon this subject, endeavour to evince, that infants were baptized even in the apostolical age. It is certain, Tertullian pleads strongly against giving baptism to infants; which shows, at least, that there was some such practice in his age, though he disapproved of it. It is certain, the ordinary subjects of this sacrament, in the first ages, were converts from Judaism and Gentilism, who, before they could be admitted to baptism, were obliged to spend some time in the state of catechumens, to qualify them to make their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> of faith, and a Christian life, in their own persons: for, without such personal professions, there was ordinarily no admission of them to the privilege of baptism. Those baptized in their sick-beds were called clinic; and were held in some reproof, as not being reputed true Christians. Hence several canons, in councils and ecclesiastical writers, of clinic baptism. This clinic baptism was not sufficient to qualify the person, in case of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>, for ordination. Some had their baptism put off by way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, when they fell into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> and scandalous crimes, which were to be expiated by a longer course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> and repentance. This was sometimes 5, 10, 20 years, or more; even all their lives to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, when their crimes were very flagrant. In the earliest ages of the church, there was no stated time or place for the reception of baptism. Afterwards Edifier, Whitfuntide, and Epiphany, became solemn seasons, out of which baptism was not administered, except in cases of necessity. The catechumens who were to receive it at these times, were called competences; and to these it is that St Cyril addresses his catecheses. In the apostolical age, and some time after, before churches and baptisteries were generally erected, they baptized in any place where they had convenience; as John baptized in Jordan, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> baptized the eunuch in the wilderness, and Paul the jailor in his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. But in after ages, baptisteries were built adjoining to the church; and then rules were made, that baptism should ordinarily be administered nowhere but in these buildings. Julian, in one of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOVELS">novels</a>, refers to ancient laws, appointing that none of the sacred mysteries of the church should be celebrated in private houses. Men might have private oratories for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> in their own houses; but they were not to administer baptism or the eucharist in them, unless by a particular license from the bishop of the place. Such baptisms are frequently condemned in the ancient councils, under the name ἀποκατεστημένων, baptisms in private conventicles. As to the attendant ceremonies and manner of baptism in the ancient church: The person to be baptized, if an adult, was first examined by the bishop or officiating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, who put some questions to him; as, first, Whether he abjured the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> and all his works; secondly, Whether he gave a firm assent to all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of the Christian faith; to both which he answered in the affirmative. If the person to be baptized was an infant, these interrogatories were answered by his sponsors, or godfathers. Whether the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of sponsors was old as the apostles' days, is uncertain; perhaps it was not, since <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-JUSTIN_MARTYR">Justin <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr</a>, speaking of the method and form of baptism, says not a word of them.—After the questions and answers, followed exorcism; the manner and end of which was this: The minister laid his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on the person's head, and breathed in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, implying thereby the driving away or expelling of the devil from him, and preparing him for baptism, by which the good and holy spirit was to be conferred upon him.—After exorcism, followed baptism itself: and first the minister, by prayer, consecrated the water for that use. Tertullian says, "any waters may be applied to that use: but then God must be first invoked; and then the Holy Ghost presently comes down from heaven, and moves upon them, and sanctifies them." The waters being consecrated, the person was baptized "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost;" by which, "dedication of him to the blest Trinity, the person (says Clemens Alexandrinus) is delivered from the corrupt trinity, the devil, the world, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>." In performing the ceremony of baptism, the usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> (except in clinical cases, Baptism. or where there was scarcity of water), was to immerse and dip the whole body. Thus St Barnabas, describing a baptized person, says, "We go down into the water full of sin and filth, but we ascend <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> fruit in our hearts." And this practice of immersing the whole body was so general, that we find no exceptions made in respect either to the tenderness of infants, or the frailty of the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, unless in case of sickness or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISABILITY">disability</a>. But to prevent any indecency, men and women were baptized apart. To which end, either the baptisteries were divided into two apartments, one for the men, the other for the women, as Bingham has observed; or the men were baptized at one time and the women at another, as is shown by Volhus, from the Ordo Romanus, Gregory's Sacramentarium, &c. Add, that there was anciently an order of deaconesses, one part of whose business was to assist at the baptism of women. The precautions, however, rather indicate a scrupulous <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to delicacy, than imply any indecency in the circumstance of immersion itself. From the candidates being immersed, there is at least no reason to infer that they were naked: The present Baptists never baptize naked, though they always immerse. After immersion, followed the unction; by which (says St Cyril) was signified that they were now cut off from the wild olive, and were ingrafted into Christ, the true olive tree; or else to show that they were now to be champions for the gospel, and were anointed thereto, as the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHLETE">athlete</a> were against their solemn games.
