With this anointing was joined the sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, made upon the forehead of the person baptized; which being done, he had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> garment given him, to denote his being washed from the defilements of sin, or in allusion to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>, "As many as are baptized in Christ have put on Christ." From this custom the feast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENTECOST">Pentecost</a>, which was one of the annual feasts of baptism, came to be called Whitewashday, i.e. White-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">sunday</a>. This garment was afterwards laid up in the church, that it might be an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> against such persons as violated or denied that faith which they had owned in baptism.—When the baptism was performed, the person baptized, according to Justin Martyr, "was received into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the faithful, who then sent up their public prayers to God, for all men, for themselves, and for those who had been baptized." The ordinary ministers, who had the right of administering this sacrament, that is, of applying the water to the body, and pronouncing the formula, were presbyters or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>; though on extraordinary occasions laymen were admitted to perform the same. As to the present form of administering baptism, that is, of applying the water to the body, and pronouncing the formula, were presbyters or bishops; though on extraordinary occasions laymen were admitted to perform the same. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> forms in the church of Rome uses the following. When a child is to be baptized, the persons who bring it wait for the priest at the door of the church, who comes thither in his surplice and purple stole, attended by his clerks. He begins with questioning the godfathers, whether they <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, in the child's name, to live and die in the true catholic and apostolic faith, and what name they would give the child. Then follows an exhortation to the sponsors; after which the priest, calling the child by its name, asks it as follows: What dost thou demand of the church? The godfather answers, Eternal life. The priest goes on: If you are desirous of obtaining eternal life, keep God's commandments, thou shalt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> the Lord thy God, &c. After which he breathes three times in the child's face, saying, Come out of this child, thou evil spirit, and make room for the Holy Ghost. This said, he makes the sign of the cross on the child's forehead and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, saying, Receive the sign of the cross on thy forehead, and in thy heart. Then taking off his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, he repeats a short prayer; and laying his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> gently on the child's head, repeats a second prayer; which ended, he blesses some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; and putting a little of it into the child's mouth, pronounces these words, Receive the salt of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>. All this is performed at the church-door. The priest, with the godfathers and godmothers, coming into the church, and advancing towards the font, repeat the apostles' creed and the Lord's prayer. Being come to the font, the priest exorcises the evil spirit again; and taking a little of his own spittle, with the thumb of his right-hand, rubs it on the child's ears and nostrils, repeating, as he touches the right <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, the same word (Epiphania, be thou opened) which our Saviour made use of to the man born <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEAF_AND_DUMB">deaf and dumb</a>. Lastly, they pull off its swaddling-clothes, or strip it below the shoulders, during which the priest prepares the oils, &c. The sponsors then hold the child directly over the font, observing to turn it due east and west: whereupon the priest asks the child, Whether he renounces the devil and all his works? and the godfather having answered in the affirmative, the priest anoints the child between the shoulders in the form of a cross. Then taking some of the consecrated water, he pours part of it thrice on the child's head, at each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERORATION">peroration</a> calling on one of the Persons of the Holy Trinity. The priest concludes the ceremony of baptism with an exhortation.—The Romish church allows midwives, in cases of danger, to baptize a child before it comes entirely out of its mother's womb; where it is to be observed, that some part of the body of the child must appear before it can be baptized, and that it is baptized on the part which first appears: if the head, it is not necessary to rebaptize the child; but if only a foot or hand appears, it is necessary to repeat baptism. A stillborn child thus baptized may be buried in consecrated ground. The Greek church differs from the Romish, as to the rite of baptism, chiefly in performing it by immersion, or plunging the infant all over in the water. The forms of administering baptism among us being English too well known to require a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, we shall only mention one or two of the more material differences between the form, as it stood in the first liturgy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward, and that in the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> Prayer Book at present. First, the form of consecrating the water did not make a part of the office, in King Edward's liturgy, as it does in the present, because the water in the font was changed, and consecrated, but once a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. The form likewise itself was something different from that now used; and was introduced with a short prayer, that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, upon whom (when he was baptized) the Holy Ghost came down in the likeness of a dove, would send down the same Holy Spirit, to sanctify the fountain of baptism; which prayer was afterwards left out, at the second revision.—By King Edward's first book, the minister is to dip the child in the water thrice; first, dipping the right-side; secondly, the left; the third time, dipping the face toward the foot. This trine immersion was a very ancient. client practice in the Christian church, and used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the Holy Trinity; though some later writers say, it was done to represent the death, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of Christ, together with his three days continuance in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>. Afterwards, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a> making an ill use of it, by persuading the people that it was used to denote that the three Persons in the Trinity were three distinct substances, the orthodox left it off, and used only one single immersion. By the first common-prayer of King Edward, after the child was baptized, the godfathers and godmothers were to lay their hands upon it, and the minister was to put on him the white vestment commonly called the chrysosome, and to say, "Take this white vesture, as a token of the innocency, which, by God's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, in this holy sacrament of baptism, is given unto thee; and for a sign, whereby thou art admonished, so long as thou livest, to give thyself to innocence of living, that after this transitory life thou mayest be partaker of the life everlasting. Amen." As soon as he had pronounced these words, he was to anoint the infant on the head, saying, "Almighty God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath regenerated thee by water and the Holy Ghost, and hath given unto thee <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMISSION">remission</a> of all thy sins; may he vouchsafe to anoint thee with the unction of his Holy Spirit, and bring thee to the inheritance of everlasting life. Amen." This was manifestly done in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the practice of the primitive church. The custom of sprinkling children, instead of dipping them in the font, which at first was allowed in case of the weakness or sickness of the infant, has so far prevailed, that immersion is at length quite excluded. What principally tended to confirm the practice of affusion or sprinkling, was, that several of our Protestant divines, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> into Germany and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> during the bloody reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, and returning home when Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> came to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, brought back with them a great zeal for the Protestant churches beyond <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, where they had been sheltered and received; and having observed, that at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a> and some other places, baptism was administered by sprinkling, they thought they could not do the church of England a greater piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> than by introducing a practice dictated by so great an oracle as Calvin. This, together with the coldness of our northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, was what contributed to banish entirely the practice of dipping infants in the font. Many different notions have been entertained concerning the effects of baptism, which it would be useless to enumerate.—The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMONSTRANTS">Remonstrants</a> and Socinians reduce baptism to a mere sign of divine grace. The Romanists, on the contrary, exalt its power; holding, that all sin is entirely taken away by it; that it absolutely confers the grace of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a>, and consequently grace ex opero operato. Some also speak of an indelible character impressed on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> by it, called character dominicus, and character regius; but this is held, by others, a mere chimera; for that the spiritual character, conferred in regeneration, may easily be effaced by mortal sins. Dodwell maintained, that it is by baptism the soul is made immortal; so that those who die without it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not rise again. It must be added, he restrains this effect to episcopal baptism alone. From the effects ordinarily ascribed to baptism, even by ancient writers, it should seem, that the ceremony is as much of heathen as Jewish origin; since Christians do not restrain the use of it, like the Jews, to the admission of new members into the church, but hold, with the heathens, a virtue in it for remitting and washing away sins. The Brahmans are still said to baptize with this latter view, at certain seasons, in the river Ganges; to the waters whereof they have annexed a cleansing or sanctifying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and hence it is that they flock from all parts, even of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, driven by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of their being eased of their load of sins. But, in this point, many Christians seem to have gone beyond the folly of the heathens. It was only the smaller sins of infirmity which these latter held to be expiable by washing; for crimes of a blacker dye, they allowed no water could efface them, nor purgation could discharge them. The Christian doctrine of a total remission of sins by baptism could not fail, therefore, to scandalize many among the heathens, and furnished Julian an occasion of satirizing Christianity itself: "Whoever (says he) is guilty of rapes, murders, sacrilege, or any abominable crime, let him be washed with water, and he will become pure and holy." In the ancient church, baptism was frequently conferred on Jews by violence: but the church itself never seems to have allowed of force on this occasion. By a canon of the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, it is expressly forbidden to baptize any against their wills. That which looks most like force in this case, allowed by law, were two orders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>; one of which appoints the heathens, and the other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SAMARITANS">Samaritans</a>, to be baptized, with their wives and children and servants, under pain of confiscation. By the ancient laws, baptism was not to be conferred on image-makers, stage-players, gladiators, aurige or public drivers, magicians, or even strolling beggars, till they quitted such professions. Slaves were not allowed the privilege of baptism without the testimony and consent of their masters; excepting the slaves of Jews, Heathens, and heretics; who were not only admitted to baptism, but, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> thereof, had their freedom. Voissus, c. 11, § 17, has a learned and elaborate <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> De Baptismo, wherein he accurately discusses all the questions concerning baptism according to the doctrine of the ancients. Baptism by Fire, spoken of by St John the Baptist, has occasioned much conjecture. The generality of the fathers held, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a>, before they enter paradise, are to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through a certain fire, which is to purify them from all pollutions remaining on them unexpiated. Others, with St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, understand it of the fire of hell; others, of that of tribulation and temptation. Others, with St Chrysostom, will have it denote an abundance of graces. Others suppose it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of the Holy Ghost on the apostles, in form of fiery tongues. Lastly, others maintain, that the word fire here is an interpolation; and that we are only to read the text, He that shall come after me will baptise you with the Holy Ghost. In reality, it is not found in divers manuscript copies of St Matthew. The ancient Selucians and Hermians, understanding the passage literally, maintained, that material fire was necessary in the administration of baptism. But we do not find how or to what part of the body they applied it, or whether they were satisfied with obliging Baptism the person baptized to pass through the fire. Valentius rebaptized all who had received water-baptism, and conferred on them the baptism of fire. Bis docuit tincti, traductoque corpore flamma. TERTULL. Carm. contr. Marc. l. 1. Heraclon, cited by Clemens Alexandrinus, says, that some applied a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> to the ears of the person baptized, as if to impress some mark upon him. Baptism of the Dead, a custom which anciently prevailed among some people in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, of giving baptism to the dead. The third council of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a> speaks of it as a thing that ignorant Christians were fond of. Gregory Nazianzen also takes notice of the same superstitious opinion prevailing among some who delayed to be baptized. In his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to this kind of men, he asks, whether they stayed to be baptized after death? Philadrius also notes it as the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of the Montanists or Cataphrygians, that they baptized men after death. The practice seems to be grounded on a vain opinion, that, when men had neglected to receive baptism in their life-time, some compensation might be made for this default by receiving it after death. Baptism of the Dead was also a sort of vicarious baptism, formerly in use, when a person dying without baptism, another was baptized in his stead. St Chrysostom tells us, this was practiced among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARCIONITES">Marcionites</a> with a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of ridiculous ceremony; which he thus describes: After any catechumen was dead, they hid a living man under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the deceased; then coming to the dead man, they asked him, whether he would receive baptism; and he making no answer, the other answered for him, and said, he would be baptized in his stead; and so they baptized the living for the dead. Epiphanius affirms us, the like was also practiced among the Corinthians. This practice they pretended to found on the Apostle's authority; alleging that text of St Paul for it, If the dead rise not at all, what shall they do who are baptized for the dead? A text which has given occasion to a great variety of different systems and explanations. Vossius enumerates no less than <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> different opinions among learned divines concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the phrase, being baptized for the dead. St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a> and Walfrid Strabo seem clearly of opinion, that the apostle had respect to such a custom then in being; and several moderns have given into the same opinion, as Baronius, Jof. Scaliger, Justellus, and Grotius. Several among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, as Bellarmin, Salmeron, Menochius, and a number of schoolmen, understand it of the baptism of tears, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>, and prayers, which the living undergo for the dead; and thus allege it as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of purgatory in St Paul's days. Hypothetical Baptism, that formerly administered in certain doubtful cases, with this formula: If thou art baptized, I do not rebaptize; if thou art not, I baptize thee in the name of the Father, &c. This sort of baptism, enjoined by some ancient constitutions of the English church, is now fallen into disuse. Solemn Baptism, that conferred at stated seasons; such, in the ancient church, were the Paschal baptism, and that at Whitetide. This is sometimes also called Lay Baptism. Lay Baptism, we find to have been permitted by both the Common-prayer Books of King Edward and that of Queen Elizabeth, when an infant is in immediate danger of death, and a lawful minister cannot be had. This was founded upon the mistaken notion of the impossibility of salvation without the sacrament of baptism; but afterwards, when they came to have clearer notions of the sacraments, it was unanimously resolved in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>, held in the year 1575, that even private baptism, in a case of necessity, was only to be administered by a lawful minister. Baptism is also applied, abusively, to certain ceremonies used in giving names to things inanimate. The ancients knew nothing of the custom of giving baptism to inanimate things, as bells, ships, and the like, by a superstitious consecration of them. The first notice we have of this is in the Capitulars of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the Great, where it is only mentioned to be censured; but, afterwards, it crept into the Roman offices by degrees. Baronius carries its antiquity no higher than the year 968, when the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a> of the church of Lateran was christened by Pope John III. At last it grew to that superstitious height, as to be thought proper to be complained of in the Centum Gravamina of the German <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, drawn up in the public diet of the empire held at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> anno 1581; where (after having described the ceremony of baptizing a bell, with godfathers, who make responses as in baptism, and give it a name, and clothe it with a new garment as Christians were used to be clothed, and all this to make it capable of driving away tempests and devils) they conclude against it, as not only a superstitious practice, but contrary to the Christian religion, and a mere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEDUCTION">seduction</a> of the simple people. Baptism, in the sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a ceremony in long voyages on board merchant ships, practiced both on persons and vessels who pass the tropic or line for the first time. The baptizing the vessels is simple, and consists only in washing them throughout with sea-water; that of the passengers is more mysterious. The oldest of the crew, that has past the tropic or line, comes with his face blacked, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a> cap on his head, and some sea-book in his hand, followed by the rest of the seamen dressed like himself, each having some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> utensil in his hand, with drums <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a>; he places himself on a seat on the deck, at the foot of the mainmast. At the tribunal of this mock <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, each passenger not yet initiated, swears he will take care the same ceremony be observed, whenever he is in the like circumstances: Then, by giving a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> by way of gratification, he is discharged with a little sprinkling of water; otherwise he is heartily drenched with streams of water poured upon him; and the ship boys are enclosed in a cage, and ducked at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>.—The seamen, on the baptizing a ship, pretend to a right of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the beak-head unless redeemed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>. Baptismal, something belonging to baptism; thus we say baptismal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a>, presents, &c. Baptismal Vow or Covenant, a profession of obedience to the laws of Christ, which persons in the ancient church made before baptism. It was an indispensible Baptismal penitent part of the obligation on catechumens, before they were admitted to the ceremony of regeneration. It was made by turning to the east; for what mystical reasons, is not well agreed on. BAPTISMAL Prefects are in use in Germany, made by the sponsors to the infant, consisting of money, plate, or even sometimes fees of lands; which by the laws of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> are to be kept for the child till of age, the parents having only the trust, not the right, of disposing of them. An anonymous author has published a discourse express on this occasion, entitled, De pecunia lufrica.

BAPTIST

Pages 435-435

John Monnoyer, a painter of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and fruit, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LILLE">Lille</a> in 1635, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, where he perfected himself in the knowledge of his art, and in his first years was intended for a painter of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>: but having soon observed that his genius more strongly inclined him to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> of flowers, he applied his talents to those subjects, and in that style became one of the greatest masters. His pictures are not so exquisitely finished as those of Van Huysum, but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> and colouring are in a bolder style. His flowers have generally a remarkable freedom and loveliness, as well in the disposition as in the pencilling; together with a tone of colouring that is lively, admirable, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> itself. The disposition of his objects is surprisingly elegant and beautiful; and in that respect his compositions are easily known, and as easily distinguished from the performances of others. He died in 1699.—He left a son, Anthony, who painted flowers in the same style and manner, and had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> merit.

BAPTISTERY

Pages 436-436

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> is performed. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> it was one of the exedrae <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> buildings distinct from the church itself; and consisted of a porch or anti-room where the persons to be baptized made their confession of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and an inner room where the ceremony of baptism was performed. Thus it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the fifth century, when the baptisteries began to be taken into the church-porch, and afterwards into the church itself. The ancient baptisteries were <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called *fontes*, *photiferia*, q.d., places of illumination; an appellation sometimes given to baptism. Or they might have the name for another reason, because they were the places of an illumination, or instruction, preceding baptism: for here the catechumens seem to have been trained up, and instructed in the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the Christian faith. Those baptisteries were anciently very capacious; because, as Dr Cave observes, the stated times of baptism returning but seldom, there were usually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> multitudes to be baptized at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>: and then the manner of baptizing, by immersion, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, made it necessary to have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> font likewise. In Venantius Fortunatus, it is called *aula baptifinatis*, the large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of baptism; which was indeed so capacious, that we sometimes read of councils meeting and sitting therein. This hall, or chapel, was always kept shut during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>, and the door sealed up with the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, not to be opened till Maunday-Thursday. The baptistery was always reputed a sacred place. In the Roman order, we find the ceremonies used in the consecration of the baptisteries: they were to be built of a round <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and distinguished with the image of St John the Baptist; over the basin or font was a figure of a dove in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> or silver, to represent the Holy Ghost. The name baptistery is sometimes also given to a kind of chapel in a large church, which served for the same office. It is an observation of some learned men, that anciently there was but one baptistery in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and that at the bishop's church; and that afterwards they were set up in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> churches, with the special allowance however of the bishop.

BAPTISTS

Pages 435-436

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, (from βαπτίζω, baptize); a denomination of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, distinguished from other Christians by their particular opinions respecting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> and the subjects of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>. Instead of administering the ordinance by sprinkling <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pouring <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, they maintain that it ought to be administered only by immersion. Such, they insist, is the meaning of the word βαπτίζω; so that a command to baptize is a command to immerse. Thus it was understood by those who first administered it. John the Baptist, and the apostles of Christ, administered it in Jordan and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and places where there was much water. Both the administrators and the subjects are described as going <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into, and coming up again out of, the water; and the baptized are said to be buried in baptism, and to be raised again: which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> could not, they say, be properly adopted on supposition of the ordinance being administered in any other manner than by immersion. Thus also, they affirm, it was in general administered in the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Thus it is now administered in the Russian and Greek church: and thus it is, at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, directed to be administered in the church of England, to all who are thought capable of submitting to it in this manner. With regard to the subjects of baptism, the Baptists say, that this ordinance ought not to be administered to children or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> at all, nor to grown up persons in general; but to adults only of a certain character and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. Our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to his apostles, by which Christian baptism was instituted, is to go and teach all nations, baptizing them; that is, say they, not to baptize all they meet with; but first to instruct them—to teach all nations, or to preach the gospel to every creature—and whoever receives it, him to baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. To such persons, and to such only, baptism appears to have been administered by the apostles, and the immediate disciples of Christ. They are described as repenting of their sins, as believing in Christ, and as having gladly received the word. Without these qualifications, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> acquaints those who were converted by his sermon, that he could not have admitted them to baptism, Philips holds the same language in his discourse with the eunuch; and Paul treats Lydia, the jailor, and others, in the same manner. Without these qualifications, Christians in general think it wrong to admit persons to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>; and, for the same reasons, without these qualifications, at least a profession of them, the Baptists think it wrong to admit any to baptism. Therefore they withhold it, not only from the impenitently vicious and profane, and from infidels who have no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; but also from infants and children, who have no knowledge, and are incapable of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> civil and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>. They further insist, that all positive institutions depend entirely upon the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of the institutor; and therefore, that reasoning by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> from abrogated Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> is to be rejected, and the express commands of Christ respecting the mode and subjects of baptism ought to be our only rule. The Baptists in England form one of the denominations of Protestant Dissenters. They separate from the establishment for the same reasons as their brethren of the other denominations do; and from additional motives derived from their particular tenets respecting baptism. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of their churches, and their modes of worship, are congregational or independent; in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of which they are protected, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with other dissenters, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of toleration. Before this act, they were liable to pains and penalties as <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NONCONFORMISTS">nonconformists</a>, and often for their peculiar sentiments as Baptists. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> was issued out against them, and some of them were burnt in Smithfield in 1558. They bore a considerable share in the persecutions of the last and of the preceding centuries; and, as it should seem, in those of some centuries before; for there were several among the Lollards and the followers of Wickliff, who disapproved of infant-baptism. There were many of this persuasion among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> and reformers abroad. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, Germany, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>, they went by the names of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a>, and Mennonites; and, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a> and the South, they were found among the Albigenses and Waldenses. See the histories of the Reformation, and the above <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>. The Baptists subsist under two denominations, viz. the Particular or Calvinistical, and the General or Arminian. The former is by far the most numerous. Some of both denominations allow of mixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, viz. of persons who have been sprinkled in their infancy, and therefore unbaptized in the view of the Baptists; others disallow it; and some of them observe the seventh day of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> as the Sabbath, apprehending the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> that enjoined it not to have been repealed by Christ or his apostles. But a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, respecting these and other matters, is not peculiar. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISTERY">Baptistery</a> peculiar to the Baptists: it is common to all Christians, and to all bodies of men who think and judge for themselves.

BAR

Pages 436-438

formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of France, now the department of Meuse, is bounded on the east by Lorraine, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Luxembourg, on the west by Champagne, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and by Franche Comté. It is crossed by the river Meuse from north to south, and watered by several other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, which render it very fertile. It was divided into four bailiages, viz. Ballilly, Bar, St Michael, and Bar-le-duc and Clermont. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Bar-le-duc, Clermont, St Michael, Longuey, Pont à Mousson, and Stenay. In 1736, it was given to Stanislaus then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. Bar-le-duc, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the late duchy of Bar, in the department of Meuse, is seated on the declivity of a hill. It is divided into the higher and lower town; the lower is watered by the rivulet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORNE">Orne</a>, which abounds with excellent trouts. The wines are excellent, and not inferior to those of Champagne. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 30'. N. Lat. 48° 35'. Bar-le-Mont, a town of the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in Hainault, situated on the river Sombre. E. Long. 3° 40'. N. Lat. 50° 10'. Bar sur Aube, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of France, in the department of Aube, seated at the foot of a mountain. It is much celebrated for excellent wines. E. Long. 4° 50'. N. Lat. 48° 14'. Bar sur <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, a town of France, in the duchy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, now in the department of Aube, seated between a mountain which covers it on the west, and the river Seine which runs on the east. E. Long. 4° 30'. N. Lat. 48° 5'. Bar-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a>, among miners, the person who keeps the gauge, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a>, for measuring the ore. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARA">Bara</a>, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Adriatic, opposite to Brundusium: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHAROS">Pharos</a> of Melia. Also a fifth or arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Britannia Secunda (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); supposed to be the Murray frith. Bara, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a> or Western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Scotland. It is a small rock, only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in circumference, being part of a chain called the Long Island, the whole cluster appearing at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> as one island. Bara is altogether barren; but abounds with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of sea-fowl, such as fulan geese, guillemotes, puffins, &c. Bara, the name of a festival celebrated with much magnificence at Messina, and representing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSUMPTION">assumption</a> of the Virgin. The bara, though used as the general denomination of this festival, signifies more particularly a vast machine 50 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, at the top of which a young girl of 14, representing the Virgin, stands upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of an image of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ. Round him turn vertically, in a circle, 12 little children which represent the seraphims; below them, in another circle, which turns horizontally, are 12 more representing the cherubims: below these a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> turns vertically, with a child at the extremity of each of the four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> radii of his circle, who ascend and descend with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a>, yet still stand upright. Below the sun is the lowest circle, about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet from the ground, in which 12 boys turn horizontally without interruption; these are intended for the twelve apostles, who are supposed to surround the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of the Virgin at the moment when she ascends into heaven. This complication of superstitious whirligigs may have already nearly turned the stomachs of some of our readers, or at least rendered them squeamish. But think of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> little cherubims, seraphims, and apes, who are twirled about in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>! for, says Mr Houel "some of them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> asleep, many of them vomit, and several do still worse;" but these unseemly effusions are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWBACK">drawback</a> upon the edification of the people; and nothing is more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> than to see fathers and mothers soliciting with ardour for their boys and girls the pious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> of puking at the bara. This machine is not drawn by asses or mules, but by a multitude of robust monks. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARABINZIANS">Barabinzians</a>, a tribe of Tartars, living on both sides of the river Irtis. They seem to derive their name from the Barabaian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> supply them abundantly with fish, on which and their cattle they chiefly subsist. They have plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> and wild-fowl of every kind, particularly ducks and puffins. Most of them are heathens, but Mahometanism daily gains ground among them. Some of them pay tribute to the emperors of Kufia, and others to the Khan Taisha. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARACOA">Baracoa</a>, a town in the north-east part of the island of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUBA">Cuba</a>. W. Long. 76° 10'. N. Lat. 21° 5'. Baralipston, among logicians, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> denoting the first indirect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of syllogism. A syllogism in baralipston, is when the two first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> are general, and the third particular, the middle term being the subject in the first proposition and the predicate in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. The following is of this kind: BA. Every evil ought to be feared; RA. Every violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> is an evil; LIP. Therefore something that ought to be feared is a violent passion. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARALLOTS">Barallots</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, who had all things in common, even their wives and children. Their facility in complying with all manner of debauchery made them get the name obedientiæ, "compliers." Baranca de Malambo, a town of Terra Firma in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, with a bishop's see and a good haven. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of great trade, and is seated on the river Magdalene. W. Long. 75° 30'. N. Lat. 11° 10'. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARANGI">Barangi</a>, officers among the Greeks of the lower empire. Cujas calls them in Latin protectoriæ, and others give them the name of fecurigeri. It was their business to keep the keys of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> gates, where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> resided. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARANWAHR">Baranwahr</a>, a town of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, taken by the emperor of Germany from the Turks in 1684. It is seated between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUDA">Buda</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGRADE">Belgrade</a>, in E. Long. 10° 5'. N. Lat. 46° 0'. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARATHRUM">Barathrum</a>, in Antiquity, a deep dark pit at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, into which condemned persons were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> headlong. It had sharp spikes at the top, that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> might escape out; and others at the bottom, to pierce and torment such as were cast in. Its depth and capaciousness made it to be applied proverbially to a covetous person: to a glutton, called Barabro by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> (Lucretius, Horace), and Barathrum in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> (Horace); and for a common prostitute (Plautus). Baratiere, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, a most extraordinary instance of the early and rapid exertion of mental faculties. This surprising genius was the son of Francis Baratiere, minister of the French church at Schwoebach near <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a>, where he was born Jan. 10th 1721. The French was his mother tongue, together with some words of High Dutch; but by means of his father insensibly talking Latin to him, it became as familiar to him as the rest; so that, without knowing the rules of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, he at four years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> talked French to his mother. Baratiere, mother, Latin to his father, High Dutch to the maid or neighbouring children; and all this without mixing or confounding the respective languages. About the middle of his fifth year he acquired Greek in like manner; so that in 15 months he perfectly understood all the Greek books in the Old and New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, which he readily translated into Latin. When he was five years and eight months old, he entered upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>; and in three years <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was so expert in the Hebrew text, that from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, he could give the sense of the original in Latin or French; or translate extempore the Latin or French versions into Hebrew, almost word for word; and had all the Hebrew psalms by heart. He composed at this time a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> of rare and difficult Hebrew words, with critical remarks and philological observations, in about 400 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> in 4to; and, about his tenth year, amused himself for twelve months with the Rabbinical writers. With these he intermixed a knowledge of the Chaldaic, Syriac, and Arabic; and acquired a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> antiquity, by studying the Greek fathers, and councils of the first four ages of the church. In the midst of these occupations, a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of globes coming into his possession, he could in 8 or 10 days time resolve all the problems on them; and in about three months, in Jan. 1735, devised his project for the discovery of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, which he communicated to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and the Royal Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1731, he was matriculated in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALTDORF">Altdorf</a>; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the year 1732, he was presented by his father at the meeting of the reformed churches of the circle of Franconia; who, astonished at his wonderful talents, admitted him to assist in the deliberations of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a>; and to preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of so singular an event, it was ordered to be registered in their acts. In 1734, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MARGRAVE">margrave</a> of Brandenburgh Anspach granted this young scholar the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of whatever books he wanted from the Anspach library, together with a pension of 50 florins, which he enjoyed three years; and his father receiving a call to the French church at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STETTIN">Stettin</a> in Pomerania, young Baratiere was, on the journey, admitted master of arts, with universal applause, at the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>; at Berlin he was honoured with several conversations with the king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, and was received into the Royal Academy. Towards the close of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he acquired a taste for medals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, and antiquities; metaphysical inquiries, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, intervening occasionally between these studies. He wrote several essays and dissertations; made astronomical remarks, and laborious calculations; took great pains toward a history of the heresies of the anti-trinitarians, and of the 30 years <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in Germany; his last publication, which appeared in 1740, was on the succession of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of Rome. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> he engaged in, and for which he had gathered <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> materials, was Inquiries concerning the Egyptian Antiquities. But the substance of this blazing <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a> was now almost exhausted: he was always weak and sickly; and died October 5, 1740, aged 19 years 8 months and 16 days. He published 11 different pieces, and left 29 <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> on various subjects, the contents of which may be seen in his life written by M. Formey professor of philosophy at Berlin.

BARANA

Pages 451-451
or Burdock.** See Arctium, Botany Index. **BARDARIOTÆ,** in Antiquity, were a kind of ancient guard attending the Greek emperors, armed with rods, wherewith they kept off the people from crowding too near the prince when on horseback. Their captain, or commander, was denominated primusvirius.—The word was probably formed from the bardic, or housings on their horses. **BARDAS,** the brother of the empress Theodora, and uncle of the famous Photius, is said to have had no other good quality besides that of loving the sciences and polite literature, which he established in the Eastern

BARATZ

Pages 438-438

Turkish, letters-patent granted by the Turkish emperors to the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, &c., for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> functions. This Baratz gives the bishops full power and authority to establish and depose the inferior clergy, and all other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> persons; to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> licenses for marriages, and issue out divorces; to collect the revenues belonging to the churches; to receive the pious legacies bequeathed to them; in short, to enjoy all the privileges and advantages belonging to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> station: and all this (as it is expressed in the baratz itself) "according to the vain and idle ceremonies of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>."

BARBACAN

Pages 438-438
or BARRICAN, an outer defence or fortification to a city or castle, used especially as a fence to the city or walls; also an aperture made in the wall of a fortress, to fire through upon the enemy. See CASTLE. BARBACAN is also used to denote a fort at the entrance of a bridge, or the outlet of a city, having a double wall with towers.

BARBADOESES

Pages 438-440

the most easterly of all the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and, according to the best geographers, lying between 59° 30' and 60° 2' of west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and between 12° 56' and 13° 16' of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> is not certainly known: the most general <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is, that it is 25 miles from north to south, and 15 from east to west; but these measurements are subject to so many difficulties and uncertainties, that it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> perhaps convey a more adequate idea of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> to tell the reader that in reality it does not contain above 107,000 acres. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is hot, but not unwholesome, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> being qualified by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-breezes; and a temperate regimen renders this island as safe to live in as any climate south of Great Britain; and, according to the opinion of many, as even Great Britain itself. This island has on its east side two streams that are called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and in the middle is said to have a bituminous <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> which sends forth a liquor like tar, and serves for the same uses as pitch <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. The island abounds in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> of good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and has several reservoirs for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>-water. Some parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> are said to be hollowed into caves, some of them capable of containing 300 people. These are imagined to have been the lurking-places of runaway <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, but may as probably be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> excavations. The woods that formerly grew upon the island have been all cut <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and the ground converted into <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> plantations. When those plantations were first formed, the soil was prodigiously fertile, but has since been worn out, inasmuch, that about the year 1732, the planters were obliged to raise cattle for the sake of their dung, by which means the profit of their plantations was reduced to less than a tenth of its usual value. Notwithstanding the smallness of Barbadoes, its soil is different; Barbadoes, different; being in some places <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and others rich, and in others spongey; but all of it is cultivated according to its proper <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, so that the island presents to the eye the most beautiful appearance that can be imagined. Oranges and lemons grow in Barbadoes in great plenty, and in their utmost perfection. The lemon juice here has a peculiar fragrancy. The citrons of Barbadoes afford the best drams and sweetmeats of any in the world, the Barbadoes ladies excelling in the art of preserving the rind of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a> fruit. The juice of the limes, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a> lemons, is the most agreeable souring we know, and great quantities of it have of late been imported into Britain and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. The pine apple is also a native of Barbadoes, and grows there to much greater perfection than it can be made to do in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> by any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> means. A vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of different trees peculiar to the climate are also found to flourish in Barbadoes in great perfection; such as the aloe, mangrove, calabash, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, cotton, mastic, &c. Here likewise are produced some sensitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, with a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of garden stuff, which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in other places. In short, a native of the finest, the richest, and most diversified <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in Europe, can hardly form an idea of the variety of delicious and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> nutritive vegetable productions with which this island abounds. When Barbadoes was first discovered by the English, few or no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> were found upon it, except hogs, which had been left there by the Portuguese. For convenience of carriage to the sea side, some of the planters at first procured camels; which undoubtedly would in all respects have been preferable to horses for their fugar and other works; but the nature of the climate disagreeing with that animal, it was found impossible to preserve the breed. They then applied for horses to Old and New England: from the former they had those that were fit for thow and draught; from the latter those that were proper for mounting their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, and for the saddle. They had likewise some of an inferior breed from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CURACAO">Curacao</a>, and other settlements. They are reported to have had their first breed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONAVISTA">Bonavista</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Mayo; they now breed upon the island, and often do the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of horses. Their asses are very serviceable in carrying burdens to and from the plantations. The hogs of Barbadoes are finer eating than those of Britain, but the few sheep they have are not near so good. They likewise have goats, which when young are excellent food. Racoons and monkeys are also found here in great abundance. A variety of birds are produced on Barbadoes, of which the humming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> is the most remarkable. Wild fowl do not often frequent this island; but sometimes teal are found near their ponds. A bird which they call the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, is said to meet ships at 20 leagues from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and their return is, to the inhabitants, a sure sign of the arrival of these ships. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows from the south and south-west, they have flocks of curlews, plovers, snipes, wild pigeons, and wild ducks. The wild pigeons are very fat and plentiful at such seasons, and rather larger than those of England. The tame pigeons, pullets, ducks, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> of all kinds, that are bred at Barbadoes, have also a fine flavour, and are accounted more delicious than those of Europe. Their rabbits are scarce; they have no hares; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they have deer of any kind, they are kept as curiosities, Barbadoes. The insects of Barbadoes are not venomous, nor do either their snakes or scorpions ever sting. The muskettos are troublesome, and bite, but are more tolerable in Barbadoes than on the continent. Various other insects are found on the island, some of which are troublesome, but in no greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> than those that are produced by every warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> in England. Barbadoes is well supplied with fish; and some caught in the sea surrounding it are almost peculiar to itself; such as the parrot-fish, snappers, grey cavallos, terbums, and coney-fish. The mullets, lobsters, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a>, caught here are excellent; and the green turtle is perhaps the greatest delicacy that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> can boast of. At Barbadoes this delicious shell-fish seldom sells for less than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, and often for more. There is found in this island a kind of land crab which eats herbs wherever it can find them, and shelters itself in holes and hollows of trees. According to report, they are a shell-fish of passage; for in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> they travel to the sea in great numbers. See Cancer. The inhabitants may be reduced to three classes; viz. the masters, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> servants, and the blacks. The former are either English, Scots, or Irish: but the great encouragement given by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to the peopling of this and other West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> islands, induced some Dutch, French, Portuguese, and Jews, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> among them with their estates; by which, after a certain time, they acquire the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of naturalization in Great Britain. The white servants, whether by covenant or purchase, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> more easy lives than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>-labourers in England; and when they come to be overseers, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> and other allowances are considerable. As to the treatment of the negro slaves in this and the other islands, that falls to be spoken of under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Negro, Slave, West Indies; which see. The manners of the white inhabitants, in general, are the same as in most polite <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and counties in Europe. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the island is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">Bridge</a>-Town; see that article. As the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this island furnishes no very remarkable events, the following short hints concerning it may suffice. When the English, some time after the year 1625, first landed here, they found it the most <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> and desolate <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> they had hitherto visited. It had not the least appearance of ever having been peopled even by savages. There was no kind of beasts of pasture or of prey, no fruit, no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, no root fit for supporting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of man. Yet as the climate was so good, and the soil appeared fertile, some gentlemen of small fortune in England resolved to become adventurers thither. The trees were so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and of a wood so hard and stubborn, that it was with great difficulty they could clear as much ground as was necessary for their subsistence. By unremitting perseverance, however, they brought it to yield them a tolerable support; and they found that cotton and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a> agreed well with the soil; and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, which was beginning to come into repute in England, answered tolerably. These proposals, together with the storm between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, which was beginning to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out in England, induced many new adventurers to transport themselves into this island. And what is extremely Barbadoes tremely remarkable, so great was the increafe of people in Barbadoes, 25 years after its firft settlement, that in 1650 it contained more than 50,000 whites, and a much greater number of negro and Indian slaves. The latter they acquired by means not at all to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>: for they feized upon all thofe unhappy men, without any pretence, in the neighbouring islands, and carried them into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>; a practice which has rendered the Caribbee Indians irreconcilable to us ever since. They had begun a little before this to cultivate sugar, which soon rendered them extremely wealthy. The number of slaves, therefore, was still augmented; and in 1676 it is supposed that their number amounted to 100,000, which, together with 50,000 whites, make 150,000 on this small spot; a degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> unknown in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, or any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world most renowned for numbers. At this time Barbadoes employed 400 sail of ships, one with another of 150 tons, in their trade. Their annual exports, in sugar, indigo, ginger, cotton, and citron-water, were above 350,000l. and their circulating cash at home was 200,000l. Such was the increafe of population, trade, and wealth, in the course of 50 years. But since that time this island has been much on the decline; which is to be attributed partly to the growth of the French sugar colonies, and partly to our own eftablifhments in the neighbouring fides. Their numbers at prefent are said to be 20,000 whites and 100,000 slaves. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> confits of the same articles as formerly, though they deal in them to lefs extent. **BARBADORS-Tar**, a mineral fluid of the nature of the thicker fluid bitumens, of a nauseous bitterill taffe, very strong and disagreeable fmell, found in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> trickling down the fides of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and fometimes floating on the surface of the waters. It has been greatly recommended in coughs and other diforders of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> and lungs.

BARBARA

Pages 440-440

among Logicians, the firft <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of the firft <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of syllogifms. A syllogifm in barbara is one whereof all the proportions are univerfal and affirmative; the middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> being the fubject of the firft proposition, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. *Examp.* <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">Bar</a>. Every wicked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is miserable; Ba. All tyrants are wicked men; Ra. Therefore all tyrants are miserable.

BARBARIAN

Pages 440-440

a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to all who were not of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> were not initiated in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, manners, and cuftoms. In this fenfe, the word signified with them no more than foreigner; not signifying, as among us, a wild, rude, or uncivilized perfon.

BARBARISM

Pages 440-440

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, an offence againft the purity of style <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; or an ungrammatical way of speaking or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, contrary to the true idiom of any particular language.

BARBAROSSA

Pages 440-440

Aruch**, and Hayradin, two famous corsairs, the sons of a potter in the ile of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>; who, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> pirates, carried on their depredations with fuch fuccefs and conduct, that they were foon poifefled of 12 galleys besides smaller veffels. Of this fleet Aruch the elder <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, called Barbarossa from the refuels of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, and Hayradin the fecond in command; they called themselves the friends of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and the enemies of all who failed upon it; and their names became terrible from the straits of Dardanelles to thofe of Gibraltar. With fuch a power they wanted an eftablifhment; and the opportunity of fettling themfelves offered in 1516, by the inconfiderate application of Eutemi <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Algiers to them for affiftance againft the Spaniards. Aruch, leaving his brother to command the fleet, carried 5000 men to Algiers, where he was received as their delver; and fecretly murdering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> he came to aid, caufed himfelf to be proclaimed king in his stead. To this ufurpation he added the conqueft of Tremece; when his exploits and piracies inducef the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. to furnifh the marquis de Gomarez governor of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORAN">Oran</a> with troops to suppress him; by whom he was defeated and killed near Tremece. His brother Hayradin, known alfo by the name of Barharoffa, affumed the fceptre at Algiers with the fame abilities, and with better fortune; for the Spaniards, fufficiently employed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, giving him no disturbance he regulated the interior <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, carried on his naval operations with vigour, and extended his conquefts on the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. He put his dominions under the protection of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Signior, Solyman the Magnificent; and obtained the command of the Turkifh fleet. With fo powerful a protector, he acquired the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a> in a manner fimilar to that by which his brother gained Algiers. Since the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Barbaroiffas, Algiers has been underftood to be dependent on the Porte; but this dependence is now little more than merely nominal.

BARBARUS

Pages 440-441

Daniel**, of the fame family with the preceding, was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of Aquileia, and famous for his learning. He was ambaffador from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> to Eng- <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">BAR</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>; and was one of the fathers of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, where he acted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> zeal for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the pope. He wrote, 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> upon Vitruvius. 2. Catena Graecorum Patrum in quinquaginta Psalmos Latine versio. 3. La Pratica della Perspicuita. He died in 1569, at 41 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

BARBARY

Pages 441-446

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, including the states of Algiers, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>; (see those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>.) This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> contains almost the whole of what the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> possessed of the continent of Africa, excepting <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. It stretches itself in length from east to west, beginning at the southern limits of Egypt, to the straits of Gibraltar full 35 degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>; and from thence to Santa Cruz, the utmost western edge of it, about six more, in all 41 degrees; so that the utmost length of Barbary from east to west is computed at above 759 German leagues. On the south, indeed, it is confined within much narrower bounds, extending no farther than from 27 to 35½ degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude; so that its utmost breadth from north to south, does not exceed 128 German miles. More particularly, Barbary begins on the west of the famed Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, called by the Arabs <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AY">Ay</a> Duaal, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Al Duacal, enclosing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kingdoms of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a> and Dela, now provinces of Morocco; thence stretching north-eastward along the Atlantic to the pillars of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINISTERRE">Finisterre</a>, then along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Mediterranean, it is at last bounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> in Egypt. Concerning the origin of the name Barbary, there are many conjectures. According to some, the Romans, after they had conquered this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> country, gave it that name out of contempt and dislike to the barbarous manners of the natives, according to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of calling all other people but themselves Barbarians.
