PAOLO ANTONIO, da Cento, painter of still <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and animals, was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Guercino, and born at Cento in 1596. He chose for his subjects fruit, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, insects, and animals; which he painted after <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with a lively tint of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> tenderness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, and a strong character of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and life. He died in 1640.

BARBITOS

Pages 446-446
or BARBITON, an ancient instrument of music, mounted with three, others say seven, strings; much used by Sappho and Alceus, whence it is also denominated Lefbonum.

BARBLES

Pages 446-446
or BARBS, in Farriery, the knots or superfluous flesh that grow up in the channels of a horse's mouth; that is, in the intervals that separate the bars, and lie under the tongue. These, which are also called barbes, obtain in black cattle as well as horses, and obstruct their eating. For the cure, they call the beak, take out his tongue, and clip off the barbles with a pair of scissors, or cut them with a sharp knife; others choose to burn them off with a hot iron.

BARBOUR

Pages 446-446

JOHN, archdeacon of Aberdeen, was esteemed an excellent poet in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> I. He wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Robert the Bruce, in an heroic poem, which is still extant, and which contains many facts and anecdotes omitted by other historians. The latest edition of this book is that of Glasgow, 8vo. printed in the year 1672. It is entitled, "The acts and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of the most victorious conqueror Robert Bruce <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Scotland; wherein also are contained the martial deeds of the valiant princes Edward Bruce, Sir James Dowglas, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Thomas Randel, Walter Stewart, and sundry others." In one passage, he calls it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>; but that word was then of good reputation: every body knows that the 'Romant of romants' has been innocently applied to true history, as well as the 'Ballad of ballads' to a sacred song.

BARBUDA

Pages 446-447

one of the British <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, about 20 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 12 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. It is low <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, but fruitful and pretty populous. The inhabitants employ themselves in husbandry, and find always a ready market for their corn and cattle in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> islands. Barbuda is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the Codrington family, who have have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> here as well as in Barbadoes. It lies in W. Long. 61° 3'. N. Lat. 18° 5'.

BARCA

Pages 447-447

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, lying on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, between the kingdoms of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, extending itself in length from east to west from the 39th to the 46th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and in breadth from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south about 30 leagues, as is generally supposed. It is for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, especially in the middle, a dry <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY_DESERT"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>: on which account the Arabs call it Sabora, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ceyart Barka, that is, the desert or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> of whirlwinds or hurricanes. It labours almost everywhere under a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> scarcity of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and except in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages, where the ground produces some small quantities of grain, such as millet and some maize, the rest is in a manner quite barren and uncultivated, or, to speak more properly, uncultivable: and even of that small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> which those few spots produce, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> inhabitants are obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> some part with their indigent neighbours, for dates, sheep, and camels, which they stand in greater need of than they, by reason of their great scarcity of grains and other proper food; for want of which, those that are brought to them seldom thrive or live <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. In this country stood the famed temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a>; and notwithstanding the pleasantness of the spot where it stood, this part of the country is said to have been the most dangerous of any, being surrounded with such quick and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> sands as are very detrimental to travellers; not only as they sink under their feet, but being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and heated by the rays of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, are easily raised by every breath of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it chance to be in their faces, almost burns their eyes out, and stifles them for want of breath; or if vehement, often overwhelms whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a>. Against this temple Cambyses <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> dispatched an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 50,000 men. They set out from Thebes in Upper Egypt, and under the conduct of proper guides reached the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Oaïs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days' journey from that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>: but what was their fate afterwards is uncertain; for they never returned either to Egypt or to their own country. The Ammonians informed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, that, after the army had entered the sandy desert which lies beyond Oaïs, a violent wind began to blow from the south at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their dinner, and raised the sand to such a degree, that the whole army was overwhelmed and buried alive. Concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of this country we know nothing certain. Most probably the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> towns are under the protection of the Porte: but whether under the bailiwick of Egypt or Tripoli, or whether they have formed themselves into independent states like those of Algiers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, we cannot say; only we are told that the inhabitants of the maritime towns are more civilized than those that dwell in the inland parts. The first professed Mahometanism, and have imbibed some notions of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; whilst the latter, who have neither <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> nor any sign of worship among them, are altogether <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> and brutish. They are a sort of Arabs, and like them live entirely upon theft and plunder. By them this tract, which before was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> desert, was first inhabited. At their first coming in, they settled themselves in one of the best places of the country; but as they multiplied, and had frequent wars with one another, the strongest drove the weakest out of the best spots, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a> sent them to wander in the desert parts, where they live in the most miserable manner, their country hardly affording one single necessary of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Hence it is that they are said to be the ugliest of all the Arabs: their bodies having scarcely any thing but skin and bone, their faces meagre, with fierce ravenous looks; their garb, which is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> what they take from the passengers who go through these parts, tattered with long wearing; while the poorest of them have scarce a rag to cover their nakedness. They are most expert and resolute robbers, that being their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> employment and livelihood; but the travellers in these parts are so few, that the Barcans are often necessitated to make distant excursions into <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, and other southern countries. Those that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> are made to drink plenty of warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; then they hang them up by the feet, and shake them, in order to make them vomit up any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> they think they have swallowed; after which, they strip them of all their clothes, even to the last rag: but with all this inhumanity, they commonly spare their life, which is more than the other African robbers do. Yet notwithstanding every artifice they can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, the Barcans are so poor, that they commonly let, pledge, or even sell, their children to the Sicilians and others from whom they have their corn, especially before they set out on any long excursion.

BARCALON

Pages 447-447

an appellation given to the prime minister of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>. The barcalon has in his department every thing relating to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, both at home and abroad. He is likewise superintendant of the king's magazines.

BARCELONA

Pages 447-448

a handsome, rich, and strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Catalonia, of which it is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. This city was originally founded by Hamilcar Barcas, and from him called Barcino. It was reduced by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> subject to them till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Spain was overrun by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> and Vandals, and afterwards by the Saracens <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Moors. In the beginning of the 9th century, Barcelona was in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Moors, and under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of one Zade. This governor having more than once abused the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, at last irritated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Aquitain, and son to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>, to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that he gave orders to his generals to invest the city, and not to rise from before it till they had put Zade into his hands. The Moor made a most obstinate resistance, so that the siege lasted many months: at last, finding it impossible to preserve the city much longer, and being destitute of all hopes of relief, he determined, or rather was compelled by the inhabitants, to go to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> and implore the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s mercy; but here he was no sooner arrived than he was arrested and sent prisoner to Charlemagne, who condemned him to perpetual banishment. The people gaining nothing by this expedient, continued to hold out for six weeks longer, when the king of Aquitain himself took the command of the siege. To him they made a proposal, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he would allow them to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> out and go where they pleased, they would surrender the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Lewis having agreed to this, made his public entry into Barcelona, where he formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of extending his father's dominions as far as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EBRO">Ebro</a>; but being recalled before he could put his design in execution, Barcelona, he appointed one Bera <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Barcelona. The city continued subject to him and his successors, who still enjoyed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of counts of Barcelona, from the year 802 to 1131; during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> we find nothing remarkable, except that the city was once taken by the Moors, but soon after retaken by the affluence of Lewis IV. king of France. In 1131 it was united to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Arragon by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Raymond V. count of Barcelona with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Don Ramiro the monk, king of Arragon. In 1465 the Catalonians revolted against Don Juan II. king of Arragon, out of hatred to his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> Donna Juanna; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which was, that Barcelona was besieged by that monarch in 1471. Various efforts were made by Lewis XI. of France and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Lorraine in order to raise the siege, but without effect. Things at length were brought to the utmost extremity, when the king offered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> them all, without the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> either in person or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, provided they would submit; but these terms they rejected, chiefly through the influence of the Count de Pailhars, who had been pardoned the year before. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, was very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> on being led on to the assault, in hopes of plunder. The king, however, wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the citizens, dated the 6th of October, in terms as affectionate as if he had been <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> to his children, bewailing the miseries they had brought on themselves, and concluding with a protestation that they, and not he, must be answerable for the consequences. Upon this, at the persuasion of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> who had a reputation for sanctity, they sent deputies to the king, and made a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a> on the 17th of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. In this the king acknowledged they had taken up arms on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> motives; and forgave everybody except Pailhars, who was, however, suffered to escape. On the 22d of October the king made his entry into the city, and confirmed all their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> privileges. In 1697, Barcelona was taken by the French, after a bloody siege of 52 days; and the loss of this city had a considerable effect in disposing the Spaniards to agree to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Ryswick. In Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s time it was taken by the allies under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Peterborough; but being afterwards shamefully denied affluence by the English ministry, was obliged to submit to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. by whom the whole province was deprived of its ancient privileges; for a particular account of which, see the article Spain. Barcelona is situated by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-side, of a form between a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> and an oval. It is surrounded with a good brick wall, round which is another, with 14 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>-works, ramparts, and ditches; the ramparts are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and spacious, inasmuch that 100 coaches may be seen every evening driving thereon for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. The city is divided into two parts, the Old and the New, which are separated from each other by a wall and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ditch; the streets are handsome, well paved with large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, wide, and very clean. It is the residence of the viceroy, is a bishop's see, has a fine university, a mint, a good port, and is adorned with handsome buildings. Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>, which the inhabitants look upon as an advantage. The remarkable buildings are the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, which is large, handsome, and adorned with two high towers, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the bishop, that of the inquisition, and several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses; add to these the palace of the viceroy; the arsenal, which contains arms for 1000 men; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> meet; the taverna, where they build the galleys; and the palace where the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> meet, called La <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASA">Casa</a> de la <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPUTATION">Deputation</a>. This last is built with fine large freestone, and adorned with columns of marble: there is in it a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, with a gilt ceiling and a handsome portico, wherein persons may either walk or sit; the hall is adorned with the portraits of all the counts of Barcelona. There are several fine squares, particularly that of St Michael, into which all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> streets run. The port is wide, spacious, deep, and safe; defended on the one side by a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a>, and on the other sheltered from the west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> that advance into the sea, and form a kind of promontory: the mole is 750 paces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, with a quay, at the end of which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and a small fort. One of the mountains, called Mont Joy, is very high, and rises in the middle of the plain near the city: it is covered with gardens, vineyards, groves of trees, and has a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the city. This mountain, being a rock, yields an inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a> of fine hard freestone. Barcelona is a place of great trade, on account of the conveniency of its harbour; and it has a manufacture of knives greatly esteemed in Spain, as also of blakets. Here are also several glass-houses. The inhabitants are diligent, and equally fit for labour and trade; they are also very civil to strangers. The women are well shaped, and as handsome as any in Spain; they are brisk and lively in their conversation, and more free and unrestrained in their behaviour than in other parts of Spain. E. Long. 2° 5'. N. Lat. 41° 26'.

BARCELONETTA

Pages 448-448

a town of France, in the department of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, formerly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Dauphiny, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the valley of its own name. It belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy, and was ceded to France by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a> in 1712. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 40'. N. Lat. 44° 26'.

BARCELOR

Pages 448-448

a town of Afia, in the East Indies, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Malabar. It is a Dutch <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a>, where they carry on a considerable trade in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 74° 15'. N. Lat. 13° 45'.

BARCELOS

Pages 448-448

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. It is festled on the river Cavado, over which there is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 0'. N. Lat. 41° 20'. BARCINO in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Terraconensis in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Laletani. Now <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCELONA">BARCELONA</a>. See that article.

BARCLAY

Pages 448-450

ALEXANDER, a learned monk in the reign of Henry VIII. Where he was born, though of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance, was nevertheless a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of virulent contention among his former biographers. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">Bale</a>, who was his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a>, is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> he was born in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>. There is indeed a village of his name, and a numerous family, in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. Pitts thinks he was born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. Mackenzie is positive he was a Scotchman; but without <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, unless we admit as such his name Alexander. He was, however, educated in Oriel-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. After leaving the university he went abroad, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and Germany, where he acquired a competent knowledge of the languages of those countries, as appears from several translations of books, which which he afterwards published. On his return to England, he was made chaplain to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> the bishop of Tyne, who likewise appointed him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, at the college of Ottery in Devonshire, founded by Grandison bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his patron, he became a Benedictine monk of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, he first obtained the vicarage of St Matthew at Wokey in Somersetshire; and, in 1549, being then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, was presented to the vicarage of Much Bede in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>. In 1552, he was appointed rector of Allhallows, Lombard-street, which he lived to enjoy but a very short time. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROYDON">Croydon</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1552. He is generally allowed to have improved the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and to have been one of the politest writers of his time. He composed several original works; but was chiefly remarkable for his translations from the Latin, Italian, French, and German languages. His version from Sallust of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of Jugurtha is accurate, and not without elegance. His lives of several saints, in heroic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, are still unpublished. His *Stultifera navis*, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> *The ship of fools*, is the most singular of his performances. It was printed by Richard Pynson at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1509, in folio; and contains a variety of wooden plates, which are worthy the inspection of the curious. Barclay, William, a learned civilian, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABERDEENSHIRE">Aberdeenshire</a> in the year 1541. He spent the early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and much of his fortune, at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Mary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Scots, from whose favour he had reason to expect preferment. In 1573 he went over to France, and at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURGES">Bourges</a> commenced student of civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> under the famous Cujacius. He continued some years in that seminary, where he took a doctor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; and was soon after appointed professor of civil law in the university of Pont-à-Mousson, the first founded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Lorraine. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> afterwards made him counsellor of state and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of requests. Barclay, in the year 1581, married Ann de Mallaville, a French lady, by whom he had a son, who became a celebrated author, and of whom the reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find an account in the next article. This youth the Jesuits would gladly have received into their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. His father refused his consent, and for that reason these disciples of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> soon contrived to ruin him with the duke his patron. Barclay now embarked for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. offered him considerable preferment, provided he would become a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England; but not choosing to comply, he returned to France in 1624; and, soon after his arrival, was appointed professor of civil law in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGERS">Angers</a>, where he died the year following, and was buried in the Franciscan church. He was esteemed a learned civilian; and wrote elaborately in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of kings, in answer to Buchanan and others. The titles of his works are, 1. *De regno et regali potestate*, &c. 2. *Commentarius in tit. pandectarum de rebus creditis, et de jure jurando*. 3. *De potestate papæ*, &c. 4. *Primitia in vitam Agricolæ*. Barclay, John, son of the former, was, as we have above mentioned, so great a favourite of the Jesuits, that they used all their efforts to engage him in their society. His father would not consent, and carried his son with him into England, who was already an author, for he had published "A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> upon Barclay on the Thebais of Statius," and a Latin poem on the coronation of King James, and the first part of *Euphorbia*, 1603. He returned to France with his father; and after his father's death went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and soon after came back to London; he was there in 1626. He published "The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">Gunpowder</a> Plot," a pamphlet of six leaves, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>. He published at London in 1610 "An Apology for the Euphorbia," and his father's treatise *De potestate papæ*. And at Paris, 1612, he published a book entitled *Pietas*, in answer to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Bellarmine, who had written against William Barclay's book concerning the power of the Pope. Two years after he published *Icon Animorum*. He was invited to Rome by Pope Paul V. and received a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of civility from Cardinal Bellarmine, though he had written against him. He died at Rome in 1621, while his *Argenis* was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> at Paris. This celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> has since gone through a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of editions, and has been translated into most languages. M. de Peirello, who had the care of the first edition, caused the effigies of the author to be placed before the book; and the following epitaph, written by Grotius, was put under it: *Gente Caledonius, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLUS">Gallus</a> natalibus, hic est, Romam Romano qui docet ore loqui.* Barclay, Robert, one of the most eminent among the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Barclay, descended of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family of Barcleys, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> in 1648. He was educated under an uncle at Paris, where the Papists used all their efforts to draw him over to their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. He joined the Quakers in 1669, and distinguished himself by his zeal and abilities in defence of their doctrines. In 1676 he published in Latin at Amsterdam his "Apology for the Quakers;" which is the most celebrated of his works, and esteemed the standard of the doctrine of the Quakers. The *Thebes Theologicae*, which were the foundation of this work, and addressed to the clergy of what sort soever, were published before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> of the *Apology*, and printed in Latin, French, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a>-Dutch, Low-Dutch, and English. The dedication of his *Apology* to King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., is very remarkable for the uncommon frankness and simplicity with which it is written. Amongst many other extraordinary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>, we meet with the following: "There is no king in the world who can so experimentally testify of God's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a> and goodness; neither is there any who rules so many free people, so many true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; which thing renders thy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>, thyself more considerable, than the accession of many nations filled with lascivious and superstitious souls. Thou hast tasted of prosperity and adversity; thou knowest what it is to be banished thy native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to be overruled as well as to rule and sit upon the throne; and being oppressed, thou hast reason to know how hateful the oppressor is both to God and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, after all those warnings and admonishments, thou dost not turn unto the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> with all thy heart, but forget him who remembered thee in thy distresses, and give thyself up to follow lust and vanity, surely great will be thy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a>."—He travelled with the famous Mr William Penn through the greatest part of England, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, Holland, and Germany, and was everywhere received with the highest respect; for though both his conversation and behaviour were suitable to his principles, yet there was such liveliness and spirit in his discourse, and such serenity and cheerfulness in his deportment, as rendered him extremely agreeable to all sorts of people. When he returned to his native country he spent the remainder of his life in a quiet and retired manner. He died at his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Ury on the 3rd of October 1690, in the 42nd year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

BARCOCHEBAS

Pages 450-450
or rather BARCOCHAB, a Jewish impostor, whose real name was Akiba; but he took that of Barcochab, which signifies the Son of a Star; in allusion to the prophecy of Balaam, "There shall a star arise out of Jacob." He proclaimed himself the Messiah; and talking of nothing but wars, victories, and triumphs, made his countrymen rise against the Romans, by which means he was the author of innumerable disorders: he ravaged many places, took a great number of fortresses, and massacred an infinite multitude of people, particularly the Christians. The emperor sent troops to Rufus, governor of Judea, to suppress the sedition. Rufus, in obedience, exercised a thousand cruelties, but could not finish his attempt. The emperor was therefore obliged to send Julius Severus, the greatest general of that time; who attained his end without a direct battle: he fell on them separately; cut off their provisions; and at last the whole contest was reduced to the siege of Bitter, in the 18th year of Hadrian. The impostor perished there. This war cost the Romans a great deal of blood.

BARD

Pages 451-452

Eastern empire; for he was treacherous, cruel, and ambitious. In the year 856, he assassinated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a>, general of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Michael's forces, and obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>. At length he caused the disgrace of the empress Theodora; and St Ignatius, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of Constantinople, reproaching him for his vices, he had him deposed in 858, in order to make room for Photius. Bardas was assassinated by Basilus the Macedonian, in 866.

BARDE

Pages 452-452

a strong and rich town of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Pomerania, with a castle and spacious harbour. It is subject to the Swedes; and is situated near the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 20. N. Lat. 54. 23.

BARDED

Pages 452-452

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is used in speaking of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> that is caparisoned. He bears <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, a cavalier d'<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, the horse larded, argent.

BARDESANISTS

Pages 452-452

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heretics, thus denominated from their leader Bardanes, a Syrian of Edessa in Mesopotamia. Bardanes, born in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, became eminent, after his conversion to Christianity, for his zeal against heretics; against whom, we are informed by St Jerome and Eusebius, he wrote a multitude of books: yet had he the misfortune to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, himself, into the errors of Valentinus, to which he added some others of his own. He taught, that the actions of men depend altogether on fate, and that God himself is subject to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. His followers went further, and denied the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of the body, and the incarnation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of our Saviour; holding that these were only apparent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> phantastical.

BARDEWICK

Pages 452-452

a town of Germany, in the circle of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNENBURG">Lunenburg</a>; formerly a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; but being ruined in 1189, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Saxony, has never yet recovered itself. It is seated on the river Ilmenau, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 6. N. Lat. 53. 40.

BARE

Pages 452-452

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies not covered. Hence we say bare-headed, bare-footed, &c. The Roman women, in times of public distress and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>, went bare-headed, with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> loose.—Among both Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and Barbarians, we find a feast called Nudipedia.—The Abyssinians never enter their churches, nor the palaces of kings and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men, but bare-footed. Bare-Foot Carmelites and Augustines, are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> of the order of St Carmel and St Austin, who live under a strict observance, and go without shoes, like the capuchins. There are also bare-foot fathers of mercy. Formerly there were bare-foot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a>, and even bare-foot nuns of the order of St Augustine.

BAREITH

Pages 452-452

a town of Germany in Franconia, in the margravate of Culembach, with a famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MARGRAVE">margrave</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> Bareith. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 50. N. Lat. 50. 0.

BARENT

Pages 452-452

Diteric, an excellent painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, and was the son of a very industrious painter. He studied in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and became the favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Titian, with whom he lived a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but at length returned to Amsterdam, where he painted many extraordinary pieces. He died in 1582, aged 48.

BARFLEUR

Pages 452-452

a town of France, in Normandy, now the department of the Channel. It was ruined, and had its harbour filled up by the English in 1346. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> of that name is 12 miles east of Cherbourg, and near it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the French fleet was destroyed in 1692. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 6. N. Lat. 49. 40. BARGAIN and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">SALE</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of conveyance in the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. It is a kind of a real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, whereby the bargainer for some pecuniary consideration bargains and sells, that is, contracts to convey, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of the bargainer; and becomes by such bargain a trustee for, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> seized to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, the bargainer; and then the statute of uses completes the purchase: or, as it hath been well expressed, the bargain first vests the use, and then the statute vests the possession. But as it was foreseen that conveyances, thus made, would want all those benefits of notoriety which the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-law assurances were calculated to give; to prevent therefore clandestine conveyances of freeholds, it was enacted in the same session of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> by statute 27 Hen. VIII. c. 16., that such bargains and sales should not endure to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> a freehold, unless the same be made by indenture, and enrolled within six months in one of the courts of Westminster-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, or with the cyfoes rotulorum of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. Clandestine bargains and sales of chattel interests, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a> for years, were thought not worth regarding, as such interests were very precarious till about six years before; which also occasioned them to be overlooked in framing the statute of uses: and therefore such bargains and sales are not directed to be enrolled. But how impossible is it to foresee, and provide against, all the consequences of innovations! This omission has given rise to the species of conveyance by LEASE and RELEASE.

BARGE

Pages 452-453

a vessel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> of state, furnished with elegant apartments, canopies, and cushions; equipped with a band of rowers, and decorated with flags and streamers: they are generally used for processions on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, by noblemen, officers of state, or magistrates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cities. Of this sort, too, we may naturally suppose the famous barge or galley of Cleopatra, which, according to Shakespeare, Like a burnish'd throne, Burnt on the water: the poop was beaten <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>: Purple her sails; and so perfumed, that The winds were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>-sick with them: the oars were silver, Which to the tune of flutes kept <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and made The water which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> to follow faster, As amorous of their strokes. At the helm A feeming <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERMAID">mermaid</a> steer'd: the filken tackles Swell'd with the touches of those flower soft <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> That rarely form'd their office. There are likewise other barges of a smaller kind, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of admirals and captains of ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. These are of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> frame, and may be easily hoisted into and out of the ships to which they occasionally belong. Barge is also the name of a flat-bottomed vessel of burden, for lading and discharging ships, and removing their cargoes from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place in a harbour. Barge-Coupler, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a beam mortised into another, to strengthen the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. Barge-Courier, with bricklayers, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the tiling which projects over without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> rafters, in all sorts of buildings where there is either a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GABLE">gable</a> or a kirkin-head.

BARGHMASTER

Pages 453-453

BARMER, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">BAR</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">MASTER</a>,** in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> or judge of the barmote.—The bar-master is to keep two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> courts of barmote yearly; and every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> a small one, as occasion requires.

BARGHMOTE

Pages 453-453
or BARMOT,** a court which takes cognizance of causes and disputes between miners.—By the custom of the mines, no person is to sue any miner for ore-debt, or for ore, or for any ground in variance, but only in the court of barmote, on penalty of forfeiting the debt, and paying the charges at law. **BARI,** a very handsome and rich town of Italy, in the kingdom of Naples; the capital of Terra di Bari, and an archbishop's see. It is well fortified, is seated on the gulf of Venice, and had formerly a good harbour, but it was destroyed by the Venetians. E. Long. 17° 45'. N. Lat. 41° 31'.

BARI

Pages 453-453
or Terra di Bari,** a territory of Italy, in the kingdom of Naples, of which the above-mentioned city is the capital. It is bounded on the north by the Capitanata, on the north-west by the Ulterior Principato, on the south by the Basilicata, on the south-east by the Terra de Otranto, and on the north-east by the gulf of Venice. It has no considerable river except the Offanto, which separates it from the Capitanata. The air is temperate; and the soil produces plenty of corn, fruit, and saffron; but there are a great many serpents, and spiders called tarantulas. See ARANEA. The principal towns are Bari the capital, Frani, Andria, Bavo, Bilonto, Conversano, Monopoli, Polignano, Barletta, and Molfetto. The two first are archiepiscopal, and all the rest episcopal.

BARILLA

Pages 453-454
or BARILHA,** the name of a plant cultivated in Spain for its ashes, from which the purest kinds of mineral alkali or soda are obtained. There are four plants, which, in the early part of their growth, bear so strong a resemblance to each other as would deceive any but the farmers and nice observers. These four are, barilla, gazul (or, as some call it, algazal), soza, and salicornia or salicor. They are all burnt to ashes; but applied to different uses, as being possessed of different qualities. Some of the rough farmers mix more or less of the three last with the first; and it requires a complete knowledge of the colour, taste, and smell of the ashes to be able to detect their knavery. Barilla is sown fresh every year. Its greatest height above ground is four inches: each root puts out a vast number of little stalks, which again are subdivided into smaller sprigs resembling samphire; and all together form a large spreading tufted bush. The colour is bright green; as the plant advances towards maturity, this colour vanishes away till it comes at last to be a dull green tinged with brown. Gazul bears the greatest affinity to barilla, both in quality and appearance: the principal difference consists in its growing on a still drier falter earth, consequently it is impregnated with a stronger salt. It does not rise above two inches out of the ground, spreading out into little tufts. Its sprigs are much flatter and more pulpy than those of barilla, and are still more like samphire. It is sown but once in three, four, or five years, according to the nature of the soil. Soza, when of the same size, has the same appearance as gazul; but in time grows much larger, as its natural soil is a strong salt marsh, where it is to be found in large tufts of sprigs, treble the size of barilla, and of a bright green colour, which it retains to the last. Salicor has a stalk of a deep green colour inclining to red, which last becomes by degrees the colour of the whole plant. From the beginning it grows upright, and much resembles a bush of young rosemary. Its natural soil is on the declivities of hills near the salt marshes, or on the edges of the small drains or channels cut by the husbandmen for the purpose of watering the fields; before it has acquired its full growth, it is very like the barilla of those seasons in which the ground has been dunged before sowing. In those years of manuring, barilla, contrary to its usual nature, comes up with a tinge of red; and when burnt falls far short of its wonted goodness, being bitter, more impregnated with salts than it should be, and raising a blister if applied for a few minutes to the tongue. Barilla contains less salt than the others: when burnt, it runs into a mass resembling a pungent stone, with a faint cast of blue. Gazul, after burning, comes as near barilla in its outward appearance as it does while growing in its vegetable form; but if broken, the inside is of a deeper and more glossy blue. Soza and salicor are darker, and almost black within, of a heavier consistence, with very little or no sign of sponginess. All these ashes contain a strong alkali; but barilla the best and purest, though not in the greatest quantity. Upon this principle, it is fitted for making glaas and bleaching linen; the others are used in making soap. Each of them would whiten linen; but all, except barilla, would burn it. A good crop of barilla impoverishes the land to such a degree, that it cannot bear good barilla a second time, being quite exhausted. For this reason the richer farmers lay manure upon the ground, and let it lie fallow for a season; at the end of which it is sown afresh without any danger, as the weeds that have sprung up in the year of rest have carried off all the pernicious effects of the dung. A proper succession of crops is thus secured by manuring and fallowing the different parts of the farm, each in their turn. The poorer tribe of cultivators cannot pursue the same method for want of capital; and are therefore under the necessity of sowing their lands immediately after manuring, which yields them a profit just sufficient to afford a present scanty subsistence, though the quality and price of their barilla be but trifling. The method used in making barilla is the same as that followed in Britain in burning kelp. The plant as soon as ripe is plucked up and laid in heaps, then set on fire. The salt juices run out below into a hole made in the ground, where they run into a vitrified lump, which is left about a fortnight to cool. An acre may give about a ton. **BARING OF TREES,** in Agriculture, the taking away some of the earth about the roots, that the winter-rain and snow-water may penetrate farther into into the roots. This is frequently practised in the autumn.

BARIUM

It is now called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>; see that article.

Our northern mariners, who are trained in the coal-trade, apply this distinction to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> sterned ship which carries no ornamental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> on the stern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prow. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a>-BARES, are little vessels used in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> for the carriage of fresh water to places where it is want-

NOTWITHSTANDING ALL THESE DISCOVERIES BY

Pages 23-37

g all these discoveries by means of telescopes, it was evident that they still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in a very imperfect state, and their imperfections at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> appeared to be without remedy. One defect was the enormous length requisite to admit of any very considerable magnifying power; and another was the incorrectness of the image arising from the aberration of the rays, as was then supposed, by the spherical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the glass. To obviate these inconveniences, Mercenius is said to have first proposed, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Descartes, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of reflectors instead of lenses in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of telescopes; but this he did in such an obscure manner, that the latter laboured to persuade him of the falsehood of the principle on which his scheme was founded. In 1663, however, James Gregory of Aberdeen showed how such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a> might be constructed. He showed also, that, in order to form a perfect image of an object in this manner, the figure of the speculum ought to be parabolic; but Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, who applied himself to the framing of telescopes of the reflecting kind, found it impracticable to grind them of the desired figure. Laying aside the idea of reflecting telescopes, therefore, he applied himself to the execution of a scheme formed by Descartes, viz. that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> lenses of the figure of one of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONIC_SECTIONS">conic sections</a>. In prosecuting this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, he discovered, that the greatest errors to which telescopes were subject arose from the different refrangibility of the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, for which he could not then find any remedy. He therefore returned to the scheme he had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> abandoned; and, in the year 1672, presented to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> two reflectors which were constructed with spherical speculums, as he could not procure any other. The inconveniences arising from the different refrangibility of the rays of light, have since been in the fullest manner corrected by Mr Dollond, the excellency of whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACHROMATIC">achromatic</a> telescopes is too well known to need any encomium. About the beginning of the present century, the practical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> seemed to languish for want of proper instruments. Roemer, indeed, had invented some new ones, and Dr Hooke had turned his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> towards this subject in a very particular manner; but either through want of skill in the arts, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some other unfortunate circumstance, it happened that nothing effectual was done. But at the very time when this was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with practical astronomy, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> part was carried in a manner to its utmost pitch by the labours of the immortal Newton, whose Principia gave an entire new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> to the science. It was not, however, for many years relished by the foreign philosophers, though almost immediately adopted at home, and has continued ever since to spread its reputation farther and farther, so that now it is in a manner established all over the world. "But (says Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>) that, after Newton's system had for so long a time been neglected, it should all at once be universally received and approved of, is not to be attributed to chance, or the caprice of fashion, as some who are ignorant of it are apt to think, and from thence to expect that some other system <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> hereafter take its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> it in oblivion. The system of Newton, like that of Copernicus, is so agreeable to the phenomena of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and so well put together, that it must last as long as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and reason endure, although time may perhaps bring the word <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> into disuse; and though it may no longer be thought inherent in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, yet the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a>, as they are now called, and on which this system is founded, will never be forgotten." It was also in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> that the first improvements in astronomical instruments took place. The celebrated... mechanic and watchmaker, Graham, carried the accuracy of his instruments to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> which surprised every one. He also greatly improved the principles of watchwork, and made clocks to go with much greater regularity than before. The old eight feet mural <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> was also constructed by him; as was a small equatorial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECTOR">sector</a> for making observations out of the meridian; but he is chiefly remarkable for contriving the zenith sector of 24 feet radius, and afterwards one of 12½ feet, by which Dr Bradley discovered the aberration of the fixed stars. The reflecting telescope which had been invented by Gregory, and executed by Newton, was greatly improved by Mr Hadley, and a very complete and powerful <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of that kind was presented to the Royal Society in 1719. The same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> has also immortalized his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the reflecting <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a>, which he presented to the Society in 1731, which is now in universal use at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and without which all improvements of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> would have been useless for determining the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, through the want of an instrument proper to make the observations with. It however appears, that an instrument, exactly similar to this in its principles, had been invented by Sir Isaac Newton, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it, together with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, given by the inventor to Dr Halley, when he was preparing for his voyage to discover the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> in 1701. About the middle of this century, the constructing and dividing of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> astronomical instruments was carried to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> degree of perfection by Mr John <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">Bird</a>; reflecting telescopes were equally improved by Mr Short, who first executed the divided object-glass micrometer. This had indeed been thought of by M. Louville, and several other persons long before; and a description of one nearly agreeing with that of Mr Short had been published in the Philosophical Transactions for 1753; but had it not been for the great skill of Mr Short in figuring and centering glasses of this kind, it is very probable the scheme might never have been executed. About this time also Mr Dollond brought refracting telescopes to such perfection, that they became superior to reflectors of equal length; though all of them are now excelled by those of Mr Herschel, whose telescopic discoveries have been far more numerous and surprising than those of any other astronomer. We shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> with a short account of the labours of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> astronomers since the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the royal observatories at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> and Greenwich, and the appointment of Mr Flamsteed to the office of astronomer royal. This gentleman not only made observations on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a> which appeared in his time, but on the fixed stars also, of which he gave a catalogue of 3000; many of them so small that they cannot be discerned without the help of a telescope: he also published new solar tables, and a theory of the moon according to Horrox. He published a very curious tract on the doctrine of the sphere, in which he showed how to construct eclipses of the sun and moon, as well as occultations of the fixed stars by the moon, geometrically; and it was upon his observations that Halley's tables and Newton's theory of the moon were constructed. Mr Caffini also distinguished himself very considerably. He erected the gnomon, and drew the famous meridian line in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Petronia at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>. He enjoyed his office more than 40 years, making many observations on the sun, moon, planets, and comets, and greatly amended the elements of their motions; though the result of his labours was much inferior to Mr Flamsteed's. The office was continued in his family, and his grandson still enjoys it. Roemer, a celebrated Danish astronomer, first discovered the progressive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of light by observing the eclipses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and read a dissertation upon it before the Royal Academy of Sciences at Paris in the year 1675. He was also the first who made use of a meridional telescope. Mr Flamsteed was succeeded in 1719 by Dr Halley, "the greatest astronomer (says M. de la Lande) without <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> in England;" and, adds Dr Long, "I believe he might have said in the whole world." He had been sent, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 21, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of St Helena, in order to make a catalogue of the southern stars, which was published in 1679. In 1705, he published his Synopsis Astronomiae Cometicae, in which, after immense calculation, he ventured to predict the return of one in 1758 or 1759. He also published many learned dissertations in the Philosophical Transactions concerning the use that might be made of the next transit of Venus in determining the distance of the sun from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. He was the first who discovered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCELERATION">acceleration</a> of the moon, and gave a very ingenious method of finding her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLAX">parallax</a> by three observed phases of a solar eclipse. He compiled tables of the sun, moon, and all the planets; and, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years in which he was at Greenwich, made near 1500 observations of the moon; all which he compared with the tables, and noted the differences; and these, he thought, would return in about 18 years. He recommended the method of determining the longitude by means of the moon's distance from the sun and certain fixed stars. He was convinced of its superior excellence; and has since been adopted by all the most eminent astronomers in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It is at present the only sure guide to the mariner; and the great perfection to which it is now brought is much owing to the industry and exertions of Dr Maskelyne, the present astronomer-royal, to whom we are indebted for the publication of the Nautical <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALMANACK">Almanack</a>, the Requisite Tables, and other works of the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to practical astronomy. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time an attempt was made in France to True figure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> a degree of the earth, which occasioned a very fine warm dispute concerning the figure of it. Caffini, from Picart's measure, concluded that the earth was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> spheroid; but Newton, from a consideration of the laws of gravity and the diurnal motion of the earth, had determined the figure of it to be an oblate spheroid, and flattened at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>. To determine this point, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XV. resolved to have two degrees of the meridian measured; one under, or very near the equator; and the other as near the pole as possible. For this purpose the Royal Academy of Sciences sent M. Mauupertuis, Clairault, Camus, and Le Monier, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>. They were accompanied by the Abbé Outhier, a correspondent of the same academy. They were joined by M. Celsius professor of anatomy at Upsal; and having set out from France in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the year 1736, returned to it in 1737, after having fully fully accomplished their errand. On the southern expedition were despatched M. Godin, Condamine, and Bouguer, to whom the king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> joined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> George Juan and Don Anthony de Ulloa, two very ingenious gentlemen and officers of the marine. They left Europe in 1735; and after enduring innumerable hardships and difficulties in the execution of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, returned to Europe at different times, and by different ways, in the years 1744, 1745, and 1746. The result of this arduous task was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of Newton's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>. Picart's measure was revised by Cassini and De la Caille; and, after his errors were corrected, it was found to agree very well with the other two. On this occasion too it was discovered, that the attraction of the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> had an effect on the plumb-line of one of their largest instruments, drawing it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight seconds from the true perpendicular. Dr Halley, dying in 1742, was succeeded by Dr Bradley, who, though inferior as a mathematician, greatly exceeded him as a practical astronomer. He was the first who made observations with an accuracy sufficient to detect the lesser inequalities in the motions of the planets and fixed stars. Thus he discovered the aberration of light, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUTATION">nutation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> axis, and was able to make the lunar tables much more perfect than they had ever been. He also observed the places, and computed the elements of the comets which appeared in the years 1723, 1736, 1743, and 1757. He made new and more accurate tables of the motions of Jupiter's satellites, from his own observations and those of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">Pound</a>; and from a multitude of observations of the sun, moon, and stars, was enabled to give the most accurate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of mean refractions yet extant, as well as the best methods of computing the variations of those refractions arising from the different states of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> as indicated by the thermometer and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a>. In 1759, having procured a very large transit instrument made by Mr Bird, and a new mural quadrant of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> eight feet radius, he began to make observations with redoubled industry; so that between this time and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1762, he made observations for settling the places of all the stars in the British catalogue, together with near 1500 places of the moon, much the greater part of which he compared with the tables of Mr Mayer. In the meantime the French astronomers were afflu- duous in their endeavours to promote the science of astronomy. The theory of the moon, which had been given in a general way by Sir Isaac Newton, began to be particularly considered by Messrs Clairault, D'Alembert, Euler, Mayer, Simpson, and Walmly; though Clairault, Euler, and Mayer, distinguished themselves beyond any of the rest, and Mr Euler has been particularly happy in the arrangement of his tables for the ease and expedition of computation. He was excelled in exactness, however, by Mayer, who published his tables in the Göttingen Acts for 1753. In these the errors in longitude never exceeded two minutes; and having yet farther improved them, he sent a copy to the lords of the British <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> in 1755; and it was this copy which Dr Bradley compared with his observations, as already mentioned. His last corrections of them were afterwards sent over by his widow; for which she and her children received a reward of 3000l. Accurate tables for Jupiter's satellites were also composed by Mr Wargentin a most excellent Swedish astronomer, and published in the Upsal Acts in 1741; which have since been corrected by the author in such a manner as to render them greatly superior to any ever published before. Amongst the many French astronomers who contributed to the advancement of the science, we are particularly indebted to M. de la Caille, for a most excellent set of solar tables, in which he has made allowances for the attractions of Jupiter, Venus, and the moon. In 1750 he went to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, in order to make observations in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> with the most celebrated astronomers in Europe, for determining the parallax of the moon, as well as of the planet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, and from thence that of the sun; from whence it appeared that the parallax of the sun could not greatly exceed ten seconds. Here he re-examined and adjusted the places of the southern stars with great accuracy, and measured a degree of the meridian at that place. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> the science was cultivated with the greatest fidelity by Signor Bianchini, Father Bofcovich, Frili, Manfredi, Zanotti, and many others; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> by Wargentin already mentioned, Blingenforn, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a>, and Planman; and in Germany, by Euler elder and younger, Mayer, Lambert, Grischow, &c. In the year 1760 all the learned <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> in Europe began to prepare for observing the transit of Venus over the sun, foretold by Dr Halley upwards of 80 years before it happened, showing, at the same time, the important use which might be made of it. Unfortunately, however, for the cause of science, many of the astronomers sent out to observe this phenomenon were prevented by unavoidable accidents from reaching the places of their destination, and others were disappointed by the badness of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. It happened also, that the circumstances of the phenomenon were much less favourable for the purpose of determining the sun's parallax than had been expected by Dr Halley, owing to the faults of the tables he made use of; so that notwithstanding all the labours of astronomers at that time, they were not able to determine the matter; and even after their observations in 1769, when the circumstances of the transit were more favourable, the parallax of the sun remained still uncertain. Dr Bradley was succeeded in his office of astronomer-royal by Mr Bliss Savilian professor of astronomy at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; who, being in a very declining state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> at the time of his accession to the office, did not enjoy it long. He was succeeded by the learned Nevil Maskelyne, D.D., the present astronomer-royal, whose name will be rendered immortal by his fidelity and success in bringing the lunar method of determining the longitude at sea into general practice. Such was the general state of astronomy, when Dr Herschel's great discovery of augmenting the power of telescopes, beyond the most sanguine hopes of astronomers, opened at once a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> altogether unlooked for. By this indefatigable observer we are made acquainted with a new primary planet attended by six secondaries belonging to our solar system; so that the latter now appears to have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the bounds formerly assigned to it; this new planet being at least twice the distance of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> from the sun.
